This establishes a guest-visible decoder/exception mismatch against that reference, not that Moira should provide functional MMU translation or that the reference no-op is a complete hardware model. No maintained in-tree guest caller requiring these encodings was found.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated M68040 guest executes MOVEC with one of those MMU-register encodings. Moira raises an illegal-instruction exception where the bundled Musashi reference accepts the instruction as a no-op; software that depends on the accepted instruction behavior can take a different guest exception path under m68kemu. **Affected configuration:** the optional AROS m68kemu target, whose bridge selects M68040 mode; practical impact depends on guest software using these encodings, and no in-tree guest caller was established. **Confidence:** high for the Moira/reference behavior difference; medium that it is an AROS compatibility bug because the reference no-op does not implement register state or MMU behavior. No instruction or guest was run; source-only. See the [MOVEC dispatch recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9094).

<a id="ek10161"></a>
### EK10161 — Concurrent AddResetCallback calls can lose reset registrations.

`AddResetCallback()` inserts the supplied interrupt node into `ResetHandlers` by calling `Enqueue()` and then returns TRUE, with no lock or exclusion around the operation (`rom/exec/addresetcallback.c:53-63`). `Enqueue()` scans for the insertion point and updates the predecessor/successor links in separate stores (`rom/exec/enqueue.c:53-107`). If two concurrent callers insert nodes with the same priority at the same tail position, both can read the same predecessor and successor; each then writes those neighbors' links, and the later insertion detaches the earlier node from the list. The API reports success for both registrations, but reset traversal cannot see the detached node (`rom/exec/doresetcallbacks.c:115-120,185-207`).

**Trigger and consequence:** two callers concurrently register reset callbacks of equal priority at the same insertion point. One callback can be omitted when reset callbacks are traversed, so its required shutdown/reset action does not run despite `AddResetCallback()` returning TRUE. A repository-wide direct-call census did not establish an overlapping selected in-tree pair. For example, the two i386 serial HIDD registration sites are reached from per-unit construction during `serial.device` Open, but `kernel-pc-i386-serial` is commented out of the boot manifest, and that i386 target has no ExecSMP path (`arch/i386-pc/boot/mmakefile.src:61`; `arch/i386-pc/drivers/serial.hidd/mmakefile.src:15`). Those optional single-CPU calls are serialized while `OpenDevice()` retains `Forbid()`; they do not demonstrate the race. The finding remains conditional on external or future concurrent API clients. It is distinct from EK59, which concerns removal of a saved successor during reset-time traversal. **Affected configuration:** builds using the generic Exec `AddResetCallback()`/`Enqueue()` path where registration can overlap; the race does not require SMP if callers can be preempted during insertion, though overlapping callers are required. **Confidence:** high for the unsynchronized four-link insertion and lost-node interleaving; medium for practical reachability because no selected overlapping in-tree pair was found. No callback was registered or reset run; source-only. See the [insertion-order recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9097).

<a id="ek10162"></a>
### EK10162 — genmodule can read past a long MUI dispatcher name.

For a configured BOOPSI class dispatcher, `config.c` stores the supplied string with `strdup()` and applies no length check (`tools/genmodule/config.c:1202-1207`). Both MUI/MCC generation branches then copy a custom name into local `char disp[256]` with `strncpy(disp, cl->dispatcher, 256)` and pass it to `fprintf(..., "%s", disp)` (`tools/genmodule/muisupport.c:62-68,100-106,72-95,110-132`). A name 256 bytes or longer leaves `disp` without a terminating NUL, so `%s` scans beyond the local array while genmodule emits the generated class startup source. Config parsing grows input lines dynamically, so the parser does not impose the needed bound (`tools/genmodule/config.c` and line reader path: [coverage trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8642)).

**Trigger and consequence:** a custom MUI/MCC/MCP configuration supplies an explicit dispatcher name at least 256 bytes long and genmodule reaches the corresponding class writer. The generated source can contain bytes read beyond the local name buffer or generation can fail unpredictably; the issue occurs at build-time for that custom configuration. A checkout-wide case-insensitive search found no checked-in explicit `dispatcher` setting, so no maintained target failure is claimed. **Affected configuration:** custom/future genmodule configurations using an explicit MUI/MCC/MCP dispatcher; default generated names use bounded `snprintf()` and are not affected by this path. **Confidence:** high for the unterminated copy and `%s` read; no generator or build was run. Source-only. See the [dispatcher boundary recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8642).

<a id="ek10163"></a>
### EK10163 — m68kemu formatting thunks pass a null argument stream after allocation failure.

`m68k_to_native_fmt_stream()` returns NULL when its temporary `AllocMem()` fails (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:255-276`). The generated Locale `FormatString` thunk passes that result directly to native `FormatString()` without checking for failure (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6598-6608`). For a format containing an argument conversion, `InternalFormatString()` computes each argument address from `dataStream` and dereferences it in the conversion handlers; there is no NULL-stream error return (`workbench/libs/locale/formatstring.c:26-42,258-302,339-352,461-495`). The same unchecked result reaches the generated Utility `VSNPrintf()` thunk (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:7133-7143`), whose implementation immediately calls `RawDoFmt()` to count the output (`rom/utility/vsnprintf.c:64-67`). The manual DOS `VPrintf()` and `VFPrintf()` wrappers also forward the possibly NULL stream to `RawDoFmt()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1144-1163`; `rom/dos/vprintf.c:68-69`; `rom/dos/vfprintf.c:81-82`). `RawDoFmt()` fetches a parameter from that stream for an argument-bearing format, with no allocation-failure branch (`rom/exec/rawdofmt.c:83-108,257-303`). These are additional registered paths for the same converter-allocation failure, not separate findings.

**Trigger and consequence:** a m68kemu guest invokes Locale `FormatString()`, Utility `VSNPrintf()`, DOS `VPrintf()`, or DOS `VFPrintf()` with at least one argument conversion, and allocation of the converted argument stream fails. The native formatter then reads an argument through the NULL stream and may fault instead of reporting allocation failure. Literal-only formats, which return NULL by design and do not dereference arguments, are excluded. **Affected configuration:** optional m68kemu integration with the generated Locale and Utility thunks and manual DOS formatting thunks; requires a conversion-bearing format and temporary allocation failure. **Confidence:** high for unchecked propagation and the native conversion dereference; no guest call or allocation failure was run. Source-only. See the [format-stream caller census](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8572).

<a id="ek10164"></a>
### EK10164 — Withdrawn as a separate finding; its current public-call effect is covered by EK10173.

The manual DOS table registers `thunk_dos_VFWritef` at offset 354, but the checked-in DOS LVO constants place `VFPrintf` at -354 and `VFWritef` at -348 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1202-1203`; `workbench/devs/diskimage/LVOs.i:316-317`). Thus a caller using the documented `VFWritef` vector does not reach this helper; it reaches the `VFPrintf` thunk. The converter's 32-bit-packed `%C` values versus the native `VFWritef()` `const IPTR *` slots would misalign later arguments on 64-bit hosts if this helper were reached, but that is not an independent documented-call trigger in the current table. Keep the observable public-vector defect under EK10173 rather than counting this dormant helper mismatch separately. Existing source-body credit is unchanged. No guest format or output was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10165"></a>
### EK10165 — Withdrawn as a separate finding; its current public-call effect is covered by EK10173.

The manual DOS table places `thunk_dos_VFWritef` at the `VFPrintf` vector rather than the documented `VFWritef` vector (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1202-1203`; `workbench/devs/diskimage/LVOs.i:316-317`). The helper's converter does not translate uppercase `%S` or BCPL `%T/%t` guest addresses, but a documented `VFWritef` call currently dispatches elsewhere; the observable format/pointer mismatch through the crossed vectors is part of EK10173. No separate `VFWritef` API trigger is established for this helper behavior. Existing body credit is unchanged. No guest format or output was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10166"></a>
### EK10166 — Withdrawn as a separate finding; the crossed-vector return effect is covered by EK10173.

`thunk_dos_VFWritef()` discards the native byte count and returns zero (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1166-1174`), but the manual table registers it at offset 354, which the DOS LVO constants identify as `VFPrintf`, while `VFWritef` is at -348 (`:1202-1203`; `workbench/devs/diskimage/LVOs.i:316-317`). The zero result therefore manifests through the crossed `VFPrintf` dispatch and is a consequence of EK10173's single vector-registration defect, not a separate `VFWritef` call-path finding. The consolidated report records it as an additional observable effect. Existing source credit is unchanged. No guest call or file write was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10167"></a>
### EK10167 — Locale FormatString reads past a format ending in a lone percent sign.

The selected Locale `FormatString()` path calls `InternalFormatString()` with the caller's template, and its `GetDataStreamFromFormat()` prepass does not reject a trailing `%` (`workbench/libs/locale/locale_intern.h:159-166`; `compiler/alib/getdatastreamfromformat.c:99-193`). When `InternalFormatString()` sees `%` at the end, the format state advances to the terminating NUL; the faulty-conversion default copies that NUL into its output byte, and the common `template_pos++` moves the cursor past the string (`workbench/libs/locale/formatstring.c:51-107,503-510`). The next OUTPUT iteration reads `fmtTemplate[template_pos]` before checking whether it is NUL (`:61-81`), so it accesses beyond the supplied format buffer and may continue scanning until an incidental NUL is encountered.

**Trigger and consequence:** a caller supplies a Locale format template whose final character is a lone `%`. Formatting reads beyond the terminating NUL and can emit unrelated following bytes or continue scanning outside the template. This concerns malformed input; no valid-format failure is claimed, and no checked-in caller format ending in `%` was found. **Affected configuration:** builds including the Locale `FormatString()` implementation; requires a malformed template. **Confidence:** high for the parser cursor transition and unchecked next read; no malformed format or formatter call was run. Source-only. See the [trailing-percent parser trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8574).


<a id="ek10168"></a>
### EK10168 — Locale FormatString indexes outside its argument-offset array for `%0$` conversions.

`GetDataStreamFromFormat()` parses positional argument numbers and stores offsets at `indexStream[argpos - 1]` (`compiler/alib/getdatastreamfromformat.c:80-140,190-228`). A `%0$s` conversion underflows the one-based `argpos - 1`; the helper leaves the index count at zero but does not reject the format (`:80-140,190-261`). The selected Locale parser then accepts the same zero position and evaluates `ARG(0)`, whose macro indexes `indexStream[(x)-1]` (`workbench/libs/locale/formatstring.c:34,91-130,461-495`). The resulting access is outside the index array: it is the preceding element on 32-bit arithmetic and a very large positive index on 64-bit arithmetic. The format requires a string argument, so the parser subsequently dereferences the invalid offset as a string pointer.

**Trigger and consequence:** a Locale `FormatString()` caller supplies a positional conversion with argument index zero, such as `%0$s`, and the formatter processes it. The helper/parser access outside the offset array can produce an invalid data-stream address and fault or read incorrect data. This is a malformed-format case; the checked-in positional example uses indexes 1–4, and a repository search found no `%0$` format. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting the Locale formatter; requires a caller-supplied zero positional index. **Confidence:** high for unsigned underflow and out-of-bounds index use; no malformed format or formatter call was run. Source-only. See the [helper and caller reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8578).

<a id="ek10169"></a>
### EK10169 — m68k bootstrap diagnostics can overrun the resident ID-string buffer.

The selected m68k bootstrap's `ConvertCSTR()` allocates 257 bytes for a BCPL string, clamps the length byte to 255, but then copies the original `rt_IdString` with unbounded `strcpy()` (`arch/m68k-amiga/c/AROSBootstrap.c:184-197`). The debug path calls this helper for each entry in the KickTag resident lists after ROM loading and before `BootROM()` (`:1287-1303,1488-1493`); `DEBUG` is compile-time enabled in this source (`:18`), so the runtime `DEBUG/S` option does not gate these list conversions.

**Trigger and consequence:** a ROM-loaded resident has an `rt_IdString` longer than 255 bytes. `strcpy()` writes beyond the 257-byte temporary allocation during boot diagnostics and can corrupt adjacent allocator memory or fault before the ROM handoff. Shorter strings fit the allocated BCPL buffer. **Affected configuration:** m68k Amiga `AROSBootstrap` with the selected debug build and a loaded ROM containing a long resident ID string. **Confidence:** high for the missing bound and selected diagnostic caller; no ROM, resident string, or boot was used. Source-only. See the [Resident string bounds review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8585).

<a id="ek10170"></a>
### EK10170 — m68kemu Icon and IFFParse thunks expose native objects to guest code. *(withdrawn; duplicate of EK9432)*

**Disposition:** the Icon `DiskObject *` and IFFParse object-pointer bridge failures are now documented under [EK9432](#ek9432), which covers the shared guest/native pointer and structure boundary. The generated thunk offset pass found no separate vector-table mismatch. This optional m68kemu observation is not a distinct candidate. See the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9317).

<a id="ek10171"></a>
### EK10171 — m68kemu CreateIORequest sizes native requests and guest shadows for only the base type.

The generated Exec thunk passes the guest-supplied size directly to native `CreateIORequest()`, then creates a guest shadow by the base type name `IORequest` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2289-2297`). Native `CreateIORequest()` allocates exactly that size and records it in `mn_Length` for later freeing (`rom/exec/createiorequest.c:57-73`). The checked-in m68k layout table defines `IORequest` as 32 guest bytes/72 native bytes but `IOStdReq` as 48 guest bytes/96 native bytes (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_shadow_layouts.h:2165-2200`; public definitions in `compiler/include/exec/io.h:19-42`). Thus the ordinary guest request size of 48 bytes produces a 48-byte native allocation and only a 32-byte guest shadow, despite later I/O wrappers treating the request as an `IOStdReq`. Even initial shadow creation applies the 72-byte native `IORequest` layout to the 48-byte allocation, reading its pointer/command fields beyond the allocation. Before request submission, native `OpenDevice()` also initializes `io_Unit` at offset 56 and `io_Device` at offset 48 (`rom/exec/opendevice.c:98-103`), both outside that 48-byte allocation.

`DoIO()`, `CheckIO()` and `WaitIO()` call `io_sync_back()`, which always applies the full `IOStdReq` layout (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2091-2107,2117-2125,2128-2135`). That synchronization reads native fields at offsets through 91, beyond the 48-byte allocation, and writes guest fields through offset 47, beyond the 32-byte shadow allocation (`m68kemu_shadow.c:94-99`; layout offsets above). A standard device request can therefore read past its native allocation during completion synchronization and overwrite adjacent emulator-heap data with the guest tail fields; the underlying device can also access the missing native tail fields.

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k guest creates the usual 48-byte `IOStdReq` and opens a device with it. `OpenDevice()` immediately writes two native pointer fields outside the 48-byte native allocation. A later `DoIO()`, `CheckIO()` or `WaitIO()` applies the 48-byte `IOStdReq` layout to a 32-byte guest shadow and reads native fields beyond the same 48-byte allocation; the resulting out-of-extent accesses can corrupt request state or adjacent allocations and produce incorrect I/O results. The exact neighboring data affected depends on allocator layout.

**Affected configuration:** an explicitly built and loaded `m68kemu.library` on a supported 64-bit host, with a guest using `CreateIORequest()` for an `IOStdReq`. The module is optional and not in the checked-in default package edges (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:14-17`; `rom/mmakefile.src:4-18,83-98,114-128`). No maintained in-tree guest caller was established. **Confidence:** high for the size mismatch and unconditional IOStdReq synchronization; actual adjacent-memory effects depend on allocation layout and device use. No guest request or runtime operation was performed; source-only. See the [IORequest lifecycle coverage note](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8599).

<a id="ek10172"></a>
### EK10172 — m68kemu CloseDevice removes a still-live I/O-request shadow.

The generated `CloseDevice()` thunk resolves the request, calls native `CloseDevice()`, and then unconditionally removes the guest/native shadow mapping (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2079-2088`). Native `CloseDevice()` closes the device/unit reference but does not free the request allocation (`rom/exec/closedevice.c:59-98`). The normal matching `DeleteIORequest()` thunk subsequently tries to resolve the same guest address; after the shadow has been removed, `m68k_to_host_or_shadow()` falls back to `ctx->mem + addr` for an in-range guest address (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2299-2308`; `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_intern.h:114-125`). It then passes that guest-arena pointer to native `DeleteIORequest()`, whose implementation reads `mn_Length` using the native `Message` layout and calls `FreeMem()` on the supplied pointer (`rom/exec/deleteiorequest.c:43-48`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a guest creates and opens a request, then follows the normal close-then-delete lifecycle. The close thunk discards the only mapping while the native allocation remains live; deletion then supplies the emulator's guest-memory address to the native allocator instead of the native request. This can cause an invalid free or allocator failure, and the original native request allocation is left unreleased.

**Affected configuration:** an explicitly built and loaded `m68kemu.library` on a supported 64-bit host, with an emulated guest that calls `CloseDevice()` followed by `DeleteIORequest()` for the same shadowed request. The module is optional and not in the checked-in default package edges (see EK10171). No maintained in-tree guest caller was established. **Confidence:** high for the mapping removal, fallback resolution, and native free path; no guest lifecycle or runtime operation was performed. Source-only; see the [IORequest lifecycle coverage note](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8599).

<a id="ek10173"></a>
### EK10173 — m68kemu DOS manual thunks are registered at incorrect LVOs.

The manual DOS thunk table contains four offsets that disagree with the public DOS LVO constants (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1188-1203`; `workbench/devs/diskimage/LVOs.i:316-317,339-340,358`): `SystemTagList` is registered at 604 rather than 606; `CreateNewProc` at 492 rather than 498, colliding with generated `Cli` at 492; and `VFPrintf`/`VFWritef` are swapped at 348/354. Manual entries are checked before generated thunks (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:223-290`). Consequently the `CreateNewProc` vector reaches the wrong manual wrapper while its expected -498 slot reaches the `RunProcess` zero-return stub; `SystemTagList` has no matching manual entry at its expected offset. Calls to `VFWritef` and `VFPrintf` enter each other's wrappers, which use different format languages; the misrouted VFWritef wrapper also discards the native result and returns zero (`m68kemu_thunks.c:1155-1174`). The prior standalone EK10164–EK10166 helper findings are consolidated here because their documented-call effects pass through this same reversed registration.

**Trigger and consequence:** a m68kemu guest calls one of the affected DOS vectors. `CreateNewProc`, `SystemTagList`, or the two formatting APIs can dispatch to an unrelated implementation or stub, yielding incorrect process creation, missing system-tag behavior, incompatible formatting, or a lost return count. The optional emulator's current guest/API callers were not established, so these are conditional compatibility defects rather than claims about a default boot path. **Affected configuration:** optional m68kemu DOS bridge. **Confidence:** high for the four table/constant mismatches and manual-first dispatch; practical impact depends on guest use. No emulated call, process creation, formatter, or file output was run; source-only. See the [manual DOS vector recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8645).

<a id="ek10174"></a>
### EK10174 — Windows KrnSetProtection drops the access mode for cache-inhibited mappings.

The MinGW32 `KrnSetProtection()` implementation derives the Windows access mode from `MAP_Readable`/`MAP_Writable` and shifts it for executable mappings, but then replaces the entire value with `PAGE_NOCACHE` when `MAP_CacheInhibit` is set (`arch/all-mingw32/kernel/setprotection.c:13-41`; flag definitions in `compiler/include/aros/kernel.h:28-39`). Windows defines `PAGE_NOCACHE` as a protection modifier used with a base access protection; the wrapper instead passes the modifier by itself to `VirtualProtect()` (`arch/all-mingw32/kernel/host_mmu.c:14-19`; [Microsoft Memory Protection Constants](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/memory/memory-protection-constants)). The host interface returns `VirtualProtect()`'s result, but the public `void` wrapper discards it.

**Trigger and consequence:** a MinGW32 kernel client requests cache-inhibited protection. The call omits the requested read/write/execute mode from `flNewProtect`; Windows rejects a protection value without a base access mode, and the ignored result leaves the caller unable to detect that the requested protection change did not take effect. The current protection remains whatever it was before the call.

**Affected configuration:** MinGW32 builds where a direct or external client calls `KrnSetProtection()` with `MAP_CacheInhibit`. The selected generic `KrnAllocPages()`/`KrnFreePages()` paths request ordinary access or no access and do not set this flag (`rom/kernel/allocpages.c:70-82`; `rom/kernel/freepages.c:47-51`). The other checked-in `CreateSegList()` protection call is under `__AROSPLATFORM_WXSEG__` and does not request cache inhibit (`compiler/arossupport/createseglist.c:95-99`); no checked-in MinGW32 caller of the affected flag was established.

**Confidence:** high for the overwrite, `VirtualProtect()` forwarding and discarded result; caller-visible effect is conditional on an explicit cache-inhibit request. No Windows mapping was called. Source-only; see the [MinGW32 protection review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8610).

<a id="ek10175"></a>
### EK10175 — The MinGW IRQ switcher indexes past its pending array after a wait-set error.

`TaskSwitcher()` passes `Ints_Num` and `IntObjects` to `WaitForMultipleObjects()`, then immediately treats the returned `DWORD` as an index into `PendingInts` (`arch/all-mingw32/kernel/host_intr.c:140-149`). The Windows API limits the wait set to `MAXIMUM_WAIT_OBJECTS` (64) and returns `WAIT_FAILED` (`0xffffffff`) on failure ([Microsoft WaitForMultipleObjects contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/synchapi/nf-synchapi-waitformultipleobjects)). `KrnAllocSystemIRQ()` can allocate up to 256 event slots and grows `Ints_Num` as sequential slots are allocated (`host_intr.c:379-403`), with no corresponding limit check before the wait call.

**Trigger and consequence:** an extension or other MinGW32 client allocates enough system IRQs for `Ints_Num` to exceed the Windows wait limit. `WaitForMultipleObjects()` fails; the unvalidated `WAIT_FAILED` value is then used as `PendingInts[obj]`, writing outside the 256-byte array. The task-switcher thread can fault, stopping host IRQ delivery; the exact host-process outcome depends on the resulting invalid access.

**Affected configuration:** MinGW32 builds with more than 64 active event objects in the host IRQ set. The checked-in callers allocate three WingDI IRQs, two socket IRQs and one emul.handler IRQ; this census does not establish an in-tree path to the limit. The exported allocator remains able to grow the set beyond it. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked failure result and unbounded count relative to the Windows API limit; no checked-in trigger above the limit was found. No IRQ or wait failure was induced. Source-only; see the [MinGW host IRQ review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8613).

<a id="ek10177"></a>
### EK10177 — m68k Utility Tag-array APIs read guest values in host byte order.

The generated `TagInArray()` wrapper passes the guest `Tag *` array directly through `THUNK_PTR()` to native Utility code (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6879-6885`; `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.h:34-38`). Native `TagInArray()` compares each host-loaded `Tag` until `TAG_DONE` (`rom/utility/taginarray.c:59-65`), while `Tag` is a 32-bit value and guest m68k memory stores it big-endian (`compiler/include/utility/tagitem.h:17,32-42`). On the supported little-endian m68kemu hosts, non-byte-symmetric array entries are read as different values. The `FilterTagItems()` thunk has the same direct-pointer issue for its `filterArray`; its native implementation uses that array in `TagInArray()` membership checks (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6887-6895`; `rom/utility/filtertagitems.c:67-89`). Its converted `tagList` mutations are separately covered by EK9198 and are not counted as this finding.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated guest calls `TagInArray()` with a terminated array containing a tag whose four bytes are not symmetric under reversal, or calls `FilterTagItems()` with such a filter array. Native comparisons fail to match the guest's intended values, so membership and filtering results can be wrong. For example, the guest representation of `TAG_USER` (`0x80000000`) is read as `0x00000080` on a little-endian host.

**Affected configuration:** an explicitly built and loaded 64-bit little-endian `m68kemu.library` target with a guest using these Utility vectors. The module is optional and not in the checked-in default package edges (see EK9432). No maintained in-tree guest caller was established. **Confidence:** high for direct guest-memory forwarding, 32-bit tag width and differing byte order; practical effect depends on guest array values. No guest array or Utility API call was run. Source-only; see the [Tag[] endian recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8634).

<a id="ek10178"></a>
### EK10178 — ARM task argument setup can misalign the entry stack.

`NewAddTask()` rounds the initial task stack pointer down to `AROS_STACKALIGN` (16 bytes on the ARM and ARMeb targets) before calling the architecture context preparer (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:274-284`; `arch/arm-all/include/aros-armel/cpu.h:50`; `arch/arm-all/include/aros-armeb/cpu.h:50`). `PrepareContext()` then places stack arguments by decrementing a `STACKULONG *` once per slot, without restoring double-word alignment afterward (`arch/arm-all/exec/preparecontext.c:25-27,47-72`; the ARMeb implementation is byte-identical). Each slot is 4 bytes. Its `numargs` is the highest specified stack argument from ARG5–ARG8, including zero-filled gaps.

**Trigger and consequence:** a task is created with ARG5 or ARG7 as the highest stack argument (one or three 4-byte stack slots). The entry SP is then 4 modulo 8 rather than double-word aligned at the public entry interface, contrary to [AAPCS32 §6.2.1.2](https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/main/aapcs32/aapcs32.rst#6212-stack-constraints-at-a-public-interface). A task entry that relies on the ABI alignment can mis-handle aligned stack data or fault on an alignment-sensitive operation. Even counts of stack arguments preserve 8-byte alignment.

**Affected configuration:** ARM and ARMeb builds using `NewAddTask()`/`NewCreateTaskA()` with stack arguments. A source search found no maintained `TASKTAG_ARG5`–`TASKTAG_ARG8` caller in this checkout, so this remains a conditional API-client issue; ordinary task entry without these tags is not implicated. **Confidence:** high for the alignment arithmetic and ABI requirement; no in-tree triggering caller or runtime effect was established. No task was created. Source-only; see the [ARM stack-argument caller review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8651).

<a id="ek10179"></a>
### EK10179 — ARM StackSwap makes Exec calls with a misaligned stack.

The ARM and ARMeb legacy `StackSwap()` vector begins with an AAPCS-aligned public-entry SP, then pushes three registers before calling `FindTask()` (`arch/arm-all/exec/stackswap.S:12-23` and the selected ARMeb implementation `arch/armeb-all/exec/stackswap.S:12-23`). That 12-byte save leaves SP 4 modulo 8 at the call. Before `Disable()`, it pushes five registers (20 bytes), again leaving SP 4 modulo 8 (`stackswap.S:26-31`). The selected ARM/ARMeb Exec stub for Disable/Enable saves two plus six registers (32 bytes total), preserving the incoming misalignment at its C-helper call (`arch/arm-all/exec/execstubs.s:15-27,33-37`; selected ARMeb stub: `arch/armeb-all/exec/execstubs.s:15-27,33-37`). After switching stacks, the assembly also pushes three registers before calling `Enable()` (`stackswap.S:46-56`), so that call is misaligned when the supplied stack pointer is 8-byte aligned.

AAPCS32 requires SP to be double-word aligned at public interfaces ([§6.2.1.2](https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/main/aapcs32/aapcs32.rst#6212-stack-constraints-at-a-public-interface)). **Trigger and consequence:** ARM or ARMeb code invokes the deprecated `StackSwap()` API. Its FindTask/Disable/Enable calls enter public routines with SP 4 modulo 8, and the Disable/Enable stubs preserve that misalignment into their C helpers. A callee that relies on the required alignment can mis-handle stack data or fault on an alignment-sensitive operation; no claim is made that every current helper fails.

**Affected configuration:** ARM and ARMeb builds where a client explicitly enables the deprecated API (`rom/exec/stackswap.c:48-55`). The checked-in `developer/debug/test/exec/stackswap.c:94-100` does so via `developer/debug/test/exec/mmakefile.src:9-10`, but that developer test is optional and no product-default caller was established. **Confidence:** high for the push arithmetic and stub preservation; runtime effects depend on compiler-generated callees and stack use. No test or target was run. Source-only; see the [ARM StackSwap review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8654).

<a id="ek10180"></a>
### EK10180 — ARM alert backtraces assume every saved r11 is a frame pointer.

The ARM and ARMeb CPU alert path stores the fault context's saved r11 in `iet_AlertStack` (`rom/exec/traphandler.c:100-112,129`). `FormatAlertExtra()` treats that value as a linked frame pointer after checking only `TypeOfMem(fp)` (`rom/exec/alertextra.c:149-168`). The selected ARM/ARMeb `UnwindFrame()` unconditionally reads `frame[0]` as the caller and `frame[-1]` as the previous frame (`arch/arm-all/exec/alert_cpu.c:34-39`; ARMeb implementation is identical). The ARM target does not require the compiler to preserve r11 as a frame pointer; optimized code can use it as a general callee-saved register.

**Trigger and consequence:** a CPU alert occurs while r11 does not point to a valid two-word frame record, but its value still passes `TypeOfMem()`. The diagnostic can print a false/truncated backtrace; if the accepted pointer is near an allocation boundary, `frame[-1]` or `frame[0]` may read outside that allocation. `TypeOfMem()` establishes that the address belongs to some memory block, not that it is a frame record or that both words are in bounds.

**Affected configuration:** ARM and ARMeb alert formatting with frame-pointer omission or any fault context where r11 is not a valid frame-chain pointer. The exact compiler output and saved register value for an affected task were not established. **Confidence:** high for the unconditional frame-record interpretation and insufficient extent check; wrong trace depends on the saved r11 value, while an out-of-allocation read additionally requires a boundary-adjacent value. No alert or exception was induced. Source-only; see the [ARM saved-r11 trace review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8660).

<a id="ek10181"></a>
### EK10181 — OpenSBI PCIDT accepts an MSI source outside the PLIC range.

The OpenSBI PCIDT driver reads its `msi` source from the matching position in a firmware `interrupts` property (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/hidd/pcidt/pcidt_driverclass.c:567-600`). When MSI initialization succeeds, it sets `b->msiReady` before the driver registers the controller source with `KrnModifyIRQA()` (`pcidt_access.c:363-385`; `pcidt_driverclass.c:728-763`). The PLIC's `krnPLICEnable()` rejects source 0 or any source greater than firmware's `riscv,ndev`, then returns without enabling it (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_plic.c:150-164`). However, OpenSBI's `KrnModifyIRQA()` calls that void helper and returns `TRUE` after storing the controller mapping (`kernel/modifyirq.c:102-122`); the PCIDT caller ignores even that result.

**Trigger and consequence:** firmware describes a nonzero PCIDT `msi` source above the PLIC's declared `riscv,ndev`, and a downstream endpoint uses MSI. PCIDT retains `msiReady`, and `ObtainVectors()` can proceed to program an endpoint MSI (`pcidt_deviceclass.c:145-174`), but the PLIC refuses to enable the controller source. The endpoint's messages therefore have no deliverable interrupt path through that PLIC source.

**Affected configuration:** OpenSBI RISC-V systems with an inconsistent or malformed FDT source assignment and a PCIe endpoint using MSI. No checked-in board FDT was found to establish an affected shipped configuration. **Confidence:** high for the PLIC range check, success-reporting path and PCIDT readiness/use path; occurrence depends on firmware data and endpoint MSI use. No board, interrupt, device or build was exercised. Source-only; see the [OpenSBI PCIDT MSI source review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8893).

<a id="ek10182"></a>
### EK10182 — m68kemu GetMsg can drop an Intuition message if shadow creation fails.

The manual m68kemu `GetMsg()` thunk first calls native `GetMsg()`, which removes the head message from the port's queue (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:621-632`; `rom/exec/getmsg.c:61-77`). It then tries to create an `IntuiMessage` guest shadow. If guest-heap allocation fails or `shadow_register()` reaches the fixed 256-entry limit, `shadow_create()` returns zero and the thunk returns zero without requeueing, replying to, or freeing the already-dequeued native message (`m68kemu_shadow.c:80-91`; `m68kemu_thunks.c:444-455,628-632`). The normal guest `ReplyMsg()` route requires a registered shadow and returns immediately when lookup fails; only the success path replies and destroys the shadow (`m68kemu_thunks.c:643-652`). Intuition's reply-port worker normally frees replied IDCMP messages (`rom/intuition/inputhandler.c:415-417`; `freeintuimessage.c:54-67`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated guest retrieves an IDCMP message through `GetMsg()` while its shadow heap allocation fails or its shadow registry is full. The message has already left the window's port, but the guest receives zero and cannot reply to that message through the bridge. Intuition does not receive it on the reply port to reclaim it, so that message allocation remains outstanding until other teardown cleanup, if any.

**Affected configuration:** an explicitly built and loaded 64-bit m68kemu target with a guest receiving IDCMP events; requires guest-shadow allocation failure or 256 live shadow registrations. The emulator is optional and no maintained in-tree guest was established. **Confidence:** high for dequeue-before-shadow ordering and the failure return without ownership recovery; accumulation depends on the stated failure condition. No guest event, allocation failure, shadow exhaustion or runtime operation was induced. Source-only; see the [IDCMP GetMsg failure-path review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8768).

<a id="ek10183"></a>
### EK10183 — m68k `RI` context display dereferences its NULL serial-output buffer.

The `RI` branch of `InternalDebug()` calls `FormatCPUContext(NULL, ...)` after validating the task (`rom/exec/debug_internal.c:158-172`). The selected m68k implementation chooses `RAWFMTFUNC_SERIAL` when `buffer` is NULL and `RawDoFmt()` emits each character through `RawPutChar()` (`arch/m68k-all/exec/alert_cpu.c:26-37`; `rom/exec/rawdofmt.c:123-134`). It then unconditionally evaluates `strlen(buffer)` at line 38, dereferencing the NULL pointer before the rest of the register/segment context formatting.

**Trigger and consequence:** a user invokes the m68k internal `RI` command for a valid task. Context text is sent to the serial output path, then `FormatCPUContext()` calls `strlen(NULL)`, so the diagnostic command can fault before it completes the context display. The ordinary alert formatter passes a non-NULL string buffer and is not implicated by this specific path.

**Affected configuration:** m68k builds using `arch/m68k-all/exec/alert_cpu.c` and the internal `RI` debugger command. **Confidence:** high for the NULL argument, serial formatter selection and unconditional `strlen()`; no debugger command or serial output was run. Source-only; see the [m68k RI caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8783).

<a id="ek10184"></a>
### EK10184 — m68k DMA cache maintenance skips boundary protection when the MMU is disabled.

The selected 68040/060 `CachePreDMA_40` and `CachePostDMA_40` paths detect an unaligned cache-line boundary for memory-changing DMA, but only call `cacheprepostset` to disable and restore copyback on the first/last page when `MMU_Level_A` is nonzero (`arch/m68k-all/exec/cachepredma_.S:91-118`; `cachepostdma_.S:113-132`). With no MMU, both paths skip that boundary protection and continue with the data-cache clear. SetPatch can still enable the 040/060 data cache unless its `NOCACHE` option is supplied (`arch/m68k-amiga/c/SetPatch.c:155-172,225-231`).

The selected Deneb DMA device permits word-aligned, long inbound transfers directly into caller-provided storage and brackets them with `CachePreDMA()`/`CachePostDMA()` (`arch/m68k-amiga/usb/denebusb/uhwcmd.c:4251-4297`; DMA device selected by `denebusb/mmakefile.src:18-45`). Its alignment checks do not require 16-byte cache-line alignment. **Trigger and consequence:** on a 68040/060 booted without an active MMU, an inbound Deneb DMA buffer starts or ends inside a 16-byte cache line, and the CPU writes neighboring bytes in that same line while the asynchronous transfer is active. Because the boundary page remains copyback-cacheable, a dirty cached line can be pushed during post-DMA maintenance and overwrite bytes just received from the device. Aligned boundaries or no concurrent writes to neighboring bytes are not implicated.

**Affected configuration:** m68k Amiga 68040/060 with the no-MMU boot path, data cache enabled, the selected Deneb DMA device, and a partial-line inbound buffer with neighboring CPU writes during transfer. No checked-in trace establishes that the Deneb client or a task writes those neighboring bytes concurrently; this remains a conditional API/caller contract defect. **Confidence:** high for the missing no-MMU branch and cache-mode mechanism; actual overwrite requires the stated DMA/cache interleaving. No cache operation, transfer, concurrent access, boot or hardware was exercised. Source-only; see the [m68k DMA cache-boundary review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8792).

<a id="ek10185"></a>
### EK10185 — m68k DMA cache cleanup changes write-through pages to copyback.

For partial cache-line DMA ranges, the selected 68040/060 `CachePreDMA_40` path clears descriptor bit 5 on each unaligned edge page, while the paired `CachePostDMA_40` path calls the same helper with its mode argument set to one (`arch/m68k-all/exec/cachepredma_.S:93-118,132-175`; `cachepostdma_.S:115-131`). In `copybackchange()`, the post path unconditionally sets descriptor bit 5 for any cacheable edge page; it does not save or restore that page's previous cache mode. The m68k descriptor encodings define `CM_WRITETHROUGH` as zero and `CM_COPYBACK` as one, with bit 6 marking noncacheable/serialized pages (`arch/m68k-all/kernel/kernel_intern.h:6-9`; descriptor construction in `mmu.c:410-430`). Thus an edge page that was write-through before the DMA call becomes copyback after completion.

The public `KrnSetProtection()` and `KrnMapGlobal()` paths both support `MAP_WriteThrough` and encode it as `CM_WRITETHROUGH` (`arch/m68k-all/kernel/setprotection.c:23-33`; `mapglobal.c:24-29`; flag in `compiler/include/aros/kernel.h:32`). The selected 040/060 hooks therefore can alter a mapping established through the maintained API. The partial-line branch is skipped for cache-line-aligned ranges, and the `DMA_ReadFromRAM` direction skips this boundary-mode handling; the affected case is a memory-changing transfer with at least one unaligned edge.

**Trigger and consequence:** on MMU-enabled m68k 68040/060, a caller maps an edge page write-through, then performs a non-cache-line-aligned DMA transfer that takes the `CachePreDMA_40`/`CachePostDMA_40` boundary path. After `CachePostDMA()`, the affected page is copyback rather than write-through. Later CPU/device access can therefore observe cache-coherency behavior different from the caller's requested mapping attributes; the report does not claim a particular corruption without a conflicting DMA/access sequence.

**Affected configuration:** MMU-enabled 68040/060 and an external or future client combining `MAP_WriteThrough` with partial-line DMA. The selected Deneb driver uses the hooks for inbound transfers, but the checked-in caller census found no m68k C/C++ caller requesting `MAP_WriteThrough`, and no maintained route establishing that Deneb's buffer is such a mapping. Keep the in-tree impact conditional. **Confidence:** high for the descriptor-bit transition and public mapping mode; practical consequence requires a caller relying on the preserved write-through mode. No mapping, DMA, cache operation or device was used. Source-only; see the [cache-mode trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8796).

<a id="ek10186"></a>
### EK10186 — m68k `CachePreDMA` returns virtual addresses for non-identity mappings.

The public `CachePreDMA()` contract accepts a virtual address and requires its result to be the physical DMA address; it also requires `*length` to report the contiguous physical extent (`rom/exec/cachepredma.c:28-48`). The selected m68k `_00` and `_40` assembly implementations both return the original A0 address unchanged and never update A1's length (`arch/m68k-all/exec/cachepredma_.S:70-79,83-130`). The C dispatch selects `_40` when `AFF_68040` is set and `_00` otherwise (`arch/m68k-all/exec/cachepredma.c:31-47`), so the mismatch spans the maintained m68k backends, including 68030 when the 040 flag is absent.

The m68k kernel supports non-identity mappings: `KrnMapGlobal(virt, phys, ...)` passes distinct virtual and physical bases through to `map_region()` (`arch/m68k-all/kernel/mapglobal.c:15-29`), and `map_region2()` writes the supplied physical base into the page descriptor while advancing virtual and physical addresses (`mmu.c:382-445`). The selected Amiga boot MMU also invokes `KrnMapGlobal(addr, newmem, ...)` for FASTREMAP (`arch/m68k-amiga/boot/mmu.c:127-143`; `FASTREMAP` is enabled at `:23`). The separate `KrnVirtualToPhysical()` implementation only translates configured ROM-image ranges and otherwise returns its input (`arch/m68k-all/kernel/virtualtophysical.c:22-41`); `CachePreDMA()` does not call it or inspect page descriptors.

**Trigger and consequence:** a DMA caller passes a virtual address backed by a non-identity mapping, or a range that crosses a physical discontinuity, to `CachePreDMA()`. The routine returns the virtual address as if it were physical and leaves the requested length unchanged. A DMA engine can then access the wrong physical location or be given a length extending past the contiguous physical segment, causing failed or misdirected I/O and possible memory corruption. Identity-mapped and physically contiguous buffers do not expose this mismatch.

**Affected configuration:** MMU-enabled m68k Amiga 68030 or 68040/060 builds with a DMA client using a non-identity or discontinuous mapping. Deneb's selected DMA path passes its caller-provided data pointer directly to `CachePreDMA()` and uses the returned address for the transfer (`arch/m68k-amiga/usb/denebusb/uhwcmd.c:4279-4300`); however, the checked-in sources do not establish that a Deneb request buffer is allocated from a non-identity/discontinuous range. The boot FASTREMAP mapping is maintained, but no checked-in DMA use of the remapped ranges was confirmed. Keep the practical in-tree trigger conditional. **Confidence:** high for the API/implementation mismatch and available non-identity mappings; consequence depends on DMA use of such a mapping. No MMU mapping, DMA, device or build was used. Source-only; see the [backend and mapping review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8798).

<a id="ek10188"></a>
### EK10188 — AArch64 SMP exception-stack watchdog uses one ceiling for every CPU.

`krnCheckExcStack()` stores the first exception frame's top in one function-static `sp_ceiling`, then compares every later frame against that value and replaces it whenever a higher frame is seen (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/intr.c:106-120`). Both synchronous exceptions and IRQs call this checker before dispatch (`:65-73,127-133`; vector entries pass each CPU's current exception-frame pointer to these handlers in `vectors.S:263-309`). AArch64 uses a downward-growing exception stack, so a higher frame top can indicate upward movement only relative to that CPU's own initial ceiling.

The selected BCM27xx SMP startup gives the boot CPU a static `stack_super` region (`kernel_startup.c:47-48,64-66,428-429`) but allocates a separate stack for each secondary CPU and installs its top in the secondary startup trampoline (`platform_bcm27xx.c:367-375`; `kernel_cpu.c:101-104`). The watchdog does not key its state by CPU and does not establish a per-core baseline. Consequently, if a healthy CPU's valid stack lies above the first recorded CPU's frame top, the next exception on that CPU is reported as stack corruption and moves the shared ceiling. If a CPU's valid stack lies below the shared ceiling, upward movement on that stack can remain below the shared threshold and go undetected. Concurrent first exceptions or ceiling updates on different CPUs are also unsynchronized.

**Trigger and consequence:** on AArch64 BCM27xx ExecSMP with multiple CPUs online, an exception on a CPU whose stack top is higher than the first CPU's recorded frame top can produce a false stack-corruption diagnostic; after the shared ceiling is raised, a lower-address CPU can move upward without crossing it. Concurrent exceptions can race the shared sample/update. This affects the diagnostic only; the checker does not modify exception frames or stack pointers.

**Affected configuration:** selected AArch64 BCM27xx SMP startup with at least two online CPUs and differing per-core exception-stack addresses. Single-CPU execution does not have the cross-core baseline mismatch. **Confidence:** high for the single shared variable and distinct selected stack setup; whether a particular boot's allocated addresses cause false positives or missed movement depends on linker placement and allocator results. No exception, SMP schedule, board, or build was run. Source-only; see the [coverage trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8881).

<a id="ek10189"></a>
### EK10189 — ARM bootstrap ELF relocation diagnostics use the unresolved extended string-table sentinel.

`checkHeader()` copies `eh->shstrndx` into `int_shstrndx` and, when it equals `SHN_XINDEX`, resolves the actual section-name table index from section header zero's `sh_link` (Efika `arch/arm-efika/boot/elf.c:25-57`; Raspberry Pi ARM32 `arch/arm-raspi/boot/elf.c:28-59`; AArch64 `arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/elf.c:77-97`). In all three loaders, the undefined-symbol and COMMON-symbol diagnostic branches in `relocate()` do not use that resolved value. They index `sh[eh->shstrndx]` while constructing the section name (Efika `:238-255`; ARM32 `:253-272`; AArch64 `:350-369`). For an ELF file using extended section-name indexing, the raw field remains the sentinel value 65535. When the actual section-header count is at most 65535, that diagnostic indexes beyond the section-header array before printing the error.

The affected branches follow processing of a relocation against a symbol whose section index is `SHN_UNDEF` or `SHN_COMMON`; ARM32 and Efika skip `R_ARM_V4BX`, while AArch64 skips `R_AARCH64_NONE` before the diagnostic. A loadable ELF with another such relocation normally reaches the diagnostic during `loadElf()`'s relocation pass. The Efika boot path invokes `loadElf()` for its embedded kernel and for ELF or packaged modules (`arch/arm-efika/boot/boot.c:298-309,315-339`). Raspberry Pi ARM32 and AArch64 manifests include `elf` in their `FILES` lists (`arch/arm-raspi/boot/mmakefile.src:6-8`; `arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/mmakefile.src:6-8`); those loaders use the same routines for boot ELF content.

**Trigger and consequence:** an ELF object accepted by `checkHeader()` uses `e_shstrndx == SHN_XINDEX`, has a resolved extended section-name index, has a section count no greater than 65535, and contains a relocation that is not skipped by that target's special-case handling and references an undefined or COMMON symbol. The loader's error-reporting path reads a section header out of bounds while trying to print the relocation's section name; this can fault or print invalid data instead of reporting the unresolved symbol. It does not establish an out-of-bounds access on ordinary successful relocation paths.

**Affected configuration:** explicit Efika ARM, Raspberry Pi ARM32, and Raspberry Pi AArch64 bootstrap/loader targets whose manifests select these files. The ARM Efika boot/package edges are active `#MM` rules (`arch/arm-efika/boot/mmakefile.src:11-22`); Raspberry Pi package selection is also target-specific, so these remain platform-specific boot paths. **Confidence:** high for the duplicated source defect and conditional out-of-range access; no affected packaged ELF was identified. No ELF, package, boot or build was used. Source-only; see the [loader review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8894).

<a id="ek10190"></a>
### EK10190 — m68k 040/060 bus-error recovery can dereference an unset zero-page descriptor.

`buserror040`/`buserror060` special-case a long data read from address 4 after an ATC fault. The handler loads the zero-page descriptor pointer from VBR slot 253 and immediately writes through it (`arch/m68k-all/kernel/buserror.S:49-68`). `enable_mmu040()` installs these bus-error vectors and stores `PlatformData.zeropagedescriptor` into that slot without checking it (`arch/m68k-all/kernel/mmu.c:218-264,289-298`). `map_region2()` sets the pointer only after it has successfully obtained the level-A and level-B tables for address zero (`:389-405`); either descriptor allocation can fail (`:54-67`), causing the map operation to return FALSE before the pointer is published (`:391-399`).

The selected Amiga MMU resident opts into `ZeroPageInvalid` only when the command line contains `debugmmu` (`arch/m68k-amiga/boot/mmu.c:195-208`). It may first try to map address zero while processing RAM headers, then calls `KrnSetProtection(0, PAGE_SIZE, 0)` to invalidate the page (`:242-268,276-280`). The m68k `KrnSetProtection()` wrapper discards `map_region()`'s BOOL result (`arch/m68k-all/kernel/setprotection.c:15-35`), and the resident proceeds to `enable_mmu()` regardless (`boot/mmu.c:328-329`). Therefore, if every address-zero mapping attempt fails before `map_region2()` reaches the descriptor-pointer assignment, the MMU can be enabled with the special handler installed and a NULL pointer in slot 253. A later ExecBase read at address 4 takes the recovery branch and faults again while writing through NULL, preventing the intended recovery.

**Trigger and consequence:** m68k Amiga 68040/68060 startup with `debugmmu`, where the VBR/handler setup is active and allocation failure prevents all address-zero page-table mapping attempts from publishing `zeropagedescriptor`. Ordinary 040/060 startup without `debugmmu` does not intentionally invalidate page zero; a successful earlier zero-page mapping also sets the descriptor and avoids this NULL case. This is distinct from EK9405's FASTREMAP partial-mapping and leaked-buffer path. **Confidence:** high for the null publication and handler dereference; the failure requires the stated debug option and low-memory failure at every relevant zero-address mapping attempt. No allocation failure, exception, boot, build or hardware was exercised; source-only. Coverage: [selected handler and caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8912), [debugmmu trigger qualification](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8934).

<a id="ek10191"></a>
### EK10191 — x86-64 PC ACPI sleep transition leaves interrupts disabled.

`krnLeaveSupervisorRing()` constructs an IRETQ frame using its supplied RFLAGS value (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_intern.h:58-72`). The shared `FLAGS_INTENABLED` constant is `0x3002` (`:74`): it sets IOPL bits 12–13, but leaves IF bit 9 clear. The selected ACPI S5 path calls this macro immediately before `AcpiEnterSleepStatePrep(ACPI_STATE_S5)`, despite its explicit comment that ACPICA requires user mode with interrupts enabled (`arch/all-pc/kernel/acpi_pm.c:80-94`). The transition therefore enters user mode with interrupts still disabled during sleep preparation.

**Trigger and consequence:** x86-64 PC systems that invoke the selected ACPI `PM_STATE_OFF` handler and reach the S5 preparation path. The function runs with IF clear contrary to its caller's stated precondition, so required interrupt servicing may be unavailable during ACPICA preparation; no specific ACPICA failure is asserted. The same macro is used at BSP boot and AP startup, but those callers have later initialization behavior and are not part of this finding. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC with ACPI shutdown support and a working S5 path. **Confidence:** high for the pushed RFLAGS value and clear IF bit; the downstream ACPI effect depends on ACPICA's runtime need for interrupts. No shutdown, firmware call, interrupt-state change, or build was run; source-only. Coverage: [header and caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8913).

<a id="ek10192"></a>
### EK10192 — Relative-library wrappers dereference the offset table after its allocation fails.

The startup relative-base provider initializes `__rel_slot` lazily. `__rel_ensure_slot()` leaves it zero if `task.resource` cannot be opened or `AllocTaskStorageSlot()` returns zero (`compiler/startup/relbases.c:54-67`); the public allocator documents zero as its failure result (`rom/task/AllocTaskStorageSlot.c:17-34`). The registered `__rel_init()` callback discards that failure and always returns `TRUE` (`relbases.c:109-113`). Later, `__aros_getoffsettable()` returns NULL when slot provisioning fails or when its per-task table allocation fails (`relbases.c:70-80`). Generated relative-library accessors do not check that result: they add the library's stored offset and dereference the resulting pointer (`tools/genmodule/writegetlibbase.c:43-57`; prototype macro `writeincproto.c:91-98`). Thus a caller can continue past startup initialization and fault on its first relative-library base access after provisioning failure.

**Trigger and consequence:** an executable using the startup-provided relative-library wrappers encounters failed task.resource/slot provisioning or failed per-task table allocation, then calls a relative-library function. The generated accessor performs pointer arithmetic on NULL and reads the presumed base, causing an invalid access rather than returning a clean initialization error. Propagate initialization failure or make the accessor handle a missing table before dereferencing it. **Affected configuration and reachability:** startup-linked programs using the relative link libraries; the checked-in target-manifest search found no standalone executable that establishes this provider as a current in-tree caller, so external or future clients are the supported trigger. The llvmpipe and softpipe HIDDs use module-local generated tables and are excluded. **Confidence:** high for the failure-to-NULL-to-unchecked-dereference chain; low for current in-tree reachability. No allocation failure, wrapper call or build was run. See the [provider/caller reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8931).

<a id="ek10193"></a>
### EK10193 — PC alert rendering can deadlock while logging a nested fault.

The PC debug-output lock is enabled when `DEBUG_USEATOMIC` is defined; both selected PC architecture initializers set `_arosdebuglock = 1` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_debug.h:35-50`; x86-64 `kernel_debug.c:11-13`). `krnDisplayAlert()` acquires `KRNDEBUGLOCK` and retains it while rendering every character through `krnPutC()` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/_displayalert.c:72-112`). The selected x86-64 `krnPutC()` disables local interrupts around `con_Putc()` and then restores the saved flags (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_debug.c:15-48`). If that synchronous console callback faults, the PC exception handler logs the exception error code with `bug()` before entering `cpu_Trap()` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/cpu_intr.c:420-470`). The bug path calls `krnBug()`, which attempts to acquire the same lock (`arch/all-pc/kernel/bug.c:26-43`; `_bug.c:31-40`). Because this is the interrupted CPU and the alert frame cannot release the lock until output returns, the nested logger spins indefinitely.

**Trigger and consequence:** a synchronous fault occurs in the console output callback while a PC alert is being rendered with the atomic debug lock enabled. The exception diagnostic path deadlocks on the lock held by the interrupted alert, stalling further diagnostics and recovery on that CPU. **Affected configuration:** PC builds where `DEBUG_USEATOMIC` enables this lock, including the reviewed ExecSMP setup. **Confidence:** high for the lock ordering and nested-fault consequence; low that ordinary selected use causes the secondary console fault. This is distinct from EK9393's cross-CPU output race. No alert, fault, interrupt or build was run. See the [source and caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8991).

<a id="ek10194"></a>
### EK10194 — PC SMP dispatch can use a task after remote removal frees it.

`core_Dispatch()` removes an eligible task from `TaskReady` while holding `TaskReadySpinLock`, then unlocks and continues using the pointer while its state is still `TS_READY` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:304-322,344-383`). In the selected x86-64 PC path, `RemTask()` sends `TS_REMOVED` through `krnSysCallReschedTask()` (`rom/exec/remtask.c:97-105`; `arch/all-pc/exec/exec_platform.h:17`). The syscall handler selects the ready-list lock from the task state, calls `Remove()` for states other than invalid/tombstoned, and then marks a removal request `TS_TOMBSTONED` (`arch/all-pc/exec/platform_init.c:269-295,323-335`). It then returns to `RemTask()`, which deletes the context, cleans the ETask, and frees the task's memory entries (`remtask.c:109-128,165-181`). The dispatcher still holds its local pointer and continues through state checks and task preparation; the selected `cpu_Dispatch()` then reads task flags, ETask/context fields, exception state and timing data before transferring control (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:90-115,162-205`).

**Trigger and consequence:** on PC ExecSMP, a remote remover catches a task after `core_Dispatch()` has detached it from the ready list but before that CPU finishes dispatching it. The syscall path can free the selected task while the dispatcher and `cpu_Dispatch()` still dereference it, causing invalid reads or a fault during scheduling. Pin the selected task across the dequeue-to-dispatch interval or defer its reclamation until the dispatch CPU acknowledges completion. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC ExecSMP with `EXEC_REMTASK_NEEDSSWITCH`; other architecture paths are not included. **Confidence:** high for the unlocked pointer lifetime and cleanup sequence; the race requires the stated interleaving and was not run. This is distinct from EK473's freeing of a task still executing remotely and EK830's competing cleanup owners. The second `Remove()` of an already-detached node is not claimed as a separate list-corruption finding. See the [scheduler and caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9015).

<a id="ek10195"></a>
### EK10195 — PC SMP halt paths stop only the calling CPU.

`X86_HandleSysHaltSC()` only executes `cli; hlt` in a local infinite loop; its `__AROSEXEC_SMP__` branch is still a TODO and sends no stop request to other CPUs (`arch/all-pc/kernel/syscall.c:134-144`). The selected x86-64 PC configuration enables ExecSMP for its `smp` variant (`configure.in:1667-1670`). The same local-only handler is reached by three system-stop routes: framebuffer dead-end alerts after printing “System halted” (`displayalert.c:26-35`); `PM_STATE_OFF` when ACPI S5 preparation/entry fails (`acpi_pm.c:82-95`; dispatched by `powerstate_handlers.c:62-76`); and the emergency shutdown fallback (`powerstate_handlers.c:70-76`).

**Trigger and consequence:** one of these stop paths reaches `X86_HandleSysHaltSC()` on an x86-64 PC ExecSMP system. The calling CPU halts, but other processors are neither stopped nor asked to halt, so the machine can continue running work on those CPUs after the initiating path reports a system stop. Add an SMP-wide halt rendezvous or broadcast before entering the local halt loop. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC ExecSMP; the dead-end-alert route additionally requires a framebuffer, while the ACPI route requires failed S5 entry. Non-SMP and successful ACPI power-off are not claimed. **Confidence:** high that this handler only halts its current CPU and the SMP branch is unimplemented; manifestation depends on another CPU continuing useful work. No alert, shutdown, syscall, IPI or build was run. See the [halt-handler and caller census](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9006).

<a id="ek10196"></a>
### EK10196 — VMM x86 fault queues use local Forbid instead of cross-CPU locking.

The optional VMM x86 page-fault handler removes a `TrapStruct` from the shared `Free` list under `Forbid()`/`Permit()`, fills it, and appends it to the shared `PageReq` list under a second `Forbid()`/`Permit()` pair (`workbench/system/VMM/x86/traphandler_x86.c:36-84`). These lists are initialized by the VMM manager (`VM_Manager_Init.c:249-250`). Other selected VMM producers and consumers mutate the same lists through `AddFree()`, `AddPageReq()`, and `RemHead()` in the page handler (`fault.c:10-25,845-888`; `pagehandler.c:313-327,468-482`). The source protects these operations only with `Forbid()`; Exec explicitly documents that on ExecSMP this is local-CPU task-switch prevention and that cross-CPU data needs a spinlock (`rom/exec/forbid.c:55-60`).

The selected PC ExecSMP exception dispatcher snapshots its handler list under a spinlock, releases that lock, then invokes the copied callbacks (`rom/kernel/addexceptionhandler.c:144-185`). Therefore concurrent user page faults on different CPUs can enter `TrapPageFault()` simultaneously; the exception-list lock does not serialize the VMM callbacks. Without a cross-CPU lock on the VMM lists, concurrent `RemHead()`/`AddTail()` operations can corrupt list links or allocate the same `TrapStruct` twice, leading to lost requests, reused fault state, or a fault in the page-handler path.

**Trigger and consequence:** an x86 ExecSMP VMM configuration has multiple CPUs handling eligible page faults at once, or overlaps a fault callback with a page-handler list operation. The local `Forbid()` calls do not serialize those CPUs, so the shared `Free`/`PageReq` list state can be corrupted. Use a cross-CPU lock for each shared queue and its ownership transitions.

**Affected configuration and reachability:** the x86 handler is selected by the explicitly buildable VMM handler module (`workbench/system/VMM/mmakefile.src:24-27,45-53`), and the active `workbench-system-vmm` target includes the handler (`workbench/system/VMM/mmakefile.src:47-52`); the VMM MUI app contributes that target to `workbench-system` (`workbench/system/VMM/MUI/mmakefile.src:18-21`). The checked-in AROS `AllocAddressRange()` path still leaves `VirtAddrStart`/`VirtAddrEnd` unset and `MarkAddress()` is a no-op in the relevant configuration (EK9906); `ShouldHandleFault()` rejects addresses outside that range (`traphandler_x86.c:22-33`). Consequently, no functioning checked-in AROS paging route to concurrent callbacks was established. **Confidence:** high that the queue operations are not cross-CPU synchronized and the PC dispatcher can invoke callbacks concurrently; practical reachability on this checkout remains low/conditional until the VMM address-range setup is implemented or supplied. No fault, queue operation, schedule, or build was run. Source-only; see the [VMM queue and target review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9019).

<a id="ek10197"></a>
### EK10197 — Hosted AArch64 cache-clear override leaves loaded code instructions unsynchronized.

The AArch64-wide Exec manifest selects a hosted `CacheClearE()` implementation that ignores the address, length, and requested cache flags (`arch/aarch64-all/exec/mmakefile.src:22-28`; `cachecleare.c:13-34`). DOS enables cache clearing for both supported load formats, and its shared adapter forwards requests to `CacheClearE()` (`rom/dos/mmakefile.src:30`; `internalloadseg_support.c:124-127`). The ELF and AOS loaders call it for loaded hunks with both data- and instruction-cache flags (`internalloadseg_elf.c:1818-1828`; `internalloadseg_aos.c:535-542`).

On the Linux-hosted path, the Unix page allocator rejects `MEMF_EXECUTABLE` requests so loaders fall back to the already RWX AROS memory pool (`arch/all-unix/kernel/allocpages.c:69-82`). No executable-page protection transition follows for that fallback. The Unix `KrnSetProtection()` implementation calls the host instruction-cache invalidation API only under `HOST_OS_darwin`; Linux performs no such invalidation (`arch/all-unix/kernel/setprotection.c:32-40`). Thus neither the no-op `CacheClearE()` nor the Linux protection path synchronizes the instruction cache after the DOS loader writes code.

**Trigger and consequence:** on Linux-hosted AArch64, load or relocate executable code into the RWX AROS pool and then execute it while the corresponding instruction-cache contents are stale. Execution can observe old instructions instead of the newly loaded bytes. Provide host-supported instruction-cache maintenance for the loaded range. **Affected configuration:** Linux-hosted AArch64; this does not describe native Raspberry Pi AArch64, whose selected cache-clear override is different. **Confidence:** high that the selected load paths request maintenance and both Linux implementations omit it; the stale-fetch manifestation depends on cache state and was not observed. No code was loaded, cache operation or build was run. See the [loader and allocator caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9024).

<a id="ek10198"></a>
### EK10198 — Sam440 startup dereferences a NULL command line when the Parthenope menu entry has no appended arguments.

`entry_alloc()` initializes each Parthenope menu entry with `append = NULL` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/menu.c:46-57`). In both supported menu formats, the `kernel`/`EXEC` parser only duplicates appended text when the remainder after the kernel filename is nonempty (`menu.c:261-275,440-455`), so an ordinary entry without command-line arguments keeps the NULL value. `testboot_aros()` emits a `KRN_CmdLine` tag unconditionally and uses `menu->append` as its data (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/parthenope.c:163-227`). The Sam440 kernel startup copies that tag data with `strcpy()` into the static `CmdLine[200]` buffer without checking for NULL (`arch/ppc-sam440/kernel/kernel_startup.c:97,258-265`).

**Trigger and consequence:** boot the AROS kernel from a Parthenope menu entry with no appended arguments. The kernel startup passes a NULL source to `strcpy()`, causing an invalid read before normal startup can continue. Provide an empty string for absent arguments or skip the copy when the tag data is NULL. **Affected configuration:** the Sam440 Parthenope boot path when built for AROS; this does not claim all Sam440 boot methods are affected. **Confidence:** high for the source-level NULL flow and invalid string access; no menu or boot was run. See the [selected caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L837).

<a id="ek8851"></a>
### EK8851 — DynModule bootstrap leaks its console path and can leak an opened console handle.

`dynmodule__InternalBootstrapDynMod()` allocates `outputfmt`, formats the port-specific console path into it, and calls `Open()` (`compiler/dynmodule/dynmodule_modules.c:83-94`). It never frees `outputfmt`, regardless of whether opening the console succeeds. It then allocates `commandline`; if this allocation fails, the function immediately returns NULL without closing a successful `output` handle (`:95-139`). The selected sole caller treats NULL as failed bootstrap and only destroys its dynamic-module entry and reply port (`compiler/dynmodule/dynmodule_loadmodule.c:101-109`), so that caller does not recover either resource.

**Trigger and consequence:** an optional DynModule client asks to bootstrap a module and the `outputfmt` allocation succeeds; the allocated pathname is leaked on every such call. If `Open()` also succeeds and the later `commandline` allocation fails, the output file handle is leaked as well. Repeated bootstrap failures can accumulate path allocations and, in the second case, open handles.

**Affected configuration:** explicit builds/loads of the `linklibs-dynmod` target. Its module target is defined in `compiler/dynmodule/mmakefile.src:12-23`, while the aggregate dependency is commented; no maintained in-tree `dynmoduleLoadModule()` caller was found. No default package inclusion is claimed. **Confidence:** high for the unconditional pathname leak and conditional handle leak; resource accumulation requires repeated bootstrap attempts. No module, console, allocation failure or build was exercised. Source-only; see the [bootstrap cleanup trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9026).

<a id="ek8853"></a>
### EK8853 — DynModule RemoveModule reverses the message-port allocation check.

`dynmoduleRemoveModule()` enters its request path only when `CreateMsgPort()` returns NULL (`compiler/dynmodule/dynmodule_removemodule.c:22-44`). With the normal successful allocation it instead calls the declared `DYNMODULE_Exit(0)` hook without looking up the module port or sending `DMIFMSG_Dispose`; if that hook returns, the function also reaches its return with `dmmport` uninitialized. On allocation failure, if `FindPort(ifport)` finds the module, the code places the NULL `replyport` in the stack message, sends it, then calls `GetMsg(NULL)` in the polling loop. Exec's `GetMsg()` requires a valid port and immediately reads `port->mp_MsgList` (`rom/exec/getmsg.c:48-62`), so this failure path cannot wait for the module's disposal reply. `DeleteMsgPort(NULL)` itself is explicitly supported, and is not the defect (`rom/exec/deletemsgport.c:24-33,47-56`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a caller invokes the public `dynmoduleRemoveModule()` API. On ordinary reply-port allocation success, it calls the exit hook instead of sending the dispose request; if execution continues, its return value is indeterminate. If reply-port allocation fails while the named module is still registered, the function sends a request with no reply port and then passes NULL to `GetMsg()`, which dereferences it. Allocate the port on the success branch and return an error if allocation fails before sending any request.

**Affected configuration:** clients explicitly linking `linklibs-dynmod` (`compiler/dynmodule/mmakefile.src:12-23`); the aggregate dependency is commented and no maintained in-tree call to `dynmoduleRemoveModule()` was found. The function is declared in the target's public header (`compiler/dynmodule/include/dynmodule.h:54`), so external API callers remain in scope. **Confidence:** high for the inverted branch, NULL `GetMsg()` path, and missing disposal request; the ordinary-success consequence depends on the caller-provided `DYNMODULE_Exit()` behavior. No module, port, allocation failure, or build was exercised; source-only. See the [RemoveModule recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#dynmodule-removemodule-create-port-result-ek8853).

<a id="ek693"></a>
### EK693 — DynModule glue tests an uninitialized port-name pointer after ReadArgs fails.

The DynModule glue declares automatic pointer `pname` without initialization, and assigns it only inside the success branch of `ReadArgs("PORT/A", ...)` (`compiler/dynmodule/dynmodule_glue.c:85-93,106-118`). `PORT/A` is required; DOS documents that omitting a required argument causes `ReadArgs()` to fail (`rom/dos/readargs.c:157-158`), and its error path returns NULL after cleanup (`:912-932`). Execution then reaches `if (!pname)` without any assignment on that path (`dynmodule_glue.c:119-124`). Reading the indeterminate pointer has undefined behavior; depending on its value, the code may skip the fallback and pass a garbage port pointer to `__dynglue_InitIFPort()`, or take the fallback path by accident.

**Trigger and consequence:** start the DynModule glue without its required PORT argument, or with another command line that makes `ReadArgs()` fail. Before selecting its fallback name, the entry point evaluates an uninitialized pointer; it can continue with an invalid port name and fail or fault during interface-port creation.

**Affected configuration:** explicit builds and use of the optional `linklibs-dynmodglue` target. The target is defined in `compiler/dynmodule/mmakefile.src:12-13,28-30`; the `core-linklibs` aggregate edge is commented at `:3-5`, and no checked-in module consumer was found. **Confidence:** high for the failure branch reaching the uninitialized read; the resulting behavior is undefined and depends on compiler/runtime state. No module launch, parser failure or build was run. Source-only; see the [ReadArgs failure-path review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9029).

<a id="ek694"></a>
### EK694 — Escaped quote port name can underflow the glue stack-copy length.

The DynModule bootstrap quotes the module name and port in a command string (`compiler/dynmodule/dynmodule_modules.c:29-30,118`). DOS `ReadArgs()` treats `*"` inside a quoted argument as a literal quote (`rom/dos/readitem.c:129-165`). Thus a port name consisting of the two input characters `*"` arrives in the glue as a one-character string containing `"`. The glue recognizes that first character as its wrapper quote and computes `int prtlen = strlen(argpname) - 2` (`compiler/dynmodule/dynmodule_glue.c:106-113`). Since `strlen()` is unsigned, subtracting two from one wraps to `SIZE_MAX`; conversion of that value to `int` is implementation-defined. If the selected compiler converts it to a negative value (as the target's usual two's-complement conversion does), `strncpy()` converts it back to a huge unsigned count, and the following `prttmp[prtlen] = 0` also indexes before the 255-byte local array. The selected `strncpy()` implementation continues zero-padding for the full count (`compiler/crt/stdc/strncpy.c:47-57`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an optional DynModule caller supplies the short port string `*"` and the selected compiler converts the wrapped length to a negative `int`. The glue then writes outside `prttmp`, potentially corrupting its stack or faulting before it can create the interface port. This finding does not assert the same result for compiler implementations that convert the unsigned value differently.

**Affected configuration:** explicit use of the optional `linklibs-dynmodglue` target; its aggregate edge is commented and no maintained module consumer was found (`compiler/dynmodule/mmakefile.src:3-5,28-30`). **Confidence:** high for the quote decoding, unsigned underflow and unchecked signed-to-size conversion; manifestation is compiler-dependent. No module, command parser or build was run. Source-only; see the [escaped-quote and caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9032).

<a id="ek125"></a>
### EK125 — task.resource can fault and retain its task-list lock after iterator allocation fails.

With `TASKRES_ENABLE`, `LockTaskList()` obtains the shared task-resource semaphore before allocating its private iterator record. If `AllocMem()` fails, it returns the still-NULL `taskList` without releasing the semaphore (`rom/task/LockTaskList.c:66-80,95`). `NextTaskEntry()` initializes `taskList` from the returned handle, then dereferences `taskList->tlp_Flags` before its later `if (taskList)` guard (`rom/task/NextTaskEntry.c:58-71`). Thus callers that pass the failed result directly to `NextTaskEntry()` fault while the semaphore remains held.

The selected `C:TaskList`, SysMon refresh, TaskTrace lookup, VMM task page, and `Break` NAME scan paths pass the result to `NextTaskEntry()` without checking whether `LockTaskList()` returned NULL (`workbench/c/TaskList.c:193-201`; `workbench/system/SysMon/tasks.c:977-978`; `developer/debug/shellcommands/TaskTrace.c:92-100,113-120`; `workbench/system/VMM/MUI/task_page.c:435-440`; `workbench/c/Break.c:169-179`). In the enabled task.resource implementation, `NextTaskEntry(NULL)` faults at its early `tlp_Flags` read before the later NULL guard (`rom/task/NextTaskEntry.c:58-71`). The selected Security task snapshot and `Who` check the handle but skip `UnLockTaskList()` on NULL (`rom/security/security_task.c:358-363`; `workbench/c/security/Who.c:134-141`), retaining the semaphore without that secondary fault.
