If the requested DMA range crosses from the starting page into a physically discontiguous next page, `CachePreDMA()` returns the first physical address but leaves the full requested byte count in `*length`. A caller following that result can transfer past the first physical run, accessing an unrelated physical range instead of the rest of the virtual buffer. No checked-in CHRP `CachePreDMA()` caller was found, so the consequence is conditional on an external or future caller using the API for a cross-page buffer.

**Trigger and consequence:** a DMA request spans a virtual page boundary whose next physical page is not adjacent to the first, and the caller uses the returned physical address and unchanged `*length` as one contiguous transfer. The transfer can read or write the wrong physical bytes after the first-page extent. **Affected configuration:** CHRP/PPC builds selecting `arch/ppc-chrp/exec/cachepredma.c`, including Efika's PTE-based translation path. **Confidence:** high for the contract mismatch; conditional on a cross-page noncontiguous buffer and a caller relying on the returned length. No DMA operation or hardware was used. Source-only; see the [CHRP DMA translation trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7247).

<a id="ek343"></a>
### EK343 — The PC bootstrap ELF loader reads beyond boot-module extents.

The PC bootstrap records an ELF module's starting address in `ELFNode.eh` but does not retain the Multiboot module end address (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:341-363`; `bootstrap/include/elfloader.h:12-18`). The shared ELF loader then requests the ELF header and section-header table using offsets and sizes from that header (`bootstrap/elfloader.c:489-535`). The PC memory backend carries no module length: `open_file()` returns the stored pointer, `load_block()` returns `file + offset`, and `read_block()` copies from `file + offset` without checking the module end (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/memory_io.c:8-35`). For package members, `pkg_next()` validates the member range while locating the payload, but `ELFNode` still stores only the payload pointer, discarding its end (`bootstrap/bootstrap.c:295-337,389-420`). Raw Multiboot modules provide a start/end pair, but the ELF branch stores only the start and performs no ELF-range validation against the supplied end (`bootstrap.c:341-363`).

A malformed or truncated ELF module can therefore advertise a section table or section payload extending past the module or package-member boundary. The loader can directly dereference the out-of-range header/table pointer or copy bytes beyond the module while sizing/loading the kernel, potentially reading unrelated memory or faulting during bootstrap. The kernel image's section offsets and sizes are untrusted relative to the containing module because the backend has no length with which to validate them.

**Trigger and consequence:** a PC boot supplies an ELF module whose ELF header or section offsets/sizes point beyond the actual module/member extent. The bootstrap reads outside that object while determining kernel size or loading sections; outcome depends on adjacent memory and may corrupt the load or stop boot. **Affected configuration:** all-PC Multiboot bootstrap builds using the selected `memory_io.c` backend; raw Multiboot modules and package-contained ELF members are both affected by the lost extent. **Confidence:** high that extent is discarded and reads are unchecked; conditional on malformed/truncated module metadata. No module or boot was loaded. Source-only; see the [PC memory-backed ELF module extent trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5067).

<a id="ek347"></a>
### EK347 — PC archive iteration dereferences a NULL cursor after rejecting a member header.

The PC bootstrap's archive walker uses `ar_next()` as the increment expression in both the GNU long-name scan and the ELF-member scan (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:423-439`). `ar_next()` returns NULL when a member header's two-byte archive magic is not `0x60 0x0a` (`:227-233`). Neither loop checks that result before comparing the cursor with `mod_end` and entering another iteration. Since NULL compares below a nonzero archive end, the next iteration passes the NULL cursor to `ar_name()` or `ar_data()`, both of which dereference the supplied header (`:211-225,254-286`). In the second scan, an invalid-magic header also makes `ar_data()` return NULL, which is then passed to `memcmp()` as the ELF signature buffer (`:435-440`).

A malformed archive member header can therefore cause the bootstrap to dereference address zero while scanning boot modules, instead of rejecting the archive entry. This is separate from EK9031's truncated-record extent checks: this finding is specifically the invalid archive magic path returning a NULL next cursor or data pointer without caller validation.

**Trigger and consequence:** a PC boot archive contains a member with invalid archive magic and otherwise reaches the ar member loop. The bootstrap can dereference NULL during either archive scan and stop before loading the kernel. **Affected configuration:** all-PC Multiboot bootstrap builds accepting an ar archive as a boot module. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked NULL return and subsequent dereferences; conditional on malformed archive input. No archive or boot was used. Source-only; see the [PC ar iterator recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7993).

<a id="ek348"></a>
### EK348 — The PC bootstrap can overrun its fixed BSS-section tracker.

The PC bootstrap reserves a fixed 32,768-byte `__bss_track` array and passes it to `LoadKernel()` (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:140,747`). The shared ELF loader counts one `KernelBSS_t` record for each allocated `SHT_NOBITS` section in `GetKernelSize()` (`bootstrap/elfloader.c:573-585`), but the PC caller passes NULL for the optional `bss_size` output (`bootstrap.c:662`). `LoadKernel()` appends a record for every such section in `load_hunk()` and writes a zero terminator after all modules, with no capacity parameter or bound check (`bootstrap/elfloader.c:73-103,612,735-737`). Each tracker record has two loader-width `elf_uintptr_t` fields (`bootstrap/elfloader.c:45-50`), so the 32 KiB array holds 2,048 records for ELF64 or 4,096 for ELF32, including the terminator. The bootstrap library rules select the ELF width for their target (`bootstrap/mmakefile.src:12-22`).

An ELF image with at least as many nonempty allocated `SHT_NOBITS` sections as the configured record capacity causes the final record or terminator to pass the array end. `__bss_track` shares the protected bootstrap tables section with the tag list, memory map and VBE structures (`bootstrap.c:140-145`; `ldscript.lds`), so the overflow can corrupt adjacent bootstrap state before the kernel handoff. The loader's computed `bss_size` does not prevent this because the PC caller discards it and no runtime capacity is supplied to `LoadKernel()`.

**Trigger and consequence:** the PC bootstrap loads enough ELF modules with nonempty allocated `SHT_NOBITS` sections to exceed 2,047 records. The loader writes beyond the 32 KiB tracker, potentially corrupting neighboring boot data and causing incorrect handoff or boot failure. **Affected configuration:** all-PC bootstrap builds using the shared ELF loader and fixed tracker. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked append/terminator and capacity; conditional on an unusually high BSS-section count in the boot modules. No ELF image or boot was loaded. Source-only; see the [BSS tracker sizing and caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7996).

<a id="ek349"></a>
### EK349 — BSD extended-name ar entries make the PC bootstrap skip subsequent archive members.

For a BSD `#1/<len>` archive member, the declared `ar_size` includes the embedded filename bytes as well as the file payload. The in-tree archive writer follows that convention by setting the size to `k + payload_size` before writing the embedded name and data (`tools/fd2pragma/fd2pragma.c:7965-8000,8682-8717`). The PC bootstrap's `ar_next()` first advances by the declared size, rounds it to even alignment, and then adds the BSD filename length and its padding a second time (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:227-251`). Both archive scans use this result as their next member pointer (`:423-439`).

When a BSD extended-name member is followed by another member, the cursor advances past the next member's start by the embedded-name length. This can cause the long-name scan to miss a later GNU `//` table and the ELF scan to skip a following kernel module or interpret a later payload as a header. The name-bearing member itself is still located at `header + sizeof(ar_header)` by `ar_data()`; the defect is the doubled size contribution in iteration.

**Trigger and consequence:** a PC boot archive contains a valid BSD `#1/` member with a subsequent member, with the declared size including the embedded filename as the format and in-tree writer do. The bootstrap advances too far and can omit subsequent archive entries, including a kernel module needed for boot. **Affected configuration:** all-PC Multiboot bootstrap builds that accept ar archives. **Confidence:** high for the size arithmetic and selected loops; conditional on a BSD extended-name entry preceding a needed member. No archive or boot was parsed. Source-only; see the [BSD ar size and iterator recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7993).

<a id="ek350"></a>
### EK350 — PC bootstrap workspace exhaustion turns module metadata allocation failures into NULL dereferences.

The PC bootstrap's `__bs_malloc()` uses a fixed 16 MiB workspace and returns NULL when an aligned allocation would exceed its end (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/support.c:64-89`). The archive-name helper does not check that result: after `tmp = __bs_malloc(len + 1)`, it immediately copies into `tmp` and writes the terminator (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:254-292`). The module-record helper likewise writes `mo->Next` and links `mo` after an unchecked allocation (`:177-198`). These helpers are called while scanning ar entries and registering raw/package ELF modules (`:357-400,423-440`). In the archive long-name search, every member name is allocated, compared, and retained in the bootstrap workspace rather than freed, so a sufficiently large archive can exhaust the arena during the scan itself.

When the workspace is exhausted, `ar_name()` writes through NULL; module registration can independently write through a NULL `ELFNode`. The bootstrap may fault while parsing boot metadata before loading the kernel. This is distinct from EK347's invalid archive magic and EK9031's truncated-record reads; it is the allocation-failure handling of otherwise parseable inputs.

**Trigger and consequence:** archive/module metadata consumes the 16 MiB bootstrap workspace until `__bs_malloc()` fails, including through accumulated archive-name copies. The unchecked caller dereferences NULL and stops bootstrap parsing. **Affected configuration:** all-PC Multiboot bootstrap builds using the selected fixed workspace. **Confidence:** high for allocation failure and unchecked writes; conditional on exhausting the arena with sufficiently large or numerous boot metadata. No workspace exhaustion or boot was induced. Source-only; see the [PC bootstrap workspace exhaustion trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8002).

<a id="ek358"></a>
### EK358 — WaitForPort frees a timer request and reply port while timer.device may still own them.

`WaitForPort` submits a `UNIT_VBLANK` request with `BeginIO()` before entering a wait that also listens for Ctrl-C and Ctrl-D (`workbench/c/WaitForPort.c:102-120`). Either break signal exits immediately, without aborting the request or waiting for its reply. Cleanup calls `CloseDevice()`, then `DeleteIORequest()` and `DeleteMsgPort()` (`:149-166`). The timer device's configuration has no custom `CLOSEDEV` hook (`rom/timer/timer.conf`); the generated close path therefore only performs the generic device close/open-count handling (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1441-1463`; `compiler/libinit/libinit.c:53-92`). It does not remove the request from the timer's wait list. `UNIT_VBLANK` `TR_ADDREQUEST` inserts the request into `tb_Lists[UNIT_VBLANK]` (`rom/timer/lowlevel.c:185-214`), and `TimerProcessVBlank()` later removes completed entries and calls `ReplyMsg()` through each request (`:354-379`). `DeleteIORequest()` simply frees the request allocation (`rom/exec/deleteiorequest.c:15-49`), while deleting the message port frees its storage (`rom/exec/deletemsgport.c:15-58`).

If the user breaks out before the next VBlank completion, the timer list retains pointers into the freed request and its deleted reply port. A later timer tick can read the freed request while comparing its deadline and then reply through the stale message/port fields, causing memory corruption or a fault. The `timer.device` no-expunge setting avoids claiming device unload as a consequence; the defect is the outstanding request lifetime.

There is also a narrower ExecSMP completion window. The selected timer VBlank handler removes a due request from its list and calls `ReplyMsg()` in interrupt context (`rom/timer/lowlevel.c:354-379`; `rom/timer/timervblank.c:17-24`). `ReplyMsg()` sets `mn_Node.ln_Type = NT_REPLYMSG` before `InternalPutMsg()` locks and links through the reply port, then signals the task (`rom/exec/replymsg.c:52-64`; `rom/exec/putmsg.c:71-105`). If another CPU delivers Ctrl-C/D and wakes `WaitForPort` while that interrupt call is still in progress, the command's break-first test can enter cleanup. `CloseDevice()` does not join that interrupt path, so cleanup can free the request and port while `InternalPutMsg()` is still using the port (and, before insertion, the request). This extends the same missing request-cancellation/join defect; it is not counted as a separate finding. This additional race is limited to ExecSMP with the timer interrupt and command task running on different CPUs.

**Trigger and consequence:** Ctrl-C or Ctrl-D arrives while the one-second VBlank request remains queued, or—on ExecSMP—while the timer interrupt is still executing `ReplyMsg()`/`InternalPutMsg()` for that request. Cleanup frees the request and port without `AbortIO()`/`WaitIO()`; a later timer-list pass or the still-running reply path can access freed storage. **Affected configuration:** runs of the selected `C:WaitForPort` command that open timer.device version 36 or newer and break during one of those intervals. The reply-path overlap additionally requires ExecSMP and execution on different CPUs. **Confidence:** high for the missing abort/wait and queued-request ownership; each manifestation depends on its stated timing condition. No command, timer request or interrupt was run. Source-only; see the [WaitForPort timer and cleanup trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8008).

<a id="ek359"></a>
### EK359 — WaitForPort checks late and can exceed its documented ten-second wait.

The command documentation says it waits up to 10 seconds for the named port (`workbench/c/WaitForPort.c:7-34`). However, after opening timer.device it submits a one-second `UNIT_VBLANK` request before its first `FindPort()` call (`:86-106,120-127`). A port that already exists when the command starts is therefore not observed until the first timer completion, adding up to roughly one interval of unnecessary delay. If the port never appears, `wait_time` starts at zero and increases by one second per timer reply; the timeout check is `wait_time > wait_limit`, with `wait_limit` set to ten seconds (`:98-100,126-135`). The command thus exits on the eleventh reply, approximately 11 seconds after starting the timer, rather than at ten.

**Trigger and consequence:** the named port exists at invocation, or remains absent for the full timeout. The initial lookup is delayed until the first one-second request completes; in the absent-port case, the command waits one extra interval beyond the documented ten-second limit. **Affected configuration:** the selected `C:WaitForPort` command when timer.device version 36 or newer opens successfully. **Confidence:** high for the source ordering and strict comparison; actual interval timing follows the selected VBlank timer implementation. No command or timer was run. Source-only; see the [WaitForPort timing trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8008).

<a id="ek364"></a>
### EK364 — LeakWatch dereferences a failed GadTools library open during its first snapshot.

`open_libs()` stores the result of `OpenLibrary("gadtools.library", 0L)` without checking it (`workbench/c/LeakWatch.c:692-695`). `main()` proceeds to `NewResourcesState()` (`:718-728`), whose `AddOpenedResources()` unconditionally reads private GadTools class fields through `GadToolsBase` (`:415-435`). The snapshot only returns early if an earlier resource-list collection fails; when those collections succeed but GadTools cannot be opened, the first snapshot dereferences NULL.

**Trigger and consequence:** `gadtools.library` is unavailable or cannot be opened, and preceding snapshot collection succeeds. LeakWatch faults during its initial resource snapshot instead of reporting the failed dependency or exiting cleanly. **Affected configuration:** the selected `C:LeakWatch` command on any target where this open can fail. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked open and subsequent dereference; conditional on library-open failure. No open failure or command was run. Source-only; see the [LeakWatch full-body and caller pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2174).

<a id="ek365"></a>
### EK365 — LeakWatch's CTRL-E baseline copy drops resource type labels in changed-count rows.

`CopyResourcesNode()` duplicates the name, address and count from each snapshot node but never copies its `type` field (`workbench/c/LeakWatch.c:651-659`). `CopyResourcesState()` uses this helper for the CTRL-E baseline (`:662-687`); when a later snapshot changes an existing resource's count, `NewStateDiff()` takes `other->type` from that baseline (`:554-569`). The static baseline node therefore has a NULL type label. The diff formatter passes it to `%s` (`:619-621`); Exec `RawDoFmt` substitutes an empty string for a NULL C-string argument (`rom/exec/rawdofmt.c:276-282`), so the resource row loses its type label but is still displayed.

**Trigger and consequence:** CTRL-E establishes a baseline, then a resource present in both snapshots changes its open count. The output row has a blank type field, reducing diagnostic clarity. **Affected configuration:** the selected `C:LeakWatch` command on all targets; only CTRL-E changed-count rows are affected. **Confidence:** high for the omitted copy and formatter behavior. No command was run. Source-only; see the [LeakWatch full-body and caller pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2174).

<a id="ek366"></a>
### EK366 — LeakWatch's never-reclaimed snapshot pools turn capacity exhaustion into unchecked NULL use.

LeakWatch's static pools have finite capacities (`MAX_ORN=30000`, `MAX_TR=3000`, `MAX_RD=300`, `MAX_STR=300000`, `MAX_MR=2000`) and monotonic allocation counters; every `release_*()` function and `StrFree()` is empty (`workbench/c/LeakWatch.c:115-119,166-208,210-230`). Some exhaustion paths are handled: `NewResourcesState()` returns NULL when its tracker or a resource-node allocation fails, and callers of that constructor exit the command. Other paths do not handle it. `CopyResourcesNode()` returns NULL when the node pool is exhausted, but `CopyResourcesState()` passes that NULL to `Enqueue()` without checking (`:651-682`). `StaticStrDup()` returns NULL at string-pool exhaustion, but collection and copy paths store that result without checking; later diff comparison calls `strcmp()` on snapshot names (`:216-224,252-262,543-557,656-681`). Finally, `NewStateDiff()` returns NULL when the diff or modified-resource pool is exhausted (`:537-563,576-578`), while CTRL-E/F call `DisplayStateDiff()` without checking (`:761-763,776-778`), and the display routine immediately dereferences `rd` (`:596-603`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a long LeakWatch session consumes its fixed pools through repeated snapshots/diffs, or a sufficiently large snapshot exhausts node/string capacity. Depending on the exhausted pool, baseline copying can insert a NULL list node, a NULL name can reach `strcmp()`, or diff-pool exhaustion can pass NULL to the display routine; the command can corrupt its list or fault instead of reporting capacity exhaustion. **Affected configuration:** the selected `C:LeakWatch` command on all targets; requires enough accumulated snapshots/resources or names to cross the fixed limits. **Confidence:** high for the monotonic counters, unchecked return paths and resulting invalid inputs; exact exhaustion threshold depends on resource counts and name lengths. No capacity limit was exercised. Source-only; see the [LeakWatch full-body and caller pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2174).

<a id="ek367"></a>
### EK367 — LeakWatch walks shared Exec lists under CPU-local Forbid without their ExecSMP list locks.

`AddLibs()`, `AddDevs()`, and `AddNodeNames()` traverse Exec's library, device, resource, interrupt, port, and semaphore lists under `Forbid()` only; `AddFonts()` similarly traverses `GfxBase->TextFonts` without the Graphics font semaphore (`workbench/c/LeakWatch.c:243-342,395-412`). On ExecSMP, `Forbid()` prevents task switches only on the calling CPU; it does not exclude concurrent list mutation on another CPU (`rom/exec/permit.c:49-55`). The selected Exec list operations use dedicated spinlocks for these shared lists (`rom/exec/exec_locks.c:30-68`), and Graphics font add/open/close/remove paths obtain `fontsem` (`rom/graphics/addfont.c:57-61`, `openfont.c:63-91`, `closefont.c:55-62`, `remfont.c:56-84`). LeakWatch does not acquire those locks while following links or reading node fields.

**Trigger and consequence:** with ExecSMP enabled, another CPU adds or removes an entry during a snapshot. The walk can observe an inconsistent list or continue through an entry whose lifetime ended during traversal, making the snapshot incomplete or causing an invalid access. The same issue applies to concurrent font-list changes without `fontsem`. **Affected configuration:** builds with ExecSMP enabled; the race requires a concurrent mutation of one of the traversed lists. **Confidence:** high that the required locks are omitted and that `Forbid()` is CPU-local; the concrete outcome depends on interleaving and node lifetime. No concurrent operation was run. Source-only; see the [LeakWatch full-body and caller pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2174).

<a id="ek369"></a>
### EK369 — LeakWatch narrows pointer-sized free-memory changes to a signed LONG before displaying them.

`TrackedResources.freeMem` is pointer-sized `IPTR`, but `ResourceDiff.memLost` is signed `LONG` (`workbench/c/LeakWatch.c:131-150`). `NewStateDiff()` subtracts the two free-memory values and assigns the result directly to that narrower field (`:591`); `DisplayStateDiff()` then formats it as a signed long (`:602`). On a 64-bit target, a free-memory delta outside the signed 32-bit range is narrowed before display and can be reported with a wrong value or sign.

**Trigger and consequence:** a 64-bit build observes a change in total free memory whose signed delta does not fit in `LONG`. LeakWatch's memory-loss figure is truncated or mis-signed. **Affected configuration:** 64-bit targets, for sufficiently large free-memory changes; narrower targets are not affected by this width mismatch. **Confidence:** high for the type-width mismatch; the displayed error requires a delta outside the `LONG` range. No large-memory change was induced. Source-only; see the [LeakWatch full-body and caller pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2174).

<a id="ek370"></a>
### EK370 — Avail HUMAN formatting writes past ten-byte buffers for large 64-bit memory values.

`printm()` uses ten-byte output buffers (`buf` and, for the table form, `tmp`) and passes them to `fmtlarge()` when `HUMAN` is selected (`workbench/c/Avail.c:290-329`). For GiB values, `fmtlarge()` formats a nonzero fractional part with `%iu.%02iu`, then appends the `G` suffix and a NUL (`:236-287`). When the rounded whole-GiB part has six digits and the hundredths are nonzero, the formatted value occupies nine characters; the suffix fills byte 10 and the final NUL is written one byte past the buffer. `RawDoFmt()` itself fits the nine characters plus its terminator in the ten-byte destination, so the overflow is specifically the suffix terminator. `AvailMem()` returns `IPTR` (`rom/exec/availmem.c:37-72`), allowing these values on 64-bit targets. The default summary and explicit `TOTAL HUMAN` path both reach this formatter (`Avail.c:187-213,178-185`); the table branch uses `tmp[10]`.

**Trigger and consequence:** on a 64-bit build, request `Avail HUMAN` (or `TOTAL HUMAN`) when a reported memory value is at least 100,000 GiB and its rounded hundredths are nonzero. `fmtlarge()` writes the final NUL one byte beyond the destination, corrupting adjacent stack storage and potentially affecting the command's output or control flow. Exact consequences depend on stack layout. **Affected configuration:** 64-bit targets with enough reported memory to cross this threshold; ordinary smaller memory values and non-HUMAN output do not reach the overlong representation. **Confidence:** high for the size calculation and out-of-bounds NUL write; threshold conditions are explicit, while impact depends on the runtime stack layout. No command or large-memory value was used. Source-only; see the [Avail formatter and caller pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7276).

<a id="ek311"></a>
### EK311 — `UnLockTaskList()` can free a different same-owner iterator handle.

`LockTaskList()` allocates a private iterator handle, records the current task in `tlp_Node.ln_Name`, records the requested flags, and appends the handle to `trb_LockedLists` (`rom/task/LockTaskList.c:62-80`; `rom/task/task_intern.h:83-90`). `UnLockTaskList(tlist, flags)` releases the semaphore, then searches that list using only the current task and `tlp_Flags`; it never compares a record to the supplied `tlist` (`rom/task/UnLockTaskList.c:53-74`). Thus two valid nested handles acquired by the same task with identical flags are indistinguishable to the search. The first matching record is removed and freed, even when it is not the handle being unlocked. `NextTaskEntry()` dereferences the private handle it receives (`rom/task/NextTaskEntry.c:58-110`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a task acquires two task-list handles with the same flags, unlocks the later handle first, then continues using the earlier handle that remains logically held. `UnLockTaskList()` may have freed that earlier handle, so a subsequent `NextTaskEntry()` can read freed storage; a later unlock can also remove the remaining record instead. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting the `task.resource` implementation with `TASKRES_ENABLE` (enabled in `rom/task/task_intern.h`); applies when clients use valid nested same-flags handles. **Confidence:** high for handle omission and first-match freeing; the stale-handle consequence requires this API call order. No nested iterator or task schedule was run. Source-only; see the [task.resource iterator reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8937).

<a id="ek312"></a>
### EK312 — ExecSMP task-list iterator bookkeeping can lose handles or free entries still held by an iterator.

`LockTaskList()` obtains a *shared* `trb_Sem` for ordinary read handles, then reads `trb_TaskList`'s head and appends its new handle to the shared `trb_LockedLists` without `TaskListSpinLock` (`rom/task/LockTaskList.c:66-80`). Multiple readers can therefore publish handles concurrently. `UnLockTaskList()` releases `trb_Sem` before unlinking its record and calling `task_CleanList()` (`rom/task/UnLockTaskList.c:61-77`). The cleanup tests whether `trb_LockedLists` is empty before obtaining `TaskListSpinLock`, then removes and frees every tombstoned task entry (`rom/task/task_support.c:13-48`). On ExecSMP, task removal marks an entry as a tombstone while any iterator record exists (`rom/task/task_execfuncs.c:133-164`). Neither iterator creation nor `NextTaskEntry()` protects its list cursor with `TaskListSpinLock` (`LockTaskList.c:77-79`; `NextTaskEntry.c:70-93`).

This leaves two related coordination gaps: concurrent shared readers can race while adding/removing `trb_LockedLists` nodes, and a new iterator can publish a cursor to a tombstone after cleanup has observed an empty lock list but before cleanup frees tombstones. In the latter interleaving, `NextTaskEntry()` may follow or dereference a freed `TaskListEntry`; registry corruption can also make cleanup's “no readers” decision incorrect.

**Trigger and consequence:** with ExecSMP enabled, concurrent `LockTaskList()`/`UnLockTaskList()` calls overlap task removal and tombstone cleanup. The registry may become inconsistent, or an iterator may retain a cursor to an entry freed by cleanup, causing an invalid read and potentially an incomplete task listing or fault. **Affected configuration:** ExecSMP builds using the selected task.resource iterator implementation; requires concurrent iterator lifecycle and task removal. **Confidence:** high for the missing synchronization and cleanup ordering; the resulting corruption or stale-cursor access depends on interleaving and cursor position. No iterator, task removal or schedule was run. Source-only; see the [task.resource iterator reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8937).

<a id="ek313"></a>
### EK313 — task.resource inserts task-list entries without the ExecSMP list lock.

The task.resource prelaunch hook allocates a `TaskListEntry`, then checks whether `trb_LockedLists` is empty and appends the entry to either `trb_TaskList` or `trb_NewTasks` (`rom/task/task_execfuncs.c:20-43`). It takes neither `TaskListSpinLock` nor another shared lock. ExecSMP task removal and task-list cleanup do use `TaskListSpinLock` around `trb_TaskList` mutations (`rom/task/task_execfuncs.c:133-164`; `rom/task/task_support.c:20-47`), and iterator list access is likewise expected to coexist with these operations. The hook is installed by task.resource's `NewAddTask` wrapper and is invoked by Exec's task-launch path (`rom/task/task_execfuncs.c:68-86`; `rom/exec/newaddtask.c:25-43,67-71`). Concurrent task creation on separate CPUs can therefore execute the unsynchronized emptiness check and list insertion at the same time.

**Trigger and consequence:** on ExecSMP, two tasks are launched concurrently while task.resource is active. Their prelaunch hooks race while reading the shared lock-holder list and appending to a shared task list. Concurrent link updates can lose or corrupt entries, so task enumeration can omit tasks or traverse inconsistent list links. **Affected configuration:** ExecSMP builds with task.resource selected; requires overlapping task launches. **Confidence:** high that insertion omits the synchronization used by the selected task-list writers; corruption requires concurrent execution. No task launch or list race was run. Source-only; see the [task.resource insertion and launch recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7884).

<a id="ek419"></a>
### EK419 — Repeated m68k `FindTask()` calls leak guest heap blocks and eventually return an unusable Task pointer.

The optional m68kemu Exec vector implements `FindTask()` by looking up the native task, allocating a fresh m68k `Process`-sized block, registering it as a `Task` shadow, syncing fields, and returning the guest address (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:116-169,706-710`). It neither checks the return from `shadow_register()` nor reuses an existing shadow or releases the allocated block. Process results with a CLI can allocate further CLI and command-name blocks (`:132-167`). The emulator has a fixed 256-entry shadow table (`m68kemu_intern.h:92-94`); when full, `shadow_register()` logs and returns zero (`m68kemu_thunks.c:444-455`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated guest repeatedly calls `FindTask()` for a name that resolves to a native task. Each successful lookup consumes guest heap; once the shadow table is full, the thunk still returns the newly allocated but unregistered address. A later guest API such as `Signal()` resolves that address through `m68k_to_host_or_shadow()`, whose fallback treats any in-range unregistered address as ordinary emulator memory (`m68kemu_intern.h:114-125`); the generated Signal thunk passes the resulting pointer to native Exec (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2012-2018`). Native `Signal()` then interprets guest-layout bytes as a host `Task`, so the call can access invalid task fields or corrupt memory. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built/loaded m68kemu on a supported 64-bit host; it is an optional target, and no maintained guest caller was found. **Confidence:** high for per-call allocation, ignored registration failure, bounded table, pointer fallback and native consumer; guest exhaustion and exact consequence depend on call count and later API use. Reuse/release task shadows and return failure when registration fails. No guest program, repeated lookup, heap exhaustion, signal call, or build was run; source-only. See the [m68k FindTask and shadow-table trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8841).

<a id="ek426"></a>
### EK426 — Concurrent ExecSMP system alerts can overwrite each other’s shared alert record.

`Exec_SystemAlert()` queues a non-dead-end alert whenever the single shared `SAT.sat_IsAvailable` flag is true: it writes the alert number and current task into `SAT.sat_Params[0..1]`, then signals `sat_Task` (`rom/exec/systemalert.c:63-70`). The producer has no shared lock or reservation around the availability check and two parameter writes. Although `Alert()` wraps the call with `Disable()`, Exec documents that this disables interrupts only on the current CPU in ExecSMP builds (`rom/exec/alert.c:170-179`; `rom/exec/disable.c:58-61`). The consumer copies the parameters after waking and marks the slot unavailable (`rom/exec/supervisoralert.c:39-48`), then later marks it available before clearing the old parameter words (`:95-102`). These accesses are likewise only locally interrupt-masked.

**Trigger and consequence:** two CPUs concurrently queue non-dead-end system alerts while the Supervisor Alert Task is available, or a new producer publishes as the consumer marks the slot available and clears the previous record. Producers can overwrite or interleave the alert-code/task pair, or a new record can be cleared by the consumer; the displayed alert can therefore be lost or associated with the wrong alert code/task. Dead-end alerts take the direct display path and are not part of this slot race. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC SMP and Raspberry Pi ARM/ARMeb SMP variants (`configure.in:1437-1461,1667-1671,2113-2199`); non-ExecSMP configurations do not have cross-CPU producers. **Confidence:** high that the shared record and availability flag have no cross-CPU synchronization; the exact interleaving and user-visible alert are conditional and were not reproduced. Protect availability and parameter publication/consumption with one SMP-safe synchronization protocol, and clear the old record before republishing availability. No alert or schedule was run; source-only. See the [shared alert-slot trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8145).

<a id="ek474"></a>
### EK474 — POSIXC `vfork()` reads its freed control block while forming the parent return value.

On the parent completion path, `__vfork_exit_controlled_stack()` saves the jump environment, frees `udata`, and then evaluates `GetETaskID(udata->child)` as the value passed to `vfork_longjmp()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/__vfork.c:437-445`). That expression reads `child` from the freed `vfork_data` block. The selected `system_sh()` caller uses a positive return as the PID for `waitpid()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/system.c:111-124`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a successful `vfork()` child completes and the parent reaches the controlled-stack return path. The child ID is read after its containing block is freed; allocator reuse or changed contents can produce an invalid PID or fault before `system()` can wait for the child. **Affected configuration:** POSIXC `vfork()` users; the checked-in direct caller is `system_sh()` in `system()`, and selected x86-64 and AArch64 wrappers reach the common C implementation. **Confidence:** high for the read-after-free ordering; wrong return value or fault depends on allocator reuse and was not reproduced. Read/save the child ID before freeing `udata`. No vfork, child process, allocator reuse, or build was run; source-only. See the [completion path trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4601).

<a id="ek475"></a>
### EK475 — Failed POSIXC `vfork()` setup leaks its parent signal/control state and leaves `VFORK_PARENT` set.

`parent_createchild()` allocates a parent signal, sets `PosixCBase->flags |= VFORK_PARENT`, and then attempts `CreateNewProc()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/__vfork.c:488-502`). If process creation fails, it frees `udata` and returns `-1` through the saved jump, but does not `FreeSignal(parent_signal)` or clear `VFORK_PARENT` (`:504-510`). If the child is created but the launcher cannot open its required POSIXC/StdC/StdCIO libraries, the launcher signals setup failure and the parent jumps out at the `child_errno` branch; that path also bypasses the later signal/control-block cleanup and the normal `VFORK_PARENT` clear (`:164-181,514-527`). These are distinct from failure to allocate `parent_signal`, which is handled before setting the flag and frees `udata` (`:490-497`).

**Trigger and consequence:** after the parent signal is allocated, either `CreateNewProc()` fails or the launched child fails POSIXC setup. `vfork()` returns `-1`, while the parent retains the allocated signal bit and `VFORK_PARENT`; the launcher-setup failure also leaves `vfork_data` allocated. Later POSIXC startup and descriptor paths test `VFORK_PARENT` to select special inheritance behavior (`compiler/crt/posixc/__posixc_nixmain.c:66-78,101-103`; `__fdesc.c:767-775`), so the stale flag can cause later process/file-descriptor setup to take the vfork branch. The selected `system_sh()` caller returns `-1` on the failure result (`system.c:111-134`). **Affected configuration:** POSIXC `vfork()` users, including the checked-in `system_sh()` path; child-creation and launcher library-open failures are conditional. **Confidence:** high for the omitted cleanup and persistent flag; downstream effect depends on later POSIXC startup/descriptor use and was not reproduced. Unwind the parent signal, control block and flag on each failure path. No process-creation or library-open failure was induced; source-only. See the [failure unwind trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4604).

<a id="ek504"></a>
### EK504 — ELF I/O callbacks can treat short reads as successful when the error indicator they inspect remains clear.

The hosted and ARM CEBoot `read_block()` adapters call `fread(dest, length, 1, file)`, which returns zero when it cannot read the complete one-element block; they then return `errno` or `GetLastError()` rather than checking the stream error/EOF state or the actual byte count (`arch/all-hosted/bootstrap/elf_io.c:79-91`; `arch/arm-native/ceboot/elf_io.c:84-96`). When the read is short and the inspected error indicator remains zero, the adapter reports success. Hosted `load_block()` then returns its allocated buffer with the unread tail uninitialized (`elf_io.c:97-115`), and the common loader trusts the result for ELF headers, section tables and section contents (`bootstrap/elfloader.c:514-530,89-105`). The PC Multiboot adapter is separate and is not included in this finding.

**Trigger and consequence:** boot loading a truncated or concurrently shortened ELF module through the hosted or CEBoot callback while `errno` (hosted) or the Win32 last-error value (CEBoot) remains clear after a short `fread()`. The loader may accept incomplete metadata or copy/relocate a section whose unread tail was not supplied by the file, causing module-load failure, corrupted module contents or a later boot fault. **Affected configuration:** hosted bootstrap and ARM CEBoot images using the shared ELF loader; the CEBoot instance additionally depends on the Windows CE CRT leaving last-error clear for the short read. **Confidence:** high that the adapters confuse the error indicator with read completeness and that the loader consumes success as a complete block; actual truncated-image acceptance depends on returned bytes and metadata. Check the byte count/EOF/error state and require exactly `length` bytes. No ELF file, short read, bootstrap or build was run; source-only. See the [adapter and shared-loader trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L6045).

<a id="ek508"></a>
### EK508 — Hosted bootstrap silently continues after it fails to add a configured kernel module.

For every `module` configuration line, hosted bootstrap calls `AddKernelFile(c)` and ignores its return (`arch/all-hosted/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:247-251`). `AddKernelFile()` returns zero when its `malloc()` for the module node/path fails, without linking that node (`arch/all-hosted/bootstrap/elf_io.c:25-44`). The parser continues, and later successful module lines are appended. `GetKernelSize()` validates only the nodes present in `FirstELF` and returns success after iterating them (`bootstrap/elfloader.c:489-595`). `LoadKernel()` likewise iterates only that partial list, chooses the first `SHF_EXECINSTR` section it sees as `kernel_entry`, and does not fail if no executable section was found (`:604-665,735-743`). Hosted bootstrap then calls `kick(kernel_entry, km)` (`arch/all-hosted/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:366,415`); `kernel_entry` is a local variable without an initializer (`:170`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a hosted bootstrap `module` line fails `AddKernelFile()` allocation, while one or more later module additions succeed. The loader calculates and loads this incomplete configured set without reporting the missing entry. If no surviving module has executable content, `LoadKernel()` still returns success and bootstrap passes its uninitialized `kernel_entry` to `kick()`; if a later executable module remains, it can instead become the first selected entry. Missing required modules can also make startup fail after handoff. **Affected configuration:** hosted bootstrap with a module configuration file; the failure requires allocation failure for a configured module and a partial list that proceeds through sizing/loading. **Confidence:** high for ignored return, partial-list acceptance and missing-entry validation; the allocation/follow-on pattern and exact handoff result are conditional and were not reproduced. Treat an `AddKernelFile()` failure as fatal and require `LoadKernel()` to confirm an executable entry before returning success. No allocation failure, ELF load, bootstrap, or build was run; source-only. See the [hosted callback and partial-list trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1285).

<a id="ek515"></a>
### EK515 — Failed Android hosted-bootstrap retries retain module state and host allocations.

The hosted bootstrap keeps the module list in process-global `FirstELF`/`LastELF` state. Android's arch-specific makefile reuses the shared hosted bootstrap sources, and JNI `Load()` calls `bootstrap()` (`arch/all-android/bootstrap/mmakefile.src:4-11`; `arch/all-android/bootstrap/main.c:40-68`). A `GetKernelSize()` failure returns without `FreeKernelList()` (`arch/all-hosted/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:339-340,366-372`); this can leave earlier nodes' allocated ELF and section headers live (`bootstrap/elfloader.c:499-538`; `arch/all-hosted/bootstrap/elf_io.c:47-59`). A later `LoadKernel()` failure likewise returns before the success-only `FreeKernelList()` call (`bootstrap.c:366-372`). The bootstrap allocates AROS RAM before sizing and the code/data/BSS areas before loading (`bootstrap.c:304-364`), but its `Host_FreeMem()` call is in the child-exit signal handler, which only runs after `kick()` has launched the AROS child (`arch/all-android/bootstrap/kickstart.c:53-73,89-95`). A pre-start bootstrap failure therefore retains those host allocations; a retry overwrites the static allocation pointers as it requests new mappings/blocks (`arch/all-unix/bootstrap/memory.c:17-27,40-54,78-101,111-120`).

On Android, `AROSActivity.onSizeChanged()` calls `ColdBoot()` while `main.started` is false; a failed native `Load()` does not reach `WarmBoot()`, so a later size-change callback can retry (`AROSActivity.java:195-229`; `AROSBootstrap.java:75-104`). The retry reparses the config and `AddKernelFile()` appends another set of nodes to the retained list; bootstrap does not reset the globals at entry (`bootstrap.c:238-250`; `elf_io.c:22-44`). If the failure clears, `GetKernelSize()` and `LoadKernel()` traverse both sets, duplicating modules in the boot image; earlier retained ELF metadata may also be overwritten without being freed. **Affected configuration and trigger:** Android hosted bootstrap, after a pre-start `GetKernelSize()` or `LoadKernel()` failure and another size-change callback before the app exits. **Confidence:** high for the skipped cleanup, persistent list/memory state, and append-on-retry; duplicate module loading requires the retry to succeed. No Android run, failure, retry or boot was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek529"></a>
### EK529 — The Sam440 ext2 boot-device factory dereferences an unchecked allocation.

After a successful ext2 block-device setup and probe mount, ext2_create() closes the probe filesystem, allocates its boot-device object through the Parthenope context malloc wrapper, then immediately writes the callback fields without checking the result (arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/ext2.c:71-100; context.c:109-117). If the U-Boot-provided c_alloc_mem_for_anythingelse callback returns NULL, the first field assignment dereferences NULL. The primary device-selection path calls ext2_create() only after DOS and SFS factories return NULL, but its boot == NULL fallback check occurs after the factory returns (parthenope.c:345-370); menu magic-load has the same DOS/SFS/ext2 fallback and only checks dev after the call (menu.c:608-620). Thus the caller cannot apply its fallback or skip policy for this allocation failure.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** an explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 bootloader, when DOS and SFS do not provide a boot device, ext2 probe mount succeeds, and the callback allocation fails. The active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` target depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`); this path is selected when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked allocation and NULL field write; trigger requires the stated low-memory condition on this optional path. Check the allocation and return NULL before initializing the object. No allocation failure, filesystem mount, or boot was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek530"></a>
### EK530 — The Sam440 SFS boot reader does not compare a block's computed checksum with its stored checksum.

Parthenope's calcchecksum() clears the block's stored checksum field, sums the block words from an initial value of one, and returns the negated sum, which is the checksum value that should have been stored (arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/sfs.c:36-49). Both metadata readers then test only whether this computed replacement checksum is zero; neither compares it with the original stored checksum (sfs.c:81-90,131-145). By contrast, the selected SFS writer stores the negative checksum after clearing the checksum field, and the filesystem validator checks the complete block sum including its stored checksum for zero (rom/filesys/SFS/FS/filesystemmain.c:3855-3874; rom/filesys/SFS/SFSchecksum/SFSchecksum.c:91-105). Consequently, a corrupted directory-container or extent-tree block whose recomputed checksum is nonzero passes Parthenope's check even when it differs from the stored value; a valid block whose expected checksum is zero is reported as invalid. These checks protect directory lookups and extent-tree traversal used to load boot files, so bad metadata may be followed as if verified or a valid edge-case block may be rejected.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 using SFS media and reading directory-container or extent-tree metadata. The active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` target depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`); this path is selected when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the incorrect predicate and checksum algorithm mismatch; which media blocks encounter either outcome is data-dependent. Compare the computed value to the saved field or validate the full block sum without destroying the stored checksum. No disk image or boot was used; source-only.

<a id="ek532"></a>
### EK532 — Parthenope passes fixed-size buffers to a file loader that has no capacity argument.

The Parthenope boot-device interface passes only a filename and destination pointer; it has no destination-capacity parameter (arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/device.h:26-29). The selected DOS, SFS, ext2 and CD readers copy or read the full file length into that pointer: DOS uses the on-disk byte_size and copies until it reaches zero (dos.c:258-289), SFS uses the object file size and copies extents until that length is read (sfs.c:177-195), ext2 passes ext2fs_open()'s file length to ext2fs_read() (ext2.c:35-62), and CD calls cdrom_read() for the complete discovered size (cdrom.c:446-456). None receives or checks the destination capacity. The TFTP callback delegates to U-Boot and is excluded because its transfer bounds are external.

Checked-in callers provide fixed-size destinations: a 5 MiB kernel buffer, 64 KiB menu buffer, 18 MiB Linux initrd buffer, 10 MiB AROS module staging buffer and 16 MiB AOS module buffer (parthenope.c:129-132,168,287-291,372-374; menu.c:584-597). A file larger than the respective buffer therefore makes a local backend write beyond the destination before the caller can parse or reject the returned length. The affected paths include kernel images, menu files, initrds and modules; the exact outcome depends on which loader mode and backend is used.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 with DOS, SFS, ext2 or CD boot media containing a file larger than the selected caller's buffer. The active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the capacity-free interface, fixed-size callers and full-length local copies; trigger requires a file exceeding the particular buffer. Add a capacity argument and reject files larger than the caller's destination before copying. No large file or boot was used; source-only.

<a id="ek536"></a>
### EK536 — The Parthenope CD backend reports missing or failed file loads as success.

fs_cdrom_find_file() returns zero when it cannot find a path, including when a directory-record read fails; it sets a positive file size when an entry is found (arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:273-275,303-312,417-435). fs_cdrom_load_file() initializes size to zero, calls cdrom_read() only for a positive found size, ignores cdrom_read()'s negative error return, then returns size unchanged (cdrom.c:116-177,446-456). Thus a missing file is reported as zero rather than a negative load error, and a failed read of a discovered nonempty file is reported as a successful positive byte count.

The selected callers use these results inconsistently. The kernel path rejects only negative values, so a missing file's zero result continues to format probes on the allocated but unwritten kernel buffer (parthenope.c:372-379). AROS module loading likewise rejects only negative results, so a positive failed read reaches load_elf_file() with incomplete contents (parthenope.c:184-192). The menu loader treats zero as a miss and tries its alternate menu paths, but a positive failed read enters the parser with incomplete contents (menu.c:584-598). Linux initrd status handling is separately recorded in EK9235 and is not duplicated here.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 using its CD backend; trigger is a missing kernel/module path or a block-read failure after a nonempty file was found. The active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for zero/positive status propagation and caller behavior; actual block-read failure depends on the firmware device callback. Return a negative status for missing/read failures and propagate cdrom_read() errors. No media, firmware callback, or boot was exercised; source-only.

<a id="ek537"></a>
### EK537 — The CD path splitter writes past its fixed component array for deep menu paths.

fs_cdrom_find_file() allocates a local elements array with ISO9660_MAX_DEPTH + 1 entries; ISO9660_MAX_DEPTH is eight, so it has nine pointer slots (arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:39,273-278). It stores the first component, then adds one pointer for every slash without checking depth (cdrom.c:294-300). A path with ten components has nine separators, so the last insertion writes elements[9] past the array. The later traversal loops to depth and reads the out-of-range pointer as another path component (cdrom.c:306 onward), risking stack corruption or a fault during lookup.

The sole caller is fs_cdrom_load_file(), which passes filenames through from Parthenope's boot-device callback (cdrom.c:446-456). Those filenames come from menu entries and include kernel, initrd and module paths; menu discovery also uses this callback (parthenope.c:129-132,184-192,372-379; menu.c:584-598). **Affected configuration and trigger:** explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 using the CD backend with a configured file path of ten or more components. The active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the out-of-bounds pointer write at ten components; whether adjacent stack state causes a visible fault or wrong lookup depends on compiler layout. Reject paths deeper than the supported maximum before appending components. No path or boot was run; source-only.

<a id="ek541"></a>
### EK541 — AArch64 secondary-start failure leaves Exec and the processor resource using dense CPU IDs for a sparse online set.

The BCM27xx AArch64 startup iterates secondary IDs 1 through 3 and continues to later IDs after a PSCI `CPU_ON` error or a startup timeout (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/platform_bcm27xx.c:362-428`). A core that registers sets its numbered bit in `ARMI_AffinityMask` (`kernel_cpu.c:323-330`), while `KrnGetCPUCount()` returns the population count, not the highest ID plus one (`getcpucount.c:11-22`). If CPU 1 fails and CPU 2 registers, the online mask is `{0,2}` but the reported count is 2.

Selected consumers treat that population count as a dense ID range. The generic `processor.resource` initializer creates topology entries 0 and 1 for count 2 (`rom/processor/init.c:27-49`). AArch64 does not select the ARM-specific `Processor_Init()` probe: that manifest builds only `raspi-arm` and `raspi-armeb` (`arch/arm-native/processor/mmakefile.src:7-21`). Exec's AArch64 `Exec_ARMCPUInit()` likewise creates affinity-pinned idle tasks for IDs 0 and 1 and stores them at those array indices (`arch/aarch64-native/exec/platform_init.c:39-99`). `SetTaskAffinity()` and `TaskTag_CPUAffinity` query only IDs 0 through count-1 (`rom/task/SetTaskAffinity.c:83-121`; `rom/task/QueryTaskTagList.c:141-150`), while `KrnGetCPUMask()` sets the requested numeric bit (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/getcpumask.c:14-24`). Consequently CPU 1 can be accepted as an affinity target although it is offline, while online CPU 2 is omitted from the public topology and cannot be selected through the ordinary affinity API. The CPU-load lookup also finds no idle-task record for CPU 2 and returns zero (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/getsystemattr.c:32-44`).

**Affected configuration and trigger:** AArch64 BCM27xx Raspberry Pi ExecSMP, when CPU 1 startup fails or times out but a later CPU (for example CPU 2) successfully registers. **Confidence:** high for the population-count/dense-ID mismatch and its topology, affinity, idle-task and load-query consequences; the sparse online set requires the stated startup outcome. Track online CPU IDs separately from their population count, and iterate actual registered IDs in these consumers. No boot, PSCI failure, affinity operation or CPU-load query was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek543"></a>
### EK543 — The Sam440 SFS boot reader leaks directory, extent-tree and root-object allocations.

The Sam440 Parthenope SFS reader retains heap buffers that have no matching release. `sfs_findobject()` allocates one block-sized buffer for each directory search and returns an object pointer into that buffer when it finds a match (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/sfs.c:73-101`). Path traversal replaces `root` with each matched directory object without releasing the prior directory buffer (`:105-129`); the final matched object buffer is also never released after `sfs_loadfile()` copies the file. The checksum-error return from `sfs_findobject()` additionally skips `free(buffer)`.

`get_bnode()` allocates a block buffer for each extent-tree lookup and returns a `BNode *` into it (`:131-163`). `sfs_loadfile()` uses the returned node to read `blocks` and `next`, but neither function releases that tree buffer (`:165-195`), so each extent lookup leaks one block. At construction, `sfs_create()` copies the root object into a separate allocation (`:237-242`), but `sfs_destroy()` frees only the device structure and not `this->root` (`:198-202`). The checked menu path calls `destroy()` after scanning a device (`menu.c:615-628`); kernel boot also destroys the chosen device on its normal return path (`parthenope.c:372-383`). Those calls do not reclaim the retained root, directory, or extent-tree allocations.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 using the SFS backend; repeated path lookups, directory traversal, or loading files with one or more extent-tree lookups accumulate leaked memory, including during menu discovery across SFS partitions. The active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` target depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`); this path is selected when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the unreleased allocations; exhaustion depends on lookup count and available bootloader memory. Give lookup buffers explicit ownership and release them after consumers finish, and free the copied root in `sfs_destroy()`. No disk image, allocation, or boot was used; source-only.

<a id="ek544"></a>
### EK544 — A missing SFS extent-tree node is dereferenced by the file loader.

`get_bnode()` can return `NULL`: it starts with a null result and returns it when the selected B-tree block fails checksum validation, when no node key is less than or equal to the requested key, or when the block-read loop ends without finding a node (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/sfs.c:131-163`). `sfs_loadfile()` does not check that result before dereferencing `sebn->blocks` and later `sebn->next` (`:181-193`). A missing extent key, corrupt tree block, or failed tree-block read therefore turns a recoverable lookup/read failure into a null-pointer dereference during file loading.

The filesystem abstraction forwards sector reads through the boot context (`context.c:98-102`), and the same `sfs_loadfile()` callback is used for menu discovery and kernel/module loads (`menu.c:590-598`; `parthenope.c:184-191,290-303,372-379`). Thus malformed SFS extent metadata or an I/O error in the extent-tree lookup can fault the optional bootloader while loading a menu, kernel, or module instead of returning a file-load error. `get_bnode()`'s retained lookup buffer is separately tracked as the leak in EK543; unchecked allocation failure is separately tracked as EK9913.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 using the SFS backend, when a file's extent-tree lookup has no qualifying node or its tree block is invalid/unreadable. The active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` target depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`); this path is selected when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked null dereference; reaching `NULL` requires inconsistent/corrupt metadata or a failed tree-block read. Check the lookup result and propagate a load error before reading node fields. No disk image, read error, or boot was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek545"></a>
### EK545 — The Sam440 SFS loader reports a truncated file as a successful positive-length read.

`SfsObject.file.size` supplies the requested byte count, but `sfs_loadfile()` stops when either that count is reached or the extent chain reaches block zero (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/sfs.c:172-195`). If the chain ends early, it returns `readed` unchanged as a positive count. No check compares `readed` with the stored file size before success is reported. This is distinct from EK544: here each extent lookup can succeed and the chain terminates normally, but describes fewer blocks than the file's recorded size.

Selected callers treat any nonnegative return as success. Menu discovery parses any positive prefix as a menu (`menu.c:590-598`); the OS4 loader allocates a module using the returned short length, copies that many bytes and passes it onward (`parthenope.c:290-303`). The main kernel path rejects only negative results before dispatching the image to boot-format handlers (`:369-380`). Thus a truncated SFS file can be accepted as loaded data; for OS4 modules the recorded module size is explicitly shortened to the incomplete byte count. Other format-specific handlers may reject some truncated images, so no universal successful boot claim is made.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 using the SFS backend, with a file whose metadata size exceeds the data reachable through its extent chain. The active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` target depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`); this path is selected when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high that early chain exhaustion returns a positive short count and selected callers accept it; the underlying inconsistent file metadata is the trigger. Require the final byte count to equal the declared size and report truncation as an error. No disk image or boot was used; source-only.

<a id="ek546"></a>
### EK546 — SFS boot-device construction dereferences three unchecked allocations.

`sfs_create()` performs three allocations without checking any result (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/sfs.c:210-242`). If the device-structure allocation fails, the next statement writes `boot->partition`. If the 32 KiB initial buffer allocation fails, its NULL pointer is passed to `loadsector()` and then read as the SFS root block. If the copied root-object allocation fails, `memmove()` writes to NULL. Each low-memory case can fault while probing a partition.

Both selected factory paths call `sfs_create()` after `dos_create()` returns NULL and only try `ext2_create()` if the SFS factory returns normally with NULL (`parthenope.c:348-359`; `menu.c:605-618`). These unchecked failures therefore bypass the intended backend fallback. The allocator is the context-provided bootloader allocator (`context.c:118-123`).

**Affected configuration and trigger:** explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 when SFS probing follows a failed DOS probe and any of the three allocations fails. The active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` target depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`); this path is selected when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked NULL uses and fallback ordering; occurrence requires allocation failure at the corresponding stage. Check each allocation and unwind before dereferencing or copying. No allocation failure, disk image or boot was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek550"></a>
### EK550 — The m68k `OpenLibrary` thunk ignores the requested minimum version for disk-loaded libraries.

The m68k Exec vector passes the requested minimum library version in D0 (`rom/exec/exec.conf:165`; `rom/exec/openlibrary.c:23-27`). The selected manual thunk reads A1 for the name but never reads D0; after fake-library lookup fails, it calls `M68KEmu_LoadM68KLibrary(ctx, name)` and returns any nonzero base (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:68-84`). The loader reads the disk library's Resident version and stores it in the emulated `lib_Version` field, but does not compare it with the requested minimum (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_m68klib.c:170-172`). Therefore, a library below the caller's requested version is still returned as if `OpenLibrary()` succeeded. Guest code can then call vectors or access fields introduced after that older version, producing incorrect behavior or a guest-side fault.

The candidate is limited to the disk fallback: fake generated-library lookup returns before the fallback and is a separate behavior. The m68kemu module is explicitly available for x86-64, AArch64 and RISC-V hosted targets, and is not selected on m68k (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:8-17,40-44`). **Trigger and consequence:** an emulated guest requests a minimum version greater than the `lib_Version` of a library found in `LIBS68K:`, `LIBS:m68k/` or `LIBS:`; the thunk returns that older library instead of NULL. **Affected configuration:** an explicitly built m68kemu library on one of its listed hosted targets, with a guest that uses disk-library fallback. **Confidence:** high for the discarded D0 value and missing version comparison; requires an older fallback library and a caller relying on the minimum-version contract. Pass the requested version through the fallback and reject incompatible library bases. No guest library or binary was loaded; source-only.



<a id="ek551"></a>
### EK551 — Repeated m68k `OpenLibrary` calls reload disk libraries into separate bases.

`thunk_exec_OpenLibrary()` first calls `M68KEmu_OpenLibrary()`, which checks the context's fake-library name map and generated library list; when neither matches, the thunk calls `M68KEmu_LoadM68KLibrary()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:37-84`). The disk loader parses the file and allocates a new set of hunks and a new emulated jump table on each call, then returns the new base without registering its name in `ctx->libs` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_m68klib.c:27-68,145-178`; hunk allocation in `m68kemu_memory.c`). Therefore a second open of the same disk-only library repeats the file load and returns another base. The `CloseLibrary` thunk does nothing (`m68kemu_thunks.c:93-96`), so neither close nor a matching later open reclaims or reuses those copies. Repeated guest open/close cycles can consume the finite emulation heap until later allocations fail.

This finding is restricted to disk-loaded libraries: generated fake libraries are in the context map and are returned by name. The m68kemu module is explicitly available for x86-64, AArch64 and RISC-V hosted targets and is not selected on m68k (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:8-17,40-44`). **Trigger and consequence:** an emulated guest repeatedly opens a library that is absent from the generated fake-library set but available through `LIBS68K:`, `LIBS:m68k/` or `LIBS:`; each open loads another copy, and close leaves it resident until context teardown. **Affected configuration:** explicit hosted m68kemu builds using disk-library fallback. **Confidence:** high for lack of disk-library caching/registration, repeated allocations and no-op close; exhaustion depends on guest call count, library size and arena capacity. Cache disk libraries by name with open counts and release/unload their hunks when the last reference closes, or explicitly retain one shared copy per context. No guest library or repeated open was run; source-only.



<a id="ek552"></a>
### EK552 — The m68k disk-library loader returns AUTOINIT libraries without applying their initialization data or initializer.

For an AUTOINIT resident, `M68KEmu_LoadM68KLibrary()` reads the initialization table's `dataSize`, `funcTable`, `dataInit` and `initFunc` fields (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_m68klib.c:116-123`). It allocates the library base and writes jump-table entries, `lib_Version` and `ln_Name`, but never applies `dataInit` or invokes `initFunc` before returning the base (`:139-178`). The OpenLibrary thunk accepts that base as a successful disk-library open (`m68kemu_thunks.c:77-82`). Thus an AUTOINIT library whose data table or initializer establishes required fields/state is exposed to guest code without those required initialization steps; its functions may use absent configuration or invariants and return incorrect results or fault.

This applies only to the disk-library fallback. Generated fake libraries have separate setup logic, and non-AUTOINIT residents are explicitly rejected. The m68kemu module is an optional library for x86-64, AArch64 and RISC-V hosted targets, not m68k (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:8-17,40-44`). **Trigger and consequence:** a guest opens an AUTOINIT library found through the m68k disk paths whose `dataInit` or `initFunc` performs required setup; the loader returns its base without that setup. **Affected configuration:** explicit hosted m68kemu builds using disk-library fallback. **Confidence:** high that both table fields are read but neither operation is applied; the visible failure depends on the library requiring that initialization. Implement the AUTOINIT data and function initialization, or reject unsupported nontrivial tables instead of returning a usable base. No guest library or binary was loaded; source-only.

<a id="ek553"></a>
### EK553 — Rejected m68k disk libraries retain their successfully loaded hunk allocations until the emulation context ends.

`M68KEmu_LoadM68KLibrary()` first loads a syntactically accepted hunk file into the context heap. If subsequent Resident/AUTOINIT admission fails, it returns zero without releasing those successfully loaded hunk blocks: rejection includes no Resident match, unsupported non-AUTOINIT, missing function table, empty function table, or failure to allocate the library base (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_m68klib.c:66-178`). The guest OpenLibrary thunk reports failure for that attempt, but the hunk blocks remain allocated and unavailable to later guest loads (`m68kemu_thunks.c:77-84`; `m68kemu_memory.c:62-104`). Repeated attempts with rejected but parseable libraries can consume the finite context heap and cause unrelated later allocations or library loads to fail.

The lower-level hunk parser does free partially allocated blocks when parsing itself fails (`m68kemu_memory.c:270-390`); the leak is specifically the successful-parser / failed-library-admission path. All context memory is reclaimed when the emulation context is destroyed, so this is bounded to the guest run rather than a host-lifetime leak (`:55-60`; `m68kemu_run.c:171-181,224-231`). **Trigger and consequence:** a guest opens a parseable disk library whose loaded hunks do not contain a supported Resident/AUTOINIT layout, or the loader rejects it after hunk loading; repeated attempts retain those hunks until context teardown. **Affected configuration:** explicit hosted m68kemu builds using disk-library fallback. **Confidence:** high for the post-parse return paths lacking `M68KEmu_HeapFree()` and eventual whole-context cleanup; exhaustion depends on rejected library sizes and retry count. Track the loaded hunk addresses and release them on each post-parse rejection. No guest library or binary was loaded; source-only.

<a id="ek554"></a>
### EK554 — An overflowing AUTOINIT size sum can make the m68k library loader allocate less space than it writes.

The loader bounds the function-table scan at 1,000 entries, so `jt_size = numFuncs * 6` is at most 6,000 bytes; however, it adds that value to the 32-bit Resident `dataSize` without overflow checking (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_m68klib.c:135-151`). If the addition wraps, the small `total` is passed to `M68KEmu_HeapAlloc()`, which allocates only that many bytes (plus its internal header; `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_memory.c:62-95`). The loader then sets `base = region + jt_size` and writes the full jump table in the range beginning at `region`, followed by library fields at `base` (`m68kemu_m68klib.c:153-177`). The `m68k_write16/32()` helpers enforce only the full arena bound, not the allocated block boundary (`m68kemu_intern.h:149-164`).

A malformed disk library with `dataSize` near the 32-bit limit can therefore make a small allocation succeed while these writes extend beyond it, corrupting other guest allocations or the reserved guest-stack area within the containment arena. The source does not establish host-memory access through these helpers, so this finding is limited to guest-arena boundary corruption and resulting emulator/guest-state failure. **Trigger and consequence:** a disk-loaded AUTOINIT library advertises a sufficiently large `dataSize` such that `dataSize + jt_size` wraps to a small nonzero value; jump-table and base-field writes then exceed the allocated block. **Affected configuration:** explicit hosted m68kemu builds using disk-library fallback with malformed library input. **Confidence:** high for unchecked 32-bit addition, bounded function count, small-size allocation and allocation-boundary-unchecked writes; exploitability or host impact is not claimed. Reject overflow before allocation and validate that the whole jump table and base fit the allocated block. No malformed library or guest was loaded; source-only.

<a id="ek555"></a>
### EK555 — The m68k KOBJ wildcard places Resident end markers before module read-only data.

The selected Amiga-m68k KOBJ linker script emits `.text.romtag`, then `*(.text .text.* .stub)`, then `.rodata`, and finally a dedicated `*(.text.moduleend)` rule (`arch/m68k-amiga/boot/kobj-romtag.ld:28-37`). The earlier `.text.*` wildcard also matches `.text.moduleend`, so it consumes that input section before the dedicated rule. The generated End object is appended after ordinary module objects by the KOBJ recipe (`config/make.tmpl:2609,2763`); its marker is emitted in `.text.moduleend` (`tools/genmodule/writeend.c:21-30`). Selected manual Resident tags also point to markers in that section, including CIA and the alert hook (`arch/m68k-amiga/cia/cia_init.c:82-98`; `rom/alerthook/alerthook.c:38-52`).

The KOBJ script folds each input `.rodata` section into its output `.text` after the wildcard. The Amiga ROM link then places each KOBJ object's `.text` before its `.rodata` (`arch/m68k-amiga/boot/mmakefile.src:225-264`), so `rt_EndSkip` points before the folded read-only bytes rather than at the module tail. `krnScanResident()` resumes two words before `rt_EndSkip`, then advances through the marker and subsequent contents while searching for the next Resident (`rom/kernel/kernel_romtags.c:263-278`). The guaranteed effect is that the scanner still walks module read-only data that the KOBJ marker is intended to skip. If those bytes contain a Resident-shaped record with a matching self-pointer, the scanner may accept it; no such checked-in match or boot failure has been established.

**Trigger and consequence:** the selected Amiga-m68k KOBJ link includes a module with `.text.moduleend` and folded `.rodata`; its Resident scan continues through the module's read-only data. Matching data could be mistaken for a Resident, but that consequence is conditional and unobserved. **Affected configuration:** `AROS_TARGET_ARCH=amiga`, `AROS_TARGET_CPU=m68k`, for modules linked with `KERNEL_KOBJ_LDSCRIPT` (`config/make.cfg.in:212-220`; `config/make.tmpl:2175,2763`). **Confidence:** high for the wildcard match and marker placement; medium for a false Resident because no matching payload was found. Exclude `.text.moduleend` from the earlier wildcard (or place it in a section name outside `.text.*`) so the dedicated tail rule can collect it after `.rodata`. No KOBJ/ROM link or scan was performed; source-only.

<a id="ek559"></a>
### EK559 — m68k Exec AVL traversal thunks pass guest nodes and comparators to native code without ABI conversion.

The generated Exec thunks for `AVL_FindPrevNodeByAddress()`, `AVL_FindNextNodeByAddress()`, `AVL_FindFirstNode()`, `AVL_FindLastNode()`, `AVL_FindPrevNodeByKey()`, and `AVL_FindNextNodeByKey()` call native functions after applying only `THUNK_PTR()` to guest arguments (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2420-2464`; signatures in `rom/exec/exec.conf:227-233`). That macro uses `m68k_to_host_or_shadow()`, which either resolves a registered shadow or maps a guest address into the emulator containment arena; it does not convert an `AVLNode` layout or wrap a guest comparator (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.h:36-37`; `m68kemu_intern.h:115-125`). There is no AVL-node shadow descriptor in the generated layout table. On the selected 64-bit host builds, guest `AVLNode` stores three 32-bit pointers and a 32-bit balance value (16 bytes), while native `AVLNode` stores three host pointers and a `LONG` balance value (32 bytes) (`compiler/include/exec/avl.h:16-20`; `rom/m68kemu/INTERNALS.md`, “Address Map” and shadow-layout notes). The native AVL walkers therefore interpret guest node bytes at host offsets and may follow invalid pointers. Key-based traversal wrappers also pass a guest comparator address as a native function pointer; native code cannot execute that guest address as a host callback. Any native node pointer returned by the traversal is narrowed directly into the guest's 32-bit D0 by the dispatcher, without `host_to_m68k()` conversion (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:257-275`; conversion helper in `m68kemu_intern.h:128-131`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k guest calls one of the generated AVL address/key traversal vectors with nodes allocated in its containment arena, or uses a guest comparator in a key traversal. The host implementation reads node fields at incompatible offsets, can traverse invalid addresses, and may return a native pointer that is not a valid guest address. Key traversals additionally attempt to call guest code through the native callback ABI. The operation can fail or corrupt the guest's AVL traversal state; exact failure depends on node values, host address layout, and whether the function needs to invoke the comparator.

**Affected configuration:** optional `kernel-m68kemu-library` builds on supported 64-bit hosts. The generated traversal vectors are available through the emulator's generated Exec thunk table; no maintained in-tree guest caller was found, so no default-image or current guest trigger is asserted. The manual zero-return mutation/search stubs are separately recorded under EK52. **Confidence:** high for the missing node/callback/result conversion and 16/32-byte layout mismatch; runtime manifestation was not tested. No guest AVL operation or build was run. Source-only; see the [generated AVL thunk and layout trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L6159).

<a id="ek560"></a>
### EK560 — PowerPC `Supervisor()` drops an already-supervisor caller into user mode on return (conditional wrong-mode return; high source confidence).
