Roll back descriptor edits on failure or make the range operation transactional before reporting failure. No mapping, allocation failure, controller initialization or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8824"></a>
### EK8824 — Concurrent AArch64 global mappings can lose one caller's page-table edits.

`mmu_map_range()` and `mmu_unmap_range()` walk and update shared page tables without serializing the walk. When a partial mapping needs to split an existing L2 block, `mmu_next()` reads the parent descriptor, allocates and fills a new L3 table, then stores its pointer into the parent slot (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/mmu.c:139-161,203-224`). There is no lock or compare-and-swap around that sequence.

If two callers both read the same valid L2 block before either publishes its table, each can allocate a different L3 table initialized with equivalent block mappings. They then store different table pointers into the same L2 slot and write their requested leaf into their respective tables. The later parent-slot store discards the earlier table from the walk. Both range calls can reach `mmu_commit()` and report success, although the mapping held only in the overwritten table is absent from the published page-table tree. The discarded table allocation is also no longer reachable for reclamation.

The Raspberry Pi AArch64 package selects RP1 and PCIe devices whose driver paths call `KrnMapGlobal()` (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/mmakefile.src:160-165`; `arch/arm-native/soc/broadcom/2712/rp1/rp1_pci.c:182-208`; `arch/arm-native/soc/broadcom/2712/hidd/pci-bcm2712/driverclass.c:245-265,327-382`). The same package selects `USBHardware/pcixhci` and the standard/SuperSpeed hub classes (`boot/mmakefile.src:217,226-227`). Each hub class starts a task for its hub (`rom/usb/classes/hub/hub.class.c:105-115`); its task allocates endpoint pipes (`:845-852`), and Poseidon synchronously invokes the HCD `phw_PrepareEndpoint` callback from `psdAllocPipe()` (`rom/usb/poseidon/poseidon.library.c:1673-1695,4468-4643`). The selected xHCI HCD registers `xhciPrepareEndpoint()` for that callback (`rom/usb/pcixhci/uhwcmd.c:595-596`); when an endpoint ring is absent, that path calls `xhciInitEP()` and `pciAllocAligned()` (`xhci_hcd.c:2133-2240`; `pcixhci_arospci.c:474-500`), which reaches the selected PCI HIDD DMA mapping method. `xhciPrepareEndpoint()` does not take the controller's `xhc_DevLock`; the checked lock sites are in disconnect/teardown (`xhci_hcd.c:418-438,2335-2417`). This establishes a maintained path from independent hub tasks to the mapper without per-controller serialization, but not that two calls overlap while splitting the same block or that their allocations occupy the same 2 MiB block. The trigger therefore remains conditional. The AArch64 kernel source also has unresolved build prerequisites under EK8902, so current target buildability is not established.

**Trigger and consequence:** two callers concurrently split the same existing L2 block before either publishes its replacement table, then update different leaf entries. One caller can return success even though its mapping is lost from the published table; the overwritten table allocation is leaked. **Affected configuration:** conditional AArch64 SMP builds using this MMU implementation and concurrent `KrnMapGlobal()`/`KrnUnmapGlobal()` operations on the same L2 block. **Confidence:** high for the unsynchronized publication mechanism; no checked-in caller overlap is established, and current AArch64 target buildability remains unresolved by EK8902. Serialize page-table walks/publication or use an atomic split protocol that preserves both callers' edits. No mapping, concurrency or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8825"></a>
### EK8825 — Genmodule can report success after generated-file output is incomplete.

The selected `genmodule` dispatcher invokes output writers as `void` functions and returns zero after the selected command finishes (`tools/genmodule/genmodule.c:14-90`). Several writers do not check output errors, and writers that call `ferror()` do so before `fclose()` and ignore the close result. For example, `writefd()` exits on pre-close `ferror()` but ignores `fclose(out)` at `:132-139`; `writemakefile()` has the same pattern (`tools/genmodule/writemakefile.c:151-160`). `writeincdefines()` closes its output without checking either `ferror()` or the close result (`tools/genmodule/writeincdefines.c:225-233`). A buffered write that fails only during final flush is therefore not propagated by these paths.

These are consumed by selected build rules: the generated include rule runs `genmodule writeincludes` and then touches its include stamp (`config/make.tmpl:1541-1549`); the module FD rule invokes `writefd` for ABI builds (`:2482-2496`). With a write/flush error, the generator can exit successfully and make can accept or stamp a truncated generated header/FD file. Other generated source and makefile writers have similar unchecked finalization; the `WRITEFUNCLIST` branch is excluded from this selected Exec/kernel finding because it was not established on the `%build_module` path.

**Trigger and consequence:** a selected generated-output command encounters a stream write or final flush/close error. `genmodule` can still return success; the build may consume incomplete generated output, and the include rule may mark incomplete output current. **Affected configuration:** builds using the selected `%build_module` generator rules, including Exec and kernel ABI generation. **Confidence:** high for ignored writer/finalization errors and dispatcher success behavior; the failure requires a filesystem/stream error and no generated-output fault was induced. Check every write and finalization result, return failure to make, and create stamps only after verified output completion. No generator or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8828"></a>
### EK8828 — PC SMP bring-up dereferences a failed per-CPU scheduler-state allocation.

During PC AP startup, `smp_Wake()` obtains the AP's TLS block and then allocates `X86SchedulerPrivate` into its `ScheduleData` field without checking the allocation result (`arch/all-pc/kernel/smp.c:247-253`). It immediately passes that pointer to `core_InitScheduleData()`, which writes `Granularity` and `Quantum` through it (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:55-61`). This occurs before the AP wake request (`smp.c:274-280`).

`smp_Initialize()` calls `smp_Wake()` after successful SMP setup (`arch/all-pc/kernel/smp.c:362-370`). The affected branch is specifically failure of the scheduler-state allocation after a usable TLS block was allocated; a NULL TLS result is a separate failure covered by EK8830. The BSP never reaches the AP wake for this failed scheduler-state allocation.

**Trigger and consequence:** during PC ExecSMP initialization with at least one AP, allocation of `sizeof(struct X86SchedulerPrivate)` fails after the AP TLS allocation succeeds. `core_InitScheduleData(NULL)` writes through NULL before the AP is launched, faulting or halting the bootstrap CPU and interrupting SMP startup. **Affected configuration:** all-PC ExecSMP builds that enter `smp_Wake()` with an AP to start. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked allocation and immediate writes; no allocation failure or AP startup was induced. Check the allocation and abort/roll back AP setup before initializing scheduler state. Keep EK8830's TLS failure and EK8831's ready-lock-array allocation failure separate. Source-only.

<a id="ek8829"></a>
### EK8829 — PC SMP initializes only part of each AP's scheduler state.

`smp_Wake()` allocates each AP's `X86SchedulerPrivate` with `MEMF_PUBLIC` but without `MEMF_CLEAR`, then calls `core_InitScheduleData()` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/smp.c:247-253`). That initializer sets only `Granularity` and `Quantum` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:55-61`). The structure also contains `ScheduleFlags`, `Elapsed`, `IDNestCnt`, and `TDNestCnt` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.h:15-25`). `cpu_BootStrap()` sets `RunningTask`, initializes the APIC, and calls `Permit()` and `Enable()` before creating its idle task (`arch/all-pc/kernel/smp_exec.c:193-229`). The selected PC Exec macros decrement/read the per-CPU nesting counters and inspect the switch flag in these calls (`arch/all-pc/exec/exec_platform.h:82-99,143-159,235-277`). The APIC heartbeat also reads `Elapsed` and can set scheduler flags (`arch/all-pc/kernel/apic_heartbeat.c:134-143`).

Consequently, those fields can be consumed with allocator-residue values before an ordinary task dispatch assigns the per-CPU nesting count and resets quantum state (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:348-356`). The exact effect depends on the prior contents: nesting checks can be wrong, and residual scheduling flags or elapsed ticks can cause an early or delayed scheduling decision. `RunningTask` is explicitly set before the bootstrap calls, so it is not included in this finding. EK8828 remains the separate NULL allocation case.

**Trigger and consequence:** an AP's scheduler-state allocation reuses nonzero contents and the AP reaches its initial `Permit()`/`Enable()` or heartbeat before the affected fields are overwritten. The AP can make interrupt-nesting or scheduling decisions from stale counters/flags/timer state during startup. **Affected configuration:** PC ExecSMP AP startup. **Confidence:** high that the fields are not initialized before these consumers; the concrete effect depends on allocator contents and timing, and no specific boot manifestation was established. Zero the scheduler-state structure or initialize every field before the AP can consume it. No AP startup or memory-pattern case was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8830"></a>
### EK8830 — x86-64 PC SMP does not handle failed per-core GDT or TLS allocation.

The selected PC AP loop stores `PlatformAllocGDT()` and `PlatformAllocTLS()` results without checking them (`arch/all-pc/kernel/smp.c:247-255`). The allocators return NULL on allocation failure, and their address-rounding leaves a NULL result unchanged (`arch/all-pc/kernel/platform_post.c:52-82`).

Two distinct failure paths follow. On an ExecSMP build, if TLS allocation fails, `smp_Wake()` assigns the NULL pointer to `apicTLS` and dereferences it to store `ScheduleData` before sending the AP wake request (`smp.c:249-253`). If GDT allocation fails but TLS and scheduler-state setup succeed, the AP is started and calls `core_SetupGDT()` with a NULL GDT; that routine immediately writes its descriptor fields through `gdtPtr` (`smp.c:86-92`; `arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:672-706`). The AP does not reach the ready-lock release after its bootstrap path (`smp.c:118-145`), so the BSP waits until its readiness timeout before proceeding.

**Trigger and consequence:** on x86-64 PC SMP, the per-AP TLS allocation fails in an ExecSMP build, causing a NULL dereference in the BSP before the AP is launched; or the per-AP GDT allocation fails, causing the AP to dereference NULL during descriptor setup and miss the ready handshake. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC SMP; the TLS dereference applies to ExecSMP builds, while the GDT use is in the 64-bit AP entry. **Confidence:** high for each unchecked result and its immediate consumer; no allocation failure or AP startup was induced. Check both allocation results and report the AP as failed before publishing or launching it. This is distinct from EK8828's `ScheduleData` allocation failure and EK8831's ready-lock-array allocation failure. Source-only.

<a id="ek8831"></a>
### EK8831 — PC SMP leaves the AP-ready lock array unchecked and unreleased.

`smp_Wake()` allocates a per-AP ready-lock array without checking the result, then immediately initializes the first AP's lock (`arch/all-pc/kernel/smp.c:228-245`). The selected PC `KrnSpinInit()` writes `lock->lock` and `lock->s_Owner` without a NULL check (`arch/all-pc/kernel/spininit.c:16-27`). This path is reached only when `apic_count > 1` and `smp_Initialize()` enters `smp_Wake()` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/smp.c:321-374`). Thus array-allocation failure faults the bootstrap CPU during AP setup, before the first AP wake.

On the successful path, `smp_Wake()` returns after all AP iterations without freeing or publishing the array (`:283-318`). When every AP has acknowledged its ready lock, no later user of those handshake locks is established, leaving one bounded array allocated for the rest of the boot. The timeout/error path is excluded from this leak claim because an AP that acknowledges late may still access its lock storage.

**Trigger and consequence:** with more than one discovered CPU, allocation of `sizeof(spinlock_t) * apic_count` fails and the first `KrnSpinInit(NULL)` writes through NULL; independently, when every AP acknowledges, the ready-lock array remains allocated after its final use. **Affected configuration:** PC SMP initialization with at least one AP. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked allocation, selected initializer writes, and success-path lack of release; no allocation failure or AP startup was induced. Check the allocation before entering the loop and release the array after all APs have acknowledged and no shared trampoline reference remains. No AP, timeout or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8839"></a>
### EK8839 — ARM32 Raspberry Pi high-window virtual-to-physical conversion uses tag-record addresses instead of tag values (conditional incorrect physical address).

`arch/arm-native/kernel/virtualtophysical.c:22-29` returns low addresses unchanged, but for addresses at or above `0xf8000000` it obtains `lowest` and `physlowest` with `krnFindTagItem()` and uses those pointers as address bases. `krnFindTagItem()` returns the address of the matching `TagItem` (`arch/arm-native/kernel/tags.c:41-52`); the corresponding helper `krnGetTagData()` reads `ti_Data` (`:55-67`). The ARM Raspberry Pi bootloader maps the kernel at `KERNEL_VIRT_ADDRESS` (`0xf8000000`) while retaining its physical load address, and places those distinct values in `KRN_KernelLowest` and `KRN_KernelPhysLowest` boot-tag data (`arch/arm-raspi/boot/include/boot.h:19`; `boot.c:586-603`). Therefore a high-window input is translated using the addresses of the two tag records instead of their virtual and physical base values, producing an incorrect physical address.

**Trigger and consequence:** an ARM32 Raspberry Pi caller invokes `KrnVirtualToPhysical()` with an address in the high-mapped kernel range. The returned address is not the corresponding physical address; a caller that submits it to a DMA engine or physical mapping operation can target the wrong memory. `CachePreDMA()` is a selected ARM-native caller and returns this translation (`arch/arm-native/exec/cachepredma.c:20-35`). The checked-in SD-card ADMA path also calls the translator, but its descriptor and bounce allocations are explicitly constrained below 2 GiB (`rom/devs/sdcard/sdcard_bus.c:668-690`), so that path does not establish this trigger. Other checked ARM callers translate allocator-supplied buffers, but this source review did not establish that those allocations occupy the high kernel window. **Affected configuration:** ARM32 Raspberry Pi images using the `arm-raspi` boot mapping with the `arm-native` kernel implementation; only high-window inputs take the faulty branch. **Confidence:** high that the branch uses TagItem record addresses and conflicts with the selected boot-tag values; conditional for a current in-tree caller supplying an address in that range. No DMA, physical mapping, boot, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8845"></a>
### EK8845 — ExecSMP child cleanup can reuse a parent link cached before `ChildOrphan()`.

`Exec_CleanupETask()` tests `et->et_Parent` and caches the corresponding parent ETask before it acquires that parent's `iet_TaskLock` (`rom/exec/exec_util.c:271-275,314-322`). `ChildOrphan()` takes the same lock, clears the child's `et_Parent`, and either removes that child (`rom/exec/childorphan.c:86-105`) or clears all parent pointers and resets the children list (`:66-84`). On ExecSMP, `Forbid()` prevents scheduling only on the local processor (`rom/exec/forbid.c:58-60`), so another CPU can complete this orphan operation after cleanup cached `parent` but before cleanup obtains the parent's lock.

Cleanup does not recheck `et->et_Parent` after acquiring that lock. It unconditionally removes the ETask and, for an `NT_PROCESS` with `PRF_NOTIFYONDEATH`, adds it to the cached parent's child-message list; after releasing the lock it signals the port's task when present (`exec_util.c:314-329`). Thus the exit is still reported through the former parent after `ChildOrphan()` has detached the child, contrary to the API's stated purpose of suppressing further child events (`rom/exec/childorphan.c:23-40`).

The single-child branch has an additional conditional list effect: the `Remove()`/`REMOVE()` operations leave the detached node's `ln_Pred` and `ln_Succ` values intact (`rom/exec/remove.c:55-60`; `compiler/include/exec/lists.h:136-145`). `Exec_InitETask()` adds a newly created child at the head under the same parent lock (`exec_util.c:217-229`). If the orphaned child was the old head and a new child is inserted before cleanup repeats `REMOVE(et)`, the detached node's stale predecessor still points to the list head and its stale successor to the former next child; the repeated removal writes the old successor back into the head, bypassing the new child while leaving that child's `et_Parent` set. This requires the intervening task creation and is not claimed for every double removal.

**Trigger and consequence:** ExecSMP is enabled; child cleanup caches a non-NULL parent; the parent concurrently calls `ChildOrphan()` for that child or all children; then cleanup proceeds using the cached pointer. If the exiting process has `NP_NotifyOnDeath`/`PRF_NOTIFYONDEATH`, cleanup can enqueue and signal an exit notification despite the orphan call. If a new child is inserted at the head in the single-child ordering above, the repeated removal can bypass it in the parent list. **Affected configuration:** ExecSMP builds with an external or indirect `ChildOrphan()` caller; the public vector is declared in `rom/exec/exec.conf:200`, but no maintained direct C caller was found. **Confidence:** high for the cached-parent/recheck omission and notification path; the interleaving requires concurrent CPUs, and the sibling-loss consequence additionally requires a list change between removals. No task exit, orphan operation, or SMP schedule was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8861"></a>
### EK8861 — The OpenSBI early FDT parser trusts the string-block offset and property-name offsets.

`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_fdt.c` checks only the FDT magic before deriving `strings` from `off_dt_strings` (`:91-97`). It does not validate that this offset and `size_dt_strings` lie within `totalsize`. For every property token it also forms `pname = strings + nameoff` without checking `nameoff` against the string-table size (`:129-145`). The resulting pointer is compared against property literals by `str_eq()` (`:42-46`), which reads through the compared literal's length; a bad offset can therefore cause reads outside the string block and potentially outside the DTB, or make the parser classify a property from unrelated bytes. The code has no string-table error return before those reads.

`krnParseFDT()` is compiled into the selected OpenSBI kernel (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/mmakefile.src:26`) and is called during early startup; a false return selects the EFI/default memory fallback, but invalid string offsets do not cause that return (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:515-568`). The same unchecked `strings + nameoff` derivation is used by `krnDumpFDT()` (`kernel_fdt.c:320-323,359-377`), which compares and prints every property name. The early parser can skip reading the name of an unrelated property under a deeper node, but the diagnostic dump reads it; startup invokes that dump when the parsed bootargs match `dumpdt` (`kernel_startup.c:641-645`). **Trigger and consequence:** OpenSBI supplies a malformed or truncated FDT with an invalid strings-block offset or property `nameoff`. The early parser may read outside the supplied blob, fault before fallback, or consume an unrelated byte sequence as a property name and derive incorrect boot metadata. An invalid name offset on an otherwise ignored property can also fault in the optional pre-MMU `dumpdt` walk. **Affected configuration:** the build-selected RISC-V OpenSBI kernel when its firmware-provided FDT has inconsistent string-table extents or offsets; the diagnostic-only route additionally requires `dumpdt` in bootargs. **Confidence:** high that the offsets/extents are unchecked and both readers dereference the derived pointer; the resulting fault or metadata effect depends on the malformed blob and adjacent address mapping. No malformed FDT, boot, or dump was exercised. Source-only. This finding is limited to property-name string-table validation; other token/node/property extent issues remain separate candidates.

<a id="ek8862"></a>
### EK8862 — OpenSBI EFI retry can hand the kernel a stale memory-region snapshot.

`efi_stub_entry()` obtains the initial map size, allocates a buffer with eight descriptor slots of extra capacity, then successfully reads the map and passes it to `efi_collect_memory()`/`efi_collect_firmware()` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/efi_stub.c:838-853`). On success, UEFI writes the actual returned map size back through `MemoryMapSize`; the stub does not retain the larger allocation capacity separately. If the first `ExitBootServices()` fails, the retry calls `GetMemoryMap()` with that actual size as the input buffer capacity, ignores the status, and immediately calls `ExitBootServices()` again (`:864-869`). If the map has grown beyond the prior actual size, `GetMemoryMap()` can return `EFI_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL`; no refreshed map/key is then established, yet the stub proceeds to retry shutdown and returns `EFIERR(9)` if that call fails. UEFI specifies that `MemoryMapSize` is in/out, reports the required size on `EFI_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL`, and that the map key is returned on success; the current key is required for `ExitBootServices()` ([UEFI 2.10 `GetMemoryMap`](https://uefi.org/specs/UEFI/2.10/07_Services_Boot_Services.html#efi-boot-servicesgetmemorymap), [UEFI 2.10 `ExitBootServices`](https://uefi.org/specs/UEFI/2.10/07_Services_Boot_Services.html#efi-boot-servicesexitbootservices)).

Separately, if the retry map read succeeds, the stub still does not rerun either collector. The kernel later prefers `__efi_regions` when publishing allocator memory ranges (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:575-608`) and uses `__efi_fwregions` to map firmware/ACPI areas (`kernel_mmu.c:435-445`); both arrays therefore continue to describe the pre-failure snapshot. A changed map can leave usable ranges omitted or stale firmware/ACPI classifications and mappings handed to the kernel.

**Trigger and consequence:** on the selected RISC-V OpenSBI UEFI boot path, the first `ExitBootServices()` fails. If the refreshed map is larger than the previous successful map, the retry uses an undersized capacity, ignores `EFI_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL`, and can abort the boot on the second exit attempt. If refresh succeeds but descriptor ranges/types changed, the kernel receives stale allocator/firmware-region arrays, which can omit RAM or leave firmware tables unmapped. **Affected configuration:** the RISC-V OpenSBI core image booted through UEFI; `efi_stub.c` is selected in `arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/mmakefile.src:20-44`. **Confidence:** high for both unchecked retry behaviors and their consumers; whether a given firmware's failed first exit grows or materially changes the map is conditional and was not observed. No UEFI firmware, boot, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8863"></a>
### EK8863 — OpenSBI can leave later EFI ACPI/runtime regions unmapped after its firmware-range table fills (conditional boot-time mapping fault; high source confidence).

`efi_collect_firmware()` stores at most 24 nonempty, non-coalesced EFI descriptors of types runtime code/data and ACPI reclaim/NVS (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/efi_stub.c:287-290,526-556`). Its loop terminates as soon as the 24-entry count is reached, silently skipping every later qualifying descriptor. When the EFI configuration table supplies an ACPI RSDP, `krnInitMMU()` maps only the retained `__efi_fwregions` entries (`kernel_mmu.c:435-445`). Later, if the FDT did not provide a PLIC base, kernel startup calls `krnACPIPLICInfo()` after enabling that MMU (`kernel_startup.c:659-668`); the ACPI parser follows the RSDP/XSDT/RSDT to find the MADT (`kernel_acpi.c:265-302,320-330`). A table in a skipped region may therefore be inaccessible after the MMU switch and fault the boot-time ACPI lookup, unless it happens to be covered by another mapping. The ACPI dump option runs before MMU setup and is not itself evidence of this post-switch fault.

**Trigger and consequence:** a UEFI memory map contains more than 24 non-coalesced, nonempty runtime/ACPI descriptors, and a later omitted region contains an ACPI root or table needed after MMU setup (in particular, the MADT when the FDT has no PLIC description). The fixed array truncates that region; a later ACPI lookup can fault on its unmapped address and prevent interrupt-controller initialization. **Affected configuration:** RISC-V OpenSBI core image booted through UEFI with an EFI RSDP and the described fragmented firmware map; the behavior is conditional on the skipped table and whether another mapping covers it. **Confidence:** high that qualifying descriptors after the cap are dropped and only retained entries are mapped; conditional for a current firmware's descriptor fragmentation and for the omitted table's later use. No EFI map, MMU transition, ACPI lookup, or boot was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8864"></a>
### EK8864 — RISC-V OpenSBI drops usable EFI RAM ranges after the eighth.

The EFI stub coalesces adjacent usable descriptors but can retain up to 16 disjoint ranges in `__efi_regions` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/efi_stub.c:299-302,481-520`). Startup copies only the first `KRN_MAX_MEMREGIONS` entries, which is eight, into `fdtinfo.regions` (`kernel_intern.h:108,123`; `kernel_startup.c:581-595`). The MMU maps only `fdtinfo.mem_base..mem_base+mem_size` plus those retained additional regions (`kernel_mmu.c:374-397`), and after Exec starts, startup uses the same list to create additional MemHeaders (`kernel_startup.c:934-1015`). Thus any usable EFI ranges after the eighth are neither mapped as extra banks nor made allocatable, even though the stub collected them.

**Trigger and consequence:** the UEFI map contains at least nine nonempty, non-coalesced usable ranges within the first 16 ranges retained by the stub. Ranges after the eighth are silently absent from `fdtinfo.regions`; memory in those banks is omitted from the additional-bank mappings and Exec MemList, reducing available RAM and making those ranges inaccessible through the normal allocator. The earliest/largest primary range can still be mapped through `mem_base/mem_size`; this finding concerns the remaining banks. **Affected configuration:** the RISC-V OpenSBI core image booted through UEFI, with a fragmented EFI map that exceeds the kernel's eight-region capacity after coalescing. **Confidence:** high that the stub can collect 16 while startup processes only eight and uses that list for mapping/allocation; actual lost capacity depends on firmware presenting more than eight distinct usable ranges. No EFI map, allocator, MMU setup, or boot was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8866"></a>
### EK8866 — SMP `TaskLaunch()` publishes a task before launch setup is complete

The task.resource `NewAddTask()` wrapper gives Exec a prelaunch hook that allocates a `TaskListEntry` and stores the child pointer (`rom/task/task_execfuncs.c:20-43,48-88`). In the SMP `TaskLaunch()` path, Exec first publishes the task as ready through `krnSysCallReschedTask()` and reenables local interrupts, then invokes the hook (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:25-70,118-123`). The ready task can therefore run on another eligible CPU before the creator reaches the hook. If it exits, the task.resource `RemTask()` wrapper searches the new/task lists, finds no entry yet, and then calls Exec's removal path (`rom/task/task_execfuncs.c:96-179`). Exec can reclaim the removed task asynchronously through its service-task cleanup (`rom/exec/remtask.c:135-141`; `rom/exec/service.c:73-90`). The creator can subsequently reach `TaskRes_PreLaunch()` and publish the now-freed task pointer. `NextTaskEntry()` dereferences `tle_Task->tc_State` while iterating (`rom/task/NextTaskEntry.c:82-92`). The same interval leaves `TaskLaunch()` itself using the published task: after `krnSysCallReschedTask()` makes it ready and local interrupts are re-enabled, the creator continues reading task fields for the CPU-affinity and priority decisions, then invokes the prelaunch hook (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:25-70,90-102`). If the child removes itself on the eligible remote CPU and the service task reclaims it before those reads, the creator can also dereference the freed task directly.

**Trigger and consequence:** on an ExecSMP configuration, a newly created task is eligible on another CPU, starts and removes itself before the creator finishes `TaskLaunch()`, and the service task reclaims its TCB before the creator's later task-field reads. The creator can dereference freed memory during `TaskLaunch()`; this consequence does not require task.resource. If task.resource's NewAddTask/RemTask wrappers are installed, the same ordering also lets its late prelaunch hook publish the removed task pointer, so a later task-list iterator can read freed memory. **Affected configuration:** ExecSMP builds; an eligible remote CPU and sufficiently early task exit are required for the direct `TaskLaunch()` consequence, while the stale task-list entry additionally requires task.resource wrappers. **Confidence:** high for publication-before-setup and the unchecked later reads; exact reclamation timing is source-inferred and unrun. No task or race was executed; source-only. See the [task.resource late-prelaunch reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7352) and [task.resource wrapper audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2140).

<a id="ek8867"></a>
### EK8867 — ARM SMP startup can leave the boot task eligible on every CPU after both affinity-mask allocations fail.

The ARM32 and AArch64 kernel `platform_PostInit()` paths try to allocate a CPU mask for the primordial boot task before calling `ARMI_Init()` to release secondary CPUs; both silently leave its affinity NULL if allocation fails (`arch/arm-native/kernel/platform_init.c:85-108`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/platform_init.c:85-108`). Exec retries pinning in its later `Exec_ARMCPUSMPInit()` hook, but likewise ignores a failed allocation (`arch/arm-native/exec/platform_init.c:245-285`; `arch/aarch64-native/exec/platform_init.c:245-285`). Both selected SMP schedulers treat NULL affinity as “run anywhere” (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:39-54`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:39-54`). The Raspberry Pi `smp` configure variant enables ExecSMP (`configure.in:2195-2199`).

**Trigger and consequence:** both boot-task CPU-mask allocations fail, and after secondary release an SMP scheduler selects the still-running boot task on a secondary CPU during cold-start initialization. The boot task then runs with boot-CPU/stack-local state on the wrong CPU, which the platform source identifies as unsafe; startup can crash or corrupt initialization state. **Affected configuration:** ARM32/AArch64 Raspberry Pi SMP builds using these native platform and Exec hooks. **Confidence:** high that both failures leave affinity unset and NULL matches any CPU; medium for the exact migration window, which depends on secondary scheduling and is further qualified by the earlier EK153/EK726 bootstrap-list findings. No allocation failure, CPU startup, or migration was run; source-only. See the [ARM32/AArch64 boot-task affinity failure recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L6295).

<a id="ek8868"></a>
### EK8868 — AArch64 Raspberry Pi SMP startup uses unchecked trampoline, secondary-stack and TLS allocations.

In the `__AROSEXEC_SMP__` branch, `bcm27xx_init()` allocates the shared trampoline and immediately copies/patches through the result without a NULL check (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/platform_bcm27xx.c:321-353`). In the per-secondary loop it allocates a stack, computes and publishes the stack pointer without checking `cpu_stack`, then allocates TLS and immediately writes `SysBase`, `KernelBase`, `ThisTask`, and CPU number through `__tls` (`:371-383`). The selected `AllocMem()` contract returns NULL on allocation failure (`rom/exec/allocmem.c:113-125`). There is no common rollback or boot-failure return for these three allocations.

**Trigger and consequence:** memory pressure causes any of these allocations to fail during AArch64 BCM27xx SMP initialization. Trampoline failure reaches `bcopy()` and subsequent pointer writes with a NULL destination; stack failure publishes an invalid secondary stack address; TLS failure faults on the first field store. Depending on which allocation fails, startup can fault before or during secondary-core release rather than report a controlled initialization failure. **Affected configuration:** AArch64 BCM27xx builds with `__AROSEXEC_SMP__` enabled (Raspberry Pi SMP variants); the allocation block is excluded from uniprocessor builds. **Confidence:** high for unchecked NULL results and immediate uses; runtime manifestation depends on which allocation fails and the memory state at startup. No allocation failure or boot was run; source-only. See the [AArch64 BCM27xx secondary allocation report-detail pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8952). PSCI refusal after successful stack/TLS allocation is tracked separately as EK8870.

<a id="ek8870"></a>
### EK8870 — BCM27xx PSCI refusal leaks the allocated secondary stack and TLS block.

In the AArch64 BCM27xx SMP startup loop, the code allocates a per-core stack and TLS block, fills the TLS fields, and publishes their addresses into the shared trampoline before calling PSCI `CPU_ON` (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/platform_bcm27xx.c:371-390`). When PSCI returns a nonzero error, the branch logs the failure, unlocks `startup_lock`, and continues to the next CPU without freeing either allocation (`:392-404`). The core was not successfully handed the trampoline on this error path, so the secondary has no startup cleanup owner for these blocks.

**Trigger and consequence:** a device-tree-selected PSCI CPU-enable method is used and firmware returns a nonzero result for `CPU_ON` after the stack and TLS allocations succeed. The failed secondary's stack and TLS allocations remain reserved for the life of the kernel; repeated refusal across CPUs leaks one pair per failed launch. **Affected configuration:** AArch64 BCM27xx SMP builds where a secondary's selected enable method is PSCI; spin-table launches do not take this branch. **Confidence:** high for the allocated-before-call ordering and missing free on the refusal branch; occurrence depends on PSCI refusing a requested CPU start. No PSCI response or boot was exercised; source-only. See the [AArch64 BCM27xx secondary startup and per-core timer caller recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5839) and [allocation report-detail pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8952). The unchecked-allocation faults are tracked separately as EK8868.

<a id="ek8869"></a>
### EK8869 — ARM32 BCM2836 secondary-core startup uses unchecked stack and TLS allocations.

For BCM2836, `platform_bcm2708.c` allocates a normal stack and FIQ stack for each secondary core, computes their top pointers, and publishes those addresses into the trampoline without checking either allocation (`arch/arm-native/kernel/platform_bcm2708.c:78-88,115-123`). It then allocates per-core TLS and immediately writes its fields through the result (`:125-133`; the allocation size includes `cpu_ipidata` under `__AROSEXEC_SMP__`). The multicore loop is outside the ExecSMP conditional, so this path also runs in the selected non-SMP BCM2836 configuration. `AllocMem()` returns NULL on failure (`rom/exec/allocmem.c:113-125`). The secondary trampoline loads the published FIQ and normal stack pointers and TLS before entering `cpu_Register()` (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:103-120,150-181`); `cpu_Register()` releases the startup lock only after its initialization path (`:212`).

**Trigger and consequence:** memory pressure causes a secondary stack, FIQ stack, or TLS allocation to fail during BCM2836 multicore startup. TLS failure dereferences NULL immediately on the boot CPU. A failed stack allocation is still published; the secondary may fault before it reaches the startup-lock release, leaving the boot CPU blocked on that lock. **Affected configuration:** ARM32 BCM2836 platform builds (Raspberry Pi 2/3); not limited to ExecSMP, though the TLS allocation size differs when SMP is enabled. **Confidence:** high for unchecked results and their immediate consumers; the exact secondary fault/lockup depends on which allocation fails and whether that core is released. No allocation failure or boot was run; source-only. See the [ARM32 BCM2836 secondary allocation recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2839). This is separate from AArch64 EK8868 and the PSCI refusal leak EK8870.

<a id="ek8875"></a>
### EK8875 — Duplicate identifier consolidated under EK10363.

This earlier entry described the same `Cause()` race and self-linked soft-interrupt queue as [EK10363](#ek10363), with no distinct root cause or consequence. EK10363 is the canonical finding and retains the full implementation analysis plus the caller traces collected under both IDs, including the optional RTL8139 and PCIUSB examples originally documented here. EK8875 remains as a cross-reference because older coverage notes cite this identifier; it is not a separate bug.

<a id="ek8799"></a>
### EK8799 — `WaitIO()` can complete and release a request while `ReplyMsg()` is still publishing it.

`ReplyMsg()` sets the message node to `NT_REPLYMSG` before calling `InternalPutMsg()` (`rom/exec/replymsg.c:57-64`). `CheckIO()` treats that type as completion (`rom/exec/checkio.c:48-59`), and `WaitIO()` skips its wait when the type is no longer `NT_MESSAGE`, then calls `Remove()` for `NT_REPLYMSG` (`rom/exec/waitio.c:55-82`). The reply port is not locked until `InternalPutMsg()` later reaches its `AddTail()` (`rom/exec/putmsg.c:71-93`); after insertion it still reads the port's signal fields and signals the task (`:95-121`). `WaitIO()`'s local `Disable()` does not serialize a different CPU, and neither completion call joins the in-progress `ReplyMsg()`.

On ExecSMP, a caller awakened by an independent signal can observe `NT_REPLYMSG` during this interval, return from `WaitIO()`, and close or free the request and reply port while `InternalPutMsg()` still uses them. It can also reuse the request before the earlier reply has finished. The selected `C:Wait` and `Exec_DoResetCallbacks()` paths use `CheckIO()` before `WaitIO()` and may skip `AbortIO()` when the message type has already changed (`workbench/c/Wait.c:178-181`; `rom/exec/doresetcallbacks.c:153-163`). Although their requests begin zeroed by `CreateIORequest()` (`rom/exec/createiorequest.c:63-72`), the timer device inserts each pending request into its own timeout list, removes it on expiry, and only then calls `ReplyMsg()` (`rom/timer/lowlevel.c:365-375`). The list `REMOVE` macro leaves the node's predecessor/successor fields unchanged (`compiler/include/exec/lists.h:136-145`), so `WaitIO()` in the pre-reply-port-insertion window sees stale timer-list links, not null links. On an unchanged timer list those repeated neighbor writes may be idempotent; no separate null-dereference or timer-list-corruption consequence is claimed. The established concern is that `WaitIO()` returns before `InternalPutMsg()` finishes inserting the request and signaling its reply port, allowing caller cleanup or reuse to race accesses to the request/port.

Two maintained paths supply the independent wake. In `Exec_DoResetCallbacks()`, the launcher waits on either the callback-completion signal or a VBlank timer signal; when the callback signal wins, it checks and waits on the timeout request, then later reuses it for another callback or closes/frees it (`rom/exec/doresetcallbacks.c:143-163,185-201`). If the VBlank timer interrupt on another CPU is in `ReplyMsg()` while that callback signal wakes the launcher, the request can be retired before reply publication finishes. `C:Wait` has the same ordering when Ctrl-C wakes it independently of its VBlank timer request: it calls `CheckIO()`/`WaitIO()` and then closes the device and deletes the request and port (`workbench/c/Wait.c:167-194`). The timer completion path removes the request and calls `ReplyMsg()` from VBlank processing (`rom/timer/lowlevel.c:354-379`; `rom/timer/timervblank.c:17-24`).

A source-caller cross-check found the same completion observation in separately buildable optional clients. `C:Logger` can receive Ctrl-C while its VBlank request is outstanding, then skip `AbortIO()` when `CheckIO()` sees the early reply state, call `WaitIO()`, close the device and delete the request (`workbench/c/Logger.c:513-519,524-529,559-566`; explicit `workbench-c-logger` target at `workbench/c/mmakefile.src:152-153`). The Bluetooth event-handler task checks its timer after processing messages from a separate event port; on a completed check it waits and immediately resubmits the same request (`rom/bluetooth/bluetooth/classes.c:843,865-919,921-925`). Poseidon's popup task and library event loop likewise process application or event-port input before checking and resubmitting their VBlank request (`rom/usb/poseidon/popo.gui.c:277-290`; `poseidon.library.c:9395-9410`). The Bluetooth and Poseidon aggregate build edges are optional/commented in this snapshot (`rom/bluetooth/mmakefile.src:6-11`; `rom/usb/mmakefile.src:8-18`), so these are explicit-build instances, not default-image claims. They share EK8799's root cause rather than adding separate findings. The explicit optional PPP driver has another case: `WritePacket()` calls `CheckIO(SerTx)`, then `WaitIO()` before passing the packet to `SendPacket()`; that path reaches `send_IP_packet()` and `SendBYTES()`, which waits again and overwrites/reuses the same `SerTx` request (`workbench/devs/networks/ppp/handler.c:147-160,184-205`; `ppp.c:937-957`; `serial.c:128-138`). The selected serial driver's write-empty interrupt completes its active request with `ReplyMsg()` (`workbench/devs/serial/serial_interrupthandlers.c:132-162`). The PPP task processes new SANA requests in its unit loop (`workbench/devs/networks/ppp/init.c:154-166`), so a new network write is an independent wake while the serial interrupt is completing the previous request. On the serial side, `CMD_WRITE` leaves `STATUS_WRITES_PENDING` set while `su_ActiveWrite` is active and queues another request to `su_QWriteCommandPort` when that status remains set (`workbench/devs/serial/serial_init.c:453-545`); the interrupt calls `ReplyMsg()` before it dequeues the next queued write or clears the pending status (`serial_interrupthandlers.c:143-184`). If PPP reuses `SerTx` in the state-publication window, the reused message can be linked onto the serial write queue before the earlier `InternalPutMsg()` adds that same node to the reply port. The original reply insertion can then overwrite links of a node already on the write queue, so this caller path can corrupt queue membership in addition to racing request contents. Both PPP and serial are explicit targets outside their commented aggregate edges (`workbench/devs/networks/mmakefile.src:4-15`; `workbench/devs/networks/ppp/mmakefile.src:7-13`; `workbench/devs/serial/mmakefile.src:8-13`); no default-package inclusion is claimed. Other checked `CheckIO()`/`WaitIO()` cleanup paths that call `AbortIO()` when the request is still pending are not counted as this early-publication case; timer.device serializes those aborts against completion with its list lock. The m68k CD32 caller is outside this ExecSMP trigger scope.

A selected Intuition input-handler path supplies another independent wake and exposes a temporary-port lifetime consequence. When called outside the input.device task and `CreateMsgPort()` succeeds, `DoSyncAction()` creates a stack-local `IOStdReq`, `MsgPort`, and `InputEvent`, queues the caller's action, sets the reply port to the caller task's `SIGB_INTUITION`, submits `IND_WRITEEVENT` with an `IECLASS_NULL` event, then calls `DoIO()` (`rom/intuition/inputhandler_actions.c:583-640`). `input.device` processes that command by synchronously forwarding the event through its registered handlers before it reaches the common `ReplyMsg(ioreq)` after the command switch (`rom/devs/input/processevents.c:397-415,433`; the `IND_WRITEEVENT` case is at `:400-415`). Intuition's selected input handler calls `HandleIntuiActions()` before processing the event (`rom/intuition/inputhandler.c:1929`); that removes and invokes the queued action, sets `am->done = TRUE`, and signals the original caller before returning (`inputhandler_actions.c:678-706`). This signal uses the same bit that `DoIO()`'s temporary reply port uses. On ExecSMP, the caller can therefore wake while the input-device task is entering `ReplyMsg()`; if it observes `NT_REPLYMSG` before `InternalPutMsg()` has linked the request, `WaitIO()` returns early. Since `am->done` was already set, `DoSyncAction()` skips its follow-up wait and deletes the stack-local port before returning (`inputhandler_actions.c:625-638`). The input-device task can then continue `InternalPutMsg()` using that port and the stack request. The exact interleaving remains conditional, but this is a source-selected independent-signal route to EK8799's reply-port/request lifetime window, rather than a port that merely happens to be stack allocated. The `input.device` and Intuition modules are selected by the standard ROM module dependencies (`rom/mmakefile.src:10-25,89-105`).

**Trigger and consequence:** on an ExecSMP timer-client path, an independent callback-completion or Ctrl-C signal wakes a caller on a different CPU while the VBlank interrupt is between publishing `NT_REPLYMSG` and finishing `InternalPutMsg()`. `WaitIO()` can return early; cleanup or request reuse can race the unfinished reply operation, which still accesses request/port storage. On the explicit PPP/serial path, a new SANA write wakes the PPP unit task while the serial interrupt is in the same state-publication window; `WaitIO()` can return and `SendIO()` can queue the reused `SerTx` node before the prior reply inserts it on the reply port, corrupting queue membership as described above. **Affected configuration:** the timer-client trigger is established for ExecSMP-enabled x86-64 PC and Raspberry Pi variants (`configure.in:1667-1670,2195-2199`) using the generic Exec reply path and VBlank timer. The PPP/serial instance requires an ExecSMP target where the explicit PPP and serial modules and a matching serial HIDD are built and active; their aggregate edges are commented, so no default-image inclusion is claimed. Both triggers require the narrow cross-CPU timing window; neither was reproduced. **Confidence:** high for the state-publication order, unsynchronized completion test, and post-insertion port use; medium for occurrence of the independent-signal overlap. Coordinate reply publication with completion observation and do not release or reuse the request until the reply operation has finished. No I/O, signal, timer expiry, build, or runtime behavior was exercised; source-only.

<a id="ek9883"></a>
### EK9883 — Exec and DOS remove queued messages without the shared port lock on SMP.

`WaitIO()` calls `Disable()` and then removes a completed request with `Remove()`, but does not acquire the reply port's `mp_SpinLock` (`rom/exec/waitio.c:68-78`). On ExecSMP, `Disable()` excludes interrupts and task switches only on the current CPU (`rom/exec/disable.c:58-61`). In contrast, `InternalPutMsg()` and `GetMsg()` protect the same port list with `mp_SpinLock` (`rom/exec/putmsg.c:71-96`; `rom/exec/getmsg.c:54-70`). `Remove()` updates the node's predecessor and successor pointers as separate writes without internal locking (`rom/exec/remove.c:51-64`), so a concurrent `AddTail()` can interleave those writes and leave the list links inconsistent.
`ReplyMsg()` also changes the request node to `NT_REPLYMSG` before calling `InternalPutMsg()` to link it on the reply port (`rom/exec/replymsg.c:52-64`). Since `WaitIO()` waits on the port's signal bit and then rechecks only the request state (`waitio.c:57-64`), a different completion on a shared reply port can wake it while this request is in that publication window. `WaitIO()` can then observe `NT_REPLYMSG` and call the same unlocked `Remove()` before this request has been linked. This additional path requires a shared port and a signal from another message during the short window; the linked-node concurrent-append interleaving below remains independently established.

`EndNotify()` has a second removal path with the same missing port-list lock: after its synchronous `ACTION_REMOVE_NOTIFY`, it scans the request's message port and removes matching queued notifications using plain `Remove()` under only local `Disable()` (`rom/dos/endnotify.c:64,70-101`). The documented `Disable()` contract says it affects only the calling processor on ExecSMP and shared data also needs a spinlock (`rom/exec/disable.c:58-61`). A selected Workbench caller supplies the shared-port case: Wanderer creates one filesystem-notification port, registers an input handler to drain it, passes the same port to preferences and icon windows, and each volume-root icon creates a `StartNotify()` request against it (`workbench/system/Wanderer/wanderer.c:3344-3386,3777-3793`; `iconwindow.c:440-463,583`; `iconwindow_volumelist.c:1178-1190`). Destroying or disabling a root entry calls `EndNotify()` from the Wanderer task (`iconwindow_volumelist.c:1208-1255`), while other active filesystem handlers can append notifications for their requests to that shared port (`rom/filesys/ram/notification.c:413-437`; FAT `notify.c:26-80`). With separate handlers on separate CPUs, an append for another active request can interleave with the removal. For example, if A is the sole queued node and EndNotify starts `Remove(A)`, its first link write can make the head point to the tail; a concurrent `AddTail(B)` can then use A as the tail predecessor, after which Remove's second write restores the tail predecessor to the head. The head then skips B even though B's links were written. The ordering follows `Remove()` and `AddTail()`'s separate pointer stores (`rom/exec/remove.c:51-64`; `addtail.c:57-65`).

The optional, maintained AHI-Handler supplies a shared-port caller. `AllocAudio()` creates one AHI request template and reply port; `PlayAndSwap()` clones that request into both playback buffers, sends one request, then waits on the other (`workbench/devs/AHI/AHI-Handler/main.c:936-947,731-761`). The AHI device queues nonquick writes to its unit task, which completes them with `ReplyMsg()` (`workbench/devs/AHI/Device/devcommands.c:101-113,257-293`; `Device/device.c:920-929`). Consequently, while the handler's `WaitIO()` unlinks one already-replied request, the unit task can append another completion to the same port on another CPU.

The conflicting writes can strand the newly appended reply. With A as the sole queued node, `WaitIO()` first sets the port head's successor to the tail; `AddTail(B)` can then append B using A as its predecessor; `WaitIO()` next sets the tail's predecessor back to the head, and `AddTail()` finally sets it to B. The port head points to the tail while B remains linked only through stale/local links, so a waiter may never retrieve B. This exact pointer ordering is derived from `WaitIO()` (`:74-75`), `Remove()` (`remove.c:61-62`), and `AddTail()` (`addtail.c:57-65`); no list operation was executed.

**Trigger and consequence:** on ExecSMP, any of these interleavings is sufficient: (a) `WaitIO()` removes a reply already linked to a port while another CPU appends to that same port; (b) a shared reply port wakes `WaitIO()` for another completion while the target `ReplyMsg()` has set `NT_REPLYMSG` but has not linked the target request yet; or (c) `EndNotify()` sweeps queued notifications while another CPU adds or removes a message on the same caller-shared port. In each path, unsynchronized link updates or removal of a not-yet-linked node can corrupt the queue or leave messages unreachable. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC and Raspberry Pi ExecSMP builds (`configure.in:1667-1670,2195-2199`). The WaitIO trigger has the selected optional AHI-Handler caller described above; the EndNotify trigger is established for the selected Wanderer shared notification port when another active filesystem handler appends concurrently; the cross-CPU overlap is timing-dependent. **Confidence:** high for both unlocked removals and the WaitIO pointer-write interleaving; the EndNotify manifestation depends on a concurrent same-port append from another handler. Protect each removal/traversal with the same port lock used by insertion/dequeue, unlink matching messages under the lock, and reply after releasing it. No I/O, audio device, port operation, build, or SMP interleaving was exercised; source-only.

<a id="ek8877"></a>
### EK8877 — PC startup ignores allocation failure for required syscall and APIC exception handlers (conditional unhandled trap and system halt; high source confidence).

KrnAddExceptionHandler() returns NULL when the exception number is out of range or when krnAllocIntrNode() fails; the latter is an AllocMem() allocation (rom/kernel/addexceptionhandler.c:97-127; rom/kernel/kernel_objects.h:12). The selected PC startup callers ignore that return for the syscall exception on both i386 and x86-64 (arch/i386-pc/kernel/platform_init.c:85-108; arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/platform_init.c:254-274). Common PC APIC setup likewise ignores the result for the APIC error handler and every IPI vector (arch/all-pc/kernel/apic_ia32.c:1111-1121). Their IDT gates are installed separately and checked, so a failed handler-node allocation leaves a live vector without its required handler while startup continues.

If the corresponding syscall, APIC error, or IPI vector is later delivered, cpu_Trap() finds no registered handler and reaches the unhandled-exception system-halt path (arch/all-pc/kernel/cpu_traps.c:90-115). This makes a transient low-memory failure during PC platform/APIC initialization capable of turning a later system call or required kernel IPI into a system halt; an APIC error only triggers the consequence if that error vector is delivered. The spurious-vector registration is excluded from this claim because cpu_Trap() explicitly exempts that vector from the halt path. **Affected configuration and trigger:** i386-PC or x86-64-PC when the relevant KrnAddExceptionHandler() allocation fails during startup and its vector is subsequently used. **Confidence:** high for the ignored return, missing-node behavior, and unhandled-vector halt; occurrence depends on allocation failure followed by delivery. No allocation failure, boot, or trap was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek8883"></a>
### EK8883 — Raspberry Pi boot diagnostics read beyond a short GPIO property (conditional firmware input; source-level out-of-property read).

Both Raspberry Pi boot LED loops accept a gpios property when its declared length is at least eight bytes, then unconditionally format three 32-bit cells from data[0..2] (arch/arm-raspi/boot/boot.c:384-391; arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/boot.c:668-675). The FDT parser stores the property's declared byte length and points op_value directly at the property's value (arch/arm-raspi/boot/devicetree.c:40-51; arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/devicetree.c:40-51). Thus an eight-byte gpios property has only two declared cells, while the diagnostic reads a third cell beyond that property's extent. The later functional use of data[2] is correctly guarded by op_length >= 12 (boot.c:402; AArch64 boot.c:686); the confirmed consequence is limited to misleading boot diagnostics and an out-of-property read, not GPIO configuration.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** ARM32 Raspberry Pi or AArch64 Raspberry Pi boot with an enabled LED node whose gpios property contains exactly the phandle and one argument (eight bytes). The referenced GPIO provider's #gpio-cells determines whether that shape is valid; no checked-in DTS/DTB was found to establish that the selected firmware supplies it. **Confidence:** high that both readers exceed the declared property length under the stated shape; low that the shipped firmware input reaches it. No boot, DTB or hardware was used; source-only.

<a id="ek8891"></a>
### EK8891 — The PC ExecSMP dispatch-state query macro uses an undeclared scheduler pointer (conditional macro defect; high source confidence, no in-tree trigger found).

In the ExecSMP branch of the selected PC Exec platform header, FLAG_SCHEDDISPATCH_ISSET declares tls_t *__tls = TLS_PTR_GET() but then tests and dereferences __schd, which is not declared in the macro, and never uses __tls (arch/all-pc/exec/exec_platform.h:279-286). The PC TLS layout stores a ScheduleData pointer, not ScheduleFlags (arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/tls.h:12-20); adjacent scheduler-state macros obtain struct X86SchedulerPrivate *__schd = TLS_GET(ScheduleData) before reading ScheduleFlags (exec_platform.h:261-278). An ordinary expansion with no caller-scope __schd is ill-formed. If a caller happens to have a visible __schd, the macro reads that object instead of the current CPU's ScheduleData.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** an external consumer or future in-tree caller expands this macro while the PC ExecSMP branch is selected. A repository-wide C/header search found no checked-in expansion, so no current selected build failure is claimed. **Confidence:** high that the macro body is malformed and inconsistent with the PC TLS layout; no in-tree runtime/build trigger established. Use the same ScheduleData lookup as FLAG_SCHEDSWITCH_ISSET. No macro expansion or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8899"></a>
### EK8899 — m68kemu guest task entry path *(withdrawn; duplicate of EK9894)*

**Disposition:** the normal successful `TASKTAG_PC` conversion and host-context installation are now included in [EK9894](#ek9894), alongside the other missing guest-callback execution bridges. EK8899 is retained as a historical anchor; the allocation-failure case remains separately tracked by [EK9900](#ek9900). See the [task-entry trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L6043).

<a id="ek8900"></a>
### EK8900 — The shared write-locked initializer uses a bit that native ARM spinlocks do not recognize as a writer lock.

The shared spinlock header defines `SPINLOCK_INIT_WRITE_LOCKED` as `1 << 27` (`compiler/include/aros/types/spinlock_s.h:52-60`). The ARM32 and AArch64 native implementations use bit 31 as the writer marker: write acquisition stores `0x80000000`, and unlock treats a word as write-held only when bit 31 is set (`arch/arm-native/kernel/spinlock.c:26-38`, `spinunlock.c:34-49`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/spinlock.c:18-20,33-45`, `spinunlock.c:24-32`). Thus a lock statically initialized with the shared write-locked macro is interpreted as a reader count on these targets. `KrnSpinUnLock()` decrements that positive count instead of clearing the lock, leaving it nonzero; subsequent writers wait indefinitely for a lock that has no reader to release it.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** ARM-native or AArch64-native clients that use `SPINLOCK_INIT_WRITE_LOCKED` and then release the initial state through the native spinlock API. **Confidence:** high for the encoding mismatch and stuck-lock consequence. A repository-wide search finds only the macro definition, with no checked-in expansion, so this is an external/future-client contract defect, not a demonstrated in-tree failure. PC uses bit 27 consistently and is excluded. Use a target-consistent initializer or a common writer encoding. No lock operation or target was run; source-only. See the [initializer and caller census](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8734).

<a id="ek8902"></a>
### EK8902 — Raspberry Pi ARM and AArch64 kernel targets require absent architecture source files

The ARM-native kernel manifest lists `vars`, `screen_fb`, and `font8x14` in `CFILES` (`arch/arm-native/kernel/mmakefile.src:60-63`), but none of those `.c` files exists in that architecture source directory in this checkout. The AArch64-native manifest lists those same three names plus `maygetchar`, `issuper`, `virtualtophysical`, and `setprotection` (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/mmakefile.src:45-62`); none of the seven AArch64-local files exists. The similarly named ARM boot-console sources under `arch/all-native/bootconsole/` and Raspberry Pi boot sources under `arch/{arm,aarch64}-raspi/boot/bc/` are not files in the native-kernel source directories. The AArch64 generic kernel sources under `rom/kernel/` likewise do not satisfy the architecture-local entries.

`%build_archspecific` turns each listed C basename into an architecture object (`config/make.tmpl:3304-3311`) and gives those objects an explicit source prerequisite at `$(SRCDIR)/$(CURDIR)/%.c` (`:3400-3404`). The AROS ARM32 and AArch64 manifests invoke this macro for the `raspi-arm`, `raspi-armeb`, and `raspi-aarch64` kernel targets (`arch/arm-native/kernel/mmakefile.src:91-97`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/mmakefile.src:83-85`). In a clean checkout without generated or externally supplied source overlays, the missing prerequisites prevent those kernel targets from producing their object sets and therefore block the dependent Raspberry Pi kernel image.

**Affected configuration and consequence:** explicit `kernel-kernel-raspi-arm`, `kernel-kernel-raspi-armeb`, and `kernel-kernel-raspi-aarch64` target builds using these checked-in manifests and no external source overlay. The top-level Raspberry Pi distfiles/package dependency edges are commented in the boot manifests (`arch/arm-raspi/boot/mmakefile.src:26-31`; `arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/mmakefile.src:20-25`), so this finding does not claim default-image selection. **Confidence:** high that the listed sources are absent and the generated object rules require those exact paths; the resulting build failure is inferred from the make prerequisites and was not reproduced. Add the missing target-specific sources or remove/replace the stale manifest entries and their consumers. No build was run; source-only; see the [manifest and make-rule audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9053).

<a id="ek8903"></a>
### EK8903 — BCM27xx secondary startup can reuse trampoline state after a late-core timeout.

In the AArch64 BCM27xx SMP startup loop, `bcm27xx_wait_core()` waits for the global `startup_lock` to be released for one `CNTFRQ_EL0` interval. If it remains locked, the caller reports that the CPU did not report in, unlocks the global lock, and proceeds to the next CPU (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/platform_bcm27xx.c:282-298,390-428`). The next iteration writes its stack and TLS pointers into the same trampoline data slots before launching that CPU (`:373-388`). The trampoline reads those shared slots only when the secondary begins executing (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:101-110,115-119`).

This creates two possible late-start ordering errors. A secondary that enters the trampoline after a later iteration rewrites the slots can load that later CPU's stack/TLS values. A secondary that loaded its own values before the timeout can still reach `cpu_Register()`'s completion path later and call `KrnSpinUnLock(&startup_lock)` after the boot CPU has acquired that same lock for another launch (`kernel_cpu.c:128,184-192`). The boot CPU can then mistake the later launch as complete and advance before that CPU has completed bootstrap and per-core initialization. These paths can misinitialize a core or disrupt serialized SMP startup.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** AArch64 BCM27xx builds with `__AROSEXEC_SMP__`, when firmware starts a secondary but it does not reach the completion unlock within one counter-frequency interval (approximately one second). The source proves the timeout, shared-slot reuse, and shared-lock ordering; it does not establish that supported firmware can delay a secondary this long. **Confidence:** high for the ordering defect if that delay occurs; unverified for the firmware timing condition. The related unchecked allocations and PSCI-refusal leaks are covered separately by [EK8868](#ek8868) and [EK8870](#ek8870). No boot, timeout, or secondary startup was run; source-only. See the [startup and timeout recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L6248).

<a id="ek8904"></a>
### EK8904 — ARM secondary registration continues after bootstrap-task creation fails, then dereferences the missing task.

In ARM32 and AArch64 SMP builds, `cpu_Register()` calls `cpu_Init()` before trying to create the secondary's bootstrap task. `cpu_Init()` sets that CPU's bit in `ARMI_AffinityMask` (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:358-365`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:323-329`). If `cpu_InitBootStrap()` fails, `cpu_Register()` jumps to `cpu_registerfatal`, but that label is after the successful bootstrap, scheduler, and per-core timer initialization blocks. The common tail still unlocks `startup_lock` and executes `WFI`; if the wait returns, execution continues to the EL1t/task-stack transition and dereferences `__tls->ThisTask->tc_SPUpper`, although `ThisTask` is NULL (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:185-217,222-233`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:168-204`).

With EK153/EK726 still present, the constructor's MemList, task, and stack allocation failures before `AddHead()` can return NULL (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_execsmp.c:29-60`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_execsmp.c:29-56`). The later context- and ETask-failure returns are after the invalid `AddHead()` and are reachable only if that earlier list defect is fixed or execution happens to continue through its null-derived access; the ETask failure also leaks the context as separately tracked by EK10202. Because `cpu_Init()` already set the online bit and the failure path does not clear it, `KrnGetCPUCount()` counts a core whose bootstrap construction returned NULL (`arch/{arm-native,aarch64-native}/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:358-365,323-329`; `getcpucount.c:16-22`). The ARM affinity API treats CPU IDs below that population count as candidates (`rom/task/SetTaskAffinity.c:82-95`), and `Signal()` can select a task's CPU ID or affinity CPU for IPI routing (`rom/exec/signal.c:170-205`). On the ordered BCM27xx launch path, a reachable early allocation failure on a lower-numbered secondary followed by a later successful CPU can leave a hole in online IDs while count-based consumers assume a dense range. This can accept affinity for a non-operational CPU and route work there; if an interrupt later returns the failed core from `WFI`, the NULL-task dereference can fault.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** ARM32 or AArch64 native SMP, when a secondary reaches `cpu_Register()` but `cpu_InitBootStrap()` returns NULL; consequences depend on a later affinity/signal consumer or an interrupt returning the failed core from `WFI`. The checked BCM2708 and BCM27xx startup loops launch CPU IDs in ascending order (`arch/arm-native/kernel/platform_bcm2708.c:115-159`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/platform_bcm27xx.c:362-428`). **Confidence:** high for the NULL continuation and stale online bit; conditional for later service of the failed CPU. The bootstrap-context leak on `Exec_InitETask()` failure is separately tracked by [EK10202](#ek10202); optional bootstrap-name and affinity-mask allocation failures do not make `cpu_InitBootStrap()` return NULL and are excluded here. No allocation failure, interrupt, affinity request, signal, or boot was run; source-only. See the [fatal-bootstrap caller recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9139).

<a id="ek8911"></a>
### EK8911 — OpenSBI accepts checksum-invalid ACPI interrupt-controller tables (conditional firmware-data interrupt misconfiguration; high source confidence, firmware trigger unverified).

The OpenSBI EFI stub selects the ACPI 2.0 RSDP (or ACPI 1.0 fallback) from the EFI configuration table and stores its pointer without validating its signature or checksum (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/efi_stub.c:778-797`). `acpi_find()` follows the RSDP's RSDT/XSDT address, scans entries, and accepts a child table by its four-byte signature; it does not verify the RSDP, root-table, or child-table checksums (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_acpi.c:263-302`). `krnACPIPLICInfo()` then consumes MADT PLIC base/size/source-count fields and RINTC enable/context fields, also without checksum validation (`:320-397`).

When the device tree did not provide a PLIC base, startup invokes this ACPI path before `krnPLICInit()` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:659-668`). The resulting base, size, source count, and supervisor contexts configure PLIC MMIO mapping, enable/threshold initialization, and interrupt completion (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_plic.c:73-130,248-255`). A checksum-invalid table with corrupted but readable controller fields can therefore be accepted and used to configure the wrong PLIC range or contexts, leaving external interrupts misconfigured or unavailable. This finding is limited to the missing checksum validation; malformed table extents and unchecked lengths are separately covered by EK9086-EK9088.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** RISC-V64 OpenSBI boot with an EFI ACPI table and no device-tree PLIC base, where the RSDP, root table, or MADT has an invalid checksum and its consumed controller fields are wrong. **Confidence:** high that this parser path does not validate checksums; the firmware condition and resulting interrupt failure are unverified. Firmware-provided tables with invalid checksums but otherwise correct fields may have no observable effect. No ACPI table, PLIC, or boot was used; source-only. See the [ACPI parser and startup recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8402).

<a id="ek8918"></a>
### EK8918 — ARM32/ARMeb task affinity adoption leaks the ETask's initialized CPU mask.

When CPU affinity is enabled, `Exec_InitETask()` allocates and stores an initial mask in the new task's ETask (`rom/exec/exec_util.c:126-164`). ARM32 and ARMEB `PrepareContext()` process a supplied `TASKTAG_AFFINITY` by assigning the tag's pointer directly to `iet_CpuAffinity`, without freeing that initialized mask (`arch/arm-all/exec/preparecontext.c:42-45`; `arch/armeb-all/exec/preparecontext.c:42-45`). The earlier allocation is then unreachable from the task and cannot be reclaimed by its normal ETask cleanup. The selected AArch64 implementation explicitly frees an existing non-sentinel mask before replacing it (`arch/aarch64-native/exec/preparecontext.c:44-50`), which confirms the missing ownership step in the two ARM variants.

Checked-in successful tag-bearing task creation paths include ARM32 SMP per-CPU idle-task setup (`arch/arm-native/exec/platform_init.c:62-79`) and secondary processor probes (`arch/arm-native/processor/processor_init.c:52-70`). The leak occurs when affinity is enabled and `Exec_InitETask()`'s initial mask allocation succeeds; it is independent of whether the caller-provided pointer is a real mask or NULL. Task creation failure before tag adoption is a separate caller-mask ownership issue tracked by [EK8790](#ek8790). **Affected configuration and trigger:** ARM32 or ARMEB SMP task creation with a `TASKTAG_AFFINITY` tag and successful initial ETask mask allocation. **Consequence:** one abandoned CPU-mask allocation per affected task, accumulating with repeated task creation; the checked-in boot/probe paths create a bounded number. **Confidence:** high for pointer replacement and lost ownership; caller-side mask-failure behavior remains separately qualified. AArch64 is excluded because its override frees the old mask. No task creation, allocation failure, or cleanup was run; source-only. See the [ARM affinity ownership comparison](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8705).

<a id="ek8927"></a>
### EK8927 — `logRemEntry()` can remove an entry before its provider-list publication.

`logAddEntryA()` allocates and zeroes a private entry, links only its `le_Node` into the producer's list, queues an add message, and returns the public entry pointer (`rom/log/log_event.c:214-267`). The provider-list node `lep_Node` is linked later by the log service task when it dequeues that add message (`rom/log/log.c:248-255`). If a caller invokes `logRemEntry()` before that publication, it unconditionally calls `Remove(&leP->lep_Node)` (`log_event.c:278-293`). The node is still zeroed and unlinked; Exec's `Remove()` dereferences `ln_Pred` and `ln_Succ` without a membership check (`rom/exec/remove.c:51-62`), so this ordering can fault before the remove event is queued.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** any client using the log resource API that removes a newly returned entry before the service task handles its queued add event. **Confidence:** high for the unlinked-node ordering and invalid `Remove()` operation. The only checked-in C caller is standalone Logger, whose startup spool and live path remove entries after protecting the entry walk or consuming the add broadcast (`workbench/c/Logger.c:499-508,548-555`); it does not establish the trigger. Retain as a conditional external/future caller defect, not a demonstrated in-tree failure. No log resource or client was run; source-only. See the [pre-publication removal trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5509).

<a id="ek8934"></a>
### EK8934 — Generated duplicate-base OpenLib leaks earlier relative libraries when a later required dependency fails.

For per-task or per-opener bases with relative libraries, generated `OpenLib` calls `set_open_rellibraries(newlib)` before the module's OPENLIB hooks. If that call fails, the generated branch restores a previous per-task base when needed, frees `newlib`, decrements the root open count, and returns NULL; it does not call `set_close_rellibraries(newlib)` (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1386-1400`). The helper opens dependencies in order and returns immediately when a required `OpenLibrary()` fails, without closing any earlier dependency it already opened (`compiler/autoinit/libraries.c:77-109`). The successful dependency's pointer is stored inside `newlib`; freeing that base loses the pointer while leaving its library open reference outstanding.

This differs from `_set_libinit()`'s ordinary initialization rollback, which closes the relative-library set after a required dependency failure (`compiler/autoinit/functions.c:40-84`), and from EK600, where dependency opening succeeded and a later module OPENLIB hook failed. The trigger is a duplicate-base open whose relative-library list has an earlier required dependency that opens successfully and a later required dependency that fails. Selected configurations include per-task `usergroup.library` (`workbench/libs/usergroup/usergroup.conf:1-10`), `z1.library` (`workbench/libs/z/z1.conf:1-9`), and `lzma.library` (`workbench/libs/lzma/lzma.conf:1-10`); each declares the required relative libraries in `posixc`, then `stdc` order and suppresses root-base opens. The parent `workbench-libs-complete` catch-all target lists UserGroup, zlib, and lzma (`workbench/libs/mmakefile:9-62`); each module also has an explicit build target. The trigger still depends on the earlier dependency opening successfully and the later one failing.

**Affected configuration and consequence:** generated duplicate-base opens for the selected UserGroup, z1, and lzma libraries when `posixc` opens but the later required `stdc` open fails; the same generated path applies to other `pertaskbase`/`peropenerbase` modules with required relative libraries. Each affected attempt can leave the earlier library open unmatched. **Confidence:** high for the missing rollback and lost opened reference; runtime incidence is conditional on dependency-open failure ordering. No library open was run or forced to fail; source-only. See the [duplicate-base rollback trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4804).

<a id="ek8942"></a>
### EK8942 — The i386-PC SAD debugger indexes its key translation table with unmapped keyboard scan codes.

The i386-PC SAD debugger's `transl` table has 50 entries, indexed 0 through 49 (`arch/i386-pc/exec/debug_internal.c:43-47`). `GetK()` returns a keyboard make scan code after filtering only no-key and key-release values (`:452-462`); the command loop uses `transl[GetK() - 1]` directly, and the argument loop uses the same table after special-casing only space (`:65-87`). Ordinary set-1 make codes such as F1 `0x3b`, Caps Lock `0x3a`, and Num Lock `0x45` therefore index beyond the table; a space in the command-entry path also uses index `0x38` and is out of range. The argument path maps space to index 1, but other unmapped keys remain unchecked.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** i386-PC builds using this local SAD debugger, when a user presses a make code not represented by the table while entering a command or its arguments. **Consequence:** the debugger reads outside the translation array and may display or process an unrelated character; unsupported keys can corrupt command parsing. **Confidence:** high for the out-of-bounds table indexing; the particular resulting character and user-visible behavior depend on adjacent memory. The no-key `-1` and key-release filtering were checked; no keyboard input was generated. See the [scan-code bounds recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7212).

<a id="ek8944"></a>
### EK8944 — ROM-map allocation failure is dereferenced during m68k-Amiga kernel startup.

`AMiGAROMSupport_Init()` builds a local list of nonidentity ROM-window mappings for an MMU-enabled m68k-Amiga platform. When at least one mapping is found (`i > 0`), it allocates `pd->romimg` and immediately copies the positive-length mapping list and writes two terminators without checking the allocation (`arch/m68k-amiga/kernel/romsupport.c:95-109,113-157`). If `AllocMem()` fails in that branch, `CopyMem()` receives a NULL destination; its nonzero-size path writes through that pointer (`rom/exec/copymem.c:60-76`).

The trigger requires an active 68030 MMU whose translation of one or more probed ROM windows differs from the virtual address, followed by failure of the small mapping-table allocation. The normal AROSBootstrap reset path clears inherited 68030 MMU state before restarting, and direct ROM boot begins from reset; with identity translations, `i` remains zero and this allocation path is skipped. No selected default boot path establishing a changed 030 mapping was found, so retain this as an alternate/legacy-startup conditional rather than a default Amiga boot failure. 040 is excluded because its selected physical-address helper returns its input (`arch/m68k-all/kernel/mmu.c:213-215`); 060 installs no probe helper (`romsupport.c:103-109`; see the [mapping producer and boot-order check](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4670)).
