**Affected configuration and trigger:** m68k-Amiga startup with a 68030 and a retained nonidentity ROM-window mapping, plus `AllocMem()` failure while building the map. **Consequence:** a kernel-startup data-access fault before the ROM map is published. **Confidence:** high for the NULL-destination access if the conditional branch is reached; the alternate/legacy mapping trigger is not established in the selected default boot path. No allocation failure, ROM map, or boot was exercised; source-only.

<a id="ek8948"></a>
### EK8948 — The i386 PC boot allocator can advance and clear memory beyond the bootstrap's reserved boot-data area.

The common native boot allocator rounds `BootMemPtr`, computes `end = addr + size`, advances the cursor, and clears the requested bytes. Its exhaustion check is compiled only for `__x86_64__`; i386 has no corresponding `BootMemLimit` check (`arch/all-native/kernel/kernel_bootmem.c:25-46`). The i386 kernel initializes the cursor from the actual `KRN_KernelHighest` image end, while the attempted limit initialization is disabled (`arch/i386-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:177-195`).

The selected 32-bit PC bootstrap reserves image size plus alignment and a fixed `0x80000` (512 KiB) tail, but does not calculate that tail from the relocated boot-tag payloads and early descriptor allocations (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:669-690`). i386 then relocates the tag list, memory map, BSS metadata, command line and loader strings through this allocator, and allocates `KernBootPrivate`, GDT, TSS and IDT (`arch/all-native/kernel/boot_utils.c:28-56,58-84`; `arch/i386-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:197-239,253-267`). If these requests exceed the selected region's reserved tail, the unchecked `memset()` can write beyond that reserved RAM extent; `kick_end` is subsequently derived from the advanced cursor and used as the kernel exclusion end during `mmap_InitMemory()` (`kernel_startup.c:271-279,345-350`).

**Affected configuration and trigger:** i386-PC first boot through the 32-bit all-PC bootstrap, where the chosen RAM region has only the minimum tail and relocated boot data plus early allocations exceed 512 KiB. **Confidence:** high that i386 lacks a bound and clears every requested range; conditional that supported boot metadata and memory placement exceed the reserve. The bootstrap itself rejects regions too small for the fixed minimum, so absence of any reserve is not the trigger. x86-64 has a runtime limit check and panics instead; PPC and other architecture allocators/callers are separately scoped. No boot metadata was supplied and no boot or memory write was run; source-only. See the [i386 bootmem bound and caller recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4502).

<a id="ek8954"></a>
### EK8954 — Adding a new interface to a class derived from an IFMeta-created class can dereference a missing interface bucket during construction.

During IFMeta class construction, `ifmeta_allocdisptabs()` calls `calc_ht_entries()` to determine which interfaces are new (`rom/oop/metaclass.c:162-180`). For each interface in the new class description, `calc_ht_entries()` asks the superclass for `MO_meta_getifinfo`; a NULL result is expected and counted as a new interface (`:601-640`). But when the superclass is itself an IFMeta-created class and lacks that interface, dispatch reaches `ifmeta_getifinfo()`, whose hash lookup can return NULL and is immediately dereferenced for `b->NumMethods` (`:353-372`). The superclass query therefore faults before construction can treat the interface as new.

The trigger requires an IFMeta-created superclass that does not implement an interface listed by the subclass. It is distinct from the checked-in Timer example: Timer derives from Root, so its query uses BaseMeta's absent-interface implementation, which safely returns NULL. The tracked checkout census found no maintained IFMeta-to-IFMeta subclass chain; HIDDMeta-created classes use a different safe lookup implementation. **Affected configuration and trigger:** external or future OOP clients dynamically constructing an IFMeta-derived subclass that adds an interface not present in its IFMeta superclass. **Consequence:** class construction dereferences a missing bucket instead of creating the new interface table. **Confidence:** high for the conditional dispatch and NULL dereference; no current in-tree trigger was established. No class was constructed; source-only. See the [superclass-type and caller census](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5952).

<a id="ek8961"></a>
### EK8961 — The i386 alert backtrace treats a saved EBP register as a frame-chain pointer.

The i386 trap path saves the interrupted `ExceptionContext` and records `ctx->FP` (EBP) as the alert backtrace start (`rom/exec/traphandler.c:100-112,129`; `rom/exec/exec_util.h:24-27`). The i386 alert formatter's `UnwindFrame()` treats that value as a linked frame and reads two words from it as caller and previous frame (`arch/i386-all/exec/alert_cpu.c:41-48`). `alertextra.c` checks only `TypeOfMem(fp)` before invoking the unwinder; it does not validate frame-chain provenance or confirm that both words fit in the containing allocation (`rom/exec/alertextra.c:149-167`).

If the interrupted code does not maintain an EBP frame chain, the trace can follow an arbitrary saved register as though it were one, producing unrelated frames. If that value happens to fall inside an allocated region near its end, the two-word read can cross the region boundary and fault during alert formatting. **Affected configuration and trigger:** i386 builds using this alert path when a trap interrupts code compiled without frame pointers, or with an otherwise invalid EBP value that passes `TypeOfMem()`. **Confidence:** high for the assumption mismatch and unchecked two-word read; whether normal compiler settings omit frames in the interrupted code and whether a particular value causes a second fault remain conditional. The diagnostic helper itself is compiled with `-O0`, but that does not establish a frame chain for the interrupted code. No compiler output, trap, or alert was produced; source-only. See the [saved-register and selected-caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L6671).

<a id="ek8962"></a>
### EK8962 — Caller-supplied stack sizes can leave the swapped C stack misaligned on several architectures.

`pthread_attr_setstack()` accepts any positive size when a non-NULL caller-provided stack address is supplied, without checking or rounding its alignment (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:854-864`). `pthread_create()` then forms `stk_Upper = stackaddr + stacksize` and uses that value as `stk_Pointer` (`compiler/pthread/pthread_create.c:139-165`). The direct-switch `NewStackSwap()` implementations install this pointer or preserve its alignment remainder across fixed-size argument/frame setup; they do not normalize it. The selected architecture headers specify 16-byte stack alignment for i386, PPC, AArch64, RV32 and RV64, and 8-byte alignment for m68k (`arch/*/include/aros/cpu.h`, respectively). Thus an aligned base plus a valid-size custom stack whose size is not a multiple of the target alignment reaches C entry code with a misaligned stack on these paths. ARM/ARMEB likewise preserve the caller's remainder when pushing their fixed four stack arguments.

There is also a normal AArch64 Shell trigger: `Stack 40961` rounds to 40,968 bytes in pointer-sized Shell units; `RunCommand()` clamps only to the 40,960-byte minimum, then sets `stk_Pointer = stack + stacksize` without ABI realignment (`workbench/c/shellcommands/Stack.c:69-82`; `rom/dos/runcommand.c:127-141`). From an aligned allocation base this leaves the stack top 8 modulo 16, and AArch64 `NewStackSwap()` directly installs it before calling `Enable()` and the command entry (`arch/aarch64-all/exec/newstackswap.c:26-35,50-74`). The smaller `Stack 2049` example does not trigger because the minimum-stack clamp repairs its extent to 40,960 bytes.

The same caller chain has an additional RISC-V case when the Shell command and Shell command set are explicitly built. On RV32, `Stack 40961` rounds to 40,964 bytes because `CLI_DEFAULTSTACK_UNIT` is four; on RV64 it rounds to 40,968 bytes because the unit is eight. Both exceed the 40,960-byte minimum, so `RunCommand()` does not repair them. `AllocMem()` returns a 16-byte-aligned base on these targets (`AROS_WORSTALIGN` and `MEMCHUNK_TOTAL` are 16), leaving `stk_Upper`/`stk_Pointer` four or eight bytes off alignment. The RISC-V32 and RV64 `NewStackSwap()` implementations install that pointer directly and call `Enable()` and the command entry without stack realignment (`arch/riscv-all/exec/newstackswap.c:28,52-81`; `arch/riscv64-all/exec/newstackswap.c:28,52-81`). The RISC-V standard ABI requires the stack pointer to be 16-byte aligned at procedure entry and throughout standard-ABI execution ([RISC-V psABI, §2.1](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/abi/v1.0/riscv-cc-procedure-calling-convention.html)). The RISC-V boot manifests comment out the `kernel-shell` and `kernel-shellcommands` dependencies, so this is an explicit-Shell-target trigger, not a default RISC-V boot-package claim.

The same Shell input is also selected for the PPC Efika workbench path: `AROS-chrp-ppc-efika` depends on `workbench-complete` (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src`), which selects `workbench-c` and its Shell command and command set (`workbench/mmakefile.src`, `workbench/c/Shell/mmakefile.src`). PPC Shell rounds `Stack 40961` to 40,964 bytes; the minimum clamp does not change it. With a 16-byte-aligned allocation base and 16-byte PPC ABI stack alignment, the resulting upper bound is four modulo 16. PPC `NewStackSwap()` subtracts the fixed 16-byte `SP_OFFSET` and copies the caller's PPC stack frames before switching (`arch/ppc-all/exec/newstackswap.c:39-54`); PPC ABI frame sizes preserve 16-byte granularity, so the switched stack remains four modulo 16 at the call. Thus this is a selected workbench Shell path, not only a hypothetical explicit build.

**Effect:** the swapped call path violates the target's stack-alignment contract. C code or compiler-generated code that relies on the required alignment can malfunction or fault; no particular failure is established solely from the source. **Scope:** selected AROS pthread custom-stack use on the direct-switch architectures above, the AArch64 Shell `Stack 40961` path, the PPC Efika workbench Shell `Stack 40961` path; and the explicitly built RISC-V32/RV64 Shell `Stack 40961` paths (the RISC-V boot manifests do not select Shell by default). x86-64 explicitly rounds the stack pointer down to `AROS_STACKALIGN` (`arch/x86_64-all/exec/newstackswap.c:36-45`), and hosted Unix delegates to `makecontext`, so neither is included. **Confidence:** high that the accepted sizes and selected implementations can pass a misaligned pointer; runtime impact depends on the called code and was not exercised. Public `StackSwap` callers outside these traced paths and caller-provided stack bounds remain open. Source-only; no stack switch, command, build, or runtime behavior was tested. See the [alignment and selected-caller audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8925).

<a id="ek8963"></a>
### EK8963 — i386 task setup can start ordinary C entry functions with a stack alignment different from the compiler's expected function-entry alignment.

`NewAddTask()` rounds the initial i386 task stack pointer down to a 16-byte boundary (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:274-285`; `arch/i386-all/include/aros/cpu.h:53`). The selected i386 `PrepareContext()` then pushes each argument through the highest `TASKTAG_ARGn` and pushes a fallback return address, without adding ABI padding (`arch/i386-all/exec/preparecontext.c:71-89`). For one argument, an aligned initial pointer becomes 12 modulo 16 after the argument push and 8 modulo 16 after the fallback push. The ordinary i386 C function-entry state after a normally aligned call is 12 modulo 16. The i386-PC dispatcher restores the saved ESP and EIP from the task context and returns through IRET, with no call shim that could correct the difference (`arch/i386-pc/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:48-53`; `arch/i386-pc/kernel/core_interrupts.s:142-156`).

This is exercised by selected Exec initialization callers: `ServiceTask` and `SupervisorAlertTask` are passed as ordinary C entry points with `TASKTAG_ARG1, SysBase` (`rom/exec/exec_init.c:326-329,347-349`; definitions at `rom/exec/service.c:18` and `rom/exec/supervisoralert.c:28`). **Effect:** if the selected compiler-generated entry code relies on the normal 16-byte i386 incoming-call boundary, these tasks begin with a stack four bytes out of phase; stack spills or aligned operations can malfunction or fault. **Affected configuration and trigger:** i386 builds using `PrepareContext()` for a task with one, two, three, five, six, or seven supplied stack arguments; the selected one-argument Exec service and supervisor tasks are concrete cases. Even argument counts leave the expected modulo-16 entry state, while four/eight arguments add a full 16/32 bytes and preserve it. **Confidence:** high for the stack arithmetic and the direct IRET restore; compiler reliance on the incoming boundary is conditional because generated toolchain options and machine code were not inspected. No task, build, or runtime behavior was exercised. Source-only. See the [task-context and caller audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1415).

<a id="ek8965"></a>
### EK8965 — A failed kernel platform initializer leaves `kernel.resource` published as if initialization succeeded.

`Kernel_Init()` adds its newly allocated base to Exec's resource list before invoking platform INITLIB callbacks (`rom/kernel/kernel_init.c:122-138`). `AddResource()` links the node and, for `kernel.resource`, sets Exec's global `KernelBase` and initializes Exec's memory-manager page-size state (`rom/exec/addresource.c:62-100`). If an INITLIB callback returns FALSE, `set_call_libfuncs()` stops at that callback and `Kernel_Init()` returns NULL, but neither path removes the resource, clears the global pointer, or frees/rolls back its initialized state (`compiler/libinit/libinit.c:37-50`; `kernel_init.c:130-132`). The normal `InitCode()` resident walk ignores `InitResident()`'s return and continues (`rom/exec/initcode.c:89-99`), so the failed resource remains reachable through the already-published Exec state.

Selected failure branches include: x86-64 PC `Platform_Init()` failing its `PlatformData` allocation (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/platform_init.c:231-233`); i386 PC `PlatformInit()` failing its 64 KiB system-stack allocation after publishing `kb_PlatformData` (`arch/i386-pc/kernel/platform_init.c:49-63`); RISC-V64 OpenSBI failing its `PlatformData` allocation (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/platform_init.c:31-35`); and m68k-Amiga failing its `PlatformData` allocation (`arch/m68k-all/kernel/platform_init.c:27-29,51`). **Effect:** callers can still find a `kernel.resource` whose platform initialization did not complete; fields may be absent or partially initialized, and later resource-vector consumers can operate on invalid platform state. The exact later failure depends on the selected platform and which consumer runs. **Affected configuration and trigger:** one of the selected platform initialization allocations fails during kernel resource startup on the configurations above. **Confidence:** high for publication-before-failure and missing rollback; later observable failure is conditional on subsequent use of incomplete state. No allocation failure or boot was induced. Source-only; wider platform rollback and consumer-by-consumer behavior remain open. See the [resource publication and selected INITLIB callers](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4150).

<a id="ek8988"></a>
### EK8988 — MinGW IRQ registration truncates the public IRQ number before validating it.

The public kernel vector declares `KrnAddIRQHandler(uint32_t irq, ...)` (`rom/kernel/kernel.conf:47`). The generic implementation rejects values at or above `HW_IRQ_COUNT` before registering them (`rom/kernel/addirqhandler.c:75-87`; `rom/kernel/kernel_base.h:50-55`, where the MinGW limit is 240 with `INTB_KERNEL == 16`). The selected MinGW override instead declares the vector argument as `uint8_t` and immediately allocates and stores it without a range check (`arch/all-mingw32/kernel/addirqhandler.c:17-43`; selected by `arch/all-mingw32/kernel/mmakefile.src:24-30`). A caller passing 256 therefore reaches the implementation as IRQ 0 and registers successfully; the host IRQ dispatcher indexes its 256-entry `irqs` array with that stored byte (`arch/all-mingw32/kernel/kernel_intr.c:77-89`). The handler can consequently run on the IRQ-0/VBlank event even though the caller requested an invalid IRQ. Values 240–255 are also accepted despite the generic limit.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** MinGW kernel builds, when a public `KrnAddIRQHandler()` caller supplies an IRQ value outside the supported range; 256 (or another value congruent to zero modulo 256) aliases the VBlank slot. **Confidence:** high for the signature narrowing, missing check, and aliasing behavior. A search of maintained MinGW callers found only timer, Wingdi keyboard/mouse/display, and emul.handler registrations, none shown to pass an out-of-range number; the concrete bad input is therefore an external/future API-client case, not a demonstrated checked-in trigger. Reject values `>= HW_IRQ_COUNT` before narrowing and use the public-width type in the override. No IRQ was registered or raised. Source-only. See the [MinGW IRQ API and dispatch audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4764).

<a id="ek8990"></a>
### EK8990 — Generic CopyMemQuick truncates 64-bit copy sizes at 128 GiB (conditional short or omitted copy; high source confidence).

The generic `CopyMemQuick()` accepts a pointer-sized `IPTR size`, divides it by four, then stores `size / 8` in 32-bit `ULONG high` while `low` holds the remainder (`rom/exec/copymemquick.c:14-22,53-65`). Its unrolled loop copies eight `ULONG`s per `high` iteration (`:77-88`). On 64-bit builds selecting this generic body, a valid aligned, non-overlapping copy of exactly 2^37 bytes (128 GiB) makes `high` equal 2^32 before truncation, so both counters are zero and the function copies nothing. Larger sizes copy only the extent represented by the counters modulo 128 GiB, leaving the remainder of the requested range unchanged.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** 64-bit targets that use the generic implementation, with a caller requesting an aligned, ULONG-multiple size of at least 128 GiB and satisfying the documented non-overlap precondition. The source explicitly notes that 64-bit sizes are not handled yet (`rom/exec/copymemquick.c:46-47`). **Effect:** the function silently omits the requested copy or copies only a short prefix, despite the public pointer-sized length. **Confidence:** high for the arithmetic and consequence. No selected TLSF allocation path reaches the 128 GiB threshold, and the broader caller census did not establish a currently selected request of that size; practical reachability depends on a large caller-managed memory range. m68k assembly and the i386 SSE replacement are separate implementations. No large buffer or copy was used. Source-only. See the [length arithmetic and selected-caller audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1868).

<a id="ek8992"></a>
### EK8992 — Reset callback timeout setup failure leaves callback waits unbounded (conditional shutdown stall; high source confidence).

On the non-supervisor path, `Exec_DoResetCallbacks()` tries to create a timer port, allocate a timer request, and open `timer.device` (`rom/exec/doresetcallbacks.c:85-112`). Any of these failures leaves `treq == NULL`; partial setup is cleaned up, but the function deliberately continues without a timeout. For each callback task that is successfully launched, the `treq` branch uses a timed `Wait()` only when the request exists; otherwise it calls `Wait(ResetCallbackSignal)` with no timer or other deadline (`:128-180`). The support task signals this bit only after the callback returns (`:31-43`).

**Effect:** if timeout setup fails and a callback task never returns or otherwise fails before signaling, the shutdown task waits indefinitely; later reset callbacks and the selected reset/power-off performer are not reached. **Affected configuration and trigger:** any selected non-supervisor shutdown/reboot path using `Exec_DoResetCallbacks()`, when port/request allocation or `timer.device` opening fails and a launched callback does not complete. The supervisor path runs callbacks directly with interrupts disabled and does not use this wait branch. **Confidence:** high for the unbounded wait on timer-setup failure; the combined resource-failure and non-completing callback condition is required. The selected generic, AArch64 and Unix shutdown wrappers reach this function, while other architecture reset entry points also call it; timer availability and callback completion vary by platform. No resource failure, callback hang, or shutdown was induced. Source-only. See the [reset caller and timeout setup audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1883).

<a id="ek8998"></a>
### EK8998 — POSIXC directory-stream positions drift on EOF and can return `..` again.

`readdir()` and `readdir64()` decrement `dir->pos` whenever `ExNext()` fails, including ordinary `ERROR_NO_MORE_ENTRIES`, then return NULL without incrementing it (`compiler/crt/posixc/readdir.c:104-118`; `readdir64.c`, corresponding branch). In `doupath` mode, the synthetic `.` and `..` entries are returned when positions are 0 and 1 (`readdir.c:91-102`; corresponding `readdir64.c` branch). After those two entries, the first EOF changes position 2 back to 1. A later call therefore returns the synthetic `..` entry again instead of remaining at end of stream. `telldir()` exposes the drift directly (`telldir.c:39-41`), and `seekdir()` uses the same position as its logical-to-physical enumeration cursor (`seekdir.c:37-61`); its inclusive `ExNext()` loop also means restoring a saved post-entry position advances past an entry.

**Effect:** after EOF, another `readdir()`/`readdir64()` call in `doupath` mode can produce a duplicate parent entry; saved positions can resume at a different entry than the one following the saved result. **Affected configuration and trigger:** POSIXC directory streams with `doupath` enabled, after reading the synthetic entries and reaching EOF; position restoration is affected in either path mode. **Confidence:** high for the counter transitions and corresponding returned entry; no filesystem enumeration was run. Keep EOF position unchanged and define/test a consistent mapping between opaque `telldir()` tokens and `seekdir()` enumeration state. Source-only. See the [directory iterator state audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L3669).

<a id="ek8999"></a>
### EK8999 — `scandir()` treats a directory-read error as successful end of directory.

Both `scandir()` and `scandir64()` stop their scan loop when `readdir()`/`readdir64()` returns NULL, then close the stream, publish the accumulated list, and return its nonnegative count without checking whether the read ended at EOF or failed (`compiler/crt/posixc/scandir.c:70-114`; `scandir64.c`, corresponding loop). The selected `readdir()` sets `errno` for a non-EOF `ExNext()` failure but returns the same NULL used for normal end-of-directory (`compiler/crt/posixc/readdir.c:104-117`). Thus a mid-scan DOS enumeration error is exposed as a successful partial result.

**Effect:** callers can mistake an incomplete directory list for a complete one. The checked WPS helper treats any nonnegative `scandir()` count as complete and selects from the list, but its object is guarded by `CONFIG_WPS_UFD`, absent from the checked-in default configuration (`workbench/network/WirelessManager/src/wps/wps_ufd.c:58-79`); no default selected caller is established. **Affected configuration and trigger:** POSIXC clients using `scandir()`/`scandir64()` when enumeration fails after returning one or more entries. **Confidence:** high that non-EOF read errors become partial nonnegative results; application impact depends on callers treating that result as complete. No DOS enumeration error was induced. Source-only. See the [scan loop and reader error audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L3593).

<a id="ek9000"></a>
### EK9000 — `scandir()` overwrites the original `opendir()` error while cleaning up.

When `opendir(dir)` fails, `scandir()` jumps to its shared failure label with `dirp` still NULL (`compiler/crt/posixc/scandir.c:53-68`). That cleanup frees the partial result list and unconditionally calls `closedir(dirp)` before returning -1 (`:116-123`). The selected `closedir(NULL)` sets `errno = EFAULT` and returns -1 (`compiler/crt/posixc/closedir.c:49-56`), replacing the original `opendir()` error such as the path's DOS-derived not-found or access error.

**Effect:** callers receive the wrong `errno` for a failed scan, which can misclassify or mishandle the underlying path/open failure. **Affected configuration and trigger:** POSIXC `scandir()` when `opendir()` fails; the same common cleanup pattern is present in `scandir64()`. **Confidence:** high for the overwritten error value. No open failure was induced. Source-only; distinct from EK8999, which concerns a later enumeration failure being returned as a successful partial count. See the [scan cleanup and `closedir()` behavior](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L3593).

<a id="ek9002"></a>
### EK9002 — Sam440 stack-probe alerts read beyond the task's saved CPU context (conditional out-of-bounds context copy; high source confidence).

When the common scheduler detects a task stack pointer outside its bounds, `core_Switch()` suspends that task and raises `AN_StackProbe` (`rom/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:76-107`). In the supervisor alert path, `Exec_ExtAlert()` special-cases this alert and passes the task's saved `et_RegFrame` as `AT_CPU` data (`rom/exec/alert.c:95-107`). The subsequent context copy uses `sizeof(struct ExceptionContext)` from the generic PPC CPU-context definition (`:117-124`; `arch/ppc-all/include/aros/cpucontext.h:14-34`).

On Sam440, the saved context is instead the platform `context_t`: 160 bytes of CPU state plus 264 bytes of FPU state, 424 bytes total (`arch/ppc-sam440/include/asm/amcc440.h:8-28`). Sam440 sets `kb_ContextSize = sizeof(context_t)` (`arch/ppc-sam440/kernel/kernel_startup.c:625`), and its selected `PrepareContext()` stores the `KrnCreateContext()` allocation in `et_RegFrame` (`arch/ppc-sam440/exec/preparecontext.c:73-79`). The generic PPC `ExceptionContext` is 968 bytes, so the alert-copy operation reads 544 bytes past that allocated saved context.

**Effect:** stack-probe alert formatting consumes bytes beyond the saved Sam440 context. This can disclose unrelated adjacent memory in the diagnostic and may fault if the read crosses an inaccessible boundary; neither a specific adjacent-data exposure nor a secondary fault is established. **Affected configuration and trigger:** an explicitly selected/built Sam440 kernel target when a task's stack check reaches the common scheduler's `AN_StackProbe` path and the supervisor alert formatter copies its CPU context. The local manifest selects no scheduler override, so it composes with the generic scheduler. The Sam440 package and kernel-link edges are active `#MM-` target rules (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:4-16,72`); this path is selected through the Sam440 boot/package target when requested. **Confidence:** high for the context-size mismatch and overread; adjacent allocation layout and resulting observable impact remain conditional. The ordinary Sam440 `RI` debug formatter's mislabeled CPU fields are a separate finding (EK9001). No task stack fault or alert was induced. Source-only. See the [stack-probe producer and context-size audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4410).

<a id="ek9013"></a>
### EK9013 — OOP method-base allocation wraps after exhausting its 22-bit interface-ID space.

OOP reserves ten low bits of each method ID for the method offset (`rom/oop/intern.h:47-48`). `init_mi_methodbase()` takes the 32-bit `ob_CurrentMethodBase`, increments it, then shifts the result left by ten without checking whether the 22-bit interface-base field has wrapped (`rom/oop/support.c:79-96`; `intern.h:317`). After 2^22 distinct base reservations, the shifted value repeats earlier method bases. `init_methodbase()` stores the resulting base in the IID bucket, and `OOP_GetMethodID()` adds the method offset to that stored base (`support.c:108-161`; `getmethodid.c:64-77`), so distinct interfaces can produce colliding numeric method IDs. The method-base counter is not rolled back when an IID bucket is released; the only decrement in `init_mi_methodbase()` is for a duplicate interface whose existing base is returned (`support.c:88-94`).

**Effect:** after counter wrap, a newly registered interface may share the numeric method-ID range of an earlier interface, making method dispatch ambiguous or directing a call to an unintended interface method. **Affected configuration and trigger:** OOP users that cumulatively reserve at least 2^22 distinct multiple-interface method bases during one OOPBase lifetime; dynamic class teardown does not restore the counter. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked shift and repeated values; the required extreme number of distinct reservations is not established in production workloads. The checked-in examples do not approach the limit. No class or method dispatch was run. Source-only. See the [method-base counter and lifetime audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L3633).

<a id="ek9014"></a>
### EK9014 — OOP attribute-base allocation wraps and aliases earlier attribute IDs after 2^22 unique bases.

`OOP_ObtainAttrBase()` keeps the next numeric base in the 32-bit `ob_CurrentAttrBase`, pre-increments it for each newly assigned interface, then shifts it left by the ten method-offset bits without checking capacity (`rom/oop/obtainattrbase.c:71-87,97-118`; `rom/oop/intern.h:47-48,318`). After 2^22 distinct bases, the shift wraps to zero. Zero is the documented failure result, so that call reports failure even though it has already inserted the new IID bucket; the following unique interface receives base 1 again and aliases an earlier attribute-ID range. `OOP_GetAttrBase()` has a corresponding unchecked increment-and-shift when it lazily initializes a bucket's attribute base (`rom/oop/getattrbase.c:73-92`).

**Effect:** after wrap, attribute IDs from distinct interfaces can collide; the boundary call can also leave a bucket with no successful returned base/reference, and later calls can reuse a live numeric range. **Affected configuration and trigger:** OOP users cumulatively assigning 2^22 distinct attribute bases during one OOPBase lifetime through `OOP_ObtainAttrBase()` or the lazy `OOP_GetAttrBase()` path. Bucket release does not decrement the monotonic counter. **Confidence:** high for the arithmetic and zero/alias sequence; the extreme distinct-interface count is not established in production workloads. No base was allocated. Source-only. See the [attribute-base counter and bucket-lifetime audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L3636).

<a id="ek9015"></a>
### EK9015 — POSIXC readdir leaves the public directory-entry inode number uninitialized.

The POSIXC public `struct dirent` exposes `d_fileno` and aliases it as `d_ino`; `struct dirent64` has a `d_ino` field (`compiler/crt/posixc/include/aros/posixc/dirent.h:38-68`). Neither `readdir()` nor `readdir64()` assigns that field while filling an entry: they set the name, record length, and type, then return the stream's embedded entry (`compiler/crt/posixc/readdir.c:135-167`; `readdir64.c:135-166`). `opendir()` and `fdopendir()` allocate `DIR` with non-clearing `malloc()` and initialize the descriptor/position and a name terminator, not the inode field (`opendir.c:74-79,146-149`; `fdopendir.c:73-78,96-98`). Therefore callers receive an indeterminate or stale inode value, and `scandir()` copies that field into its allocated result entries (`scandir.c:93-100`; `scandir64.c:93-100`).

**Effect:** clients relying on the public inode field receive no file identity from the directory stream; the value may reflect prior heap contents. **Affected configuration and trigger:** POSIXC `readdir()`/`readdir64()` callers that read `d_ino`/`d_fileno`, including callers consuming entries copied by `scandir*()`. A repository search found no checked-in consumer of these fields, so no in-tree application consequence is claimed. **Confidence:** high that the readers leave the fields unwritten and that their stream storage is not zero-initialized; caller-visible impact requires a client to use the field. No directory was enumerated. Source-only. See the [dirent layout and reader field audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L3591).

<a id="ek9022"></a>
### EK9022 — The x86-64 StackSwap assembly calls C vectors with a misaligned stack.

The selected x86-64 `StackSwap` entry is entered through the normal C ABI with RSP 8 modulo 16. It pushes RBX, then pushes RSI before calling the `Disable` vector; that makes pre-call RSP 8 modulo 16, so the callee enters with RSP 0 modulo 16. After returning and restoring RSI, it pushes RSI again before calling `FindTask`, repeating the same misalignment (`arch/x86_64-all/exec/stackswap.S:9-28`). Under the x86-64 ABI, these C calls must have pre-call RSP aligned to 16 bytes, yielding callee-entry RSP 8 modulo 16.

**Effect:** a C callee or compiler-generated prologue that relies on the required entry alignment can use misaligned stack storage and malfunction or fault. **Affected configuration and trigger:** x86-64 builds when the deprecated `StackSwap` vector is invoked; the assembly is selected in the architecture Exec manifest (`arch/x86_64-all/exec/mmakefile.src:26-29`). Its public convenience declaration is gated by `__AROS_GIMME_DEPRECATED_STACKSWAP__` (`rom/exec/exec.conf:31-56`), and the checked-in production caller/build census did not establish that gate as enabled. Thus the assembly defect is confirmed, while an ordinary selected product caller remains unproven. The later `Enable()` call on the replacement stack assumes caller-provided alignment and is a separate condition tracked by EK8962. **Confidence:** high for the stack arithmetic and ABI mismatch; observable failure depends on the called vector code and whether this deprecated path is used. No stack swap or build was run. Source-only. See the [assembly call-site and API-selection audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L50).

<a id="ek9023"></a>
### EK9023 — The x86-64 PC page-table backend does not enforce MAP_Executable permissions.

The x86-64 PC `KrnSetProtection()` wrapper translates the flag set into present, writable, and user bits; `MAP_Executable` only participates in its present-bit test (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/setprotection.c:15-35`). It calls `core_ProtKernelArea()`/`core_ProtPage()` with no executable parameter, and the page update writes only RW, user and present bits (`mmu.c:183-250`). Initial 2-MiB PDEs explicitly set `nx = 0` (`mmu.c:66-83`), dynamically mapped 2-MiB PDEs do the same (`mapglobal.c:69-86`), and the 4-KiB split/update path never sets NX. The BSP and AP transition code enables long mode but does not enable NXE (`bootstrap/cpu.c:224-230`; `smpbootstrap.s:114-119`). Consequently a protection request that omits `MAP_Executable` does not make a present page non-executable; the backend does not distinguish executable from non-executable mappings.

**Effect:** callers cannot use this backend to revoke execute permission; code and data pages remain executable even when the requested attributes omit `MAP_Executable`. **Affected configuration and trigger:** x86-64 PC kernel mappings protected through `KrnSetProtection()` or `KrnMapGlobal()` where the caller expects a non-executable mapping. **Confidence:** high that the selected backend does not set NX and that its flag translation ignores execute permission. Practical default in-tree reachability is limited: the selected startup protection calls directly update supervisor/RW bits, the `CreateSegList()` W^X call is behind the Apple-only `__AROSPLATFORM_WXSEG__` configuration, and the checked-in x86-64 PC startup does not establish a working generic `KrnAllocPages()` caller (`kb_PageSize` has no selected assignment; see EK9024 coverage). Thus no current default caller requiring execute revocation is claimed; direct external/future kernel-resource clients remain affected. No page permission was changed, no instruction was fetched, and no hardware behavior was tested. Source-only. See the [selected permission translation and caller audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1753).

<a id="ek9024"></a>
### EK9024 — Exhausting the x86-64 PC 4-KiB split-table pool silently skips page protection changes.

The x86-64 PC MMU reserves a fixed pool of 32 page-table pages for splitting initially mapped 2-MiB PDEs into 4-KiB PTEs (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/mmu.c:16,168-172`). When `core_ProtPage()` reaches a still-large PDE after all 32 splits have been consumed, it logs exhaustion and returns without changing that page's mapping or reporting failure (`:205-220`). Its caller `core_ProtKernelArea()` is void and continues through the requested range; `KrnSetProtection()` is also void, so callers cannot detect the missed change (`:253-262`; `arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/setprotection.c:35-56`).

**Effect:** the target page remains mapped with the old permissions. If this occurs during `KrnFreePages()`, the wrapper still calls `mm_FreePages()` after the failed permission clear (`rom/kernel/freepages.c:47-52`), potentially returning pages to the allocator while their old mapping remains present; subsequent alias/use effects depend on caller and allocator behavior. **Affected configuration and trigger:** x86-64 PC after protection requests have split 32 distinct 2-MiB regions, followed by a permission change in another still-large region. Large startup protection spans could consume the pool, but the checked-in kernel-image extent does not establish that it does; no default allocator-backed free path is established because `KrnAllocPages()` returns NULL when `kb_PageSize` is zero and no selected assignment was found. Direct external kernel-resource callers remain a possible trigger. **Confidence:** high that a 33rd split request silently leaves protection unchanged and that the API exposes no status; production reachability and any resulting reuse effect are conditional. No page-table pool was exhausted, no page was freed, and no mapping was changed. Source-only. See the [split-pool and caller reachability audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1753).

<a id="ek9030"></a>
### EK9030 — RISC-V OpenSBI can reuse a stale PLIC context when ACPI fills a missing controller base.

The OpenSBI FDT parser initializes `plic_context` to -1, but can later assign a boot-hart context from a PLIC node's `interrupts-extended` property independently of whether the PLIC `reg` property supplied a usable base (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_fdt.c:85-89,190-225`). Startup invokes ACPI PLIC parsing whenever `plic_base` is zero (`kernel_startup.c:661-668`). `krnACPIPLICInfo()` resets `plic_ncontexts` but leaves the prior scalar `plic_context` unchanged; it sets a new scalar only when it collected at least one enabled RINTC context (`kernel_acpi.c:320-391`). If ACPI supplies a PLIC record but no enabled RINTC contexts, the count remains zero and the old FDT scalar survives. `krnPLICInit()` then treats that nonnegative scalar as valid, copies it into `plic_ctxlist[0]`, and enables the controller using it (`kernel_plic.c:73-97,113-130`).

**Effect:** startup can configure PLIC threshold/enable/claim operations for a context inherited from the partial FDT rather than one validated against the ACPI controller description. Interrupt delivery or completion may then target the wrong supervisor context or fail; exact hardware behavior depends on whether the stale numeric context is valid for the ACPI-described controller. **Affected configuration and trigger:** OpenSBI RISC-V startup where the EFI stub provides both an FDT and ACPI RSDP, the FDT contains a PLIC supervisor-context entry but no usable PLIC base, ACPI supplies a PLIC base, and ACPI yields no enabled RINTC context entries. The EFI stub records FDT and ACPI table pointers independently (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/efi_stub.c:757-797`). No checked-in firmware configuration establishes this inconsistent mixed description. **Confidence:** high for the stale scalar and fallback control flow; context mismatch and resulting interrupt failure are conditional on the firmware descriptions. No ACPI table, PLIC, boot, or interrupt was exercised. Source-only. See the [FDT-to-ACPI fallback and context audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1710).

<a id="ek9032"></a>
### EK9032 — GenModule can read past a stack buffer when generating a proto header for a long include name.

`tools/genmodule/config.c:1300-1305` duplicates a configured `includename` without a length limit, then creates its uppercase form at `:1422-1426`. In `writeincproto()` the generated proto path is opened before the include-name guard is built (`tools/genmodule/writeincproto.c:15-23,132-141`). For a name whose uppercase form begins with a nondigit and has at least 256 bytes, `strncpy(define, ..., sizeof define)` fills all of `define[256]` without a terminating NUL. The following `fprintf()` uses `define` as `%s` twice (`:143-155`), so formatting reads beyond the array until it encounters an unrelated NUL; generated output may contain stray bytes or the generator may fail while formatting it.

**Trigger and scope:** custom GenModule configuration with `writeincludes` and `includes` enabled, a nondigit-leading `includename` at least 256 bytes long, and an output path the host can open. The name is also used in the output filename (`:15-18`), so ordinary filesystems with a 255-byte component limit reject a single 256-byte component before reaching the copy; a longer-component filesystem or a path-like include name with usable existing directories is needed for the shown path to be reachable. Names beginning with a digit take the `snprintf()` branch and are not affected by this specific missing-terminator path. Checked-in configurations do not establish a triggering name. **Confidence:** high for the unterminated copy and subsequent out-of-bounds string read; limited/conditional practical reachability. No generator, custom configuration, or host filesystem boundary was exercised. Source-only. See the [GenModule writer review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L696).

<a id="ek9033"></a>
### EK9033 — Efika PCI unmap leaves Radeon BAR translations installed after expunge.

The Efika PCI HIDD implements `MapPCI()` by calling `KrnMapGlobal()` for the requested range, but its class method list does not override `UnmapPCI()` (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/pci/driverclass.c:155-165`; `pci-efika.conf`). OOP therefore dispatches unmap to the generic PCIDriver method, which is empty (`rom/hidds/pci/pcidriverclass.c:181-188`). The Efika package manifest includes both `pci-efika` and Radeon (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:68-75`). After successful Radeon initialization, `ATI_Expunge()` calls `HIDD_PCIDriver_UnmapPCI()` for the framebuffer, MMIO and ROM ranges before clearing its retained PCI-device pointer (`workbench/hidds/radeon/ati_init.c:329-340`); the library registers this cleanup with `ADD2EXPUNGELIB` (`:352`). Since the selected Efika method is the inherited no-op, none of the `KrnMapGlobal()` translations are removed. Efika's `KrnUnmapGlobal()` clears the corresponding PTE valid bit, while `mmu_map_page()` only chooses entries whose valid bit is clear (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/mmu.c:112-158,427-445`), so retained mappings also keep those hash-table slots unavailable for later mappings.

**Trigger and scope:** an Efika package containing the Radeon HIDD successfully initializes a supported Radeon device, then the Radeon library is expunged. The Efika package target is optional in the top-level dependency graph; no default-machine inclusion is claimed. The separate Radeon initialization-failure path is excluded because the supported-card table selects initialization routines that return success (`workbench/hidds/radeon/ids.c:10-112`; `workbench/hidds/radeon/radeon_driver.c:2265-2430`). **Effect:** framebuffer, MMIO and ROM translations remain installed after Radeon expunge, consuming Efika PTE slots and potentially causing later `KrnMapGlobal()` calls that hash into those full groups to fail. **Confidence:** high for selected dispatch, no-op cleanup, and persistent PTE entries; practical later mapping failure depends on subsequent address hashes and available PTE slots. No expunge, mapping, allocation failure, PCI operation or build was run. Source-only. See the [Efika PCI unmap caller recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L3763).

<a id="ek9035"></a>
### EK9035 — x86-64 `KrnMapGlobal()` reports success without mapping a range that ends at the top of the virtual address space (conditional missing final-page mapping; high source confidence).

The selected x86-64 PC implementation computes the exclusive aligned end with `vend = (vaddr + length + MAP_2M_MASK) & ~MAP_2M_MASK` (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/mapglobal.c:105-109`). The arithmetic is performed in unsigned `IPTR`; if the requested range ends exactly at the address-space boundary, `vaddr + length` wraps to zero, the rounded `vend` is zero, and the loop condition `vcur < vend` is false. The function therefore skips the final mapping and returns success (`:139-144`). For example, a 2 MiB-aligned mapping of length 2 MiB beginning at `0xffffffffffe00000` ends at `2^64` and takes this path.

**Trigger and scope:** caller requests a range whose exclusive end is exactly `2^64` on the selected x86-64 PC backend. The selected PCIPC, ATA, NVMe and VESAGfx caller review did not identify such a request; those callers use identity-mapped physical BAR/framebuffer ranges, and no checked-in layout establishes a boundary-ending range. The defect is in the generic public `KrnMapGlobal()` implementation for this target, so external callers remain possible. **Effect:** the API reports success although the requested final 2 MiB page was not installed; a subsequent access can still fault or use a prior mapping. **Confidence:** high for the arithmetic/control-flow case, conditional for occurrence in a maintained caller. No mapping, page fault, BAR probe or build was exercised. Source-only. See the [x86-64 global-map review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1752).

<a id="ek9042"></a>
### EK9042 — OpenSBI UEFI startup can allocate the FDT primary span as RAM after replacing it with a smaller EFI usable-region list (conditional allocation from EFI-reserved or absent memory; high source confidence).

When EFI usable regions are available, startup resets `fdtinfo.nregions` and replaces the detailed bank array, but does not reset the primary `mem_base`/`mem_size` inherited from the FDT (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:575-595`). It updates those scalar bounds only when an individual EFI region's **size** exceeds the previous FDT `mem_size` (`:591-595`). Thus if the FDT's selected bank is larger than every coalesced EFI usable region, the EFI region list becomes authoritative for later bank processing while the primary scalar extent remains the FDT extent. Startup later sets `memhigh = mem_base + mem_size` and creates the primary system MemHeader from `memlow` (aligned `__kernel_end`) through `memhigh` (`:781-788,890-895`). It does not subtract EFI-unusable holes from that primary span.

**Trigger and scope:** OpenSBI RISC-V UEFI boot with both a parseable FDT and EFI usable-region list, where the FDT-selected largest bank is larger than each EFI coalesced usable region and its end extends beyond the valid RAM containing the kernel. This requires inconsistent or stale firmware descriptions; no checked-in board/firmware map establishes it. The selected EFI stub accepts conventional, boot-services and loader memory as usable and coalesces adjacent ranges (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/efi_stub.c:481-520`), but the kernel's scalar comparison can still retain larger FDT bounds. **Effect:** the early primary MemHeader can advertise addresses beyond the EFI-usable range, so ordinary allocations may use absent or reserved physical memory and fail during later access. **Confidence:** high for the retained scalar and untrimmed primary extent; conditional on the firmware topology and physical extent mismatch. No firmware map, allocation, boot or hardware was exercised. Source-only. See the [EFI/FDT memory handoff review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1722).

<a id="ek9050"></a>
### EK9050 — PowerPC `SuperState()` enters supervisor mode but always returns the token that means no transition occurred (conditional privilege-state leak; high source confidence).

Both selected PowerPC `SuperState()` overrides issue `SC_SUPERSTATE` and then unconditionally return `NULL` (`arch/ppc-chrp/exec/superstate.c:16-22`; `arch/ppc-sam440/exec/superstate.c:17-23`). The corresponding syscall handlers save the incoming MSR in the syscall result register and clear `MSR_PR` (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/syscall.c:38-41`; `arch/ppc-sam440/kernel/syscall.c:87-90`), but the wrappers do not return that value. The public contract says a user-to-supervisor transition returns the prior supervisor stack token and reserves `NULL` for callers already in supervisor mode; callers must not invoke `UserState()` for that NULL case (`rom/exec/superstate.c:22-33`).

**Trigger and scope:** direct `SuperState()` call from user mode on PowerPC CHRP/Efika or Sam440, followed by the documented `if (token) UserState(token)` pattern. Since the override returns NULL after the syscall has cleared `MSR_PR`, the caller skips restoration and remains privileged. No selected ordinary in-tree caller following this conditional pattern was found; CHRP `PrepareContext()` deliberately calls `UserState(NULL)` for its separate task-context setup, and the PowerPC `Supervisor()` wrappers' unconditional restore-on-NULL behavior is tracked separately as EK560. **Confidence:** high for the wrapper/syscall mismatch and contract; external/direct caller impact is conditional. No privilege transition or build was exercised. Source-only. See the [PowerPC privilege-wrapper review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1626).

<a id="ek9051"></a>
### EK9051 — realtime.library can unload Pulse before its worker exits during final expunge.

The realtime expunge hook calls `FreeTimer()` and immediately returns (`workbench/libs/realtime/realtime_init.c:52-61`). `FreeTimer()` removes the VBlank server and sends CTRL-C to `rtb_PulseTask`, but does not wait for task termination (`realtime_timer.c:78-84`). The Pulse loop handles CTRL-C only after its current tick completes; during a tick it reads and mutates `RealTimeBase` state, traverses conductors and players, and may call client hooks while holding `RT_CONDUCTORS` (`pulse.c:46-57,67-76,78-159`). The worker does not own an open reference to realtime.library. Generated final expunge removes and frees the library base and returns its segment list (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1558-1587`); `CloseLibrary()` and `RemLibrary()` call the expunge vector under `Forbid()` (`rom/exec/closelibrary.c:69-75`; `remlibrary.c:64-70`), but Exec documents that `Forbid()` is processor-local on ExecSMP (`rom/exec/forbid.c:55-60`).

**Trigger and scope:** ExecSMP build, final library close/removal overlaps a Pulse task already executing a tick on another CPU. The expunge caller can free the base and unload the segment while the worker still uses library state or code; sending CTRL-C only causes it to exit after the in-progress tick. The prior UP blocked-hook scenario is not established by the selected caller audit and is excluded. **Consequence:** worker accesses freed realtime state or resumes in unloaded module code, potentially disrupting the worker and the caller-owned state it traverses. **Confidence:** high for missing join and cross-CPU Forbid semantics; actual overlap is scheduling-dependent. No expunge, tick, task or SMP interleaving was run. Source-only. See the [realtime worker/expunge review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L141).

<a id="ek9053"></a>
### EK9053 — ExternalSync publishes unlocked or stale external-time windows to the Pulse worker.

`ExternalSync()` validates `player`, `pl_Source` and `PLAYERF_EXTSYNC`, then writes `cdt_ExternalTime`, `cdt_MaxExternalTime`, and `CONDUCTF_GOTTICK` without taking `LockRealTime(RT_CONDUCTORS)` (`workbench/libs/realtime/externalsync.c:64-73`). Pulse takes that lock before reading the same fields (`pulse.c:76-107`). A tick can therefore observe a partially published window (or the writes can overlap directly on ExecSMP). Separately, `SetPlayerAttrsA(PLAYER_ExtSync)` changes the external-source flags under the same lock (`setplayerattrsa.c:263-292`), so an already validated call may be delayed while a source is disabled and another source enabled, then publish the old source's bounds and `GOTTICK` into their shared conductor (`externalsync.c:64-73`; `setplayerattrsa.c:263-292`).

**Trigger and scope:** an external client calls `ExternalSync()` while Pulse processes that conductor, or the client/source designation changes between validation and publication. This is an unsynchronized public API path; repository search found no checked-in caller, so the trigger depends on external library use. **Effect:** Pulse can consume bounds from different updates or accept stale bounds as a tick for a newly designated synchronizer, causing the conductor clock to align to or wait on an unintended time window. **Confidence:** high for the missing lock and shared fields; occurrence and timing are conditional. No sync call, tick, source switch or SMP interleaving was run. Source-only. See the [realtime shared-state review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L144).

<a id="ek9054"></a>
### EK9054 — SetConductorState races the Pulse worker and traverses a mutable player list without its lock.

`SetConductorState()` reads and writes `cdt_State`, `cdt_Flags`, and `cdt_ClockTime`, and traverses `cdt_Players`, without taking `LockRealTime(RT_CONDUCTORS)` (`workbench/libs/realtime/setconductorstate.c:86-105,108-225`). Pulse takes that lock while reading/updating conductor state and traversing the same player list (`pulse.c:76-159`). `DeletePlayer()` also takes the lock to unlink the player and possibly its conductor, then frees both objects (`deleteplayer.c:68-89`). Thus a state change can overlap a Pulse tick or a deletion despite those operations using the documented list lock; the unlocked traversal may continue through a removed/freed node.

**Trigger and scope:** selected Animation datatype start/stop/pause/shuttle methods call `SetConductorState()` (`workbench/classes/datatypes/animation/animationclass.c:1376,1443,1708,1728,1754`), while the asynchronous Pulse worker runs from the VBlank signal. An overlapping state call or player deletion can race with Pulse; independently, an unlocked `SetConductorState()` traversal can race with a concurrent `DeletePlayer()`. The same public APIs are available to external realtime.library clients. **Effect:** conductor state/time may be observed inconsistently, and traversal can use a player/conductor node after deletion; the exact outcome depends on interleaving. **Confidence:** high for the missing lock and shared mutable list/state; runtime overlap depends on scheduling and API use. No animation, API call, deletion or interleaving was run. Source-only. See the [realtime state/list synchronization review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L145).

<a id="ek9055"></a>
### EK9055 — PLAYER_ExtSync dereferences a player with no conductor instead of reporting failure.

`SetPlayerAttrsA()` handles `PLAYER_ExtSync` by first obtaining the `RT_CONDUCTORS` semaphore and then dereferencing `player->pl_Source->cdt_Flags` without checking whether `pl_Source` is NULL (`workbench/libs/realtime/setplayerattrsa.c:263-277`). `CreatePlayerA()` allocates a cleared Player and passes the caller's tags directly to this setter (`createplayera.c:127-157`); neither API documents that `PLAYER_Conductor` is mandatory, and the ExtSync tag is described as an attempt to become the external source (`createplayera.c:58-61,94-96`). A caller can therefore create or update an unassociated player with `PLAYER_ExtSync=TRUE` and enter the NULL dereference. The branch does not reach `UnlockRealTime()` after the fault (`setplayerattrsa.c:292`); that semaphore remains held if the fault returns to the system.

**Trigger and scope:** selected realtime.library `SetPlayerAttrsA()` or `CreatePlayerA()` with `PLAYER_ExtSync=TRUE` while the player has no conductor. A directly created player with no `PLAYER_Conductor` tag starts with `pl_Source == NULL`; a failed/absent conductor assignment can also leave it unassociated. **Effect:** the caller faults during tag processing, and the conductor semaphore can remain locked, blocking later conductor operations. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked dereference and missing unlock; actual caller impact depends on using the documented optional-tag combination. No API call or fault was induced. Source-only. See the [realtime player-tag review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L146).

<a id="ek9056"></a>
### EK9056 — CreatePlayerA leaks and leaves a linked player when SetPlayerAttrsA rejects a later tag.

`CreatePlayerA()` allocates a cleared Player, calls `SetPlayerAttrsA()`, and returns NULL on failure without freeing or unlinking the allocation (`workbench/libs/realtime/createplayera.c:127-157`). With `PLAYER_Conductor` before `PLAYER_ExtSync` in the tag list, the setter first inserts the new Player into the conductor list (`setplayerattrsa.c:120-158`); if that conductor already has an external synchronizer, the later ExtSync case unlocks and returns FALSE (`:263-274`). The constructor then loses the only returned pointer while the Player remains linked. The conflict branch also returns without setting the optional `PLAYER_ErrorCode` output, despite the documented output contract (`createplayera.c:97-108`; `setplayerattrsa.c:263-274`).

**Trigger and scope:** caller constructs a second player on a conductor already marked `CONDUCTF_EXTERNAL`, with tags ordered so `PLAYER_Conductor` is processed before `PLAYER_ExtSync=TRUE`. The checked-in tree has no `PLAYER_ExtSync` caller; this is a public API/client trigger. **Effect:** `CreatePlayerA()` reports failure but the allocated Player remains in the conductor's list with no caller-held pointer to delete it, retaining the Player and potentially the otherwise-empty conductor; an optional error-code variable may retain its prior value. **Confidence:** high for the allocation, enqueue, later rejection, and no-cleanup return sequence; occurrence depends on the tag sequence and existing external source. No player creation or conflict was run. Source-only. See the [realtime constructor/tag failure review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L146).

<a id="ek9057"></a>
### EK9057 — Reassigning a linked player leaves its old conductor list corrupted (conditional public API defect; high source confidence).

For every `PLAYER_Conductor` tag, `SetPlayerAttrsA()` resolves or creates a conductor, assigns it to `player->pl_Source`, then enqueues the Player into the new conductor list under `RT_CONDUCTORS` (`workbench/libs/realtime/setplayerattrsa.c:120-158`). It never removes a player that was already linked to its previous conductor. The node's `ln_Succ`/`ln_Pred` links are reused by the second `Enqueue()`, while the old list still has links to that node; this leaves the old list's chain inconsistent and the player no longer safely linked in both lists.

**Trigger and scope:** external client calls `SetPlayerAttrsA()` on an already-linked player with a `PLAYER_Conductor` tag naming a different public conductor (or re-enqueues it into the same list). The API documents the same tags for `SetPlayerAttrsA()` as `CreatePlayerA()` and does not document a one-time-only assignment restriction (`setplayerattrsa.c:41-48`; `createplayera.c:58-61`). Checked-in uses of `PLAYER_Conductor` are constructor tag lists, where the Player is new and unlinked; no maintained reassigning caller was found. **Effect:** old conductor traversal/removal can follow inconsistent list links, potentially losing nodes or traversing an invalid chain. **Confidence:** high for the missing unlink and reused intrusive-list node; practical impact requires a live reassignment. No conductor reassignment or list traversal was run. Source-only. See the [realtime player-list update review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L146).

<a id="ek9058"></a>
### EK9058 — SetPlayerAttrsA searches and adopts public conductors outside the required list lock (conditional concurrency defect; high source confidence).

`FindConductor()` walks the shared conductor list without locking and explicitly documents that callers must hold `LockRealTime(RT_CONDUCTORS)` (`workbench/libs/realtime/findconductor.c:26-40,61-74`). The `PLAYER_Conductor` case in `SetPlayerAttrsA()` calls it before taking the lock; the lock is acquired only later to enqueue the Player (`setplayerattrsa.c:130-157`). If lookup returns a conductor that is concurrently removed and freed by `DeletePlayer()` after its last member is deleted (`deleteplayer.c:74-88`), the setter can subsequently enqueue through the stale pointer. If concurrent callers both fail to find a name, each can allocate a public conductor and add it under the lock without rechecking (`setplayerattrsa.c:132-140,309-355`), leaving duplicate public names.

**Trigger and scope:** concurrent `PLAYER_Conductor` assignment or player construction against conductor creation/deletion, through selected realtime.library code on SMP or during preemptive task scheduling. No checked-in caller demonstrates concurrent conductor management; this remains a public API concurrency condition. **Effect:** a lookup/use race can access a freed conductor, while simultaneous creation can publish duplicate same-name conductors and split clients across them. **Confidence:** high for the missing required lock and lack of a creation recheck; occurrence depends on concurrent API calls. No conductor creation/deletion or interleaving was run. Source-only. See the [realtime conductor-list locking review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L146).

<a id="ek9059"></a>
### EK9059 — A conductor allocation failure can leak a Player or report success without attaching it (conditional allocation-failure defect; high source confidence).

When a `PLAYER_Conductor` tag names a missing public conductor (or requests a private one), `SetPlayerAttrsA()` calls `createConductor()`. On allocation failure that helper returns NULL and, if supplied, writes `RTE_NOMEMORY` (`workbench/libs/realtime/setplayerattrsa.c:124-140,309-323`). The caller then handles the NULL result inconsistently (`:159-166`): if `PLAYER_ErrorCode` is present it overwrites the error with `RTE_NOCONDUCTOR` and returns FALSE; if absent it falls through and ultimately returns TRUE despite not attaching the player. `CreatePlayerA()` has already allocated the Player and simply returns NULL when the setter reports failure, without freeing it (`createplayera.c:127-157`).

**Trigger and scope:** conductor allocation failure while creating a player with a `PLAYER_Conductor` tag. With an error-output tag, the Player allocation leaks and the error misreports memory exhaustion as no conductor; without it, `CreatePlayerA()` can return a non-NULL Player with `pl_Source == NULL` and no conductor membership. The tag/API allows this allocation path; no checked-in caller demonstrates memory pressure at this point. **Effect:** leaked Player on the failure-return path or a successful but unattached object on the no-error path. **Confidence:** high for the branch behavior and ownership; occurrence depends on allocation failure. No allocation failure or API call was induced. Source-only. See the [realtime constructor allocation review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L146).

<a id="ek9061"></a>
### EK9061 — PPC CacheClearU performs no cache-line maintenance for its whole-cache request.

Generic `CacheClearU()` requests a full I- and D-cache clear by calling `CacheClearE(0, ~0, CACRF_ClearI | CACRF_ClearD)` (`rom/exec/cacheclearu.c:58-64`). PPC32 selects `arch/ppc-all/exec/cachecleare.c`; it rounds `address` and `address + length` to 32-byte lines using `IPTR` arithmetic, then performs `dcbf` and `icbi` only while `start < end` (`:18-38,49-57`). With the all-cache request, the 32-bit endpoint `(0 + 0xffffffff + 31)` wraps to `0x1e`, rounds down to zero, and both loops are empty. Thus the public whole-cache call returns without executing either cache-line operation.

**Trigger and scope:** any `CacheClearU()` use on PPC CHRP/Efika or Sam440, which inherit the PPC32 `CacheClearE` implementation and do not replace `CacheClearU`. **Effect:** instruction and data cache contents remain uncleared despite the API request; callers relying on a full flush may observe stale instructions or data. The selected `SetFunction()` caller patches pointer-sized jump-vector data and does not establish stale executable code as a maintained consequence; other client reliance remains caller-dependent. **Confidence:** high for the arithmetic wrap and empty loops; impact depends on a caller needing whole-cache maintenance. No cache operation or hardware behavior was exercised. Source-only. See the [PPC cache-clear review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1581).

<a id="ek9062"></a>
### EK9062 — The optional x86-64 PC early exception screen labels several saved registers with the wrong values.

The optional early trap handler saves registers in push order RAX through R15, then passes the resulting stack pointer to `print_crash_info()` (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_early.c:347-373`). After those 15 pushes, `stack[0]` is R15, `stack[7]` is R8, `stack[8]` is RBP, `stack[9]` is RDI, `stack[10]` is RSI, `stack[11]` is RDX, `stack[12]` is RCX, `stack[13]` is RBX, and `stack[14]` is RAX; the interrupt number follows at `stack[15]`. The dump labels RAX through RBP using `stack[15]` down through `stack[9]`, shifting each by one slot, and labels saved RBP (`stack[8]`) as RSP (`:263-288`). RSP is not among the 15 saved registers. The displayed vector (`stack[15]`), error code (`stack[16]`), RIP (`stack[17]`) and flags (`stack[19]`) are correctly indexed; they are not part of this finding.

**Trigger and scope:** early exception occurs with `KERNEL_USE_EARLYTRAP` enabled in the x86-64 PC kernel build; the checked-in manifest does not enable this option by default (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/mmakefile.src:26-30`). **Effect:** the diagnostic screen misidentifies saved values for RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, RBP and the unavailable RSP value, reducing the usefulness of early crash diagnosis. **Confidence:** high for the stack layout and index mismatch. No trap or display was induced. Source-only. See the [early-trap frame audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1748).

<a id="ek9064"></a>
### EK9064 — `TaskTag_CPUAffinity` queries can retain bits from a reused output mask.

**Finding:** The `QueryTaskTagList()` contract says `TaskTag_CPUAffinity` returns the task's affinity mask (`rom/task/QueryTaskTagList.c:45-52`). Its implementation loops over allowed CPU IDs and calls `KrnGetCPUMask()` for each set bit, but never clears the caller's buffer first (`:141-151`). The selected ARM32, AArch64, and PC mask helpers add bits to the supplied storage (`arch/arm-native/kernel/getcpumask.c:21-22`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/getcpumask.c:21-22`; PC implementation and APIC helper at `arch/all-pc/kernel/getcpumask.c:20`, `apic.c:115-132`). A reused nonzero buffer therefore retains bits that are absent from the task's current affinity.

The selected in-tree `smpaffinity` test clears its output mask before each query (`developer/debug/test/smp/smpaffinity.c:59-75,94-108`), so that caller does not demonstrate the stale-bit result. Concurrent `SetTaskAffinity()`/query snapshots are a separate, unpromoted concern because the API does not promise an atomic snapshot.

**Trigger and scope:** ExecSMP caller reuses a nonzero mask buffer for `TaskTag_CPUAffinity` without clearing it before `QueryTaskTagList()`. This affects task affinity reporting on ARM32, AArch64, and PC mask implementations.

**Confidence:** High for additive output and stale-bit retention; no query was run.

<a id="ek291"></a>
### EK291 — MinGW processor expunge leaks its per-CPU power-information buffer [conditional]

When the optional `wincpu.dll` loads successfully, `wincpu_hostlib_init()` gets the host processor count and allocates `cpucount * 6 * sizeof(ULONG)` bytes into the static `wincpu_pppi` pointer (`arch/all-mingw32/processor/processor_hostlib.c:72-85`). The corresponding expunge hook closes the DLL but never frees or clears `wincpu_pppi` (`:89-100`). The pointer is used as the output buffer passed to the DLL's `win_getcpufreq()` wrapper (`:36-40`); repository search found no separate release or reassignment cleanup.

**Trigger and consequence:** the DLL loads, reports a positive CPU count, the buffer allocation succeeds, and the processor module is later expunged. The expunge releases the DLL but leaves the per-CPU buffer allocated; a subsequent module load allocates another buffer and overwrites the only stored pointer. The same leak occurs if a later processor-library initialization step fails and generated init rollback invokes this expunge hook (`compiler/autoinit/functions.c:42-72`). **Scope:** MinGW32 processor module when `Libs\Host\wincpu.dll` is available; the DLL build dependency is commented in `arch/all-mingw32/processor/mmakefile.src:22-23`, so no default DLL packaging is claimed. **Confidence:** high for the allocation and missing release; module reload/runtime was not exercised. Free `wincpu_pppi` with the matching allocation size on expunge and clear the pointer. No Windows host, module expunge, reload, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek9066"></a>
### EK9066 — The MinGW processor loader leaks allocated HostLib error strings on both lookup failures.

**Finding:** The selected MinGW processor loader requests an error string from `HostLib_Open()` and returns immediately on failure without releasing it (`arch/all-mingw32/processor/processor_hostlib.c:43-57`). If opening succeeds but a required symbol lookup fails, it closes the module and again returns without freeing `err` (`:59-66`). The selected Windows HostLib backend allocates these error strings with `FormatMessage(FORMAT_MESSAGE_ALLOCATE_BUFFER, ...)` and its `HostLib_FreeErrorStr()` implementation releases them with `LocalFree()` (`arch/all-mingw32/bootstrap/hostlib.c:12-26,28-36,50-57`; exposed through `hostinterface.c:32-42` and `arch/all-mingw32/hostlib/freeerrorstr.c:11-19`). Each failed initialization therefore leaks the allocated message buffer.

**Trigger and scope:** MinGW processor-resource initialization attempts to open the optional host CPU library and either the DLL is unavailable or a required symbol is missing. The processor module is selected by `arch/all-mingw32/processor/mmakefile.src:8-10`. The leak is limited to these failure paths; other platforms' static `dlerror()` strings do not share this allocation behavior.

**Confidence:** High for the two unmatched allocations and cleanup API. No Windows host or loader failure was run.

<a id="ek9067"></a>
### EK9067 — The generic MMU allocator does not subtract absolute allocations from its free-byte count.

**Finding:** In the generic linear MMU allocator, successful `mm_AllocAbs()` marks the requested page-map range allocated but does not decrement `mh->mh_Free` (`rom/kernel/mm_linear.c:274-327`). By contrast, ordinary `mm_Allocate()` subtracts the rounded allocation size (`:254-265`), and `mm_Free()` adds freed bytes back (`:330-358`). The public `KMS_Free` statistic reports `mh_Free` directly (`:468-486`). After an absolute reservation, free-byte accounting is therefore overstated; freeing that reservation later adds bytes that were never subtracted, increasing the discrepancy.

The generic memory allocator selects `mm_AllocAbs()` for a non-NULL requested address (`rom/kernel/kernel_mm.c:33-64`). The generic linear implementation is conditional on the generic MMU configuration; this checkout does not establish a normal selected `KrnAllocPages()` caller that reaches it after page-size and map initialization (see EK639). The page map remains authoritative for whether an actual region can be allocated, so this report claims inaccurate statistics and potentially misleading free-size prechecks, not an established overlapping allocation.

**Trigger and scope:** successful absolute allocation through an initialized generic linear MMU MemHeader, followed by `KMS_Free` query or later allocator decisions based on `mh_Free`. Generic `USE_MMU` configurations only.

**Confidence:** High for the accounting mismatch; initialization and in-tree operational reachability remain unverified. No allocation or statistics query was run.

<a id="ek9068"></a>
### EK9068 — The shared FDT reader accepts unchecked block offsets and token extents.

**Finding:** `FDT_Open()` checks only the blob pointer and magic, then publishes structure/string pointers from header offsets and derives a cell limit from `size_dt_struct`; it does not validate the header extent, `totalsize`, block offsets, or that the declared blocks fit inside the blob (`arch/riscv-all/linklibs/fdt/fdt.c:50-64`). Token readers then dereference cells and scan node/property strings without validating each token header, payload length, terminator, or property-name offset against the structure/string block boundaries (`:72-103,105-137,140-158,165-197`). A magic-valid but malformed firmware blob can therefore make selected startup/device-tree consumers read outside the declared blob or walk invalid token data, leading to boot failure or incorrect hardware discovery/configuration.

The shared FDT library is selected for the RISC-V/OpenSBI path. OpenSBI's early parser also checks magic and publishes the flattened-tree boot tag; if that parse fails, the later selected clients still receive/reopen the blob through `KRN_FlattenedDeviceTree` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_fdt.c:91-97`; startup publication and caller edges documented in the coverage trace). Selected consumers include the RISC-V processor initializer and OpenSBI I2C, UART, PCI and BattClock drivers. The optional DWMAC target is separately buildable but not included in the default network aggregate.

**Trigger and scope:** firmware supplies a DTB with valid FDT magic but inconsistent offsets, block sizes, token extents, or missing string terminators; a selected OpenSBI caller then traverses the affected data. This is a boot/input validation correctness issue. Other narrower FDT arithmetic findings remain separate.

**Confidence:** High for absent boundary checks; exact failure depends on malformed DTB contents and the caller's traversal. No DTB, boot, or device initialization was run.

<a id="ek9069"></a>
### EK9069 — The x86-64 EFI resource interprets an EFI32 system table using 64-bit field offsets.

**Finding:** The x86-64 Multiboot2 parser prefers an EFI64 tag when present, but if it is absent it accepts an EFI32 system-table pointer and publishes it unchanged as `KRN_EFISystemTable` (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/multiboot2.c:113-117,183-211`). The selected x86-64 EFI resource casts the value to the native `EFI_SystemTable` and reads fields using native pointer and `IPTR` widths (`arch/all-native/efi/efi_init.c:70-95`; layout in `compiler/include/hardware/efi/efi.h:18-34`). EFI32 and EFI64 system-table layouts differ after the shared header: on x86-64, `RuntimeServices` is read at the native 64-bit offset instead of the EFI32 offset, and the later `NumEntries`/`ConfigTable` fields are likewise misinterpreted. Initialization can reject or dereference the wrong service pointer; selected configuration-table clients can read incorrect table metadata.

**Trigger and scope:** x86-64 PC Multiboot2 handoff includes an EFI32 tag but no EFI64 tag, and the bootstrap proceeds to initialize the EFI resource. When both tags are present, the parser gives EFI64 precedence. No such firmware/bootloader handoff was tested.

**Confidence:** High for the pointer-width/layout mismatch and parser selection. The resulting failure depends on the supplied EFI32 table contents and downstream use.

<a id="ek9070"></a>
### EK9070 — OpenSBI counts failed CPU nodes as present logical processors.

**Finding:** The OpenSBI FDT parser increments `ncpus` for every direct `/cpus/cpu@...` node without checking its `status` property (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_fdt.c:114-122`). `Platform_Init()` publishes that count as `kb_HartCount` and creates a corresponding HartData record (`platform_init.c:23-49`). The selected RISC-V processor resource independently enumerates `cpu` nodes with a `reg` property and does not filter `status` (`arch/riscv64-all/processor/processor_init.c:435-457`). A node marked `status = "fail"` is therefore exposed as a logical processor record even though firmware marks it unavailable.

This finding is limited to the public CPU inventory. It does not establish that the scheduler runs the failed hart or that affinity to it necessarily succeeds. `status = "disabled"` is excluded because it can describe a present but quiescent CPU. No checked-in DTB fixture with a failed CPU node was found.

**Trigger and scope:** external OpenSBI firmware tree includes a direct `/cpus/cpu@...` node with `status = "fail"` and a `reg` property. The kernel and processor resource then advertise it in CPU counts/topology.

**Confidence:** High for the two enumerators' missing status filter and resulting inventory entry; actual firmware-tree occurrence is unverified. No boot or CPU query was run.

<a id="ek9071"></a>
### EK9071 — The 16-bit Exec semaphore queue count can falsely free a held lock or strand waiters.

**Finding:** `ss_QueueCount` and `ss_NestCount` are signed 16-bit `WORD` fields (`compiler/include/exec/semaphores.h:53-57`). Exec uses `ss_QueueCount == -1` as the free sentinel; `ObtainSemaphore()`/`ObtainSemaphoreShared()` and `AttemptSemaphore()`/`AttemptSemaphoreShared()` all increment it and treat a resulting zero as a free semaphore (`rom/exec/semaphores.c:86-98,183-194`). `Procure()` uses the same sentinel transition (`rom/exec/procure.c:68-92`). Starting from a free semaphore, 65,536 successful same-owner obtains or attempts wrap `ss_QueueCount` back to -1 and `ss_NestCount` back to zero while leaving `ss_Owner` set. The next competing obtain or attempt increments -1 to zero and is granted, overwriting the existing owner despite the outstanding holds.

There is a second threshold in the release path. When another task owns the semaphore, each queued request increments `ss_QueueCount`. `ReleaseSemaphore()` decrements it and only services the wait queue when the resulting count is nonnegative (`rom/exec/releasesemaphore.c:83-85,106-114`). With 32,769 queued task or message requests behind an exclusive owner, the signed 16-bit count wraps such that the decrement leaves it negative; the code takes the no-waiters branch, marks the semaphore free, and leaves queued requests unreplied (`:188-196`). This is distinct from same-owner count overflow; `Procure()` message waiters use the same release path.
