Restrict discovery to validated hunk sections and a compiler-table signature, or require explicit table metadata. Source-only; no guest image was run.

<a id="ek9166"></a>
### EK9166 — Repeated opens of an uncached generated m68k library consume new base slots.

`M68KEmu_SetupLibBase()` appends a fake base to `ctx->libs` until `M68KEMU_MAX_LIBS` (32), but adds its name to `ctx->libmap` only while `num_libmap < M68KEMU_MAX_LIBMAP` (16) (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_memory.c:185-245`; `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_intern.h:36,54,76-81`). `M68KEmu_OpenLibrary()` checks that map first and creates a new base for a generated library when no name match is found (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:37-64`). Once the map is full, such newly created names are never cached. Guest `CloseLibrary()` is a no-op for fake bases (`:93-97`), so these slots are not reclaimed during the run.

**Trigger and consequence:** after the name map fills, the guest repeatedly opens a generated library whose name was not recorded. Each successful call consumes another library-array entry and jump-table region. In the current 64 KiB region, the 17 distinct generated bases occupy about 52.9 KiB; only four duplicate 512-vector bases fit after that, and the next open fails the region-size check (before the 32-entry array limit). **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator with enough distinct library names to fill the 16-entry map and subsequent opens of an uncached generated library. Exec and DOS bases use two initial map entries, so up to 14 later names can be cached; subsequent name insertions are omitted. **Reachability limit:** the generated library inventory is 17 names including Exec and DOS. If all are opened once, the 16-entry name map leaves one name uncached; reopening that name can allocate four duplicate bases in the remaining region, after which SetupLibBase returns zero. The 32-record array is not the first limit reached. No maintained guest workload establishing that sequence was found. **Confidence:** high for duplicate allocation and capacity behavior; guest impact depends on reaching the threshold. Cache names independently of the fixed map or return the existing base by searching `ctx->libs`. Source-only; no guest was run.

<a id="ek9167"></a>
### EK9167 — `ReadArgs` copies native result pointers into the m68k argument array as guest addresses.

The manual `ReadArgs` thunk copies the guest `IPTR` array into a host array, calls native DOS `ReadArgs()`, then copies each host value back by narrowing it to a 32-bit `ULONG` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:883-915`). Native `ReadArgs()` stores pointers for ordinary string arguments, optional `/N` values, and `/M` results (including a pointer vector) in that array (`rom/dos/readargs.c:807-888`; API contract in `compiler/include/dos/rdargs.h:152-168`). The thunk does not copy those native allocations into guest memory or translate their addresses before writing them back.

**Trigger and consequence:** a guest uses a pointer-valued template result and dereferences the returned argument-array value. It receives a native host address narrowed to 32 bits rather than an address in the guest arena, so the guest reads an unrelated guest location or an invalid address; `/M` results can also contain a native pointer vector and native element pointers. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator calling the manual DOS `ReadArgs` thunk for pointer-valued results. **Reachability limit:** scalar switches/toggles and values not represented as pointers do not exercise this conversion defect; the manual thunk is the registered route. No maintained guest caller reproducer was established. **Confidence:** high for the missing address conversion and pointer-valued outputs; exact failure depends on guest use of those results. Copy returned buffers/vectors into guest allocations and convert every pointer, with lifetime tied to the `FreeArgs` handle. Source-only; no guest call was run.

<a id="ek9168"></a>
### EK9168 — The `ReadArgs` handle returned to guest D0 is not a guest address.

When the guest supplies a null `rdargs` argument, native `ReadArgs()` allocates its own `RDArgs` object and returns that host pointer on success (`rom/dos/readargs.c:242-251,934-942`). The manual thunk returns the pointer unchanged (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:905-915`), and the Moira dispatcher narrows every native result to 32-bit guest D0 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:256-275`). The paired `FreeArgs` thunk casts guest D1 directly back to a native pointer and calls native `FreeArgs()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:918-923`).

**Trigger and consequence:** on a 64-bit emulator host, a guest calls `ReadArgs()` with D3=0 and then passes the returned D0 handle to `FreeArgs()`. The host pointer may be truncated when returned through guest D0; `FreeArgs()` then dereferences the reconstructed invalid pointer and may fault or corrupt memory. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator on a 64-bit host using the auto-allocated RDArgs path. **Reachability limit:** a host allocation below 4 GiB could avoid truncation for the opaque round trip, but no guest-address mapping exists; the guest must not inspect the native structure. Caller-owned non-null `RDArgs` has a separate size/layout and translation issue recorded as EK9432. No maintained caller reproducer was established. **Confidence:** high for the unbridged handle and 32-bit narrowing; the immediate failure depends on host pointer placement. Return a guest handle mapped to the native object and resolve it in `FreeArgs()`, or allocate a guest-layout shadow. Source-only; no guest call was run.

<a id="ek9169"></a>
### EK9169 — Native DOS BPTR handles are truncated when returned to the 32-bit m68k guest.

The manual DOS thunks return native `BPTR` results directly for `Open`, `Input`, `Output`, `Lock`, and `CurrentDir`; the paired operations cast guest D-register values straight back to native `BPTR` for `Read`, `Write`, `Seek`, `Close`, `UnLock`, `Examine`, and related calls (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:739-795,810-823,876-880,927-930,954-980`). Native `BPTR` is `IPTR` by default and uses `MKBADDR`/`BADDR` pointer-shift encoding (`compiler/include/dos/bptr.h:20-48`). The Moira dispatcher writes native return values into 32-bit D0 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:256-275`); there is no guest-handle mapping in these thunks.

**Trigger and consequence:** on a 64-bit emulator host, the guest opens a file or obtains another native DOS BPTR and passes the returned value to a paired operation. D0 truncates the native BPTR to 32 bits; the later native DOS call reconstructs a BPTR from that truncated value, which can refer to the wrong address and fail or fault while using the handle. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator on 64-bit hosts using native DOS BPTR-returning operations. **Reachability limit:** the returned handles are intended to be opaque and round-tripped; this does not claim that guest code directly dereferences them. No maintained guest caller exercising these thunk vectors was established. **Confidence:** high for the width mismatch and missing mapping; the exact result depends on host address placement and the DOS path. Maintain a guest-handle-to-native-BPTR table and resolve handle arguments before native calls. Source-only; no DOS operation was run.

<a id="ek9170"></a>
### EK9170 — `AllocDosObject` returns unbridged native objects and `FreeDosObject` reads its pointer from the wrong register.

The manual `AllocDosObject` thunk returns a native pointer directly for every type except `DOS_FIB`, for which it creates a `FileInfoBlock` shadow (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1023-1032`). The Moira dispatcher narrows that result into 32-bit guest D0 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:256-275`), leaving objects such as `DOS_EXALLCONTROL`, `DOS_RDARGS`, `DOS_CLI`, and `DOS_FILEHANDLE` without guest-addressable storage. Separately, `dos.conf` declares `FreeDosObject(type, ptr)` in D1,D2, but its thunk passes `THUNK_PTR(2)` (`:1034-1037`); that macro reads address register A2, not data register D2 (`m68kemu_thunks.h:33-38`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated caller allocates a non-FIB DOS object and attempts to inspect or free it. The returned native pointer is not a guest-arena address and can be truncated; `FreeDosObject` then ignores the actual D2 object value and resolves A2 instead. Depending on A2, it can no-op and leak the native allocation or pass a different pointer to the native destructor. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator; pointer narrowing affects 64-bit hosts, while the D2/A2 mismatch applies wherever the thunk is used. **Reachability limit:** `DOS_FIB` has a dedicated shadow on allocation, but the free thunk's wrong-register behavior also affects that type. No maintained m68k guest caller was established. **Confidence:** high for both register and pointer-bridge defects; the specific cleanup outcome depends on A2 and host address placement. Return a guest handle/shadow for each supported object type and resolve the declared D2 argument through that mapping. Source-only; no DOS object was allocated.

<a id="ek9171"></a>
### EK9171 — `ExAll` and `ExAllEnd` read pointer arguments from address registers and use native layouts on guest buffers.

The DOS vector declarations place `ExAll` and `ExAllEnd` arguments in D1 through D5 (`rom/dos/dos.conf:126,223`), but both manual thunks pass `THUNK_PTR(2)` and `THUNK_PTR(5)` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:991-999`); `THUNK_PTR` reads A registers. Thus the buffer and control pointers come from A2/A5 rather than their declared D2/D5 values. Even when those address registers happen to resolve to guest memory, the thunks pass guest `ExAllData32`/`ExAllControl` storage directly to native DOS. On a 64-bit host the native layouts use pointer-sized fields and differ from the 32-bit guest layouts (`compiler/include/dos/exall.h:24-71,90-106`), with no field or endian conversion.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated caller invokes either vector with its documented D-register arguments. Native DOS receives unrelated or null pointers from A2/A5; if these happen to resolve to guest storage instead, native code interprets the guest 32-bit records/control object as its 64-bit structures, so fields and linked results are misread or written in the wrong layout. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator; wrong-register dispatch applies to the manual vectors generally, and structure mismatch applies on 64-bit hosts. **Reachability limit:** no maintained m68k guest caller was found; the `AllocDosObject(DOS_EXALLCONTROL)` route is separately affected by EK9170. **Confidence:** high for register mismatch and layout difference; exact failure depends on register contents and which ExAll fields are used. Read D2/D5, translate guest storage through explicit 32-to-native structures, and copy results back. Source-only; no ExAll call was run.

<a id="ek9172"></a>
### EK9172 — The m68k pattern-matching thunks pass a smaller guest `AnchorPath` as a native structure.

The manual `MatchFirst`, `MatchNext`, and `MatchEnd` thunks translate the guest address only to the backing guest-memory pointer, then pass it directly to native DOS (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1004-1018`). The guest `AnchorPath` layout is 282 bytes while the selected 64-bit native layout is 304 bytes; its embedded `FileInfoBlock` and pointer fields also differ (`compiler/include/dos/dosasl.h:52-74`; the `FileInfoBlock` definitions in `compiler/include/dos/dos.h`). Native `MatchFirst` initializes anchor pointers and `ap_Info`, `MatchNext` traverses and updates those fields, and `MatchEnd` follows the anchor pointers for cleanup (`rom/dos/matchfirst.c:55-72`; `matchnext.c:55-115`; `matchend.c:48-86`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated caller invokes any of the matching vectors with a guest `AnchorPath`. Native DOS interprets the 32-bit guest fields as host pointer-width fields and uses its larger structure layout; fields are misread or written at the wrong offsets, and native anchor pointers are stored in guest memory. Subsequent iteration or cleanup can follow invalid pointers, corrupt nearby guest state, or fail to release the native chain. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator on 64-bit hosts using `MatchFirst`/`MatchNext`/`MatchEnd`. **Reachability limit:** these calls are externally reachable through the manual DOS vectors, but no maintained m68k guest caller was found. **Confidence:** high for the direct-layout mismatch and native pointer storage; exact failure depends on caller allocation size, match results, and iteration/cleanup. Use a native AnchorPath object with explicit guest/native field conversion and keep the AChain lifetime behind a guest handle. Source-only; no pattern search was run.

<a id="ek9173"></a>
### EK9173 — m68k formatted output passes guest `%b` BSTR values to native formatting without translation.

`m68k_to_native_fmt_stream()` converts `%s` arguments to `ctx->mem + guest_address`, but for `%b` it casts the raw 32-bit guest value directly to a host pointer (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:255-315`). The converted argument stream is then consumed by native `RawDoFmt()` through DOS `VPrintf`/`VFPrintf`/`VFWritef` and generated Utility formatting paths (manual wrappers at `:1144-1174`; raw formatter `rom/exec/rawdofmt.c:257-264`). Native `%b` treats its argument as a native `BSTR` and applies `BADDR()` before reading the length/data (`compiler/include/dos/bptr.h:20-48,70-83`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a guest formats a BCPL string with `%b`. The native formatter shifts and dereferences the raw guest BSTR value in the host address space rather than translating the encoded guest address into the emulator arena; it can read unrelated memory or fault, and does not print the guest string. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator using a formatting API with a `%b` conversion. The known Utility `VSNPrintf` thunk shares the same conversion helper. **Reachability limit:** ordinary `%s` and scalar conversions use separate conversion cases; no maintained guest call using `%b` was found. **Confidence:** high for the missing BSTR address translation and native dereference; exact fault depends on the guest value and host mapping. Decode the guest BSTR address, resolve its bytes within the emulator memory, and supply a host-compatible BSTR representation. Source-only; no formatter was run.

<a id="ek9174"></a>
### EK9174 — m68k packet thunks read D-register packet arguments from A registers and pass guest packets natively.

`dos.conf` declares `SendPkt` and `ReplyPkt` packet/port parameters in D1-D3, and `DoPkt`'s port in D1 (`rom/dos/dos.conf:94-97`). The manual thunks use `THUNK_PTR(1..3)` for those arguments, which reads A1-A3 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1118-1139`; `m68kemu_thunks.h:33-38`). Even if an address register happens to contain a resolvable guest address, `SendPkt` and `ReplyPkt` pass the guest `DosPacket` bytes directly as the native structure. Native helpers mutate its pointer fields, queue links, and result fields (`rom/dos/sendpkt.c:68-74`; `replypkt.c:58-75`); guest and selected 64-bit native `DosPacket` fields have different widths/layouts (`compiler/include/dos/dosextens.h:511-529`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated caller invokes `DoPkt`, `SendPkt`, or `ReplyPkt` with the documented D-register arguments. The wrappers instead resolve A-register values; `SendPkt`/`ReplyPkt` can then pass an unrelated pointer or guest-layout storage to native queue/mutation code, causing failure, invalid memory access, or corrupted packet/message state. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator using these manual DOS vectors; structure mismatch is specific to 64-bit hosts. **Reachability limit:** no maintained m68k guest caller was found; the vectors are externally callable. **Confidence:** high for the register mismatch and direct structure-layout crossing; exact outcome depends on A-register contents and packet state. Resolve D-register values and marshal packets/ports through native objects with guest handles. Source-only; no packet operation was run.

<a id="ek9175"></a>
### EK9175 — `DoPkt` zero-extends negative m68k packet arguments on 64-bit hosts.

The manual `DoPkt` thunk passes D3-D7 values, returned as `ULONG`, directly to native `SIPTR` parameters (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1118-1121`). `SIPTR` is a signed native-width integer (`compiler/include/exec/types.h:89-91`), and native `DoPkt` stores these values in the native-width `dp_Arg1`–`dp_Arg7` fields (`rom/dos/dopkt.c:119-128`; `dosextens.h:511-529`). On a 64-bit host, an m68k value such as `0xffffffff` is converted from unsigned 32-bit to positive 64-bit `4294967295`, rather than sign-extended to `-1`.

**Trigger and consequence:** a guest sends a negative 32-bit argument through `DoPkt` and the receiving handler interprets that field as signed. The handler receives the wrong positive value, which can alter the requested packet operation or its result. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator on a 64-bit host calling the manual `DoPkt` vector. **Reachability limit:** only argument positions whose protocol meaning is signed and whose value is negative are affected; many packet arguments are unsigned values or pointers. No maintained guest caller demonstrating a negative value was found. **Confidence:** high for C integer conversion and packet-field storage; the application-level effect depends on handler/action semantics. Sign-extend each guest 32-bit argument according to the m68k ABI before calling native DOS. Source-only; no packet call was run.

<a id="ek9176"></a>
### EK9176 — `WaitPkt` returns a native `DosPacket` pointer and layout to the m68k guest.

The manual thunk returns native `WaitPkt()` directly (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1131-1134`); Moira narrows the pointer into 32-bit guest D0 (`m68kemu_moira.cpp:256-275`). Native `WaitPkt()` takes a message from the current native process port and returns the `DosPacket *` stored in the message node (`rom/dos/waitpkt.c:54-58,63-96`). No guest shadow or packet-field conversion is applied, and native `DosPacket` contains host-width pointers and `SIPTR` fields (`compiler/include/dos/dosextens.h:511-529`).

**Trigger and consequence:** guest code calls `WaitPkt()` and a packet is available on the native process port. The guest receives a narrowed host address; if it reads or replies to the packet as an m68k `DosPacket`, its fields are not at the native offsets and pointer values are not guest addresses. It can misread packet data or pass an invalid handle into another packet thunk. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator when a native packet is queued for the process running the emulation; layout mismatch is specific to 64-bit hosts. **Reachability limit:** the runner uses its containing native process context; no maintained guest caller or queued packet sequence was established. **Confidence:** high for raw pointer return and layout mismatch; trigger depends on packet arrival. Return a guest packet handle backed by a converted packet shadow. Source-only; no wait or packet exchange was run.

<a id="ek9177"></a>
### EK9177 — m68k record-lock arrays are traversed with the larger native entry stride.

The generated `LockRecords` and `UnLockRecords` thunks resolve D1 to backing guest memory and pass the array directly to native DOS (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1045-1066`). The m68k guest `RecordLock32` has 16-byte entries; selected x86-64 native `RecordLock64` entries are 32 bytes because `AROS_FAST_BPTR` makes BPTR pointer-sized and the two ranges are `UQUAD` (`compiler/include/dos/record.h:26-48`; `arch/x86_64-all/include/aros/cpu.h:84`). Native loops read fields using that structure and advance `recArray++` until a zero `rec_FH` sentinel (`rom/dos/lockrecords.c:53-72`; `unlockrecords.c:47-59`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k caller supplies one or more 16-byte records to `LockRecords` or `UnLockRecords`. Native code reads the guest `rec_FH` together with the next guest field as one pointer-sized handle, interprets later values at different offsets, and advances 32 bytes per entry. This can send invalid file/offset/length/mode values to record-lock operations, skip guest entries, and read beyond the guest array while searching for its sentinel. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator on x86-64 hosts; other 64-bit targets require checking their BPTR ABI separately. **Reachability limit:** requires a guest call using the array APIs; no maintained m68k caller was found. **Confidence:** high for the 16-byte versus 32-byte stride mismatch and unconverted native iteration. Convert entries into a temporary native array, preserve the guest sentinel count, and copy any modified fields back explicitly. Source-only; no record lock was acquired.

<a id="ek9178"></a>
### EK9178 — m68k window/screen teardown leaks child shadows and mishandles CloseScreen results.

`setup_window_shadow()` allocates a guest Window, RastPort and UserPort and registers each native/guest pair; `CloseWindow()` closes the native window and destroys only the top-level Window shadow (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:518-568,601-606`). Native `CloseWindow()` owns and disposes the `UserPort`, but its guest allocation/mapping is not removed; the RPort allocation/mapping also remains. `OpenScreen()` registers the top-level Screen and its embedded ViewPort/RastPort shadows, while `CloseScreen()` removes only the Screen entry (`:1262-1290`). Both setup paths ignore `shadow_register()` failure. The fixed table holds 256 entries (`m68kemu_intern.h:92-93`), and a failed registration returns zero (`m68kemu_thunks.c:444-455`); setup still returns the allocated guest object address. The close thunk also ignores native `CloseScreen()`'s BOOL result, destroys the Screen shadow unconditionally, and itself always returns zero (`:1286-1291`). Native `CloseScreen()` returns FALSE when the screen still has an open window (`rom/intuition/closescreen.c:102-113`), leaving the native screen live; the thunk then frees its guest shadow anyway. On successful closes, the guest also receives FALSE instead of the native success value.

**Trigger and consequence:** repeated window/screen creation and closure leaves auxiliary entries in the fixed table and leaks guest allocations. When the table is full, a later setup can return a guest Window/Screen without registering its top-level native object. The matching close thunk cannot resolve it and skips the native close, leaving a native GUI object and guest allocation behind. Stale auxiliary mappings can also resolve guest fields to native RastPort/UserPort/ViewPort objects that have already been closed. Separately, a guest closes a screen while it still has an open window: native `CloseScreen()` refuses, but the thunk frees the guest Screen shadow while leaving the native screen open; even successful native closure is reported as FALSE. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator using the manual Intuition window/screen vectors. **Reachability limit:** registry exhaustion requires accumulated shadow entries; the close-result mismatch is reachable whenever a guest calls `CloseScreen()` and a failed-close case is induced by an open window. No guest GUI lifecycle was run. **Confidence:** high for auxiliary retention, ignored registration failures, and the ignored native BOOL result; registry exhaustion is conditional on accumulated shadows. Remove all child mappings/allocations on close, check every registration result, unwind native object creation on failure, and preserve the Screen shadow when native closure fails while returning the native BOOL result. Source-only; no GUI object was opened or closed.

<a id="ek9179"></a>
### EK9179 — Window and screen RastPort shadows are not synchronized with native graphics state.

Window setup allocates a 100-byte guest RastPort block and registers it against the native `w->RPort`, but writes only the guest Window's `RPort` pointer; it does not initialize RastPort fields (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:534-543`). OpenScreen similarly registers the embedded guest RastPort address against `scr->RastPort` without copying fields (`:1276-1280`). Graphics thunks resolve these guest addresses to the native RastPort and invoke native operations, with no writeback to guest storage (`:1350-1387`). For example, `SetAPen()` updates native `FgPen` and related state, and `Move()` updates native `cp_x`, `cp_y`, flags and line pattern state (`rom/graphics/setapen.c:53-56`; `move.c:54-62`).

**Trigger and consequence:** guest code calls a graphics operation such as `SetAPen()` or `Move()` on a window/screen RastPort and then reads the public RastPort fields from guest memory. Those fields remain at their initially zeroed or reused stale values rather than reflecting the native state, so later guest logic sees stale pens/current position/flags. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator using its manual Graphics thunks with an Intuition-created window or screen. **Reachability limit:** no maintained m68k guest caller reading these fields after the named operations was found; consumers that only call graphics APIs may not observe the mismatch. **Confidence:** high for missing initialization/writeback and native mutation; effect depends on direct guest field reads. Synchronize public fields after native operations or route guest field reads through a coherent shadow. Source-only; no GUI or graphics call was run.

<a id="ek9180"></a>
### EK9180 — `OpenScreen` leaves the guest ViewPort shadow unsynchronized.

The manual `OpenScreen` thunk allocates a guest Screen block, registers its embedded ViewPort address against native `scr->ViewPort`, and writes selected Screen fields; it never copies any ViewPort fields into the guest record (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1262-1282`). The context memory is initially cleared (`m68kemu_memory.c:25-27,36-50`), and the heap allocator does not clear reused blocks. The public `Screen.ViewPort` begins at guest offset 44 (`m68kemu_offsets.h:128`); its `ColorMap` field is at offset 4, while the generated ViewPort field map records that field at guest offset 4 and native offset 8 (`m68kemu_shadow_layouts.h:3969-3981`). The ViewPort dimensions and offsets are also public fields, and native `OpenScreen()` initializes them from the selected display and screen geometry (`compiler/include/graphics/view.h:82-102`; `rom/intuition/openscreen.c:1363-1382,1406-1444,1491-1539`). A successful open has a native ColorMap; allocation failure sets the open result to failure.

This is visible through supported graphics vectors, not only direct structure inspection. A guest reading `Screen.ViewPort.ColorMap` from a fresh shadow gets zero. The generated `GetRGB32()` thunk resolves that guest zero to NULL and passes it to native `GetRGB32()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:4030-4038`; `m68kemu_intern.h:115-124`). For a positive color count, native `GetRGB32()` calls `color_get()` without validating `cm`; `color_get()` dereferences `cm->ColorTable` (`rom/graphics/getrgb32.c:62-65`; `color_support.c:87-99`). Thus a guest that uses the opened screen's documented `ViewPort.ColorMap` with `GetRGB32()` can fault instead of reading its palette. Direct guest reads of the ViewPort dimensions/offsets also see zero or stale values. Other thunk calls that pass the embedded ViewPort address itself can still resolve the registered native object, which does not repair the missing guest field values.

**Trigger and consequence:** successfully open a screen in the optional m68k emulator, read `screen->ViewPort.ColorMap`, and pass it with at least one color to the supported `GetRGB32()` vector. The missing guest pointer becomes NULL at the thunk boundary and native color lookup dereferences it. Direct guest reads of public ViewPort dimensions/offsets likewise see zero/stale data. **Affected configuration:** optional `kernel-m68kemu-library` integration on the supported 64-bit hosted targets, with guest code using `OpenScreen()` and the returned public ViewPort fields. **Reachability limit:** no checked-in m68k guest reproducer was found; this is conditional on guest API use. **Confidence:** high for the missing synchronization and the NULL-to-dereference path; no guest, screen, or color query was run. Populate the guest ViewPort scalars and create valid guest mappings for pointer fields such as ColorMap; do not place native pointers in guest memory. Source-only; no emulated call or build was run.

<a id="ek9181"></a>
### EK9181 — `OpenWindow` omits initialized IDCMP and size-limit fields from the guest Window shadow.

The manual `OpenWindow` thunk reads `IDCMPFlags` and min/max dimensions from the guest `NewWindow` and passes them to `OpenWindowTags()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:489-511`). Native Intuition installs the IDCMP mask through `ModifyIDCMP()` and initializes/clamps `Window.MinWidth`, `MinHeight`, `MaxWidth`, and `MaxHeight` (`rom/intuition/openwindow.c:711-714,950-961`). But `setup_window_shadow()` copies only edges, dimensions, mouse coordinates, flags and selected pointer fields into the returned guest Window; it does not write IDCMP or min/max fields (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:525-568`). These fields are public in `struct Window` (`compiler/include/intuition/intuition.h:486-534`), and the guest shadow allocation starts from cleared/reused emulator memory.

**Trigger and consequence:** after a successful emulated `OpenWindow`, guest code reads the returned Window's `IDCMPFlags` or size limits. It sees zero/stale shadow values rather than the values Intuition installed, so guest logic can make incorrect event-mask or resize decisions. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulator using manual `OpenWindow` or `OpenWindowTagList` and direct public-field reads. **Reachability limit:** native APIs that resolve the Window through the shadow can still act on the native object; the mismatch affects guest reads of these public fields. No maintained m68k caller reading them was found. **Confidence:** high for native initialization and omitted guest writes; effect depends on direct field consumers. Copy these fields into the guest Window shadow after successful native creation and update them after later native changes. Source-only; no window was opened.

<a id="ek9182"></a>
### EK9182 — The Android alert bridge drops the final character of each alert message.

The selected Android kernel alert path sends `AlertBuffer` to the host through `SendAlert()` as a command plus a string address (`arch/all-android/kernel/_displayalert.c:34-49`). `Alert_DisplayKrnAlert()` always prefixes the buffer with the alert title and a newline before calling `KrnDisplayAlert()` (`rom/exec/systemalert.c:14-30`), and the Java `cmd_Alert` handler calls native `GetString()` and displays the resulting text (`arch/all-android/bootstrap/app/src/org/aros/bootstrap/AROSBootstrap.java:267-274`). `GetString()` sets `size = strlen(addr)`, allocates a byte array of that size, but copies only `size - 1` bytes (`arch/all-android/bootstrap/main.c:91-98`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an Android-hosted kernel alert is sent. Since this selected path supplies a nonempty title/newline-prefixed string, the copy omits its final character and leaves the last array byte zero-initialized; the displayed alert is truncated at the end. **Affected configuration:** Android-hosted AROS kernel using the JNI alert bridge. **Reachability limit:** this does not establish behavior for empty input to `GetString()`; the selected system-alert producer always prefixes a title and newline. **Confidence:** high for the size/copy mismatch and selected caller path. Copy `size` bytes for nonempty strings, or allocate/copy the terminator consistently with the Java decoder. Source-only; no Android alert was sent.

<a id="ek9190"></a>
### EK9190 — A nested x86-64 interrupt can fault on the unaligned XMM save area.

The selected x86-64 PC entry stub runs same-ring interrupts on the interrupted stack. For a no-error vector, hardware pushes 24 bytes and the stub pushes a dummy error plus vector (16 bytes); for an error-code vector, hardware pushes 32 bytes and the stub pushes only the vector (8 bytes). Both paths therefore add 40 bytes mod 16. `core_EnterInterrupt` then pushes 32 bytes of segment slots, 120 bytes of GPRs and 8 bytes of flags, followed by fixed 8+64+8-byte subtractions; the XMM save-area pointer is captured after the first 8+64 bytes (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/core_interrupts.s:10-24,98-139`). With interrupted RSP mod 16 = 8, the stored `FXSData` pointer is 8 mod 16. `core_IRQHandle()` immediately uses `movaps` stores to that address, which requires 16-byte alignment (`arch/all-pc/kernel/cpu_intr.c:379-386`). A concrete selected route is `SoftIntDispatch()`: it calls `KrnSti()` before invoking an ordinary C callback (`rom/exec/cause.c:182-189`), so a nested IRQ may arrive at callback entry, where the x86-64 ABI has RSP mod 16 = 8.

**Trigger and consequence:** a hardware IRQ arrives at the callback-entry stack state described above. The first `movaps` in `core_IRQHandle()` targets an address not aligned to 16 bytes and raises #GP before the device IRQ callback is handled; the selected unhandled trap path can halt the system. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC kernel with an interrupt arriving while a SoftInt callback runs after interrupts have been re-enabled. **Reachability limit:** requires that particular nested interrupt timing and the same-ring path; no interrupt was induced. **Confidence:** high for stack arithmetic and the alignment requirement; runtime trigger timing is conditional. Compute an aligned save address from the actual interrupted stack or use an unaligned-safe store while retaining enough space for all saved data. Source-only; no assembly or boot was run.

<a id="ek9191"></a>
### EK9191 — x86-64 PC IRQ callbacks can clobber unsaved interrupted XMM state.

The x86-64 PC interrupt entry allocates a 64-byte temporary area and `core_IRQHandle()` saves/restores only XMM0–3 on the return-without-task-switch path (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/core_interrupts.s:137-141`; `arch/all-pc/kernel/cpu_intr.c:379-386,548-561`). The public `KrnAddIRQHandler()` contract describes the handler as an ordinary C function and does not state a vector-register preservation rule (`arch/all-pc/kernel/addirqhandler.c:24-57`). Under the selected x86-64 C ABI, XMM registers are caller-saved. The implementation's private comment instead requires IRQ/soft-interrupt code to preserve XMM5–15, but omits XMM4. General-register-only flags apply to the kernel and Exec objects, not to all selected driver callback modules.

**Trigger and consequence:** an x86-64 PC IRQ callback uses XMM4–15 and returns without a task switch. Because those interrupted values are not saved and restored, the interrupted task or kernel callback resumes with changed vector state; XMM4 is additionally absent from the private preservation instruction. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC builds with a raw IRQ callback compiled to use vector registers; this also applies to ordinary Exec interrupt callbacks if their callback code uses them. **Reachability limit:** the selected in-tree raw callback bodies checked so far do not establish a current clobbering callback, and no interrupt was run. The candidate is therefore conditional on a callback's generated code or explicit XMM use. **Confidence:** high for the save/restore boundary and ABI mismatch; conditional reachability. Document a callback preservation contract consistent with the ABI, or preserve the interrupted vector state around callbacks. Source-only; no build or runtime operation was performed.

<a id="ek9200"></a>
### EK9200 — m68k `FindNamedObject()` and `NamedObjectName()` return native pointers instead of guest addresses.

The selected generated Utility thunks resolve guest arguments through `THUNK_PTR`, but return `FindNamedObject()` and `NamedObjectName()` results as raw native pointers (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:7068-7074,7085-7089`). In contrast, `AllocNamedObjectA()` explicitly wraps its native result with `shadow_create_by_name()` (`:7051-7058`). The emulator's `THUNK_PTR` accepts a registered guest shadow or an address inside emulated memory; it cannot translate an arbitrary native pointer back to a guest handle (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.h:37`; `m68kemu_intern.h:115-125`). Native `FindNamedObject()` increments the use count and returns the native object for a named match (`rom/utility/findnamedobject.c:96-100`); `NamedObjectName()` returns the native `ln_Name` pointer (`rom/utility/namedobjectname.c:60-63`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k guest performs a successful named lookup, or calls `NamedObjectName()` on a valid guest shadow. D0 receives a native host pointer rather than the corresponding guest address. The guest cannot reliably read the result, and passing the lookup result to `ReleaseNamedObject()` cannot resolve the acquired native object through the shadow table, leaving its use count held. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k guest emulation on the 64-bit x86-64, AArch64, or RISC-V hosts selected by `rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:14-17`. **Reachability limit:** checked-in `FindNamedObject()` clients are native DataTypes/Workbench code; no checked-in m68k guest reproducer was established. The generated guest vector is selected for external guest programs. This finding concerns named lookup; the native NULL-name enumeration semantics are tracked separately in EK9500. **Confidence:** high for the pointer conversion mismatch and native reference increment; guest-trigger reachability is conditional. Return an existing shadow address or create/synchronize one, and translate the name pointer into guest memory. Source-only; no guest call was run.

<a id="ek9201"></a>
### EK9201 — m68k `FreeNamedObject()` leaves the freed object's guest shadow allocated and registered.

The generated `AllocNamedObjectA()` thunk creates a `NamedObject` guest shadow for the native object (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:7051-7058`). Its matching `FreeNamedObject()` thunk resolves that guest handle and calls native `FreeNamedObject()`, but does not call `shadow_destroy()` (`:7077-7082`). Native `FreeNamedObject()` releases the optional object/name-space storage and then the `IntNamedObject` allocation (`rom/utility/freenamedobject.c:60-74`). `shadow_destroy()` is the helper that removes the registry entry and returns the guest shadow block to the emulator heap (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_shadow.c:101-107`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k guest allocates a named object through the selected `AllocNamedObjectA()` vector and frees it through `FreeNamedObject()`. Each lifecycle leaves the guest shadow block and table slot behind, pointing at freed native storage; repeated lifecycles consume the fixed shadow capacity and heap, and a stale guest handle can continue resolving to that freed (or later reused) native address. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k guest emulation on the 64-bit x86-64, AArch64, or RISC-V hosts selected by `rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:14-17`. **Reachability limit:** native Utility callers use their native allocator/free path; no checked-in m68k guest lifecycle was established. This is conditional on guest use of the generated vectors. **Confidence:** high for the missing shadow teardown and its resource consequence. Preserve the guest shadow address before resolution, then unregister and free it when native free succeeds. Source-only; no allocation/free sequence was run.

<a id="ek10219"></a>
### EK10219 — m68k `AllocNamedObjectA()` leaks the native object when guest-shadow creation fails.

The selected generated thunk allocates the native object first, then returns `shadow_create_by_name()` directly (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:7051-7058`). `shadow_create()` returns zero if guest-heap allocation fails; if registration fails because the fixed shadow table is full, it frees only the guest shadow block and returns zero (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_shadow.c:75-92,101-107`; `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:444-458`). The thunk does not call native `FreeNamedObject()` on either failure path, so the guest sees allocation failure while the native allocation remains live and inaccessible.

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k guest calls `AllocNamedObjectA()` when the emulator heap cannot allocate a shadow or the shadow table is full. The vector returns NULL but leaks the successfully allocated native NamedObject; repeated calls under table saturation can accumulate host allocations. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k guest emulation on x86-64, AArch64, or RISC-V hosts selected by `rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:14-17`. **Reachability limit:** conditional on native allocation succeeding while shadow allocation/registration fails; no checked-in m68k guest caller or allocation-failure run was established. This is distinct from EK9201, which concerns teardown after a guest shadow was successfully created. **Confidence:** high for the missing rollback and inaccessible native allocation. Call `FreeNamedObject(_ret)` when shadow creation fails. Source-only; no allocation failure was induced.

<a id="ek9202"></a>
### EK9202 — m68k `RemNamedObject()` passes a guest `Message` buffer as a native 64-bit structure.

The generated thunk resolves both arguments with `THUNK_PTR` and passes the guest message buffer directly to native `RemNamedObject()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:7100-7105`). For ordinary guest memory, `THUNK_PTR` returns `ctx->mem + guest_address`; it does not create a `Message` shadow (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.h:37`; `m68kemu_intern.h:115-125`). The selected x86-64 shadow-layout table records `Message` as 20 bytes for m68k and 48 bytes for native AROS (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_shadow_layouts.h:2640-2641,4582`). Native `RemNamedObject()` writes `message->mn_Node.ln_Name` at native Node offset 24 and later calls `ReplyMsg()` on the same pointer (`rom/utility/remnamedobject.c:97-125`); native ReplyMsg reads `mn_ReplyPort` at the native Message offset.

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k guest calls `RemNamedObject()` with a non-NULL, correctly initialized guest Message for an object in a namespace. On the selected 64-bit hosts, the native write lands beyond the 20-byte guest structure, and the native reply path reads `mn_ReplyPort` at its 64-bit layout offset rather than the guest offset. This can overwrite adjacent guest memory and can reply through an invalid port pointer. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k guest emulation on x86-64, AArch64, or RISC-V hosts; the recorded 48-byte native layout is generated for x86-64 and other host layouts should be checked independently. **Reachability limit:** a repository-wide caller census found only `AttemptRemNamedObject()` and `ReleaseNamedObject()` call `RemNamedObject()` in checked-in code, and both pass NULL; no maintained guest caller using a message was found. **Confidence:** high for the direct layout mismatch and native field accesses; trigger is conditional on a guest-supplied non-NULL message. Translate the message into native storage and copy back reply fields, or provide a message shadow with the required lifetime. Source-only; no message was sent.

<a id="ek9203"></a>
### EK9203 — m68k tag-output thunks let 64-bit `IPTR` stores overwrite adjacent guest data.

Generated m68k TagItem wrappers convert the guest list to a native array, but resolve in-range output addresses in `ti_Data` to direct pointers into guest backing memory (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_shadow.c:139-163`). The wrappers then call native APIs and free the temporary TagItem array without copying outputs back in guest format. Affected output paths include DataTypes `GetDTAttrsA()` (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:681-689`; native `IPTR *` stores in `workbench/libs/datatypes/getdtattrsa.c:72-88`), GadTools `GT_GetGadgetAttrsA()` (`:2863-2871`; its `ti_Data` is an `IPTR *` passed to `GetAttr()` at `workbench/libs/gadtools/gt_getgadgetattrsa.c:40-42,64-67`), DOS `GetSegListInfo()` (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1828-1835`; recognized `GSLI_ElfHandle`/`GSLI_68KHUNK` stores in `rom/dos/getseglistinfo.c:78-96`), and Utility `UnpackStructureTags()` (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:7031-7040`; documented `IPTR *` outputs at `rom/utility/unpackstructuretags.c:35-43,100-153`). Graphics `GetRPAttrsA()` has the same output-slot width defect (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:4238-4245`; native stores at `rom/graphics/getrpattrsa.c:98-118`). On supported 64-bit hosts, native `IPTR` is eight bytes while m68k guest `IPTR` slots are four bytes.

**Trigger and consequence:** a guest supplies a four-byte output slot and invokes one of these APIs with a matching output tag/attribute (and, for `GetSegListInfo()`, a segment handle that matches a DOS-tracked native segment). The native store writes eight bytes into guest memory, overwrites the following four bytes, and leaves a host-endian value where the guest expects a big-endian one; a slot at the arena boundary can also cross the allocation boundary. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k guest emulation on supported 64-bit hosts. No maintained in-tree m68k guest caller was established for these output paths; native in-tree callers use host-width storage. **Confidence:** high for the conversion, output contracts and width mismatch; triggers are conditional on guest API use and matching tags. Marshal outputs through native temporaries and encode/copy back using the guest ABI width and byte order. The pack-table endian mismatch in `PackStructureTags()`/`UnpackStructureTags()` remains separate under EK10213. Source-only; no guest call or output buffer was used; see the [TagItem output-thunk recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#m68kemu-tagitem-output-thunk-recheck-ek9203-2026-11-02).

<a id="ek9204"></a>
### EK9204 — the m68k `RawDoFmt()` thunk ignores its output callback.

The public RawDoFmt contract calls `PutChProc` for every formatted character and supports the `STRING`, `SERIAL`, and `COUNT` sentinel callbacks (`rom/exec/rawdofmt.c:123-150,459-477`). The m68k manual thunk reads format, DataStream, and PutChData but never reads A2/`PutChProc`; it instead formats into a local buffer and copies that buffer to PutChData when non-NULL (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:318-367`).

The same replacement delegates each parsed conversion to host `snprintf()` (`:338-353`), although AROS RawDoFmt handles unknown conversion characters by emitting them literally without consuming an argument (`rom/exec/rawdofmt.c:350-354`). For `%n`, `translate_fmt_args()` takes its default branch and passes the raw 32-bit guest word as an `IPTR`, without guest-to-host pointer translation (`m68kemu_thunks.c:217-231`). Host `snprintf()` treats `%n` as a count-store conversion and interprets that value as a host pointer; consequently this unsupported guest conversion can fault the optional emulator instead of producing the literal `n` that the native RawDoFmt implementation produces. The argument scanner excludes escaped `%%` from its argument count (`:217-231`), but the output loop sends `%%` through `snprintf()` while still incrementing `ai` (`:338-353`). In a format such as `%% %d`, the escaped percent consumes the only translated argument index, so the later `%d` is copied literally rather than formatted. Native RawDoFmt emits one `%` for `%%` without consuming the following conversion's argument (`rom/exec/rawdofmt.c:340-354`). This is another observable mismatch in the same manual replacement, not a separate callback finding. No checked-in guest caller using `%n` or the affected mixed `%%`/conversion sequence was found.

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k guest calls RawDoFmt with `RAWFMTFUNC_SERIAL`, `RAWFMTFUNC_COUNT`, or a custom callback. Serial output is lost when PutChData is NULL; count mode does not increment the counter and may overwrite it with text; custom callbacks are never invoked. A guest format containing unsupported `%n` also reaches the host formatter's count-store behavior through an untranslated guest value and may fault. A format such as `%% %d` with one data argument prints the escaped percent but then emits `%d` literally because the thunk consumes the translated argument index while rendering `%%`. String mode is the only output mode approximated by the buffer copy, and its return value is separately wrong (EK10220). **Affected configuration:** optional m68k guest emulation on supported 64-bit hosts, through the manual Exec RawDoFmt vector. **Reachability limit:** no checked-in m68k guest call was established; native in-tree callers do not use this thunk. **Confidence:** high for the ignored A2 argument, escaped-percent argument-index mismatch, and `%n` host-format interpretation; impact depends on guest format and callback. Implement the native RawDoFmt parsing/output contract and marshal guest callbacks through an emulator callback bridge. Source-only; no formatter or callback was run.

<a id="ek9205"></a>
### EK9205 — m68k `RawDoFmt()` writes past its fixed output buffer after `snprintf()` truncates.

The thunk formats into `char buf[1024]`, calls `snprintf()` with at most `1020 - (out - buf)` bytes remaining, then advances `out` by `snprintf()`'s return value (the length that would have been produced) and unconditionally stores a terminator through `*out` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:330-360`). If PutChData is non-NULL, it then copies `out - buf + 1` bytes from the same buffer (`:364-365`).

**Trigger and consequence:** on a 64-bit host, a guest formats `%1024ld` with a zero LONG argument into string output. `snprintf()` returns 1024 although only 1019 output bytes plus NUL fit in the passed 1020-byte region; `out` becomes `buf + 1024`, and `*out = 0` writes one byte past the stack array. The subsequent copy reads 1025 bytes, also one byte past the array. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k guest emulation on 64-bit hosts. **Reachability limit:** requires a guest format whose rendered conversion reaches at least 1024 bytes; no guest formatter call was run. **Confidence:** high for the truncation arithmetic and boundary; exact stack effects depend on compiler layout. Clamp the produced length to the remaining capacity and track truncation before advancing or copying. Source-only.

<a id="ek10220"></a>
### EK10220 — the m68k `RawDoFmt()` thunk returns output length instead of the remaining DataStream pointer.

Native `RawDoFmt()` returns the pointer to the unconsumed part of DataStream (`rom/exec/rawdofmt.c:83-103,409-410,484-485,544`). The manual m68k thunk translates arguments for formatting but discards the consumed guest-stream position and returns `out - buf`, the formatted character count (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:327-368`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a guest calls the vector and uses its documented RAWARG result. Even a no-argument call with `DataStream == NULL` returns the number of output characters instead of NULL; an argument-bearing call likewise returns a small count rather than the guest address after the consumed arguments. The caller cannot continue walking the original DataStream correctly. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k guest emulation on supported hosts, through the manual Exec RawDoFmt vector. **Reachability limit:** no checked-in m68k guest caller using the return value was established. **Confidence:** high for the native result contract and the thunk's length return; consequence requires caller use of the result. Preserve and return the appropriate guest-stream cursor after parsing. Source-only; no guest call was run.

<a id="ek9206"></a>
### EK9206 — m68k formatted-output conversion packs `%i` and `%p` arguments at the wrong width.

`m68k_to_native_fmt_stream()` reserves eight bytes per argument on 64-bit hosts, but its parser recognizes only the `l` size modifier. `%i` falls through to the four-byte ULONG case; `%p`/`%P` also fall through to that case, while native RawDoFmt sets those pointer conversions to IPTR width and fetches eight bytes (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:255-315`; `rom/exec/rawdofmt.c:118-121,288-296`). The converter therefore advances its output cursor by four bytes where the native consumer advances by eight.

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k caller uses `%id` with a negative 32-bit value, or mixes `%i`/`%p`/`%P` with later conversions, through a thunk using this converter. Negative `%id` is zero-extended into the native 64-bit SIPTR slot and prints as a positive value; the four-byte cursor advance also places subsequent arguments at offsets the native formatter does not consume, producing incorrect later fields. The affected bridge consumers include DOS `VPrintf()`/`VFPrintf()`, Utility `VSNPrintf()`, and Locale `FormatString()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1144-1173`; `m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6598-6608,7133-7143`). **Affected configuration:** optional m68k guest emulation on 64-bit hosts. **Reachability limit:** no checked-in guest caller was established; native in-tree formatters use host-native streams. VFWritef's fixed-IPTR slot mismatch for other specifiers is separate (EK10164), as is the little-endian pack-table interpretation issue (EK10213). **Confidence:** high for width/cursor mismatch and signed extension; guest-visible output depends on these formats being used. Repack each argument using the native consumer's exact width and sign extension, preserving matching offsets. Source-only; no formatter or guest call was run.

<a id="ek9207"></a>
### EK9207 — m68k `FormatString()` returns NULL or a freed native stream pointer instead of the guest argument cursor.

The generated Locale `FormatString()` thunk converts the m68k argument stream into a temporary native stream, calls native `FormatString()`, frees the temporary, and returns the native result unchanged (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6598-6608`). `m68k_to_native_fmt_stream()` returns NULL when the format has no conversions; for argument-bearing formats it allocates and returns a separate native buffer (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:255-282,303-322`). Native `InternalFormatString()` returns its stream unchanged when there are no formatted arguments, and otherwise returns a pointer at the end of the highest referenced argument (`workbench/libs/locale/formatstring.c:560-575`). Thus the no-argument path returns NULL, while an argument-bearing call returns a pointer into the temporary after it has been freed. Neither result is translated to the corresponding cursor in the guest's original argument stream.

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k guest calls the generated Locale vector and uses the returned `APTR` as its post-format argument cursor. A format with no conversion yields NULL; a format with converted arguments yields a dangling native pointer, not a usable guest address. The precise downstream symptom depends on whether the guest uses or compares the returned cursor. This finding is about return-cursor ownership/translation; the separate positional-argument loss is tracked under [EK9209](#ek9209), and the Hook callback ABI is covered by [EK9894](#ek9894).

**Affected configuration:** an explicitly built and loaded m68kemu library on a supported 64-bit host, for guest calls through the selected Locale `FormatString()` vector. The m68kemu target is optional and excluded from checked-in default package edges (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:14-17`; `rom/mmakefile.src:4-18,83-98,114-128`). No maintained in-tree emulated guest caller was established.

**Confidence:** high that no-argument conversion returns NULL, that argument-bearing conversion allocates a temporary, and that the wrapper frees it before returning the native cursor; guest-visible impact requires a caller to consume the returned cursor. No guest call, formatter operation, allocation failure, or build was run. Source-only; see the [Locale thunk review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5002).

<a id="ek9208"></a>
### EK9208 — Locale guest Hook forwarding *(withdrawn; duplicate of EK9894)*

**Disposition:** the Locale `FormatDate()`, `FormatString()`, and `ParseDate()` Hook paths are covered by [EK9894](#ek9894), which documents the guest/native Hook layout mismatch and the missing m68k callback execution bridge across the selected callback vectors, including these three Locale APIs. EK9208 is retained as a historical anchor; it is no longer a separate active finding. See the [Locale callback trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L10191).

<a id="ek9209"></a>
### EK9209 — m68k Locale `FormatString()` does not translate positional argument slots.

The generated m68k `FormatString()` thunk converts the guest stream with `m68k_to_native_fmt_stream()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6598-6608`). That helper counts conversion occurrences, scans flags/width, and handles sequential `%s`/`%b`, but does not parse the `$` positional index (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:255-315`). Native Locale `FormatString()` does parse `arg_pos$` and reads `ARG(arg_pos)` through a positional offset table (`workbench/libs/locale/formatstring.c:110-160,249-260,560-575`); its format prepass stores argument widths by position (`compiler/alib/getdatastreamfromformat.c:115-191`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k guest calls Locale `FormatString()` with a positional template such as `%2$s%1$s`. The thunk treats `$` as the conversion character, copies raw guest argument words into sequential four-byte slots, and does not translate their string addresses. Native Locale then looks up eight-byte host pointer slots by argument position; it can read the wrong slot or beyond the temporary allocation and may dereference a guest address as a host pointer before emitting output. **Affected configuration:** optional m68k emulation on 64-bit hosts, through the generated Locale `FormatString()` vector. **Reachability limit:** no checked-in guest caller was established. The ordinary guest Hook callback is independently unbridged (EK9894), so successful output is not claimed; the wrong argument reads/dereferences occur while the native formatter resolves the conversion, before its per-character callback. **Confidence:** high for the converter/parser mismatch and positional slot calculation; guest trigger remains conditional. Build the native stream by argument position and width, translating pointer arguments for guest memory. Source-only; no guest format was run.

<a id="ek9210"></a>
### EK9210 — m68k locale open routines return native Locale/Catalog pointers that their paired thunks cannot resolve.

The generated `OpenLocale()` and `OpenCatalogA()` thunks return their native pointers as `IPTR`, without creating guest shadows (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6717-6732`). The Moira vector dispatcher narrows the native result to the guest's 32-bit D0 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:256-275`). `OpenLocale(NULL)` increments the current Locale's open count and returns its native `IntLocale` address; a named Locale is also returned as its native structure (`workbench/libs/locale/openlocale.c:176-191`). `OpenCatalogA()` returns a cached native Catalog after incrementing `ic_UseCount`, or returns the embedded native Catalog for a newly loaded entry (`opencataloga.c:148-173,285-299`). The checked-in layout map records Locale as 168 guest / 312 native bytes and Catalog as 28 / 56 bytes (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_shadow_layouts.h:334-346,2512-2518`).

The paired `CloseLocale()` and `CloseCatalog()` thunks resolve their arguments using `THUNK_PTR()` but do not translate the truncated pointer back to the native object (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6555-6568`). The resolver accepts only exact registered shadow addresses or addresses within the guest arena (`m68kemu_intern.h:115-125`); neither open thunk registers a shadow. Native close then reads the host object fields directly (`workbench/libs/locale/closelocale.c:50-72`; `closecatalog.c:56-71`). Consequently, a guest cannot reliably inspect or release the acquired handle: the open reference may be left held, and a later close can resolve an unrelated guest address or fail depending on the truncated value. The object-layout differences also prevent treating the raw native structure as a valid guest Locale/Catalog.

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k guest calls `OpenLocale()` or `OpenCatalogA()` through the generated vectors, then accesses the returned record or passes it to the matching close routine. On the selected 64-bit hosts, D0 truncates the native pointer; the close thunk subsequently applies guest/shadow resolution rather than recovering the original pointer. The exact failure depends on the resulting 32-bit value and guest-memory range; no claim is made that every close faults.

**Affected configuration:** an explicitly built and loaded m68kemu library on a supported 64-bit host, with guest use of these Locale vectors. The m68kemu target is optional and excluded from the checked-in default package edges (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:14-17`; `rom/mmakefile.src:4-18,83-98,114-128`). No maintained in-tree emulated guest caller was established. `LocalePrefsUpdate()` also returns an old native Locale pointer, but its own documentation marks it internal for IPrefs, and the reviewed tree establishes no guest-side valid Locale producer/caller; it is not used to broaden this trigger.

**Confidence:** high that the open thunks return unshadowed native pointers, D0 narrows them, and paired close thunks cannot recover them through the selected resolver. Guest-visible resource retention or bad close behavior is conditional on an emulated client using the returned handle. No locale call, object access, close, or build was run. Source-only; see the [Locale object/string pointer review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5008).

<a id="ek9211"></a>
### EK9211 — m68k locale string-return APIs expose host string pointers directly to guest D0.

The generated `GetLocaleStr()` and `GetCatalogStr()` thunks return native `CONST_STRPTR` values as `IPTR` without translating them into guest addresses (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6611-6625`). The dispatcher narrows the result into the guest's 32-bit D0 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:256-275`). `GetLocaleStr()` returns a pointer from the native Locale's language-function table (`workbench/libs/locale/getlocalestr.c:55-61`). `GetCatalogStr()` returns either a catalog-owned string or the supplied fallback string (`getcatalogstr.c:59-86`); its thunk first translates the guest fallback to a host pointer, but does not map the returned pointer back. Neither API creates or returns a string shadow/handle.

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k guest calls either vector and reads or retains the returned string pointer. Native catalog/locale strings are host addresses narrowed into D0, and even the `GetCatalogStr(NULL, ..., defaultString)` path returns the host-mapped fallback address rather than the original guest address. The result is not a valid guest string address; any subsequent guest read can address unrelated guest memory or fail. The native APIs document Locale strings as read-only and valid while their Locale remains open, and catalog-owned strings as valid while the Catalog remains open; the fallback string instead retains its caller-owned lifetime. In every case the bridge fails to provide a usable guest pointer.

**Affected configuration:** an explicitly built and loaded m68kemu library on a supported 64-bit host, with guest use of these Locale vectors. The m68kemu target is optional and excluded from checked-in default package edges (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:14-17`; `rom/mmakefile.src:4-18,83-98,114-128`). No maintained in-tree emulated guest caller was established; native Workbench/Prefs callers use the host-native library path.

**Confidence:** high that each wrapper returns a native pointer through 32-bit D0 without guest mapping, including the fallback-string route; guest-visible impact requires guest code to consume the returned address. No string lookup or guest memory read was run. Source-only; see the [Locale object/string pointer review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5008).

<a id="ek9215"></a>
### EK9215 — m68k `NewCreateTaskA()` returns an unregistered native Task pointer to guest D0.

The generated m68kemu thunk converts the guest tag list, calls native `NewCreateTaskA()`, and returns the native `Task *` unchanged (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2466-2472`). The Moira thunk dispatcher narrows every `IPTR` return to a 32-bit guest D0 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:233-244`). Unlike `FindTask()` and `FindTaskByPID()`, which allocate/register Task shadows, this thunk creates no guest shadow for the returned task (`m68kemu_thunks.c:116-129`; generated `FindTaskByPID` at `m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2475-2482`). A subsequent `Signal()` resolves its guest A1 only through the shadow table or guest arena (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2012-2018`; `m68kemu_intern.h:115-125`), so the returned D0 value does not reliably identify the native task and cannot be used as a valid guest Task handle.

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k guest calls `NewCreateTaskA()` and then uses the returned Task pointer with a task-taking Exec vector such as `Signal()`. The pointer is truncated and unregistered; resolution may return NULL or an unrelated guest-arena address, so the operation does not target the created task. **Affected configuration:** optional `m68kemu` on supported 64-bit hosted targets; the target is not in the checked-in default package edge. No maintained in-tree emulated guest caller of `NewCreateTaskA()` was found, so use depends on guest software. **Confidence:** high for the raw native-pointer return, D0 narrowing, and shadow-aware argument resolution; no guest task was created. Register and return a Task shadow, or provide a guest-handle mapping used consistently by task APIs. No guest call or task was run; source-only. See the [m68kemu task-return trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5034).

<a id="ek9216"></a>
### EK9216 — CD device creation dereferences a failed boot-object allocation.

`cdrom_create()` first obtains a copied block-device descriptor through `get_dev()`, then allocates the enclosing `cdrom_boot_dev_t` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:485-494`). Initialization and failure cleanup are inside `if (boot)`, but the function's final `return &boot->dev` is outside that guard (`:497-605`). If the boot-object allocation returns NULL after a CD descriptor was found, execution reaches the member-address expression through NULL and faults instead of reporting factory failure. The separately allocated descriptor is also lost on that path; normal successful teardown's descriptor leak is recorded independently as EK9218.

**Trigger and consequence:** a CD backend is explicitly requested, `get_dev()` finds a drive, and the later `malloc(sizeof(cdrom_boot_dev_t))` fails. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the unguarded allocation result and return path; occurrence requires the stated allocation failure. Return NULL on allocation failure and release the copied descriptor. No allocation failure, media or boot was exercised; source-only. See the [Parthenope CD factory trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5332).

<a id="ek9217"></a>
### EK9217 — The CD reader can treat uninitialized cache metadata as a valid sector.

`cdrom_boot_dev_t` stores the one-sector cache tag `sector_in_buf` without initializing it (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:104-114`). `cdrom_create()` obtains the object with `malloc()` and initializes `phys`, the callbacks, and `rr`, but not this cache tag (`:485-514`). Its first descriptor read requests block 16, offset 0, for the primary volume descriptor (`:514-516`). The partial-sector path in `cdrom_read()` skips the physical read whenever the tag already equals the requested block, then copies bytes from `tmpbuf` (`:160-174`). Thus if the uninitialized tag happens to equal 16, the first read consumes uninitialized cache bytes and may reject a valid CD or proceed using fabricated descriptor fields. The later magic check does not make the read safe; matching stale bytes can pass it.

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 CD backend allocates a boot object whose stale `sector_in_buf` value is 16 before its first descriptor read. The tag then falsely marks `tmpbuf` as containing that sector, so the descriptor read is skipped. **Affected configuration:** explicit `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the uninitialized field, unchecked cache-hit comparison, and first-read path; occurrence depends on the allocator's prior contents. Initialize the tag to a guaranteed invalid state or track cache validity separately. No CD, allocation, firmware callback, or boot was exercised; source-only. See the [Parthenope CD source and caller ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5039).

<a id="ek9218"></a>
### EK9218 — Destroying a CD boot device leaks its separately allocated descriptor copy.

`get_dev()` allocates a standalone `block_dev_desc_t` and copies the matching U-Boot scan entry into it (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:459-483`). `cdrom_create()` stores that allocation in `boot->phys` (`:488,508`). The registered destroy callback, `fs_cdrom_destroy()`, frees only the enclosing `cdrom_boot_dev_t` (`:440-444`); it never frees the separately allocated `phys` copy. The selected boot path invokes `boot->destroy(boot)` after loading and probing the selected formats (`parthenope.c:383`), so each successful CD backend teardown leaks one descriptor-sized allocation. The descriptor is a copy, not the scan handle itself, and no other checked-in owner frees it.

**Trigger and consequence:** the optional CD backend is created successfully and reaches its destroy callback. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the allocation, stored ownership and incomplete destructor. Free `this->phys` as part of CD backend teardown. No boot, allocation or device operation was performed; source-only. See the [Parthenope CD factory trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5039).

<a id="ek9219"></a>
### EK9219 — CD device discovery writes through an unchecked descriptor allocation.

When `get_dev()` finds a U-Boot scan entry of type `DEV_TYPE_CDROM`, it allocates a standalone `block_dev_desc_t` and immediately copies the scan entry into it without checking the allocation result (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:469-475`). If that allocation fails, `memmove()` receives a null destination before `get_dev()` can finish the scan or return a clean failure. The caller `cdrom_create()` has a NULL check for a returned descriptor, but it cannot handle this earlier fault (`:485-491`).

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicitly built Parthenope CD backend encounters a CDROM scan entry while descriptor allocation fails. The copy then faults rather than returning NULL so the factory can reject the device. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked allocation and immediate copy; occurrence requires the stated allocation failure with a CDROM entry present. Check `bdev` before copying and end the scan cleanly on failure. No allocation failure, scan, device or boot was exercised; source-only. See the [Parthenope CD factory trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5039).

<a id="ek9220"></a>
### EK9220 — The CD factory reads the SUSP area without validating its size, allocation, or read.

After reading the ISO root directory record, `cdrom_create()` derives the System Use Area position and size directly from the on-media `len` and `namelen` fields (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:532-546`). It allocates `sua` without checking the result, ignores `cdrom_read()`'s return, casts the pointer to an SUSP entry, and reads `entry->sig` unconditionally (`:548-555`). For a valid plain ISO root entry with no SUA, the derived size is zero; the zero-length read does not populate the buffer, but the code still accesses the first two signature bytes. A NULL result from `malloc(0)` yields a null dereference; a non-NULL zero-size result still does not designate readable SUSP data. For a positive size, allocation failure or media-read failure likewise leaves no valid entry before the same dereference. Malformed length underflow is tracked separately under EK9228.

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 CD backend reads a plain ISO root record without SUSP data, or encounters SUA allocation/read failure. The factory accesses an absent or uninitialized entry before it can decide that Rock Ridge is not present, so a normal non-Rock-Ridge disc or a transient read failure can fault or misclassify the volume. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high that zero/failed allocation or read is unchecked before `entry->sig`; the exact failure form depends on zero-size allocation behavior and buffer contents. Validate record geometry, require a positive SUSP extent before parsing, and check both allocation and read status. No CD, allocation failure, read failure or boot was exercised; source-only. See the [Parthenope CD factory trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5039).

<a id="ek9221"></a>
### EK9221 — Parthenope's SUSP iterator leaks its allocated entry buffer when a media read fails.

`iterate_entries()` allocates an SUA buffer, then returns `-1` directly if the initial `cdrom_read()` fails, without freeing the buffer (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:185-193`). For a CE entry, it frees the old buffer, allocates the continuation buffer, and also returns directly on a failed continuation read without freeing that replacement (`:199-214`). `get_entry()` discards `iterate_entries()`'s return value and returns only its result pointer (`:254-270`), so the selected Rock Ridge and NM-name callers see the failed scan as a missing entry and continue (`:332-340,562-568`).

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicit Parthenope Sam440 CD backend allocates an SUA buffer and a later block read fails during an initial or CE continuation scan. The current buffer remains allocated with no retained owner; repeated failed lookups can accumulate the leaked buffer sizes, though repeated failures or exhaustion are not established on the selected boot path. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the early-return cleanup omission and lost buffer; occurrence depends on a failed firmware block read after allocation. Free the active SUA buffer on every read-error exit and propagate scan failure separately from “entry not found.” No CD, media error or boot was exercised; source-only. See the [Parthenope SUSP iterator trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5043).

<a id="ek9222"></a>
### EK9222 — Malformed SUSP data can make Parthenope loop indefinitely while parsing an ISO image.

`iterate_entries()` advances its SUSP cursor only by the current entry's on-media `len` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:224-231`). A zero-length entry leaves `ptr` unchanged, so for a remaining SUA extent larger than one byte the outer `do` loop revisits the same entry forever. The CE continuation loop is also unbounded: it replaces the current buffer with the referenced block/offset/length and repeats while the new entry is CE, without checking visited extents or limiting continuation count (`:199-216`). A cyclic CE reference therefore repeats the same read and parse indefinitely. `get_entry()` invokes this iterator during initial Rock Ridge detection and later NM filename lookup (`:254-270,332-340,562-568`).

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 CD backend scans an ISO image containing a zero-length SUSP record or a CE chain that cycles. Factory initialization or path lookup can then stop making progress, preventing boot-menu or image loading from completing. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high that the cursor/continuation logic has no progress or cycle bound; occurrence requires malformed on-media SUSP data. Reject entries shorter than the SUSP header, enforce that each entry advances within the remaining extent, and bound or detect repeated CE extents. EK9223 and EK9228 separately cover out-of-extent entry copying and directory-record bounds; this finding is limited to non-progress. No malformed image or boot was used; source-only. See the [Parthenope SUSP parser trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5178).

<a id="ek9223"></a>
### EK9223 — Parthenope copies a matching SUSP entry past the end of its allocated SUA buffer.

`iterate_entries()` allocates `sua` for the caller-supplied extent and passes an entry pointer to the callback without first validating `e->len` against the bytes remaining in that allocation (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:185-197,224-231`). When the signature matches, `my_iteration()` allocates `e->len` bytes and copies that entire length from the source pointer (`:244-249`). A matching entry near the end of the SUA whose declared length extends beyond the remaining extent therefore makes `memcpy()` read beyond the allocated source buffer. `get_entry()` uses this callback for the root RR lookup and for NM filename lookup on Rock Ridge volumes (`:254-270,332-337,562-565`).

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 CD backend scans Rock Ridge SUSP data containing a matching NM or RR record whose declared length exceeds the bytes remaining in the current SUA. The copy reads adjacent memory beyond the allocated record buffer and can fault or produce invalid metadata. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked source extent and copy length; occurrence requires malformed SUSP input with a matching signature. Check the declared length against the current remaining SUA before callback dispatch and copying. EK9228 separately covers the outer ISO directory-record and SUA extent derivation; EK9222 covers non-progress. No malformed image or boot was used; source-only. See the [Parthenope SUSP entry-copy trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5047).

<a id="ek9224"></a>
### EK9224 — A failed SUSP-entry copy allocation is dereferenced immediately.
