It stores the segment in `segArray[3]` only after allocating the segment array (`:505-514`). The common creation-failure cleanup frees the array when published, then frees the process and local allocations, but never calls `UnLoadSeg()` for the synthesized entry segment (`:594-650`). `UnLoadSeg()` is only called in the normal `DosEntry()` completion path (`:945-953`). `CreateSegList()` allocates the wrapper and its release path distinguishes normal `AllocMem()` from W^X page allocation (`compiler/arossupport/createseglist.c:60-103`; `rom/dos/unloadseg.c:25-46`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a caller supplies `NP_Entry` without `NP_Seglist`, wrapper allocation succeeds, and a later fallible step fails before the child reaches normal `DosEntry()` cleanup. The wrapper then leaks. Confirmed later failure points include segment-array allocation and task insertion; on `__AROSPLATFORM_WXSEG__` targets, the leak retains the dedicated page mapping as well as the segment. **Affected configuration:** all selected `CreateNewProc()` callers using a synthesized entry; the checked-in pthread creator follows this path (`compiler/pthread/pthread_create.c:263-278`). **Confidence:** high for the missing cleanup once the wrapper exists; trigger requires a subsequent creation failure. No allocation failure, task insertion failure, or process creation was induced; source-only. See the [CreateNewProc synthesized-entry ownership/error-path recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#createnewproc-synthesized-entry-ownershiperror-path-recheck-ek9874-retained-2026-10-26).

<a id="ek9507"></a>
### EK9507 — `Date2Amiga()` signed overflow from calendar year 2047.

`Date2Amiga()` stores `date->year` in a `UWORD` and evaluates `year * 31536000` before adding it to the `ULONG` seconds total (`rom/utility/date2amiga.c:49-57,73-78`). On the selected 32-bit-`int` targets, integer promotions make this multiplication signed: for year 2047 the relative year is 69 and the product is 2,175,984,000, above `INT_MAX`, so the expression has signed overflow before conversion to `ULONG`. `CheckDate()` permits years from 1978 upward without an upper-year bound and returns this conversion result (`rom/utility/checkdate.c:77-85,120-122`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a caller converts a valid date in calendar year 2047 or later. The signed multiplication is undefined; the resulting seconds value can be incorrect, and callers that derive DOS dates or timestamps from it can receive a corrupt date. Checked-in paths include CDVDFS directory timestamps, whose year is read from the disc record and passed through `CheckDate()` (`rom/filesys/CDVDFS/src/iso9660.c:765-770`), plus the optional Zune Calendar class (`workbench/classes/zune/calendar/calendar.c:145-170,182-192`; `MUIA_Calendar_Year` is declared as UWORD in `calendar.h:23`). FAT's on-disk year range reaches 2107 and also calls the function (`rom/filesys/fat/date.c:54`), subject to the format's source fields. **Affected configuration:** selected Utility library clients on targets with 32-bit `int`; the Zune Calendar target is optional, while CDVDFS and FAT use depends on filesystem selection. **Confidence:** high for the signed-overflow expression and year threshold; exact downstream date corruption depends on compiler treatment of undefined overflow. No date conversion or filesystem/UI operation was run; source-only. See the [Utility date arithmetic pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#utility-date-arithmetic-filtering-and-named-object-lifecycle-pass-ek9505-ek9507-added-2026-10-25).

<a id="ek9508"></a>
### EK9508 — generic `SDivMod32()` drops its documented remainder result.

The public vector contract returns quotient in the high 32 bits and remainder in the low 32 bits for non-m68k HLL callers (`rom/utility/utility.conf:60`; `rom/utility/sdivmod32.c:21-35`). The selected generic implementation instead returns only `dividend / divisor` (`sdivmod32.c:67-69`). On targets where `QUAD` is a native signed 64-bit value, this sign-extends the quotient; on targets where `QUAD` is the `{high, low}` pair, a scalar quotient does not construct the required pair. The m68k architecture supplies an assembly vector override returning quotient and remainder in D0/D1 (`arch/m68k-all/utility/sdivmod32.s:22-55`), so this finding is limited to the generic implementation.

**Trigger and consequence:** a client calls the generic Utility vector and interprets the returned 64-bit value according to the documented packed contract. The quotient is not placed in the high word and the remainder is absent, so both fields are wrong for ordinary non-exact divisions. The checked-in source search found no maintained AROS C caller consuming the packed result; the sound datatype's legacy `__MAXON__` macro uses the API as quotient-only arithmetic, so no in-tree user consequence is asserted. **Affected configuration:** targets using generic `rom/utility/sdivmod32.c`, excluding the m68k vector replacement. **Confidence:** high for the implementation/contract mismatch; practical impact depends on clients using the documented packed result. No division call was run; source-only. See the [Utility arithmetic and structure-tag body pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#utility-arithmetic-and-structure-tag-body-pass-ek9508-added-2026-10-25).

<a id="ek9509"></a>
### EK9509 — PC x86 interrupt entry calls C with DF inherited from the interrupted context.

Both selected PC entry stubs preserve registers and then transfer to the shared C `core_IRQHandle()` without first clearing the x86 direction flag: i386 executes `call core_IRQHandle` (`arch/i386-pc/kernel/core_interrupts.s:97-128`), while x86-64 jumps to it (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/core_interrupts.s:98-139`). `core_SetIDTGate()` installs interrupt gates with DPL 3 (`arch/all-pc/kernel/cpu_intr.c:200-236`), and the i386 PC startup installs the syscall vector as a user-callable gate (`arch/i386-pc/kernel/platform_init.c:85-90`; x86-64 uses the shared PC syscall setup). The shared `core_SysCallHandler()` reaches C list traversal and handler dispatch before its `cli; cld` at `arch/all-pc/kernel/syscall.c:41-75`. Similarly, the shared IRQ handler reaches its C body before the `cli; cld` on the user-return path (`arch/all-pc/kernel/cpu_intr.c:370-390,525-536`).

**Trigger and consequence:** user-mode code sets DF and enters the user-callable syscall vector, or a PC interrupt arrives while DF is set. The processor preserves the interrupted flags on the return frame but does not make the current DF suitable for C; entry then invokes C with DF set, contrary to the expected x86 C calling convention. If generated or inlined C string operations rely on forward direction, they can process memory backwards and corrupt data or fault. The later `cld` does not protect earlier C work. **Affected configuration:** selected i386-PC and x86-64-PC kernels using the shared all-PC interrupt handlers. **Confidence:** high that both entry stubs omit the clear and that user code can enter the syscall gate with DF set; actual corruption depends on the C instructions emitted and the affected operation. No interrupt, syscall, or user code was run; source-only. See the [i386 interrupt-entry coverage row](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1441).

<a id="ek8848"></a>
### EK8848 — i386-PC dispatch unconditionally uses Pentium-only `RDTSC`

The i386-PC build selects `arch/i386-pc/kernel/kernel_cpu.c`, whose `cpu_Dispatch()` unconditionally executes `RDTSC()` when it starts each task (`:25-72`, especially `:71`). The selected all-PC `RDTSC()` helper emits the raw instruction with no feature check or fallback (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_arch.h:175-185`); `KrnTimeStamp()` also calls it directly (`arch/all-pc/kernel/timestamp.c:14-20`). Intel documents that `RDTSC` was introduced with Pentium, while the i386 configuration is compiled with `-march=i486` (`configure.in:1364-1382,1436-1448`) and the i386 interrupt-controller path permits operation without APIC by falling back to the 8259A PIC (`arch/all-pc/kernel/apic.c:21-31`; `ictl.c:95-134`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an i386-PC system with a CPUID-capable 486-class processor that lacks TSC boots far enough to dispatch its first task. The unconditional instruction raises invalid-opcode (#UD), preventing task dispatch; any earlier `KrnTimeStamp()` call has the same unsupported-instruction risk. The configuration flag establishes an i486 compiler baseline, but the source tree does not document a supported runtime CPU floor, so the trigger is conditional on such a 486 being a supported boot target. **Affected configuration:** the explicit `pc-i386` kernel target using the shared all-PC kernel code. **Confidence:** high that the selected path executes `RDTSC` without checking support and that Intel introduced the instruction with Pentium; medium that the repository intends to support every i486-compatible system because its compiler baseline does not by itself define the product's hardware support policy. Require TSC support before selecting this path or provide a non-TSC fallback, and document a Pentium-or-later minimum if that is the actual platform contract. No CPU or build was exercised; source-only.

<a id="ek9510"></a>
### EK9510 — x86-64 PC task CPU-time conversion overflows after a long scheduling interval.

The selected x86-64 PC `cpu_Switch()` computes elapsed TSC ticks and converts them to nanoseconds with `(timeCur * 1000000000) / cpu_TSCFreq` (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:208-225,311-340`). `timeCur` is `UQUAD`, so the multiplication wraps modulo 2^64 before division. It overflows when the interval exceeds `UINT64_MAX / 1,000,000,000` TSC ticks, about 6.15 seconds at 3 GHz. The resulting `timespec` increment is then added to the task's accumulated CPU time. That value is exposed by `QueryTaskTagList(TaskTag_CPUTime)` (`rom/exec/etask.h:49`; `rom/task/QueryTaskTagList.c:153-160`).

**Trigger and consequence:** on the selected x86-64 PC kernel, one task runs without a scheduling/accounting switch for longer than the frequency-dependent threshold. Local `Forbid()` prevents task switching on its processor while active (`rom/exec/forbid.c:58-60`), providing a source-level route to a long interval. When the task is next switched, the wrapped conversion adds an incorrect CPU-time increment, so `TaskTag_CPUTime` underreports or otherwise misstates that task's accumulated runtime. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC builds selecting `arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_cpu.c`; the threshold varies with the measured TSC frequency. **Confidence:** high for unsigned multiplication wrap and the public accounting path; triggering requires an unusually long uninterrupted scheduling interval. No task interval or CPU-time query was exercised; source-only. See the [x86-64 PC scheduler CPU-time conversion and API trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#x86-64-pc-scheduler-cpu-time-conversion-and-api-trace-ek9510-added-2026-10-26).

<a id="ek9511"></a>
### EK9511 — Optional x86-64 trap backtracing dereferences an unchecked interrupted frame pointer.

When `KERNEL_USE_TRAPDEBUG` is enabled, the x86-64 PC build includes `kernel_trapdebug.c` (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/mmakefile.src:7,42-46`), whose trap-dump path passes the saved exception RBP to `KrnBacktraceFromFrame()` (`kernel_trapdebug.c:291-303`; saved context layout: `arch/x86_64-all/include/aros/cpucontext.h:47-86`). The selected x86-64 walker immediately reads `rbp[0]` and `rbp[1]`, then checks only the saved next-frame pointer for monotonicity and alignment (`arch/x86_64-all/kernel/backtracefromframe.c:23-39`). It does not validate the initial pointer.

**Trigger and consequence:** with optional trap debugging enabled, an exception occurs while the interrupted task has a nonzero invalid RBP. The diagnostic unwinder reads through that pointer and can fault again while reporting the original exception, replacing or obscuring the original trap report and potentially preventing normal trap handling. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC builds with `KERNEL_USE_TRAPDEBUG` enabled; the makefile leaves it disabled by default. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked first dereference and conditional secondary-fault path. No trap, invalid frame, or debug build was run; source-only. See the [optional x86-64 trap-backtrace frame validation pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#optional-x86-64-trap-backtrace-frame-validation-pass-ek9511-added-2026-10-26).

<a id="ek9515"></a>
### EK9515 — DOSBoot divides by zero while scanning an RDB partition with zero cylinder geometry.

`AddPartitionVolume()` rejects an unknown DosType, but after that it calculates `blockspercyl` as `DE_BLKSPERTRACK * DE_NUMHEADS` and unconditionally evaluates `i % blockspercyl` (`rom/dosboot/bootscan.c:145-150,204-212`). The selected RDB parser accepts a checksummed PART block and copies its declared DosEnvec fields into the partition handle without validating these geometry fields (`rom/partition/partitionrdb.c:277-303,479-496`). DOSBoot's leaf-table scan calls `AddPartitionVolume()` when a child partition table cannot be opened (`rom/dosboot/bootscan.c:253-272`). For RDB entries the path does not replace the reported geometry with whole-device defaults.

**Trigger and consequence:** DOSBoot scans a recognized, sufficiently sized RDB PART entry with a valid checksum and nonzero DosType, but with either `DE_BLKSPERTRACK` or `DE_NUMHEADS` set to zero. If treated as a leaf, `blockspercyl` is zero and the remainder operation faults before filesystem lookup or BootNode creation. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting DOSBoot and the RDB partition backend; the failure occurs while scanning the affected disk, before boot-node creation. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked source path and zero-divisor consequence; trigger requires malformed or unusual RDB geometry. No disk, RDB table, or boot scan was run; source-only. See the [DOSBoot zero-geometry scan recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#ek9515-zero-geometry-rejection-and-selected-scan-recheck-2026-10-26).

<a id="ek9516"></a>
### EK9516 — MinGW bootstrap may consume an invalid error pointer when Windows cannot format a loader failure.

`GetErrorStr()` passes the caller's `char **` directly to `FormatMessage(FORMAT_MESSAGE_ALLOCATE_BUFFER | FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_SYSTEM, ...)`, ignores its return value, and does not initialize `*error` before the call (`arch/all-mingw32/bootstrap/hostlib.c:12-20`). `Host_HostLib_Open()` and `Host_HostLib_GetPointer()` invoke it after `LoadLibrary()` or `GetProcAddress()` fails (`:28-36,50-57`). The selected kernel startup caller declares `errstr` without initialization and, for either failure, uses it as a `%s` argument and passes it to `Host_HostLib_FreeErrorStr()` (`arch/all-mingw32/kernel/kernel_startup.c:35-37,90-108`; free wrapper: `hostlib.c:23-26`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a DLL load or symbol lookup fails, and the follow-up `FormatMessage` call also fails without storing a valid allocated string through the output pointer. Startup may then read an indeterminate pointer while formatting the diagnostic and pass it to `LocalFree`, so error reporting itself can fault or mis-handle memory. Initialize `*error` to `NULL` before formatting and check the return value before exposing/freeing the string. **Affected configuration:** MinGW hosted bootstrap when loading `Libs\Host\kernel.dll` or resolving one of its required symbols fails and system-message formatting also fails. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked output and caller dataflow; medium for reaching the secondary formatting failure and its exact manifestation. No Windows loader or formatting failure was run. See the [selected bootstrap and caller recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1110).

<a id="ek9517"></a>
### EK9517 — MinGW warm reboot omits the shared-RAM marker and leaves its inherited mapping handle open.

`Host_Shutdown(TRUE)` formats the shared mapping handle/address into `AROS\x1b.RAM`, calls `putenv()`, then starts the replacement process with `CreateProcess(..., bInheritHandles=TRUE, ..., lpEnvironment=NULL, ...)` (`arch/all-mingw32/bootstrap/shutdown.c:31-50`). In the selected MinGW CRT, `putenv()` updates the CRT-local environment; it does not update the operating-system environment block used when raw `CreateProcess` is passed a NULL environment. The child therefore inherits the prior OS environment, without the newly formatted marker. The mapping handle itself was created with `SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES.bInheritHandle=TRUE` (`arch/all-mingw32/bootstrap/memory.c:63-79`), so it is inherited by the child. With no marker, the child's `AllocateRAM32()` creates and stores a new mapping handle, leaving the inherited old mapping handle untracked and open for the child's lifetime (`memory.c:46-93`). The code explicitly builds the marker to preserve the shared mapping across this restart, but this path does not deliver it to the child.

**Trigger and consequence:** use the maintained MinGW warm-reboot path (`ColdReboot()` calls the HostInterface callback with `warm=TRUE`) and let `CreateProcess` succeed. The new process starts with a fresh RAM mapping instead of reusing the old one and retains an unused inherited file-mapping handle until that process exits. This wastes a kernel handle and defeats the source's intended shared-RAM handoff; no RAM contents are claimed to survive reboot. Avoid the CRT-only environment change or pass a constructed environment block, and close unconsumed inherited handles. **Affected configuration:** MinGW hosted bootstrap warm-reboot path; the selected source supports x86 and x86-64. **Confidence:** high that the marker is not in the child OS environment and the mapping handle is inherited/untracked; medium for practical impact beyond the per-process handle/resource leak. No restart or Windows process was run.

A separate, less reachable case remains conditional: if an external launcher supplies a valid `AROS\x1b.RAM` marker in the OS environment and invokes the 64-bit bootstrap with the corresponding inheritable handle, a cold reboot's CRT-only attempt to clear it does not remove it from the child environment. For a memory request above 512 MiB, the x64 bootstrap first consumes the marker in `AllocateRAM()` for the high portion and then in `AllocateRAM32()` for the low portion (`arch/all-hosted/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:306-329`; `arch/all-mingw32/bootstrap/memory.c:97-145,46-93`). The second fixed-address map collides with the first; larger high portions can exceed the referenced mapping size earlier. This can abort bootstrap, but no maintained in-tree producer of an OS-level marker was found, so treat it as an external-launcher condition with low reachability confidence.

The CRT environment behavior is documented for [`_putenv`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/c-runtime-library/reference/putenv-wputenv?view=msvc-170); a NULL environment pointer makes `CreateProcess` inherit the process environment, and its handle inheritance is enabled here ([`CreateProcess`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessa), [handle inheritance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sysinfo/handle-inheritance)). See the [allocator and restart-path recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1111).

<a id="ek9518"></a>
### EK9518 — DOSBoot dereferences a missing device-enable array in Boot Options.

`dosboot_Init()` counts the Expansion MountList, then allocates a two-part `devicesEnabled` array only when at least one device exists (`rom/dosboot/dosboot_init.c:215-231`). If `AllocVec()` fails, the assignment leaves `LIBBASE->devicesEnabled == NULL`; initialization nevertheless proceeds into `bootmenu_Init()` (`:233-235`). When the user opens Boot Options, `initScreen()` selects `PAGE_BOOT`, whose `populateGadgets_PageBoot()` first copies every device state into the backup half of that array without checking the pointer (`rom/dosboot/menu.c:244-248`). Its later device-list rendering and toggle handlers also dereference the same array (`:371-396,685-690`). The final MountList reorder explicitly handles a NULL array as “leave all devices enabled” (`dosboot_init.c:259-273`), so the allocation failure is otherwise supported outside this page.

**Trigger and consequence:** DOSBoot has a nonempty MountList, the optional `devicesEnabled` allocation fails, and the user enters Boot Options (through the main page's Boot Options button or another selected menu entry path). The backup loop dereferences NULL before populating the page, so the boot-menu path can fault instead of continuing with the default all-enabled device set. Keep Boot Options unavailable when the array is absent or make the page use the same default-enabled behavior as the final reorder. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting the DOSBoot module and its menu (`rom/dosboot/mmakefile.src:19-39`); requires low memory, at least one MountList entry, and Boot Options selection. **Confidence:** high for the allocation-failure state and unguarded page dereference; the failure/UI sequence was not induced. See the [allocation and menu caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7051).

<a id="ek9520"></a>
### EK9520 — m68k AROSBootstrap's `LoadSegment` free callback only removes bookkeeping and leaks the allocation.

The m68k bootstrap supplies `aosAlloc` and `aosFree` as the allocation callbacks to DOS `LoadSegment()` from `LoadResidents()` (`arch/m68k-amiga/c/AROSBootstrap.c:582-605,822-845`). `aosAlloc()` uses `aosAllocMem()`, which allocates the requested span plus two `ALLOCATION_EXTRA` headers and records the range in the bootstrap MemList (`:558-580,589`). The paired `aosFree()` reconstructs the base and expanded size, then calls only `remMemList()`; it never calls `FreeMem()` (`:593-605`). `remMemList()` marks the reservation slot free and unlinks the node, but does not release the underlying Exec allocation (`:343-357`).

The selected AOS Hunk loader calls that callback for its 2,048-byte buffered-read allocation at the common return on both success and failure (`rom/dos/internalloadseg_aos.c:36-45,583-591`; callback dispatch: `rom/dos/internalloadseg.h:39-55`). Thus every configured AOS Hunk module loaded by `LoadResidents()` loses at least the read-buffer allocation (2,048 bytes plus the bootstrap's two allocation headers) after the loader returns. On parse/read failure, the AOS loader also sends allocated hunk vectors and its hunk table through the same callback (`internalloadseg_aos.c:583-590`; vector free dispatch: `rom/dos/internalloadseg.c:159-184`), leaking those allocations too. Successful resident hunks themselves remain intentionally reserved for the boot handoff; the temporary read buffer is not part of that retained module state.

**Trigger and consequence:** run m68k `AROSBootstrap` with one or more `MODULES` entries that reach the AOS Hunk loader. Each such load leaks its 2,048-byte parser buffer; malformed or unreadable Hunk modules can additionally leak temporary hunk/table allocations during error cleanup. Repeated entries consume bootstrap-available memory, with the configured module count bounded by the command parser. Have `aosFree()` release the reconstructed base/size with `FreeMem()` after removing the reservation, while preserving allocations intentionally retained for successful handoff. **Affected configuration:** `AROSBootstrap` built by `arch/m68k-amiga/c/mmakefile.src` and included by the m68k-Amiga boot image; requires configured AOS Hunk modules (the malformed-load excess is conditional). **Confidence:** high for the missing `FreeMem()` and the loader's successful/failure callback paths; no module load or allocation was run. See the [loader callback and memory-reservation trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7107).

<a id="ek9521"></a>
### EK9521 — Hosted Unix accepts IRQ registrations that are reserved or outside its signal-dispatch range.

The selected Unix kernel uses `IRQ_COUNT=32` (`arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel_arch.h:1-3`). Its installed interrupt handler calls `krnRunIRQHandlers()` only when the delivered signal number is below that limit (`arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel.c:125-162`). However, the generic `KrnAddIRQHandler()` checks only `irq < HW_IRQ_COUNT` before allocating and publishing a handler (`rom/kernel/addirqhandler.c:79-110`). With `INTB_KERNEL=16`, the default bound is 240; maintained i386/x86-64 CPU headers set `HW_IRQ_BASE=32`, making the bound 208 (`rom/kernel/kernel_base.h:50-55`; `compiler/include/exec/interrupts.h:84-87`; `arch/i386-all/include/aros/cpu.h:18-19`; `arch/x86_64-all/include/aros/cpu.h:18-19`). Thus signal-like IDs from 32 up to the selected bound are accepted and stored but never reached by Unix `core_IRQ()`; Unix installs handlers only for its selected timer, I/O, trap, and internal software/syscall signals (`kernel.c:271-324`).

The same generic admission check accepts the host's `SIGUSR1` and `SIGUSR2` IDs. Unix reserves `SIGUSR1` for syscall/context transitions (`arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel.c:322-323,346-358`; `arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:68-73`) and `SIGUSR2` for `KrnCause()` software interrupts (`kernel.c:316-320`; `arch/all-unix/kernel/cause.c:12-18`). `core_SysCall()` unconditionally walks the handler chain for its signal before interpreting task state (`kernel.c:71-82`); the `SIGUSR2` route enters `core_IRQ()` and walks its chain when the signal is below 32 (`kernel.c:153-160`). A client that registers either reserved ID therefore gets its handler called as part of syscall or software-interrupt processing, rather than only for an independent device interrupt.

**Trigger and consequence:** an external kernel.resource client registers an IRQ ID outside the Unix dispatch domain, or registers `SIGUSR1`/`SIGUSR2` as a device IRQ. Out-of-range registrations return a non-NULL handle but are never dispatched; reserved-signal registrations run at internal syscall/soft-interrupt times and can invoke device handlers spuriously. Reject IDs not explicitly supported by the selected Unix signal table and exclude the internal control signals from public IRQ registration. **Affected configuration:** hosted Unix targets using `arch/all-unix/kernel`; the numeric generic bound is 208 for maintained i386/x86-64 headers and 240 where `HW_IRQ_BASE` is unset, while Unix dispatch remains capped at 32. **Confidence:** high for the admission/dispatch mismatch and reserved-signal routing; practical in-tree reachability is not established because checked-in Unix IRQ callers use only `SIGALRM`/`SIGIO`. No IRQ was registered or signal delivered. See the [Unix IRQ registration/dispatch trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1310).

<a id="ek9522"></a>
### EK9522 — EFI GetTime advertises the wrong capabilities structure type.

The shared EFI runtime-services header defines `struct EFI_Time_Caps` with the RTC resolution, accuracy, and `SetsToZero` fields, but the `GetTime` function pointer instead accepts `struct EFI_Time_Cap *` (`compiler/include/hardware/efi/runtime.h:39-43,58-61`). The singular tag is never defined in the EFI headers. In C, that pointer declaration is legal as a pointer to an incomplete struct, so this is not a header parse failure; it makes the public function-pointer type incompatible with the provided capabilities structure type. A consumer passing `struct EFI_Time_Caps *` gets an incompatible-pointer diagnostic and must use a cast or a locally invented tag to call the service through this declaration.

**Trigger and consequence:** an EFI consumer uses `GetTime` and requests capabilities using the structure type supplied by this header. The mismatch impedes type-safe use and can hide caller mistakes behind casts; both pointer representations are the same on supported C targets, and no direct memory-corruption consequence is established from this declaration alone. **Affected configuration:** any build consuming `hardware/efi/runtime.h`; no checked-in `GetTime` caller was found. **Confidence:** high that the declared tag does not match the defined public structure; practical impact is limited to consumers of this API. The [UEFI 2.10 GetTime prototype](https://uefi.org/specs/UEFI/2.10/08_Services_Runtime_Services.html#efi-runtime-services-gettime) names `EFI_TIME_CAPABILITIES *`. No firmware call or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek9523"></a>
### EK9523 — EFI shared service declarations use incorrect native-width types on 32-bit targets.

The EFI type header fixes several ABI-native types at 64 bits regardless of target: `EFI_STATUS` is `QUAD`, `EFI_TPL` and `EFI_HANDLE` are `UQUAD`, and allocation, memory, and interface type values are also `UQUAD` (`compiler/include/hardware/efi/types.h:19-25`). The shared Boot Services and Runtime Services tables then use `UQUAD` for native-width sizes/counts and pointers-to-handles, including `GetMemoryMap`, `AllocatePages`, image exit-data lengths, variable data sizes, and `SetVirtualAddressMap` (`compiler/include/hardware/efi/boot.h:19-45,118-151`; `compiler/include/hardware/efi/runtime.h:76-105`). In the 32-bit EFI ABI these positions use `UINTN`/pointer-sized or 32-bit enum types, while this header describes 64-bit values; calls made through these function-pointer types therefore do not faithfully describe the firmware ABI and can pass or receive arguments with the wrong width/layout. The maintained x86-64 EFI calling-convention branch is separate and these widths are appropriate there.

The Runtime Services table also declares `GetNextHighMonotonicCount(UQUAD *)` (`runtime.h:109-111`), but UEFI specifies `UINT32 *`. Firmware writes only four bytes: a consumer treating the output as a 64-bit count can retain an indeterminate/stale half, with which half affected depending on byte order and initialization. The [UEFI 2.10 service prototypes](https://uefi.org/specs/UEFI/2.10/08_Services_Runtime_Services.html#efi-runtime-services-get-next-high-monotonic-count) specify native-width parameters and a 32-bit high-count output.

**Trigger and consequence:** a 32-bit EFI consumer calls a service through these shared declarations, or a consumer treats the high monotonic output as a 64-bit value. Width mismatches can make service arguments/results disagree with firmware expectations; the high-count mismatch can leave part of a caller's 64-bit object unwritten. **Affected configuration:** 32-bit EFI consumers of `hardware/efi/{types,boot,runtime}.h`. The i386 PC BSP manifest lists `efi` in its resource set (`arch/i386-pc/boot/mmakefile.src:69`), and the selected Multiboot2 parser accepts an EFI32 system-table tag (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/multiboot2.c:194-201,206-210`). Its checked-in runtime caller is `ResetSystem()` (`arch/all-native/efi/efi_init.c:25-50`); that invocation supplies zero for the width-mismatched status, size, and data arguments, so the ABI mismatch does not establish a failure for that call. No checked-in consumer invokes the affected Boot Services or other width-sensitive Runtime Services through these declarations. The remaining consequence is conditional on external or future 32-bit EFI clients using the public declarations. **Confidence:** high for the header/spec type mismatches; actual effect depends on an external or future 32-bit EFI consumer invoking the affected entries. No EFI firmware call or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek9524"></a>
### EK9524 — TLSF corruption diagnostics omit frames on generic-stub targets.

When TLSF detects free-list corruption, `tlsf_fail_corruption()` captures up to 16 PCs with `KrnBacktraceFromFrame()` and prints the returned depth (`rom/kernel/tlsf.c:336-338,371-377`). The common implementation selected when an architecture does not supply an override unconditionally returns zero (`rom/kernel/backtracefromframe.c:80-82`). The checked target manifests select architecture implementations only for x86-64, AArch64, and RISC-V64/OpenSBI (`arch/x86_64-all/kernel/mmakefile.src:20`; `arch/aarch64-all/kernel/mmakefile.src:22`; `arch/riscv64-all/kernel/mmakefile.src:27`). The generic implementation is therefore used by the verified i386-PC, ARM-native, and RISC-V SiFive-U targets. Each of these has a selected TLSF startup path by default (`arch/i386-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:175,320-321`; `arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_startup.c:279-293`; `arch/riscv-native/sifive_u/kernel/kernel_startup.c:188-202`); the latter two can opt out with `notlsf`, and i386-PC uses its `notlsf` allocator selection.

**Trigger and consequence:** a TLSF consistency check detects corruption on one of those default-TLSF configurations. The diagnostic prints the corruption metadata and then a backtrace header reporting zero frames, losing the allocator call-site context that could help identify the source. The corruption path still terminates via `__builtin_trap()`; this finding concerns diagnostic quality only. **Affected configuration:** i386-PC, ARM-native Raspberry Pi, and RISC-V native SiFive-U when TLSF is selected; x86-64, AArch64 and RISC-V64/OpenSBI use architecture overrides and are excluded. **Confidence:** high for the zero-depth common implementation and selected caller/configuration path. No corruption or backtrace was induced; source-only. See the [target and caller census](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8919).

<a id="ek9525"></a>
### EK9525 — Concurrent x86-64 protection calls can overwrite each other’s split page table.

The x86-64 PC `KrnSetProtection()` vector directly calls `protect_pages()` and then `core_ProtKernelArea()`; it adds no serialization around page-table edits (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/setprotection.c:25-61`). In `core_ProtPage()`, a 2 MiB PDE is split by copying its current mapping into a 4 KiB table, taking a slot from the shared `mmu_PDEPageUsed` counter, and publishing the new table pointer back into the PDE (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/mmu.c:183-250`). The check/increment, table population, and PDE publication are not protected by a lock. If two CPUs enter while the same PDE is still a large-page mapping, both can copy the original permissions into separate tables; after one caller changes a PTE and publishes its table, the other can publish its stale copy over that PDE and erase the first permission update. The shared split-table counter is also not synchronized during this path.

**Trigger and consequence:** concurrent calls to the public kernel `KrnSetProtection()` vector on x86-64 PC target the same not-yet-split 2 MiB PDE, with one publication occurring after the other caller's PTE update. The later stale table publication can silently restore the old permissions for the affected page; concurrent counter updates can also make split-table allocation inconsistent. Startup's direct protection calls occur before AP startup, and the checked-in post-startup caller census found no selected concurrent route; this remains conditional on external or future clients invoking the public vector concurrently. It is distinct from split-pool exhaustion and stale remote TLB handling. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC kernel with SMP-capable CPUs and concurrent public `KrnSetProtection()` clients; no claim for other architecture implementations. **Confidence:** high for the unsynchronized split/publish sequence; no selected in-tree concurrent trigger was established. No protection call or interleaving was run; source-only. See the [caller and page-table recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8437).

<a id="ek9526"></a>
### EK9526 — DOSBoot drops a whole-disk fallback when all child registrations fail.

`CheckTables()` returns TRUE whenever `OpenPartitionTable()` succeeds, regardless of whether any child `DeviceNode` is created or accepted by `AddBootNode()` (`rom/dosboot/bootscan.c:260-280`). `AddPartitionVolume()` ignores the `AddBootNode()` result and also returns without reporting failure when `MakeDosNode()` returns NULL (`bootscan.c:240-249`). After the scan, `CheckPartitions()` unconditionally removes the original whole-disk BootNode and re-enqueues it only when `CheckTables()` returned FALSE; the detached BootNode allocation is not freed on the successful-table path (`bootscan.c:283-316`). `AddBootNode()` can reject a duplicate name or fail its BootNode allocation (`rom/expansion/addbootnode.c:134-168`).

**Trigger and consequence:** DOSBoot scans a whole-disk node, opens a partition table successfully, and every child volume creation/registration fails (for example, allocation failure or duplicate DOS names). `CheckTables()` still reports success, so the original whole-disk entry is removed and not restored; DOS loses that mount/boot fallback. The detached BootNode record also leaks whenever an opened table is treated as successful. If at least one child registration succeeds, that child may remain available, so the fallback-loss consequence is limited to the all-child-fail case. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting DOSBoot and `partition.library`; requires a pre-DOS whole-disk BootNode and successful partition-table open. **Confidence:** high for result propagation, list removal, and missing free; the failure sequence was not induced. No disk, boot, or allocation failure was exercised; source-only. See the [DOSBoot table and BootNode trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7151).

<a id="ek9527"></a>
### EK9527 — Concurrent ExecSMP dead-end alerts can interleave the shared diagnostic text.

When the Supervisor Alert Task is unavailable or the alert is marked `AT_DeadEnd`, `Exec_SystemAlert()` calls `Alert_DisplayKrnAlert()` directly. That formatter builds the complete alert in the single `PrivExecBase(SysBase)->AlertBuffer` and passes it to `KrnDisplayAlert()` (`rom/exec/systemalert.c:14-30,39-75`; buffer field: `rom/exec/exec_intern.h:96`). The caller in `Alert()` first invokes `Disable()` (`rom/exec/alert.c:168-186`), but the ExecSMP contract explicitly says this disables only the current CPU and does not protect shared data from other CPUs (`rom/exec/disable.c:56-61`). Two CPUs can therefore format into the same buffer concurrently; one alert can overwrite or interleave with the other's text before display.

**Trigger and consequence:** on an ExecSMP configuration, two CPUs concurrently enter the direct alert path, such as separate dead-end alerts or alerts when the supervisor alert task is unavailable. The displayed diagnostic may contain mixed or overwritten text, making the alert's identifying details unreliable. This finding does not assert a lost alert or alter alert control flow. Non-dead-end alerts queued to the Supervisor Alert Task are outside this direct shared-buffer race; concurrent SAT parameter publication is covered separately by EK426. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC SMP and Raspberry Pi SMP target variants (`configure.in:1437-1461,1667-1670,1516-1555,2195-2198`); ordinary non-ExecSMP builds do not have cross-CPU callers. **Confidence:** high that the direct path writes the shared buffer without cross-CPU serialization; overlap is conditional and was not induced. No alert or interleaving was run; source-only. See the [configuration and caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7160).

<a id="ek9528"></a>
### EK9528 — pthread can invoke a PosixC thread hook after delayed expunge has unloaded its code.

`pthread` worker startup snapshots registered CRT hook function pointers while holding the registry semaphore, releases the semaphore, and only then invokes the saved pointers (`compiler/pthread/pthread_create.c:63-89,132-134`). PosixC registers `posixc_thread_enter()` in that registry during library initialization and removes it during expunge (`compiler/crt/posixc/__threadhook.c:132-179`). The callback's first library-lifetime action is `OpenLibrary("posixc.library", 0)`, which occurs only after control has entered the callback (`__threadhook.c:76-82`). Thus the snapshot does not itself retain a library reference, and removing the registry entry does not invalidate a pointer already copied by a worker.

Generated library expunge sets `LIBF_DELEXP` when `RemLibrary()` requests expunge while the library remains open; a later close of the last open reference invokes expunge and frees the generated library base/code (`rom/exec/remlibrary.c:54-67`; `tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1506-1522,1550-1590`). If that final expunge lands after a worker snapshots the hook but before it calls the function, the worker can branch to the PosixC callback after its code is unloaded. The callback's own `OpenLibrary()` is too late to prevent that interval.

**Trigger and consequence:** an external client calls `RemLibrary()` on PosixC while it is open, then the last reference closes during the worker's snapshot-to-call window. The worker can attempt to execute an unloaded enter-hook address, preventing normal pthread startup. A direct checkout search found no in-tree `RemLibrary()` caller for PosixC, so this is a conditional public-API lifecycle issue, not an ordinary close path. **Affected configuration:** builds that include both `compiler/pthread` and `compiler/crt/posixc`, with delayed expunge requested on PosixC. **Confidence:** high for the unpinned snapshot/call interval and generated delayed-expunge lifecycle; medium for occurrence because the required external `RemLibrary()` interleaving is not selected in-tree. No library expunge or worker interleaving was run; source-only. See the [hook lifetime and expunge recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8446).

<a id="ek9529"></a>
### EK9529 — ConClip shutdown can leave a synchronous request unanswered.

ConClip's `handleall()` takes a single `Wait(SIGBREAKF_CTRL_C | portmask)` signal snapshot, drains the message port only when that snapshot contains `portmask`, then exits immediately when it contains Ctrl-C (`workbench/c/ConClip.c:388-427`). Its cleanup removes the edit hook and deletes the rendezvous port (`:115-121`). A request posted after a Ctrl-C-only snapshot, or after the last drain and before port deletion, is not replied to before shutdown. The requesters use private reply ports and wait synchronously: the ConClip edit hook calls `PutMsg()` then `WaitPort()` (`ConClip.c:212-231`); the selected console-handler paste path does the same (`rom/filesys/console_handler/support.c:759-790`), as does the CharMap copy path (`rom/devs/console/charmapconclass.c:1340-1394`).

**Trigger and consequence:** ConClip receives Ctrl-C while a synchronous copy/paste request is queued after the loop's final port drain and before `DeletePort()`. The requester's message is discarded with the deleted port without `ReplyMsg()`, so its `WaitPort()` can wait indefinitely. Requests drained before shutdown are replied normally, and requests sent after port removal fail their `FindPort()` lookup; the race is limited to the teardown interval. **Affected configuration:** ConClip running with its edit hook or a selected synchronous console-handler/CharMap client. **Confidence:** high for the one-snapshot/drain/exit ordering and the wait-without-timeout callers; no interleaving was induced. No message or shutdown was run; source-only. See the [shutdown and synchronous-caller recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8449).

<a id="ek516"></a>
### EK516 — Apple Silicon ELF loading can leave code hunks non-executable after an RWX mapping fallback.

The Darwin hosted `KrnAllocPages()` first requests `PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE|PROT_EXEC`; if that mapping fails, it retries with `PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE` and returns the successful mapping without recording that executable permission was omitted (`arch/all-unix/kernel/allocpages.c:60-73,119-130`). The ELF loader marks `SHF_EXECINSTR` sections `MEMF_EXECUTABLE` and allocates their hunk through this callback (`rom/dos/internalloadseg_elf.c:254-305`; callback setup: `rom/dos/loadseg.c:47-88`). It fills the section and clears the data/instruction caches at the end of loading, but does not call `KrnSetProtection()` to change a successful R/W fallback mapping to R/X (`internalloadseg_elf.c:1747-1755,1823-1830`). On Apple Silicon, the AROS host configuration selects this W^X path (`configure.in:1809-1811`).

**Trigger and consequence:** load an ELF object with executable sections on Apple Silicon where the initial W/R/X mapping is refused but the read/write retry succeeds. Loading returns a segment whose code pages remain non-executable; attempting to run the code can fault under host W^X enforcement. A successful initial executable mapping is not affected, and this is distinct from the allocation-failure fallbacks in EK8947 and EK712. **Affected configuration:** AROS hosted AArch64 on Darwin/Apple Silicon. **Confidence:** high for mapping retry and missing protection transition; no mapping, ELF load or execution was attempted. Source-only. See the [loader/allocator trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8201).

<a id="ek8947"></a>
### EK8947 — Apple Silicon LoadSeg can fall back to non-executable RAM after page allocation fails.

The selected DOS `LoadSeg()` allocator sends executable hunks to `KrnAllocPages()` but falls back to ordinary `AllocMem()` when the page request returns NULL (`rom/dos/loadseg.c:47-88`). On Apple Silicon, the hosted bootstrap maps the ordinary AROS RAM pool read/write without execute permission (`arch/all-unix/bootstrap/memory.c:58-77,117-125`). `LoadSeg()` returns the resulting hunk chain without a later protection transition for this pool allocation; its `FreeFunc` routes pool memory to `FreeMem()` (`loadseg.c:92-108`). The selected Shell path loads commands with `LoadSeg()` and executes the returned segment through `RunCommand()` (`workbench/c/Shell/Shell.c:429,555`).

**Trigger and consequence:** on Apple Silicon, an executable hunk's `KrnAllocPages()` request fails, but the subsequent `AllocMem()` succeeds. The segment is returned from non-executable host RAM; executing it can fail under W^X enforcement. This is distinct from EK516, where page allocation succeeds with R/W permissions, and EK712, which concerns a `CreateSegList()` jump vector. **Affected configuration:** AROS hosted AArch64 on Darwin/Apple Silicon; requires page-allocation failure followed by pool-allocation success and later execution. **Confidence:** high for the fallback and pool permissions; the allocation/command sequence was not exercised. Source-only. See the [LoadSeg allocation and execution-caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1266).

<a id="ek712"></a>
### EK712 — Apple Silicon CreateSegList can return a non-executable jump segment when allocation or protection fails.

On the Apple Silicon W^X configuration, `CreateSegList()` requests a page allocation for the generated jump-vector segment. If `KrnAllocPages()` returns NULL, it clears the `KernelBase` pointer and falls back to `AllocMem()` (`compiler/arossupport/createseglist.c:57-82`). It writes the full jump vector into the returned memory, but the later `KrnSetProtection()` call is conditional on `KernelBase`; the fallback therefore skips the R/X transition (`:87-99`). The selected DOS bootstrap caller passes `internalBootCliHandler()` to `CreateSegList()` and launches the resulting segment (`rom/dos/cliinit.c:177-197`; caller and packet path: [coverage trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7064)). The ordinary Darwin AROS RAM pool is mapped read/write, not executable (`arch/all-unix/bootstrap/memory.c:58-77,117-125`). There is a second failure path after page allocation succeeds: the selected Unix `KrnSetProtection()` translates the requested R/X bits and calls host `mprotect()` but discards its result (`arch/all-unix/kernel/setprotection.c:15-35`). Its public vector returns void, so `CreateSegList()` cannot learn that the permission change failed; it returns the segment without checking status (`createseglist.c:95-99`). The selected Darwin/AArch64 build sets `__AROSPLATFORM_WXSEG__` (`configure.in:1805-1811`), and the DOS bootstrap caller later launches the segment (`cliinit.c:177-197`).

**Trigger and consequence:** either `KrnAllocPages()` fails while `AllocMem()` succeeds, or page allocation succeeds but the host rejects the R/W-to-R/X `mprotect()` transition; in either case, later entry of the returned jump vector can fault under W^X enforcement. The second trigger is conditional on host policy/runtime conditions that reject this otherwise page-backed transition; no such rejection was reproduced. This remains distinct from the ELF and DOS hunk paths in EK516 and EK8947. **Affected configuration:** AROS hosted AArch64 on Darwin/Apple Silicon with the W^X segment option. **Confidence:** high for both unchecked source paths and the selected caller; actual host rejection conditions and runtime behavior remain unverified. No allocation failure, protection change, or boot was induced. Source-only. See the [CreateSegList failure and caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7064).

<a id="ek8761"></a>
### EK8761 — HPET initialization succeeds after its unit-array allocation fails, leaving an invalid resource state.

`hpet_Init()` counts the units described by ACPI HPET tables into `base->unitCnt`, then allocates `base->units`. If this allocation fails, it skips semaphore initialization, the second table scan, and kernel clock-source registration, but still closes ACPICA and returns TRUE (`arch/all-pc/hpet/hpet_init.c:68-97`). The positive `unitCnt` remains published while `units` is NULL. `GetCSUnitAttrsA()` checks only `unit < base->unitCnt` and then reads `base->units[unit]` (`arch/all-pc/hpet/hpet_getcsunitattrsa.c:51-68`); `AllocCSUnit()` and `FreeCSUnit()` likewise index the array after their range check. The selected ShowConfig and SysExplorer diagnostics enumerate units from zero and call the getter after opening the resource (`workbench/c/ShowConfig/ShowConfig.c:239-255`; `workbench/tools/SysExplorer/computer_page_cl.c:369-372,494-505`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a PC system exposes at least one memory-mapped HPET unit and the `HPETUnit` array allocation fails during resource initialization. Initialization nevertheless reports success, so a later selected unit query passes the retained count check and dereferences NULL, potentially faulting the diagnostic task. The kernel clock-source registration is skipped on this failure branch, so no broken clock source is claimed. **Affected configuration:** i386-PC and x86-64-PC images including the selected HPET resource; requires HPET presence, allocation failure, and a unit-querying client. **Confidence:** high for the partial initialization and unchecked access; no allocation failure or query was induced. Source-only. See the [HPET partial-init and caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8276).

<a id="ek9875"></a>
### EK9875 — CLI startup leaks synthesized stdout when opening stderr fails.

`internal_CliInitAny()` synthesizes stdout with `Open("*", MODE_NEWFILE)` when a console exists, or `Open("NIL:", MODE_NEWFILE)` otherwise (`rom/dos/newcliproc.c:200-215`). If that succeeds but the subsequent equivalent stderr `Open()` fails, the function sets the process error and jumps to `exit` without closing `cos` (`:216-239,334-341`). The handle is still only in the local variable: `me->pr_COS` is not assigned until the successful stream-setup path (`:242-245`). The `AROS_CLI` startup macro returns immediately when `CliInitRun()`/`CliInitNewcli()` reports this error (`compiler/include/dos/cliinit.h:161-165`), before its normal shell stream cleanup. `SystemTagList()` may leave output inherited from `Output()` or allow `SYS_Output` to replace it, and initializes the error stream as BNULL unless `SYS_Error` replaces it (`rom/dos/systemtaglist.c:133-155`); on the selected child-process path it also initializes `NP_Output` and `NP_Error` to BNULL, so later process cleanup does not own this locally synthesized stdout (`:402-415,443-446`; `createnewproc.c:920-934`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a CLI startup reaches `internal_CliInitAny()` with `dp_Arg3` (stdout) and `ea_CES` (stderr) both BNULL, stdout synthesis succeeds, and stderr synthesis fails. This can occur for a streamless startup or an explicit BNULL output/error pair; ordinary calls inheriting live streams are outside this trigger. The stdout file handle and its open handler reference are abandoned without `Close()`. **Affected configuration:** DOS CLI startup through `CliInitRun()` or `CliInitNewcli()` on targets selecting this shared implementation; no architecture-specific branch is required. **Confidence:** high for the local-handle ownership and error-return path; occurrence depends on the stated stream inputs and stderr-open failure. Close any locally synthesized stdout on this failure path before returning. No stream-open failure or CLI startup was induced; source-only; see the [stream ownership trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7444).

<a id="ek9876"></a>
### EK9876 — PC bootstrap framebuffer console clears an oversized mirror beyond its fixed workspace.

The PC bootstrap initializes `fb_Mirror` to the start of its 16 MiB static `workspace` (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:595-598`; `arch/all-pc/bootstrap/support.c:55-68`). For graphical Multiboot1/2 input, `con_InitMultiboot()`/`con_InitMultiboot2()` pass the bootloader's pixel dimensions to `fb_Init()` before the parser calls `AllocFB()` (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/multiboot1.c:73-81`; `multiboot2.c:120-124`; `arch/all-native/bootconsole/init_multiboot.c:14-38`; `init_multiboot2.c:15-78`). The VESA setup path likewise calls `con_InitVESA()` before `AllocFB()` (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/vesa_setup.c:121-123`). `fb_Init()` converts dimensions to text cells using the selected 8-by-14 font and calls `fb_Resize()`; `fb_Resize()` calls `fb_Clear()` (`arch/all-native/bootconsole/screen_fb.c:95-113`; `font8x14.c:5-6`). `fb_Clear()` clears `scr_Width * scr_Height` bytes through `fb_Mirror` (`screen_fb.c:115-129`). Only afterward does `AllocFB()` ask `__bs_malloc()` to reserve that many bytes and discard its result (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:459-466`). The allocator returns NULL when the rounded reservation would exceed the fixed workspace (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/support.c:64-92`), but this does not protect the earlier clear.

**Trigger and consequence:** PC bootstrap receives a graphical mode with a valid framebuffer mapping and more than 16,777,216 text cells, with the cell product still representable in `unsigned int`. Console initialization clears beyond the 16 MiB workspace before the later reservation fails; the clear can overwrite adjacent bootstrap data or fault. This requires an exceptionally large mode and is not claimed for ordinary PC modes. **Affected configuration:** i386-PC or x86-64-PC bootstrap using graphical Multiboot1/Multiboot2 framebuffer input or the selected VESA mode path. **Confidence:** high for initialization order, clear length, fixed workspace size and ignored reservation result; practical reachability is low and depends on the bootloader supplying a valid very-large mode. Bound the mirror clear to a successful reservation and reject dimensions whose cell count exceeds the workspace. No boot or framebuffer operation was run; source-only; see the [capacity and initialization-order trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7363). The older EK344 mirror-reuse claim remains withdrawn; this is a separate first-clear-before-reservation overrun.

<a id="ek9879"></a>
### EK9879 — ARM processor frequency queries violate the mailbox buffer cache-line alignment contract. *(withdrawn; duplicate of OD3527)*

**Disposition:** rechecked `vcQueryClock()`'s 48-byte allocation and 16-byte pointer alignment against the selected mailbox resource's 64-byte exclusive-cache-line requirement and `MBoxCall()`'s cache-maintenance path. The processor-frequency instance is already included in [OD3527](AROS-other-drivers.md#od3527), together with the two battclock callers under the same mailbox-buffer contract violation. Withdraw this Exec/Kernel entry as a duplicate; retain the issue and full trigger/consequence in the Other Drivers report. No separate kernel defect or runtime cache effect is claimed. See the [caller and cache-line recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7431).

<a id="ek9880"></a>
### EK9880 — The m68k processor resource returns cache sizes in bytes despite documenting kilobytes.

The common `GetCPUInfo()` documentation specifies that `GCIT_L1CacheSize`, `GCIT_L1DataCacheSize`, `GCIT_L1InstructionCacheSize`, and the L2/L3 size tags return kB (`rom/processor/getcpuinfo.c:86-108`). The m68k initializer instead stores byte counts in the cache fields: for an MC68040 it assigns `1024 << 2` (4,096 bytes) to each L1 cache, and for an MC68060 assigns `1024 << 3` (8,192 bytes) (`arch/m68k-all/processor/processor_init.c:117-118,98-99`). The m68k `GetCPUInfo()` writes these fields, and their sum for `GCIT_L1CacheSize`, directly to the caller without converting to kB (`arch/m68k-all/processor/getcpuinfo.c:82-95`). Thus the MC68040 query returns 4,096 for each cache and 8,192 for the combined L1 tag where the documented values are 4, 4, and 8. The selected developer diagnostic prints these tags with `kB` labels (`developer/debug/test/misc/getcpuinfo.c:165-168,191-194`), so it displays the inflated values. The m68k-specific ShowConfig formatter labels its results in bytes (`workbench/tools/ShowConfig/cpu_m68k.c:27-28`), so that caller is consistent with the implementation and is not itself affected.

**Trigger and consequence:** a client queries any of the m68k cache-size tags on a processor with a reported nonzero cache and interprets the result according to the public kB contract. The reported size is in bytes, overstating cache capacity by 1,024 for the 040/060/080 values that are whole kB; clients can display incorrect sizes or make incorrect size-based decisions. **Affected configuration:** m68k builds selecting `arch/m68k-all/processor/getcpuinfo.c` and `processor_init.c`; the developer diagnostic is an explicit test target. **Confidence:** high for the public unit contract, byte-valued initializer fields, and unconverted tag writes; impact requires a client to use the documented units. Return kB consistently or change the public API contract and all consumers together. No processor query or diagnostic was run; source-only; see the [m68k cache-unit trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7433).

<a id="ek9881"></a>
### EK9881 — i386 PC ACPI power-off enters ACPICA with maskable interrupts disabled.

The i386 PC `krnLeaveSupervisorRing()` macro pushes its argument as EFLAGS in the IRET frame (`arch/i386-pc/kernel/kernel_intern.h:51-65`). `FLAGS_INTENABLED` is `0x3002` (`:67`): it sets IOPL to 3 but leaves IF (bit 9) clear. The shared ACPI power-off handler states that ACPICA requires user mode with interrupts enabled, then uses this macro immediately before `AcpiEnterSleepStatePrep(ACPI_STATE_S5)` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/acpi_pm.c:80-94`). Thus the i386-PC path enters ACPICA with maskable interrupts disabled despite the caller's stated precondition.

**Trigger and consequence:** an i386 PC shutdown that selects the ACPI S5 handler and reaches sleep preparation. ACPICA executes with IF clear; interrupt servicing it needs may be unavailable during preparation. No particular ACPICA failure is asserted. The x86-64 PC instance is tracked separately as EK10191. **Affected configuration:** i386 PC with ACPI shutdown support and a working S5 path. **Confidence:** high for the pushed EFLAGS value and clear IF bit; downstream effects depend on ACPICA's runtime interrupt requirements. No shutdown, firmware call, interrupt-state change, or build was run; source-only. See the [header and caller reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1444).

<a id="ek9882"></a>
### EK9882 — The optional PC SMP IPI diagnostic block calls `core_DoCallIPI()` with too few arguments.

The PC IPI API declares six parameters: hook, CPU mask, async flag, argument count, argument array, and kernel base (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_ipi.h:25`; implementation at `kernel_ipi.c:92`). The two diagnostic calls in `KernelPost()` pass only four arguments (`arch/all-pc/kernel/platform_post.c:210-220`); the fourth is `KernelBase`, which is not a replacement for the required `nargs`, `args`, and `_KB` parameters. When this code is compiled, both calls fail the function-argument-count check.

**Trigger and consequence:** manually enable `TEST_SMP_IPI` in `platform_post.c` and compile the PC kernel. Compilation fails at the two diagnostic calls, so this optional IPI self-test cannot be built as written. **Affected configuration:** i386-PC and x86-64-PC source configurations that build `arch/all-pc/kernel/platform_post.c` with its local `TEST_SMP_IPI` define uncommented. The define is commented out in this snapshot, and no selected manifest/configuration enables it; the default PC kernel is unaffected. **Confidence:** high for the prototype/call arity mismatch; this is limited to the disabled diagnostic block. Supply the intended argument count, argument array, and kernel base at both call sites. No manual define, compile, IPI, or boot was performed; source-only; see the [diagnostic-block recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L3837). Historical EK749 references name this same optional candidate; EK9882 is the canonical report ID.

<a id="ek9884"></a>
### EK9884 — Native AArch64 `CacheClearE()` walks 4 GiB for a documented whole-address request with a non-NULL start.

The public `CacheClearE()` documentation says a length of `$FFFFFFFF` indicates that all addresses should be cleared (`rom/exec/cachecleare.c:32-40`). The AArch64 vector wrapper forwards its 32-bit `ULONG` length in x1 (`arch/aarch64-native/exec/cachecleare.c:18-31`), and the SVC receiver reads that value into a 64-bit length (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/syscall.c:280-289`). The native helper recognizes the whole-cache sentinel only when both `addr == NULL` and `length == 0xffffffff`; only then does it use set/way data-cache maintenance and `ic iallu` (`syscall.c:85-101`). With a non-NULL address and the documented sentinel length, it instead rounds `addr`/`addr + length` to 64-byte boundaries and walks that virtual range (`:103-110,126-158`). For a normal low address such as `0x1000`, this is about 67 million cache-line operations over a 4 GiB range. The helper itself notes that walking unmapped virtual-address blocks can raise translation faults on real hardware (`:88-91`). `CacheClearU()` uses a NULL address (`rom/exec/cacheclearu.c:63`), and the maintained call-site census found no non-NULL all-address sentinel caller.

**Trigger and consequence:** an AArch64 caller passes a non-NULL `address`, `length == 0xffffffff`, and `CACRF_ClearD`, `CACRF_InvalidateD`, or `CACRF_ClearI`. Instead of performing the documented whole-cache operation, the helper performs a 4 GiB virtual-address walk; this can take a very long time and can fault when the range includes unmapped addresses. **Affected configuration:** native AArch64 Exec/kernel callers using the documented sentinel form with a non-NULL start; no maintained in-tree caller was found. **Confidence:** high for the contract/branch mismatch and 64-byte loop extent; actual time and fault depend on cache flags and address mappings. Treat the sentinel as whole-cache regardless of the address, or document and enforce a NULL-address precondition. No cache operation, SVC, or boot was run; source-only; see the [sentinel caller and helper trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7653). This is distinct from EK9082, which covers ordinary pointer-sized lengths narrowed by the AArch64 vector wrapper.

<a id="ek9885"></a>
### EK9885 — pthread advertises 18 attribute and concurrency APIs absent from its selected link library.

The copied public `compiler/pthread/pthread.h` declares these functions, but the active `linklibs-pthread` recipe includes only `pthread.c`, `sched.c`, `semaphore.c`, and the explicitly listed `PTHREADFUNCS` sources. A checkout-wide definition search found no implementation for any of them:

- Scheduling attributes: `pthread_attr_getschedpolicy`, `pthread_attr_setschedpolicy`, `pthread_attr_getinheritsched`, `pthread_attr_setinheritsched`, `pthread_attr_getscope`, and `pthread_attr_setscope` (`pthread.h:423-428`).
- Concurrency level: `pthread_setconcurrency` and `pthread_getconcurrency` (`:454-455`).
- Process sharing: `pthread_mutexattr_getpshared` and `pthread_mutexattr_setpshared` (`:472-473`); `pthread_condattr_getpshared` and `pthread_condattr_setpshared` (`:494-495`); `pthread_barrierattr_init`, `pthread_barrierattr_destroy`, `pthread_barrierattr_getpshared`, and `pthread_barrierattr_setpshared` (`:514-517`); `pthread_rwlockattr_getpshared` and `pthread_rwlockattr_setpshared` (`:533-534`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an application includes the installed pthread header and calls any listed function. Compilation accepts the declared call, but linking against the selected pthread archive cannot resolve the symbol. No checked-in caller of these functions was found, so this is an external-client/API completeness issue, not a demonstrated in-tree build failure. The single-user platform may need to implement unsupported process-sharing operations as documented errors, but the published declarations still need linkable definitions. **Affected configuration:** applications using the selected AROS pthread link library. **Confidence:** high for the declaration/definition mismatch and conditional unresolved-symbol consequence. The active library source list and copied-header rule are in `compiler/pthread/mmakefile.src`; the separate device-style module build directive is commented out and does not provide these symbols. No application link or target build was run; source-only. See the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#pthread-public-api-link-library-census-ek617-detail-2026-10-13).

<a id="ek9886"></a>
### EK9886 — m68k GadTools bridge omits CreateContext and CreateGadgetA vectors.

The public GadTools function list exports `CreateGadgetA` at LVO −30 and `CreateContext` at LVO −114 (`workbench/libs/gadtools/gadtools.conf:35,49`). The selected m68k emulator registers only 17 GadTools thunk offsets; its table starts at 36, then jumps from 108 to 120, and therefore omits both vectors (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:7505-7525`). A checkout search found no manual override for either call. The native implementations exist (`workbench/libs/gadtools/creategadgeta.c:22-42`; `createcontext.c:20-26`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated m68k client calls either library vector. The A-line dispatcher finds the GadTools library but no matching generated or manual LVO, then pops the return address and returns D0=0 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:280-290`). The call silently fails: `CreateContext()` does not initialize the caller's gadget-list pointer, and `CreateGadgetA()` does not create the requested gadget. GadTools clients commonly use `CreateContext()` to seed the list before adding gadgets, so the missing first vector also blocks the normal gadget-construction sequence. **Affected configuration:** applications running through `m68kemu.library` on supported hosted targets that use GadTools. **Confidence:** high for the missing entries and zero-return behavior; the user-visible effect depends on the guest's handling of the NULL result. No guest program or emulator was run; source-only. See the [vector comparison and wrapper review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#generated-gadtools-thunk-table-versus-public-vectors-ek9886-added-full-17-wrapper-section-re-read-no-pathloc-credit-2026-10-27).

<a id="ek9887"></a>
### EK9887 — m68k diskfont bridge omits OpenDiskFont and NewScaledDiskFont vectors.

The public diskfont function list exports `OpenDiskFont` at LVO −30 and `NewScaledDiskFont` at LVO −54 (`workbench/libs/diskfont/diskfont.conf:13,19`). The selected m68k emulator registers only three diskfont thunk offsets: `AvailFonts` (−36), `NewFontContents` (−42), and `DisposeFontContents` (−48) (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:7268-7274`). A checkout search found no manual override. Native implementations exist (`workbench/libs/diskfont/opendiskfont.c:22-28`; `newscaleddiskfont.c:13-20`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated m68k client calls either missing diskfont vector. The A-line dispatcher finds no thunk and returns D0=0 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:280-290`), so opening a font or requesting a scaled disk font fails as if the native operation returned NULL. **Affected configuration:** applications running through `m68kemu.library` on supported hosted targets that use these diskfont APIs. **Confidence:** high for the missing entries and zero-return behavior; application impact depends on whether it uses either API and how it handles NULL. No guest font call or build was run; source-only. See the [vector comparison and manifest evidence](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#generated-diskfont-vector-reconciliation-ek9887-added-no-pathloc-credit-2026-10-27).

<a id="ek9888"></a>
### EK9888 — m68k utility bridge omits the NextTagItem vector.

The selected public Utility function list declares `NextTagItem(struct TagItem **tagListPtr)` at LVO −48 (`rom/utility/utility.conf:40`; native vector implementation `rom/utility/nexttagitem.c:16-27`). The generated m68k Utility thunk table has entries at offsets 42 and 54 but no entry at 48 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:7986-8030`). The emulator source search found no manual Utility thunk. The generated source is selected by `rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:33`.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated m68k client calls `NextTagItem()` on a nonempty list. The library dispatcher finds no matching LVO and returns D0=0 without calling the native iterator (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:280-290`). Because zero is also the normal end-of-list result, the guest silently treats the first call as completion and skips the remaining tags; the guest cursor is not advanced by the missing call. **Affected configuration:** applications using Utility `NextTagItem()` through `m68kemu.library` on supported hosted targets. **Confidence:** high for the absent vector and zero-return path; application effect depends on using this iterator and whether an empty iteration is meaningful to the caller. No guest tag list or emulator run was used; source-only. See the [public-vector and generated-dispatch reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#m68k-utility-public-vector-versus-generated-dispatch-reconciliation-ek9888-retained-2026-10-28).

<a id="ek9890"></a>
### EK9890 — PowerPC CachePostDMA can discard adjacent CPU writes in a shared cache line.

On standalone PPC, `CachePostDMA()` for device-to-memory transfers calls `CacheClearE(address, *length, CACRF_InvalidateD | CACRF_ClearI)` (`arch/ppc-chrp/exec/cachepostdma.c:23-27`; same branch in `arch/ppc-sam440/exec/cachepostdma.c:27-31`). The shared PPC implementation rounds the range outward to 32-byte boundaries, then the selected Efika and Sam440 `SC_INVALIDATED` handlers execute `dcbi` on every covered line (`arch/ppc-all/exec/cachecleare.c:25-48`; `arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/syscall.c:75-88`; `arch/ppc-sam440/kernel/syscall.c:99-112`). This invalidation discards a modified cache line without writing its other bytes back to memory.

**Trigger and consequence:** a device writes a buffer whose first or last byte shares a 32-byte line with adjacent CPU-owned data, and the CPU dirties that adjacent data after `CachePreDMA()` but before `CachePostDMA()`. The outward-rounded `dcbi` invalidates the whole line, discarding the neighboring CPU write along with the device buffer's stale cache contents. A checked-in Efika OHCI caller passes `msg->buffer` and its requested length directly for input transfers, then calls `CachePostDMA()` on that same range before returning (`workbench/devs/USB/drivers/OHCI/ohcidriverclass.c:964-971,1135-1137`); the overlap and concurrent neighbor write remain conditional. **Affected configuration:** standalone PPC Efika and Sam440 CachePostDMA paths; the Efika OHCI caller is explicitly present in its boot manifest, though its parent aggregate edge is optional. No Pegasos standalone handler path is claimed. **Confidence:** high for outward rounding and invalidation behavior; conditional for actual data loss because the edge-line sharing and concurrent adjacent write must occur. No DMA transfer or cache operation was run; source-only. See the [PowerPC invalidation and OHCI caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#powerpc-cachepostdma-invalidation-caller-target-audit-ek9890-added-2026-10-27).

<a id="ek9891"></a>
### EK9891 — m68k generated object lifecycles retain guest shadow mappings.

`shadow_create()` allocates a new guest block and appends a mapping for every call; it does not deduplicate a native pointer already in the table. `shadow_destroy()` is the helper that removes a mapping and frees the guest block (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_shadow.c:75-107,122-132`), and each context has only 256 shadow entries (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_intern.h:92-94`). The following selected generated lifecycle paths create a guest shadow but have no matching shadow teardown:

- `CreateMsgPort()` / `DeleteMsgPort()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2311-2324`): DeleteMsgPort releases the native port while retaining its guest allocation and mapping.
- `GetDeviceProc()` / `FreeDeviceProc()` (`:1467-1482`): the native routine can reuse and return the same supplied DevProc during successful multi-directory assign iteration (`rom/dos/getdeviceproc.c:357-368,371-419`), but each successful generated return creates another guest mapping; terminal exhaustion frees the native structure (`:375-383,388-404`), and FreeDeviceProc releases it without removing its mapping. One iteration can therefore retain several guest shadows for the same native object.
- `CreateMenusA()` / `FreeMenus()` (`:2728-2744`) and `AllocNamedObjectA()` / `FreeNamedObject()` (`:7050-7082`): each matching free releases the native allocation but leaves the guest block and mapping behind.
- GadTools message filtering (`:2769-2783,2812-2827`): `GT_GetIMsg()` creates a shadow for each returned message wrapper. In the no-context path, `GT_ReplyIMsg()` eventually frees a `GT_IntuiMessage` allocated by `GT_FilterIMsg()`; its guest shadow is not removed. In the context-gadget path, the native wrapper is embedded and reused, but each returned wrapper still receives another mapping; destroying that context can leave mappings to freed embedded storage. The separately exposed `GT_FilterIMsg()` / `GT_PostFilterIMsg()` wrappers also create shadows for successful results and have no paired shadow cleanup. The original Intuition message returned by post-filter remains sender-owned and is not claimed to be freed by GadTools.
- `GetScreenDrawInfo()` / `FreeScreenDrawInfo()` (`:5808-5823`): Get returns the screen's embedded DrawInfo and creates a fresh guest shadow. The native Free routine is a no-op, and the thunk retains the guest block/table entry. This case does not leak a native DrawInfo; the embedded pointer's lifetime remains tied to its screen.
- `LockPubScreen()` / `UnlockPubScreen()` (`:5578-5594`): each successful lock creates a new guest Screen shadow, but unlock releases only the public-screen lock and leaves the allocated guest block and mapping. The native screen remains owned by Intuition, so repeated ordinary lock/unlock cycles consume table/heap capacity without freeing the screen.
- `ObtainGIRPort()` / `ReleaseGIRPort()` (`:5641-5657`): Obtain clones a native RastPort and creates a guest shadow; Release frees the cloned RastPort but does not remove the shadow mapping or guest block, leaving a mapping to freed native storage.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated caller repeatedly uses one of these successful acquisition/release sequences. Every retained guest block reduces emulator heap capacity and every mapping consumes a bounded table entry; after the table fills, a later shadow creation fails and its wrapper returns zero. In paths that free the native object, the old guest handle also remains mapped to a freed native address, so reusing it can pass a dangling pointer into native code. The borrowed DrawInfo and reusable GadTools cases share the capacity loss but only become stale when their owning screen/context storage is destroyed. These effects depend on guest code using the optional vectors; no maintained in-tree m68k guest caller was established.

**Scope exclusions:** the generated `DeleteIORequest()` path removes its registry entry but fails to free the guest block; that distinct partial-cleanup case is tracked under EK410. Graphics `DisposeRegion()` / `FreeColorMap()` / `FreeBitMap()` lifecycles are tracked under EK9438. A suspected Layers release pair remains excluded because the generated constructors do not establish a valid guest handle route (EK9432).

**Affected configuration:** the optional m68kemu library when explicitly built and loaded on a supported 64-bit x86-64, AArch64, or RISC-V target (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:14-17`; `rom/mmakefile.src:4-18,83-98`).

**Confidence:** high that the listed wrapper paths allocate shadows without matching teardown and that the table is bounded; guest-visible exhaustion requires repeated successful use by an emulated client. Stale native translation is asserted only for cases whose native allocation is freed or whose containing context is destroyed. No guest message, menu, port, DrawInfo, or filesystem operation was run. Source-only; see [EK9275](#ek9275) for the distinct repeated-shadow problem on borrowed lookups.

<a id="ek9892"></a>
### EK9892 — Exec's minimum-version diagnostic passes a packed array to a variadic formatter.

When the weak `__aros_libreq_SysBase` requirement exceeds the loaded Exec version, `SysBase_autoinit()` builds `IPTR arr[] = { task name, required version, actual version }` and calls `__showerror("%s: Requires exec.library v%ld, found v%ld\n", arr)` (`rom/exec/exec_autoinit.c:32-38`). The `__showerror` macro forwards that as one variadic argument to `___showerror()` (`compiler/autoinit/autoinit.h:21-22`); it does not expand the array into separate arguments. The selected Exec module links `exec_autoinit` (`rom/exec/mmakefile.src:94`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an Exec image is built with a nonzero minimum-version requirement greater than the available Exec version. The formatter interprets the address of `arr` as the `%s` task-name pointer, then consumes two more variadic arguments that were never supplied. The diagnostic can display garbage or access an invalid string/argument location; behavior depends on the formatter branch and stack contents. `___showerror()` forwards its variadic stream through `AROS_SLOWSTACKFORMAT_ARG()` to VPrintf, EasyRequestArgs, or RawDoFmt (`compiler/autoinit/__showerror.c:29-80`), so none of those branches repairs the caller mismatch. Startup returns failure after attempting the diagnostic. **Affected configuration:** Exec builds with an unmet `__aros_libreq_SysBase` requirement. **Confidence:** high for the argument mismatch and selected call path; the exact displayed text or fault is environment-dependent. No version-mismatch startup was run; source-only. See the [caller and formatter trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#exec-minimum-version-diagnostic-caller-reconciliation-ek9892-added-2026-10-27).

<a id="ek9893"></a>
### EK9893 — The m68k Commodities bridge passes a guest NewBroker layout to native CxBroker without translating it.

The generated `CxBroker()` thunk converts A0 with `THUNK_PTR(0)` and passes that address directly to native `CxBroker()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:119-125`). This preserves the guest arena bytes; it does not translate the pointed-to structure. The public m68k `NewBroker` fields occupy 26 bytes, with pointers at offsets 2, 6, 10, and 20 (`compiler/include/libraries/commodities.h:25-37`).
