The registered shadow-layout description records a 56-byte native layout, placing those pointer fields at offsets 8, 16, 24, and 40 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_shadow_layouts.h:2800-2810`), but this thunk does not create that shadow. Native `CxBroker()` and its `BrokerFunc()` consumer dereference the structure using host offsets and pointer width (`workbench/libs/commodities/cxbroker.c:38-40,90-105`; `createcxobj.c:151-165`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated m68k client passes a guest-allocated `NewBroker` to `CxBroker()`. On supported 64-bit little-endian m68kemu hosts, native code reads pointer fields from the wrong offsets and interprets guest 32-bit big-endian data as host pointers. Broker name/title/description, message port, flags, and priority can therefore be misread, causing broker creation to fail or use invalid data. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built `kernel-m68kemu-library` on supported 64-bit hosts; its parent kernel/package edges are commented out, so no default-image claim is made. **Confidence:** high for the guest/native layout mismatch and direct pointer forwarding; exact failure depends on guest field contents and the native dereference path. No emulated broker call or build was run; source-only. See the [NewBroker layout and thunk trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#generated-m68k-thunk-source-order-pass-started-ek9893-added-2026-10-27-partial-body-only).

<a id="ek9894"></a>
### EK9894 — m68kemu forwards guest callbacks to native callback call sites without an execution bridge.

Generated wrappers resolve callback addresses as ordinary guest data pointers. `THUNK_PTR` maps a guest address into the emulator arena (or an exact existing shadow); it does not create a host-callable thunk into the m68k interpreter (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.h:36-37`; `m68kemu_intern.h:108-125`). The generated public `Utility/CallHookPkt` vector passes that pointer directly to native `CallHookPkt()`, whose `CALLHOOKPKT` macro loads `Hook.h_Entry` and invokes it as a native function (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6898-6904`; `rom/utility/callhookpkt.c:64-67`; `compiler/include/utility/hooks.h:82-87`). The guest Hook layout is 20 bytes versus 40 bytes for the selected x86-64 host layout, and the generated layout maps only list links and `h_Data`, not `h_Entry` or `h_SubEntry` (`m68kemu_shadow_layouts.h:1837-1842,4530`). The affected generated wrappers do not create or populate a Hook shadow.

The same missing execution bridge appears in other selected vectors: Locale `FormatDate()` and `FormatString()` forward the guest Hook pointer, then native Locale calls its `h_Entry` directly for output characters; `ParseDate()` forwards the same raw pointer and directly calls its entry while reading input (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6587-6607,6734-6742`; `workbench/libs/locale/formatdate.c:366-372`; `formatstring.c:72-95`; `parsedate.c:123-127`). IFFParse `EntryHandler()`, `ExitHandler()`, and `InitIFF()` pass guest hooks that IFFParse later invokes through `CallHookPkt()` (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:4727-4748,4916-4923`; `workbench/libs/iffparse/openiff.c:71-74`; `basicfuncs.c:297-308`); Graphics `SetCollision()` stores its guest callback for later `DoCollision()` dispatch, and `DoRenderFunc()`/`DoPixelFunc()` pass guest code addresses to direct native callback calls (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:3022-3030,4407-4428`; `rom/graphics/setcollision.c:31-44`; `gfxfuncsupport.c:67-77,218-227`). The generated `SetDisplayDriverCallback()` vector stores the guest function pointer unchanged; Graphics later invokes it directly as a native C function on display-driver insertion/removal (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:3698-3705`; `rom/graphics/setdisplaydrivercallback.c:29-49,75-78`; `rom/graphics/graphics_display.c:242-243,336-339`). This callback slot is normally populated by Intuition with its native `DisplayDriverNotify()` during initialization (`rom/intuition/intuition_init.c:300`; `monitorclass.c:50`), so a guest call through the optional thunk can also replace the maintained native callback with an unbridged guest address. CyberGraphX `DoCDrawMethodTagList()` invokes the supplied hook through `CallHookPkt()` (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:504-512`; `workbench/libs/cgfx/docdrawmethodtaglist.c:179-181,236-237`). The selected layers Hook vectors also retain guest Hook pointers and later invoke `h_Entry` through native ABI calls (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6410-6476`; `rom/hyperlayers/basicfuncs.c:110-163`); additionally, `CollectPixelsLayer()`'s generated vector forwards its guest Hook unchanged, and the native Layers implementation calls it through `CallHookPkt()` in simple-refresh, smart-refresh and remaining-background branches (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6543-6549`; `rom/hyperlayers/collectpixelslayer.c:125-135,211-218,278-289`). Its sole checked-in C caller is the native Lens demo (`developer/demos/lens.c:202-204`), so this extends only the optional m68kemu guest API scope. The generated `AVL_FindPrevNodeByKey()` and `AVL_FindNextNodeByKey()` vectors likewise pass a guest comparator address unchanged (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2427-2449`); Exec invokes it through native `AROS_UFC2()` calls when traversing a nonempty tree (`rom/exec/avl.c:894,1041`; `asmcall.h:314-321`), so these keyed searches cannot execute an m68k guest comparator through the native function ABI. The comparator type is explicitly a user callback (`compiler/include/exec/avl.h:31`); the only checked-in call found is the native AVL test (`developer/debug/test/exec/avltest.c:203`), not an emulated guest caller. The generated `ScanVars()` path is also already covered as a raw guest Hook/native `CallHookPkt()` boundary under EK9432 (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1819-1825`; `rom/dos/scanvars.c:69-83`), and is not duplicated here. This consolidated coverage supersedes the narrower historical Locale-only duplicate EK9208. The generated `NewCreateTaskA()` path has the same execution-bridge failure for a valid guest `TASKTAG_PC`: tag conversion maps it into the guest arena, native task creation consumes it as `initpc`, and native `PrepareContext()` stores it as the host instruction pointer (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2466-2472`; `m68kemu_shadow.c:139-163`; `rom/exec/newcreatetaska.c:113-124,248-258`; selected architecture `preparecontext.c` files).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated guest supplies a callback or Hook to one of these APIs and the selected native path invokes it. Native code reads guest Hook storage using host offsets or calls an m68k code address using the host calling convention; the callback therefore does not execute as an m68k guest callback and the operation can fault or fail. Retained callbacks can fail later when the corresponding native event occurs. **Affected configuration:** an explicitly built and loaded m68kemu library on a supported 64-bit host; it is optional and excluded from the checked-in default package edges. No maintained in-tree emulated guest caller was established. **Confidence:** high for the direct pointer forwarding, incompatible Hook layout, and native callback invocation paths; exact manifestation depends on guest-supplied callback data and the operation that invokes it. No guest Hook, callback, IFF operation, graphics render, or build was run. Source-only; see the [generated callback-path coverage notes](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7738).

<a id="ek9895"></a>
### EK9895 — m68kemu passes guest semaphore structures to native Exec without layout conversion.

The generated semaphore thunks resolve `SignalSemaphore *` and `SemaphoreMessage *` through `m68k_to_host_or_shadow()`/`THUNK_PTR()` and pass the resulting address directly to native Exec (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2195-2258,2327-2341`). For a guest-owned object with no exact registered shadow, the resolver returns an address inside the guest arena (`m68kemu_intern.h:114-125`). The checked-in layout table records m68k `SignalSemaphore` as 46 bytes versus 512 bytes natively, and `SemaphoreMessage` as 24 versus 56 bytes (`m68kemu_shadow_layouts.h:3546-3557,3574-3590,4633-4636`).

These are active native data accesses, not merely unused layout differences. Native `AddSemaphore()` calls `InitSemaphore()` on the supplied pointer before linking it into the global list (`rom/exec/addsemaphore.c:52-63`); native initialization writes the wait-list pointers, owner, queue count, and SMP spinlock at host-layout offsets (`rom/exec/initsemaphore.c:48-68`). `Procure()` reads the bid message's shared marker, updates the semaphore owner/nesting state, and can write `ssm_Semaphore` or the waiter link in place (`rom/exec/procure.c:46-105`). `Vacate()` similarly reads and updates the message and native wait queue (`rom/exec/vacate.c:47-90`). No structure conversion is performed on these wrapper paths. The manual `InitSemaphore()` thunk is a no-op (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:370-371`); that separate behavior is not needed to establish this finding.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated guest supplies its guest-sized semaphore, or a guest-sized semaphore message, to a generated vector such as `AddSemaphore()`, `Procure()`, or `Vacate()`. Native Exec interprets guest fields at host offsets and can read or write beyond the guest allocation; list, owner, and queue state can also be misinterpreted, so semaphore operations may fault, corrupt adjacent guest-arena data, or fail to coordinate correctly. **Affected configuration:** an explicitly built and loaded m68kemu library on a supported 64-bit host, when a guest uses caller-owned semaphore structures through the generated vectors. The module is optional and excluded from checked-in default package edges; no maintained in-tree emulated caller was established. **Confidence:** high for the size/layout mismatch and native field accesses; actual manifestation depends on which API and guest-owned objects are used. No semaphore operation, allocation failure, or build was run. Source-only; see the [semaphore thunk/layout trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7710).

<a id="ek9896"></a>
### EK9896 — generated m68k thunks discard non-void native API results.

The affected generated wrappers call native functions with non-void results but unconditionally return zero to the emulated caller. The checked wrapper/declaration sweep identified these vectors:

- Exec `AbortIO()` discards its `LONG` result (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2138-2145`; `rom/exec/exec.conf:153`; `rom/exec/abortio.c:16-71`), and `ChildOrphan()` discards its error status (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2350-2356`; `exec.conf:200`; `rom/exec/childorphan.c:60-118`).
- Graphics `BltBitMap()` discards the native plane count (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2878-2895`; `rom/graphics/graphics.conf:45`; `rom/graphics/bltbitmap.c:112-113,333`). `MrgCop()` and `MakeVPort()` discard their ULONG results (`:3108-3124`; `graphics.conf:75-76`; `rom/graphics/mrgcop.c:112-127`; `rom/graphics/makevport.c:71-75,100-103,235-245`). `WritePixelLine8()` and `WritePixelArray8()` discard the native pixel counts (`:3862-3875,3888-3902`; `graphics.conf:174,176`; `rom/graphics/writepixelline8.c:64-70`; `rom/graphics/writepixelarray8.c:66-76`). `SetWriteMask()` discards its declared ULONG result (`:4144-4152`; `graphics.conf:210`; `rom/graphics/setwritemask.c:15-49`).
- Intuition `AddGadget()`, `AddGList()`, and `RemoveGList()` discard their returned gadget positions/counts (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:4982-4990,5461-5480`; `rom/intuition/intuition.conf:59,126-127`; `rom/intuition/addgadget.c:17-99`; `rom/intuition/addglist.c:20,157`; `rom/intuition/removeglist.c:31,160-165`). `ModifyIDCMP()` drops its BOOL result (`:5109-5117`; `intuition.conf:77`; `rom/intuition/modifyidcmp.c:15,108-141`), `RemoveGadget()` drops the removed gadget's position (`:5207-5215`; `intuition.conf:90`; `rom/intuition/removegadget.c:16-51`), and `SetAttrsA()` drops the class-defined `OM_SET` result (`:5745-5754`; `intuition.conf:165`; `rom/intuition/setattrsa.c:16,89-99`). `SetMenuStrip()` also discards its BOOL (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:5256-5263`; `intuition.conf:96`): native Intuition can return FALSE when the window is invalid or menu-handler setup fails, and TRUE after attaching the strip (`rom/intuition/setmenustrip.c:60-63,98,120-122`). `ActivateGadget()` discards its BOOL as well (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:5498-5505`; `intuition.conf:130`); native code returns the activation success result (`rom/intuition/activategadget.c:67-111,131-146).
- Layers `DeleteLayer()` drops its success/failure LONG (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6265-6273`; `rom/hyperlayers/layers.conf:29`; `rom/hyperlayers/deletelayer.c:23-57,74,150`). `InstallClipRegion()` likewise discards the previous Region pointer returned by the native API (`:6380-6388`; `layers.conf:40`; `rom/hyperlayers/installclipregion.c`); this pointer-return case is part of the same wrapper defect, though guest ownership/round-trip limitations are separately tracked under EK9432.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated caller invokes one of these vectors and relies on its documented result. The guest always receives zero regardless of the native count, status, error, or class result. For example, `MakeVPort()` can report an allocation/display error natively while the wrapper returns zero (`MVP_OK`), and `ModifyIDCMP()` can report port-allocation failure while the wrapper hides it; callers also lose pixel counts and gadget positions. `InstallClipRegion()` callers cannot receive the prior region pointer. **Affected configuration:** an explicitly built and loaded m68kemu library on a supported 64-bit host; it is optional and excluded from checked-in default package edges. No maintained in-tree emulated caller was established for these vectors; native in-tree clients call the native library directly. **Confidence:** high for the discarded native return values and affected declarations; user-visible impact depends on guest code consuming the result. No guest API, graphics, GUI, layer, or device operation was run. Source-only; see the [return-value reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8126).

<a id="ek9897"></a>
### EK9897 — Concurrent AArch64 Raspberry Pi diagnostics can corrupt bootstrap framebuffer output.

The AArch64 kernel's `krnPutC()` forwards each character from `bug()`/`KrnBug()` directly to the bootstrap framebuffer callback and serial callback, with no output lock (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_debug.c:14-31`; generic formatter path `rom/kernel/bug.c:21-63`, `rom/kernel/_bug.c:18-20`). The Raspberry Pi bootloader publishes `fb_Putc` as `KRN_FuncPutC` when framebuffer initialization succeeds (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/boot.c:718-731`). The selected callback uses shared `scr_XPos`/`scr_YPos`, `fb_Mirror`, and framebuffer bytes; `fb_Putc()` updates them and may scroll/render a full screen without synchronization (`arch/all-native/bootconsole/screen_fb.c:42-85,135-213`). The selected Raspberry Pi `fbgfx` handoff sends marker `0x03` when `DEBUGDISPLAY` is not defined (`arch/aarch64-raspi/hidd/fbgfx/fbgfx_support.c:42-50`); `kernel_debug.c:20-25` then clears the framebuffer callback. The handoff immediately follows this with `ClearBuffer()`, which `memset`s the handed-off framebuffer (`fbgfx_support.c:71,130-133`). Neither the callback clear nor this framebuffer clear waits for a diagnostic that already loaded the callback pointer.

On Raspberry Pi AArch64 SMP startup, two CPUs can format diagnostics at once while the bootstrap callback remains installed. Their characters and cursor/scroll operations can interleave, overwriting mirror positions and producing missing, duplicated, or garbled framebuffer text. There is also a transition window: a concurrent diagnostic can enter `krnPutC()` and load `ARMI_PutChar` before `RawPutChar(0x03)` clears it, then continue drawing while `FBGfx_Init()`'s `ClearBuffer()` zeros the same framebuffer. This can leave stray or incomplete console pixels after takeover. The source supports output corruption; this report does not claim an out-of-bounds write or broader memory damage. The serial path is also called per character and is not serialized by this code, but the reviewed candidate is specifically the framebuffer's shared cursor/mirror state and the framebuffer takeover overlap.

**Trigger and consequence:** overlapping `bug()`/`KrnBug()` output from different CPUs before graphics handoff detaches `fb_Putc`, or a diagnostic already inside `krnPutC()` when the handoff clears the callback and immediately zeroes the framebuffer. The unsynchronized framebuffer cursor and scroll updates can corrupt or lose diagnostic text; a callback crossing the clear can leave framebuffer contents dependent on write ordering. **Affected configuration:** AArch64 Raspberry Pi SMP boot with a working bootstrap framebuffer console, during concurrent diagnostic output or the selected `fbgfx` takeover (default path with `DEBUGDISPLAY` undefined); single-CPU runs and output after callbacks have drained are outside this finding. **Confidence:** high for unsynchronized shared-state mutation, direct selected callbacks, and the clear-after-detach ordering; manifestation requires the stated cross-CPU overlap. No boot or concurrent output was run. Source-only; see the [AArch64 bootstrap console cross-CPU trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7876).

<a id="ek9898"></a>
### EK9898 — m68kemu I/O-request size mismatch *(withdrawn; duplicate of EK10171)*

**Disposition:** this recovered candidate is the same `CreateIORequest()` guest/native extent mismatch already fully detailed under [EK10171](#ek10171), including the fixed `IORequest` shadow type, later `IOStdReq` synchronization, and native allocation size. EK10171 is the canonical finding; EK9898 is retained only as a historical anchor. See the [I/O request lifecycle coverage note](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8599).

<a id="ek9900"></a>
### EK9900 — m68kemu can create a task with a null entry point when tag conversion fails.

The generated `NewCreateTaskA()` thunk converts the guest tag list with `m68k_to_native_taglist()` and passes the result directly to native Exec (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2466-2472`). For a nonzero guest address, that converter allocates a native `TagItem` array and returns `NULL` if `AllocVec()` fails (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_shadow.c:139-150`). The thunk does not distinguish conversion failure from a null input list.

Native `NewCreateTaskA()` treats a null tag list as an empty list, leaving its local `initpc` null, and proceeds to allocate a task before calling `NewAddTask()` (`rom/exec/newcreatetaska.c:101-123,198-258`). The selected x86-64 `PrepareContext()` does not reject a null `entryPoint`; after creating the context it stores that value in `ctx->rip` and returns success (`arch/x86_64-all/exec/preparecontext.c:22-38,103-111`). `NewAddTask()` then publishes the prepared task with `TaskLaunch()` (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:285-345`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a guest calls `NewCreateTaskA()` with a nonempty list containing `TASKTAG_PC`, conversion-array allocation fails, and subsequent task/context allocations succeed. The thunk silently drops the requested entry point, and Exec can return a task whose initial instruction pointer is zero; dispatch cannot start the requested task code and is expected to fault when that task runs. This is distinct from EK9894, which covers the normal successful translation of a guest code address into native task execution without an m68k interpreter bridge. **Affected configuration:** an explicitly built and loaded m68kemu library on an x86-64 host; the module is optional and is not in the checked-in default package edges (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:14-17,40-42`; `rom/mmakefile.src:4-18,83-98,114-128`). No maintained in-tree emulated caller was established. **Confidence:** high for the allocation-failure-to-null-PC path and task publication; the consequence requires later task dispatch. No allocation failure, guest call, task dispatch, or build was run. Source-only; see the [NewCreateTaskA conversion-failure trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7868).

<a id="ek9909"></a>
### EK9909 — m68k Exec bridge leaves SumKickData unimplemented *(withdrawn; internal API, no guest contract established)*

**Disposition:** the generated thunk table does omit `SumKickData()` and the unknown-LVO path returns zero, but `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunkgen.py` explicitly lists it among functions skipped as “manual, dangerous, or internal.” Its checked-in callers are the AROS Exec/Amiga boot paths (`rom/exec/initkicktags.c:230`; `arch/m68k-amiga/boot/start.c:1018`), not emulated guest clients. No m68kemu contract promising this internal checksum vector to guest applications was found. Therefore the omission alone does not establish a supported API defect, and EK9909 is withdrawn rather than retained as a bug candidate. This does not withdraw EK9910, which concerns the native `SumKickData()` checksum implementation used by those boot paths. See the [vector census and caller disposition](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#ek9909-disposition).

<a id="ek9910"></a>
### EK9910 — SumKickData omits trailing entries in multi-entry MemList nodes.

`SumKickData()` checks each `KickMemPtr` node by adding `sizeof(struct MemList) / sizeof(ULONG)` words starting at the structure address (`rom/exec/sumkickdata.c:74-93`). The `MemList` allocation convention supports `ml_NumEntries` entries beyond the inline `ml_ME[0]`: `NewAllocEntry()` sizes and copies the record using that count (`rom/exec/newallocentry.c:82-103`). `InitKickTags()` likewise iterates every entry when reserving kick memory (`rom/exec/initkicktags.c:250-269`). On the selected m68k-Amiga AROS bootstrap path, a valid old ExecBase's `KickMemPtr` and saved checksum are copied into the new ExecBase, then compared with a fresh `SumKickData()` result before `InitKickMem()` (`arch/m68k-amiga/boot/start.c:997-1005,1017-1020`). A change confined to an entry after `ml_ME[0]` therefore is not included in the checksum and can pass this comparison, after which initialization consumes the changed range.

**Trigger and consequence:** warm boot with a multi-entry `KickMemPtr` node whose later entry changes while the saved checksum remains unchanged. The checksum does not detect that change before the later entry is used to reserve memory. This is a conditional integrity-check gap; the checked-in source search found no producer of a multi-entry `SysBase->KickMemPtr`, and the selected bootstrap's local `BootStruct.mlist` is a separate source, so no ordinary in-tree trigger is established. Treat historical or externally supplied warm-boot state as the remaining possible trigger. Include every declared `ml_NumEntries` entry in the checksum, with checked bounds. **Affected configuration:** m68k-Amiga AROS warm-boot path; multi-entry kick-memory state is not established by checked-in producers. **Confidence:** high that checksum coverage is one inline entry while initialization consumes all declared entries; low that a supported current configuration produces the required multi-entry state. No boot or memory mutation was run. See the [source and producer census](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2002).

<a id="ek9911"></a>
### EK9911 — DOS signals a null parent when an orphaned notifying process exits.

`ChildOrphan()` detaches a selected child by setting its `ETask.et_Parent` to NULL; the all-children branch does this to each child, and the single-child branch does it before unlinking the child (`rom/exec/childorphan.c:66-100`). Its public contract says the detached child will no longer participate in child-task actions (`:23-40`), but it does not clear the child's DOS `PRF_NOTIFYONDEATH` flag. `NewProc()` sets that flag from `NP_NotifyOnDeath` (`rom/dos/createnewproc.c:460-468`). Later, `DosEntry()` tests the flag and unconditionally calls `Signal(GetETask(me)->et_Parent, SIGF_CHILD)` (`rom/dos/createnewproc.c:997-1002`). The selected `Signal()` implementation dereferences its task argument to update its signal state (`rom/exec/signal.c:296-303`), so the orphaned process exit passes NULL into a routine that requires a task pointer.

**Trigger and consequence:** a client creates a process with `NP_NotifyOnDeath`, successfully orphans that process with `ChildOrphan()`, and the process later exits through `DosEntry()`. Its exit cleanup attempts to signal the cleared parent and can fault instead of completing normally. Skip notification when `et_Parent` is NULL, or clear the notification flag when orphaning. **Affected configuration:** builds that include the selected Exec and DOS implementations; the sequence requires a caller to combine the public `ChildOrphan()` and `NP_NotifyOnDeath` APIs. No maintained direct `ChildOrphan()` caller was found, so in-tree occurrence is not established. **Confidence:** high for the NULL state and unconditional signal call; conditional for client reachability and observed failure. No process was run. See the [orphan and exit-path trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8136).

<a id="ek9912"></a>
### EK9912 — The Sam440 SFS file loader ignores failed data-block reads.

`sfs_loadsector()` forwards the block request to the Parthenope context callback (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/sfs.c:51-57`; `context.c:98-102`). `get_bnode()` treats a zero result as a failed read by terminating its `while (sfs_loadsector(...))` loop (`sfs.c:138-162`), but `sfs_loadfile()` discards the result for every file-data block and immediately copies from the reusable scratch buffer and advances `readed` (`sfs.c:177-195`). The callback can therefore report failure without stopping this path; the buffer may contain prior block data or indeterminate contents. `sfs_loadfile()` returns the nominal positive byte count when the extent loop otherwise completes. Selected Parthenope consumers reject only negative `load_file()` results for the kernel and module paths (`parthenope.c:184-191,286-303,369-379`), so this read failure is accepted as a successful load.

**Trigger and consequence:** the SFS `loadsector` callback reports a data-block read failure as zero while the scratch allocation succeeds and the file has a data extent. Parthenope copies non-file data into the destination and can pass the resulting buffer to ELF parsing or module loading as though the read succeeded. Check the sector-read result and return an error before copying or increasing the completed byte count. **Affected configuration:** explicitly buildable Sam440 Parthenope boot target using its SFS fallback; the parent build dependency is commented, so default-image inclusion is not claimed. **Confidence:** high for the ignored result and successful return path; occurrence depends on a failed callback read, which was not induced. This is distinct from EK545's positive short return on early extent-chain exhaustion and EK9913's read-time allocation failures. No disk image, media read, or boot was used. See the [read and caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8143).

<a id="ek9913"></a>
### EK9913 — SFS file lookup uses unchecked temporary-allocation results.

The Parthenope context `malloc()` wrapper forwards to the boot context allocator and may return NULL (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/context.c:110-113`). Four temporary buffers in the SFS read path are consumed without checking that result. For a pathname containing `/`, `sfs_find()` writes the extracted component through its `directory` pointer (`sfs.c:105-128`); `sfs_findobject()` passes its block buffer to `sfs_loadsector()` and then reads its checksum and object fields (`:73-102`); `get_bnode()` passes its tree buffer into the sector-read loop and parses the B-tree node (`:131-162`); and `sfs_loadfile()` passes its extent-read buffer to the sector callback and copies from it (`:165-195`). A failed allocation can therefore reach a NULL destination/read buffer, or cause lookup to return a NULL B-node which `sfs_loadfile()` dereferences at `sebn->blocks` (`:183-184`). The checked menu path calls each boot device's `load_file()` and treats positive lengths as success (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/menu.c:584-597`); boot consumers also proceed on nonnegative results (`parthenope.c:184-191,286-303,369-379`).

**Trigger and consequence:** low memory causes one of the lookup or read-time allocations to return NULL while SFS lookup/loading continues. Depending on which buffer fails and the callback outcome, the path can fault during component copying, sector I/O, B-tree parsing, or file-data copying; a failed B-node buffer can instead produce NULL that is dereferenced by the file loader. Check each allocation and propagate a load error before using its buffer or node. **Affected configuration:** explicitly buildable Sam440 Parthenope boot target; its parent dependency is commented, so default-image inclusion is not claimed. These read-time allocations are separate from EK546's unchecked constructor allocations. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked results and subsequent consumers; the failure is conditional on allocation failure and was not induced. No allocation failure, media read, or boot was performed. See the [allocation and caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8149).

<a id="ek9914"></a>
### EK9914 — Concurrent m68kemu opens can leak a DOS library reference.

`M68KEmu_Open()` checks the shared `base->dosBase` and, if NULL, opens DOS and stores the result without synchronization (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_init.c:21-25`). Exec `OpenLibrary()` releases the library-list lock before invoking the library's Open vector (`rom/exec/openlibrary.c:73-91`); the generated Open vector runs the `ADD2OPENLIB` function before incrementing `lib_OpenCnt` (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1295-1302`). In ExecSMP, `Forbid()` is local-CPU only (`rom/exec/forbid.c:42-60`), and the library-list read lock permits concurrent open lookups.

**Trigger and consequence:** two CPUs concurrently perform the first `OpenLibrary("m68kemu.library", 0)` calls. Both can observe `dosBase == NULL`, each open `dos.library` (incrementing its open count), and then store the same DOS base pointer. Each m68kemu open succeeds and is later paired with a close, but `M68KEmu_Close()` does not release DOS; when m68kemu finally expunges, `M68KEmu_Expunge()` closes the shared pointer only once (`m68kemu_init.c:27-41`). One DOS open reference remains unbalanced. The selected DOS library is `noexpunge` (`rom/dos/dos.conf:7`), so no unload blockage is claimed. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built m68kemu on an ExecSMP hosted target, with concurrent first opens; the m68kemu dependency is optional and omitted from default package edges (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:14-17`). Checked-in paths that can open it include DOS `RunCommand()` and process startup (`rom/dos/runcommand.c:109-113`; `createnewproc.c:860-864`). **Confidence:** high for the unsynchronized check/store and unmatched reference under the stated interleaving; this requires simultaneous first opens. No concurrent open/close or expunge was run; source-only. See the [first-open concurrency trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#ek9914-first-open-concurrency-recheck).

<a id="ek9915"></a>
### EK9915 — CHRP Efika package repeats generic modules instead of its Efika-specific set.

The Efika package manifest declares `PKG_EFI_RSRC := battclock bootloader openfirmware processor`, `PKG_EFI_DEVS := timer ata`, and `PKG_EFI_HIDDS := radeon pci-efika` (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:72-76`). However, the `kernel-package-chrp-ppc-efika` `%make_package` invocation passes `PKG_GEN_RSRC`, `PKG_GEN_DEVS`, `PKG_GEN_HANDLERS`, and `PKG_GEN_HIDDS` instead (`:77-80`). The package macro constructs its archive member list from exactly the passed `res`, `devs`, `handlers`, and `hidds` arguments (`config/make.tmpl:3750-3767,3795-3797`), so the Efika package repeats generic modules and leaves its target-specific resources, timer/ATA devices, and Radeon/PCI-Efika HIDDs out. The checked-in Efika boot menu loads both the generic and Efika package files (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/menu.lst:7-10`), so the second package does not get those members from the generic package under their Efika-specific names.

**Trigger and consequence:** build the explicit CHRP Efika package using the checked-in package rule. The resulting `aros-ppc-efika.pkg` omits the modules named by the `PKG_EFI_*` lists; booting an image from that package set can lack its Efika timer/ATA and board-specific HIDD/resource modules. **Affected configuration:** explicit CHRP Efika package/image build. The target is not asserted to be part of the default image. **Confidence:** high for the wrong variable references and package member construction; generated archive contents and hardware behavior were not built or booted. Pass the `PKG_EFI_*` lists to the Efika package rule. Source-only; see the [package-manifest reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#chrp-efika-package-content-manifest-full-pass-ek9915-added-2026-10-28).

<a id="ek329"></a>
### EK329 — `OpenAsync()` can close a DOS FileHandle twice when async setup fails

`OpenAsync()` opens the requested file and calls `AS_OpenAsyncFH()` with `closeIt=TRUE`; if that helper returns NULL, the wrapper unconditionally calls DOS `Close()` on its original handle (`workbench/libs/asyncio/src/OpenAsync.c:35-52`). The helper itself closes that handle on both failure routes: when append-mode `Seek(..., OFFSET_END)` fails (`OpenAsyncFH.c:24-45`) and when its retry loop cannot allocate the `AsyncFile` and buffers (`OpenAsyncFH.c:75-99,185-198`). It then returns NULL without clearing the wrapper's local BPTR. DOS `Close()` frees the FileHandle and does not make a repeated close idempotent (`rom/dos/close.c:52-78`), so the wrapper can close a stale handle after the helper already consumed it.

**Trigger and consequence:** `OpenAsync()` calls the helper with a handle-owning mode and async setup fails. The append-seek case depends on a failing filesystem seek; the allocation failure is reachable from the maintained AHIRecord caller, which opens an output file before requesting the async wrapper. The second close can access a freed DOS FileHandle and corrupt memory or fail during cleanup. Give handle closure to one layer, or clear/transfer ownership before returning failure. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting the AsyncIO library and a caller using `OpenAsync()`; no default-image claim is made. **Confidence:** high for the duplicate-close ownership path; failure timing and manifestation were not run. See the [failure ownership trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9155).

<a id="ek10200"></a>
### EK10200 — Repeated console SCREEN options leak earlier screen-name allocations

The CON open-parameter parser handles each accepted `SCREEN` option by allocating a new string and assigning it directly to `fh->screenname` (`rom/filesys/console_handler/support.c:348-354`). It does not free the previous value before overwriting the pointer. On close, the handler frees only the string still stored in that field (`rom/filesys/console_handler/con_handler.c:441-442`). Thus an open string containing multiple `/SCREEN...` options leaks every successfully allocated value except the last one.

**Trigger and consequence:** open a console stream with two or more accepted SCREEN options and allow the corresponding allocations to succeed. The stream remains usable with the final parsed screen name, but each earlier name allocation is lost until process/system reclamation. Free the old value before replacement or reject duplicate options. **Affected configuration:** the console handler's option-parsing path. **Confidence:** high for the pointer overwrite and cleanup ownership; no console stream was opened. See the [parser and cleanup review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L531).

<a id="ek10202"></a>
### EK10202 — ARM32/AArch64 secondary bootstrap leaks its CPU context when ETask allocation fails [conditional]

Both native ARM32 and AArch64 secondary-CPU bootstrap paths create a context before calling `Exec_InitETask()` (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_execsmp.c:64-106`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_execsmp.c:59-96`). `Exec_InitETask()` returns FALSE when its initial `AllocMem(sizeof(struct IntETask), ...)` fails (`rom/exec/exec_util.c:101-126`). Each caller then frees the bootstrap stack, task and MemList and returns NULL, but neither calls `KrnDeleteContext()` for the already-created `bsctx`. The selected context destroyer frees that allocation using the matching context size (`rom/kernel/deletecontext.c:50-55`; AArch64 creation in `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/createcontext.c:31-36`).

**Trigger and consequence:** during ARM32 or AArch64 SMP secondary bootstrap, context creation succeeds but `Exec_InitETask()` cannot allocate the ETask. The CPU startup path fails and the context allocation is leaked. In both implementations this branch follows `AddHead(&bstask->tc_MemEntry, ...)` before `NEWLIST(&bstask->tc_MemEntry)` (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_execsmp.c:65,80`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_execsmp.c:60,75`); the earlier zeroed-list insertion defects are tracked separately as EK153 and EK726. The context-leak branch is therefore conditional on reaching it despite that earlier defect or after the list initialization order is corrected. Add `KrnDeleteContext(bsctx)` to both failure cleanups. **Affected configuration:** native ARM32/AArch64 builds using ExecSMP; the trigger is a low-memory ETask-allocation failure after context creation, subject to the preceding list issue. **Confidence:** high for the missing cleanup and bounded leak; reachability is conditional. No allocation failure or CPU startup was induced. See the [bootstrap cleanup trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9127).

<a id="ek10203"></a>
### EK10203 — ARM MinGW CE is selectable but lacks its kernel CPU backend.

The MinGW configure branch accepts ARM targets, sets `aros_target_cpu="arm"`, and chooses the `arm-mingw32ce-` kernel tool prefix (`configure.in:2348-2360`). The selected MinGW kernel manifest always includes `cpu_$(CPU)` in its architecture-specific C source list (`arch/all-mingw32/kernel/mmakefile.src:24-30`), so this target requests `arch/all-mingw32/kernel/cpu_arm.c`. That file is absent; the repository contains `cpu_i386.c` and `cpu_x86_64.c` in the MinGW directory, and the only other `cpu_arm.c` implementations are for unrelated tools and the Unix backend. `%build_archspecific` constructs the object list from the given source names, and its C pattern rule requires the corresponding source in the current architecture directory (`config/make.tmpl:3297-3304,3415-3423`). Thus an ARM MinGW CE kernel build reaches a missing-source prerequisite rather than an ARM implementation.

The ARM context header itself matches the public ARM register layout for the 17 copied words, but that does not supply the missing CPU translation table or other CPU-specific implementation. In addition, an explicit `kernel-kernel-mingw32-native` DLL build selects `leaveinterrupt_$(CPU)` (`mmakefile.src:35-36,52-55`), which requests absent `leaveinterrupt_arm.s`; its dependency from the main kernel target is commented at line 22, so this separate failure is scoped to requests for that native target.

**Trigger and consequence:** configure/build the ARM MinGW CE target; the selected kernel build cannot resolve `cpu_arm.c`. If the native DLL target is separately requested, it also cannot resolve the ARM interrupt-exit assembly source. Supply the missing ARM backend(s) or reject this configuration before generating build targets. **Affected configuration:** ARM MinGW CE (`target_cpu` matching `*arm*`); the missing native trampoline additionally affects explicit `kernel-kernel-mingw32-native` builds. **Confidence:** high for the source-list and missing-file mismatch; no build was run. See the [ARM context and target-selection review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1123).

<a id="ek10204"></a>
### EK10204 — m68k bootstrap debug diagnostics dereference a failed Resident-name allocation.

`ConvertCSTR()` allocates its 257-byte temporary BCPL string with `AllocMem()` and immediately writes `bname[0]` without checking for NULL (`arch/m68k-amiga/c/AROSBootstrap.c:184-197`). The selected compile-time debug path calls it for each Resident in the original and newly loaded KickTag lists after ROM loading and before `BootROM()` (`:1287-1303,1488-1493`; `DEBUG` is defined as 1 at `:18`). Thus a Resident list containing at least one item and a failed temporary allocation cause a NULL write during bootstrap diagnostics. This failure path is separate from EK10169's long-string overwrite after successful allocation.

**Trigger and consequence:** m68k Amiga `AROSBootstrap` reaches the enabled debug `DumpKickTags()` path with a nonempty resident list, and the 257-byte `AllocMem()` in `ConvertCSTR()` fails. The bootstrap dereferences NULL and aborts before the ROM handoff instead of skipping or reporting the unavailable diagnostic string. **Affected configuration:** m68k Amiga bootstrap builds selecting `arch/m68k-amiga/c/AROSBootstrap.c`; requires allocation failure and at least one Resident entry. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked result and unconditional debug caller; no allocation failure or boot was induced. Source-only. See the [bootstrap allocation and diagnostics review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8585).


<a id="ek10205"></a>
### EK10205 — Generic and architecture dispatchers invoke a task's `tc_Launch` callback twice.

The generic `core_Dispatch()` calls `task->tc_Launch` when the selected task has `TF_LAUNCH` (`rom/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:163-170`; the generic resource manifest includes `kernel_scheduler` in `rom/kernel/mmakefile.src:34-39`). The Sam440 arch-specific additions omit a scheduler replacement (`arch/ppc-sam440/kernel/mmakefile.src:20-35`), and the OpenSBI `CFILES` omit one (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/mmakefile.src:20-48`); both selected `cpu_Dispatch()` functions independently test the same flag and call the callback after `core_Dispatch()` returns (`arch/ppc-sam440/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:48-73`; `arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:165-215`). `NewAddTask()` sets `TF_LAUNCH` whenever `tc_Launch` is non-NULL (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:312-317`), and the public `Task` layout describes the callback as running when the task gets CPU (`compiler/include/exec/tasks.h:61`). Neither selected dispatcher clears the flag, so on these two target paths the callback runs twice per dispatch, not just twice on first launch. ARM-native, AArch64-native and native RISC-V explicitly select their own `kernel_scheduler.c` in their `CFILES` and are excluded (`arch/arm-native/kernel/mmakefile.src:24-29`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/mmakefile.src:20-27`; `arch/riscv-native/kernel/mmakefile.src:4-5`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a task with a non-NULL `tc_Launch` is selected by `core_Dispatch()` on a target that also calls the callback in its architecture dispatcher. The generic scheduler implementation is selected for Sam440 and RISC-V OpenSBI, and both corresponding CPU dispatchers invoke the callback after `core_Dispatch()` returns; the flag is not cleared, so the callback runs twice on every dispatch of such a task on those targets. The normal self-removal caller reaches this same dispatch route through `RemTask()` → `KrnDispatch()` → `SC_DISPATCH` → `core_SysCall()` → `cpu_Dispatch()` (`rom/exec/remtask.c:146-164`; `rom/kernel/dispatch.c:53-55`; `rom/kernel/kernel_intr.c:78-80`; Sam440 syscall entry `arch/ppc-sam440/kernel/syscall.c:154-161`; OpenSBI trap entry `arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_traps.c:169-178`). **Affected configuration:** Sam440 and RISC-V OpenSBI builds using the generic `rom/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c`. ARM-native, AArch64-native, and native RISC-V use architecture-specific `kernel_scheduler.c` implementations and are excluded; their `core_Dispatch()` functions do not make the generic callback call. The only checked-in direct `tc_Launch` assignment is the Efika idle hook, which uses a separate custom scheduler and is not affected. No maintained caller exercising the duplicate path was found, so no in-tree user-visible consequence is claimed. **Confidence:** high for the duplicate on the two selected target paths; medium for practical impact because checked-in users were not found. No task callback or scheduler was run. Source-only; see the [dispatch and launch-callback caller census](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9427).


<a id="ek8810"></a>
### EK8810 — Raspberry Pi AArch64 boot does not handle device-tree allocation failure

The selected Raspberry Pi AArch64 bootstrap includes `devicetree.c` in its boot `FILES` list (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/mmakefile.src:6-7`). Its private bump allocator is limited to `BOOT_TMP_SIZE` (256 KiB) and returns NULL when the requested allocation exceeds remaining space (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/include/boot.h:18`; `support.c:111-128,131-135`). `dt_build_node()` checks whether a node allocation succeeded, but it does not propagate failure to its caller. On a failed child-node allocation it returns without consuming that node's FDT name or structure; the parent ignores the NULL return and resumes its token loop from the child-name bytes (`devicetree.c:13-37`). The parser can therefore lose token synchronization and return an incomplete tree without reporting failure (`:109-131`).

Property-node allocation is more direct: after `malloc(sizeof(of_property_t))`, the parser immediately writes `p->op_length` without checking for NULL (`devicetree.c:40-50`). If the bump allocator is exhausted while parsing a property, this dereferences NULL during boot. The first parse is called unconditionally in the selected boot path (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/boot.c:432-438`); later boot code uses the parsed tree to locate required `/soc` data, and halts if that node is absent (`:475-528`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a sufficiently large or property/node-dense firmware DTB exhausts the 256 KiB bootstrap parse allocator. Property allocation failure faults immediately; node allocation failure desynchronizes the global parser cursor and leaves `dt_parse()` without a reliable failure result, so later boot-tree lookups can fail or consume an incomplete tree. **Affected configuration:** Raspberry Pi AArch64 boot targets selecting this parser; requires allocator exhaustion while parsing the firmware DTB. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked property dereference, ignored node-allocation failure and cursor desynchronization; the required DTB size/shape is conditional and no selected firmware DTB is shown to exceed the allocator. Check and propagate every allocation failure and make `dt_parse()` return an explicit failure before boot consumes the tree. No DTB, allocation failure, or boot was exercised; source-only; see the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1004).


<a id="ek10206"></a>
### EK10206 — ARM Efika bootstrap writes past its fixed kernel-tag array for many ATAG memory ranges.

The ARM Efika bootstrap stores outgoing `TagItem`s in `tags[128]` (`arch/arm-efika/boot/boot.c:34-37`). For every `ATAG_MEM`, `parse_atags()` appends both `KRN_MEMLower` and `KRN_MEMUpper` without checking the remaining array capacity (`:51-62`). The ATAG header explicitly permits multiple memory records (`arch/arm-efika/boot/atags.h:34-43`), and the shared kernel-tag contract also permits repeated memory-range pairs (`compiler/include/aros/kernel.h:81-85`). After parsing, `boot()` appends kernel-lowest/highest tags and, when a memory upper bound was supplied, a BSS tag and final `TAG_DONE` without checking capacity (`boot.c:276-280,347-354,359-362`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an ATAG list with at least 62 non-wrapping memory ranges reaches the fixed tag-array boundary: the repeated range pairs consume 124 entries, before the bootstrap's own tag and later kernel tags/terminator. The writes to the kernel-bound/BSS entries or final terminator then land beyond `tags[128]`, potentially corrupting adjacent bootstrap state and leaving the outgoing tag list malformed. No claim is made about how common such a fragmented map is. **Affected configuration:** the explicitly built ARM Efika bootstrap (`arch/arm-efika/boot/mmakefile.src:6,36-43`); its `arosboot-efika` aggregate edges are commented (`:11-22`), so no default-image path is claimed. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked appends and table arithmetic; triggering depends on an ATAG map with many memory ranges. No ATAG input, build, package or boot was used. Source-only. See the [ATAG parser and caller review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1335).


<a id="ek10207"></a>
### EK10207 — EfikaMX ARM kernel startup copies a long memory-tag list past its 64-entry buffer.

The kernel startup's temporary boot-message storage is a union with exactly 64 `TagItem` slots (`arch/arm-efika/kernel/kernel_startup.c:68-71`). When the bootstrap passes its separate `tags[128]` array, `startup()` copies each item into `temporary.tags` until it reaches `TAG_DONE`, without checking the destination capacity (`:106-116`). The bootstrap emits one `KRN_BootLoader` item, two items for every `ATAG_MEM`, then `KRN_KernelLowest`, `KRN_KernelHighest`, `KRN_KernelBss` when memory was found, and the terminator (`arch/arm-efika/boot/boot.c:34-37,51-62,276-280,347-362`). Multiple memory tags are explicitly allowed by the ATAG definition (`arch/arm-efika/boot/atags.h:34-43`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a valid non-wrapping ATAG map with 30 or more `ATAG_MEM` records and a command-line record yields at least 65 non-terminator kernel tags; with no command line, 31 or more memory records suffice. The copy writes past `temporary.tags[64]` before it reaches the terminator, potentially corrupting adjacent startup state. The source-side 128-entry overflow at 62 or more memory records is separately tracked as [EK10206](#ek10206); this destination overflow occurs earlier and does not depend on the source array being exceeded. **Affected configuration:** checked-in EfikaMX ARM startup when entered with such a fragmented memory map; the explicit boot target's aggregate edges are commented, so no default-image path is claimed. **Confidence:** high for tag-count arithmetic and the unchecked copy; occurrence depends on the supplied map. No tag list or boot was used. Source-only; see [EK9484](#ek9484) and the [Efika startup ledger entry](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1346).


<a id="ek547"></a>
### EK547 — Efika ARM debug input returns UART status bits as character data.

The selected Efika `KrnMayGetChar()` implementation tests `USR2_RDR` and then returns the complete 32-bit `URXD` register value without applying the register's data mask (`arch/arm-efika/kernel/maygetchar.c:18-26`). The same hardware header defines `UART_URXD_RX_DATA_MASK` as `0xFF` and separate receive-status flags in bits 10–15 (`arch/arm-efika/include/hardware/mx51_uart.h:55-62`). The common `RawMayGetChar()` forwards the value, and the selected debug.library `KGetChar()` loops only on `-1` before returning the raw result (`rom/exec/rawmaygetchar.c`; `rom/debug/kgetchar.c:10-20`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a received byte is reported ready while one or more upper `URXD` status bits are set. The caller receives those status bits ORed with the byte instead of an ASCII value; consumers may treat the result as an invalid or unrelated character. This report does not claim which status bits accompany ordinary reads on physical MX51 silicon. Mask with `UART_URXD_RX_DATA_MASK` before returning the character. **Affected configuration:** EfikaMX ARM kernel builds selecting `arch/arm-efika/kernel/maygetchar.c` and clients using `RawMayGetChar()`/debug.library `KGetChar()`. The checked-in startup currently parks before initializing the kernel resource (EK9484), so this is a backend defect with no normal checked-in boot route at this revision. **Confidence:** high for the unmasked source dataflow and public return contract; medium for hardware occurrence of status bits on a read. No UART read or character input was performed. Source-only; see the [Efika input path review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1347).


<a id="ek345"></a>
### EK345 — A zero VESA refresh request reaches a division by zero in the PC bootstrap.

The PC bootstrap passes the suffix of a `VESA=` command-line option to `setupVESA()` (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:477-498`). When the option contains `@`, `vesa_setup.c` parses the following decimal value with `strtoul()` and sets `set_refresh`, but does not reject zero (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/vesa_setup.c:22-54`). `findMode()` calls `calcTimings(vfreq)` for a valid selected mode when the VBE controller reports version 3.0 or newer (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/vesa.c:294-304`); the first timing calculation divides by `vfreq` (`:154-156`).

**Trigger and consequence:** boot with an explicit VESA option ending in `@0` (or `@` with no digits), a VBE 3.0+ controller, and a listed mode that `findMode()` accepts. The parsed zero reaches the division in the standalone 32-bit bootstrap before `setVbeMode()` is called. This raises the processor's divide-error exception; the resulting boot behavior depends on the active IDT/exception handling and is not established here. **Affected configuration:** i386-PC and x86-64-PC bootstrap VESA mode-setting path, only when custom refresh timing is enabled and a valid VBE 3.0+ mode is found. **Confidence:** high for the parser-to-division path and zero divisor; runtime exception handling and firmware mode availability are unverified. Reject zero or select a documented default before calling `calcTimings()`. No boot, BIOS call, or invalid option was exercised. Source-only; see the [VESA option and timing review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2149).


<a id="ek126"></a>
### EK126 — x86-64 task.resource register queries omit index zero and return incorrect vector data.

`task.resource` publishes register counts and indexed tag bases: 15 general registers from `TaskTag_REG_General0`, eight floating-point registers from `TaskTag_REG_Float0`, and 32 vector values of 16 bytes from `TaskTag_REG_Vec0` (`rom/task/task.h:27-37`). In `QueryTaskTagList()`, the general and floating-point handlers require the tag to be strictly greater than the corresponding base (`rom/task/QueryTaskTagList.c:86-111`). A query using the base tag for index zero therefore falls through without writing the caller's output. The selected TaskTrace caller constructs its general-register tags as `TaskTag_REG_General0 + i` for indices 0 through 14 (`developer/debug/shellcommands/TaskTrace.c:176-192`); its zero-initialized first result consequently remains zero, although TaskTrace only consumes index 14 for its frame pointer.

The x86-64 vector handler has a separate mapping error. It accepts only tags strictly above `TaskTag_REG_Vec0` and below `TaskTag_REG_Vec0 + 0x18`, so indices 0 and 24 through 31 are not handled. For the accepted tags it stores through an `IPTR *` (eight bytes on x86-64), despite `TaskTag_REG_VecSize` reporting 16, and derives the source from `&regs->rax` using the general-register tag base rather than from `regs->FXSData`/`XSData` (`QueryTaskTagList.c:115-125`). These reads select unrelated portions of the context/FPU save area, not the requested vector value. The pointer is outside the `ExceptionContext` structure proper, but the selected x86-64 context allocation includes adjacent FPU state; this review does not establish an out-of-allocation read.

**Trigger and consequence:** a caller queries index-zero general/floating-point tags or requests x86-64 vector-register tags. The first general/floating output remains whatever the caller supplied; vector outputs contain partial, unrelated values or remain unwritten for indices outside the accepted range. The direct C caller census found no in-tree vector-register consumer, and TaskTrace's selected use only needs RBP, which its index-14 query maps correctly; vector impact therefore depends on external or future API clients. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 task.resource builds for the implemented indexed-register paths. i386's nonzero reported register counts but absent indexed copy implementation are tracked separately in EK611. **Confidence:** high for the tag comparisons, vector output width and source address calculation; caller impact is conditional for vector tags. No register query or task inspection was run. Source-only; see the [register-query implementation and caller review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2128).


<a id="ek10208"></a>
### EK10208 — RISC-V OpenSBI load sampling drops elapsed time from the running task's CPU-time total.

When the OpenSBI timer closes a load window, `krnTimerTick()` folds the current running ETask's elapsed ticks into `iet_private2` and then advances `iet_private1` to `now` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_timer.c:345-353`). The normal switch-out path in `cpu_Switch()` also uses `iet_private1` as the start of the current run segment, but it is the only selected RISC-V OpenSBI path that converts elapsed ticks into `iet_CpuTime` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:137-155`). The timer fold therefore consumes the pre-sample interval for the CPU-time accumulator without adding it there. `krnTaskUsage()` only converts and clears `iet_private2` for `iet_CpuUsage`; it does not update `iet_CpuTime` (`kernel_timer.c:68-80`). A source-wide search of the selected OpenSBI tree found no other `iet_CpuTime` producer. `TaskTag_CPUTime` returns that accumulator to callers (`rom/task/QueryTaskTagList.c:153-160`; contract in `rom/task/task.h:24`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an ETask is still the current task when a load-sampling window closes (nominally once per second after `__timebase_freq` ticks). Its elapsed pre-sample slice is counted in task CPU usage, but is excluded from `TaskTag_CPUTime`; the later switch-out only accounts from the advanced timestamp. A task spanning multiple sample windows loses each such slice, so its reported cumulative CPU time can substantially undercount actual running time. **Affected configuration:** RISC-V64 OpenSBI kernel builds with task load sampling enabled and a current ETask at a sample boundary. **Confidence:** high for the timestamp and accumulator dataflow; no task or timer boundary was exercised. Add the folded interval to `iet_CpuTime` when advancing the timestamp, or maintain a separate timestamp for load sampling. Source-only; see the [OpenSBI timer and task-accounting ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L9698).


<a id="ek10209"></a>
### EK10209 — Linux x86-64 task switches preserve only legacy FXSAVE state while the HIDD can execute AVX2.

The Linux x86-64 hosted kernel's signal-context macros save and restore only `sizeof(struct FPFXSContext)` bytes through `uc_mcontext.fpregs` (`arch/all-linux/kernel/cpu_x86_64.h:204-219`); that structure is the 512-byte legacy FXSAVE image (`arch/x86_64-all/include/aros/cpucontext.h:23-40`). For Linux x86-64, `configure` selects the emulation flavour (`configure:10638-10643`), while the x86-64 CPU initializer enables extended XSAVE sizing and `ECF_FPXS` only under `AROS_FLAVOUR_STANDALONE`; the selected emulation path allocates only the FXSAVE context and sets `ECF_FPFXS` (`arch/x86_64-all/kernel/cpu_init.c:19-27,90-97`; `createcontext.c:38-57`). The hosted switch therefore drops the AVX YMM upper halves when it saves a task, and restoring a task overwrites only the legacy 512-byte portion of the Linux signal frame.

The omitted state is reachable in the checked-in x86-64 graphics path: the x86-64 HIDD target depends on the x86 AVX implementation (`arch/x86_64-all/hidd/gfx/mmakefile.src:12-22`), which is built with `-mavx2` (`arch/i386-all/hidd/gfx/mmakefile.src:40-45`). Its dispatcher selects those routines after AVX and AVX2 CPUID checks (`arch/x86_64-all/hidd/gfx/rgbconv_arch.c:67-77,102-124`), installs them during color-conversion initialization (`rom/hidds/gfx/colorconv_init.c:23-29`), and the bitmap conversion caller invokes the selected function pointer (`rom/hidds/gfx/gfx_bitmapconvertpixels.c:618-630`). The AVX2 routines use live `__m256i` values across multiple instructions and stores (`arch/i386-all/hidd/gfx/rgbconv_avx.c:34-61`). A second checked-in route exists when the x86-64 CyberGraphics target is built: `arch/x86_64-all/cgfx/mmakefile.src` selects `processpixelarray_opblur` and `processpixelarray_avx_opblur`; the public `ProcessPixelArray()` operation dispatches POP_BLUR to `ProcessPixelArrayBlurFunc()` (`workbench/libs/cgfx/processpixelarray.c:109`), whose x86-64 implementation checks AVX2 and calls the AVX implementation (`arch/x86_64-all/cgfx/processpixelarray_opblur.c:30-42,501-512`). That implementation uses YMM values in its vectorized horizontal and vertical blur loops (`arch/x86_64-all/cgfx/processpixelarray_avx_opblur.c:47-120,146-221`). This CyberGraphics route is scoped to builds that select that optional library target; it is not claimed as part of every default image. Linux x86 signal frames can include extended XSAVE state beyond the legacy FXSAVE prefix; see the [Linux x86 signal-context ABI](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/arch/x86/include/uapi/asm/sigcontext.h) and [signal-frame definition](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/arch/x86/include/asm/sigframe.h).

**Trigger and consequence:** on an x86-64 Linux emulation build running on a host that exposes usable AVX2, an AROS task enters either an AVX2 graphics conversion or (when the x86-64 CyberGraphics target is built) its AVX2 blur path and is asynchronously switched out; another task changes YMM upper halves before the first task resumes. Because neither task context stores/restores those halves, resumed vector code can use corrupted values and produce incorrect pixels. The trigger requires an AVX2 path and a task switch during live vector state; no runtime manifestation is claimed. **Affected configuration:** Linux x86-64 hosted/emulation flavour with the x86-64 HIDD AVX2 target, or the optional x86-64 CyberGraphics target, enabled and AVX2 available to the process. **Confidence:** high for the incomplete state copy and the two selected AVX2 call paths; practical frequency depends on workload and scheduling. Preserve the full enabled XSAVE state in hosted task contexts or keep AVX code out of a backend that saves only FXSAVE. No build, signal, or runtime test was performed; source-only.

<a id="ek10210"></a>
### EK10210 — Linux PowerPC task switches do not preserve FPSCR.

The Linux PowerPC context macros mark only `ECF_FULL_GPRS|ECF_FPU` and copy the 32 FPR values in `SAVEREGS()` (`arch/all-linux/kernel/cpu_ppc.h:62-82`). `RESTOREREGS()` writes those FPRs back but never copies the FPSCR (`:89-112`). The saved context has a separate `fpscr` field, and `ECF_FULL_FPU` is explicitly documented as indicating that FPSCR is present (`arch/ppc-all/include/aros/cpucontext.h:27-42`). The Linux PPC32 signal ABI carries FPSCR as the final value of the FPR state (`mc_fregs`); the Linux ptrace layout names its register slot `PT_FPSCR` (`PT_FPR0 + 2*32 + 1`). See the [Linux PPC32 ucontext layout](https://codebrowser.dev/linux/linux/arch/powerpc/include/uapi/asm/ucontext.h.html), [register-slot definitions](https://codebrowser.dev/linux/linux/arch/powerpc/include/uapi/asm/ptrace.h.html), and [signal FPR save/restore path](https://codebrowser.dev/linux/linux/arch/powerpc/kernel/signal_32.c.html). The selected Unix switch calls `SAVEREGS()` before scheduling and `RESTOREREGS()` for the dispatched task (`arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:90,131-136`). AROS's PPC `fesetround()` changes FPSCR directly with `mtfsf` (`arch/ppc-all/include/aros/fenv.h:168-179`).

**Trigger and consequence:** in a successfully built Linux PPC32 hosted/emulation target, one AROS task changes its rounding mode or FPSCR exception state, then a task switch occurs. The next task inherits the outgoing task's FPSCR; when the first task resumes, its prior value is not restored. Floating-point operations can consequently use the wrong rounding mode or exception state, producing incorrect results or status. **Affected configuration:** Linux `powerpc*` selecting `AROS_TARGET_CPU=ppc` and the Unix kernel's PPC context macros; `configure` contains this target branch (`configure:10671-10678`), although nearby configuration comments say the PPC nightly target still needs work, so a successful build for a specific toolchain remains unverified. **Confidence:** high that the save/restore macros omit a distinct ABI field and that this field controls supported PPC floating-point environment operations; actual target buildability and runtime manifestation were not tested. Save and restore the signal-frame FPSCR and set the matching context flag. Source-only; no build or runtime test was performed.

<a id="ek10211"></a>
### EK10211 — m68k thunk regeneration loses DOS D-register pointer translations without prototype headers.

`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunkgen.py` defines DOS D-register pointer overrides for `FRead`, `FWrite`, and `FGets` at lines 192–218, including D2 for each buffer argument. A later assignment to `DPTR_OVERRIDES` at lines 249–255 replaces that entire map with five graphics-specific entries. In `gen_param_line()` lines 452–469, a D-register argument without a parsed prototype is translated with `THUNK_DPTR` only when its function/register pair is in the surviving map; otherwise it is emitted as `ULONG arg = THUNK_D(n)`. The command-line usage and module docstring explicitly allow omitting the optional NDK prototype directory, and `parse_clib_protos()` returns an empty map in that mode (lines 5–8, 296–300, 632–647).

The affected DOS declarations include D2 buffers for `FRead(BPTR, APTR, ...)`, `FWrite(BPTR, CONST_APTR, ...)`, and `FGets(BPTR, STRPTR, ...)` (`rom/dos/dos.conf:108–110`; implementations in `rom/dos/fread.c:17–23,63–76`, `fwrite.c:15–22,64–78`, and `fgets.c:14–19,49–76`). The overwritten first map also includes active generated path APIs: `FilePart(path=D1)`, `PathPart(path=D1)`, and `AddPart(dirname=D1, filename=D2, size=D3)` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1690–1717`). Their checked-in prototype-aware wrappers translate those arguments through `m68k_to_host()` (`:1691–1717`), while the generator's no-prototype path would emit `ULONG` values from `THUNK_D()` because the surviving map no longer contains these entries. Native `FilePart()` and `PathPart()` traverse their string arguments (`rom/dos/filepart.c:63–81`; `pathpart.c:53–72`); `AddPart()` reads both strings and writes the destination buffer (`addpart.c:80-125`). `THUNK_DPTR` translates guest offsets through `m68k_to_host_or_shadow()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.h:38`); fallback `THUNK_D` does not. Thus a no-prototype regeneration passes guest offsets as host pointers. The buffer APIs write or read through those invalid host addresses, while the path APIs can read from invalid addresses and `AddPart()` can also write through one, so calls can fail or access the wrong host memory.

**Trigger and consequence:** regenerate thunk source with a valid FD directory but without the optional NDK prototype directory, then call one of the affected DOS vectors with a guest buffer. The generated wrapper does not translate D2 and native DOS receives an invalid host pointer. **Affected configuration:** users of this documented no-prototype regeneration mode; the checked-in generated file is unaffected and contains correct buffer translations (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1106–1132`). The normal m68kemu build compiles that checked-in file and does not run this generator (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:33–39`), so no defect in the current build output is claimed. **Confidence:** high for the shadowed map and emission behavior; no generated output or DOS call was executed. Merge the two override maps or make the later graphics entries additive. Source-only.


<a id="ek10212"></a>
### EK10212 — Efika ELF section alignment zero collapses the load destination to address zero.

`load_hunk()` uses `sh->addralign` directly in its alignment expressions for both section-placement cursors (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/elf.c:82-104`). ELF permits `sh_addralign` 0 to mean that no alignment is required. With zero, the read-only expression `((ptr_ro + addralign - 1) & ~(addralign - 1))` becomes `(ptr_ro - 1) & 0`, and the writable expression also masks its computed address to zero. The function records that zero in `sh->addr`, then copies a non-NOBITS section there with `read_block()` or clears a NOBITS section with `bzero()` (`:106-119`). The selected OpenFirmware loader checks only ELF magic, ET_REL and EM_PPC before processing the section headers (`:59-76,231-255`); it does not normalize this valid alignment value. In-tree comparison supports the expected semantics: the selected ARM Efika loader treats zero as one (`bootstrap/elfloader.c:82-89`), and the AArch64 Raspi loader explicitly comments that zero means no constraint before normalizing it to one (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/elf.c:156-162,220-225`).

**Trigger and scope:** the CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware loader processes a structurally valid ELF32 PPC relocatable image containing a nonempty `SHF_ALLOC` section with `sh_addralign == 0`. Bootstrap passes the loaded kernel or module image to `load_elf_file()` (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/bootstrap.c:48-86,269-286`). The format value is valid; this finding is distinct from EK9113's malformed or truncated section-table/extent case. **Effect:** section copying or BSS clearing targets address zero instead of the current placement cursor, potentially faulting or overwriting low memory and preventing boot/module loading. **Confidence:** high for the arithmetic and subsequent zero-address write; no checked-in Efika ELF artifact was available to establish whether the normal image contains such a section. Treat zero as one before aligning. No ELF image, boot, memory write or build was exercised. Source-only.


<a id="ek10213"></a>
### EK10213 — m68k Pack/UnpackStructureTags reads guest pack-table words in host byte order.

The generated Utility thunks pass `packTable` through `THUNK_PTR()` directly to native `PackStructureTags()` and `UnpackStructureTags()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:7021-7038`). `THUNK_PTR()` resolves the guest address to the backing byte array without converting its contents (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.h:37`; `m68kemu_intern.h:115-124`). The public pack format defines `PACK_STARTTABLE`, `PACK_ENTRY`, and control/offset fields as 32-bit `ULONG` words (`compiler/include/utility/pack.h:20-26,56-67`). The native implementations dereference those words directly to read the base tag, sentinels, control bits, tag offsets, and structure offsets (`rom/utility/packstructuretags.c:69-90,123-142`; `unpackstructuretags.c:71-100`). In contrast, the emulator's `m68k_read32()` explicitly assembles guest bytes in big-endian order, and the wrappers convert the TagItem list through that reader before calling the native functions (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_intern.h:141-147`; `m68kemu_shadow.c:139-163`).

**Trigger and consequence:** m68k guest code calls either API with a pack table containing ordinary non-byte-symmetric tag/control words on a little-endian host. Native `ULONG` loads see each guest word byte-reversed; the base tag and entry fields no longer describe the guest table. Pack operations can miss requested tags or select the wrong field/offset; unpack operations can read from the wrong offset or skip the intended entries. There is a second guest-boundary mismatch after table decoding: PackStructureTags writes selected UBYTE/UWORD/ULONG fields by native typed stores into the guest `pack` buffer (`rom/utility/packstructuretags.c:99-151`). On little-endian hosts, multi-byte values are stored in host byte order, so a guest structure field such as a 16-bit value `0x1234` is left as bytes `34 12` instead of `12 34`. UnpackStructureTags likewise reads multi-byte fields with native typed loads (`rom/utility/unpackstructuretags.c:107-148`), interpreting guest big-endian fields in host order; this is an independent wrong-value consequence from its separately tracked native-width output-pointer write (EK9203). **Affected configuration:** an explicitly selected `kernel-m68kemu-library` on a 64-bit little-endian host, when guest software calls either Utility vector with its m68k-encoded pack table. The module is optional; no in-tree m68k guest caller was established. **Confidence:** high for raw guest-memory forwarding, the word-based public table format, and direct native word reads; no guest call or runtime output was exercised. Decode each guest table word to host `ULONG` representation before invoking native Utility code, or provide a guest-endian-aware table walker. Source-only.


<a id="ek10214"></a>
### EK10214 — Parthenope reports an RDB partition one block shorter than its geometry.

The Parthenope firmware reader stores
`(apg_HighCyl - apg_LowCyl + 1) * apg_BlockPerTrack * apg_Surfaces - 1`
in `disk_partition_t.size` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/rdb.c:131-133`). The local structure documents `size` as the **number of blocks** (`src/uboot.h:81-87`), so the inclusive cylinder count and geometry product already give the count; subtracting one makes every valid nonempty partition one block shorter. Parthenope passes this record to the external U-Boot `ext2fs_set_blk_dev_full()` callback (`src/ext2.c:74-78`), which supplies the resulting partition length to the ext2 mount path. The DOS and SFS backends use the start and block size but do not consume this length field in their local code.

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicitly built Sam440 Parthenope bootloader reads an RDB partition with a nonzero, representable geometry product. Its partition descriptor advertises one fewer block than the inclusive geometry specifies; a one-block partition is reported with size zero. The selected ext2 integration therefore receives an undersized length, though the exact last-block behavior depends on the external U-Boot callback. DOS/SFS sector access is not claimed to use this field. **Affected configuration:** explicit `parthenope-sam440` firmware target; the Sam440 aggregate's Parthenope dependency is commented out, so this is not claimed for every Sam440 build. **Confidence:** high for the arithmetic and field contract, medium for filesystem-level consequences because the callback implementation is external. Use the full inclusive block count. No RDB, filesystem, boot, or build was exercised; source-only.

<a id="ek10215"></a>
### EK10215 — RISC-V unmapping a large 2 MiB-leaf range can exhaust the fixed page-table pool and halt the kernel.

The OpenSBI RISC-V mapper installs a 2 MiB leaf whenever virtual and physical addresses are 2 MiB aligned and at least 2 MiB remains (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_mmu.c:149-196`). The unmapper instead advances in 4 KiB increments and calls `krnPTWalk()` for each page (`:200-220`). When that walk encounters a 2 MiB leaf, it calls `krnPTSplit()` to allocate a 4 KiB leaf table (`:84-109`); each split consumes one page from the static 128-page pool, and `krnPTAlloc()` loops forever in `wfi` once the pool is exhausted (`:34-57`). A 256 MiB aligned range mapped as 2 MiB leaves requires 128 such splits to unmap, while the mapping itself already requires the root table and at least one intermediate table. The pool therefore exhausts before the unmap finishes. The pool allocator has no reclamation path, and the operation halts rather than returning the documented-style failure value.

**Trigger and consequence:** a caller maps a 256 MiB or larger aligned range with `KrnMapGlobal()` and later unmaps it through `KrnUnmapGlobal()` while the pool has fewer than 128 free pages; a 256 MiB mapping alone exceeds the available capacity because its root and intermediate tables are already allocated. The unmap can permanently halt the OpenSBI RISC-V kernel partway through clearing the mapping. **Affected configuration:** `riscv64-opensbi`, for use of the exported mapping API with a range covered by 2 MiB leaves. The repository-wide C-call search found no checked-in `KrnUnmapGlobal()` caller, so no current in-tree trigger is claimed; the API is exposed to external clients. **Confidence:** high for the walker, allocation count, and exhaustion behavior; conditional on an external caller requesting the described unmap. Avoid allocating one L0 table per 2 MiB leaf during teardown, or fail without halting when the page-table pool cannot satisfy the split. No mapping, unmapping, or boot was run; source-only.
<a id="ek10216"></a>
### EK10216 — PC Multiboot2 accepts a truncated EFI64 tag as a firmware pointer.

The selected PC Multiboot2 bootstrap walks records using the overall handoff pointer but never checks `total_size`, per-tag bounds, or the minimum size for a known tag (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/multiboot2.c:120-150,183-195`). In an x86-64 build, the `MB2_TAG_EFI64` case reads the 64-bit `pointer` field even when the record declares only the 8-byte common header. The next tag is 8-byte aligned, so with an end tag immediately following, the read uses that end tag's `type` and `size` fields as the alleged pointer. The parser publishes any resulting nonzero value as `KRN_EFISystemTable` (`:206-211`). The selected x86-64 PC image includes the EFI resource (`arch/x86_64-pc/boot/mmakefile.src:62`), whose `efi_Init()` trusts the boot tag and dereferences `EFIBase->System->Hdr` before validating its signature (`arch/all-native/efi/efi_init.c:67-82`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an x86-64 PC Multiboot2 handoff contains an `MB2_TAG_EFI64` record with `size == 8` followed by the required end tag. The parser reads across the record boundary, treats the end-tag bytes as an EFI system-table address, and hands that bogus pointer to the selected EFI resource; EFI initialization then reads through it and can fail or fault instead of rejecting the malformed tag. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC boot through the selected Multiboot2 bootstrap with malformed external bootloader metadata. The checkout contains no producer of such a record. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked field read and selected consumer path; conditional on a truncated external record. Validate each tag's declared extent and type-specific minimum size against the handoff's `total_size` before reading fields. No boot record or EFI resource was exercised; source-only.



<a id="ek10217"></a>
### EK10217 — i386-PC task dispatcher never delivers pending task exceptions

Exec sets TF_EXCEPT when a task receives a signal covered by its exception mask, and SetExcept() also sets the flag when the new mask matches already received signals; both paths request rescheduling (rom/exec/signal.c:306-342; rom/exec/setexcept.c:68-83). The generic scheduler treats TF_EXCEPT as an unconditional reason to schedule away from the current task (rom/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:28-57). Its scheduling syscall reaches the selected CPU dispatcher through core_SysCall() (rom/kernel/kernel_intr.c:70-80), and interrupt exits use the same cpu_Switch()/cpu_Dispatch() pair when scheduling is requested (:30-53).

The i386-PC manifest selects arch/i386-pc/kernel/kernel_cpu.c for the pc-i386 kernel target (arch/i386-pc/kernel/mmakefile.src:12-34). In cpu_Dispatch(), the task is dequeued by core_Dispatch(), but the only exception-delivery block is commented out as a TODO; the function proceeds directly to restoring the task context (kernel_cpu.c:25-53). core_Dispatch() does not call Exec's Exception(). By comparison, the selected x86-64, ARM, AArch64, and Sam440 dispatchers call Exception() after choosing a task. Exception() clears TF_EXCEPT, drains matching received exception signals, and invokes tc_ExceptCode when it is set (rom/exec/exception.c:54-81).
