**Trigger and consequence:** on an i386-PC kernel, a task with tc_ExceptCode configured receives a signal enabled by SetExcept(), or SetExcept() enables a signal already pending. Exec forces a reschedule, but dispatch resumes the task without invoking its exception callback or clearing TF_EXCEPT. The exception remains undelivered. Since `core_Schedule()` bypasses its ready-list/priority/quantum early returns whenever TF_EXCEPT remains set, each later scheduling point forces another switch; if this is the only ready task, it is immediately selected again without the flag being cleared. This is repeated scheduling overhead, not an in-dispatch infinite loop. The explicit test-exec-public target's `exceptiontest` provides a direct maintained trigger (`developer/debug/test/exec/mmakefile.src:19-36; developer/debug/test/exec/exceptiontest.c:38-53`): it installs a callback, enables a signal as an exception, signals the current task with that signal, then prints `s`, which only the callback assigns. On this dispatcher path the callback is skipped, so the test's callback result remains at its static zero initialization. That test target is not in the default aggregate. **Affected configuration:** the pc-i386 kernel target built from the i386-PC manifest; arch/i386-pc/boot/mmakefile.src currently comments out the aggregate boot dependency, so this finding does not claim the default aggregate boots this target. **Confidence:** high for the missing call and its consequences in the selected scheduler path. No exception signal, kernel, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10218"></a>
### EK10218 — Concurrent public BOOPSI class registration can publish duplicate class IDs

`MakeClass()` checks for an existing public class ID with `FindClass()` while holding only a shared class-list lock, then releases that lock before returning the new class (`rom/intuition/makeclass.c:115-125,170-177`). Publication is a separate `AddClass()` call. `AddClass()` takes the exclusive list lock but unconditionally inserts the class without rechecking its ID (`rom/intuition/addclass.c:60-63`); its own documentation explicitly says duplicate names are unprotected and make system behavior undefined (`:32-35`). Two clients creating the same public ID can both observe it absent in `MakeClass()` and then both insert their classes. `FindClass()` walks from the list head and returns the first matching ID (`rom/intuition/findclass.c:69-89`), so subsequent lookup can select either registered implementation according to insertion order, while objects or subclasses created from the other class retain a different class pointer.

**Trigger and consequence:** two independently scheduled class-registration paths call `MakeClass()` for the same non-NULL `classID` before either calls `AddClass()`. Both `MakeClass()` calls succeed and both later publish; name lookup becomes order-dependent, and callers can instantiate or subclass a different class from the one another registrant expects. **Affected configuration:** Intuition/BOOPSI clients on all targets; concurrency can arise from simultaneously starting libraries or class modules with a colliding public ID. No in-tree duplicate-ID pair was established, so this is conditional on client ID collision and overlapping registration. **Confidence:** high for the missing atomic duplicate check and unconditional insertion; conditional for occurrence and downstream impact. Make registration atomic with respect to duplicate IDs or reject an already-present ID in `AddClass()`. No class-registration race or application was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10221"></a>
### EK10221 — 64-bit TLSF pooled allocations around 126 GiB index past the bucket tables

On 64-bit builds, TLSF defines `MAX_FLI` as 37 and `REAL_FLI` as 31, then sizes both `slbitmap` and the first dimension of `matrix` with `REAL_FLI` (`rom/kernel/tlsf.c:35-49,111-125`). `MAPPING_SEARCH()` rounds a request to a first-level class and subtracts `FLI_OFFSET` (`:166-180`). For a rounded request at or above `2^37 - (2^31 - 1)` bytes, that calculation yields `fl == 31`; `FIND_SUITABLE_BLOCK()` immediately reads `slbitmap[fl]` and can also read `matrix[fl][sl]`, with no range check (`:184-209`). The file's stated 64-bit limit is 128 GiB, but this class-rounding boundary is reached earlier, at approximately 126 GiB.

The request can reach this code through a managed pool: `CreatePool()` obtains a managed `MemHeaderExt` using `AllocMemHeader()` (`rom/exec/createpool.c:134-143`), which inherits the source header's allocator callbacks and initializes TLSF state (`rom/exec/memory.c:898-956`). `AllocPooled()` forwards its `IPTR memSize` directly to `mhe_Alloc()` for managed pools (`rom/exec/allocpooled.c:32-33,72-83`); it does not first narrow the request to `ULONG`. `tlsf_malloc()` performs the class lookup before checking whether a suitable block exists (`rom/kernel/tlsf.c:489-513`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a 64-bit client requests roughly 126 GiB or more from a pool backed by a TLSF-managed memory header. The allocator reads beyond its first-level bucket arrays before it can return an ordinary allocation failure; depending on adjacent state, it can also derive a bogus block pointer or take an undefined-width bitmap shift. The direct source-supported defect is the out-of-bounds bucket lookup; subsequent allocator failure or state damage depends on the adjacent values. **Affected configuration:** 64-bit targets using TLSF-backed managed memory pools, including x86-64 PC (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:74,374`) and RISC-V64 OpenSBI (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:860-870`), where TLSF is the default unless `notlsf` is supplied. Ordinary non-managed pools and requests below the bucket boundary are not affected by this finding. A source census of 503 pooled-allocation call expressions found no literal near-boundary request; dynamic size expressions have not all been traced. **Confidence:** high for the index calculation and unchecked table access; conditional on a caller requesting a boundary-sized block from a TLSF-backed pool. Reject or safely fail requests whose mapped first-level index is outside `REAL_FLI` before indexing either table. No allocation, pool operation, build, or runtime behavior was exercised; source-only.

<a id="ek10222"></a>
### EK10222 — 32-bit TLSF class rounding wraps large requests into zero or invalid buckets

On a 32-bit target, `IPTR` is unsigned 32-bit and TLSF uses `MAX_FLI == 32` (`compiler/include/exec/types.h:79-86`; `rom/kernel/tlsf.c:35-49`). `tlsf_malloc()` first rounds the request, then `MAPPING_SEARCH()` adds a class-rounding mask to that value without checking overflow (`:166-180,489-505`). For example, a valid ULONG-aligned request of `0xfd000010` bytes remains unchanged through `ROUNDUP()`. Its first-level mask is `0x03ffffff`; the 32-bit `tr = size + tmp` wraps to `0x0100000f`, maps to `fl == 18, sl == 0`, and the rounded request written back through `*r = tr & ~tmp` becomes zero. The zero-size early return has already happened, before this mapping.

A managed pool makes the bad size survive the no-block path: `CreatePool()` uses `AllocMemHeader()` when backed by a managed header (`rom/exec/createpool.c:129-143`); TLSF's pool initializer installs an autogrow callback and a minimum 4096-byte puddle (`rom/kernel/tlsf.c:1419-1435`). When the first lookup has no matching class-18 block, `tlsf_malloc()` computes its autogrow request from the now-zero size, adds a small puddle, and repeats `MAPPING_SEARCH()` with zero (`:517-545`). The retry then searches for a zero-byte block, and the normal split/return path can mark a block of size zero busy and return its address (`:550-590`).

**Trigger and consequence:** on a 32-bit TLSF-backed managed pool, a client requests `0xfd000010` bytes (or another aligned size in the wrapping top range), and the pool can successfully autogrow a normal puddle. The allocator can return a non-NULL pointer backed by a zero-size block instead of failing the unfulfillable request; subsequent use of the requested extent exceeds the returned allocation, and TLSF's free-size accounting is not reduced by the split. **Affected configuration:** 32-bit targets using TLSF-backed memory pools, including i386-PC (`arch/i386-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:175,320-322`) and ARM-native (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_startup.c:279-293`) when TLSF is enabled; `notlsf` paths are excluded. No in-tree near-limit pooled request was found in the source census. **Confidence:** high for the unsigned class-rounding wrap and its invalid mapped values; the zero-size allocation requires the selected lookup/autogrow path to obtain a free block, while the negative-shift subcase has compiler-dependent execution because it invokes undefined behavior. Reject requests whose rounded mapping overflows or becomes zero before searching or growing the pool. No allocation, pool operation, build, or runtime behavior was exercised; source-only.

<a id="ek10224"></a>
### EK10224 — Failed detached-stream duplication silently starts without inherited I/O

The `detach.o` startup routine duplicates the launching process's input and output handles and converts the copied locks back into file handles (`compiler/startup/detach.c:83-88`). Neither result is checked before both are passed as `NP_Input` and `NP_Output` to `CreateNewProc()` (`:90-108`). `DupLockFromFH()` can return `BNULL` when its filesystem copy action fails (`rom/dos/duplockfromfh.c:49-57`), and `OpenFromLock()` can fail when given a null lock, when allocating a filehandle, or when the filesystem action fails (`rom/dos/openfromlock.c:51-80`). The `OpenFromLock()` contract explicitly says that on error its non-null input lock must still be freed (`:26-28`). Because detach nests `DupLockFromFH()` directly inside `OpenFromLock()` and does not retain the temporary lock, a failure inside `OpenFromLock()` after a successful lock duplication leaks that lock. `CreateNewProc()` explicitly accepts `BNULL` input/output handles as NIL and still proceeds with process creation; its documentation states that `NP_Arguments` will not work when `NP_Input` is `BNULL` (`rom/dos/createnewproc.c:79-83`). Its argument injection is conditional on both `pr_Arguments` and `pr_CIS` being nonzero (`:516-523`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a CLI-launched program linked with `detach.o` encounters a failed input or output handle conversion, while later `CreateNewProc()` setup succeeds. The child starts with NIL for that stream instead of the inherited handle; if input conversion failed, its startup arguments are not injected into the child input stream. When `DupLockFromFH()` succeeded but `OpenFromLock()` then failed, the duplicated lock is also lost without the required `UnLock()`. The successfully converted other stream is passed to the child; its cleanup is handled by the detach handshake, so no leak is claimed for that case. **Affected configuration:** programs explicitly linked with the `detach.o` startup object and launched from a CLI; ordinary `startup.o` programs are unaffected. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked results, NIL-handle acceptance, skipped argument injection, and lock ownership contract; occurrence requires a filesystem or allocation failure during handle duplication/open. Check each result, retain and free an unconsumed lock on conversion failure, and unwind successful handles if detachment is aborted. This is distinct from EK689's successful filehandle duplicates leaked when `CreateNewProc()` itself fails. No process, handle failure, or runtime operation was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek10223"></a>
### EK10223 — TLSF bitmap masks use undefined signed left shifts

`FIND_SUITABLE_BLOCK()` forms both bitmap masks by left-shifting `~0` (`rom/kernel/tlsf.c:188-205`). The unsuffixed literal `0` has type `int`; integer promotion leaves `~0` as signed `int` with value -1 on the selected two's-complement targets. The shift occurs before the result is combined with the unsigned bitmap, so assigning the final expression to `IPTR bitmap_tmp` does not make the shift unsigned. C defines a left shift of a negative signed operand as undefined behavior. The first mask is evaluated on every call; the second is evaluated when the first-level sub-bitmap has no matching entry. Both call sites of this helper are in `tlsf_malloc()` (`:508,542`).

The same file has a second signed-shift case in `SetBit()` and `ClrBit()`: each uses `1 << (nr & 31)` before combining it with an `ULONG` bitmap (`:144-152`). `MAX_SLI` is 32 and the mapping routines produce second-level indices in the range 0..31 (`:35-36,154-183`), so valid bucket updates can shift signed `int` 1 into bit 31. For example, a free block with `GET_SIZE(b) == 1008` maps to `fl == 3, sl == 31` (`MS(1008) == 9`; `1008 >> 4 == 63`). The helpers are used on ordinary free-list insertion/removal paths (`:236-250,453-484,1048-1058`). This is the same undefined signed-bitmap-shift class as the search-mask expression, but has a distinct source expression and bucket-update path; use unsigned operands in both search-mask shifts and both bit-update helpers.

**Trigger and consequence:** any nonzero allocation request that reaches TLSF's bucket search evaluates `(~0 << *sl)`, including the zero shift case. The C implementation therefore has undefined behavior during ordinary block lookup; the compiler is not required to preserve the intended all-ones mask, so allocation selection and failure behavior are not portable or source-guaranteed. This report does not claim a particular observed compiler output or a specific runtime corruption. **Affected configuration:** builds that use `rom/kernel/tlsf.c` for managed allocations, including default TLSF on i386-PC, x86-64 PC, and ARM-native; `notlsf` configurations are excluded. **Confidence:** high that the source expression shifts a signed negative value; the concrete effect depends on compiler/version/optimization. Form masks with an explicitly unsigned type, such as `~(ULONG)0`, before shifting. No build, allocator operation, or runtime behavior was exercised; source-only.


<a id="ek10226"></a>
### EK10226 — OpenSBI RISC-V runs relocated boot modules without synchronizing instruction fetch

`krnLoadModule()` copies each allocatable ELF section into the bump-allocated RAM range and applies relocations by writing the destination sections (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_elf.c:258-405`). After `krnLoadPackage()` succeeds, startup changes the module range's page permissions with `krnMMUSetPerms()` and passes that range to Exec's resident scan (`kernel_startup.c:813-829,928`). The permission helper executes `sfence.vma`, which synchronizes address translation, not instruction fetch (`kernel_mmu.c:264-279`). Exec later invokes package initializers through `InitCode(RTF_SINGLETASK, 0)` and then `InitCode(RTF_COLDSTART, 0)` (`kernel_startup.c:1044-1048`; `rom/exec/initcode.c:68-96`). No `fence.i` or SBI remote-fence call lies between the section writes/relocations and that first execution.

This matters on RISC-V implementations whose instruction-fetch stream is not coherent with data stores. The RISC-V specification does not guarantee that a hart's subsequent instruction fetch will see preceding stores to instruction memory until that hart executes `FENCE.I` ([Zifencei specification](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/zifencei.html)). The selected OpenSBI Exec port provides the needed firmware path: `CacheClearE_SBI()`/`CacheClearU_SBI()` call `sbi_remote_fence_i()` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/exec/cpu_init.c:40-64`; helper selection and dispatch in `arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_sbi.h:142-160`), and `cpu_Init()` installs those overrides when SBI RFENCE or legacy FENCE.I is available (`cpu_init.c:196-223`). However, those cache-clear functions are registered during Exec initialization and are not called to synchronize the already-loaded boot package before its first resident initializers run. Startup calls the single-task initializer before cold start (`kernel_startup.c:1044-1048`). `SetFunction()` does not incidentally issue a cache clear on RISC-V: its call is guarded by `__AROS_USE_FULLJMP` (`rom/exec/setfunction.c:101-108`), which is not defined for the selected RISC-V target. `krnMMUSetPerms()`'s `sfence.vma` is not a substitute.

**Trigger and consequence:** boot an OpenSBI RISC-V64 configuration with a noncoherent instruction-fetch path and a boot package containing relocated modules. The initializers may be fetched using stale or otherwise unsynchronized instruction bytes, so a module can fail or behave incorrectly during cold start. The affected configuration is the explicit `boot-opensbi-riscv64` flow when it supplies `aros-bsp.pkg` to a system requiring instruction-fetch synchronization (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/boot/mmakefile.src:114-120,136-165`); the parent aggregate edge is commented, and coherent implementations are unaffected. **Confidence:** high that the selected loader writes executable sections and reaches resident initialization without an instruction-fence call; the stale-fetch manifestation is architecture/cache-state dependent and was not reproduced. Synchronize the loaded module range before the resident scan or before the first module initializer executes. No package, boot, cache operation, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek869"></a>
### EK869 — Amiga SAD and serial.device can consume the same UART input

On the m68k-Amiga kernel, `KrnObtainInput()` returns success without taking ownership of or masking the low-level debug UART (`arch/m68k-amiga/kernel/obtaininput.c:14-23`). The generic `Debug()` entry calls `InternalDebug()`, which checks this result and then polls `RawMayGetChar()` in its command-input loop (`rom/exec/debug.c:54-59`; `rom/exec/debug_internal.c:37-46,425-435`). The selected Amiga `KrnMayGetChar()` delegates to `DebugMayGetChar()`, which checks `SERDATR_RBF` and reads the byte from `SERDATR` (`arch/m68k-amiga/kernel/maygetchar.c:14-23`; `arch/m68k-amiga/boot/debug.c:39-50`).

If the optional Amiga serial HIDD is active, opening unit 0 through the optional `serial.device` initializes its HIDD unit and installs an `INTB_RBF` server. That server reads `SERDATR` and forwards the byte to the serial.device callback (`workbench/devs/serial/serial_init.c:170-174`; `arch/m68k-amiga/hidd/serial/SerialUnitClass.c:113-122,145-176`). `InternalDebug()` does not mask interrupts around its polling loop, so an arriving byte can be consumed by the serial HIDD server before SAD's next poll sees it. SAD then continues waiting for command input that has been diverted to serial.device. `KrnReleaseInput()` is also a no-op (`arch/m68k-amiga/kernel/releaseinput.c:14-23`), so this target does not implement the documented handback operation either.

**Trigger and consequence:** enter SAD from ordinary task context with interrupts enabled while the optional `serial.device` unit 0 has installed its receive server; a byte arriving between SAD polls may be delivered to serial.device instead, leaving SAD without that command byte and potentially waiting for more input. The source proves the competing reads and missing arbitration; which consumer wins a particular byte depends on interrupt timing. **Affected configuration:** m68k-Amiga with the kernel's generic SAD and both optional `amiga-m68k-hidd-serial` and `workbench-devs-serial` targets built, with serial.device unit 0 open. Both modules' parent aggregate edges are commented in this revision, so no default-package occurrence is claimed. **Confidence:** high for the ownership gap and competing receive paths; the precise byte-routing outcome is timing-dependent and was not reproduced. Acquire exclusive debug-input ownership before entering SAD and restore the serial receive path on release. No debugger, serial device, interrupt, or build was run; source-only; see the coverage ledger.


<a id="ek10227"></a>
### EK10227 — Moira division overflow paths can leave the carry flag set

The selected `m68kemu` configuration uses `MOIRA_MIMIC_MUSASHI=true` (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/MoiraConfig.h:84`). Its signed and unsigned word-divide helpers set V on quotient overflow but do not clear C (`MoiraALU_cpp.h:777-779,801-804`); their `execDivsMusashi()` and `execDivuMusashi()` callers write the returned dividend without a later flag update (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:4276-4305,4404-4434`). The selected 64-bit-dividend signed and unsigned DIVL helpers have the same omission in their quotient-overflow branches (`MoiraALU_cpp.h:896-905,927-936`), reached through `execDivlMusashi()` (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:4600-4634`). Their successful paths explicitly clear C. Motorola's M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual specifies C as always cleared for DIVS/DIVU and that detected overflow sets V while leaving operands unaffected ([NXP-hosted Motorola manual, pp. 194-201](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/M68000PM.pdf)). N/Z are undefined on overflow and are not part of this finding.

**Trigger and consequence:** begin with C=1 and execute a quotient-overflowing divide: for example DIVS.W or DIVU.W with D0=`0x00010000` and source word 1; signed or unsigned 64-bit DIVL with dividend `0x0000000100000000` and divisor 1. The helper sets V and preserves the dividend/destination as appropriate, but C incorrectly remains set. **Affected configuration:** the explicitly built `m68kemu.library` using the checked-in Musashi-compatible Moira configuration; the library is not selected by the normal ROM aggregate. **Confidence:** high for the helper branches, selected callers and documented carry behavior; no guest instruction was run. Clear C on every quotient-overflow path. No build or runtime operation was performed; source-only; see the [ALU coverage entry](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1768).


<a id="ek10228"></a>
### EK10228 — Moira's dump-number-format setter changes instruction formatting instead

The public `Moira::setDumpNumberFormat()` inline setter passes `instrStyle` to `setNumberFormat()` (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/Moira.h:166-168`). The class keeps a separate `dataStyle` (`Moira.h:39-40`), and each `dump8/16/24/32()` routine constructs its `StrWriter` with `dataStyle` (`MoiraDasm_cpp.h:71-113`). Consequently, calling the dump setter changes instruction disassembly's number format and leaves all data dump output unchanged. This is not an invalid-argument or formatting-contract ambiguity: `setDasmNumberFormat()` separately targets `instrStyle` (`Moira.h:157-158`), while dump indentation correctly targets `dataStyle` (`:169-170`). The selected configuration enables disassembly (`MoiraConfig.h:59-61`). A search found no checked-in caller of `setDumpNumberFormat()` in the AROS bridge or Moira runner, so the defect is reachable through the public C++ Moira interface but no current in-tree user impact is claimed.

**Trigger and consequence:** a Moira client calls `setDumpNumberFormat()` and then requests a data dump. The dump continues using its previous number format, while instruction disassembly uses the newly supplied format. **Affected configuration:** consumers of the Moira class built with disassembly enabled; the AROS `m68kemu` bridge does not expose or call this setter in the checked-in sources, so impact there depends on a future or external C++ client. **Confidence:** high for the setter/consumer mismatch; no output was generated at runtime. Pass `dataStyle` to `setNumberFormat()` in this setter. Source-only; see the [Moira interface coverage entry](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1762).


<a id="ek10229"></a>
### EK10229 — An ordinary guest read at the m68kemu return sentinel stops emulation

`AROSMoira::read16()` treats every read at `SENTINEL_ADDR` (`0x00DEAD00`) as the emulator's return: it clears `ctx->running` and returns a fabricated STOP instruction (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:14,141-151`). This virtual callback is used for both program and data reads; it does not know whether the CPU is fetching an instruction or reading guest data (`MoiraDataflow_cpp.h:353-405`). The sentinel is inside the allocated 32 MiB guest arena (`m68kemu_intern.h:20`; `m68kemu_memory.c:25-44`). It is also within the heap's available address interval, which starts at `0x10400` and extends to `mem_size - stack_size`, with no sentinel reservation (`m68kemu_intern.h:25-26`; `m68kemu_memory.c:40-45`). The actual sentinel return address is pushed on the guest stack at startup (`m68kemu_moira.cpp:338-342`), but the callback does not distinguish that instruction fetch from an ordinary data read.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated guest performs a word read whose effective address is `0x00DEAD00` (or a long read beginning there). The callback marks the guest run complete; after the current instruction returns, `M68KEmu_Execute()` exits its run loop and returns the current D0 value, even though the guest did not return. **Affected configuration:** explicit `m68kemu.library` guest execution; no default-package inclusion is claimed. **Confidence:** high for the unconditional sentinel check, shared program/data read hook, and address's inclusion in guest RAM/heap; no guest access was run. Reserve the sentinel outside guest-accessible memory or detect it only when the CPU is fetching the return instruction. Source-only; see the [Moira wrapper review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8557).


<a id="ek10230"></a>
### EK10230 — The m68k disk-library loader silently truncates function tables at 1,000 entries

`M68KEmu_LoadM68KLibrary()` counts function-table entries until it sees `M68K_FUNCTABLE_END`, but stops scanning once `numFuncs` reaches 1,000 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_m68klib.c:127-134`). It does not distinguish finding the terminator from reaching that cap. Any nonempty table therefore proceeds as a successful load, and the loader allocates and builds jump slots only for those first 1,000 functions (`:136-166`). If the table contains more entries, guest vectors at indices 1,000 and above are left without the corresponding generated JMP slot even though `OpenLibrary()` returns the base as usable (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:77-82`). A call through such a vector can execute unrelated guest-memory bytes from below the allocated jump table instead of the function address.

**Trigger and consequence:** the disk fallback loads an AUTOINIT library whose function table contains more than 1,000 entries. The loader returns a base after silently building only the first 1,000 vectors; guest use of a higher vector jumps through an uninitialized/non-table address and can execute incorrect guest code or fail. **Affected configuration:** explicit hosted `m68kemu.library` builds using disk-library fallback. No checked-in disk library with more than 1,000 vectors was identified; reachability depends on the loaded guest library. **Confidence:** high for the cap, missing terminator check and truncated returned table; medium for practical impact because no in-tree library with this size was established. Reject the table when the cap is reached without seeing its terminator, or support the full table. No guest library or vector call was run; source-only; see the [disk-library loader review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1791).


<a id="ek10231"></a>
### EK10231 — Moira misses overflow for signed 32-bit DIVSL.L INT32_MIN divided by minus one

The selected M68040 opcode table enables DIVL and the AROS configuration selects the Musashi-compatible implementation (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/MoiraInit_cpp.h:883-886`; `MoiraConfig.h:84`). For the signed DIVSL.L 32-bit-dividend form, `execDivlMusashi()` reads the low dividend register and calls `divlsMusashi<Word>()` (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:4616-4623`). That helper calculates the signed quotient in `i64` but, for `S == Word`, unconditionally sets V=0 and C=0 without checking whether the quotient fits in signed 32 bits (`MoiraALU_cpp.h:878-888`). The caller then writes both returned remainder and quotient registers without checking V (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:4616-4623`). Motorola's M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual defines DIVSL.L with a 32-bit dividend and 32-bit quotient/remainder and says overflow occurs when the quotient exceeds a signed 32-bit integer; when overflow is detected, V is set and operands are unchanged ([NXP-hosted Motorola manual, pp. 194-197](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/M68000PM.pdf)).

**Trigger and consequence:** execute signed DIVSL.L with the 32-bit dividend `0x80000000` and divisor `0xffffffff` (−1), using distinct quotient and remainder destination registers. The mathematical quotient is +2,147,483,648, outside signed 32-bit range. Moira leaves V clear and writes the quotient/remainder pair, instead of reporting overflow and leaving the destination registers unchanged. **Affected configuration:** the explicitly built `m68kemu.library` on its selected M68040 path; m68kemu is not part of the normal ROM aggregate. **Confidence:** high for the selected dispatch, missing range check and documented overflow rule; no guest instruction was run. Check the quotient range before writing the destination registers. This is distinct from EK10159's 64-bit signed host-division overflow and EK10227's carry-flag omission on detected overflow. No build or runtime operation was performed; source-only; see the [DIVL selection and arithmetic review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8648).


<a id="ek10232"></a>
### EK10232 — M68040 CAS and CAS2 omit the failed-compare destination writeback

The selected AROS Moira bridge fixes the emulated CPU model to M68040 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:317`). Its selected CAS handlers are registered for byte, word and long sizes, and CAS2 for word and long sizes (`MoiraInit_cpp.h:673-699`). On a failed CAS comparison, `execCas()` updates the compare data register and advances to prefetch, without writing the memory destination (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:1433-1479`). On a failed CAS2 comparison, `execCas2()` writes the compare registers and prefetches, but does not write either memory operand (`:1486-1549`). Motorola's M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual states that on an M68040 failed comparison writes the destination operand (or CAS2 destination 1) back to memory to complete the locked access; the instructions use locked/read-modify-write transfers ([NXP-hosted manual, pp. 169-171](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/M68000PRM.pdf)).

This omission is observable through the selected bridge's custom-chip write callback. A mismatching word CAS to `$DFF02A` (`VPOSW`) should write the read destination value back; `write16()` routes that address to `customWrite16()`, which updates the emulated frame/vertical-position state (`m68kemu_moira.cpp:69-82,161-168`). The CAS failure branch never reaches that callback. Ordinary RAM retains the same final data value, but the missing write transaction means mapped device state and M68040 locked-access behavior differ.

**Trigger and consequence:** guest code executes a word CAS against `$DFF02A` with a compare value that does not equal the emulated read value (zero). The compare register is updated, but the required writeback is skipped, so the VPOSW emulation does not apply the written value to `beam_lof`/`beam_v`. A failed CAS2 similarly omits its required destination-1 writeback. **Affected configuration:** explicit `m68kemu.library` execution using the selected M68040 model; the module is not in the normal ROM aggregate. **Confidence:** high for the handler branches, selected model, callback mapping and manual requirement; no guest instruction was run. Perform the M68040 failed-compare writeback on CAS and destination-1 writeback on CAS2. The bundled Musashi reference also omits this writeback and therefore does not override the processor manual. No build or runtime operation was performed; source-only; see the [Moira CAS/CAS2 coverage pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L10570).


<a id="ek10233"></a>
### EK10233 — CHK2/CMP2.B/W truncates address-register operands before range checking

The selected Moira configuration enables `MOIRA_MIMIC_MUSASHI` (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/MoiraConfig.h:84`), and the M68040 opcode table registers the shared CHK2/CMP2 byte, word, and long encoding under `Instr::CHK2` (`MoiraInit_cpp.h:723-742`). The extension word's bit 11 distinguishes CHK2 from CMP2: `execChkCmp2()` takes the CHK exception only when that bit is set (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:1722-1725`), and the disassembler emits CMP2 when it is clear (`MoiraDasm_cpp.h:733-737`). In the selected handler branch, `readR<S>(dst)` clips either a data or address register to the operation size, then sign-extends only Dn (`dst < 8`), leaving an An comparison truncated for byte and word forms (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:1693-1698`; `Moira.cpp:574-578`). The NXP-hosted Motorola reference manual specifies that byte/word An forms compare the full 32-bit An against sign-extended bounds; Dn forms compare the corresponding low-order register part ([M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual, pp. 4-82–4-83](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/M68000PM.pdf)). The alternate, unselected Moira branch reads the full register for An (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:1707-1719`), confirming that the selected branch differs. The long form is unaffected because `readR<Long>()` retains all 32 bits. This affects both the trap decision for CHK2 and the C/Z results for CMP2.

**Trigger and consequence:** with An selected, execute CHK2.B or CHK2.W using bounds 1 and 2 and A0=`0x00010001`. The handler truncates A0 to 1 and reports it in range; CHK2 with the extension trap-enable bit set therefore suppresses the required CHK exception. On the same operands, CMP2 incorrectly sets Z and clears C, instead of clearing Z and setting C for an out-of-range A0. **Affected configuration:** explicit `m68kemu.library` execution on the selected M68040/Musashi-compatible path; the module is not in the normal ROM aggregate. **Confidence:** high for the shared dispatch, `readR<S>` truncation, register-type branch, and manual rule; no guest instruction was run. Preserve the full address-register value for An checks and sign-extend only the bounds. No build or runtime operation was performed; source-only; see the [Moira CHK2/CMP2 coverage pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L10572).



<a id="ek10234"></a>
### EK10234 — M68040 CLR reads a custom-register destination before clearing it

The AROS Moira bridge selects `Model::M68040` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:317`), which uses Moira's C68020 execution core. The selected CLR handler takes the `C == Core::C68020` branch and calls `readOp()` on every destination before `writeOp()` clears it (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:1745-1765`). Motorola's instruction reference manual explicitly limits the read-before-clear behavior to MC68000/68008; the later M68020/030/040 forms clear the destination without that read ([NXP-hosted M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual, pp. 4-73–4-74](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/M68000PRM.pdf)). The bundled Musashi CLR memory handlers also write without first reading (`Runner/Musashi/m68kops.c:10417-10526`).

This extra read is observable in the selected bridge's custom-register map. A word read at `$DFF02A` routes to `customRead16(0x02A)`, whose common entry advances the emulated beam by two color clocks before returning zero through its default case (`m68kemu_moira.cpp:43-66,143-150`). The subsequent write routes to `customWrite16(0x02A, 0)`, which writes the VPOSW alias and updates the emulated field/vertical-position state (`:69-77,161-166`). Thus the selected CLR performs an unintended beam-advancing read before the write; a later VHPOSR read can observe a shifted beam position. This is a concrete bridge-visible consequence, beyond the general CPU bus-cycle mismatch.

**Trigger and consequence:** guest code executes `CLR.W $DFF02A` in an explicit `m68kemu.library` run. Moira advances the emulated beam by two color clocks during the operand read before applying the VPOSW clear, shifting subsequent emulated VHPOSR observations. **Affected configuration:** explicit m68kemu execution using the selected M68040 model; the module is not claimed to be part of the default ROM aggregate. **Confidence:** high for the selected handler, manual's model distinction, address decode, and beam callback side effect; no guest instruction was run. Use the no-read CLR path for the selected C68020/M68040 execution core. No build or runtime operation was performed; source-only; see the [Moira CLR/TST/NEG coverage pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L10595).

<a id="ek10235"></a>
### EK10235 — M68040 RTE rejects valid format-3 and format-7 frames

The AROS Moira bridge selects `Model::M68040` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:317`), which dispatches RTE through Moira's C68020 core. In `execRte()`, the selected frame parser accepts formats 0, 1, 2, and 0xB, then sends every other format to `execException(FORMAT_ERROR)` (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/MoiraExec_cpp.h:5060-5180`). It rejects valid M68040 format 3 (floating-point post-instruction) and format 7 (30-word access-error) frames, which RTE must restore and consume. Conversely, it accepts format B, which the M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual identifies as the long bus-cycle frame for MC68020/MC68030, not the M68040 frame set ([NXP-hosted M68040 User's Manual, §§8.4.4–8.4.6](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68040UM.pdf); [M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual, Figure B-12](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/M68000PRM.pdf)). An M68040 RTE should reject this foreign format, but the selected parser consumes its fields as a valid frame and resumes at its stored PC. The base M68040 manual explicitly says it does not generate or recognize format 4, so format 4 is not included in this finding.

**Trigger and consequence:** guest supervisor code executes RTE with a valid M68040 format-3/7 frame or a format-B frame on the active supervisor stack. For format 3 or 7, the selected handler enters the format-error path instead of restoring the saved state. For format B, it accepts a frame that M68040 does not recognize, consumes it, restores its SR/PC fields, and continues. **Affected configuration:** explicit `m68kemu.library` execution using the selected M68040 model; this optional module is not part of the normal ROM aggregate. **Reachability qualification:** address-error emulation is disabled (`MoiraConfig.h:44`) and the bridge's memory callbacks return zero/ignore out-of-range writes (`m68kemu_moira.cpp:130-168`), so no checked-in format-7 access-fault producer was found. The bridge's FPU handlers throw an unsupported-instruction exception (`MoiraExecFPU_cpp.h:121-187`), so no in-bridge format-3 producer was found either. No selected bus-error producer creates format B. These cases therefore require a guest-supplied or restored frame. **Confidence:** high for the parser dispatch and manual's frame definitions; medium for practical reachability in this bridge. Correct the selected M68040 format dispatch to consume formats 3/7 and reject format B. No exception frame or instruction was executed; source-only; see the [RTE format inventory reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L10617).

<a id="ek10236"></a>
### EK10236 — M68040 master-mode interrupts keep both exception frames on the master stack

The selected AROS bridge fixes Moira to `Model::M68040` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:317`), which dispatches interrupt handling through `execInterrupt<Core::C68020>()`. That handler saves the incoming SR, raises the IPL, calls `setSupervisorMode(true)`, then writes a format-0 frame and, if `reg.sr.m` is still set, a format-1 frame (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/MoiraExceptions_cpp.h:514-565`). `setSupervisorMode(true)` preserves the M bit; only `setSupervisorFlags()` changes stack banks, and it is not called to clear M here (`Moira.cpp:528-560`). As a result, the format-1 frame is pushed on the MSP too, and the live M bit remains set. M68040 interrupt processing requires the format-0 frame on the MSP, then clears M and creates the format-1 throwaway frame on the ISP with supervisor mode and the new interrupt mask; the post-exception state has M clear ([NXP-hosted M68040 User's Manual, §8.2.9](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68040UM.pdf)).

**Trigger and consequence:** Moira is in supervisor master mode (`S=1,M=1`) when an accepted interrupt reaches `execInterrupt()`. The emulator leaves the handler on the master stack with M set and places both frames there, instead of switching to the interrupt stack. Interrupt handling therefore observes the wrong active stack and SR, and RTE/frame consumption follows a state different from M68040 behavior. **Affected configuration:** Moira's selected M68040 core, including explicit `m68kemu.library` execution if its caller drives the public IPL input while master mode is active. **Reachability qualification:** repository search found no `setIPL()` caller in the selected AROS bridge, so a current in-tree interrupt trigger was not established; the issue is conditional on a Moira client injecting an interrupt. **Confidence:** high for the selected handler's stack/M-bit behavior and the manual's required transition; medium for reachability in the AROS bridge. No interrupt or instruction was run; source-only; see the [master-mode interrupt frame pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L10613).

<a id="ek10237"></a>
### EK10237 — M68040 cache-maintenance instructions raise Line-F instead of performing maintenance

The AROS bridge selects `Model::M68040` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:317`). The M68040 opcode table registers CINV and CPUSH variants for that model (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/MoiraInit_cpp.h:1964-1983`), but all of their selected handlers call `execLineF()` (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:5673-5691`). That helper raises the Line-F exception (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:62-70`) instead of executing cache maintenance or applying the required privilege check. Motorola documents CINV and CPUSH as M68040 supervisor instructions: in supervisor state they invalidate selected cache lines or push/invalidate dirty data lines; in user state they trap for privilege violation ([NXP-hosted M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual, §§3.1.10, 6-3–6-4](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/M68000PRM.pdf)). The emulator has no modeled instruction/data caches, so a supervisor-mode no-op can represent the cache effect, but Line-F is not the specified behavior.

**Trigger and consequence:** guest code executes any selected CINV or CPUSH encoding under the M68040 model. Supervisor code receives a Line-F exception instead of the cache operation; user code receives Line-F instead of privilege violation. **Affected configuration:** explicit `m68kemu.library` execution on the selected M68040 model; the module is not part of the normal ROM aggregate. **Confidence:** high for model-specific registration, handler dispatch and documented privilege/operation semantics; no guest instruction was run. Implement the cache operation as a no-op in the cacheless emulator while preserving the supervisor-mode guard. No build or runtime operation was performed; source-only; see the [Moira M68040 CINV/CPUSH pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L10623).

<a id="ek10238"></a>
### EK10238 — M68040 MOVE16 encodings raise Line-F instead of copying a memory line

The AROS bridge selects `Model::M68040` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:317`). Its selected M68040 opcode table registers all five MOVE16 forms: postincrement-to-postincrement, postincrement/absolute-long in both directions, and address-register-indirect/absolute-long in both directions (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/MoiraInit_cpp.h:1987-2004`). Every associated handler delegates to `execLineF()` instead of transferring the 16-byte line (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:5694-5741`; generic Line-F dispatch at `:62-70`). The M68040 instruction reference defines these forms as 16-byte block transfers, aligning both line addresses to 16 bytes and incrementing postincrement address registers by 16 ([NXP-hosted M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual, p. 4-126](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/M68000PRM.pdf)).

**Trigger and consequence:** guest code executes a MOVE16 opcode under the selected M68040 model. Instead of copying the source line to the destination, the emulator takes a Line-F exception; no destination bytes are written and postincrement registers are not advanced. **Affected configuration:** explicit `m68kemu.library` execution on the selected M68040 model; the module is not part of the normal ROM aggregate. **Confidence:** high for the five registrations, direct Line-F handler path, and documented instruction operation; no guest instruction was run. Implement the 16-byte transfer and the addressing-form-specific postincrements. No build or runtime operation was performed; source-only; see the [Moira M68040 MOVE16 pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L10625).

<a id="ek10239"></a>
### EK10239 — M68040 CHK2/CMP2.B misreads PC-relative bounds as unsigned bytes

The M68040 initializer selects CHK2/CMP2.B with PC-displacement and PC-indexed effective addresses (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/MoiraInit_cpp.h:733-742`; the mask admits `Mode::DIPC` and `Mode::IXPC`). `execChkCmp2()` reads each byte through `readM<..., Byte>()`, which returns the zero-extended `u8`, then the selected `MOIRA_MIMIC_MUSASHI` branch deliberately skips `SEXT<Byte>()` for these two PC-relative modes (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:1690-1696`; `MoiraDataflow_cpp.h:362-398`; `MoiraConfig.h:84`). The other selected byte-bound EA forms sign-extend the same bytes. Bundled Musashi also sign-extends PC-relative bytes: its `m68k_op_chk2cmp2_8_pcdi/pcix()` stores `m68ki_read_pcrel_8()` in signed bounds, matching the explicit `(int8)` casts in its indirect/indexed forms (`Runner/Musashi/m68kops.c:9911-9950,9963-9975`). The Motorola manual allows PC-relative control addressing for CHK2/CMP2 and defines signed bound comparisons; the selected Moira behavior changes solely with the EA encoding ([M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual, pp. 4-82–4-83](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/M68000PM.pdf)).

**Trigger and consequence:** execute the byte form with D0's low byte `0x80` and PC-relative bounds bytes `0x80,0x81` (the extension's D/A bit selects Dn; bit 11 selects CHK2 versus CMP2). The expected signed interval is `[-128,-127]`, so D0 equals the lower bound: C is clear and Z is set. The selected handler sign-extends D0 to −128 but treats the bounds as +128 and +129, so it sets C and clears Z; CHK2 takes a spurious CHK exception when its trap bit is set, while CMP2 returns incorrect condition codes. This applies to both PC-displacement and PC-indexed forms. **Affected configuration:** explicit `m68kemu.library` execution on its selected M68040/Musashi-compatible path; not claimed for the normal ROM aggregate. **Confidence:** high for the source-level sign-extension mismatch and its selected extension/handler path, supported by the bundled Musashi implementation and manual's signed-bound semantics; no guest instruction was run. Sign-extend PC-relative byte bounds consistently with the other selected EA forms. No build or runtime operation was performed; source-only; see the [CHK2/CMP2 coverage pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L10643).

<a id="ek10240"></a>
### EK10240 — PC ExecSMP dispatch can link a stack-rejected task into both Running and Wait

In the selected x86-64 PC ExecSMP scheduler, `core_Dispatch()` removes a candidate from `TaskReady`, then `SET_THIS_TASK(newtask)` adds its node to `TaskRunning` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:304-355`; `arch/all-pc/exec/exec_platform.h:295-304`). If the saved stack pointer is outside the task bounds, the dispatcher changes the state to `TS_WAIT` and enqueues that same node on `TaskWait` without first removing it from `TaskRunning` (`kernel_scheduler.c:358-395`). The rejected candidate then takes the `!launchtask` path through `core_Switch()` (`:399-405`). On ExecSMP, `core_Switch()` unconditionally removes its current task node under `TaskRunningSpinLock` (`:205-215`) and, because its state is still `TS_WAIT`, enqueues it on `TaskWait` again (`:273-287`). The task node is intrusive and has only one pair of list links. `Enqueue()` writes the node's links and the destination list's neighbors without unlinking any prior membership (`rom/exec/enqueue.c:87-97`); `Remove()` follows the node's current links and has no list argument (`rom/exec/remove.c:55-62`). Inserting it into Wait while it is still linked from Running therefore leaves Running's neighbors pointing at a node whose links now belong to Wait; the later removal/re-enqueue operates through those rewritten Wait links and does not repair Running's neighbors. A source census of active PC task-list insertions confirms the distinction: `core_Switch()` removes the current node from Running before its state-based requeue (`kernel_scheduler.c:205-287`), task-priority changes remove Ready nodes before reinsertion (`rom/exec/settaskpri.c:104-112`), and new-task publication enters TaskLaunch from `TS_ADDED` before its first scheduler-list insertion (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:238,327`; `TaskLaunch()` at `:25-43`). The other direct PC insertion into Ready is inside a disabled `#if (0)` block (`arch/all-pc/exec/platform_init.c:122-138`). The invalid-stack branch is the selected PC path found to enqueue a task into Wait before removing it from Running.

**Trigger and consequence:** x86-64 PC ExecSMP selects a ready task whose saved `tc_SPReg` fails the explicit stack-bound check. The scheduler's rejection path can corrupt the Running-list linkage and disturb later scheduler/list traversal; no claim is made that ordinary stack use reaches this condition. **Affected configuration:** the x86-64 PC `smp` variant, which enables `__AROSEXEC_SMP__` (`configure.in:1648-1669`); the PC scheduler is selected through `arch/all-pc/kernel/mmakefile.src:68-75`. **Confidence:** high for the source-ordered double membership and intrusive-list inconsistency; the trigger requires a selected ready task with an invalid saved stack pointer. Keep the rejected node off Running before placing it on Wait, and do not pass an already-waiting candidate through a path that assumes it is on Running. No scheduler operation, invalid stack or build was run; source-only; see the [Exec/Kernel coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#pc-execsmp-invalid-stack-dispatch-list-membership-pass).

<a id="ek9025"></a>
### EK9025 — Failed CDFS handler startup leaves its shared semaphore published

`CDFS_Init()` allocates the shared `struct CDFS`, opens `utility.library`, initializes its semaphore, and publishes it with `AddSemaphore()` (`rom/filesys/cdfs/cdfs.c:222-248`). The newly started handler then calls `CDFS_DeviceOpen()` (`:291-305`). If its device-record allocation fails or `BCache_Create()` returns an error, the handler replies with failure and returns without removing the newly published semaphore or closing the utility-library reference. `CDFS_DeviceOpen()` has not linked a device on either failure path (`:130-152`). The only shared-object teardown is at the end of a successfully opened handler's loop, after `CDFS_DeviceClose()`, when both device and volume lists are empty (`:611-625`).

**Trigger and consequence:** the first handler creates the shared CDFS object, then the handler's device allocation or cache creation fails. The handler exits while the empty `CDFS` semaphore remains in Exec's public semaphore list and the object retains its `utility.library` open reference. The retained object may be reused by a later handler, but absent later successful CDFS activity the startup failure leaves those resources held. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `kernel-fs-cdfs` module builds (`rom/filesys/cdfs/mmakefile.src:1-12`). **Confidence:** high for both failure returns and the missing rollback/only teardown site; no allocation or cache failure was induced. Roll back the newly created singleton and library reference when first-handler device setup fails. Source-only; see the [CDFS startup coverage pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L3704).

<a id="ek10241"></a>
### EK10241 — CDFS can use its shared state after the last handler frees it

`CDFS_Init()` wraps `FindSemaphore("CDFS")` in `Forbid()` and returns the found `struct CDFS *` after `Permit()` (`rom/filesys/cdfs/cdfs.c:222-248`). The Exec semaphore-list lock protects the lookup only while `FindSemaphore()` traverses the list; it does not pin the returned object's lifetime (`rom/exec/findsemaphore.c:48-61`). The new handler does not register itself as a device until after `CDFS_Init()` returns and `CDFS_DeviceOpen()` has allocated a device and completed `BCache_Create()` (`cdfs.c:291-305,130-152`). Meanwhile, the last existing handler can close its device, acquire `cb_Semaphore`, observe both lists empty, remove the public semaphore, release the lock, close `utility.library`, and free the `struct CDFS` (`cdfs.c:611-625`). If the new handler found the object before that removal, it can continue into device setup with the stale pointer. If it reaches `ObtainSemaphore()` while teardown owns the lock, `ReleaseSemaphore()` can hand ownership to the waiter, after which teardown still frees the object without waiting for the awakened task to finish (`rom/exec/releasesemaphore.c:107-194`; `rom/exec/obtainsemaphore.c:55-79`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a new CDFS handler startup overlaps the last handler's shutdown: `FindSemaphore()` returns the current singleton, the old handler wins the final empty-list teardown, and the new handler then uses or waits on the freed object. This can make `BCache_Create()` completion or semaphore acquisition/update access freed storage. The caller-side `Forbid()` does not span device registration and does not pin the object across CPUs; on a single CPU the post-`Permit()` interval also permits the shutdown task to run. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `kernel-fs-cdfs` module builds with overlapping handler startup/shutdown on a preemptive AROS target, including SMP. **Confidence:** high for the unpinned lookup, registration gap, final free, and stale-pointer use sequence; the interleaving was source-traced, not run. Make lookup and handler registration atomic with respect to last-user removal, for example with a separately stable owner/reference protocol. No CDFS handler, semaphore, device, or build was run; source-only; see the [CDFS shared-lifetime caller pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#cdfs-shared-semaphore-lifetime-caller-pass).

<a id="ek10242"></a>
### EK10242 — Bifteck reports success after an interrupted or failed log write

The optional Bifteck command initializes `result` to `RETURN_OK`, then ignores the return values from `FPutC()` while copying the in-memory log (`developer/debug/bifteck/Bifteck.c:41-45,76-89`). If Ctrl-C is detected, the loop sets `error = ERROR_BREAK` and exits, but the next statement overwrites `error` with `IoErr()` (`:78-85`). A failed `FPutC()` can likewise set the DOS error while the loop continues; neither case changes `result`. The final status branch therefore takes the success arm, calls `SetIoErr(0)`, and returns `RETURN_OK` (`:118-125`). The final newline write and `Close()` result are also unchecked (`:87-99`), so late buffered output failures can be lost as well.

**Trigger and consequence:** invoke the Bifteck target with an output stream that fails during a character write or close, or press Ctrl-C while the log is being copied. The command can leave a truncated log but report successful completion and clear the caller's DOS error. **Affected configuration:** explicit `debug-tools-bifteck` target when selected in a Workbench build; this is an optional diagnostic command. **Confidence:** high for the ignored write/close results, overwritten break error, and unconditional success return on these paths; no output failure or interruption was induced. Set failure status when `FPutC()`/`Close()` fails and preserve the break result. No command or build was run; source-only; see the [Bifteck caller review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#remaining-named-findsemaphore-caller-census-closure).

<a id="ek10243"></a>
### EK10243 — PosixC pthread workers leak an opened library base when task-slot storage fails

The PosixC thread-enter hook opens a private `posixc.library` base, then stores its pointer in the worker's task-storage slot without checking `SetTaskStorageSlot()`'s Boolean result (`compiler/crt/posixc/__threadhook.c:76-83`). The matching leave hook can recover and close the base only by reading that slot (`:85-96`). `SetTaskStorageSlot()` returns `FALSE` if it cannot allocate or grow the task's storage array (`rom/task/SetTaskStorageSlot.c:70-92`), leaving the opened base unpublished. The leave hook then reads NULL and skips `CloseLibrary()`. The generated `posixc.library` configuration selects `pertaskbase` (`compiler/crt/posixc/posixc.conf:1-6`); its per-task duplicate is released through the matching close path, and task exit does not substitute for that explicit library close.

There is a second way the hook can run without a usable slot. `__posixc_threadhook_init()` calls `AllocTaskStorageSlot()` when the saved slot is unset, but registers the enter/leave callbacks regardless of whether the result is zero (`__threadhook.c:132-154`). `AllocTaskStorageSlot()` returns its initial zero result when the current task has no `IntETask` (`rom/task/AllocTaskStorageSlot.c:45-83`). If PosixC is first initialized in that context, the generated library initializer also saves zero as its own `__pertaskslot` without checking it (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1147-1150`). The generated base getter/setter use that slot, and the setter ignores its failure result (`:312-322`); later worker opens therefore cannot publish the PosixC base for the rel wrappers. The registered enter callback still opens a private base but skips saving it because its separate tracking slot is zero, and leave skips the close. The pthread hook interface returns no status to stop the worker from entering user code (`compiler/pthread/pthread_create.c:94-119,171-212`).

The zero slot also exposes a separate getter-side failure within this same scenario. `SetTaskStorageSlot()` rejects `slotid < 1` (`rom/task/SetTaskStorageSlot.c:84-90`), but `TaskGetStorageSlot()` checks only whether storage exists and whether its capacity is less than the ID, then returns `tsstorage[slotid]` (`rom/task/GetTaskStorageSlot.c:63-77`). Index zero is the array's capacity field (`rom/task/task_intern.h:91`; `SetTaskStorageSlot.c:76,80,95`), so `GetTaskStorageSlot(0)` returns that positive count whenever the worker already has a task-storage array. Generated `OpenLib()` treats the getter result as a duplicate base and dereferences its task and library-name fields before validating it (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1317-1345`). Thus, on a worker that already has storage for another slot, the failed zero-ID reservation can produce an invalid small pointer in the open path rather than a clean NULL/missing-base result. When no storage array exists, the getter returns NULL and the prior missing-base path applies.

**Trigger and consequence:** either a pthread worker's slot write fails after its private base opens, or PosixC's init hook runs in a task without an `IntETask`, reserves no slot, but still registers the callbacks used later by pthread workers. In both cases the worker cannot retrieve/close the opened base at leave; when PosixC was first initialized without an `IntETask`, its generated per-task slot is also zero, so the worker cannot obtain the CRT base needed by the selected PosixC rel wrappers. If that worker already has task-storage data for another slot, the unguarded zero-ID getter can instead return the array-capacity word as a bogus base; generated OpenLib dereferences it while checking for a reusable duplicate and may fault or read unrelated data. Repeated workers can leak per-task library bases and retain PosixC open references, consuming memory and potentially preventing library expunge. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting both `linklib-pthread` and the per-task-base `compiler/crt/posixc` library; each path requires a successful worker base open and the stated storage failure/initialization context. **Confidence:** high for the ignored slot results, zero return without an `IntETask`, callback registration despite zero, getter's capacity-word result, and missing leave-time close; the cross-task sequence after plain-Task initialization and the worker's possession of another slot were not observed. Reject nonpositive IDs in the getter, do not register callbacks unless a positive slot was reserved, and close the opened worker base if publication fails. No worker or library lifecycle was run; source-only; see the [PosixC thread-hook coverage row](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L593).



<a id="ek8785"></a>
### EK8785 — task.resource leaks per-task storage when a task removes itself

`SetTaskStorageSlot()` allocates or grows a task's slot array with `AllocMem()` and publishes it through `et_Reserved[ETASK_RSVD_SLOTID]` (`rom/task/SetTaskStorageSlot.c:70-108`). task.resource replaces Exec's `RemTask` vector with its wrapper during `taskres_Init()` (`rom/task/task_init.c:75-78`). The wrapper saves the slot-array pointer, calls the original Exec `RemTask()`, and only afterward frees that array (`rom/task/task_execfuncs.c:167-188`). That cleanup works for remote removal, where the original vector returns. For self-removal, Exec queues the task for service cleanup and calls `KrnDispatch()` with an explicit note that it will never return to the task (`rom/exec/remtask.c:130-163`). The wrapper therefore never reaches its `FreeMem(tsstorage, ...)` block. Exec's ETask cleanup frees the ETask structure (`rom/exec/exec_util.c:361-369`), and the service task only frees the task's `tc_MemEntry` allocations (`rom/exec/service.c:66-90`); neither sees the separately allocated task-storage array. The array allocation is not added to `tc_MemEntry` by `SetTaskStorageSlot()`.

**Trigger and consequence:** a task successfully creates a task-storage array by setting a task-storage slot, then removes itself with `RemTask(NULL)` or the equivalent self-exit path. Its slot array, sized from the first slot-count word, remains allocated after the ETask pointer is destroyed. Repeated short-lived tasks that use task storage, including tasks opening generated `pertaskbase` libraries, can accumulate these allocations. **Affected configuration:** builds that include task.resource (`rom/task/mmakefile.src` builds `kernel-task`, which is included in maintained native boot targets). **Confidence:** high for the non-returning self-removal path, the cleanup placement after it, and the absence of another selected owner of the allocation; no task exit or memory leak was run. Free the saved slot array before invoking the non-returning self-removal path, while retaining the existing post-call cleanup for remote removals. Source-only; see the [task.resource RemTask coverage row](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2140).


<a id="ek10244"></a>
### EK10244 — CDFS cache teardown closes a pointer field instead of its I/O request

`BCache_Create()` stores the separately allocated request in `bp->bp_IOStdReq` after creating its message port and opens the backing device through that request (`rom/filesys/cdfs/bcache.c:85-91`). The successful cache remains owned by the CDFS device until `CDFS_DeviceClose()` calls `BCache_Delete()` (`rom/filesys/cdfs/cdfs.c:155-165,611`). `BCache_Delete()` passes `&bp->bp_IOStdReq` to `CloseDevice()` instead of the request pointer `bp->bp_IOStdReq` (`bcache.c:251-259`). Exec's `CloseDevice()` dereferences the supplied object as an `IORequest` and dispatches through its `io_Device` field (`rom/exec/closedevice.c:63-85`); the address of the pointer field is not an `IORequest`, so this normal close path reads unrelated cache-state bytes as request fields and can dispatch through an invalid device pointer. The function then frees the cache object without `DeleteIORequest()` or `DeleteMsgPort()`, leaving the separately allocated request and its port without cleanup even if the close call happens not to fault.

**Trigger and consequence:** a mounted CDFS device is closed, including normal handler shutdown after its device list empties. The malformed request can fault or call an invalid device vector during teardown; if execution continues, the opened device reference, I/O request allocation, and message port are not released. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting the optional `kernel-fs-cdfs` target and a successful `BCache_Create()`; the CDFS target is selected by its module manifest but this finding does not claim it is present in every default image. **Confidence:** high for the wrong argument, the Exec request-field dereference, and omitted request/port destruction; runtime manifestation was not exercised. Pass `bp->bp_IOStdReq` to `CloseDevice()`, then delete the request and its port in ownership order. No device close or runtime operation was run; source-only; see the [CDFS BCache teardown pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#cdfs-bcache-teardown-pass).


<a id="ek10245"></a>
### EK10245 — CDFS decimal volume dates subtract the wrong digit base

`ascdec()` accepts decimal characters but accumulates each digit as `*val - '9'` (`rom/filesys/cdfs/iso9660.c:43-54`) instead of subtracting `'0'`. `ascdate2stamp()` uses it for every ASCII date component (`:59-72`), including the primary volume descriptor's creation date copied into `dl_VolumeDate` during mount (`:596-598`). A normal digit such as `'2'` contributes a negative value that wraps in the unsigned accumulator, so the mounted volume date is computed from wrapped values rather than the descriptor's year, month, day and time.

**Trigger and consequence:** mount an ISO9660 image with a primary volume descriptor. Its reported volume creation timestamp is incorrect even when all date digits are valid. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting the optional `kernel-fs-cdfs` target and an ISO9660 image with a primary descriptor. **Confidence:** high for the digit-base error and selected assignment path; no image was mounted. Subtract `'0'` and validate the fixed-width date fields. Source-only; see the [CDFS ISO9660 body pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#cdfs-iso9660-body-pass).

<a id="ek10246"></a>
### EK10246 — CDFS directory reads index a sector buffer with the absolute directory offset

`isoReadDir()` selects the correct sector with `extent + (offset / 2048)` and then indexes the returned sector buffer with the unnormalized `offset` (`rom/filesys/cdfs/iso9660.c:316-328`). `BCache_Read()` returns a pointer to the start of the requested block (`bcache.c:431-469`). The directory walkers pass offsets that advance through the full directory (`isoFindCmp():380-403`; `ISO9660_ExamineNext():824-848`), so once an entry offset reaches 2048 the code reads `buff[2048]` or later even though `buff` addresses one 2048-byte cache block.

**Trigger and consequence:** locate or examine a directory whose records extend past its first 2048-byte sector. The parser reads directory-record fields outside the cached sector, returning incorrect entries or faulting the CDFS handler. **Affected configuration:** optional `kernel-fs-cdfs` builds reading a multi-sector ISO9660 directory. **Confidence:** high for the sector selection and absolute buffer index; no image or directory operation was run. Index within the buffer using `offset % 2048` after selecting the sector. Source-only; see the [CDFS ISO9660 body pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#cdfs-iso9660-body-pass).

<a id="ek10247"></a>
### EK10247 — CDFS drops Rock Ridge names and Amiga comments when their payloads fit

The `RR_SystemUse_NM` branch copies a name only when its length is greater than the remaining filename capacity (`rom/filesys/cdfs/iso9660.c:252-260`); when the payload fits, the branch does nothing. The Amiga `RR_SystemUse_AS` comment branch uses the same condition (`:216-224`), so ordinary comments that fit are also omitted. The filename comparator later matches only the `FileInfoBlock` name (`:416-426`), while the base ISO identifier has already been copied and version-suffix-trimmed (`:151-169`). Thus a valid short Rock Ridge name is not made available for lookup, and a fitting Amiga comment is not reported.

**Trigger and consequence:** read directory records with a valid NM name or AS comment whose payload length is within the corresponding available buffer space. The name remains the ISO identifier instead of the extension name, and the comment remains empty; longer payloads take the copy path but are truncated to the cap. **Affected configuration:** optional `kernel-fs-cdfs` builds reading ISO images using these extensions. **Confidence:** high for the conditional copy behavior and downstream name comparison; no image was read. Copy the bounded payload whenever space is available, truncating only when necessary. Source-only; see the [CDFS ISO9660 body pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#cdfs-iso9660-body-pass).

<a id="ek10248"></a>
### EK10248 — CDFS leaks parsed path-table allocations when unmounting an ISO volume

When a primary volume descriptor advertises a nonempty path table, `isoReadPathTables()` allocates and retains both the raw table buffer and an array of pointers into it (`rom/filesys/cdfs/iso9660.c:467-520`). `ISO9660_Unmount()` frees only `vol->cv_Private` (`:648-653`); it does not free either path-table allocation. CDFS calls the filesystem unmount operation before freeing the `CDFSVolume` on eject/device unmount (`rom/filesys/cdfs/cdfs.c:86-126`). The path table is separately released only if a parsed Rock Ridge PX record causes it to be discarded (`iso9660.c:291-299`).

**Trigger and consequence:** mount an ISO image with a usable path table, do not reach the Rock Ridge discard branch, then unmount/eject it. The path-table pointer array and data remain allocated; repeating media swaps accumulates memory loss. **Affected configuration:** optional `kernel-fs-cdfs` builds and ISO images with a nonempty, successfully parsed path table. **Confidence:** high for both allocations and the missing normal-unmount frees; no mount or eject was run. Release both owned allocations before freeing the volume-private structure. Source-only; see the [CDFS ISO9660 body pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#cdfs-iso9660-body-pass).

<a id="ek10249"></a>
### EK10249 — CDFS skips the rest of a directory sector after an ignored record

`isoParseDir()` returns false for hidden/associated ISO records and Rock Ridge relocated entries (`rom/filesys/cdfs/iso9660.c:121-123,272-276`). `isoReadDir()` maps that result to `ERROR_OBJECT_WRONG_TYPE` before writing the record length to its output `size` (`:325-335`). Both `isoFindCmp()` and `ISO9660_ExamineNext()` tolerate that result, advance using the unchanged `size`, and round the offset up to the next 2048-byte boundary (`:387-403,826-848`). This skips visible records later in the same sector. There is an additional resume-path defect: `ISO9660_ExamineNext()` initializes `size` only when the incoming `fib_DiskKey` is zero (`:811-817`); the selected `ACTION_EXAMINE_NEXT` packet path forwards the caller's FileInfoBlock to it (`rom/filesys/cdfs/cdfs.c:439-449`), so a continuation uses the caller-supplied nonzero key. On that path, an ignored record makes `isoReadDir()` return without writing `size`, and the caller reads that uninitialized local at `:832-838`. The resulting offset is indeterminate and can skip entries or terminate enumeration incorrectly.

**Trigger and consequence:** a directory contains a hidden, associated, or relocated entry. Lookup can skip later visible records in that sector; enumeration resumed with a nonzero disk key can additionally advance using an uninitialized size. **Affected configuration:** optional `kernel-fs-cdfs` builds reading ISO9660 directories with ignored entries. **Confidence:** high for both source paths and their consequences; no image or directory operation was run. Have `isoReadDir()` report the raw record length even when suppressing an entry, then advance by that length without skipping the rest of the sector.

<a id="ek10250"></a>
### EK10250 — CDFS accepts a truncated ISO path-table record and later reads beyond it

`isoReadPathTables()` counts entries by reading the name-length byte and advancing by the implied record size, but never checks that the fixed eight-byte header or the full record fits in the remaining table bytes (`rom/filesys/cdfs/iso9660.c:492-503`). It then stores pointers into the allocation and publishes the count (`:513-529`). For a nonzero table shorter than eight bytes, the count loop still creates an entry; `isoFindCmp()` later reads `ExtentLocation` and `ParentDirectory` from that pointer (`:361-373`), beyond the allocated path-table data.

**Trigger and consequence:** an ISO primary descriptor advertises a nonzero path-table length containing a truncated final record (including a table shorter than the fixed record header). Path-table lookup reads fields outside the allocated table and can return bogus locations or fault the handler. **Affected configuration:** optional `kernel-fs-cdfs` builds when malformed/truncated path-table metadata is present. **Confidence:** high for the missing extent check and later field reads; no malformed image was used. Validate each fixed header and complete padded record against remaining bytes before publishing entries; reject or ignore an invalid table. Source-only; see the [CDFS ISO9660 body pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#cdfs-iso9660-body-pass).


<a id="ek10251"></a>
### EK10251 — CDFS leaks a temporary lock on a path from a file

`ISO9660_Locate()` allocates the result `ISOLock` before walking path components (`rom/filesys/cdfs/iso9660.c:677-678`). Inside the slash-component loop, if the current lock is neither a directory nor root, it returns `ERROR_DIR_NOT_FOUND` without freeing that allocation (`:730-737`). CDFS passes `LOCATE_OBJECT` requests to this operation and on failure returns an error without receiving or closing an output lock (`rom/filesys/cdfs/cdfs.c:510-537`).

**Trigger and consequence:** issue a locate request with at least one slash-separated component while the starting lock, or a prior resolved component, is a file. Each rejected request leaks one `ISOLock` allocation. **Affected configuration:** optional `kernel-fs-cdfs` builds using `ISO9660_Locate()`. **Confidence:** high for the allocation, error return, and absence of caller ownership on failure; no packet was sent. Free `fl` before returning `ERROR_DIR_NOT_FOUND`. Source-only; see the [CDFS ISO9660 Locate cleanup follow-up](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#cdfs-iso9660-locate-cleanup-follow-up).

<a id="ek10252"></a>
## EK10252 — Overlapping reset calls overwrite shared callback-completion state

The non-supervisor path stores its launcher, signal mask, and running handler in the single `IntExecBase` fields `ResetCallbackWaiter`, `ResetCallbackSignal`, and `ResetCallbackTask` (`rom/exec/exec_intern.h:98-100`). Each invocation of `Exec_DoResetCallbacks()` writes those fields without acquiring a serialization lock (`rom/exec/doresetcallbacks.c:85-92,140-153`); the public `ShutdownA()` and `ColdReboot()` paths both enter it (`rom/exec/shutdowna.c:58`; `rom/exec/coldreboot.c:51`). On handler completion, `ResetCallbackHandler()` clears and signals the current shared fields rather than the state belonging to the invocation that launched it (`doresetcallbacks.c:31-43`).

**Trigger and consequence:** two non-supervisor reset/shutdown calls overlap while their callback support tasks are running or sleeping. Each handler clears and signals the *current global* fields, not the state of its own invocation. If call A's handler finishes after call B has published its waiter and signal bit, it can wake B's launcher; if B has already launched a handler, that stale wake can let B advance while its handler is still active. A's launcher can remain asleep or fall through its timeout path, and a timeout can demote B's handler through the shared task pointer (`:160-180`). This can violate callback ordering and permit concurrent callback execution. **Affected configuration:** task-context reset-callback use where the selected `ShutdownA()` or `ColdReboot()` vector reaches `Exec_DoResetCallbacks()`: the generic ROM vectors, plus the maintained `aarch64-native`, `all-unix`, `arm-native` ColdReboot, `m68k-amiga` ColdReboot, `ppc-chrp` ColdReboot, `ppc-sam440` ColdReboot, and `riscv-native` ColdReboot implementations. Their source manifests select those overrides (`rom/exec/mmakefile.src:18,35`; corresponding `arch/*/exec/mmakefile.src` entries). MinGW32 overrides do not call the shared dispatcher and are excluded; PowerPC CHRP `ShutdownA()` uses RTAS directly, while its `ColdReboot()` still dispatches callbacks. The supervisor-only branch does not use the shared completion fields. Selected clients include the separate `Reboot`/`Shutdown` commands (`workbench/c/mmakefile.src:35,47`; `Reboot.c:61-72`; `Shutdown.c:29`) and Wanderer (`workbench/system/Wanderer/mmakefile.src:8-15`; `wanderer.c:2904-2920`). On ExecSMP, task callers can overlap across CPUs; on a single CPU the overlap requires a callback task to yield. These source paths establish possible callers, not a reproduced interleaving. **Confidence:** high for the shared-state race and its conditional consequences; medium for reachability, with ExecSMP providing the direct concurrent-task configuration. Use per-invocation completion state or serialize/reject overlapping calls. No reset, callback, or interleaving was run. Source-only; see the [reset-callback shared-state concurrency pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#reset-callback-concurrent-invocation-pass).


<a id="ek10253"></a>
### EK10253 — CDFS uses unchecked ISO path-table parent indices

`isoReadPathTables()` validates neither the contents nor the 1-based parent number of a complete path-table entry (`rom/filesys/cdfs/iso9660.c:492-529`). `isoParseDir()` converts `ParentDirectory` to a zero-based index and immediately reads that pointer (`:121-124`); `ISO9660_Locate()` performs the same unchecked lookup while traversing `..` (`:708-713`). During ordinary path-table search, `isoFindCmp()` parses each candidate entry after finding the current directory's path-table record (`:361-375`), so this is reachable from normal name lookup when a malformed entry is present.

**Trigger and consequence:** an ISO path table contains a structurally complete entry whose `ParentDirectory` is zero or greater than the number of parsed entries. CDFS indexes before or beyond the allocated pointer array and dereferences the result; lookup or parent traversal can fault or use an unrelated extent. **Affected configuration:** optional `kernel-fs-cdfs` when mounting malformed ISO9660 path-table metadata. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked index and reachable lookup; no malformed image was used. Validate parent indices against the published entry count before using them. Source-only; see the [CDFS path-table parent-index follow-up](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#cdfs-path-table-parent-index-follow-up).


<a id="ek10254"></a>
### EK10254 — CDFS path-table lookup searches unrelated directories

When the current extent is found in the ISO path table, `isoFindCmp()` loops over every path-table entry except the current one and passes each to the name comparator (`rom/filesys/cdfs/iso9660.c:361-375`). It never checks that a candidate's `ParentDirectory` identifies the current directory.
