The shared full-format indexed-EA decoder also does not reject reserved fields: `BD SIZE=00` and `I/IS=100` are specified as reserved, and `IS=1` with `I/IS=101..111` is reserved (NXP M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual, Table 2-2, [official manual](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/M68000PRM.pdf)). `computeEAfull()` treats `BD SIZE=00` like a null displacement and interprets `I/IS=100` as postindexed; with index suppression, it also accepts `I/IS=101..111` as postindexed (`MoiraDataflow_cpp.h:157-198`; field-width helpers at `:695-714`). The selected M68040 bridge maps to the C68020 execution core, so these full-format EAs are active. As one concrete selected route, the M68040 `MOVE` registrations admit indexed mode 6 for source and destination effective addresses (`MoiraInit_cpp.h:1088-1120`; the registration macro maps the mode-6 mask bit to `Mode(6)` at `:91-100`); generic `readOp()` and `writeOp()` then call `computeEA()` before memory access (`MoiraDataflow_cpp.h:206-255`). No runtime invalid-extension validation intervenes in that route. A call-site census finds `isValidExt()` only in GNU-syntax disassembly routines (`MoiraDasm_cpp.h:520,637,664,725,1554,1606`), not the runtime handlers. The MC68040 User's Manual defines an illegal instruction as a bit pattern that does not correspond to a valid M68040 instruction (§8.2.4; [NXP-hosted manual](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68040UM.pdf)).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated guest executes one of the listed instructions with a reserved extension field set while the remaining fields specify an operation, or executes a selected instruction using a full-format indexed EA with one of the reserved combinations above. Moira proceeds through the selected operation instead of taking the illegal-instruction exception; malformed CAS/CAS2 encodings can reach their memory compare/update path, malformed CHK2 or bit-field encodings can update flags/registers or modify the target field, and the EA decoder computes an address from the invalid full-format extension (performing an indirect pointer read for the reserved I/IS values it treats as postindexed). For register-offset/width bit-field forms, the trigger is specifically a nonzero bit in a field documented as reserved for that selected mode. **Affected configuration:** explicit `m68kemu.library` builds using the selected M68040/Musashi-compatible configuration; the parent ROM aggregate edges are commented (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:15-17`), so default inclusion is not asserted. **Confidence:** medium; the formats, handler field use, and absence of runtime validation are source/reference-supported, but malformed encodings were not run on hardware or in the emulator. Validate each instruction extension and full-format EA before operand side effects and take the illegal-instruction exception when its encoding is invalid. Source-only. See the [extension validation coverage pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#moira-extension-word-validation-families-ek10298).

<a id="ek10299"></a>
### EK10299 — Register-width bit-field arithmetic overflows signed `int` for valid high-bit values

In both selected register-direct and memory-EA bit-field handlers, `reg.d[]` is `u32`, but the dynamic width is copied into signed `int` and decremented before its low five bits are selected (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/MoiraTypes.h:286`; `MoiraExec_cpp.h:1044-1066,1144-1163`). On the selected 32-bit-`int` AROS toolchains, a width register value such as `0x80000000` converts to `INT_MIN`; `rawWidth - 1` then overflows signed `int` at `:1059,1063`. The width operand is architecturally modulo 32, with zero meaning 32, so this register value is a valid way to request width 32, not a reserved encoding ([NXP M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual, bit-field width definition](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/M68000PRM.pdf)). The selected M68040 bridge uses the C68020 execution core, and `MoiraInit_cpp.h` registers register-direct bit-field operations to this handler (`:314-321`; `MoiraInit_cpp.h:491-537`). The bundled Musashi comparison uses an unsigned `uint width` before the same modulo calculation (`Runner/Musashi/m68kops.c:5280-5299,6261-6278,7027-7049`), avoiding signed overflow.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated guest executes a register-direct or memory-EA bit-field operation with the extension selecting a Dn width and that Dn containing `0x80000000` (or another value converting to `INT_MIN`). This reaches signed-overflow undefined behavior before the mask or operation is computed; the resulting width and therefore the affected register result/flags can depend on compiler and optimization. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built `m68kemu.library` on its selected x86-64, AArch64, or RISC-V 64-bit target; the optional library is not claimed as part of the default ROM aggregate. **Confidence:** high that the valid input reaches signed overflow on the supported 32-bit-`int` ABIs; medium for a particular wrong runtime result because no target compiler output or instruction execution was produced. Perform the modulo operation in an unsigned type before narrowing. No guest instruction, emulator, compiler experiment, or build was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10300"></a>
### EK10300 — Moira executes MOVES with nonzero reserved extension bits

The selected M68040 opcode table registers `MOVES` for memory-alterable addressing modes and byte, word, and long sizes (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/MoiraInit_cpp.h:1225-1229`). Its handler branches on extension bit 11 and uses the register selector, but does not validate bits 10–0 before doing the selected SFC/DFC memory transfer (`MoiraExec_cpp.h:3527-3631`). The execution dispatcher calls the registered handler directly (`Moira.cpp:251-263`). `Moira::availabilityMask(Instr::MOVES, ..., ext)` does reject a nonzero `ext & 0x7ff`, but that availability check is metadata and has no call in instruction execution (`Moira.cpp:693-728`; the only `isAvailable()` uses are public query/disassembly paths). The Motorola M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual's MOVES extension format shows bits 10–0 fixed to zero (pp. 6-24–6-25, [NXP-hosted manual](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/M68000PRM.pdf)); the MC68040 User's Manual defines invalid instruction bit patterns as illegal instructions (§8.2.4, [NXP-hosted manual](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68040UM.pdf)).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated guest executes a MOVES instruction with any of extension bits 10–0 set. The handler ignores those bits and performs its alternate-function-code memory transfer rather than taking an illegal-instruction exception, so malformed instruction behavior diverges from the selected M68040 model. **Affected configuration:** explicit `m68kemu.library` builds using the selected M68040 model; default ROM inclusion is not claimed. **Confidence:** medium; the selected handler path, metadata-only check, and documented zero fields are source/reference-supported, but malformed encodings were not run on hardware or in the emulator. Validate the MOVES extension before address-register side effects or memory access and raise the illegal-instruction exception for invalid encodings. No instruction, guest, emulator, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10302"></a>
### EK10302 — CHRP Exec bootstrap cannot preprocess its `InitETask` call

The architecture-specific CHRP Exec source includes `exec_util.h` (`arch/ppc-chrp/exec/exec_init.c:30-35`), which resolves to the only checked-in `rom/exec/exec_util.h`. That header defines `InitETask(t,p)` as a two-argument macro expanding to `Exec_InitETask(t,p,SysBase)` (`rom/exec/exec_util.h:163`). The CHRP initializer invokes it with three arguments at `arch/ppc-chrp/exec/exec_init.c:378`. There is no other checked-in definition or `#undef` for this macro, so preprocessing this selected source reports that `InitETask` was passed three arguments although the macro takes two; the translation unit cannot compile.

**Trigger and consequence:** assemble the CHRP PPC `kernel-exec` architecture target. Its manifest selects `exec_init.c` in `CFILES` and passes the directory as the `kernel-exec` architecture override (`arch/ppc-chrp/exec/mmakefile.src:12-14,28-41`). The explicit Efika link target consumes `exec_library.o` (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/mmakefile.src:8,13-16`), although its aggregate dependency edge is commented and default-image inclusion is not claimed. The CHRP Exec module build fails at preprocessing before an Efika image can be linked.

**Affected configuration and confidence:** explicit CHRP PPC `kernel-exec` builds that select this override, including the Efika object path when requested. High confidence: the macro definition, call arity and active manifest are direct source facts. No build was run. Update the stale call to the current `InitETask` interface and reconcile ownership of the separately allocated `IntETask` before compiling. Source-only.


<a id="ek10303"></a>
### EK10303 — PC ExecSMP SetTaskPri can requeue a task while its dispatcher moves it to Running

On the selected x86-64 PC SMP path, `core_Dispatch()` removes a task from `TaskReady` and releases `TaskReadySpinLock` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:304-322`). The task remains `TS_READY` while `SET_THIS_TASK()` adds its same intrusive node to `TaskRunning` (`kernel_scheduler.c:344-355`; `arch/all-pc/exec/exec_platform.h:295-303`); only afterward does the dispatcher set `tc_State = TS_RUN` (`kernel_scheduler.c:358-370`). Meanwhile, `SetTaskPri()` takes `tc_SpinLock`, reads `tc_State`, and treats `TS_READY` as proof that the node is on `TaskReady`; it then removes and reinserts that node using only `TaskReadySpinLock` (`rom/exec/settaskpri.c:72-112`). The PC dispatcher does not take the task lock across its dequeue/list/state transition. ARM32 and AArch64 dispatchers do take `tc_SpinLock` before removing an eligible task from `TaskReady` (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:263-287`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:241-261`), so this finding is scoped to the PC path.

**Trigger and consequence:** on x86-64 PC ExecSMP, one CPU dequeues a ready task while another calls `SetTaskPri()` for that task before the dispatcher publishes `TS_RUN`. The interleaving does not require a changed numeric priority: every call that observes `TS_READY` unconditionally removes and re-enqueues the node (`rom/exec/settaskpri.c:102-112`). `SetTaskPri()` can reinsert the detached node into `TaskReady`; if the dispatcher has already linked it to `TaskRunning`, the setter can also unlink it under the wrong list lock. The task can then be linked on both lists or the Running list can be corrupted, allowing another CPU to select the same task while the first dispatcher is preparing to run it. `ChangeTaskPri PROCESS` is a maintained caller (`workbench/c/ChangeTaskPri.c:86-104`; `workbench/c/mmakefile.src:5-11`), and its local `Forbid()` does not exclude another CPU (`rom/exec/forbid.c:58-61`). The selected optional pthread link library provides another direct route: `pthread_setschedparam()` resolves a thread record and passes its `Task` to `SetTaskPri()` (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:1033-1049`; `compiler/pthread/mmakefile.src:11-15,52-54`). **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC ExecSMP with concurrent dispatch and priority change of the same ready task; the API-level trigger does not depend on the command being in a default image. **Confidence:** high for the state/list ordering and unsynchronized caller path; the double-dispatch or list-corruption consequence requires the stated SMP interleaving. Serialize the PC dequeue, Running publication and `TS_RUN` transition with the task lock using a lock order compatible with `SetTaskPri()`. No priority change, scheduler interleaving or build was run; source-only; see the [Exec/Kernel coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#pc-execsmp-settaskpri-dispatch-list-race-ek10303).

<a id="ek10304-moira-disassembler-uses-cpu-cpi-model"></a>
<a id="ek10304"></a>
### EK10304 — Moira's higher-model disassembler omits coprocessor instructions based on the CPU model

`Moira::createJumpTable(cpuModel, dasmModel)` explicitly builds the disassembler registrations from `dasmModel` first (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/MoiraInit_cpp.h:157-185`). The inner registration routine initializes every opcode's execution and disassembly handler to `ILLEGAL` (`:188-200`), but gates all coprocessor-interface registrations on `hasCPI()` (`:1904-1928`). That helper tests the object's `cpuModel` field, not the `model` parameter being used to build the disassembler table (`Moira.cpp:109-119`). The public two-model overload is documented to let the disassembler target a broader, higher-end model than the emulated CPU, including M68030 (`Moira.h:150-152`; `Documentation/HowTo/HowToUseTheCpu.md:40-48`). `cpGEN` is available on M68020 and M68030 (`Moira.cpp:612-615`).

**Trigger and consequence:** with `MOIRA_ENABLE_DASM=true`, set `cpuModel=M68000` and `dasmModel=M68030`, then disassemble a valid coprocessor-general instruction using a non-GNU syntax. `hasCPI()` returns false while building the M68030 disassembly table, leaving that opcode on the default `dasmIllegal` handler. The disassembler prints it as `ILLEGAL` and reports a two-byte instruction, whereas the registered `dasmCpGen()` path would consume a long extension and return six bytes (`MoiraDasm_cpp.h:9-21,213-231,845-858`). This can mislabel valid instructions and desynchronize subsequent disassembly. **Affected configuration:** consumers of the explicitly buildable `kernel-m68kemu-library` Moira C++ API that use the documented separate CPU/disassembler model setting. The checked-in AROS bridge calls only the one-model overload (`m68kemu_moira.cpp:317`), and a repository-wide call search found no in-tree two-model caller, so no current in-tree runtime trigger or default-ROM inclusion is claimed. **Confidence:** high for the table-selection mismatch and disassembly result under the stated API call; the candidate is conditional because no checked-in caller selects separate models. Gate CPI registration on the model argument used for the disassembler table. No disassembly, instruction stream, build or runtime operation was run; source-only; see the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#moira-disassembler-cpi-model-selection-ek10304).


<a id="ek10308"></a>
### EK10308 — m68kemu manual thunks read byte fields beyond the guest arena

Several manual m68k Intuition and Graphics thunks read byte-sized structure fields directly from `ctx->mem` without checking the address against the guest arena size. `OpenWindow()` reads `NewWindow.DetailPen` and `BlockPen` this way (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:487-488`; offsets 8 and 9 in `m68kemu_offsets.h:81-82`); `OpenScreen()` does the same for `NewScreen` offsets 10 and 11 (`:1244-1245`; offsets `:114-115`). `translate_intuitext()` reads the three initial `IntuiText` bytes directly (`:1298-1300`; offsets `:133-135`), and the manual `OpenFont()` thunk directly reads the `TextAttr` style and flags at offsets 6 and 7 (`:1489-1490`; offsets `:167-168`). The neighboring 16- and 32-bit fields use `m68k_read16()`/`m68k_read32()`, which attempt arena-bound checks; these direct byte reads bypass those checks. `m68kemu` allocates a fixed 32 MiB arena (`m68kemu_memory.c:25-37`), and the byte accesses do not validate the complete guest structure extent before indexing.

For example, a `TextAttr` pointer at `ctx->mem_size - 7` leaves its style byte inside the arena but places its flags byte exactly one byte past the allocation. Corresponding truncated guest structures can reach the `BlockPen` or `DrawMode` reads in the other listed thunks. The out-of-range byte load is undefined host C behavior and can read beyond the allocated arena or fault while the thunk is translating the guest call.

**Trigger and consequence:** an m68k guest calls one of the listed vectors with a non-NULL pointer to a truncated structure positioned so a directly read byte falls at or beyond `ctx->mem_size`. The thunk indexes outside the guest allocation instead of rejecting the incomplete structure; behavior can include an emulator fault or an invalid field value passed to native Intuition/Graphics. **Affected configuration:** optional `m68kemu.library` builds that include the manual OpenWindow, OpenScreen, AutoRequest, or OpenFont vectors; no default ROM inclusion or checked-in guest caller is claimed. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked byte indexing and boundary offsets; the resulting host behavior depends on allocation layout and the invalid guest input. No guest call, memory fault, or build was run. Validate each field extent before access or use a bounds-checked byte accessor. Source-only; see the [manual thunk bounds pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L11831).


<a id="ek10305"></a>
### EK10305 — m68kemu `GetDrawInfoAttr()` writes a host-width result into a guest-width slot

The generated Intuition thunk maps the guest `errorPtr` address directly into emulator memory and passes it to native `GetDrawInfoAttr()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6067-6074`; public signature in `rom/intuition/intuition.conf:210`). The native API types the optional result as `IPTR *`, and `SetResult(TRUE)` writes through that pointer before handling the requested attribute (`rom/intuition/getdrawinfoattr.c:17-18,98`; failure branches also write FALSE at `:124,132,231`). On supported 64-bit hosts, `IPTR` is eight bytes, while an m68k guest `IPTR` result slot is four bytes. For any non-NULL guest result pointer, the initial native store writes four bytes beyond the guest slot and overwrites the following guest bytes; if the slot is at the end of the guest arena, the write also crosses the arena boundary.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated m68k caller invokes `GetDrawInfoAttr()` with a non-NULL `errorPtr`. The call corrupts the next four bytes in guest memory even when the attribute query succeeds; invalid/unsupported queries may perform additional writes to the same slot. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded m68kemu on supported 64-bit x86-64, AArch64, or RISC-V hosts. No maintained in-tree emulated caller was found. **Confidence:** high for the direct pointer forwarding, unconditional `IPTR` store and 8-versus-4-byte width difference; no guest call was run. Marshal the status into a temporary native `IPTR` and copy it back with a four-byte guest write. Source-only; see the [GetDrawInfoAttr thunk pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L11808).


<a id="ek10309"></a>
### EK10309 — m68kemu disk-library scan can select a Resident from another loaded hunk file

`M68KEmu_LoadHunksFromMemory()` allocates each Hunk independently and records only the first hunk's address as `entry_point` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_memory.c:312-319`). `M68KEmu_HeapAlloc()` splits the free block from its high-address end (`:77-86`), so later hunks in a file occupy lower addresses than its first hunk. After loading a disk library, `M68KEmu_LoadM68KLibrary()` scans upward from that first-hunk address to the end of the entire 32 MiB arena, rather than checking the addresses and extents of the hunks belonging to this file (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_m68klib.c:76-90`). This misses a Resident record stored in a later hunk. It can also encounter a matching Resident in a previously loaded library: successful disk-library hunks remain allocated in the context, and the loader does not register disk libraries in the fake-library map (EK551; `m68kemu_m68klib.c:145-178`, `m68kemu_thunks.c:68-84`). The scan then accepts that unrelated record and uses its AUTOINIT table, function pointers, name and version to construct a base for the newly requested library (`m68kemu_m68klib.c:99-178`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an optional m68kemu guest opens a disk-backed library whose Resident is outside its first allocated hunk after another disk library with a Resident has already been loaded in the same context. The scan can bind the earlier library's Resident to the new request, return a base with the wrong version/name and vector targets, and report the requested library as successfully opened. If no earlier Resident is encountered, the valid later-hunk Resident is missed and the load fails. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built m68kemu with a disk-library fallback from `LIBS68K:`, `LIBS:m68k/`, or `LIBS:`; the module is optional and no default inclusion or in-tree guest reproducer is claimed. **Confidence:** high for the scan/allocation mismatch and false match; availability of a library with its Resident in a later hunk is input-dependent. Track and scan each loaded hunk range, and reject matches outside the current file's ranges. Source-only; no guest library or build was run.

<a id="ek10310"></a>
### EK10310 — Graphical boot consoles underflow their row index on a sub-glyph framebuffer

`fb_Init()` computes `scr_Height` as `height / fontHeight`, with the selected font height fixed at 14 pixels, and does not reject a nonzero framebuffer height below 14 (`arch/all-native/bootconsole/screen_fb.c:95-107`; `font8x14.c:5-8`). The selected PC Multiboot1, Multiboot2, and VBE initializers pass the bootloader's graphical dimensions through to this function without a minimum-height check (`init_multiboot.c:34-38`; `init_multiboot2.c:74-78`; `common.c:22-40`). The separate Raspberry Pi AArch64 boot requests a default 1024×768 mode when the initial query is zero, but later replaces those dimensions with any nonzero values echoed by firmware and performs no minimum-height check before `fb_Init()` (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/vc_fb.c:55-76,139-160,177-194`). If the echoed height is 1–13 pixels, either implementation sets `scr_Height` to zero. On the first output character, `fb_Putc()` sees `scr_YPos >= scr_Height` and assigns `scr_Height - 1` to the unsigned row index; this wraps to `UINT_MAX`. On PC, after Exec memory setup, startup requests a replacement mirror with `AllocMem(scr_Width * scr_Height)`; the zero-row height makes this `AllocMem(0)`, which is specified to return NULL, and `fb_SetMirror()` assigns that NULL to `fb_Mirror` (`arch/i386-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:401-405`; `arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:579-583`; `rom/exec/allocmem.c:94-107`; `arch/all-native/bootconsole/util_fb.c:7-18`). On the next nonzero framebuffer-console character, `fb_Putc()` calls `lineLen(fb_Mirror)` and reads through the NULL pointer when `scr_Width` is nonzero (`arch/all-native/bootconsole/screen_fb.c:29-37,136-152`). Before that replacement, the early mirror points at `KRN_ProtAreaEnd` (`arch/i386-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:96-99`; x86-64 `:127-133`); its available capacity is not established. The independent unsigned-row underflow still makes the scroll/character path invalid even if mirror handling changes. The AArch64 callback is published after `vcfb_init()` succeeds (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/boot.c:718-724`); its framebuffer `fb_Putc()` has the same unsigned underflow, causing an enormous mirror scan or, if mirror allocation failed, an underflowed framebuffer copy (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/bc/screen_fb.c:135-205`). The PC bootconsole's `con_Putc()` is enabled by the parsed `debug` option, and selected PC `krnPutC()` paths forward output to it (`common.c:79-119`; `arch/i386-pc/kernel/kernel_debug.c:19-50`; `arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_debug.c:19-46`). AArch64 kernel `krnPutC()` sends output through the published callback (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_debug.c:17-30`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a PC bootloader supplies a graphical framebuffer 1–13 pixels high, or Raspberry Pi firmware echoes such a nonzero mode after `SETRES`, and kernel output reaches the framebuffer console. On PC, a normal nonzero text width makes the post-setup debug character dereference the NULL mirror immediately; the row subtraction also wraps and yields an invalid scroll/render path. On AArch64, the existing mirror path scans beyond its rounded one-row allocation or the no-mirror fallback uses an underflowed copy. Diagnostics can fault or fail to make progress. **Affected configuration:** i386-PC and x86-64-PC Multiboot1/2 or VBE framebuffer paths when the `debug` console is enabled; AArch64 Raspberry Pi boot when the firmware returns a nonzero sub-glyph height and the selected callback is used. **Confidence:** high for zero-row calculation, unsigned underflow and loop/copy bounds; practical reachability depends on unusual bootloader metadata or a firmware response that has not been observed. No framebuffer, boot, or firmware response was exercised. Reject graphical modes that provide fewer than one font row or disable the graphical console before output. Source-only; see the [zero-row framebuffer caller pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#zero-row-framebuffer-caller-pass-ek10310-added-2026-10-31).


<a id="ek10311"></a>
### EK10311 — M68040 MOVEC rejects its MMU control-register encodings

The AROS Moira bridge fixes the emulated CPU model to M68040 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:317`), and the MOVEC opcode is registered for this model (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/MoiraInit_cpp.h:1155-1159`). The execution handlers validate control-register encodings using the `C == Core::C68020` whitelist, which accepts only `000`, `001`, `002`, `800`, `801`, `802`, `803`, and `804` (`rom/m68kemu/Moira/Moira/MoiraExec_cpp.h:3197-3207,3251-3261`). Because M68040 maps to the C68020 execution core, valid M68040-only encodings `003`–`007` and `805`–`807` take `execIllegal()` before the transfer switch. The M68040-specific registers are named in the MOVEC availability table (`Moira.cpp:711-718`) and disassembler (`StrWriter_cpp.h:599-612`); the Motorola M68000 Family Programmer's Reference Manual lists them as M68040/MC68LC040 MOVEC registers (TC, ITT0/1, DTT0/1, MMUSR, URP and SRP; pp. 6-23–6-24, [NXP-hosted manual](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/M68000PRM.pdf)).

**Trigger and consequence:** supervisor-mode M68040 guest code executes MOVEC to or from one of those valid control registers. The selected handler raises an illegal-instruction exception instead of transferring the register value, so guest code that reads or configures these M68040 MMU controls cannot execute as specified. **Affected configuration:** explicit `kernel-m68kemu-library` use of the AROS bridge's M68040 model; this optional module is not claimed as part of the default ROM aggregate. No checked-in guest caller or runtime instruction was established. **Confidence:** high that the valid encodings are rejected by the selected handler and are specified for M68040; guest impact depends on whether external guest code uses them. Add model-specific M68040 register handling and state, or constrain the exposed CPU model to the controls actually implemented. Source-only; no guest instruction, emulator, or build was run. See the [MOVEC coverage pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#moira-movec-m68040-register-coverage-ek10311).


<a id="ek10313"></a>
<a id="ek10313-dup2-can-replace-another-processs-global-posixc-descriptor-reservation"></a>
### EK10313 — dup2 can replace another process's global POSIXC descriptor reservation

Each ordinary POSIXC process owns its own local `fd_array` (`compiler/crt/posixc/__fdesc.c:45-51`), while `fd.library` tracks descriptor numbers and a single owner/data entry in a system-wide table (`workbench/libs/fd/fd_alloc.c:146-196,414-445`). `dup2()` documents that `newfd` is the caller's target descriptor and that an already-valid target is deallocated before return; its only usage restriction is that it must not be called from a shared library or threaded application (`compiler/crt/posixc/dup2.c:17-56`).

When process A calls `dup2(oldfd, newfd)` and `newfd` is empty in A's local array but currently holds a POSIXC descriptor in process B, `__getfdslot()` does not close a local target and skips `FD_Reserve()` whenever `FD_GetOwner(newfd) == FD_OWNER_POSIXC` (`compiler/crt/posixc/__fdesc.c:237-299`). It therefore returns the number as if the reservation were A's. `__setfdesc()` then publishes A's local `fdesc` and calls `FD_SetData(newfd, FD_OWNER_POSIXC, desc)`, which accepts the matching owner class and overwrites the one global data pointer (`__fdesc.c:184-201`; `fd_alloc.c:414-445`). Process B's local table still contains its old `fdesc`, so both local tables now claim the same globally reserved number.

When either process later closes that descriptor, `close()` clears its local slot and calls `FD_Free(newfd, FD_OWNER_POSIXC)` (`compiler/crt/posixc/close.c:43-45,109-112`; `__fdesc.c:184-201`). This frees the shared reservation even though the other process still has a local entry. The remaining process's next `__getfdesc()` sees an owner other than `FD_OWNER_POSIXC` and rejects its local entry (`__fdesc.c:122-143`); `close()` then has no owner hook to use and returns `EBADF`, leaving that local descriptor and its FCB reference stranded (`close.c:43-54`).

**Trigger and consequence:** two separate POSIXC processes have distinct local descriptor arrays. Process A can explicitly call `dup2(oldfd, newfd)` while process B holds `newfd` only in B's local table. The same collision is reachable through ordinary `dup(oldfd)`: `dup()` first finds a globally free number with `__getfirstfd(0)`, then calls `dup2()` in a separate step (`compiler/crt/posixc/dup.c:56`; `__fdesc.c:199-224`). If process B reserves and publishes that number between A's scan and `__getfdslot()`'s owner check, A mistakes B's `FD_OWNER_POSIXC` reservation for its own and overwrites its data pointer. The `dup()` usage restriction forbids shared-library/threaded use, not concurrent ordinary processes. Either process then closes the colliding number. The other process loses access to its descriptor and cannot close it through the POSIXC close path, leaking its descriptor/FCB reference. The `dup()` interleaving is between ordinary processes; it does not require a threaded POSIXC caller. **Affected configuration:** POSIXC with `fd.library` available and ordinary separate processes using an explicit colliding `dup2()` target or concurrently allocating through `dup()`. **Confidence:** high for the separate local tables, global owner/data table, same-owner reservation skip, and close/rejection path; no checked-in selected caller was found that deliberately chooses another process's descriptor number. Treat the owner as belonging to a specific POSIXC process/table, or fail the target reservation when it belongs to another process. No process, descriptor, or `dup2()` call was run; source-only. See the [cross-process target reservation trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-dup2-cross-process-target-reservation-ek10313).

<a id="ek10315"></a>
### EK10315 — `SetTaskAffinity()` can modify an affinity mask while task teardown frees it

`SetTaskAffinity()` checks the supplied task and ETask pointers at entry, reads `iet_CpuAffinity` once before locking to decide whether to allocate a replacement, then rereads the field after taking `task->tc_SpinLock`; when it points to an allocated mask, it clears and rewrites that buffer under the lock (`rom/task/SetTaskAffinity.c:75-82,98-120`). `RemTask()` releases its state-transition synchronization before deleting the saved context and calling `CleanupETask()` (`rom/exec/remtask.c:97-128`). ARM/AArch64 `Exec_ReschedTask()` uses `tc_SpinLock` only for that transition (`arch/arm-native/exec/platform_init.c:129-193`; `arch/aarch64-native/exec/platform_init.c:114-174`); the selected x86-64 PC `X86_HandleReschedTask()` instead uses the scheduler-list lock, not `tc_SpinLock` (`arch/all-pc/exec/platform_init.c:259-335`). In all these routes, teardown proceeds after releasing its transition lock. `CleanupETask()` frees the affinity mask under `Forbid()` before its later message-port/child-list locking, without taking `task->tc_SpinLock` or clearing `iet_CpuAffinity` (`rom/exec/exec_util.c:238-260`). Exec documents that `Forbid()` only prevents task switches on the calling processor in ExecSMP; it does not exclude another CPU (`rom/exec/forbid.c:73-80`). `SetTaskAffinity()` does not recheck `tc_State` after acquiring its lock.

**Trigger and consequence:** with ExecSMP and CPU-affinity support enabled, one CPU calls `SetTaskAffinity(target, validMask)` while another calls `RemTask(target)`, and the setter's in-place mask update overlaps `CleanupETask()` freeing that mask. The setter can read or write the freed buffer, or continue through an ETask that teardown has expunged, causing a task-resource fault or allocator/ETask state corruption. This is distinct from EK714's scheduler-versus-setter stale-eligibility race and EK830's concurrent double-removal path.

**Affected configuration and reachability:** ExecSMP configurations with the Task resource and `EXECF_CPUAffinity` active, including the selected ARM32/AArch64 SMP paths and x86-64 PC SMP. The task-resource manifest explicitly builds `SetTaskAffinity` (`rom/task/mmakefile.src:40-70`). A direct C-call census found maintained `SetTaskAffinity()` calls only in the SMP affinity test; it waits for setter workers before stopping the target (`developer/debug/test/smp/smpaffinity.c:265-301`). No maintained production caller establishes the concurrent-removal sequence, so product reachability remains conditional on an application or external module using the public API this way.

**Confidence:** high that mask mutation and free have no shared lock and can overlap after the terminal-state transition; medium for occurrence in maintained workloads because no production caller was found and the API does not document a target-lifetime synchronization rule. Keep the target alive across the operation and serialize teardown with the affinity update, or add a lifetime guard shared by `SetTaskAffinity()` and cleanup. No affinity call, concurrent removal, allocation reuse, or build was run; source-only. See the [SetTaskAffinity/RemTask lifetime pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#settaskaffinity-remtask-cleanup-race-ek10315).


<a id="ek10316"></a>
### EK10316 — m68kemu `OpenWindowTagList()` passes guest `TAG_MORE` addresses to native Intuition

The manual `OpenWindowTagList()` thunk copies guest TagItems into a native-width array, but its pointer conversion handles only `WA_Title`, `WA_ScreenTitle`, `WA_PubScreenName`, and `WA_CustomScreen`; all other `ti_Data` values are copied unchanged (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:571-595`). For a valid m68k `TAG_MORE`, `ti_Data` is a 32-bit address of another guest TagItem list, and the tag terminates the current array (`compiler/include/utility/tagitem.h:34-39`). The thunk's sizing loop nevertheless scans forward in the current guest arena until it sees a literal `TAG_DONE` (`m68kemu_thunks.c:577-579`), counting entries beyond the valid current list; it then copies that whole span. It neither translates the `TAG_MORE` address nor follows the continuation while constructing the copy. Native Intuition chains the copied array through `TAG_MORE` and passes that `ti_Data` to native tag traversal (`rom/intuition/openwindowtaglist.c:286-296`; `rom/intuition/openwindow.c:177-186`; `compiler/arossupport/libnexttagitem.c:7-33`). On supported 64-bit host layouts, `struct TagItem` uses host-width `IPTR` for `ti_Data` and is 16 bytes, rather than the guest's 8-byte records in the emulator arena (`compiler/include/utility/tagitem.h:19-24`). The pre-scan can therefore copy unrelated guest words and request temporary storage proportional to the distance to a later zero tag before native traversal even reaches the untranslated continuation pointer.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated m68k caller uses a valid `TAG_MORE` entry in `OpenWindowTagList()`'s tag list. The thunk scans and copies beyond the current list while sizing its temporary array. Native Intuition then follows the unconverted guest address using host-width TagItem records, so the window open can fail or read the wrong fields. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded `kernel-m68kemu-library` on its supported 64-bit hosts. `m68kemu` remains outside the default ROM/package graph, and no checked-in guest caller was found. **Confidence:** high that a valid `TAG_MORE` terminates the current array but the thunk scans for `TAG_DONE`, and high for the untranslated continuation pointer/native-width mismatch; the amount of extra copying and allocation depends on guest memory following the list. Stop sizing at control tags and marshal the complete chain into native-width records while preserving `TAG_MORE` control flow, or traverse guest-width tags in a bridge iterator. No tag list, window, emulator, or build was run; source-only; see the [OpenWindowTagList tag-chain recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#openwindowtaglist-tag-more-translation-recheck-ek10316).


<a id="ek10317"></a>
### EK10317 — m68kemu `OpenWindowTagList()` discards its `NewWindow` argument

The manual thunk reads A1 as the tag list, never reads A0, and always calls native `OpenWindowTagList(NULL, ht)` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:571-595`). The native API accepts a `NewWindow *` for compatibility and copies its fields as the initial window specification before applying the extension tags (`rom/intuition/openwindowtaglist.c:265-278`). Thus any caller-supplied NewWindow values not overridden by converted tags are absent from the native call; the thunk instead relies on the native defaults created for a NULL NewWindow.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated m68k caller passes a non-NULL, valid `NewWindow` with one or more settings not repeated by the tag list. The created window uses defaults or omits those settings rather than honoring the supplied structure, which can change its geometry, IDCMP mask, flags, or other initial attributes. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded `kernel-m68kemu-library`; the module is outside the default ROM/package graph, and no checked-in guest caller was found. **Confidence:** high for the ignored A0 and the native API's NewWindow-copy behavior; the visible difference depends on which fields the caller supplies and tags do not override. Translate the guest NewWindow fields and pass a native structure alongside the converted tags. No window, guest call, emulator, or build was run; source-only; see the [OpenWindowTagList NewWindow-argument recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#openwindowtaglist-newwindow-argument-recheck-ek10317).

<a id="ek10337"></a>
### EK10337 — m68kemu window-opening thunks omit or mis-marshal initial gadget lists

The manual `OpenWindow()` thunk reads geometry, pens, IDCMP flags, flags, title, screen, and size limits from the guest `NewWindow`, then calls native `OpenWindowTags(NULL, ...)` without reading its `FirstGadget` field or supplying `WA_Gadgets` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:477-510`; the guest field is at offset 18 in the `NewWindow` layout, `rom/m68kemu/m68k_offsets.txt:2169`). Native Intuition copies the supplied `NewWindow` and uses `nw.FirstGadget` to size borders and attach the gadget list (`rom/intuition/openwindow.c:145-146,778-820,1126-1142`); `WA_Gadgets` is the corresponding tag route (`compiler/include/intuition/intuition.h:635`; `openwindow.c:231-233`). The thunk therefore drops a supported initial-gadget input instead of translating it into the native representation. The sibling manual `OpenWindowTagList()` path also fails to marshal an initial gadget chain supplied as `WA_Gadgets`: it copies that tag data unchanged, translating only title strings and `WA_CustomScreen` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:571-597`). Native `OpenWindowTagList()` places the tag value into `nw.FirstGadget` (`rom/intuition/openwindow.c:231-233`); native `OpenWindow()` walks `NextGadget`, reads Activation and geometry, then passes the chain to decoration and `AddGList()` (`:778-820,1126-1143`). The m68k `Gadget` is 44 bytes while the selected native layout is 80 bytes, with fields at different offsets (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_shadow_layouts.h:1686-1698`). Passing a guest address as a host pointer can make this traversal fail or fault before the gadgets are attached. This is the same missing initial-gadget marshalling gap through a second public entry point, not a separate finding.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated m68k caller opens a window with gadgets in `NewWindow.FirstGadget`, which the direct thunk drops, or supplies `WA_Gadgets` to `OpenWindowTagList()`, which the thunk forwards as a raw guest pointer. In the first case gadgets are absent; in the second, native code traverses guest-width records as host-width `Gadget` objects and may fail or fault before attachment. **Affected configuration:** explicitly building and loading the optional `kernel-m68kemu-library` target; its manifest selects `m68kemu_thunks.c` (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:16-26`), while the parent ROM/package edges remain commented. No checked-in guest caller was found. **Confidence:** high for both the direct field omission and the raw `WA_Gadgets` pointer/layout mismatch; practical impact requires a guest client supplying an initial gadget list. Translate the guest gadget chain and pass a native list through `WA_Gadgets`, or construct the native window with a translated `NewWindow`. No guest call, window, emulator, or build was run; source-only; see the [direct FirstGadget trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#openwindow-firstgadget-field-recheck-ek10337) and the [WA_Gadgets trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#openwindow-tag-gadgets-recheck-ek10337).

<a id="ek10338"></a>
### EK10338 — m68kemu `OpenScreen()` drops selected `NewScreen` fields

The manual `OpenScreen()` thunk reads geometry, depth, pens, `Type`, and `DefaultTitle`, then calls `OpenScreenTags(NULL, ...)`; it does not read `NewScreen.ViewModes`, `Font`, or `CustomBitMap`, and it passes only `Type & 0x000F` while forcing `SA_ShowTitle` true (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1232-1259`; guest offsets `ViewModes` through `CustomBitMap` in `rom/m68kemu/m68k_offsets.txt:2161-2166`; thunk constants in `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_offsets.h:109-118`). Native Intuition uses `ViewModes` to constrain `BestModeIDA()` for HAM/EHB screens (`rom/intuition/openscreen.c:1056-1061`), `Font` to open the requested screen font (`:1837-1845`), and the `CUSTOMBITMAP` type flag plus `CustomBitMap` to choose the screen bitmap (`:1165-1209`). Its `SA_ShowTitle` handler also sets or clears the corresponding type flag (`:597-605`). The mask additionally discards supported non-screen-type flags embedded in `NewScreen.Type`, including `SCREENBEHIND`, `SCREENQUIET`, and `AUTOSCROLL` (public flag definitions `compiler/include/intuition/screens.h:122-136`). Native screen publication uses `SCREENBEHIND` to append the screen rather than make it active (`rom/intuition/openscreen.c:2445-2462`); `SCREENQUIET` suppresses the screen bar (`rom/intuition/intuition_misc.c:594-655`); and `AUTOSCROLL` enables edge-driven screen scrolling in the input handler (`rom/intuition/inputhandler.c:1483-1520`). The wrapper supplies no `SA_Behind`, `SA_Quiet`, or `SA_AutoScroll` tags to preserve these requested behaviors. Although native OpenScreen may derive AUTOSCROLL from host screen-mode preferences under `SA_LikeWorkbench` (`rom/intuition/openscreen.c:319-345`), this thunk does not set that tag, so that branch does not restore the guest request; see the [preference-path check](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#openscreen-autoscroll-preference-qualification-ek10338). `OpenScreenTagList(NULL, ...)` starts with default `ViewModes`, `Type`, `Font` and `CustomBitMap` values rather than the guest structure's values (`rom/intuition/openscreentaglist.c:247-270`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated caller requests a HAM/EHB view mode, custom screen font, custom bitmap, a screen without a title bar, or `SCREENBEHIND`, `SCREENQUIET`, or `AUTOSCROLL` through `NewScreen.Type`. The opened screen uses default mode-selection constraints/font/bitmap, forces the title bar on, becomes the active/front screen instead of remaining behind, draws a screen bar that should be quiet, or fails to autoscroll when the pointer reaches a display edge, rather than preserving those requests. **Affected configuration:** explicitly building/loading the optional `kernel-m68kemu-library` target, which selects this thunk (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:16-26`); the module is outside the default ROM/package graph. No checked-in m68k guest caller was established. The native C demo `developer/demos/2View/2View.c` sets `NewScreen.Type` to `CUSTOMSCREEN|SCREENBEHIND|AUTOSCROLL` and fills `ViewModes` before `OpenScreenTagList(&newScreen, TagList)` (`:94-98,475-520`); this confirms a maintained public-API usage, but it does not run through m68kemu. **Confidence:** high that these fields/flags are omitted or overridden and that native Intuition consumes them; the SCREENBEHIND, SCREENQUIET, and AUTOSCROLL consequences follow selected screen-list, screen-bar, and input-handler branches, while visible differences require a guest caller to use the affected fields. Translate and pass each supported field, including pointed-to guest objects, through the corresponding native tags or a converted `NewScreen`. No screen, guest call, emulator, or build was run; source-only; see the [OpenScreen NewScreen-field recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#openscreen-newscreen-field-recheck-ek10338).

<a id="ek10339"></a>
### EK10339 — m68kemu `AutoRequest()` discards `IntuiText.ITextFont`

The manual AutoRequest thunk converts each guest `IntuiText` chain through `translate_intuitext()`, which unconditionally assigns `native->ITextFont = NULL` and never reads the guest field (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1293-1307,1321-1332`; the public field is part of `struct IntuiText`, `compiler/include/intuition/intuition.h:124-134`). Native `AutoRequest()` passes the body and button labels into `BuildSysRequest()` (`rom/intuition/autorequest.c:48-57`); the requester renderer calls `int_PrintIText()` for that text (`rom/intuition/requesters.c:59-78,166-174`). `int_PrintIText()` opens and uses each non-NULL `ITextFont` while rendering (`rom/intuition/printitext.c:98-125`). Since the thunk supplies NULL for every item, the native path renders them with the requester RastPort's existing font instead of the guest-requested font.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated m68k caller passes an AutoRequest body or button `IntuiText` with a non-NULL `ITextFont`. The requester text ignores that font and uses the screen/requester font, changing its appearance and potentially its fit. **Affected configuration:** explicitly building and loading the optional `kernel-m68kemu-library` target, whose manifest selects this thunk (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:16-26`); it is outside the default ROM/package graph. No checked-in guest caller was established. **Confidence:** high that conversion clears the field and that native rendering honors non-NULL fonts; practical effect requires a guest caller to specify one. Translate the guest `TextAttr` to a native-width record, preserve its storage for the request duration, and set the native field. If that conversion is corrected, the native requester still measures text using the screen font even when rendering honors a per-entry font (GD10521, Graphics/Desktop). No requester, guest call, emulator or build was run; source-only; see the [AutoRequest IntuiText font recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#autorequest-intuitext-font-recheck-ek10339).

<a id="ek10340"></a>
### EK10340 — m68kemu `AutoRequest()` truncates long `IntuiText.NextText` chains

The thunk translates the body chain with `max_chain` 8 and each positive/negative button label with `max_chain` 1 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1302-1311,1327-1329`). When the limit is reached, it writes `NextText = NULL`, silently omitting the remaining guest entries. There is also a truncation path before the limit: each recursive node is allocated with `AllocMem()`, but on failure the function leaves the zeroed `NextText` field NULL and returns; `AutoRequest()` is still called with the partial chain. Native requester sizing iterates until the chain ends (`rom/intuition/sysrequest_intern.c:535-556`), and `int_PrintIText()` likewise renders every entry (`rom/intuition/printitext.c:94-125`). The public `IntuiText` structure defines a linked `NextText` pointer without a fixed chain-length limit (`compiler/include/intuition/intuition.h:124-134`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated caller passes an AutoRequest body with more than eight linked entries, a button label with a following entry, or any chain whose native-node allocation fails during conversion. Entries after the cap or failed allocation are not measured or rendered, so the requester is incomplete and may be sized differently from native behavior; allocation failure is not reported to the caller. **Affected configuration:** explicitly building and loading the optional `kernel-m68kemu-library` target (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:16-26`); no checked-in guest caller was established. **Confidence:** high that the thunk truncates at the fixed limits and silently returns a partial chain on allocation failure; the visible effect depends on omitted guest content. Translate the full chain with a cycle/size policy and propagate allocation failure instead of calling `AutoRequest()` with partial text. No requester, guest call, allocation failure, emulator or build was exercised; source-only; see the [AutoRequest IntuiText chain recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#autorequest-intuitext-chain-recheck-ek10340).

<a id="ek10318"></a>
### EK10318 — TaskTrace can report an old register and stack snapshot for a task running on another CPU

On x86-64 PC, `cpu_Switch()` copies the outgoing task's interrupt context, including `rip`, `rsp`, and general registers, into `ETask.et_RegFrame` when that task is switched out (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:208-220,294-306`). `QueryTaskTagList()` reads PC/SP and indexed registers from that saved frame (`rom/task/QueryTaskTagList.c:86-110,256-275`). TaskTrace finds a task through task.resource, releases its iterator lock, and then queries PC, SP and RBP and walks the frame chain; it does not stop or request a consistent snapshot of the target (`developer/debug/shellcommands/TaskTrace.c:84-122,176-192,357-389`). The call-site census directly includes running tasks: `LTF_ALL` contains `LTF_RUNNING`, and `NextTaskEntry()` maps that flag to `TS_RUN` (`rom/task/task.h:16-19`; `rom/task/NextTaskEntry.c:70-85`). TaskTrace does not filter the selected state before querying; it prints `tc_State` only afterward (`TaskTrace.c:357-377`). The PC scheduler permits a task to remain `TS_RUN` on another CPU while TaskTrace executes (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:294-323).

**Trigger and consequence:** on x86-64 PC ExecSMP, TaskTrace selects a task that is running on another CPU after that task's most recent switch-out. Its ETask context still describes that earlier point, while the task's live registers and stack may have advanced. TaskTrace can therefore print an old PC/SP and unwind a stack that no longer matches the task's live state. This finding concerns snapshot accuracy only; no invalid read or fault is claimed. **Affected configuration:** ExecSMP x86-64 PC with the explicitly built optional `debug-tools-shellcommands` target containing TaskTrace. **Confidence:** high for the saved-context write/read and the absence of a target stop/snapshot protocol; occurrence depends on selecting a task running on another CPU. Use a scheduler-coordinated snapshot/rendezvous, or report that live-task register values are unavailable. No task trace, SMP schedule, or build was run; source-only; see the [TaskTrace caller and saved-context recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#tasktrace-live-task-context-snapshot-ek10318).


<a id="ek10319"></a>
### EK10319 — Handler initialization can report success without registering its handlers

For `HANDLER` configurations with handler entries, genmodule emits `InitHandler()` to open the required FileSystem/Expansion resource, create a `SegList`, and register DOS nodes or `FileSysEntry` records. It returns `FALSE` when the required resource is unavailable (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:841-853`), but a `CreateSegList()` allocation failure only skips the registration block and falls through to `return TRUE` (`:855-858,961-972`; `CreateSegList()` returns `BNULL` when allocation fails at `compiler/arossupport/createseglist.c:84-85`). For each configured `DOSNode`, the generated code also ignores `AddBootNode()`'s Boolean result (`writestart.c:875-883`); the selected `AddBootNode()` implementation can fail when it cannot allocate its boot-list node (`rom/expansion/addbootnode.c:152-157`). More directly, the generated handler `InitLib()` discards `InitHandler()`'s Boolean result and always returns `LIBBASE` (`writestart.c:1028-1037`). `InitResident()` adds a non-NULL returned base as an `NT_RESOURCE` (`rom/exec/initresident.c:134-155`), so the failed handler remains marked initialized and the cold-start resident walk does not retry it (`rom/exec/initcode.c:91-96`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a generated handler has configured DOS-node or filesystem registrations and, during resident initialization, a required resource is absent, the seglist or registration allocation fails, or `AddBootNode()` rejects/fails to publish one configured node. The resource is still installed as initialized while affected DOS handler/file-system entries are missing; for a boot-selected handler this leaves the corresponding name/device unavailable until another explicit recovery or reboot. The checked-in `con` handler has DOSNode and Resident entries (`rom/filesys/console_handler/con_handler.conf`) and is selected in the AArch64 Raspberry Pi and SiFive U boot packages (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/mmakefile.src:219-232`; `arch/riscv-native/sifive_u/boot/mmakefile.src:40-47`). **Affected configuration:** generated `HANDLER` modules with registration entries; the `con` handler is a selected example on those package targets. **Confidence:** high for the ignored error and missing-registration path; occurrence requires initialization-time resource/allocation failure. No resource failure, boot, handler or build was exercised; source-only. See the [full genmodule writer review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#genmodule-writestart-handler-init-error-propagation-recheck-ek10319).


<a id="ek10320"></a>
### EK10320 — TaskTrace can read beyond a malformed x86-64 frame record

On x86-64, TaskTrace obtains the target's saved RBP from `QueryTaskTagList()` (`developer/debug/shellcommands/TaskTrace.c:177-197`). `PrintStackTrace()` checks only whether `TypeOfMem(fp)` reports memory at that single address, then `UnwindFrame()` immediately reads both `rbp[1]` and `rbp[0]` (`TaskTrace.c:168-175,284-305`). `TypeOfMem()` is documented and implemented as a one-address classification: it calls `FindMem(address)` and returns the containing memory header's attributes (`rom/exec/typeofmem.c:27-35,48-55`). TaskTrace does not check that the 16-byte record fits in that allocation or lies within the target task's `tc_SPLower`/`tc_SPUpper`; those bounds are printed separately (`TaskTrace.c:373-382`).

**Trigger and consequence:** trace an x86-64 task whose saved RBP is malformed or overwritten to point into the final 1–15 bytes of an allocated block. `TypeOfMem(fp)` can accept the starting address while `rbp[1]` reads beyond that block; depending on the adjacent mapping this can read unrelated memory or fault while producing the diagnostic. The repeated-frame loop is capped at `TRACE_DEPTH` 10, so no unbounded walk is claimed. x86-64 target flags disable frame-pointer omission for normal configured C/C++ code (`configure.in:1662-1663`); this finding therefore requires a malformed/corrupted frame value or an external/nonstandard frame producer, not an ordinary valid in-tree frame. Check the entire record against the task stack bounds before dereferencing it. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built optional `debug-tools-shellcommands` TaskTrace on x86-64, when tracing a task with the stated malformed RBP. **Confidence:** high for the one-address check and unchecked two-word read; occurrence and whether the out-of-block access faults depend on the frame value and surrounding mappings. This is distinct from EK10318's stale-but-readable context report. No malformed task, trace, or build was used; source-only; see the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#tasktrace-frame-record-extent-check-ek10320).


<a id="ek10321"></a>
### EK10321 — DecodeLocation returns module and symbol names after releasing their lifetime lock

`DecodeLocationA()` resolves a module and symbol while holding `db_ModSem`, stores direct pointers from the module record and symbol table into the caller’s outputs, then releases the semaphore before returning (`rom/debug/decodelocation.c:245-273`). `UnregisterModule()` takes the exclusive semaphore and, when removing the module’s final segment, frees the symbol table, string tables, segment array and module record (`rom/debug/unregistermodule.c:61-99,122-151`). The API does not copy or pin the returned strings. TaskTrace’s `PrintLocation()` passes the returned module and symbol names to `Printf()` only after `DecodeLocation()` has returned (`developer/debug/shellcommands/TaskTrace.c:123-149`). The selected Exec alert formatter also uses the returned names after return in `FormatLocation()` and `FormatAlertExtra()` (`rom/exec/alertstrings.c:530-545`; `rom/exec/alertextra.c:169-190`), reached from the selected `useralert.c` path (`:102-119`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a module unloads after `DecodeLocation()` releases `db_ModSem` but before a caller finishes reading one of the returned names. The caller can then read freed module/string-table storage while formatting a diagnostic, producing corrupted output or a fault. The library remaining open does not pin each registered module. Keep the database protection through consumption or return caller-owned copies. **Affected configuration:** builds with `debug.library`, module registration/unregistration, and a concurrent caller of `DecodeLocation()` that reads returned name pointers. The maintained Exec alert path reaches `FormatLocation()` when the alert has a non-NULL location and DebugBase is available; TaskTrace is an explicit optional caller. **Confidence:** high for returned pointer ownership, lock release, and unload freeing the storage; occurrence depends on the stated overlap. This is distinct from EK9003’s stale registration after failed metadata allocation. No module unload or concurrent lookup was run; source-only; see the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#decodelocation-returned-name-lifetime-ek10321).


<a id="ek10322"></a>
### EK10322 — Kernel backtrace resolver walks module metadata while unload can free it

`debug.library` registers `Debug_SymResolver()` with `kernel.resource` during initialization (`rom/debug/debug_init.c:57-58`). The resolver deliberately walks `db_Modules`, segment arrays and symbol tables without `db_ModSem`, noting that it runs in trap context (`rom/debug/symresolver.c:1-8,18-75`). `KrnPrintBacktrace()` invokes the registered resolver and then formats its returned module, segment and symbol pointers (`rom/kernel/printbacktrace.c:14-40,110-118`). By contrast, DOS `InternalUnloadSeg()` calls `UnregisterModule()` before freeing the segment chain (`rom/dos/internalunloadseg.c:57-78`); unregister holds `db_ModSem` while it removes and frees segment records, symbol/string tables and the module record (`rom/debug/unregistermodule.c:61-99,122-151`). The resolver does not participate in that exclusion or pin the returned strings.

**Trigger and consequence:** on an ExecSMP x86-64 PC build with `debug.library` and TLSF active, a kernel backtrace overlaps another CPU unloading a registered module whose debug records can be freed without waiting on the memory-header semaphore held by the backtrace's current TLSF operation. The resolver can then traverse records as they are removed/freed, or return names that are freed before `KrnPrintBacktrace()` formats them. The resulting diagnostic can be corrupted or fault while reporting the original kernel error. The x86-64 PC target supports the `smp` variant (`configure.in:1647-1669`); TLSF is selected in `rom/kernel/mmakefile.src:61` and is the default x86-64 allocator unless the boot command line selects `notlsf` (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:74,374`). If unload frees the debug records through the same memory header whose TLSF semaphore is held, it will block before the records are freed and this specific overlap will not occur. Protect resolver-visible records with a trap-safe lifetime scheme, or avoid dereferencing unloadable metadata from the lockless resolver. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC ExecSMP, TLSF enabled, debug.library loaded, a fatal backtrace, and module metadata freeing that is not serialized by the backtrace's allocator lock. **Confidence:** high for lockless traversal and record-free behavior; low-to-medium for the selected allocator/header overlap, which depends on runtime memory-header placement and was not established from source. This is distinct from EK10321, where `DecodeLocationA()` uses the semaphore during lookup but returns borrowed names after releasing it. No allocator corruption, trap, or unload was induced; source-only; see the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#kernel-backtrace-resolver-module-lifetime-ek10322).


<a id="ek10323-private-realtime-conductor-sentinel-is-later-treated-as-a-name-pointer"></a>
<a id="ek10323"></a>
### EK10323 — Private RealTime conductor sentinel is later treated as a name pointer

`CreatePlayerA()` documents `PLAYER_Conductor = ~0` as the request to create a private conductor (`workbench/libs/realtime/createplayera.c:58-61`). `SetPlayerAttrsA()` forwards that sentinel as the `name` argument to `createConductor()` (`workbench/libs/realtime/setplayerattrsa.c:124-128`); `createConductor()` stores it in `cdt_Link.ln_Name` and adds the conductor, including private conductors, to `rtb_ConductorList` (`:325-350`). A later `FindConductor()` calls Exec `FindName()` on the entire list and only checks `CONDUCTF_PRIVATE` after the name search (`workbench/libs/realtime/findconductor.c:61-71`). `FindName()` treats every non-NULL `ln_Name` as a C string and passes it to `strcmp()` (`rom/exec/findname.c:77-84`). Since the private sentinel is non-NULL and invalid as a string pointer, traversal reaching that node can fault before `FindConductor()` can reject it as private.

**Trigger and consequence:** create a player with the documented private-conductor sentinel, then call `FindConductor()` for a name not found earlier in the list, or create a player on a new named conductor (which takes the same lookup path). The lookup reaches the private node and `strcmp()` dereferences the sentinel, disrupting conductor lookup and potentially faulting the caller. The explicitly buildable Animation datatype creates players with `PLAYER_Conductor = ~0` (`workbench/classes/datatypes/animation/animationclass.c:136-157`), establishing an in-tree source of the malformed list entry; a later unmatched lookup is the additional trigger. No checked-in caller was found that performs that lookup after the Animation path creates a private conductor, so the failing follow-up depends on a public/external `FindConductor()` call or a later named `CreatePlayerA()` call. Set the stored name to NULL for private conductors or have `FindConductor()` skip private nodes before name comparison. **Affected configuration:** an explicitly built `realtime.library` with a private conductor followed by an unmatched named lookup; the explicitly buildable Animation datatype supplies private conductors, but no checked-in follow-up lookup was found. **Confidence:** high for sentinel propagation, global-list publication, and the unconditional non-NULL string comparison; no lookup or fault was run. Source-only; see the [coverage trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#realtime-private-conductor-name-sentinel-ek10323).

<a id="ek8910"></a>
### EK8910 — `sem_timedwait` can return timeout while a semaphore permit is available

`sem_timedwait()` holds `sem->lock` while checking `sem->value` and entering `pthread_cond_timedwait()`. After the condition wait returns, it decrements `waiters_count`; if the result is nonzero, it unlocks and returns that error before checking `sem->value` again. It consumes a permit only on the zero-result path (`compiler/pthread/semaphore.c:226-263`). `sem_post()` increments `sem->value` before signaling a registered waiter, under the same mutex (`:268-294`). The selected condition implementation waits on both the timer signal and the condition waiter's signal, then gives the timer bit priority: if it is present, it returns `ETIMEDOUT` without considering the condition signal (`compiler/pthread/pthread_cond_timedwait.c:128-169`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a timed waiter starts with value zero; before its `Wait()` returns, a post publishes a permit and signals it while the timer signal is also pending. The condition wait returns `ETIMEDOUT`; `sem_timedwait()` propagates that result without consuming or rechecking the now-positive value. The caller sees a timeout even though a permit is available, and that permit remains for a later wait. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting this `linklib-pthread` implementation and an external or application caller using `sem_timedwait()`; the only maintained in-tree `sem_wait()` wrapper passes a NULL deadline, so this timed trigger is not established for an in-tree call site. **Confidence:** high for the mutex-protected publication, timer-first return and skipped count check; the finding requires the stated simultaneous timer/post signal state. Recheck the semaphore predicate after wakeup before returning timeout when a permit is available. No timed wait, post, timer race, or build was run; source-only; see the [coverage trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#sem-timedwait-timeout-with-available-permit-ek8910).

<a id="ek8952"></a>
### EK8952 — Reusing a deleted pthread key exposes stale per-thread values

`pthread_key_delete()` marks a key slot unused and clears its destructor, but leaves the per-thread `tlsvalues[]` entries intact (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:201-225`; `pthread_intern.h:104-123`). A later `pthread_key_create()` selects the first unused slot, installs the new destructor, and does not reset that slot in currently active threads (`compiler/pthread/pthread_key_create.c:26-59`). `pthread_getspecific()` then returns the saved slot value directly (`pthread_getspecific.c:26-42`), and worker-exit cleanup dispatches the newly registered destructor on any non-NULL value at that index (`pthread_create.c:180-197`). POSIX requires a newly created key to be associated with NULL in all active threads ([`pthread_key_create(3p)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_key_create.3p.html)).

**Trigger and consequence:** a live pthread thread stores a non-NULL value for key *k*; another thread deletes *k* and creates a new key before the first thread exits, with no lower-numbered key slot available, so the allocator reuses *k*. The live thread then observes its old value through `pthread_getspecific(new_key)`, and its exit path can pass that old pointer to the new key's destructor. This can associate unrelated per-thread state with the new key; if the old value was released as part of deleting the old key, the new destructor can receive an invalid pointer. Clear each active thread's value when assigning a new key generation, or otherwise distinguish generations. **Affected configuration:** applications linking the explicitly buildable `linklibs-pthread` implementation (`compiler/pthread/mmakefile.src:14-48,51-53`); the parent aggregate dependency is optional, and no checked-in caller of the key APIs was found. **Confidence:** high for slot reuse, retained values, getter/destructor consumers, and the POSIX initial-value requirement; manifestation requires a live thread with a stale non-NULL slot and index reuse. No pthread call, destructor, or thread was run; source-only. See the [TLS key reuse coverage trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#pthread-tls-key-reuse-ek8952-rechecked).

<a id="ek10324"></a>
### EK10324 — PosixC thread-exit hook can close and unload the code it is returning through

`pthread` invokes registered leave hooks from `StarterFunc()` before it publishes thread completion or reclaims detached-thread state (`compiler/pthread/pthread_create.c:199-208`). PosixC's `posixc_thread_leave()` retrieves the worker's private PosixC base and calls `CloseLibrary(base)` directly from its own code (`compiler/crt/posixc/__threadhook.c:85-97`). PosixC is built with `pertaskbase` and `rellinklib` (`compiler/crt/posixc/posixc.conf:6`). The generated close vector decrements the root library open count and, when it reaches zero with `LIBF_DELEXP`, tail-calls expunge (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1499-1518`). Generated expunge invokes the module's expunge hooks, frees its base and returns the segment list (`:1557-1590`). The selected LDDemon `CloseLibrary()` wrapper immediately passes that segment list to `UnLoadSeg()` before returning to its caller (`rom/lddemon/lddemon.c:569-592`). Therefore, when this worker's close is the final reference after a delayed expunge request, the callback returns into PosixC code that has already been unloaded.

**Trigger and consequence:** a client requests delayed expunge of `posixc.library` while it remains open (for example through `RemLibrary()`); the process/base that owns the remaining non-worker reference closes, and a pthread worker subsequently exits with its PosixC reference last. `posixc_thread_leave()` then triggers expunge from inside itself. The return address targets reclaimed module code, so the worker may execute freed/reused instructions before returning to pthread cleanup. No checked-in PosixC `RemLibrary()` caller was found; automatic LDDemon expunge skips libraries with nonzero open counts, so this is conditional on an explicit delayed-expunge request and final-reference ordering, not ordinary worker exit. Defer the last library close until after the hook returns, or otherwise hold the module code alive through callback return. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting both `compiler/pthread` and the PosixC pertask-base library, with a delayed expunge request and the stated last-reference ordering. **Confidence:** high for the callback/close/expunge/unload source order; low-to-medium for occurrence because the required explicit expunge request and last-reference sequence are not established by a checked-in caller. No library expunge, thread exit or build was run; source-only. See the [thread-hook close lifetime trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-thread-exit-hook-self-expunge-ek10324).


<a id="ek10325"></a>
### EK10325 — `SaveTaskStorage` fails to compile when task.resource debug logging is enabled

`SaveTaskStorage()` declares the saved slot count as `slots` and uses it for allocation and copying (`rom/task/SaveTaskStorage.c:52-65`), but its debug log passes an undeclared identifier `size` (`:68-70`). The `D(...)` macro expands its argument when `DEBUG` is nonzero (`compiler/arossupport/include/debug.h:22-24,298-300`), so compiling the selected task.resource source with `-DDEBUG=1` produces an undeclared-identifier error. The task.resource manifest currently leaves its local `-DDEBUG=1` option commented (`rom/task/mmakefile.src:22-25`), and `DEBUG` defaults to zero, so the ordinary selected build does not hit this compile failure. Replace `size` with the intended slot count or byte count in the diagnostic. **Affected configuration and trigger:** explicit `kernel-task` builds that enable debug logging for `rom/task/SaveTaskStorage.c`. **Consequence:** the task.resource build fails at this translation unit. **Confidence:** high for the undeclared identifier and conditional macro expansion; this is not a default-build failure. No debug build was run; source-only; see the [task-storage snapshot trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2150).


<a id="ek10326"></a>
### EK10326 — Darwin AArch64 hosted kernel cannot compile its signal-context save/restore path

The Darwin AArch64 context header's `SAVEREGS` and `RESTOREREGS` macros use `sizeof(struct VFPContext)` when copying the signal frame's NEON state (`arch/all-darwin/kernel/cpu_aarch64.h:92-123`). The selected Unix context-switch implementation expands both macros (`arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:90,135`). The AArch64 context header included by this target defines `struct ExceptionContext` and its `fpuContext` pointer but does not define `struct VFPContext` (`arch/aarch64-all/include/aros/cpucontext.h:12-34`); the only AArch64 definition in this checkout is in the native-kernel private header, which this hosted target does not include (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_intern.h:98-105`). The selected Darwin target combines the Unix kernel source list with the Darwin architecture overlay (`arch/all-unix/kernel/mmakefile.src:49-51`; `arch/all-darwin/kernel/mmakefile.src`), while `configure.in` explicitly supports the macOS arm64 target at lines 1814-1845.

**Trigger and consequence:** build the Darwin hosted kernel for AArch64/macOS arm64. Expanding `SAVEREGS`/`RESTOREREGS` requires the size of an incomplete `struct VFPContext`, so the selected `kernel_cpu.c` translation unit is rejected by the C compiler. Define and include the Darwin/AArch64 saved NEON state layout (or use the SDK's corresponding state size) before these macros are expanded, then audit allocation and initialization of `fpuContext` as a separate context-lifecycle requirement. **Affected configuration:** Darwin hosted AArch64; other Darwin CPU targets use separate CPU headers. **Confidence:** high for the selected source/macro path and missing AArch64 definition in the checkout; no build was run to confirm a particular toolchain diagnostic. Source-only; see the [Darwin AArch64 context-header review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#darwin-aarch64-signal-context-header-ek10326).


<a id="ek10327"></a>
### EK10327 — Darwin x86-64 signal switch copies beyond each task's FXSAVE buffer

The Darwin x86-64 `SAVEREGS` and `RESTOREREGS` macros copy `sizeof(struct FPXSContext)` bytes through `cc->regs.FXSData` (`arch/all-darwin/kernel/cpu_x86_64.h:176-192`). In the selected hosted configuration, `KrnCreateContext()` takes the non-standalone branch and sets `FXSData` to a 16-byte-aligned tail (`arch/x86_64-all/kernel/createcontext.c:38-58`); `cpu_Init()` reserves `sizeof(struct FPFXSContext) + 15` bytes for that tail (`arch/x86_64-all/kernel/cpu_init.c:93-97`). `FPFXSContext` is the 512-byte FXSAVE area, while `FPXSContext` adds a 64-byte XSAVE header before its flexible extended area (`arch/x86_64-all/include/aros/cpucontext.h:23-50`), so `sizeof(struct FPXSContext)` is 576 bytes. The alignment allowance is at most 15 bytes and cannot cover the extra 64-byte copy.

**Trigger and consequence:** create and dispatch an Exec task in the Darwin x86-64 hosted target. Its initial context already sets `ECF_FPFXS`, so `RESTOREREGS()` reads 576 bytes from a buffer with at most 527 allocated bytes; later `SAVEREGS()` writes 576 bytes there, extending at least 49 bytes beyond the requested context allocation. The save can overwrite adjacent Exec memory, while the restore also reads outside the task context. Copy only the 512-byte legacy FXSAVE structure on this path, or allocate and initialize a matching XSAVE buffer and use its corresponding flag/type. **Affected configuration:** Darwin hosted x86-64, selected by the macOS x86-64 branch (`configure.in:1728-1767`) and the Unix kernel's `kernel_cpu` source list. **Confidence:** high for the structure-size mismatch, hosted allocation size, and selected macro consumers; no build or task dispatch was run. Source-only; see the [Darwin x86-64 context-header review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#darwin-x86-64-signal-context-header-ek10327).


<a id="ek10328"></a>
### EK10328 — Darwin AArch64 hosted task contexts never preserve NEON state

The Darwin AArch64 signal-switch macros only copy NEON state when the AROS context has an FPU buffer (`arch/all-darwin/kernel/cpu_aarch64.h:102-107,121-123`); restore additionally requires `ECF_FPU`. The selected Darwin hosted target uses `arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel_cpu.c` and generic context code from `rom/kernel`. Its generic `cpu_Init()` sets `kb_ContextSize` to exactly `sizeof(struct AROSCPUContext)` (`rom/kernel/cpu_init.c:18-22`), and generic `KrnCreateContext()` allocates that many bytes with `MEMF_CLEAR` (`rom/kernel/kernel_objects.h:11`; `rom/kernel/createcontext.c:52-60`). Darwin AArch64's `AROSCPUContext` embeds `ExceptionContext` plus `errno_backup` (`arch/all-darwin/kernel/cpu_aarch64.h:152-157`); it allocates no trailing VFP state and leaves `regs.fpuContext` zero. The selected AArch64 `PrepareContext()` also explicitly sets `ctx->Flags = 0` (`arch/aarch64-all/exec/preparecontext.c:72-80`). A repository-wide search found no other assignment to `fpuContext`; the generic allocation is used both for new tasks (`arch/aarch64-all/exec/preparecontext.c:29-32`) and Exec's bootstrap task (`rom/exec/exec_init.c:159-164`). Therefore the save macro skips the signal frame's FP/NEON state, and the restore macro likewise skips it; task switches can expose one task's vector-register state to another and resume a task with clobbered FP/vector state. **Trigger and consequence:** run Darwin AArch64 hosted Exec tasks that use floating-point/NEON registers across scheduler or signal-driven context switches; the bootstrap task's first saved context has the same missing state. **Affected configuration:** Darwin hosted AArch64/macOS arm64. This remains independently necessary after resolving EK10326's missing `VFPContext` compile-time definition; fixing that type alone does not allocate or enable per-task FP state. **Confidence:** high for the selected allocation and guards; actual Darwin signal-frame behavior and runtime corruption were not tested. Source-only; see the [Darwin AArch64 context lifecycle pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#darwin-aarch64-fpu-context-lifecycle-ek10328).


<a id="ek153"></a>
### EK153 — ARM32 ExecSMP secondary bootstrap dereferences its uninitialized task memory list

In `cpu_InitBootStrap()`, ARM32 allocates the task object using `AllocMem(sizeof(struct Task), MEMF_PUBLIC|MEMF_CLEAR)` (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_execsmp.c:38-40`), then calls `AddHead(&bstask->tc_MemEntry, &ml->ml_Node)` at line 65 before `NEWLIST(&bstask->tc_MemEntry)` at line 80. `tc_MemEntry` is the embedded memory list in `struct Task` (`compiler/include/exec/tasks.h:62`), so `MEMF_CLEAR` leaves its `lh_Head` null. The selected Exec `AddHead()` implementation dereferences `list->lh_Head` to update its predecessor (`rom/exec/addhead.c:60-69`); the public `ADDHEAD` inline has the same sentinel-list precondition (`compiler/include/exec/lists.h:108-120`). This writes through the null list head before a valid list exists. Even if that write did not fault on a given memory map, the subsequent `NEWLIST()` would overwrite the link and detach the allocated `MemList` from the task, so its task/stack allocations would not be reclaimed through `RemTask()`.
