The selected ARM32 SMP `cpu_Register()` invokes this routine for each secondary core (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:185-186`), and the Raspberry Pi BCM2708 primary waits for the registering CPU to release `startup_lock` (`arch/arm-native/kernel/platform_bcm2708.c:143-159`). **Trigger and consequence:** bring up a configured ARM32 Raspberry Pi ExecSMP secondary after the task, stack and MemList allocations succeed. The list operation accesses a null-derived address and can fault or corrupt low memory before the secondary reaches `cpu_Register()`'s unlock; the primary's wait then does not complete. **Affected configuration:** ARM32/ARMEB Raspberry Pi native ExecSMP. **Confidence:** high that the cleared list header is passed to an operation that dereferences its null head and that NEWLIST follows too late; exact fault versus low-memory effect depends on the target mapping. No CPU was started and no runtime fault was induced. Initialize the list before inserting the MemList node. Source-only; see the [ARM32 secondary-bootstrap trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1393).


<a id="ek726"></a>
### EK726 — AArch64 ExecSMP secondary bootstrap dereferences its uninitialized task memory list

The AArch64 `cpu_InitBootStrap()` has the same ordering as ARM32: it allocates the task object with `MEMF_PUBLIC|MEMF_CLEAR` (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_execsmp.c:38-40`), calls `AddHead()` on the zeroed `tc_MemEntry` at line 60, and initializes that list only later at line 75. `AddHead()` dereferences the null `lh_Head` to update the old first node (`rom/exec/addhead.c:60-69`); the selected `ADDHEAD` inline has the same requirement (`compiler/include/exec/lists.h:108-120`). The later `NEWLIST()` would also discard the MemList node's link if execution continues. This is the same root defect as EK153, independently present in the AArch64 implementation.

The selected Raspberry Pi AArch64 SMP `cpu_Register()` reaches this constructor before its startup-lock release (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:168-169,191`); unlike ARM32, the BCM27xx primary waits with a bounded counter-based timeout and reports a CPU that did not report in before continuing (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/platform_bcm27xx.c:282-298,423-428`). **Trigger and consequence:** bring up a configured AArch64 Raspberry Pi ExecSMP secondary after its task, stack and MemList allocations succeed. The secondary encounters a null-derived list write before it can register; it may fault or corrupt low memory and does not complete CPU registration. The primary's timeout prevents this source path alone from establishing a whole-system boot hang; the separate stale-online-mask consequences remain covered by EK8904. **Affected configuration:** Raspberry Pi AArch64 native ExecSMP. **Confidence:** high for the list initialization order and startup call path; exact memory effect and subsequent firmware/core state depend on the target mapping. No CPU was started and no runtime fault was induced. Initialize the list before inserting the MemList node. Source-only; see the [AArch64 secondary-bootstrap trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1070).
<a id="ek10329"></a>
### EK10329 — `TASKTAG_TCBEXTRASIZE` can wrap the task allocation size

`NewCreateTaskA()` starts with `nml_ME[0].me_Length == sizeof(struct Task)` and adds the caller's `TASKTAG_TCBEXTRASIZE` directly to that `ULONG` without checking for overflow (`rom/exec/newcreatetaska.c:20-31,158-159`). AROS defines `ULONG` as an unsigned 32-bit type (`compiler/include/exec/types.h:37-43`), so the addition wraps modulo 2^32. The resulting length is passed unchanged to `NewAllocEntry()` (`newcreatetaska.c:190-192`), which allocates exactly each nonzero `me_Length` (`rom/exec/newallocentry.c:105-143`). `NewCreateTaskA()` then writes the task's fields, stack bounds, and embedded memory-list links through that allocation before passing it to `NewAddTask()` (`newcreatetaska.c:194-254`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a `NewCreateTaskA()` caller supplies an extra-size value whose addition wraps to a nonzero value smaller than `sizeof(struct Task)`, and the small allocation succeeds. The function treats that undersized block as a complete `Task` and writes fields beyond the allocated block; later `NewAddTask()` also consumes it as a task object. Reject values exceeding `ULONG_MAX - sizeof(struct Task)` before adding, or perform a checked size calculation. **Affected configuration:** all targets using the selected AROS `NewCreateTaskA()` implementation and 32-bit `ULONG`; the API documents the extra-size tag but specifies no upper bound. No checked-in C/header caller of `TASKTAG_TCBEXTRASIZE` was found, so reachability is through public API clients rather than a demonstrated maintained caller. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked fixed-width addition and undersized allocation/write sequence; allocation success and caller-supplied extreme value are conditional. No task or allocation was created; source-only; see the [task-extra-size overflow trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#tasktag-tcbextrasize-allocation-overflow-ek10329).


<a id="ek10330"></a>
### EK10330 — Unix SAD changes shared stderr status flags for the whole process

Unix `KrnObtainInput()` reads the current flags on descriptor 2 and sets `O_NONBLOCK` (`arch/all-unix/kernel/obtaininput.c:30-38`), but does not retain the original flags. The built-in SAD calls this before entering its input loop (`rom/exec/debug_internal.c:37-46`). That loop does not disable task switching; the Unix timer path may schedule other AROS tasks while SAD polls (`arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel.c:153-164`; `arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel_intr.c:24-55`). The Unix emulation handler represents its standard-error handle with the same descriptor number 2 (`arch/all-unix/filesys/emul_handler/emul_host_unix.c:98-105,153-155`), and its `DoWrite()` issues a host `write()` on that descriptor, maps a failed call through `err_u2a()`, and returns `-1` (`arch/all-unix/filesys/emul_handler/emul_host.c:619-635`). The host error mapping has no `EAGAIN` entry and falls through to `ERROR_UNKNOWN` (`:49-70`). `ACTION_WRITE` returns this result and error in the DOS packet reply (`arch/all-hosted/filesys/emul_handler/emul_handler.c:867-879,1372-1374`). If descriptor 2 refers to a full pipe while such a task writes during SAD, the temporary nonblocking mode can make the write fail with `EAGAIN` instead of waiting, surfacing to the guest as a failed write with `ERROR_UNKNOWN`. On normal SAD quit, `KrnReleaseInput()` clears `O_NONBLOCK` unconditionally (`arch/all-unix/kernel/releaseinput.c:30-36`); when descriptor 2 was already nonblocking before entry, the prior status is lost after release.

**Trigger and consequence:** Unix-hosted build with SAD entered through the built-in debugger; either (a) the Unix emulation handler writes to stderr while SAD has set descriptor 2 nonblocking and the pipe is full, causing `DoWrite()` to return an I/O error, or (b) descriptor 2 was initially nonblocking and SAD exits normally, leaving it blocking. The first effect requires the optional Unix emulation handler and the stated pipe/write overlap; the second requires initially nonblocking stderr. **Affected configuration:** Unix-hosted targets using `arch/all-unix/kernel/{obtaininput,releaseinput}.c`; the concurrent-write case additionally requires the Unix emulation handler and a pipe-like stderr. **Confidence:** high for the status-flag mutation, shared descriptor use, and error propagation; the trigger depends on the stated descriptor and scheduling conditions. Avoid changing shared stderr flags for polling, or preserve and restore the original state. No debugger, host descriptor, pipe, or write was exercised; source-only. See the [Unix input coverage trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#unix-sad-shared-stderr-status-flags-ek10330).

<a id="ek10331--ftime-stores-microseconds-as-milliseconds"></a>
<a id="ek10331"></a>
### EK10331 — `ftime()` stores microseconds as milliseconds

The selected POSIX C link-library implementation copies `tv.tv_usec * 1000` into `struct timeb.millitm` (`compiler/crt/posixc/ftime.c:53-61`). The public type defines `millitm` as an `unsigned short` and the function documents that field as milliseconds (`compiler/crt/posixc/include/aros/posixc/sys/timeb.h:15-22`; `ftime.c:22-28`). `gettimeofday()` supplies `tv_usec` in microseconds. The multiplication therefore converts in the wrong direction; the value assigned to the 16-bit field also wraps for most nonzero fractions. For example, 1,000 microseconds (1 ms) becomes 1,000,000, then truncates to 16,960 rather than 1.

**Trigger and consequence:** any successful `ftime()` call during a second with a fractional time other than a coincidental value reports an invalid `millitm`; consumers computing sub-second time from it get a wrong result. **Affected configuration:** programs linking the selected POSIX C `ftime` link library (`compiler/crt/posixc/mmakefile.src:311-319`). The implementation is deprecated but remains declared in the public `<sys/timeb.h>`. **Confidence:** high; the source units, destination type, and assignment are explicit. Divide `tv_usec` by 1,000 before storing. No call or clock value was exercised; source-only.

<a id="ek10332--ftime-reports-success-after-gettimeofday-fails"></a>
<a id="ek10332"></a>
### EK10332 — `ftime()` reports success after `gettimeofday()` fails

`ftime()` ignores the return value from `gettimeofday(&tv, &tz)` and unconditionally copies both automatic structures to the caller before returning 0 (`compiler/crt/posixc/ftime.c:53-63`). In the selected implementation, `gettimeofday()` returns -1 with `errno = EACCES` when the timer device cannot be opened and leaves `tv` and `tz` unwritten (`compiler/crt/posixc/gettimeofday.c:101-117`). `__init_timerbase()` leaves the per-task timer base unset when `OpenDevice()` fails (`compiler/crt/posixc/__posixc_timer.c:31-45`); timer resources are initialized per task and closed through the selected close hook (`posixc.conf:1-6`; `__posixc_timer.c:48-57`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a POSIX C task calls `ftime()` while its timer-device open fails. `ftime()` returns success and publishes indeterminate stack values as time and timezone instead of propagating the underlying failure. **Affected configuration:** POSIX C users of the selected `ftime` link library when `timer.device` cannot be opened. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked return and unwritten outputs; manifestation is conditional on timer-open failure. Return an error when `gettimeofday()` fails, without copying its outputs. No device failure or function call was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek10333"></a>
### EK10333 — ARM `GetCPUInfo()` returns incorrect model, version, and vendor identity fields

The ARM probe reads the Main ID Register and saves its implementer field in `VendorID` (`arch/arm-native/processor/processor_util.c:55-58`), but does not extract the part number, variant, or revision. Its per-core record is allocated with `MEMF_CLEAR` (`processor_init.c:47-50`), and a source-wide assignment search finds no later write to `Model`; `ARMProcessorInformation` has no version field (`processor_arch_intern.h:13-35`). `ARM_AnswerTag()` returns the untouched, zero-initialized `Model` for `GCIT_Model` and has no `GCIT_Version` case (`getcpuinfo.c:104-109,148-150`). For `GCIT_Vendor`, it stores `processor->Vendor`, a `CONST_STRPTR`, into the output (`:148-150`) even though the public ARM contract defines this tag as the numeric implementer ID (`compiler/include/resources/processor.h:30-34,65`). The numeric ID is already available as `processor->VendorID`; the separate `Vendor` field is a descriptive string (`processor_arch_intern.h:16-17`; `processor_util.c:274-299`).

Both maintained ARM-specific display clients use `ULONG` output slots for model, version, and vendor. ShowConfig then matches the vendor value against the first-byte implementer IDs and prints the model plus decoded revision/variant (`workbench/tools/ShowConfig/cpu_arm.c:33-72`); SysExplorer does the same (`workbench/tools/SysExplorer/cpu_arm.c:34-86`). On ARM32, the model and version therefore display as zero, while vendor lookup receives the string pointer value instead of the implementer ID and reports an unknown vendor. ShowConfig reaches the getter through `GetCoreInfo()`'s selected-core forwarding (`rom/processor/getcoreinfo.c:78-93`); SysExplorer passes `GCIT_SelectedProcessor` directly. These are display errors; no claim is made about CPU feature detection or scheduling.

**Trigger and consequence:** use the ARM32 `processor.resource` `GCIT_Model`, `GCIT_Version`, and/or `GCIT_Vendor` tags, as the checked-in ARM-specific ShowConfig and SysExplorer paths do. The queries return zeroed model/version values and a pointer value in the numeric vendor slot, so the displayed CPU identification is wrong. **Affected configuration:** ARM32 targets selecting `arch/arm-native/processor/getcpuinfo.c`, including the Raspberry Pi ARM processor-resource target. AArch64 uses the generic getter and is tracked separately as EK10334 because no maintained AArch64 caller was found. **Confidence:** high for the record initialization, absent field extraction/version case, vendor type mismatch, and selected display consumers; no tool or processor query was run. Extract and store the ARM MIDR part/variant/revision fields and return `VendorID` using the documented numeric output type. Source-only; see the [ARM processor identity caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#arm-processor-identity-tags-ek10333).


<a id="ek10334"></a>
### EK10334 — AArch64 processor resource leaves ARM model, version, and vendor outputs untouched

The Raspberry Pi AArch64 boot package includes `kernel-processor` (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/mmakefile.src:136,216`). The common processor module selects `init`, `getcpuinfo`, `getcoreinfo`, and `gettopology` and enables architecture-specific replacement (`rom/processor/mmakefile.src:20`), but this checkout has no AArch64 processor override directory; the package therefore uses `rom/processor/getcpuinfo.c`. The generic defaults explicitly classify `__aarch64__` as `PROCESSORARCH_ARM` (`rom/processor/defaults.h:27-32`).

The public resource header describes ARM `GCIT_Model`, `GCIT_Version`, and `GCIT_Vendor` outputs as the part number, revision/variant, and implementer ID (`compiler/include/resources/processor.h:30-34`; tag definitions at `:44-47,65`). The selected generic getter has no cases for these tags and no default branch that initializes unknown tags (`rom/processor/getcpuinfo.c:185-278`); `GetCoreInfo()` forwards per-core tags to that getter (`rom/processor/getcoreinfo.c:78-93`). Thus a caller that supplies these ARM tags receives no output update on AArch64, unlike the ARM identity values specified for the architecture family.

**Trigger and consequence:** an AArch64 Raspberry Pi client queries one or more of the ARM-specific identity tags through `GetCPUInfo()` or `GetCoreInfo()`. Its output variable remains at the caller's prior value, so processor identification is absent or stale. A repository-wide `GCIT_Model`/`GCIT_Version`/`GCIT_Vendor` caller search found no maintained AArch64 client; the trigger is limited to external or future callers, and no claim is made that current desktop tools display the defect. **Affected configuration:** Raspberry Pi AArch64 processor.resource using the generic getter. **Confidence:** high that the selected getter leaves these output locations untouched; medium that the ARM-specific tag contract is intended to apply to AArch64, with external caller reachability only. Add an AArch64 answerer or define and return an explicit unsupported/unknown result for these tags. No processor query, build, or runtime operation was performed; source-only; see the [AArch64 processor identity trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#aarch64-processor-identity-tags-ek10334).

<a id="ek10335"></a>
### EK10335 — The selected pthread library accepts asynchronous cancellation but does not deliver it asynchronously

`pthread_setcanceltype()` accepts `PTHREAD_CANCEL_ASYNCHRONOUS` and stores it in the calling thread's `ThreadInfo` (`compiler/pthread/pthread_setcanceltype.c:30-43`). When an enabled asynchronous target is canceled, `pthread_cancel()` sets `inf->canceled` and signals `SIGBREAKF_CTRL_C` (`pthread_cancel.c:34-50`). The code that turns that signal into immediate cancellation is conditional on `USE_ASYNC_CANCEL`: `StarterFunc()` installs `CancelHandler` and enables the task exception only inside that conditional (`pthread_create.c:99-130`), and the handler calls `pthread_testcancel()` (`pthread.c:910-933`). In the selected source that define is commented out (`pthread.c:40`); the selected link-library manifest includes the setters and cancel entry points (`compiler/pthread/mmakefile.src:14-48`). With the default configuration, no handler consumes the asynchronous request while ordinary user code runs. Cancellation is observed only if the target later reaches an explicit `pthread_testcancel()` or another path that checks the pending state.

**Trigger and consequence:** a thread sets its type to asynchronous, leaves cancellation enabled, and is canceled while executing code that does not reach a pthread cancellation point (for example, a compute loop). The API reports success from `pthread_cancel()`, but the target continues running instead of being canceled asynchronously; it may continue indefinitely. This finding concerns the default selected pthread implementation; builds that explicitly enable `USE_ASYNC_CANCEL` take the separate handler path. **Affected configuration:** applications linking `linklibs-pthread` with the default `compiler/pthread/pthread.c` configuration. **Confidence:** high for accepted mode, signal-only default path, and conditional handler installation; the non-termination outcome depends on the target not reaching a cancellation check. Either implement asynchronous delivery in the selected configuration or reject the unsupported cancellation type. No thread, cancellation request, build, or runtime operation was exercised; source-only.
<a id="ek10341"></a>
### EK10341 — `waitpid()` traverses the exited-child list without its port lock

The selected POSIXC `waitpid()` implementation runs `ListLength(&et->et_TaskMsgPort.mp_MsgList, exchildno)` unconditionally before its `WNOHANG` decision (`compiler/crt/posixc/waitpid.c:127-133`). `ListLength` is a plain `ForeachNode` walk over `lh_Head` and each node's `ln_Succ`; it takes no lock (`compiler/include/exec/lists.h:195-201,211-216`). On ExecSMP, `Exec_CleanupETask()` publishes a notifying child's ETask into this same list under `mp_SpinLock` (`rom/exec/exec_util.c:307-322`), and `ChildWait()`/`ChildStatus()` acquire that lock when they traverse the exited-child list (`rom/exec/childwait.c:92-108`; `rom/exec/childstatus.c:74-87`). `waitpid()`'s count walk does not. A cross-CPU child-exit publication can therefore overlap the pointer walk; unlike the subsequent protected `ChildStatus()` scan, this caller can observe the list while its links are being changed. For a specific PID, the computed count is still traversed even though the later branch does not use it; for `pid == -1`, it feeds the `WNOHANG` no-child decision. Use the same port lock for the count traversal or obtain the count through a synchronized Exec API.

**Trigger and consequence:** on an ExecSMP build, a parent calls the selected POSIX `waitpid()` while a notifying child exits on another CPU and is appended to the exited-child list. The unsynchronized traversal may follow a transient/inconsistently observed `ln_Succ` chain, causing a wrong child count or invalid list traversal; the precise manifestation depends on the interleaving and memory visibility. The active `ChildStatus()` finding EK812 concerns its separate unlocked live-child traversal and false `CHILD_NOTFOUND` window; EK10341 records the POSIX caller's additional unlocked traversal of the exited-child list. **Affected configuration:** ExecSMP builds with POSIXC `waitpid()` selected. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked traversal and concurrent locked publisher; medium for the list-corruption consequence, which depends on the cross-CPU observation. No child exit, wait, interleaving, or build was run; source-only.
<a id="ek10342"></a>
### EK10342 — `wait()` and `waitpid(-1)` fail to report `ECHILD` when the caller has no children

`waitpid()` converts `pid == -1` to `tid == 0` (`compiler/crt/posixc/waitpid.c:110-111`), but its no-child check only runs for nonzero `tid` (`:113-118`). For `WNOHANG`, it counts only already-exited children and returns zero when that list is empty (`:127-138`), without checking whether any eligible child exists. With blocking options, it passes zero to `ChildWait()`, whose loop waits for an exited child and never tests the parent's live-child list (`rom/exec/childwait.c:88-113`). `wait()` has the same blocking path: it checks only that the caller has an ETask, then directly calls `ChildWait(0)` without checking for children (`compiler/crt/posixc/wait.c:84-103`). If the caller has no child processes, `waitpid(-1, ..., WNOHANG)` therefore returns 0 instead of failing with `ECHILD`; `waitpid(-1, ..., 0)` and `wait()` wait indefinitely because no child can publish a completion or signal `SIGF_CHILD`.

The implementation's own synopsis defines `pid == -1` as waiting for any child (`waitpid.c:50-56`) and its result contract returns -1 on error (`:63-65`). POSIX specifies that `waitpid(-1, ...)` behaves like `wait()`; when the caller has no unwaited-for children, it fails with `ECHILD`, and `WNOHANG` returns zero only when at least one selected child exists but has no available status ([POSIX specification, FIPS PUB 151-2, wait/waitpid](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/FIPS/fipspub151-2.pdf#page=47)). This is distinct from EK812's concurrent false-not-found case for a specific child and EK10341's unlocked exited-list traversal.

**Trigger and consequence:** a POSIXC caller with no child processes invokes `waitpid(-1, ..., WNOHANG)` and receives a false “no status yet” result, or invokes the blocking `waitpid(-1, ..., 0)`/`wait()` and hangs instead of receiving `-1`/`ECHILD`. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting the POSIXC `wait.c` and `waitpid.c` sources (`compiler/crt/posixc/mmakefile.src:257-258`). **Confidence:** high for the source paths and API mismatch. No wait call or runtime behavior was exercised; source-only.
<a id="ek10343"></a>
### EK10343 — `WEXITSTATUS` does not parenthesize its argument

The selected POSIXC header defines `WEXITSTATUS(status)` as `(status & 0xff)` (`compiler/crt/posixc/include/aros/posixc/sys/wait.h:20`). The argument is not parenthesized before the bitwise AND. If a caller passes a conditional expression such as `WEXITSTATUS(choose_child ? status : fallback)`, C precedence parses the expansion as `choose_child ? status : (fallback & 0xff)`, so the true branch bypasses the intended low-eight-bit mask. A caller that passes a bitwise expression can similarly have only its final operand masked.

The header is included in the POSIXC copy set (`compiler/crt/posixc/include/mmakefile.src:3-5`). A repository-wide search found no maintained AROS caller passing a conditional or other precedence-sensitive expression; checked-in callers use simple variables or are in host-only code. Thus the issue is scoped to external/future POSIXC clients that pass a compound expression, and no current in-tree wrong return value is claimed. Parenthesize the parameter: `((status) & 0xff)`.

**Trigger and consequence:** a POSIXC client passes a conditional or bitwise compound expression to `WEXITSTATUS`, and the selected value contains bits above bit 7; the macro can return those bits instead of the low-byte exit code. **Affected configuration:** consumers using this POSIXC `sys/wait.h` header. **Confidence:** high for the macro expansion and precedence; no checked-in caller exercising the trigger was found. No caller or build was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10345"></a>
### EK10345 — Public OOP class lookup can race final class expunge [medium impact, high source confidence; trigger conditional]

`rom/oop/findclass.c:58-66` protects the public class-list traversal with `ob_ClassListLock` but returns the raw class pointer after releasing the lock. `rom/oop/newobject.c:75-91` then increments that class's `objectcount` only after `OOP_FindClass()` returns. Meanwhile, generated class shutdown removes the published class and immediately disposes its class object (`tools/genmodule/oopsupport.c:185-198`). `BaseMeta::Dispose()` frees the class name and dispatch tables without checking or waiting for `data->objectcount` (`rom/oop/basemetaclass.c:500-523`), before root disposal frees the class object itself (`rom/oop/rootclass.c:137-150`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a public `OOP_NewObject(NULL, classID, tags)` lookup overlaps provider expunge after `FindName()` returns but before the `objectcount` increment; shutdown can free the class in that gap, after which the creator increments freed metadata or dispatches `New()` through the freed class. A maintained second route is Workbench `MonWrapper`: when `OOP_FindClass(args.hidd)` already succeeds, `wrapper.c` skips `OpenLibrary(args.lib)` and passes the borrowed class pointer to `AddDisplayDriverA()` (`workbench/devs/monitors/wrapper/wrapper.c:69-94`; the optional `devs-monitors-wrapper` target is explicitly buildable at `workbench/devs/monitors/wrapper/mmakefile.src:29-32`). `AddDisplayDriverA()` and `driver_Setup()` retain/use that class pointer without opening its provider (`rom/graphics/adddisplaydrivera.c:166,186,237-285`; `rom/graphics/graphics_driver.c:326-380`). If the provider performs final expunge concurrently, these uses can dereference freed class state. **Affected configuration:** generated OOP class modules using standard `ADD2EXPUNGECLASSES`, including the optional monitor wrapper path, when a class is looked up without a provider reference that prevents final expunge. No checked-in concurrent expunge schedule was established; the class lifetime overlap remains timing-dependent. This is distinct from OD1687's teardown with an already-live SMBIOS IPMI instance. **Confidence:** high for the unpinned lookup, generated disposal, and maintained MonWrapper borrow/use path; medium for the required final-expunge overlap in a supported deployment. No class lookup, object creation, expunge, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10347"></a>
### EK10347 — Console handler reports bytes written after the console device accepts none

The console device retains a trailing incomplete CSI escape sequence in `icu->pendingCSI` when a `CMD_WRITE` ends with that sequence (`rom/devs/console/support.c:162-170`). On the next write, `writeToConsole()` must allocate a temporary buffer to join the pending bytes with the new data. If `AllocMem(pl + towrite, MEMF_ANY)` fails, it returns zero immediately (`:116-127`). `CMD_WRITE` stores this return in `io_Actual` (`rom/devs/console/console.c:321-332`); the device's `BeginIO()` initializes its completion error to zero and the allocation-failure return does not change it (`:270-277,404-416`).

The selected `kernel-fs-con` handler submits the DOS packet through `do_write()`, which calls `DoIO()` and discards its return value (`rom/filesys/console_handler/support.c:395-402`). `answer_write_request()` then replies with the original requested `length`, regardless of the device's `io_Actual` (`:1095-1118`). DOS `Write()` returns the handler's packet result as the number of bytes written (`rom/dos/write.c:35-43,59-73`). Thus this allocation failure makes `Write()` claim that all newly supplied bytes were written even though the device accepted zero of them; the caller can discard or advance past data that was never processed.

**Trigger and consequence:** one write leaves an incomplete CSI sequence pending, and the next console write encounters failure allocating the merge buffer. The second write returns its full requested length while the device reports zero accepted bytes. **Affected configuration:** the selected `kernel-fs-con` handler with `console.device`; the trigger requires a pending CSI sequence and allocation failure. **Confidence:** high for the result propagation mismatch and conditional data-loss consequence. No allocation failure, console write, or build was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek10346"></a>
### EK10346 — Console handler does not handle failure to allocate its read signal.

`open_con()` allocates custom signals for `conreadmp` and `conwritemp` with `AllocSignal(-1)` and stores both return values directly in byte-sized `mp_SigBit` fields without checking the documented `-1` failure result (`rom/filesys/console_handler/con_handler.c:565-581`; `rom/exec/allocsignal.c:34-44`). The read port receives asynchronous `SendIO()` requests (`con_handler.c:646-661`); the handler later computes `1L << fh->conreadmp->mp_SigBit` for its `Wait()` set (`:763-778`) and uses that mask to recognize completed reads (`:951-957`). The write port is installed on `conwriteio` (`:312,371`), and `do_write()` calls `DoIO()` (`rom/filesys/console_handler/support.c:397-401`); when the device does not complete synchronously, Exec's `WaitIO()` waits on `1 << io_Message.mn_ReplyPort->mp_SigBit` (`rom/exec/doio.c:61-68`; `rom/exec/waitio.c:72-88`). On either allocation failure, `-1` is stored as 255; shifting a 32-bit `1L` by that value is undefined in C, and the resulting wait mask cannot reliably represent the requested signal. A completed read may not be recognized and drained, or a synchronous write may remain blocked waiting for its reply signal.

**Trigger and consequence:** all allocatable task signal bits are already occupied when the handler opens a console stream, so one or both allocations fail. Depending on which one fails and whether the device completes I/O synchronously, the handler can miss an asynchronous read completion or block in `DoIO()` while waiting for a write reply. Exec's `CreateMsgPort()` checks the `AllocSignal()` result and returns failure if it cannot obtain a signal (`rom/exec/createmsgport.c:55-70`); the console handler's manual ports do not. **Affected configuration:** selected `kernel-fs-con` cooked/raw console and device-backed stream opens. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked failure and out-of-range shift; medium for the precise wait manifestation because the shift is undefined and target/compiler behavior varies. Check both `AllocSignal()` results and unwind the open if required signals are unavailable. No signal exhaustion, console I/O, or build was induced; source-only.
<a id="ek10349"></a>
### EK10349 — Hosted ARM processor initialization leaks earlier model strings

The hosted ARM processor initializer scans all of `/proc/cpuinfo`; for every line matching `Processor`, it calls `StrDup(val)` and assigns the result directly to the single `data->Model` field (`arch/arm-linux/processor/arch_init.c:164-185`). `StrDup()` allocates a new `AllocVec()` block (`compiler/alib/strdup.c:47-56`). When another matching line is read, the prior pointer is overwritten without `FreeVec()`, and only the last pointer remains reachable through `ProcessorBase->Private1` (`arch_init.c:251`). Thus each additional matching line leaks one model-string allocation for the lifetime of the processor resource. If an allocation fails, `StrDup()` returns null and the field is still overwritten; the checked-in SysExplorer and ShowConfig callers substitute “Unknown,” so no separate null-display failure is established (`workbench/tools/SysExplorer/computer_page_cl.c:219,227-228`; `workbench/tools/ShowConfig/ShowConfig.c:153,184-185`).

**Trigger and consequence:** the hosted ARM Linux `/proc/cpuinfo` contains multiple `Processor:` lines; all but the final duplicated model string are leaked during processor.resource initialization. The leak grows with the number of matching lines and is limited to this one-time resource initialization.

**Affected configuration:** hosted ARM Linux builds selecting `arch/arm-linux/processor/arch_init.c`. The trigger depends on the host file containing repeated `Processor` records; no ARM host file or resource initialization was exercised.

**Confidence:** high for the allocation and pointer overwrite; conditional for the host-file trigger. Reuse one owned model string or free the previous allocation before replacing it. Source-only; see the [hosted ARM processor initializer ownership recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#hosted-arm-processor-initializer-ownership-ek10349).

<a id="ek10351"></a>
### EK10351 — `NewCreateTaskA()` reads a nonexistent name entry for unnamed tasks

`NewCreateTaskA()` starts its allocation template with two entries: the `Task` and its stack. It increases `nml_NumEntries` to three only when `TASKTAG_NAME` is present, and to four when `TASKTAG_TASKMSGPORT` is requested (`rom/exec/newcreatetaska.c:19-32,127-153`). `NewAllocEntry()` sizes its returned `MemList` to exactly `ml_NumEntries` entries and initializes only those entries (`rom/exec/newallocentry.c:82-84,102-144`). With neither optional tag, the returned list therefore has entries 0 and 1 only. The constructor nonetheless reads `ml->ml_ME[2].me_Addr` unconditionally (`newcreatetaska.c:190-203`), reading a pointer-sized value beyond the returned MemList allocation and storing it in `tc_Node.ln_Name`. Its value depends on adjacent allocator contents. `NewAddTask()` supplies a fallback name only if that field is NULL (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:192-219`), so a nonzero value from beyond the allocation bypasses the fallback. Later name-based lookup reaches `FindName()`, which passes non-NULL node names to `strcmp()` (`rom/exec/findtask.c:63-79`; `rom/exec/findname.c:76-85`); an invalid value can therefore fault or make the task name unreliable.

**Maintained trigger:** ARM-native SMP `Processor_Init()` creates one probe task for each secondary CPU using `TASKTAG_AFFINITY`, `TASKTAG_PRI`, `TASKTAG_PC`, and three arguments, but supplies neither `TASKTAG_NAME` nor `TASKTAG_TASKMSGPORT` (`arch/arm-native/processor/processor_init.c:45-75`). The processor manifest selects this file for ARM and big-endian ARM (`arch/arm-native/processor/mmakefile.src:5-17`); the affected call occurs when SMP is enabled, a secondary CPU exists, and signal allocation succeeds. The out-of-bounds value is allocator-content-dependent; if it happens to be zero, `NewAddTask()` uses its fallback and this manifestation is absent. A second checked-in route exists in the optional m68kemu library: its generated `NewCreateTaskA()` thunk translates the guest tag list and passes it directly to native `NewCreateTaskA()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2466-2472`). `m68k_to_native_taglist()` returns NULL for a zero guest tag pointer, and otherwise copies the supplied tags without adding a task name or message-port tag (`m68kemu_shadow.c:136-161`); a guest caller omitting both tags therefore reaches the same native out-of-bounds read when this optional bridge is built. No checked-in guest program exercising this call was found. **Consequence:** unnamed tasks can be published with a non-NULL invalid/uninitialized `ln_Name`; a later task-name search or other name consumer can read through that value. **Affected configuration:** ARM-native SMP builds selecting `processor.resource`; the same API defect applies to any caller omitting both tags. **Confidence:** high for the out-of-bounds read and missing guard; medium for a bad-name consequence because the bytes beyond the allocation determine whether the fallback is bypassed. Read the task name entry only when it was allocated, or initialize the name pointer to NULL so `NewAddTask()` can supply its fallback. No task, lookup, allocation failure or build was run; source-only; see the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#newcreatetaska-unnamed-task-entry-read-ek10351).

<a id="ek10352"></a>
### EK10352 — Hosted ARM `GetCPUInfo()` leaves `GCIT_SupportsFPU` output untouched.

The public processor API lists `GCIT_SupportsFPU` as a boolean feature query (`compiler/include/resources/processor.h:86-90`; `rom/processor/getcpuinfo.c:122-145`). In the Linux ARM getter, that tag has no switch case. The default branch only writes outputs for tags in the numeric range from `GCIT_SupportsVFP` through `GCIT_SupportsThumbEE` (`arch/arm-linux/processor/getcpuinfo.c:28-85`); `GCIT_SupportsFPU` is below that range (`processor.h:88-90,119-127`). A query therefore leaves the caller's output unchanged. The ARM-native implementation explicitly handles the same tag using the VFP hardware feature bit (`arch/arm-native/processor/getcpuinfo.c:175-177`), and the hosted initializer uses VFP/VFPv3 presence to set the processor FPU attention flag (`arch/arm-linux/processor/arch_init.c:189-195`), supporting FPU as a meaningful ARM result.

The optional `developer/debug/test/misc/getcpuinfo` diagnostic requests `GCIT_SupportsFPU`, initializes its result to `FALSE`, and prints the feature only when the returned value is true (`developer/debug/test/misc/getcpuinfo.c:100-103,198-214`; selected in `developer/debug/test/misc/mmakefile.src:8-18,42-49`). Under the Linux ARM provider it therefore omits FPU even when the host reports VFP support. Other API callers that reuse or do not initialize their output can observe a stale value.

**Trigger and consequence:** a Linux-hosted ARM client queries `GCIT_SupportsFPU`; the getter does not store a boolean, so the diagnostic hides available FPU support and other clients receive unchanged output storage.

**Affected configuration:** the Linux ARM `processor.resource` implementation selected by `arch/arm-linux/processor/mmakefile.src`; the in-tree consequence is limited to the explicitly built misc diagnostic, with additional impact conditional on external clients querying this tag.

**Confidence:** high that the selected getter leaves this tag unwritten and that the documented API requires a boolean result; high that the diagnostic consequently suppresses its initialized-false output. Whether a particular host has FPU support depends on its parsed `/proc/cpuinfo`. No processor query, host file, diagnostic, or build was run. Source-only; see the [hosted ARM FPU feature-tag trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#hosted-arm-fpu-feature-output-ek10352).

<a id="ek10353"></a>
### EK10353 — GPT writer subtracts the backup table size in bytes from an LBA

`PartitionGPTWritePartitionTable()` computes `tablesize` as a byte count: it rounds `EntrySize * NumEntries` up to a multiple of the sector size (`rom/partition/partitiongpt.c:512-514`). For the backup copy it sets `backup` to the final disk LBA, then calls `GPTWriteTable(..., backup, 1, backup - tablesize, tablesize)` (`:567-574`). The fourth numeric argument is used as an LBA: `GPTWriteTable()` stores it in the header's `StartBlock` and passes it to `WritePartitionDataQ()` (`:481-505`), whose API defines `StartBlock` as a block number and multiplies it by the block size to obtain the byte offset (`rom/partition/writepartitiondata.c:28-35,53-62`). The subtraction therefore mixes bytes and sectors.

With the conventional 128 entries of 128 bytes and 512-byte sectors, `tablesize` is 16,384 bytes, or 32 sectors. The expected backup entry array begins 32 LBAs before the backup header; this code places it 16,384 LBAs before that header and records that erroneous LBA in `StartBlock`. This violates GPT's placement of the backup entry array after the last usable LBA and before the backup header, and on a disk whose partition uses the space up to the last usable LBA, the write can overwrite partition data. The primary table is separately written at LBA 2 and is not affected by this byte/LBA subtraction.

**Trigger and consequence:** a user saves a GPT partition table through the selected `HDToolBox` path (`workbench/tools/HDToolBox/gui.c:341`), and the GPT entry-array byte size is larger than one sector. The backup array is written at a location too early by a factor of the sector size; this can overwrite the tail of a partition and leaves the backup header pointing to a nonstandard array location. **Affected configuration:** explicit builds of the selected `partition.library` GPT backend (`rom/partition/mmakefile.src:5-25`) together with the explicitly buildable HDToolBox target (`workbench/tools/HDToolBox/mmakefile.src:3-24`). **Confidence:** high for the unit mismatch and computed write location; partition-data loss depends on a partition occupying the overlapped LBAs. Compute the backup-array LBA by converting `tablesize` to sectors before subtracting. No GPT disk, write operation, or build was run; source-only.



<a id="ek10354"></a>
### EK10354 — Graphics manual thunks are registered at the wrong library vectors

The manual Graphics thunk table assigns `ScrollRaster` to LVO offset 318 and `SetABPenDrMd` to offset 864 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1508-1509`). The public Graphics function list places `ReadPixel` at offset 318, `ScrollRaster` at 396, `GetBPen` at 864, and `SetABPenDrMd` at 894 (`rom/graphics/graphics.conf:93,106,190,195`); the generated table likewise registers `ReadPixel` at 318 and `GetBPen` at 864 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:7567,7648`). The emulator searches manual entries before generated entries (`m68kemu_moira.cpp:225-259`), so those manual entries shadow the correct generated `ReadPixel` and `GetBPen` handlers. The actual `ScrollRaster` and `SetABPenDrMd` offsets have no matching manual or generated entry and take the unimplemented-LVO path, which returns zero (`m68kemu_moira.cpp:270-286`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated m68k program calls `ReadPixel` at offset 318 and the manual handler instead runs `ScrollRaster` with the same RastPort register but interprets the coordinate and remaining data registers as scroll displacement and bounds; the guest receives zero instead of the pixel value, and the raster may be changed. A `GetBPen` call at offset 864 instead runs `SetABPenDrMd`, reading its RastPort from A1 although the public API passes it in A0 and applying unrelated D-register values; the guest does not receive the background pen. Calls to the correct `ScrollRaster` offset 396 or `SetABPenDrMd` offset 894 silently return zero without performing the requested operation. **Affected configuration:** the explicitly buildable `kernel-m68kemu-library` target on supported emulator hosts; the parent m68kemu aggregate edges are commented out, so no default-image inclusion is claimed (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:14-17,40`). **Confidence:** high for the offset collisions, manual-before-generated dispatch, and zero-return fallback; the exact accidental RastPort mutation depends on guest register contents and address validity. Register each manual handler at its public vector offset and remove the conflicting entries. No emulated call, graphics operation, or build was run; source-only; see the [vector reconciliation pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#graphics-m68kemu-manual-vector-reconciliation-ek10354).


<a id="ek10355"></a>
### EK10355 — m68kemu does not register the public Graphics `WeighTAMatch()` vector

`graphics.library` exposes `WeighTAMatch()` at LVO offset 804, with a `WORD` result and `TextAttr *`, `TextAttr *`, and `TagItem *` arguments (`rom/graphics/graphics.conf:179`). The native implementation is selected in `rom/graphics/weightamatch.c`; `OpenFont()` also calls it to score font matches (`rom/graphics/openfont.c:80`). The checked-in generated Graphics thunk registry has a gap at offset 804 between `ModeNotAvailable` at 798 and `EraseRect` at 810, and the manual Graphics table has no entry at 804 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:7628-7634`; `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:1496-1511`). `WeighTAMatch` is not in the generator's `SKIP_FUNCTIONS` set (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunkgen.py:32-66`). Moira handles an unregistered library vector by returning zero (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:270-286`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated m68k client calls the public `WeighTAMatch()` vector. It receives score zero instead of the native font-attribute match score and can rank or reject candidate fonts incorrectly. No maintained in-tree m68k guest caller was found; the in-tree `OpenFont()` use is native code and does not traverse this thunk. **Affected configuration:** the explicitly buildable `kernel-m68kemu-library` target on supported emulator hosts; the parent m68kemu aggregate edges are commented out, so no default-image inclusion is claimed (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:14-17,40`). **Confidence:** high that the public LVO is absent and returns zero; practical caller impact is conditional because no maintained guest caller was established. Add a thunk that translates the two `TextAttr` structures and optional tags, or document the vector as unsupported and expose that limitation to guest callers. No emulated font call or build was run; source-only; see the [Graphics vector reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#graphics-m68kemu-manual-vector-reconciliation-ek10354).


<a id="ek10356"></a>
### EK10356 — OpenSBI FDT parsing reads node names and property payloads past the declared structure

`krnParseFDT()` checks only the FDT magic before it sets `end` from `totalsize`; it neither validates `off_dt_struct`/`size_dt_struct` nor uses the declared structure size as the traversal bound (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_fdt.c:23-36,91-101`). For `FDT_BEGIN_NODE`, it scans the node name until a NUL with no remaining-length check (`:105-112`). For `FDT_PROP`, it reads the length/name-offset words without checking that both are present, then advances by the declared payload length without confirming that the payload is within the structure block or DTB (`:129-136`). The selected property branches can dereference that value immediately; for example, root `#address-cells` reads `*val` (`:138-145`).

A concrete truncated input can contain a valid FDT header, root node, valid property-name string, and an `FDT_PROP` declaring a four-byte `#address-cells` value while ending immediately after the token/length/name-offset words. The parser reaches `be32(*val)` at the declared end of the blob instead of returning failure. A node name without a terminator in the remaining structure likewise makes the name scan continue past the block. The fallback in `kernel_cstart()` only runs if `krnParseFDT()` returns false; these unchecked reads happen before such a return (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:515-568`). This is separate from EK769/EK772's root cell-count arithmetic and EK8861's property-name string-table bounds.

**Trigger and consequence:** OpenSBI supplies a truncated or malformed FDT whose structure token, node name, or property payload is incomplete or whose declared structure extent is inconsistent. The early parser can read past the declared DTB/structure, fault during startup, or consume following bytes as boot metadata before its EFI/default fallback. **Affected configuration:** the selected RISC-V OpenSBI kernel when the firmware-provided FDT has inconsistent/truncated structure data. **Confidence:** high that token, node-name, and value extents are not bounded before access; a fault or wrong metadata depends on the blob layout and accessible memory following it. Validate the header and structure block, then check each token's fixed and variable extent before dereferencing or advancing. No malformed FDT, boot, or build was used; source-only. See the [OpenSBI FDT structure-extent audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#opensbi-fdt-structure-extent-pass-ek10356).
<a id="ek10357"></a>
### EK10357 — AArch64 `KrnMapGlobal()` leaves partial mappings after a later table-allocation failure

The selected AArch64 mapper updates page-table descriptors in place as it walks the requested range (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/mmu.c:180-225`). `mmu_next()` allocates a child table and publishes it immediately (`:139-161`); each aligned 2 MiB mapping is then written into its L2 slot (`:210-216`). If a later `mmu_next()` allocation fails, `mmu_map_range()` returns 0 immediately without undoing earlier descriptors or calling `mmu_commit()` (`:203-226`). `KrnMapGlobal()` returns that result directly (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/mapglobal.c:18-28`), so the caller gets failure while part of the requested mapping remains in the live page-table hierarchy. The AArch64 target selects this implementation (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/mmakefile.src:50-57,83-85`).

There are several selected in-tree consequences. V3D's `arena_new()` requests a 32 MiB-or-larger, 2 MiB-aligned identity mapping with `MAP_WriteThrough`; on a false result it frees the raw backing allocation and metadata, but does not unmap any prefix (`arch/arm-native/soc/broadcom/2708/hidd/v3d/v3d_mem.c:73-116`). The BCM2711 and BCM2712 PCI HIDDs and RP1 each have `AllocPCIMem()` paths that return their raw allocations to Exec on map failure without unmapping (`arch/arm-native/soc/broadcom/2711/pcie/driverclass.c:248-275`; `arch/arm-native/soc/broadcom/2712/hidd/pci-bcm2712/driverclass.c:327-357`; `arch/arm-native/soc/broadcom/2712/rp1/rp1_pci.c:182-211`). The BCM2712 PCI HIDD's `MapPCI()` also returns NULL on a failed mapping without rollback (`driverclass.c:245-270`). These drivers are in the `raspi-aarch64` package (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/mmakefile.src:224-227`). A failure after earlier 2 MiB entries have been written is possible when the range crosses into a region that needs a newly allocated lower-level table and that allocation fails. The edits have not yet been TLB-committed on this return path, but they remain in the page tables and can become active after a later successful mapping calls `mmu_commit()`. Freed identity ranges can then retain altered Normal Non-Cacheable or Device attributes after their memory is reused; V3D and the three DMA allocators do not restore the failed mapping before `FreeMem()`.

**Trigger and consequence:** on `raspi-aarch64`, `KrnMapGlobal()` maps a range that needs a new lower-level table after installing one or more earlier entries, and that later table allocation fails. The selected V3D arena and BCM2711/BCM2712/RP1 DMA allocation paths free backing storage on mapping failure, while the BCM2712 `MapPCI()` path returns NULL; none rolls back a possible prefix. A later global TLB invalidation can activate the partial attribute change for memory that has since been reused, creating unexpected cacheability and possible alias/coherency problems. **Affected configuration:** the AArch64 Raspberry Pi kernel and its selected PCI/RP1 clients; the V3D HIDD is additionally optional, with its parent aggregate edge commented (`arch/arm-native/soc/broadcom/2708/hidd/v3d/mmakefile.src:6-11`). **Confidence:** high for partial descriptor publication and the callers' error cleanup; occurrence requires later page-table allocation failure after at least one range entry was written. Make mapping failure atomic by staging/rolling back edits, or require callers to unmap/restore every failed partial range before freeing backing memory. No allocation failure, mapping, reuse, build, or runtime operation was exercised; source-only.
<a id="ek10358"></a>
### EK10358 — Unix hosted tasks never receive CPU-usage samples

The selected Unix task switch records elapsed time in `iet_CpuTime` and increments `iet_private2` (`arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:88-99`; `kernel_cpusupport.c:22-33`), but neither path updates `iet_CpuUsage`. A full source search found assignments to that field only in the PC APIC heartbeat, ARM/AArch64 native schedulers, and RISC-V timer code; none is selected by `arch/all-unix/kernel/mmakefile.src`. The generic `QueryTaskTagList()` implementation returns the stored field directly for `TaskTag_CPUUsage` (`rom/task/QueryTaskTagList.c:163-168`). SysMon's task-list refresh requests this tag on each update and displays/sorts the resulting percentage (`workbench/system/SysMon/tasks.c:122-140,145-165,478-488,622-623`). The selected `C:TaskList` command also requests the tag while collecting tasks and prints a CPU Usage column (`workbench/c/TaskList.c:82-87,110-116,228-236`; `workbench/c/mmakefile.src:51`).

**Affected configuration and trigger:** Unix-hosted targets running SysMon or `C:TaskList`. SysMon is connected to `workbench-system` through its active `#MM-` virtual-target dependency (`workbench/system/SysMon/mmakefile.src:8-11`) and is selected by the normal Workbench system chain; `TaskList` is selected in the common `workbench-c` command list. Every task-list refresh reads the unmaintained field. **Consequence:** per-task CPU usage remains zero or stale, so SysMon and `C:TaskList` display CPU usage that does not represent hosted task activity, even though CPU time is accumulated. **Confidence:** high for the missing writer in the selected Unix kernel and the reader/display path; no hosted target or SysMon GUI was run. Source-only; see the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#unix-task-cpu-usage-query-and-sysmon-caller-pass-ek10358).
<a id="ek10359"></a>
### EK10359 — Generic hosted bootstrap support fallback does not compile

The explicitly declared generic `kernel-bootstrap-hosted` program selects `arch/all-hosted/bootstrap/support.c` through its default `FILES` list (`arch/all-hosted/bootstrap/mmakefile.src:4,30-32`). In `getosversion()`, the `parts` array declaration has no terminating semicolon after its initializer (`support.c:11-16`), so this translation unit is rejected before the function can be built. Even after adding the semicolon, the return calls `join_strings()` (`:18`), but the shared controller declares and defines only `join_string()` (`support.h:4`; `bootstrap.c:140`), and a repository-wide search found no `join_strings` implementation. The Unix and MinGW arch-specific manifests substitute their own `support.c` files (`arch/all-unix/bootstrap/mmakefile.src:17-19`; `arch/all-mingw32/bootstrap/mmakefile.src:15-17`), so this finding is limited to building the generic all-hosted fallback without those overrides. Its parent link-library aggregate edge is commented, though the `%build_prog` target is explicitly available.

**Trigger and consequence:** explicitly build the unoverridden `kernel-bootstrap-hosted` target using its default source list. Compilation fails at the unterminated array declaration; fixing that reveals the unresolved `join_strings` symbol at link time. **Affected configuration:** only the generic hosted fallback target; no default Unix or MinGW build impact is claimed. **Confidence:** high for both source defects and target source selection; no build was run. Source-only; see the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#generic-hosted-support-fallback-selection-and-buildability-ek10359).


<a id="ek10360"></a>
### EK10360 — ARM32 SMP processor probes can record the wrong core when affinity-mask allocation fails

The ARM-native SMP processor initializer allocates a per-secondary affinity mask with `KrnAllocCPUMask()`, but it creates the probe task even when allocation returns NULL (`arch/arm-native/processor/processor_init.c:52-70`; the allocator directly returns `AllocMem()` at `arch/arm-native/kernel/alloccpumask.c:20-26`). In the selected ARM `PrepareContext()`, the `TASKTAG_AFFINITY` tag is copied as-is into `iet_CpuAffinity` (`arch/arm-all/exec/preparecontext.c:32-45`). The ARM scheduler explicitly treats a NULL affinity pointer as eligible on every CPU (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:39-51,269-287`).

Each task is passed the record allocated for logical CPU `i`, but `ProbeCPUAndSignal()` calls `ReadProcessorInformation()` on whichever CPU runs it; that routine stores the running core's MPIDR into the supplied record (`processor_init.c:20-25`; `arch/arm-native/processor/processor_util.c:149-152`). `Processor_FillTopology()` later treats each record's array index as that processor's logical entry and copies the recorded MPIDR into its physical ID (`processor_util.c:313-345`). Therefore, after the small mask allocation fails, if the scheduler runs a probe on a CPU other than its intended index, the published processor identity/topology can associate the wrong physical CPU with that logical entry; multiple probes can also sample the same core. `GetCPUInfo()` exposes the resulting physical ID for the selected logical core (`arch/arm-native/processor/getcpuinfo.c:163-165`).

**Trigger and consequence:** ARM32/ARMeb ExecSMP processor initialization has at least one secondary CPU, a probe signal is allocated, and `KrnAllocCPUMask()` fails for that probe; the defect manifests if the unrestricted task is scheduled on a different CPU than the requested one. **Affected configuration:** `raspi-arm` and `raspi-armeb` builds selecting `arch/arm-native/processor/processor_init.c` with ExecSMP. **Confidence:** high that NULL is passed through and interpreted as unrestricted, and that the running CPU's MPIDR is stored in the index-specific record; the incorrect published mapping depends on allocation failure and scheduling the probe on another core. Treat mask allocation failure as a probe failure or probe synchronously on the requested CPU. This is distinct from EK279's unchecked task-creation and incomplete-join behavior, EK8790's caller-owned mask leak when task creation fails, and EK10351's unnamed-task entry read. No allocation failure, task, processor query, boot, or build was exercised; source-only; see the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#arm-processor-probe-affinity-mask-failure-ek10360).


<a id="ek10361"></a>
### EK10361 — Workbench `Info` reports success after initialization failures

`main()` always returns `RETURN_OK` after calling the `void` `doInfo()` (`workbench/c/Info.c:197-211`). In `doInfo()`, failure to allocate the initial `InfoData` or failure to create the pool prints `ERROR_NO_FREE_STORE` and returns without communicating failure to `main()` (`:545-567`). Consequently the command exits with a successful DOS result even though it did not perform the requested listing. This also applies when `CreatePool()` fails after the `InfoData` allocation; the resulting small leak is separately tracked as EK9060. Propagate a success/failure result from `doInfo()` and return the corresponding DOS status from `main()`.

**Trigger and consequence:** a selected Workbench `Info` invocation encounters either initial `AllocVec()` failure or `CreatePool()` failure. The diagnostic is printed, but the process result remains `RETURN_OK`, so callers cannot use the command status to detect the failed operation. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting the common `workbench-c` command, including `Info` (`workbench/c/mmakefile.src:23`). **Confidence:** high for the unconditional success return and both early error returns; no memory failure or command invocation was induced. Source-only; see the [caller and target trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#info-command-status-caller-pass-ek10361).


<a id="ek10362"></a>
### EK10362 — Early boot menu retries forever after GadTools VisualInfo allocation failure

When `WantBootMenu` is true, `bootmenu_Init()` calls `initScreen()` (`rom/dosboot/menu.c:965-974`). The initial page is `PAGE_MAIN`, and `initWindow()` opens GadTools then stores `GetVisualInfoA()` directly in `bm_VisualInfo` without checking it (`:856-875,803-810`). `populateGadgets()` passes that pointer to `CreateGadgetA()` (`:500-520`); the selected GadTools implementation returns NULL when `ng_VisualInfo` is NULL (`workbench/libs/gadtools/creategadgeta.c:87-89`). This makes page construction fail and leaves `newpage` at `-1` (`menu.c:798-800,839-854`). `initScreen()` repeats until the page equals `EXIT_BOOT` (5) or `EXIT_BOOT_WNSS` (6), so persistent VisualInfo allocation failure never reaches the boot-selection continuation (`:856-875`).

**Trigger and consequence:** on a selected m68k Amiga boot with the early menu requested through the `bootmenu` bootloader argument or the keyboard check, `GetVisualInfoA()` fails while `CreateContext()` succeeds. Gadget construction then fails and the page loop retries with the invalid `-1` page result; if the allocation keeps failing, dosboot never returns to complete boot setup. The m68k boot target includes `dosboot` (`arch/m68k-amiga/boot/mmakefile.src:154-159`), and the DOSBoot module selects `menu.c` (`rom/dosboot/mmakefile.src:19-20`). **Confidence:** high for the failure propagation and loop termination condition; manifestation requires persistent allocation failure during a requested boot menu. Handle failed page construction as an exit/fallback result rather than retrying an invalid page indefinitely. No allocation failure or boot was induced; source-only. See the [DOSBoot VisualInfo failure trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#dosboot-visualinfo-retry-loop-ek10362).


<a id="ek798"></a>
### EK798 — Per-core PC frequency query samples APERF/MPERF on the caller CPU

The PC `GetCPUInfo()` implementation reads `GCIT_SelectedProcessor` and uses that index to select the saved per-core record passed to `X86_AnswerTag()` (`arch/all-pc/processor/getcpuinfo.c:36-46,67-70`). For `GCIT_ProcessorSpeed`, that record is passed to `GetCurrentProcessorFrequency()` (`:133-135`). In the standalone PC implementation, the APERF/MPERF branch then executes `rdmsr` locally and computes a ratio from those readings, without pinning the caller or switching to the selected logical processor (`arch/all-pc/processor/processor_frequency.c:374-415`). The maximum-frequency value used to scale the ratio belongs to the selected record, but the sampled counters belong to the CPU on which the call runs. The generic `GetCoreInfo()` wrapper only forwards `coreNo` as `GCIT_SelectedProcessor`; it performs no affinity change (`rom/processor/getcoreinfo.c:78-94`).

The selected SysExplorer processor page loops over CPU indexes, requests both `GCIT_SelectedProcessor` and `GCIT_ProcessorSpeed`, and calls `GetCPUInfo()` directly (`workbench/tools/SysExplorer/computer_page_cl.c:212-224`). It does not set task affinity around the query. If that task executes on a different logical CPU than the selected index, the displayed speed combines the selected processor's maximum-frequency record with the executing CPU's APERF/MPERF ratio. Thus the value can describe the caller CPU rather than the requested CPU.

**Trigger and consequence:** on a standalone PC build where APERF/MPERF sampling is enabled for the selected record, query a different logical CPU while the caller is executing elsewhere. `GCIT_ProcessorSpeed` can then return a frequency based on another CPU's counters; repeated per-core queries may display incorrect or duplicated current-speed values. **Affected configuration:** standalone i386-PC or x86-64-PC targets with the APERF/MPERF path enabled and a caller that can run on a CPU other than the selected index; SysExplorer is a checked-in unpinned caller. **Confidence:** high for the selected-record versus local-MSR data flow and missing affinity in SysExplorer; manifestation depends on executing a query from a different logical CPU and on per-CPU APERF/MPERF values differing. Execute the sampling on the selected CPU or otherwise obtain that CPU's counters before combining them with its record. No affinity change, frequency query, MSR access, or runtime behavior was exercised. Source-only; see the [selected-core sampling trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2549).

<a id="ek10363"></a>
### EK10363 — Concurrent ExecSMP `Cause()` calls can self-link a soft-interrupt node

In `Cause()`, Exec checks `softint->is_Node.ln_Type != NT_SOFTINT` before taking the per-priority soft-interrupt spinlock (`rom/exec/cause.c:84-100`). On ExecSMP, `Disable()` masks interrupts only on the calling CPU; its own contract says shared data still requires a spinlock (`rom/exec/disable.c:44-58`). Two CPUs can therefore both observe the same interrupt node as not queued. The first caller acquires the list lock, appends the node, and marks it `NT_SOFTINT`; the second then acquires the lock but does not repeat the type check and appends that same node again.

The second `ADDTAIL` uses the node itself as the old tail, so it sets `ln_Pred` and then makes `ln_Succ` point back to the node (`compiler/include/exec/lists.h:122-134`). `SoftIntDispatch()` removes and calls queued nodes under the same list lock, but it marks the node `NT_INTERRUPT` and invokes the callback after unlocking (`rom/exec/cause.c:168-194`). With the self-linked list head, Exec's `RemHead()` sets `lh_Head` to the node's own `ln_Succ`, which is the same node, so the dispatcher can repeatedly invoke the callback and fail to drain that priority list (`rom/exec/remhead.c:58-68`). Check and insert atomically under the list lock, rechecking `ln_Type` after acquiring it.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** ExecSMP-enabled x86-64 PC SMP and Raspberry Pi SMP builds (`configure.in:1667-1670,2195-2199`) when two CPUs call `Cause()` concurrently with the same `struct Interrupt` before either queued instance is dispatched. The public `Cause()` contract permits calls from interrupt context and special device-I/O paths (`rom/exec/cause.c:40-57`). A generic in-tree route also exists through `PutMsg()` to a `PA_SOFTINT` port: `PutMsg()` permits interrupt callers, and `InternalPutMsg()` releases the port's SMP spinlock and calls `Enable()` before it invokes `Cause(port->mp_SoftInt)` (`rom/exec/putmsg.c:38-42,83-114`; `compiler/include/exec/ports.h:41-48`). Concurrent producers on separate CPUs can therefore reach `Cause()` with the same port-owned interrupt after their individually serialized message insertions; the `Cause()` node-state test still occurs outside its own priority-list lock. This is a conditional generic API trigger; no specific in-tree pair of concurrent producers to one selected `PA_SOFTINT` port is claimed here. A maintained same-object caller pairing also exists in optional USB Audio: both `nOutReqHook()` and the device-release `nReleaseHook()` call `Cause(&nam->nam_PlayerInt)` (`rom/usb/classes/audio/usbaudio.class.c:2647,2765`). The output-request hook can be reached while EHCI/OHCI completion soft interrupts queue the next isochronous transfer, or while the xHCI event task replenishes completed periodic transfers (`rom/usb/pciusb/ehci/ehci_hcd.c:1097-1133`; `rom/usb/pciusb/ohci/ohci_hcd.c:1310-1335`; `rom/usb/pcixhci/xhci_hcd.c:2765-2810`; `rom/usb/pcixhci/xhci_isoch.c:193-220`). The release hook synchronously issues `UHCMD_STOPRTISO` from the Poseidon device-release path (`rom/usb/poseidon/poseidon.library.c:5657-5675`). The path does not serialize those callbacks across CPUs: `DoIO()` invokes the device `BeginIO` vector synchronously (`rom/exec/doio.c:49-70`), and PCIUSB/xHCI `BeginIO` dispatches `UHCMD_STOPRTISO` directly to the controller stop routine (`rom/usb/pciusb/pciusb_dev.c:196-278`; `rom/usb/pcixhci/pcixhci_dev.c:198-280`). The stop routines use `Disable()` around local controller changes but do not wait for a completion callback on another CPU (`rom/usb/pciusb/uhwcmd.c:1679-1727`; `rom/usb/pcixhci/uhwcmd.c:1665-1707`). The xHCI stop path calls `xhciFinishRequest()`, which removes request back-pointers and frees request-private state while documenting that endpoint TRBs can remain on the ring until a later endpoint stop; it does not join the event task (`rom/usb/pcixhci/xhci_isoch.c:332-350`; `xhci_periodic.c:40-47`; `xhci_hcd.c:2433-2479`). This establishes a possible in-tree cross-context race when device release overlaps an output-request callback that reaches its timer-triggered `Cause()`; the exact overlap remains timing-dependent and was not reproduced. Two other maintained same-node caller pairs are conditional on explicit optional-target selection: RTL8139 timeout and transmit-completion interrupts share `rtl8139u_tx_int` (`workbench/devs/networks/rtl8139/unit.c:478-497,618-620`; initialization at `:1052-1069`), and PCIUSB task submissions share `hc_CompleteInt` across controller transfer queues (`rom/usb/pciusb/pciusb_dev.c:215-254`; `rom/usb/pciusb/uhwcmd.c:1058-1088,1109-1139,1160-1190,1213-1244`). Neither optional path is claimed as a default-image reproducer. **Consequence:** the soft-interrupt node can self-link its priority queue; dispatch may repeatedly invoke that callback and stall dispatch of later callbacks at that priority. **Confidence:** high for the unlocked precheck, missing in-lock recheck, list-link mutation, and dispatcher behavior; medium for the maintained USB Audio trigger topology, with manifestation requiring the stated overlap on optional ExecSMP USB builds. No device removal, concurrent interrupt, callback, build, or runtime behavior was exercised; source-only; see the [Cause SMP race trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#cause-smp-duplicate-enqueue-ek10363).


<a id="ek10364"></a>
### EK10364 — `NewCreateTaskA()` accepts an undersized stack after stack-size alignment wraps

`NewCreateTaskA()` rounds the `TASKTAG_STACKSIZE` value before checking the minimum stack size (`rom/exec/newcreatetaska.c:127-153,165-180`). On selected targets with 32-bit `ULONG` and 16-byte `AROS_WORSTALIGN`, `AROS_ALIGN(x)` adds 15 in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic (`arch/x86_64-all/include/aros/cpu.h:50,170`; `compiler/include/exec/types.h:37-43`). For the valid representable value `x = 0xfffffff1`, that addition wraps to zero before the mask is applied. The minimum-size check then replaces zero with `AROS_STACKSIZE` (40,960 bytes on x86-64; `cpu.h:176`). `NewAllocEntry()` allocates that reduced length (`rom/exec/newallocentry.c:105-143`), and `NewCreateTaskA()` proceeds to set the stack bounds and create the task (`newcreatetaska.c:239-254`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a caller requests a `TASKTAG_STACKSIZE` near the 32-bit limit whose round-up overflows, for example `0xfffffff1` on a 16-byte-alignment target. Instead of rejecting the unallocatable requested size, task creation can succeed with the minimum stack; a task that relies on the requested larger extent may run out of stack. The API documents this tag as the requested stack size and does not document truncation on overflow (`newcreatetaska.c:59-63`). The compatibility `CreateTask()` wrapper also forwards its caller-supplied `stacksize` directly as `TASKTAG_STACKSIZE` without validation (`compiler/alib/createtask.c:30-63`). A repository-wide call-site review found no checked-in near-limit value, so the trigger remains an external API-client case. **Affected configuration:** generic Exec task creation on maintained targets whose architecture defines `AROS_WORSTALIGN` as 4 or 16 bytes, including m68k, ARM, i386, x86-64, AArch64, PowerPC, and RISC-V. Values `0xfffffffd` and `0xfffffff1` respectively round to zero. The checked-in 8-byte value belongs to the legacy `ppc-morphos` header, for which no AROS target selection was found, so it is not included as an affected configuration. The exact stack-use consequence depends on the caller and selected architecture. **Confidence:** high for the unsigned wrap and reduced allocation; medium for downstream task failure, which depends on the caller's actual stack use. Check the alignment addition for overflow and report task-creation failure rather than silently reducing the requested stack. No task or allocation was created; source-only; see the [stack-size alignment trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#task-stacksize-align-overflow-ek10364).


<a id="ek633"></a>
### EK633 — OpenSBI boot self-tests use unchecked signal allocations and leak the boot-task signal on task-creation failure

The optional `testsched` path allocates `schedSig` in `krnSchedTest()` and immediately shifts it into a wait mask without checking whether `AllocSignal(-1)` returned `-1` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:189-203`). The optional `testfpu` path does the same for the boot task at `:138-143`. Its worker also shifts an unchecked `AllocSignal()` result at `:104-108`, but this task is newly created; selected `NewAddTask()` initializes a zero signal-allocation field to `SysBase->TaskSigAlloc` (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:249-251`), which Exec initializes to `0xFFFF` (`prepareexecbase.c:319`). Thus the worker's first allocation has a free ordinary signal on this selected path, and worker-side exhaustion is not established. `AllocSignal()` returns signed `BYTE` and uses `-1` for exhaustion (`rom/exec/allocsignal.c:45-68,89-96`). On this RV64 target, `ULONG` and Exec's `Wait`/`Signal` masks are 32-bit (`compiler/include/exec/types.h:35-43`; `rom/exec/wait.c:24-30`; `rom/exec/signal.c:117-124`), while `1UL` is 64-bit. Shifting by the returned `-1` is undefined in C; if lowered to the ordinary RV64 shift instruction, the count is reduced to 63 and the high bit is then truncated when assigned to `ULONG`, producing a zero mask. `Wait(0)` loops without any possible matching received bit, and `Signal(..., 0)` publishes no bit (`rom/exec/wait.c:75-80`; `rom/exec/signal.c:298-303`). The tests run after the two selected `InitCode()` passes (`kernel_startup.c:1027-1030,1093-1111`). A source search found no direct `AllocSignal()` use in the selected kernel/Exec/task startup trees before these helpers; the other generic allocator paths are reset callbacks and `CreateMsgPort()` (`rom/exec/doresetcallbacks.c:88-97`; `createmsgport.c:51-76`), with no direct caller in those three startup trees. So ordinary boot-time signal exhaustion is not established. A checked-in route exists when the bootargs dispatcher matches the test name repeatedly and each `NewCreateTaskA()` fails: each failed attempt leaks one boot-task signal, and after the 16 allocatable task signals are consumed a later invocation reaches the unchecked `-1` shift. Under ordinary RV64 lowering that later test can wait on zero; compiler behavior remains undefined by the C source.

After a successful boot-task signal allocation, each helper calls `NewCreateTaskA()`. If task creation fails, both print a failure message and return without `FreeSignal(sigbit)` (`:146-151,205-210`), leaving that bit allocated in the boot task. Repeated selected self-tests after task-creation failures can consume additional signal bits.

**Trigger and consequence:** the optional OpenSBI scheduler or FPU self-test is invoked with the boot task's signal pool exhausted, or a signal allocation succeeds and subsequent `NewCreateTaskA()` fails. The checked-in compound exhaustion route is repeated matching substrings in bootargs plus enough child-task creation failures to leak all 16 allocatable boot-task signal bits before a later match; ordinary startup exhaustion was not established. The boot-task exhaustion case makes the test's wait/signal protocol unreliable; under ordinary RV64 shift lowering the mask becomes zero and the boot task can wait forever for an event that cannot match, while C's undefined shift leaves other compiler outcomes unconstrained. The second case leaks the successfully allocated boot-task signal. **Affected configuration:** the RISC-V OpenSBI kernel when `testsched` or `testfpu` is requested in bootargs and the specified allocation/task-creation failure occurs. The tests are optional; no ordinary boot failure is claimed. **Confidence:** high that boot-task exhaustion reaches a negative shift count and that task-creation failure leaks an allocated signal; medium-high for the zero-mask/infinite-wait consequence because it follows ordinary RV64 shift lowering plus 64-to-32-bit truncation, but the C expression has undefined behavior. Check each allocation before constructing a mask and release the boot-task signal before returning after child-task creation failure. No signal exhaustion, task-creation failure, self-test, or boot was induced; source-only. See the [OpenSBI self-test signal trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L351).

<a id="ek8775"></a>
### EK8775 — OpenSBI boot-argument substring matching can start self-tests unintentionally

The OpenSBI startup dispatcher scans every byte of `fdtinfo.bootargs` and compares the next eight or nine bytes against `testfpu` or `testsched` without checking token boundaries (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:1093-1111`). A token such as `notestsched` or `my-testfpu-mode` therefore starts the corresponding optional self-test even though the boot argument is not that test option. The same file has a token-aware `krnArgMatch()` helper used by other boot options (`:219-241`), but this dispatch does not use it. Both test worker entry points finish with `Wait(0)` (`:115,182`), so each unintended invocation leaves an extra task blocked indefinitely; repeated matching substrings can start multiple such tasks.

**Trigger and consequence:** an OpenSBI boot-argument value contains `testsched` or `testfpu` as a substring inside another value, rather than as a standalone option. The corresponding test runs unexpectedly and leaves a sleeping worker task; this consumes task resources and can produce unexpected test output or scheduling overhead. **Affected configuration:** RISC-V OpenSBI boots using this startup dispatcher with a bootargs string containing either substring. **Confidence:** high for the missing boundary check and the persistent worker wait; the operational effect of an extra sleeping task is limited and depends on the bootargs supplied. Parse bootargs as tokens and match the complete option. No bootargs, task, or boot was exercised; source-only. See the [OpenSBI self-test signal trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L351).


<a id="ek10365"></a>
### EK10365 — `CreateIORequest()` accepts a size that `DeleteIORequest()` cannot represent

`CreateIORequest()` takes an `ULONG size`, allocates that many bytes, then stores the size in `io_Message.mn_Length` (`rom/exec/createiorequest.c:39-73`). The field is a `UWORD` (`compiler/include/exec/ports.h:55-60`), but the constructor does not reject values above `UWORD_MAX`. For an accepted 65,536-byte request, the stored length wraps to zero. `DeleteIORequest()` passes that field to `FreeMem()` (`rom/exec/deleteiorequest.c:43-48`), and `FreeMem()` explicitly returns without freeing when `byteSize` is zero (`rom/exec/freemem.c:70-75`). Thus the normal create/delete pair permanently leaves the allocated block unreleased. Larger values can also truncate to an incorrect nonzero free size, but the zero-length case alone establishes the leak.

**Trigger and consequence:** a caller requests a 65,536-byte I/O request and later deletes the returned request. If allocation succeeds, deletion is a no-op and the block remains allocated. A source-wide direct-call census found that ordinary in-tree creators pass fixed `sizeof(...)` request types, but the optional `m68kemu.library` vector forwards the guest D0 size unchanged through `thunk_exec_CreateIORequest()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2289-2297`). Thus an emulated m68k caller can request the boundary-sized block when that library is built and used. **Affected configuration:** generic Exec on targets using the declared 16-bit `UWORD`; this includes guest calls through the optional m68kemu library. **Confidence:** high for the accepted `ULONG` size, truncating assignment, and zero-size `FreeMem()` return. Reject sizes that cannot be represented in `mn_Length` or widen the recorded allocation size. No allocation/deletion was run; source-only. See the [DeleteIORequest caller and size trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#deleteiorequest-size-width-ek10365).


<a id="ek10366"></a>
### EK10366 — m68k allocation thunks leak native resources when guest-shadow creation fails
