Exec calls through the NULL callback and faults instead of continuing the search or reporting the invalid/unmatched range. **Affected configuration:** custom managed-memory providers that publish such headers in the system MemList without implementing the optional bounds callback. The in-tree TLSF provider supplies `mhe_InBounds`; no current in-tree system-MemList provider with the callback absent was found. **Confidence:** high for the inconsistent NULL handling and direct call paths; in-tree reachability is not established and the trigger is limited to external/future providers. Check the callback before dispatch and define how headers without it are skipped or bounded by `mh_Lower`/`mh_Upper`. No allocation/free or provider was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10604-tlsf-allocabs-scan-bound"></a>
<a id="ek10604"></a>
## EK10604 — TLSF `AllocAbs()` scans beyond the bucket matrix on a miss

`tlsf_t.matrix` has `REAL_FLI` rows (`rom/kernel/tlsf.c:35-45,110-120`), but `tlsf_allocabs()` iterates its first-level scan while `fl < MAX_FLI` (`:987-1020,1124-1129`). `MAX_FLI` is larger than `REAL_FLI` on both word sizes. `MAPPING_SEARCH()` can start at a valid class; if no free-list block contains the requested absolute range, the loop proceeds through all remaining first-level values and reads `tlsf->matrix[REAL_FLI][sl]` and subsequent rows. This search does not check the bucket index or terminate at the allocated row count. `tlsf_allocabs()` is installed as the MemHeader `mhe_AllocAbs` vector (`:1477-1478`) and is reached through Exec's public `AllocAbs()` -> `InternalAllocAbs()` -> `nommu_AllocAbs()` dispatch (`rom/exec/allocabs.c:72-84`; `rom/exec/memory.c:879-883`; `rom/exec/memory_nommu.c:88-130`). The distinct kernel `KrnAllocPages()` path calls the generic linear `mm_AllocAbs()` and does not dispatch to this TLSF vector (`rom/kernel/kernel_mm.c:43-53`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an `AllocAbs` request is directed to a TLSF-managed memory header and no free block contains the requested range; one ordinary case is a request for an address range already occupied by an allocated block in that TLSF area. The provider’s `tlsf_in_bounds()` accepts ranges based on area boundaries, not on whether the range is free, so this reaches the allocator search. The unsuccessful search reads beyond the matrix; depending on adjacent allocator metadata and contents, it can fault or interpret unrelated memory as a free-list pointer instead of returning allocation failure. **Affected configuration:** any architecture using this TLSF implementation and receiving an absolute allocation request against a TLSF MemHeader; no in-tree caller-specific trigger is required for the public memory vector. **Confidence:** high for the out-of-range scan and invalid row access on a miss; exact manifestation depends on adjacent memory contents. Bound the loop by `REAL_FLI` and return failure after the last valid bucket. No allocation or build was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10603-tlsf-oversized-initial-region"></a>
<a id="ek10603"></a>
## EK10603 — TLSF traps while registering a free region larger than 128 GiB

On 64-bit builds TLSF sets `MAX_FLI` to 37 and `FLI_OFFSET` to 6, so `REAL_FLI` is 31 and the largest legal first-level bucket index is 30 (`rom/kernel/tlsf.c:35-45`). `MAPPING_INSERT()` computes `fl = MS(r) - FLI_OFFSET` for large blocks (`:154-167`); any free block of at least 2^37 bytes maps to `fl == 31`. The bucket insertion validates the result and calls `tlsf_fail_corruption()` when it is outside the table (`:427-441,465-484`), whose terminal action is `__builtin_trap()` (`:336-382`).

The initial memory conversion supplies each remaining chunk as one TLSF area: `krnConvertMemHeaderToTLSF()` walks the source chunks and calls `tlsf_add_memory()` with each complete `mc_Bytes` extent (`:1512-1555`); `tlsf_add_memory()` initializes one free block and immediately sends it through `tlsf_freevec()` (`:1175-1225,810-855`). The x86-64 PC map includes a high-memory region extending to the address-space end and selects TLSF by default (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:69-75`; `notlsf` is an explicit override at `:374-375`). The PC map builder groups contiguous physical ranges into memory headers and converts them at each gap or region end (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_mmap.c:188-205,261-269`). No cap or subdivision at TLSF's stated 128-GiB limit is applied along this path.

**Trigger and consequence:** a 64-bit TLSF target exposes a single free `MemChunk` of at least 128 GiB after allocator metadata is reserved. Registering that memory maps the initial free block to the nonexistent first-level bucket 31 and takes the allocator corruption trap during boot-time memory-header conversion. **Affected configuration:** 64-bit targets using TLSF when firmware presents a sufficiently large contiguous free extent; x86-64 PC uses TLSF by default, with `notlsf` as a boot override. **Confidence:** high for the class/table mismatch and unsplit registration path; actual occurrence depends on the firmware memory map containing the stated contiguous extent. Reject, split, or represent oversized extents before inserting them. No memory map, boot, or build was exercised; source-only.


<a id="ek10602"></a>
### EK10602 — Relative-base setup leaks tables when task-slot publication fails

`__aros_getoffsettable()` allocates and clears a per-task `__rel_bases` table, calls `SetTaskStorageSlot(__rel_slot, (IPTR)t)`, ignores its Boolean result, and continues to open `posixc.library` before returning the table (`compiler/startup/relbases.c:69-101`). `SetTaskStorageSlot()` can return `FALSE` when allocating or growing the task's slot array fails (`rom/task/SetTaskStorageSlot.c:70-92`). In that case the new table was never published: the next relative-wrapper lookup still gets NULL from `GetTaskStorageSlot()` and repeats the allocation/open sequence. The original table and any successful PosixC open reference are no longer reachable through the task slot, and repeated lookups during continued allocation pressure leak another table and reference each time. This is distinct from EK10192, where provisioning or table allocation returns NULL and the generated accessor dereferences it, and from EK764, which covers the normal task-exit lifetime.

**Trigger and consequence:** a program linked with the startup relative-base provider successfully allocates its `__rel_bases` table, but task-storage array allocation/growth then fails; relative-library wrappers continue to be called. Each retry can leak the unpublished table and a successful `posixc.library` open reference, consuming memory and delaying or preventing library expunge. **Affected configuration:** startup-linked programs using the `posixc_rel`, `stdc_rel`, or `stdcio_rel` wrappers; current checked-in target manifests do not establish a standalone production client, so reachability is conditional on external or future clients. **Confidence:** high for the ignored failure result and repeated-unpublished-allocation path; manifestation requires the stated allocation failure and later wrapper calls. Check the setter result and free the table / close any opened base on failure, or make publication failure fatal to that lookup. No allocation failure, wrapper call, library lifecycle, or build was exercised; source-only; see the [relative-base publication failure trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#relative-base-slot-publication-failure-ek10602).

<a id="ek67-mungwall-stacksnoop-co-option"></a>
<a id="ek67"></a>
## EK67 — `stacksnoop` command-line option clears the earlier `mungwall` setting

The generic `PrepareExecBase()` initializer reads `KRN_CmdLine` and tests for the debug options independently (`rom/exec/prepareexecbase.c:322-345`). When it finds `mungwall`, it assigns `EXECF_MungWall` to `IntFlags`; when it later finds `stacksnoop`, it assigns `EXECF_StackSnoop`, replacing the earlier value instead of adding the second bit. The flags are independent (`rom/exec/exec_intern.h:138-142`): allocation/free paths test `EXECF_MungWall`, while `NewAddTask()` tests `EXECF_StackSnoop` (`rom/exec/allocmem.c:105`; `freemem.c:70`; `newaddtask.c:261-265`). Thus a command line containing both options enables only StackSnoop, despite both matches succeeding. This does not apply to PPC-CHRP's separate Exec initializer.

**Trigger and consequence:** boot a target using the generic initializer with both `mungwall` and `stacksnoop` in `KRN_CmdLine`. MungWall will silently remain disabled while StackSnoop is enabled, so memory-wall checks requested by the boot configuration do not run. **Affected configuration:** platforms using generic `PrepareExecBase()`; PPC-CHRP has a separate initializer. The checked-in default command lines found in the coverage pass do not contain both options, so this is conditional on a custom boot command line. **Confidence:** high for the independent matches and replacement assignment; no boot or runtime option parsing was exercised. Preserve both bits when enabling the second option (and parse complete option tokens). Source-only; see the [option co-reachability trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L136).

<a id="ek10607"></a>
### EK10607 — HDToolBox can divide by zero when a block device reports zero partition geometry

`OpenRootPartition()` accepts any successful `TD_GETGEOMETRY` result for a non-CD device and copies `dg_Heads` and `dg_TrackSectors` directly into the root DosEnvec as `de_Surfaces` and `de_BlocksPerTrack`, without validating either value (`rom/partition/openrootpartition.c:68-85`). The selected HDToolBox discovery path stores the returned root handle, then reads its `PT_DOSENVEC` into the root record (`workbench/tools/HDToolBox/harddisks.c:113-136`). When the user adds a partition, `addPartition()` computes `blocks_per_cyl = de_Surfaces * de_BlocksPerTrack` and divides `(leadin + blocks_per_cyl - 1)` by that value without a zero check (`workbench/tools/HDToolBox/partitions.c:279-335`; its GUI caller is `gui.c:399`). If a device returns success with either geometry component zero, this path divides by zero before `AddPartitionTags()` is called. The MBR backend also divides by the copied root geometry when encoding CHS fields (`rom/partition/partitionmbr.c:188-237`), so bypassing the GUI calculation would not protect direct partition-library callers.

**Trigger and consequence:** a non-CD trackdisk-compatible device opens successfully and returns a successful `TD_GETGEOMETRY` with zero heads or zero sectors per track; HDToolBox discovers the root and the user requests a new partition. The add action reaches an integer division by zero and cannot complete. The producer audit found device-response paths that can pass zero geometry through: ATA's small-LBA path copies legacy IDENTIFY head/sector fields without checking for zero (`rom/devs/ata/lowlevel.c:1878-1926`), AHCI copies IDENTIFY `nheads`/`nsectors` directly (`rom/devs/ahci/ahci_io.c:298-317`), and the ROM USB mass-storage class can mark heads/sectors as present when a mode page has a nonzero cylinder count even if its head or sectors field is zero (`rom/usb/classes/massstorage/massstorage.class.c:2424-2425,2446-2450,2561-2565`). The selected NVMe and VirtIO producers instead synthesize nonzero head/track defaults (`rom/devs/nvme/nvme_busclass.c:595-618`; `rom/devs/virtio/virtio_busclass.c:237-243`). These code paths establish that zero fields are not rejected or repaired, but no checked-in target/device response establishes that hardware supplies them, so occurrence remains conditional. **Affected configuration:** `partition.library` plus an explicit HDToolBox build (`workbench/tools/HDToolBox/mmakefile.src:7-25`); the HDToolBox aggregate dependency is commented, so default installation is not claimed. **Confidence:** high for acceptance of zero values and the downstream division; medium for occurrence because no maintained device response with zero geometry was established. Reject nonpositive heads/sectors in `OpenRootPartition()` and guard the UI/backend arithmetic. No geometry request, partition operation, device, or build was exercised; source-only; see the [geometry-validation caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#partition-root-zero-geometry-hdtoolbox-ek10607).


<a id="ek568"></a>
### EK568 — pthread timer cleanup aborts a request before it was queued

`_obtain_sema_timed()` successfully opens `timer.device`, sets `timerio.tr_node.io_Flags = 0`, and converts the absolute deadline before submitting the request (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:249-280`). When the converted relative timeval is zero, it calls `CloseTimerDevice()` and returns `ETIMEDOUT` without calling `SendIO()` (`:273-291`). The shared timer setup has already set the request message type to `NT_MESSAGE` in `OpenTimerDevice()` but has not initialized the timer request's queue links (`:129-169`). `CloseTimerDevice()` calls `CheckIO()`; because `IOF_QUICK` is clear and the message type is `NT_MESSAGE`, `CheckIO()` reports the request as still active (`rom/exec/checkio.c:49-58`). Cleanup then calls `AbortIO()` (`pthread.c:173-194`), and the timer device's abort vector removes every request whose message is not `NT_REPLYMSG`, without checking that it was ever queued (`rom/timer/abortio.c:69-83`). The zero-deadline request is therefore passed to `Remove()` with uninitialized list links before the helper can return its timeout result.

The same cleanup helper is reached on `OpenTimerDevice()` failure and on `clock_gettime()` failure in `_pthread_cond_timedwait()` (`compiler/pthread/pthread_cond_timedwait.c:60-80`). Those requests are also unsent; the failed-open case additionally leaves `io_Flags` uninitialized, so its route through `CheckIO()` and the NULL-device abort dispatch depends on stack contents. These are conditional variants of the same cleanup-state defect; they do not strengthen the primary zero-interval trigger.

**Trigger and consequence:** a contended pthread timed mutex or read/write lock reaches `_obtain_sema_timed()` with a deadline that converts to a zero timeval. The function intends to return `ETIMEDOUT`, but first invokes timer AbortIO on a request that was never submitted; the driver's unconditional `Remove()` can dereference invalid link pointers or corrupt list state. Avoid aborting requests that have not been sent, or mark/initialize request state so cleanup distinguishes submitted from unsent requests. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting `linklib-pthread` and callers of the timed mutex/read/write-lock APIs with the stated zero-interval condition. **Confidence:** high for the zero-interval path, `CheckIO()` state test and timer abort removal; the resulting memory effect depends on the uninitialized stack link values. The failed-open and condition-clock-error variants remain conditional on the uninitialized flags. No lock, timer request, failed open or clock error was induced; source-only. See the [pthread timer cleanup trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#pthread-timed-lock-cleanup-ek568).

<a id="ek9183"></a>
## EK9183 — `AddTaskHook()` dereferences a failed hook-node allocation

In the normal registration branch (`tlhe_Node.ln_Pri >= 0`), `AddTaskHook()` allocates a `TaskListHookNode` but does not check the result before storing `tHook` through it (`rom/task/AddTaskHook.c:64-69`). If that allocation fails, the next statement dereferences NULL instead of returning the function's `FALSE` failure result. The `TaskListEntry` and hook-type allocations immediately above are checked, so this unchecked allocation is a separate failure path. The queued hook-node allocation is distinct from EK8803's later list-node layout mismatch.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** builds selecting `task.resource` with `TASKRES_ENABLE`, when a task registers a queued hook (`tlhe_Node.ln_Pri >= 0`) and this node allocation fails. The checked-in startup initializes/runs a task-hook type but no in-tree `AddTaskHook()` producer was found; the trigger therefore requires an external or indirect hook client. **Consequence:** the caller task faults during registration rather than receiving `FALSE`. Check `hookEntry` and return failure before writing or linking it. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked allocation and immediate dereference; no allocation failure or hook registration was induced. Source-only; see the [AddTaskHook body and caller review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2144).


<a id="ek10608"></a>
### EK10608 - m68kemu DeleteMsgPort leaves freed port shadows registered. *(withdrawn; duplicate of EK9891)*

**Disposition:** this observation is already covered by EK9891, which lists the `CreateMsgPort()` / `DeleteMsgPort()` lifecycle, retained guest allocation and mapping, and bounded 256-entry shadow table. No separate finding is retained. See the [DeleteMsgPort shadow-lifetime recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#delete-msgport-shadow-lifetime-ek10608).


<a id="ek10609"></a>
### EK10609 - m68kemu IFFParse chunk-array thunks pass guest-endian IDs directly to native code.

The generated `PropChunks()`, `StopChunks()`, and `CollectionChunks()` wrappers translate only the `propArray` base pointer (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:4760-4803`). Their public contract is an array of `LONG` type/ID pairs (`workbench/libs/iffparse/iffparse.conf:32-36`), and the native routines read each pair as host `LONG` values (`workbench/libs/iffparse/propchunks.c:63-81`; `stopchunks.c:51-62`; `collectionchunks.c:60-78`). IFF chunk IDs are defined as four-character big-endian numeric values by `MAKE_ID()` (`compiler/include/libraries/iffparse.h:124-130`; `compiler/arossupport/include/macros.h:343-344`). On little-endian hosts, a guest array word for `FORM` stored as bytes `46 4f 52 4d` is read as `0x4D524F46`, not `0x464F524D`.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated m68k client supplies a normal guest type/ID pair to one of these array APIs on a little-endian host. The native function compares or registers byte-reversed IDs, so the intended chunks are not recognized or stopped/collected as requested; `PropChunks()` can return an error for the invalid/unsupported ID. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded m68kemu with a little-endian host. Native in-tree callers exist, but no maintained emulated guest caller was found. Copy and byte-swap each 32-bit pair into native storage before dispatch. **Confidence:** high for the direct guest pointer, native `LONG` reads, and ID encoding; exact parser outcome depends on the requested chunk pair and IFF stream. No guest array, IFF stream, or build was used; source-only. See the [IFFParse chunk-array ABI trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#iffparse-chunk-array-endian-trace-ek10609).


<a id="ek819"></a>
### EK819 — RexxSupport `OPENPORT` crashes on allocation failure and can leave a half-published port

`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/openport.c:43-76` creates a public message port, then allocates `PortNode` and its name without checking either `AllocMem()` result before `strcpy()` and field stores (`:44-52`). If either allocation fails, the RexxSupport caller dereferences NULL; the already-created message port and any successful sibling allocation are not released.

A later failure occurs after the resource has been published: the function increments the library open count, links the `PortNode` into the library's `openports` list, and calls `AddPort()` before creating the temporary reply port and Rexx message (`:53-72`). If either reply allocation fails, it returns `ERR10_003` without removing the published port/list node or releasing the name, node, port, reply port (if created), or library pin. The command reports failure while leaving an externally visible, partially initialized resource; a subsequent `OPENPORT` for the same name finds the list entry and reports that it already exists. Even when the RPC is sent, a non-`RC_OK` `RXADDRSRC` reply is only printed (`:80-93`): OPENPORT still returns the success string, leaving the public port and library pin in place although the Rexx system did not register the script-finish cleanup resource. The request's purpose is documented as registering a cleanup callback when the Rexx script finishes (`compiler/include/rexx/storage.h:67-71`).

**Trigger and consequence:** memory or signal exhaustion after initial port creation can fault the caller at the unchecked node/name allocation; a later reply-port/message allocation failure can leave a published resource and pinned library behind after an error return; or Rexx can reject `RXADDRSRC` and the command can report success while the script-finish cleanup was not registered. In the latter cases the named port can remain published and keep RexxSupport resident after the script exits. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded `workbench-libs-rexxsupport`; the local manifest defines that target, while default aggregate/package reachability is not established by the checked-in parent graph. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked allocations, missing post-publication rollback, and ignored non-success reply; no allocation failure or RPC error was induced. Check the registration result and unwind every published resource on failure. No allocation failure, Rexx command, or build was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10611"></a>
### EK10611 — NextConductor exposes private RealTime conductors through public enumeration

`PLAYER_Conductor = ~0` is documented as creating a private conductor (`workbench/libs/realtime/createplayera.c:58-61`). `createConductor()` still appends that object to the shared `rtb_ConductorList` and marks it `CONDUCTF_PRIVATE` (`workbench/libs/realtime/setplayerattrsa.c:325-350`). `FindConductor()` explicitly filters private conductors (`workbench/libs/realtime/findconductor.c:61-71`), but `NextConductor()` returns the list head or successor without checking the private flag (`workbench/libs/realtime/nextconductor.c:55-70`); its own source comment asks whether private conductors should be filtered. Thus enumeration can return a private conductor pointer to a caller using the public API, despite name lookup hiding those objects.

**Trigger and consequence:** a client creates or encounters a private conductor, then enumerates with `NextConductor()` at a position before that node. The API exposes the private conductor and its public `Conductor` structure to that client. This defeats the privacy implied by the documented private-conductor creation mode and by `FindConductor()` filtering. No checked-in `NextConductor()` caller was found, so an in-tree caller consequence is not established. The API documentation does not explicitly promise that enumeration excludes private conductors; this candidate therefore depends on the intended meaning of “private,” indicated by the flag, the `FindConductor()` behavior, and the unresolved implementation comment. Filter private nodes during enumeration if the API is intended to hide them. **Affected configuration:** an explicitly built `realtime.library` with a private conductor and an external or future `NextConductor()` client. **Confidence:** medium-low; the implementation asymmetry is direct, but the public enumeration contract is not explicit. No conductor or enumeration was run; source-only. See the [NextConductor privacy review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#nextconductor-private-conductor-enumeration-ek10611).

<a id="ek10612"></a>
### EK10612 — Timer EClock updates race across ExecSMP CPUs

The selected PC timer's `EClockUpdate()` reads the shared PIT baseline, computes elapsed ticks, updates `tb_ticks_total`, `tb_CurrentTime`, and `tb_Elapsed`, then stores the new `tb_prev_tick` without a cross-CPU lock (`arch/all-pc/timer/ticks.c:81-112`). The hardware IRQ calls it from `TimerInt()` (`arch/all-pc/timer/timer_init.c:34-49`). Task-context APIs also call it: `ReadEClock()`, `GetSysTime()`, and `GetUpTime()` each wrap the call in `Disable()` only (`rom/timer/readeclock.c:56-62`; `getsystime.c:54-61`; `getuptime.c:54-61`); `common_BeginIO()` does the same in its request paths (`rom/timer/lowlevel.c:145-180,190-225`). Exec documents that on ExecSMP, `Disable()` applies only to the calling processor and shared data needs a spinlock (`rom/exec/disable.c:58-61`). The timer list lock does not protect the preceding clock update. The selected AArch64 Raspberry Pi backend has a separate race in the same shared clock state: `EClockUpdate()` atomically advances `tbp_EClockLast` with compare-and-swap, then updates `tb_CurrentTime` and `tb_Elapsed` using ordinary, non-atomic `ADDTIME()` operations (`arch/aarch64-raspi/timer/ticks.c:23-56`). If one CPU claims sample `now1` and is delayed before the additions, a second CPU can claim a later `now2` and concurrently add its disjoint delta to the same timeval fields. `ReadEClock()`, `GetSysTime()`, and `GetUpTime()` call this routine under local `Disable()` only; the selected timer tick also calls it from `timer_ProcessTick()` (`timer_init.c:40-46`). These paths do not serialize other CPUs. The CAS avoids double-booking the same interval but does not serialize the shared timeval updates.

**Trigger and consequence:** on PC ExecSMP, a timer IRQ on one CPU overlaps a timer API call on another. Both can read the same `tb_prev_tick` and add overlapping elapsed intervals, or one can overwrite the other's newer baseline. On AArch64 Raspberry Pi ExecSMP, the timer tick or a clock API call can claim a counter sample on one CPU while another CPU claims a later sample and overlaps the non-atomic additions. Either path can make clock values inconsistent or lose elapsed time, affecting timer deadlines and elapsed-time consumers. Serialize the complete sample and update of shared clock state across CPUs, including `EClockSet()` interactions. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC ExecSMP and i386 PC SMP (`configure.in:1669-1670,2197-2199`), plus the AArch64 Raspberry Pi `smp` target (`:2197-2199`). **Confidence:** high for the unsynchronized shared state and cross-CPU caller paths; the resulting time error depends on the interleaving and was not reproduced. No timer, SMP schedule, or build was run; source-only. See the [PC and Raspberry Pi timer EClock update traces](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#pc-timer-eclock-update-smp-race-ek10612).

<a id="ek10613"></a>
### EK10613 — Raspberry Pi timer reprogramming can overwrite an earlier deadline

The Raspberry Pi AArch64 backend's `Timer_Reprogram()` conditionally obtains `tb_ListLock`, reads the MICROHZ queue head, computes a delay, releases the lock, then writes the shared system-timer compare register (`arch/aarch64-raspi/timer/ticks.c:72-116`). The selected AArch64 timer initializer does not initialize `tb_ExecLockBase` or `tb_ListLock` (`arch/aarch64-raspi/timer/timer_init.c:100-121`); the zero-cleared library base therefore leaves the lock guard false on this path (library-base allocation: `rom/exec/makelibrary.c:108-116`). The missing queue lock is recorded separately as EK10614. Even when queue locking is available, the snapshot is released before the compare write, so concurrent callers can still commit in stale order. `common_BeginIO()` calls `Timer_Reprogram()` when an insertion becomes the new head (`arch/aarch64-raspi/timer/beginio.c:17-24`), and the selected compare interrupt calls it again after processing the tick (`arch/aarch64-raspi/timer/timer_init.c:56-74`). ExecSMP is enabled for the Raspberry Pi `smp` target (`configure.in:2197-2199`), and the BCM system timer compare is shared by CPUs.

**Trigger and consequence:** a `BeginIO()` caller or compare-interrupt handler snapshots a MICROHZ head with a longer remaining delay and is delayed before writing the compare. Another CPU inserts a request with an earlier deadline, snapshots that new head, and arms its shorter delay. If the first caller then writes its stale, longer delay, the earlier request is not serviced at its deadline and can remain delayed until the stale compare fires (or another reprogramming event occurs). Keep the queue snapshot and compare programming ordered across CPUs, for example by serializing the complete operation or validating the queue generation before committing the register write. **Affected configuration:** AArch64 Raspberry Pi ExecSMP systems where the system-timer compare IRQ is delivered to the selected `Timer1Tick()` path (the BCM2837/Pi 3 route). Exclude BCM2711/BCM2712 (Pi 4/5) from the user-visible deadline claim: their selected timer code installs a VBlank-driven MICROHZ fallback because the compare interrupt is not guaranteed (`arch/aarch64-raspi/timer/timer_init.c:77-82,108-112,172-182`). The race requires overlapping MICROHZ request submissions on different CPUs. **Confidence:** high for the unlocked snapshot-to-register interval; medium for deadline delay on compare-IRQ SoCs, conditional on the stated cross-CPU ordering and interrupt path. No request, timer, SMP schedule, or build was run; source-only. See the [Raspberry Pi compare reprogramming trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#raspberry-pi-timer-compare-reprogramming-ek10613).

EK10612 follow-up: the same cross-CPU serialization gap also covers `TR_SETSYSTIME`. Shared `common_BeginIO()` writes `tb_CurrentTime` and calls `EClockSet()` while using only local `Disable()` (`rom/timer/lowlevel.c:131-142`). On Raspberry Pi AArch64, `EClockSet()` is a no-op while a concurrent `EClockUpdate()` can non-atomically add to those same timeval fields after claiming the EClock interval (`arch/aarch64-raspi/timer/ticks.c:39-63`). On PC, `EClockSet()` also resets `tb_ticks_total` and `tb_prev_tick` without cross-CPU serialization (`arch/all-pc/timer/ticks.c:115-126`). Selected in-tree setters include Date, SetClock, DOS CLI startup and Locale prefs. This is incorporated into EK10612; no separate ID is counted.


<a id="ek10614"></a>
### EK10614 — AArch64 Raspberry Pi ExecSMP timer queues have no list lock

`TimerBase` is allocated with `MEMF_CLEAR`, so fields without explicit initialization begin NULL (`rom/exec/makelibrary.c:108-116`). The selected AArch64 Raspberry Pi timer initializer installs the hardware timer and configures its tick rate but never assigns `tb_ExecLockBase` or `tb_ListLock` (`arch/aarch64-raspi/timer/timer_init.c:100-168`); a repository-wide writer search finds no assignment for either field in this architecture's timer sources. The generic initializer does not run for this architecture-specific target (`arch/aarch64-raspi/timer/mmakefile.src:6-9`). Yet the shared request insertion/completion and AbortIO paths acquire the list lock only when `tb_ExecLockBase` is non-NULL (`rom/timer/lowlevel.c:161-180,190-220,264-403`; `rom/timer/abortio.c:59-88`), and AArch64 `Timer_Reprogram()` uses the same guard (`arch/aarch64-raspi/timer/ticks.c:72-104`). On the selected ExecSMP build, that guard is false, so list operations proceed without a cross-CPU lock.

**Trigger and consequence:** on an AArch64 Raspberry Pi ExecSMP build, a timer interrupt/tick processes a request list while another CPU inserts or aborts a timer request. The concurrent linked-list operations are unsynchronized and can lose/corrupt queue membership or leave a request uncompleted. BCM2711/2712 use the VBlank-driven MICROHZ tick fallback, but that path still processes the same queue concurrently with callers. **Affected configuration:** AArch64 Raspberry Pi `smp` variant (`configure.in:2195-2199`), including the BCM2837 timer-IRQ route and BCM2711/2712 VBlank fallback. **Confidence:** high that the selected initializer leaves both fields zero and all guarded paths skip locking; the resulting queue failure depends on cross-CPU overlap. Initialize and validate the shared lock before enabling timer processing, or fail SMP timer initialization if a safe lock cannot be provided. Source-only; no request, interrupt, SMP schedule or build was run. See the [AArch64 timer initializer and queue-lock trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#raspberry-pi-timer-list-lock-missing-ek10614).


<a id="ek10615"></a>
### EK10615 — ExecSMP housekeeper can spin on a remote tombstone and delay reclamation

When the service task dequeues a `TS_TOMBSTONED` task while CPU affinity is enabled, it compares its current CPU number with the task's recorded CPU (`rom/exec/service.c:48-57`). On a mismatch, `taskRequeue` remains true; the `TS_REMOVED` case puts the same task node back on `ServicePort` and breaks only the `switch` (`:58-65`). The enclosing `while (GetMsg(...))` immediately dequeues that request again (`:22-30`), so the service task never reaches `WaitPort()` while this condition persists. The housekeeper has priority 127 and `TASKAFFINITY_ANY` (`rom/exec/exec_init.c:308-335`). The x86-64 PC, ARM32, and AArch64 `core_Schedule()` implementations scan for an affinity-eligible ready task and can request a switch after the quantum when its priority is equal to or below the running task (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:112-134`; `arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:111-140`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:101-132`). `core_Dispatch()` then selects the first affinity-eligible task in the priority-sorted ready list (`:308-319`; `arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:269-285`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:247-263`). The housekeeper is priority 127, the maximum, and `exec_TaskEnqueueReady()` uses `Enqueue()`, which inserts equal-priority nodes after existing peers and before all lower-priority tasks (`rom/exec/exec_intern.h:205-214`; `rom/exec/enqueue.c:67-90`). Thus the quantum switch does not let a lower-priority task run while the housekeeper remains eligible; absent an equal-priority eligible task ahead of it, dispatch can select the housekeeper again. Another CPU may select it while it is ready because its affinity is ANY, but an idle CPU assigned to the tombstoned task does not force that CPU to win the dispatch race.

**Trigger and consequence:** on ExecSMP with CPU affinity enabled, a tombstoned-task cleanup request is dequeued by the housekeeper on a CPU other than the task's recorded CPU, with no equal-priority eligible ready task ahead of the housekeeper. The housekeeper requeues the request at the tail and, if no other message is queued, immediately dequeues it again; it can busy-spin instead of reaching `WaitPort()`. The tombstoned task's memory list remains allocated until the housekeeper later runs on the matching CPU. Because the request moves to the tail, already queued messages ahead of it can still be processed. A priority-127 eligible peer already ahead of the housekeeper can time-slice it; lower-priority tasks cannot, because the requeued housekeeper remains first in the priority-sorted ready list. Other CPUs may take the housekeeper while it is ready, so the affected CPU and duration depend on dispatch races; the retry ends only after the housekeeper runs on the recorded CPU or CPU-affinity checking is disabled. This is distinct from EK807's conditional stale-TCB reclamation race: EK10615 concerns repeated queue processing and delayed reclamation, not use of a task after reclamation. Defer the request until the owning CPU can service it or yield between retries. **Affected configuration:** the configured x86-64 PC and Raspberry Pi ExecSMP targets (`configure.in:1669,2197`; x86-64 PC and ARM32/AArch64 Raspberry Pi scheduler paths) with CPU affinity enabled and the described scheduling state. **Confidence:** high for the immediate dequeue/requeue loop and priority-order effect; duration and system impact depend on affinity, message arrivals, equal-priority peers, and which CPU wins dispatch. No SMP schedule was run; source-only. See the [housekeeper remote-tombstone queue review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#housekeeper-remote-tombstone-queue-ek10615).


<a id="ek10616"></a>
### EK10616 — RexxSupport `GETPKT` inserts a null node when its port is empty

`rxsupp_getpkt()` accepts the registered one-argument `GETPKT` command, calls `GetMsg(data->port)`, and unconditionally passes the result to `AddTail(&data->msgs, ...)` (`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/getpkt.c:21-32`; registration in `arexxdispatch.c:36-38`). `GetMsg()` returns NULL when the message queue is empty (`rom/exec/getmsg.c:52-62`). `AddTail()` dereferences the supplied node to write `ln_Succ` and `ln_Pred` (`rom/exec/addtail.c:57-65`), so an empty-queue call writes through NULL and corrupts/faults the caller before producing its nominal pointer result. `GETPKT` does not itself wait; `WAITPKT` is a separate command. No checked-in caller or command documentation establishes a mandatory `WAITPKT`-before-`GETPKT` precondition, so the public command's empty-queue behavior remains an API-contract question, but the implementation has no safe empty result path.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `GETPKT` for a valid open port while it has no queued message (including a race where another consumer removes the message after a separate `WAITPKT`). The null node is passed into list insertion, causing invalid memory writes and potentially damaging the retained-message list used by `portcleanup()`. Return a defined empty result or an error before `AddTail()` when `GetMsg()` returns NULL. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built/loaded `workbench-libs-rexxsupport`; aggregate package selection is not established. **Confidence:** high for the NULL-to-`AddTail` failure; medium for whether an empty queue violates an intended undocumented command precondition. No command or port was run; source-only. See the [GETPKT caller/contract recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#rexxsupport-getpkt-empty-queue-ek10616).


<a id="ek10617"></a>
### EK10617 — RexxSupport `GETPKT` strands a dequeued message when its result allocation fails

`rxsupp_getpkt()` removes a message from the public port with `GetMsg()`, links it into the private `data->msgs` list, then returns the pointer to Rexx by allocating an argstring containing the pointer bytes (`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/getpkt.c:29-32`). If `CreateArgstring()` fails, it returns NULL (`workbench/libs/rexxsyslib/createargstring.c:49-56`), but `GETPKT` still returns `RC_OK`; `ArexxDispatch` forwards both values unchanged to `ReturnRexxQuery()` (`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/arexxdispatch.c:75-79`; `compiler/include/rexx/rexxcall.h:36-39`). The caller receives no message pointer for the `REPLY` command, while the message remains removed from the public port and linked in the private retained list. No rollback restores it to the public queue or replies it at this point.

**Trigger and consequence:** argstring allocation fails after a queued message is dequeued. The script cannot use the pointer needed by `REPLY`, leaving the original sender waiting and the message retained until `CLOSEPORT`/resource cleanup; EK866 means cleanup with multiple tracked messages can skip replies after the first. Return an error and restore or reply the dequeued message when the result argstring cannot be created. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built/loaded `workbench-libs-rexxsupport`. **Confidence:** high for the failed allocation, successful return code, and retained inaccessible message; downstream wait duration depends on later port closure and cleanup. No allocation failure or Rexx command was run; source-only. See the [GETPKT result-allocation failure trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#rexxsupport-getpkt-result-allocation-ek10617).



<a id="ek10618"></a>
### EK10618 — PC timer loses complete PIT wraps after a delayed update [medium impact, high source confidence; i386-PC and x86-64-PC]

The selected PC PIT backend reads a 16-bit down-counter in software-strobe mode (`arch/all-pc/timer/timer_init.c:184-196`; `ticks.c:105-112`). `EClockAdd()` calculates elapsed ticks from the previous and current `UWORD` values and adds `0x10000` at most once when it sees a rollover (`arch/all-pc/timer/ticks.c:81-96`). In PIT mode 4 the counter continues through `0xffff` after reaching zero, so its value repeats every 65,536 input clocks; the Intel 8254 datasheet describes this wrap-and-continue behavior ([Mode 4 and counter operation](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~410/doc/8254.pdf#page=16)). At the configured 1,193,180 Hz, one full counter period is about 54.9 ms (`timer_init.c:134-143`). A single modular difference cannot reveal additional full periods; after exactly 65,536 clocks, `time == tb_prev_tick`, so the rollover branch is skipped and the computed increment is zero.

**Trigger and consequence:** no `EClockUpdate()` sample is taken for more than one 65,536-clock period (for example, IRQ0 service is delayed or masked for over about 54.9 ms). The current counter then contains only the phase within its latest wrap; `EClockAdd()` loses one or more complete periods while advancing `tb_ticks_total`, `tb_CurrentTime`, and `tb_Elapsed`. The public clock and timer deadline accounting under-report elapsed time. The normal PIT reload is 23,864 clocks (about 20 ms), but a sufficiently long service gap can span multiple counter periods before the next sample.

**Affected configuration:** i386-PC and x86-64-PC targets selecting `arch/all-pc/timer`; the regular one-wrap path is unaffected when updates occur within one full counter period. **Confidence:** high for the single-wrap arithmetic and modulo counter limit; the trigger depends on a greater-than-54.9-ms gap between samples. This is distinct from EK10612, which covers concurrent unsynchronized updates even when the sample intervals are shorter. Use an independent overflow count or a wider/monotonic clock source. No interrupt delay, timer request, hardware counter or build was exercised; source-only. See the [PC timer EClock rollover audit](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#pc-timer-eclock-missed-wrap-ek10618).


<a id="ek10619"></a>
### EK10619 — PC BattClock misreads and writes a 12-hour RTC as 24-hour time [medium impact, high confidence; conditional RTC mode]

`arch/all-pc/battclock/readbattclock.c:34-58` and `writebattclock.c:38-58` inspect Status B only for its binary-versus-BCD bit (`0x04`); neither handles its 24/12-hour bit (`0x02`) or the hour register's PM bit. The MC146818-compatible RTC format uses hours 1–12 plus bit 7 for PM when 12-hour mode is selected ([MC146818 datasheet, Register B and hour formats](https://www.dosdays.co.uk/media/motorola/Motorola_MC146818.pdf)). For example, a BCD 12 AM value is `0x12` and is decoded by this code as hour 12 rather than 0; a PM value also carries bit 7 into the BCD conversion. `WriteBattClock()` emits `Amiga2Date()`'s 0–23 hour directly (BCD-encoding it when needed), which is not a valid 1–12 plus PM representation in 12-hour mode. The PC BattClock initialization does not set or normalize the RTC mode (`battclock_init.c:19-42`), and selected `SetClock` and Time preferences callers use these APIs (`workbench/c/SetClock.c:130,164`; `workbench/prefs/time/prefs.c:51`). **Trigger and consequence:** firmware or prior software leaves the RTC in 12-hour mode; `ReadBattClock()` returns a wrong time and `WriteBattClock()` stores incorrect/invalid hour values. **Confidence:** high for the mode mismatch; whether a machine enters this mode is configuration-dependent. No RTC or build was exercised; source-only. See the [PC BattClock full-body pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#pc-battclock-full-body-time-format-pass-ek10619).


<a id="ek10620"></a>
### EK10620 — Hyper-V debugger task-list command calls `kprintf` with a missing string argument [medium impact, high confidence; optional debugger]

`HVDEBUGDumpTasks()` calls `kprintf("\n[HyperV:DEBUG] %s()\n");` with a `%s` conversion and no corresponding argument (`arch/all-pc/debug/hyperv/hyperv-tasks.c:79`). The custom formatter used by `kprintf` consumes a pointer for `%s` and measures/prints the pointed-to string (`compiler/arossupport/_vkprintf.c:85-88`; `compiler/fmtprintf/fmtprintf.c:269-280,368-370`). The command table routes `tasklist` to `HVDebug_cmdTaskList()`, which calls this function (`hyperv-debug.c:133-142,73-80`); the function runs inside the registered NMI exception handler. **Trigger and consequence:** invoke `tasklist` in the optional Hyper-V debugger. The formatter consumes an unspecified value as a string pointer and reads through it, producing garbage or faulting while handling the debugger exception. **Affected configuration:** only the optional `hyperv-debug` resource, which requires the DEBUG=yes target and explicit addition to the x86-64 PC boot image (`arch/all-pc/debug/hyperv/mmakefile.src:20-21`; `notes.txt`). **Confidence:** high for the mismatched format/argument and resulting invalid string access; exact failure depends on the stray value. Supply a string argument or remove the conversion. No NMI or command was issued; source-only. See the [Hyper-V debugger task-list pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#hyperv-debugger-task-list-and-helper-full-body-pass-ek10700).


<a id="ek10621"></a>
### EK10621 — Hyper-V debugger converts an absolute TSC timestamp as task runtime [low impact, high source confidence; optional debugger]

`HVDEBUGDumpTaskStats()` converts `IntETask(etask)->iet_private1` directly to nanoseconds and labels the result `Runtime : last +...` (`arch/all-pc/debug/hyperv/hyperv-tasks.c:49-54`). In the selected x86-64 PC scheduler, that field is set to the raw `RDTSC()` counter when a task is dispatched (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:179-185`); task CPU runtime is measured separately by subtracting this start timestamp from the current counter on switch-out (`:323-329`). The debugger therefore reports an absolute counter value as a duration, not the task's current or previous run interval. Multiplying a long-running machine's raw TSC value by one billion in `UQUAD` also overflows before division by the CPU frequency. The registered `task` command calls `HVDEBUGDumpTaskStats()` directly (`hyperv-debug.c:82-86`), so this path does not pass through the separate missing-format-argument call in `tasklist` (EK10620).

**Trigger and consequence:** invoke the optional Hyper-V debugger's `task` command after a task has been scheduled. Its “last” runtime field displays a boot-relative/overflowed value instead of a task runtime interval; the accumulated `iet_CpuTime` total remains a separate field. **Affected configuration:** optional `hyperv-debug` resource explicitly included in an x86-64 PC image. **Confidence:** high for the timestamp-versus-duration mismatch; the numeric value depends on TSC uptime and frequency. Subtract the timestamp from a current TSC sample before converting, and perform the conversion without overflowing the intermediate. No command, NMI, or build was exercised; source-only. See the [Hyper-V debugger task-list and helper pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#hyperv-debugger-task-list-and-helper-full-body-pass-2026-11-03).


<a id="ek10622"></a>
### EK10622 — Hyper-V debugger walks scheduler lists without protecting an SMP snapshot [medium impact, high source confidence; optional ExecSMP debugger]

The Hyper-V debugger registers `HVExceptionHandler()` for exception vector 2 (`arch/all-pc/debug/hyperv/hyperv-debug.c:17,243-251`). That handler remains in an input loop until the user exits and has no stop-the-other-CPUs or scheduler-list snapshot step (`:185-240`). Its `tasklist` command calls `HVDEBUGDumpTasks()` (`:76-80`), which walks `TaskRunning`, `TaskSpinning`, `TaskReady`, and `TaskWait` with raw `ForeachNode` loops and reads each task while traversing (`arch/all-pc/debug/hyperv/hyperv-tasks.c:90-145`). `ForeachNode` dereferences the head/successor links directly (`compiler/include/exec/lists.h:195-201`). The corresponding ExecSMP scheduler transitions mutate these lists under their per-list spinlocks (`rom/exec/exec_intern.h:193-239`; `arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:205-213,248-286,304-321,333-350`), but the debugger takes none of them. Because this is an NMI handler, it can also interrupt the local CPU during a list-link update; acquiring the existing lock from that context could deadlock if the interrupted path held it.

**Trigger and consequence:** in an x86-64 PC ExecSMP build with the optional Hyper-V debugger included, invoke `tasklist` while the NMI handler is active and another CPU is scheduling tasks, or when the NMI interrupts the local CPU during a scheduler-list update. The walk can observe transient links, skip entries, or follow a stale/freed task pointer while reading its fields, potentially producing a partial listing or faulting in the debugger. The earlier EK10620 format mismatch occurs immediately before the list walks; this separate consequence is reachable if that formatter call returns. **Affected configuration:** optional `hyperv-debug` resource in an x86-64 PC ExecSMP image; the issue requires an overlapping scheduler-list mutation. **Confidence:** high for the unsynchronized walks and concurrent mutation path; medium for whether a particular interleaving produces a visible failure. Use a debugger-safe stable snapshot or stop/quiesce the other CPUs before walking scheduler state. No NMI, command, schedule, or build was exercised; source-only. See the [Hyper-V debugger task-list and helper pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#hyperv-debugger-task-list-and-helper-full-body-pass-2026-11-03).


<a id="ek10623"></a>
### EK10623 — Hyper-V debugger accepts command prefixes and dispatches every match [low impact, high confidence; optional debugger]

`HVDebug_CommandMatch()` returns true as soon as all characters in a command-table pattern have matched; it never requires the input to end or reach a delimiter (`arch/all-pc/debug/hyperv/hyperv-debug.c:145-171`). `HVDebug_DispatchCommand()` continues scanning and invokes every matching handler instead of stopping after a match (`:174-181`). The table includes both `tasklist` and the shorter `task` command (`:133-143`).

**Trigger and consequence:** enter `taskextra` at the debugger prompt. The `task` entry matches its prefix and runs `HVDebug_cmdThisTask()` instead of rejecting the unknown command. Enter `tasklist` and, if the longer handler returns, the shorter `task` entry also matches and prints the current task after the list. **Affected configuration:** optional Hyper-V debugger resource. **Confidence:** high; prefix acceptance and continued dispatch follow directly from the matcher, loop, and command table. Require an end-of-command or argument delimiter and stop after dispatching a single match. No debugger command or NMI was issued; source-only. See the [Hyper-V debugger task-list and helper pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#hyperv-debugger-task-list-and-helper-full-body-pass-2026-11-03).


<a id="ek10624"></a>
### EK10624 — Raspberry Pi `notlsf` boot option skips initial memory-header setup

The native ARM32 and AArch64 startup paths set `mh` to the first usable RAM address, then test whether the supplied command line contains `notlsf`. In ARM32 the plain-header setup is inside a disabled `#if (0)` block (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_startup.c:279-293`); in AArch64 the branch contains only a comment, “Plain memory header (for debugging)” (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_startup.c:342-359`). Neither branch calls `krnCreateMemHeader()` or initializes an equivalent header. Both paths nevertheless continue into `krnPrepareExecBase()` with that `mh` (`arm-native/kernel_startup.c:321-323`; `aarch64-native/kernel_startup.c:371-373`).

`krnPrepareExecBase()` immediately calls `krnRomTagScanner()` (`rom/kernel/prepareexecbase.c:17-21`). The scanner obtains its resident-list workspace through `krnGetSysMem()` (`rom/kernel/kernel_romtags.c:281-309`), which reads `mh_Attributes`, then either invokes managed-header callbacks or traverses `mh_First` and `MemChunk` fields (`:61-99`). Those fields are initialized by `krnCreateMemHeader()` (`rom/kernel/kernel_memory.c:25-75`), which the `notlsf` paths skipped. Startup therefore attempts allocator operations using uninitialized RAM as a MemHeader; this can fault or fail the resident-list allocation and halt boot.

**Trigger and affected configuration:** ARM32 Raspberry Pi or AArch64 Raspberry Pi boot where firmware's `/chosen/bootargs` contains the substring `notlsf`. The selected boot producers copy that property into `KRN_CmdLine` (`arch/arm-raspi/boot/boot.c:687-695`; `arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/boot.c:1055-1063`), which the affected startup files parse. No checked-in firmware bootargs establishing that option were found. The analogous SiFive-U branch is excluded: its startup handoff is disabled in this snapshot (EK193/EK195), so it is not a current reachable target path. **Confidence:** high that the option skips all MemHeader initialization and that Exec continues into the resident scan; the exact first invalid access and visible failure depend on the contents of the uninitialized RAM. Initialize and reserve a valid standard MemHeader in the fallback branch, or reject `notlsf` before allocator-dependent startup. No boot or memory operation was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10625"></a>
### EK10625 — OpenURL leaves its worker blocked when startup-message setup fails [optional target]

`sendRexxMsg()` starts `handler()` with `CreateNewProcTags()` before creating the caller's reply port and allocating its `startMsg` (`external/openurl/library/utils.c:208-258`). If either later allocation fails, it skips the `PutMsg()` and returns with `res == FALSE`; the only cleanup is freeing the reply port when present (`:282-288`). The spawned worker's first operation is an indefinite wait for that startup message (`external/openurl/library/handler.c:66-76`). No stop signal, process deletion, or error message reaches the worker on those allocation-failure branches.

**Trigger and consequence:** `CreateNewProcTags()` succeeds, then creation of the reply port or `startMsg` allocation fails. The OpenURL operation returns failure, while the independent handler process remains blocked on its private process port and retains its process/task resources indefinitely. Defer process creation until startup resources are ready, or terminate/wake the child on every post-spawn failure.

**Affected configuration:** explicitly buildable `external-openurl-lib` (`external/openurl/library/mmakefile.src:19-23`); the top-level OpenURL and broader `external` aggregate edges are commented (`external/openurl/mmakefile.src:5-12`). The finding is limited to use of this optional library target.

**Confidence:** high for the spawn-before-allocation ordering, early returns, and worker's initial wait; actual allocation failure was not induced. Source-only.


<a id="ek10626"></a>
### EK10626 — Sam440 CPU-feedback clock calculation falls through to the default formula [medium impact, high source confidence; conditional PPC440 clock mode]

In `SetupClocking440()`, the `CPR0_PLLC0` feedback selector is extracted from bits 25:24. Selector value 1 is explicitly labeled `CPU` and assigns `m = fbdv * fwdva`, but the case has no `break`; it falls through and overwrites `m` with the default `perdv0 * opbdv0 * fwdvb` formula (`arch/ppc-sam440/kernel/kernel_startup.c:421-437`). The resulting `m` determines `vco` and all published CPU/PLB/OPB/EPB/PCI frequencies (`:439-444`). The OPB estimate is used to program the decrementer reload (`:446-454`) and later in periodic idle accounting and reboot delays (`arch/ppc-sam440/kernel/intr.c:305-312`; `syscall.c:131-141`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a PPC440 boot where `CPR0_PLLC0[25:24]` reads 1. The CPU-feedback calculation is discarded, so the kernel publishes incorrect derived clocks and programs the decrementer/timing intervals from the default-mode result. The exact clock error and visible tick/delay change depend on the actual strap/register values. **Affected configuration:** explicitly selected Sam440 PPC kernel on a PPC440-class processor in the CPU-feedback mode; the active Sam440 aggregate boot edges select this kernel path when the corresponding platform target is built (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:4-16,72`). **Confidence:** high that the source falls through and overwrites `m`; conditional impact because no checked-in board register dump establishes selector 1 at runtime. Add a `break` after the CPU-feedback formula. No board, register, timer, boot, or build was used; source-only. See the [Sam440 kernel startup clocking pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#sam440-kernel-startup-clock-selector-review-ek10626-2026-11-03).

<a id="ek10627"></a>
### EK10627 — Raspberry Pi 4/5 `ReadEClock()` reports twice the fallback counter rate

The AArch64 Raspberry Pi timer defaults `tb_eclock_rate` to 100 and publishes that value as `SysBase->ex_EClockFrequency` (`arch/aarch64-raspi/timer/timer_init.c:128-154`). `ReadEClock()` returns this rate and copies `TimerBase->tb_ticks_total` to the result (`rom/timer/readeclock.c:56-67`); its public contract defines the return as EClock ticks per second. On BCM2711/BCM2712, the timer driver uses `MicroHZVBlankInt()` as its tick source because the GPU system-timer compare interrupt is not guaranteed (`timer_init.c:77-82,172-182`). That handler calls `timer_ProcessTick()`, which increments `tb_ticks_total` once per invocation (`timer_init.c:40-50,84-92`). The selected native kernel manifest includes both SoC files in `PLATFILES` (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/mmakefile.src:64`); they generate the `INTB_VERTB` heartbeat at 50 Hz (`platform_bcm2711.c:71,186-195`; `platform_bcm2712.c:111,294-303`). The regular AArch64 Raspberry Pi package selects `kernel-timer` (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/mmakefile.src:97-118,217-232`).

**Trigger and consequence:** boot on a BCM2711 or BCM2712 AArch64 Raspberry Pi with the default `eclock=100` setting (or any override other than 50). The fallback counter advances at 50 ticks per second while `ReadEClock()` reports 100 ticks per second. A client converting EClock deltas using the returned frequency therefore calculates about half the actual elapsed time; busy waits derived from that conversion take about twice their requested duration. A checked-in EtherLink III micro-delay helper uses the returned frequency to calculate its target EClock delta (`workbench/devs/networks/etherlink3/unit.c:2787-2805`); the timer API contract is violated independently of whether a particular client module is present in the standard Pi package. AHI's `PreTimer()` compares two deltas in the same EClock units, so this frequency mismatch does not by itself skew that ratio (`workbench/devs/AHI/Device/misc.c:463-480`). The free-running counter used by `EClockUpdate()` still advances wall-clock and timer elapsed values; this finding is limited to the public EClock value/frequency pair. Set the reported rate to the actual fallback tick rate, or advance the EClock value at the advertised rate. **Affected configuration:** standard AArch64 Raspberry Pi 4/5 BCM2711/BCM2712 package using the VBlank-driven fallback; a boot override of `eclock=50` avoids this rate mismatch. **Confidence:** high for the 50 Hz source, one-count-per-heartbeat update, and 100 Hz default report; no timer hardware or delay was exercised. Source-only; see the [Raspberry Pi EClock fallback-rate trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#raspberry-pi-eclock-fallback-rate-ek10627).

<a id="ek10628"></a>
### EK10628 — Generic and Efika timers leave unsupported-unit `TR_ADDREQUEST` requests unreplied [medium impact, high source confidence; selected timer implementations]

The generic timer device's `Timer_Open()` accepts unit numbers through `UNIT_WAITECLOCK` (`rom/timer/lowlevel.c:410-424`), including `UNIT_ECLOCK` and `UNIT_WAITECLOCK` (`compiler/include/devices/timer.h:22-27`). In `common_BeginIO()`, `TR_ADDREQUEST` is queued only for `UNIT_WAITUNTIL`, `UNIT_VBLANK`, and `UNIT_MICROHZ`; the ECLOCK/WAITECLOCK and default branch sets `IOERR_NOCMD` but leaves `replyit = FALSE` (`rom/timer/lowlevel.c:144-231`). The shared completion code replies only when `replyit` is true (`:244-253`). The Efika-specific `BeginIO()` repeats this no-reply error path for `UNIT_ECLOCK`, `UNIT_WAITECLOCK`, and its default (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/timer/beginio.c:118-164`), although the m68k override handles those two units. PC, AArch64 Raspberry Pi, and RISC-V BeginIO wrappers delegate to `common_BeginIO()` (`arch/all-pc/timer/beginio.c:29`; `arch/aarch64-raspi/timer/beginio.c:19`; `arch/riscv64-opensbi/timer/beginio.c:19`).

**Trigger and consequence:** on a target using the generic entry point or the Efika override, open either accepted but unsupported unit and submit `TR_ADDREQUEST` without `IOF_QUICK`. BeginIO records `IOERR_NOCMD` but does not send the request to a queue or reply to its message, so a synchronous `DoIO()` or a caller waiting on a `SendIO()` request can wait indefinitely. The behavior is confirmed in the generic implementation and Efika override; the m68k override completes requests for ECLOCK/WAITECLOCK, and other overrides require separate checking. **Confidence:** high for the source control flow and missing completion; no request was run. Return the error through the normal completion path (or reject unsupported units at open). Source-only; no device or build was used.

<a id="ek10629"></a>
### EK10629 — m68k timer completes future `UNIT_WAITUNTIL` requests immediately [high impact, high source confidence; m68k Amiga timer]

The m68k timer converts the requested `UNIT_WAITUNTIL` value to VBlank ticks, then tests `if (!cmp64(&tb_vb_count, &tr_time))` (`arch/m68k-amiga/timer/beginio.c:105-118`). `cmp64()` returns TRUE when its first value is greater than or equal to the second (`arch/m68k-amiga/timer/lowlevel.c:56-63`), so this branch completes a request when the current count is *less* than the target and queues it when the target is already reached. It also compares the converted absolute wall-clock deadline against `tb_vb_count`, a counter incremented from zero by VBlank interrupts, rather than the wall-clock value in `tb_CurrentTime` (`lowlevel.c:264-270`; `timer_init.c:183-185`). The checked-in `WaitX` date/time mode opens `UNIT_WAITUNTIL` and submits an absolute timestamp from `CheckDate()` (`workbench/c/WaitX.c:199,404-410`).

**Trigger and consequence:** on m68k Amiga, issue a `TR_ADDREQUEST` with `UNIT_WAITUNTIL` for a future absolute time whose converted tick value is greater than the uptime tick count. The inverted predicate takes the immediate-reply branch, so `WaitX` can execute its command before the requested date/time. A deadline at or before the compared count instead enters the wait queue. **Affected configuration:** m68k Amiga timer implementation selected by `arch/m68k-amiga/timer/mmakefile.src`. **Confidence:** high for the comparison polarity and the wall-clock/uptime counter mismatch; no request or timer was run. Compare the deadline against current system time using one consistent time base and complete only when current time has reached it. Source-only.

<a id="ek10630"></a>
### EK10630 — m68k `GetSysTime()` compares microseconds with the prior seconds value [medium impact, high source confidence; m68k Amiga timer]

After computing the current fraction in `dest->tv_micro`, the m68k `GetSysTime()` compares it with `tb_lastsystime.tv_secs + lastsystimetweak` (`arch/m68k-amiga/timer/getsystime.c:27-40`). The operands represent microseconds and seconds respectively. For a system timestamp above 1,000,000 seconds, the right-hand side is at least 1,000,000 while `tv_micro` is below 1,000,000, so the condition that resets `lastsystimetweak` is never true. Instead, the tweak increments on every call and is added to the returned microseconds. The code subtracts only one million once (`:39-45`), so after enough calls the adjustment adds seconds repeatedly and can eventually return `tv_micro >= 1,000,000`, violating the normalized timeval result.

**Trigger and consequence:** on m68k Amiga with system time above 1,000,000 seconds, call `GetSysTime()` repeatedly. The adjustment accumulates at one microsecond per call; after about one million calls it adds an extra second, and after more calls a single carry no longer normalizes the result. Consumers of the system clock can observe time running ahead and malformed timeval values. **Affected configuration:** the selected m68k Amiga timer implementation; the timer base loads `tb_CurrentTime` from BattClock when available (`arch/m68k-amiga/timer/timer_init.c:183-185`). **Confidence:** high for the mismatched units and unbounded increment; the number and rate of calls before visible drift depends on use. Compare timevals lexicographically and adjust only when the new timestamp fails to advance. No clock call or hardware was exercised; source-only.

<a id="ek10631"></a>
### EK10631 — m68k VBlank delays wrap when converted to a 32-bit frame count [low impact, high source confidence; m68k Amiga timer]

`convertunits()` converts a VBlank timeval with `ULONG v = tr->tv_secs * tb_vblank_rate`, adds the fractional-frame count, then clears `tv_secs` and stores the result in `tv_micro` (`arch/m68k-amiga/timer/lowlevel.c:19-25`). Both `tv_secs` and the product are 32-bit unsigned values on this target. `UNIT_VBLANK` requests pass through this conversion before being added to the current 64-bit VBlank counter and queued (`arch/m68k-amiga/timer/beginio.c:132-139,192-204`). The generic timer implementation instead adds the request timeval to its elapsed timeval with the shared normalized time arithmetic (`rom/timer/lowlevel.c:187-211`).

**Trigger and consequence:** submit a normalized `UNIT_VBLANK` delay with `tv_micro=0` and a seconds value above `ULONG_MAX / tb_vblank_rate`. At 60 Hz, 71,582,789 seconds converts to 44 frames after wrap; at 50 Hz, 85,899,346 seconds converts to four frames. The request is therefore queued for less than a second instead of the requested multi-year delay. No maximum duration is checked before conversion. **Affected configuration:** m68k Amiga timer implementation selected by `arch/m68k-amiga/timer/mmakefile.src`, on PAL/NTSC systems using its 50/60 Hz VBlank rate (`timer_init.c:173-175`). **Confidence:** high for the unsigned overflow and shortened result; low practical likelihood due to the multi-year threshold. Keep the conversion in a 64-bit counter or reject intervals above its representable range. No timer request or hardware was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10632"></a>
### EK10632 — POSIXC path APIs dereference failed Unix path conversions [medium impact, high source confidence]

`access()` checks only whether `path` is NULL before passing it to `__path_u2a()`, then immediately passes the result to `SplitName()` without checking it (`compiler/crt/posixc/access.c:66-70,90-93`). With Unix path handling enabled, `__path_u2a()` deliberately returns NULL and sets `ENOENT` for paths beginning `/.attbin` (`compiler/crt/posixc/__upath.c:74-82`); it also returns NULL with `ENOMEM` if its conversion-buffer allocation fails (`:93-100`). `SplitName()` dereferences its `name` argument immediately (`rom/dos/splitname.c:70-75`). The selected `remove()` wrapper likewise forwards `__path_u2a()`'s result to `__stdcio_remove()` without a check, and `rmdir()` forwards the result through `remove()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/remove.c:47`; `rmdir.c:43`). `rename()` also calls `strdup(__path_u2a(oldpath))` and then indexes `__path_u2a(newpath)` without checking either conversion; a failed old-path conversion reaches `strdup(NULL)`, while a failed new-path conversion reaches `anewpath[0]` (`compiler/crt/posixc/rename.c:55-64`). It also fails to check whether duplicating a successfully converted old path failed before forwarding it to stdio rename. `opendir()` also passes `__path_u2a(name)` directly to DOS `Lock()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/opendir.c:88-94`); when conversion returns NULL, `Lock()` passes the pointer to `strchr()` (`rom/dos/lock.c:175-179`). The stdio implementation calls DOS `DeleteFile()`, whose selected `getpacketinfo()` helper immediately passes the name to `strchr()` (`compiler/crt/stdc/remove.c:38-42`; `rom/dos/deletefile.c:56-59`; `rom/dos/packethelper.c:15-18`). Thus `access()`, `remove()`/`unlink()`, `rmdir()`, `rename()`, and `opendir()` can fault on the deliberate not-found path or a conversion allocation failure instead of returning an error; `rename()` can also forward a NULL path after its own `strdup()` allocation failure. Unix path handling is enabled by `__posixc_nixmain()` before invoking a program's main function (`compiler/crt/posixc/__posixc_nixmain.c:41-45`); all four functions are selected in the POSIXC manifest (`mmakefile.src:29,186-187,190`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a POSIXC program running with `doupath` enabled calls `access("/.attbin", mode)`, `remove("/.attbin")`/`unlink("/.attbin")`, or `rmdir("/.attbin")`; `rename("/.attbin", ...)` or `rename(..., "/.attbin")` reaches the unchecked `strdup(NULL)`/subscript paths; `opendir("/.attbin")` passes NULL to `Lock()`. A path-conversion allocation failure reaches the same unchecked result paths. The process can fault in `SplitName()`, `strchr()`, `strdup(NULL)`, or the unchecked `anewpath[0]` access rather than returning `-1` with the conversion error in `errno`. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library with Unix path handling enabled; allocation failure applies to ordinary converted paths. **Confidence:** high for the NULL-producing conversion branches and downstream dereferences. Check every conversion and duplication result before indexing or calling DOS/stdio helpers. No call, allocation failure, or build was induced; source-only. See the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-access-full-body-and-path-conversion-failure-pass-ek10632).


<a id="ek10633"></a>
### EK10633 — POSIXC creation APIs ignore requested mode and saved `umask` [medium impact, high source confidence]

The selected POSIXC `mkdir(path, mode)` implementation converts and duplicates the path, calls DOS `CreateDir()`, and returns success without reading `mode` or changing the created directory's protection (`compiler/crt/posixc/mkdir.c:35-83`). Regular-file creation has the same gap: `open(path, O_CREAT, mode)` passes the mode to `__open()`, but `__open()` uses it only in debug output and creates missing files with `Open(path, MODE_NEWFILE)` without applying protection (`compiler/crt/posixc/open.c:87-93`; `__fdesc.c:344-349,469-477`). `creat()` delegates to this path (`creat.c:47`). `mkstemp()` also creates through `open(O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_EXCL, 0600)`, so its requested owner-only permissions are ignored as well (`mkstemp.c:65-71`). The API documentation says these modes specify access permissions. POSIXC `umask()` stores and returns `PosixCBase->umask`, but its implementation explicitly says the value is not used; a checkout-wide search of POSIXC shows no other read of that field (`umask.c:24-64`). The initial mask is `S_IWGRP|S_IWOTH`, but it cannot affect creation. The target manifest selects these APIs (`compiler/crt/posixc/mmakefile.src:45,151,153,160,243`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a POSIXC program creates a directory with `mkdir()`, a regular file with `open(O_CREAT)`/`creat()`, or a temporary file with `mkstemp()`, optionally after setting `umask()`. The DOS handler receives no requested creation mode, so callers cannot establish the requested access policy through these POSIX APIs, including the owner-only mode required by `mkstemp()`. This can expose created files or directories more broadly than callers expect when they request restrictive permissions. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library; DOS handlers determine the resulting default protection. **Confidence:** high that neither argument nor saved mask is applied; exact resulting protection is handler-dependent and was not established for every filesystem. Apply `mode & ~umask` to each newly created object using the POSIXC-to-DOS protection mapping, including the owner-only mode required by `mkstemp()`, with cleanup/error handling if applying protection fails. No directory was created and no build was run; source-only. See the [mkdir and umask review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-mkdir-mode-and-umask-review-ek10633).


<a id="ek10634"></a>
### EK10634 — POSIXC path APIs dereference failed conversion and buffer allocations [medium impact, high source confidence]

After `NameFromLock()` succeeds, `getcwd()` passes its stack path to `__path_a2u()` and immediately copies the result without checking for NULL (`compiler/crt/posixc/getcwd.c:67-69`). With Unix path conversion enabled, `__path_a2u()` can return NULL and set `ENOMEM` when its `realloc_nocopy()` fails (`compiler/crt/posixc/__upath.c:177-190`). The allocating `getcwd(NULL, size)` form also calls `malloc()` and immediately `strcpy()` without checking the allocation result (`getcwd.c:91-103`). `realpath()` calls `getcwd()` in both its directory and final-component resolution paths, so it inherits these crash paths (`compiler/crt/posixc/realpath.c:135-141,181-182`). `statfs()` and `getfsstat()` also pass `__path_a2u()` results directly to `CopyMem()` without checking for NULL (`compiler/crt/posixc/statfs.c:89-91`; `getfsstat.c:128-130`); conversion-buffer allocation failure can therefore fault there too. All four public functions are selected in POSIXC (`compiler/crt/posixc/mmakefile.src:107,113,181,223`). The selected `basename()` and `dirname()` wrappers also pass their input to `__path_a2u()` and immediately index/use the result without checking it (`compiler/crt/posixc/basename.c:55-59,67`; `dirname.c:54-58,66`); a failed conversion allocation therefore reaches pointer reads in both functions. Unix-style program startup adds another caller: `__posixc_nixmain()` enables `doupath`, converts `argv[0]` with `__path_a2u()`, and immediately passes the result to `strdup()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/__posixc_nixmain.c:41-54`). If growing the shared conversion buffer fails, `__path_a2u()` returns NULL with `ENOMEM` and `strdup(NULL)` dereferences it before the existing `new_argv0 == NULL` check can run. This startup function is part of the selected POSIXC sources (`mmakefile.src:15`).

**Trigger and consequence:** call `getcwd()`/`realpath()`, `statfs()`/`getfsstat()`, `basename()`, or `dirname()` while Unix-path conversion-buffer allocation fails; separately, start a Unix-style POSIXC program while conversion of its `argv[0]` needs a buffer allocation that fails; or call `getcwd(NULL, size)` while its result-buffer allocation fails. The process can fault in `strcpy()` or `CopyMem()` instead of returning NULL with an allocation error. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library with Unix path handling enabled for conversion failure; allocating `getcwd()` form for result-buffer failure. **Confidence:** high for both unchecked NULL results and direct copy. Check conversion and allocation results before copying, preserving the conversion errno or returning ENOMEM. No allocation failure or path call was induced; source-only. See the [path-conversion allocation-failure review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-path-conversion-allocation-failure-review-ek10634).


<a id="ek10635"></a>
### EK10635 — POSIXC `symlink()` rewrites existing targets as absolute paths [medium impact, high source confidence]

When the target passed as `oldpath` exists, POSIXC `symlink()` converts it, obtains a lock, calls `NameFromLock()`, and passes that resolved path to DOS `MakeLink()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/symlink.c:56-91`). Only when `Lock()` reports `ERROR_OBJECT_NOT_FOUND` does it pass the caller's target string through unchanged (`:95-107`). POSIX symlinks store the target pathname as supplied, including relative pathnames. The selected implementation therefore gives existing and not-yet-existing relative targets different semantics. `symlink()` is selected by the POSIXC manifest (`mmakefile.src:229`); DOS `MakeLink()` accepts a soft-link destination string and does not require the target to exist (`rom/dos/makelink.c:39-48`).

**Trigger and consequence:** create a symlink with a relative target that currently resolves, then move the symlink or its containing directory. The stored link remains bound to the target's former absolute location instead of resolving the original relative text from the link's new parent; the link can become broken or refer to a different object than POSIX pathname semantics specify. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library and filesystems supporting DOS soft links. **Confidence:** high for the source rewrite and DOS call; no filesystem move or symlink was performed. Pass the converted target text directly to `MakeLink()` without resolving it through `Lock()`/`NameFromLock()`. No link operation or build was run; source-only. See the [symlink target-preservation review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-symlink-target-preservation-review-ek10635).


<a id="ek10636"></a>
### EK10636 — POSIXC `fchdir()` dereferences an invalid descriptor [medium impact, high source confidence]

`fchdir()` assigns `__getfdesc(fd)` to `fdc`, then immediately dereferences `fdc->fcb->privflags` without checking for NULL (`compiler/crt/posixc/fchdir.c:58-61`). The helper returns NULL for negative or out-of-range descriptors, empty/closed slots, and descriptors owned by another subsystem (`compiler/crt/posixc/__fdesc.c:116-139`). A later `__get_default_file()` check would set `EBADF`, but is reached only after this dereference (`fchdir.c:67-71`). `fchdir()` is selected in POSIXC (`mmakefile.src:62`).

**Trigger and consequence:** call `fchdir()` with a negative, closed, out-of-range, or non-POSIXC descriptor. The process can fault instead of returning `-1` with `EBADF`; a valid non-directory POSIXC descriptor is separately handled with `ENOTDIR`. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library. **Confidence:** high for the NULL-return branches and immediate dereference. Check `fdc` before inspecting its FCB and return `EBADF`. No descriptor operation or build was run; source-only. See the [fchdir invalid-descriptor review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-fchdir-invalid-descriptor-review-ek10636).


<a id="ek10637"></a>
### EK10637 — POSIXC `*at()` wrappers ignore unsupported flag bits [low impact, high source confidence]

`fstatat()` documents only flags 0 and `AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW`, but selects `lstat()` only when that bit is present and ignores every other bit (`compiler/crt/posixc/fstatat.c:29-35,64-68`). `unlinkat()` documents only 0 and `AT_REMOVEDIR`, then tests only that bit to choose `rmdir()` or `remove()` (`unlinkat.c:28-33,61-67`). `fchmodat()` documents only 0 and `AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW` (noting that the latter is ignored), but never validates `flags` before calling `chmod()` (`fchmodat.c:30-35,60-72`). All three are selected POSIXC sources (`mmakefile.src:64,94,246`).

**Trigger and consequence:** pass an unsupported nonzero flag bit to one of these functions. Instead of rejecting the invalid request with `EINVAL`, the wrapper proceeds: it stats, removes, or changes permissions according to the recognized subset, potentially performing an operation the caller expected to fail. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library. **Confidence:** high that arbitrary extra bits are silently ignored; no call was made. Validate the flags against each function's supported mask before changing directory state or invoking the operation. No filesystem operation or build was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC at-wrapper flag review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-at-wrapper-flag-validation-review-ek10637).


<a id="ek10638"></a>
### EK10638 — POSIXC `statvfs()` passes Unix absolute paths to DOS as relative names [medium impact, high source confidence]

The selected POSIXC `statvfs()` calls `Lock(path, ACCESS_READ)` directly and never applies `__path_u2a()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/statvfs.c:26-34`). In the same library, `statfs()` converts its POSIX path before calling `Lock()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/statfs.c:47-56`).
