With Unix paths enabled, `__path_u2a("/foo")` converts the leading slash to the current volume's root form (`compiler/crt/posixc/__upath.c:327-333,402-410`). DOS `Lock()` treats a name without a volume colon as relative to the current directory (`rom/dos/lock.c:183-201`). Therefore a POSIX absolute path such as `/foo` passed to `statvfs()` can be looked up relative to the process current directory rather than at the volume root. `statvfs()` is selected in POSIXC (`mmakefile.src:224`).

**Trigger and consequence:** with Unix-path POSIXC enabled and current directory below the volume root, call `statvfs()` on an absolute path such as `/foo`. It can report information about a same-named object under the current directory, or fail to find the root-level target. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library with Unix path handling enabled. **Confidence:** high for the missing conversion and DOS relative-path rule; no filesystem lookup was performed. Convert the path with `__path_u2a()` and propagate its error before `Lock()`. No path operation or build was run; source-only. See the [statvfs path and error review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-statvfs-path-and-error-review-ek10638).

<a id="ek10639"></a>
### EK10639 — POSIXC `statvfs()` maps every lock failure to `ENOENT` [low impact, high source confidence]

When DOS `Lock()` fails, `statvfs()` discards `IoErr()` and unconditionally sets `errno = ENOENT` (`compiler/crt/posixc/statvfs.c:29-31`). A denied path or other handler failure is consequently reported as nonexistent. The neighboring selected `statfs()` preserves `IoErr()` and translates it through `__stdc_ioerr2errno()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/statfs.c:68-76`).

**Trigger and consequence:** call `statvfs()` on an existing path whose handler reports an error other than `ERROR_OBJECT_NOT_FOUND`, such as access denied. The caller receives `ENOENT` and cannot distinguish the actual failure. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library and any handler that can fail `Lock()` with another error. **Confidence:** high for the unconditional assignment; no handler error was induced. Translate `IoErr()` with the shared DOS-to-errno mapper. No path operation or build was run; source-only. See the [statvfs path and error review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-statvfs-path-and-error-review-ek10638).

<a id="ek10640"></a>
### EK10640 — POSIXC `fstatvfs()` returns success without filling its result [medium impact, high source confidence]

The selected `fstatvfs()` validates `buf` and the descriptor, then invokes `AROS_FUNCTION_NOT_IMPLEMENTED()` and returns `0` from its `#if (1)` branch without writing any field of `*buf` (`compiler/crt/posixc/fstatvfs.c:17-34`). The macro only logs a message and does not change the return value (`compiler/arossupport/include/debug.h:397-398`). The function is selected by the POSIXC manifest (`mmakefile.src:95`).

**Trigger and consequence:** call `fstatvfs()` with a valid descriptor and output buffer. The function reports success while leaving the result unchanged, so callers can consume uninitialized or stale filesystem statistics as valid. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library. **Confidence:** high from the complete implementation and macro definition; no call was made. Implement the query or return `-1` with an appropriate unsupported-operation error until it is available. No descriptor operation or build was run; source-only. See the [fstatvfs implementation review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-fstatvfs-review-ek10640).


<a id="ek10642"></a>
### EK10642 — POSIXC stat fallback fills metadata but returns failure [medium impact, high source confidence]

Both `__stat_from_path()` and `__stat64_from_path()` initialize `res` to `-1`. When the split basename is empty or the parent handler does not implement examine, each branch fills the output structure but never changes `res` to zero (`compiler/crt/posixc/__stat.c:229-230,330-332`; 64-bit counterpart `:375-376,476-478`). The ordinary directory-entry search does set `res = 0` when it finds a match (`:338-344,484-490`). Selected `stat()` and `stat64()` enter these helpers when the target lock fails with `ERROR_OBJECT_IN_USE`; `lstat()`/`lstat64()` also enter for soft links (`compiler/crt/posixc/stat.c:93-104`; `lstat.c:76-90`; `stat64.c:93-104`; `lstat64.c:76-90`).

**Trigger and consequence:** invoke one of these calls on a path that takes the path fallback and whose parent handler reports `ERROR_NOT_IMPLEMENTED`/`ERROR_ACTION_NOT_KNOWN`, or on an empty-basename case. The helper writes default or root metadata but returns `-1`, so callers observe failure despite the output being populated; `errno` may also remain stale. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library; requires the lock-failure fallback and the specified parent path behavior. **Confidence:** high for the unmodified `res` and all four wrapper routes; no handler or stat call was run. Set `res = 0` after successfully filling the output, while retaining `-1` for actual failures. No filesystem operation or build was run; source-only. See the [stat helper fallback review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-stat-helper-fallback-review-ek10642).


<a id="ek10643"></a>
### EK10643 — POSIXC `lseek()` reports success after a short or failed zero-fill write [medium impact, high source confidence]

When `Seek()` reports `ERROR_SEEK_ERROR` for a target beyond EOF, both `lseek()` and `lseek64()` seek to EOF and loop writing zero blocks to extend the file (`compiler/crt/posixc/lseek.c:97-142`; identical logic in `lseek64.c:97-142`). They discard every `__dos64_write()` return and subtract the requested chunk size regardless of bytes written, then return the handle's resulting position as a successful seek. `__dos64_write()` returns the byte count, including partial progress, or `-1` (`compiler/crt/posixc/__dos64.c:156-175`); the underlying `Write()` and `Write64()` contracts likewise allow short writes or errors (`rom/dos/write.c:29-44`; `rom/dos64/write64.c:25-42`).

**Trigger and consequence:** seek beyond EOF on a file where the zero-fill write fails or is short, such as a write-protected file or a full filesystem. The loop still consumes the remaining count and the function can return the old or partially advanced offset as success, rather than the requested position or an error. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `lseek()`/`lseek64()` implementations on handlers that reject or short-write the extension. **Confidence:** high that write counts are ignored and the loop advances by requested lengths; no I/O failure was induced. Check each result and stop with an error if the zero-fill cannot reach the requested offset. No file operation or build was run; source-only. See the [lseek zero-fill review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-lseek-zero-fill-review-ek10643).


<a id="ek10644"></a>
### EK10644 — POSIXC mount-stat routines copy 90 bytes from shorter path strings [medium impact, high source confidence]

`statfs()` and `getfsstat()` call `CopyMem(..., MNAMELEN)` to fill `f_mntonname`, where `MNAMELEN` is 90, but the source is a variable-length result from `__path_a2u()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/statfs.c:88-89`; `getfsstat.c:133-135`; `sys/mount.h:52,66`). `__path_a2u()` allocates only `1 + size + 1` bytes for the input-derived conversion buffer (`compiler/crt/posixc/__upath.c:172-190`), and `realloc_nocopy()` requests that size from `malloc()` (`compiler/crt/stdc/realloc_nocopy.c:53-73`). A short volume name therefore supplies a source allocation far smaller than the 90-byte copy.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `statfs()` or `getfsstat()` for a normally short volume name when the conversion buffer is smaller than `MNAMELEN`. The fixed-size copy reads beyond the path buffer; trailing bytes in `f_mntonname` come from memory after the string, and the read is outside the source allocation. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library; typical short volume labels and a small/current conversion-buffer allocation. **Confidence:** high for the fixed 90-byte read and requested variable buffer size; no filesystem query was run. Copy only the bounded string length and initialize the rest of the destination field. No filesystem operation or build was run; source-only. See the [mount-stat output bounds review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-mount-stat-bounds-review-ek10644).


<a id="ek10645"></a>
### EK10645 — POSIXC `select()` and `pselect()` always report no ready descriptors [medium impact, high source confidence]

The selected implementations of both functions unconditionally return 0 without validating `nfds`, inspecting or modifying any descriptor set, waiting for readiness, or honoring the timeout (`compiler/crt/posixc/select.c:35-39`; `pselect.c:36-40`). A ready descriptor is always reported as not ready; timed waits return immediately instead of waiting. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library. **Confidence:** high from both complete function bodies; no readiness or timed wait was run. Implement descriptor readiness and timeout behavior, or return an explicit unsupported error until implemented. No descriptor operation or build was run; source-only. See the [select and pselect implementation review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-select-pselect-review-ek10645).


<a id="ek10646"></a>
### EK10646 — POSIXC `sleep()` overflows the tick conversion [low impact, high source confidence]

`sleep()` multiplies its `unsigned int seconds` argument by 50 before passing the result to DOS `Delay(ULONG)` (`compiler/crt/posixc/sleep.c:49-51`). The multiplication is therefore performed in the argument's unsigned-int type and wraps above its representable tick count. DOS documents `Delay()` ticks as 1/50 second (`rom/dos/delay.c:25-33`).

**Trigger and consequence:** request at least 85,899,346 seconds on a target with 32-bit `unsigned int`; that value produces 4 ticks after modulo wrap, so the call waits about 80 ms rather than the requested interval. Other sufficiently large values also shorten the wait unpredictably. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC implementation with 32-bit `unsigned int` and 32-bit tick multiplication. **Confidence:** high for the integer width, multiplication and Delay tick unit; no wait was run. Convert in a wider type and split waits into representable Delay intervals. No sleep call or build was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC sleep and time API review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-sleep-time-api-review-ek10646).


<a id="ek10647"></a>
### EK10647 — POSIXC `utimes()` wraps pre-1978 timestamps into future dates [medium impact, high source confidence]

`utimes()` casts `tvp[1].tv_sec` to `ULONG` before subtracting the Unix-to-Amiga epoch offset (`compiler/crt/posixc/utimes.c:74-78`). For timestamps earlier than the Amiga DateStamp epoch, the unsigned subtraction wraps instead of reporting an unrepresentable date. For example, Unix epoch zero becomes a value near 4.04 billion seconds after 1978, producing a DateStamp around year 2106. `utime()` delegates here with whole-second values (`utime.c:71-74`).

**Trigger and consequence:** call `utimes()` or `utime()` with a modification time before the 1978 DateStamp epoch. The file is assigned a far-future modification date instead of the requested historical time or a range error. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library. **Confidence:** high for the unsigned cast/subtraction and resulting wrap; no timestamp was set. Check the signed input range before conversion and reject or explicitly clamp dates the DOS representation cannot express. No filesystem operation or build was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC file-time review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-utimes-time-conversion-review-ek10647).

<a id="ek10648"></a>
### EK10648 — POSIXC `utimes()` discards subsecond modification time [low impact, high source confidence]

For a supplied timeval, `utimes()` derives `ds_Days`, `ds_Minute` and `ds_Tick` only from the integer seconds field (`compiler/crt/posixc/utimes.c:74-78`). It never reads `tvp[1].tv_usec`; the documentation states that AROS time has one-tick resolution, and the implementation already expresses seconds as `TICKS_PER_SECOND` in `ds_Tick`, so valid fractions of at least one tick are representable but discarded.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `utimes()` with a valid nonzero `tv_usec` fraction. The modification time is truncated to the whole second instead of being rounded or represented at the available tick resolution. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library. **Confidence:** high that the field is ignored and DOS DateStamp has tick precision; no timestamp was set. Convert microseconds to DateStamp ticks according to the supported resolution and validate the timeval range. No filesystem operation or build was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC file-time review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-utimes-time-conversion-review-ek10647).


<a id="ek10649"></a>
### EK10649 — POSIXC `tempnam()` reads before an empty directory string [medium impact, high source confidence]

When `TMPDIR` is set to the empty string, the first candidate-directory branch evaluates `*(f + strlen(f) - 1)` with `strlen(f) == 0` (`compiler/crt/posixc/tempnam.c:96-99`). The caller-supplied `dir` branch repeats the same expression for an empty string (`:103-106`). In either case, the code reads before the start of the valid string buffer while deciding whether to append `/`.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `tempnam()` with `TMPDIR=""`, or pass an empty non-NULL `dir`. It reads outside the supplied string before forming a candidate and may fault or choose a path based on unrelated memory. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library. **Confidence:** high for the zero-length pointer arithmetic and dereference; no environment or call was changed. Check for an empty string before examining its last character and fall back or return an error. No temp-name operation or build was run; source-only. See the [tempnam empty-directory review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-tempnam-empty-directory-review-ek10649).

<a id="ek10650"></a>
### EK10650 — POSIXC `tmpfile()` leaves its temporary file linked after close [medium impact, high source confidence]

`tmpfile()` creates a unique file with `mkstemp()` and wraps the descriptor with `fdopen()`, but the call that would unlink the pathname is commented out (`compiler/crt/posixc/tmpfile.c:111-125`). Its own function documentation says the temporary file is unlinked before return and removed when the last reference is closed (`:22-28`); a BUG note confirms that the current implementation neither removes the pathname nor follows that behavior (`:58-62`).

**Trigger and consequence:** call `tmpfile()`, close the returned stream, then inspect the temporary directory or repeat the operation. The file remains named in `T:` instead of being deleted, so temporary files accumulate until some external cleanup removes them. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library. **Confidence:** high for the omitted unlink and stated contract; no temporary file was created. Implement the specified auto-delete-on-close lifetime for the open temporary object, and unwind the descriptor/stream if that setup fails. No temporary-file operation or build was run; source-only. See the [tmpfile unlink review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-tmpfile-unlink-review-ek10650).


<a id="ek10651"></a>
### EK10651 — stdio output and flush failures can leave the error indicator clear [medium impact, high source confidence]

On invalid descriptors or DOS write errors, the selected output functions return an error without setting `stream->flags & __POSIXC_STDIO_ERROR`: `fwrite()` handles a DOS `-1` by translating `IoErr()` and returning zero (`compiler/crt/posixc/fwrite.c:56-79`), while `fputc()` and `fputs()` similarly return EOF (`fputc.c:48-64`; `fputs.c:48-65`). Per-stream `fflush()` also returns EOF on a failed DOS `Flush()` without setting the flag in POSIXC (`fflush.c:83-103`) or stdc (`compiler/crt/stdc/fflush.c:60-67`). The corresponding read paths set that flag on errors (`fread.c:63-81`; `fgetc.c` includes `__getc.c:11-19`), and `ferror()` reports only whether the flag is set (`ferror.c:41-43`). Thus the standard stream-status check can report no error after a failed output operation unless the flag was already set for another reason.

**Trigger and consequence:** an output operation or per-stream `fflush()` encounters an invalid descriptor or DOS write/flush failure; the function returns EOF/zero and sets errno as applicable, but `ferror(stream)` can still return zero. Code relying on the stream error indicator may treat the failed write as an ordinary zero-block result. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC output functions and stdc/POSIXC per-stream `fflush()`. **Confidence:** high for the un-set flag and `ferror()` implementation; no write failure was induced. Set the stream error indicator on each output and per-stream flush error path, consistently with the input operations. No I/O operation or build was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC stdio error-state review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-stdio-error-state-review-ek10651).


<a id="ek10652"></a>
### EK10652 — stdc and POSIXC `fgets()` write past a one-byte destination [medium impact, high source confidence]

Both selected stdc and POSIXC `fgets()` forward `size` unchanged to DOS `FGets()` (`compiler/crt/stdc/fgets.c:61`; `compiler/crt/posixc/fgets.c:76-77`). `FGets()` decrements the unsigned buffer length, then unconditionally reads and stores one character before writing a terminating NUL (`rom/dos/fgets.c:52-73`). With a one-byte destination and non-EOF input, it stores the character at index 0 and the terminator at index 1, outside the caller's buffer.

The same unchecked decrement also wraps a direct DOS `FGets()` call with `buflen == 0` to `ULONG_MAX` (`rom/dos/fgets.c:52`). The do/while loop then continues copying until it reads a newline or EOF, and finally writes a terminator; a zero-capacity destination can therefore be overwritten by an arbitrary amount. No checked-in caller passing a literal zero was found, so this additional case is limited to direct DOS callers or wrappers that forward a zero size.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `fgets(buf, 1, stream)` with at least one character available, or directly call DOS `FGets(buf, 0)` with a non-NULL destination. The first case writes two bytes into a one-byte destination; the second can copy until newline/EOF despite the zero capacity. **Affected configuration:** selected stdc and POSIXC `fgets()` implementations using DOS `FGets()` for size 1; all direct DOS `FGets()` callers that pass zero. **Confidence:** high for the unconditional read/store/terminator sequence, unsigned underflow, and size forwarding; no call was run. Special-case size 1 to return an empty string without consuming input, and reject unsupported nonpositive sizes before dispatch. No input operation or build was run; source-only. See the [stdio line-input boundary review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-stdio-line-input-review-ek10652).


<a id="ek10653"></a>
### EK10653 — POSIXC `fopen()`/`popen()` leak descriptors if stream allocation fails [high source confidence]

`__fopen()` opens the file and obtains its descriptor before calling `fdopen()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/__fopen.c:36-49`). If `fdopen()` cannot allocate its `FILENODE`, it returns `NULL` (`fdopen.c:99-100`) without closing the descriptor; `__fopen()` returns that `NULL` directly and does not close it. Both `fopen()` and `fopen64()` use this helper (`fopen.c:83`; `fopen64.c:76`). The selected `popen()` also creates a pipe and starts its asynchronous command before calling `fdopen()` for the parent endpoint (`popen.c:73-96`). If that stream allocation fails, it returns NULL without closing the remaining parent pipe descriptor; the child has already started and may remain blocked on that pipe. This is the same missing cleanup at the `fdopen()` failure boundary.

**Trigger and consequence:** either a file open or `popen()` pipe/process setup succeeds but the subsequent `FILENODE` pool allocation fails. The caller receives `NULL` while the descriptor remains open and unavailable; for `popen()`, the already-started child also retains a live pipe peer and can block. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC stdio and process-pipe API; requires allocation failure at stream-node creation. **Confidence:** high for the unbalanced open/close path; no allocation failure was induced. Close the opened descriptor when `fdopen()` fails, while preserving the allocation error. No file operation or build was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC fopen cleanup review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-fopen-cleanup-review-ek10653).


<a id="ek10654"></a>
### EK10654 — stdc and POSIXC `vfscanf()` ignore failure to flush a read/write stream [medium impact, high source confidence]

Both stdc and POSIXC `vfscanf()` call `Flush()` on the stream's DOS handle and ignore its return before entering `__vcscan()` (`compiler/crt/stdc/vfscanf.c:47-50`; POSIXC direct-DOS path at `compiler/crt/posixc/vfscanf.c:102-117`). A failed flush can therefore be followed by successful input parsing and a normal conversion count, hiding the failure of pending output. The DOS flush path returns failure when `InternalFlush()` cannot write the pending bytes; the DOS `Close()` result overwrite is covered by [D01](AROS-dos.md#d01); the ignored pre-seek flush is EK8884.

**Trigger and consequence:** use a readable/writable update stream with pending output, have the handler reject the buffered write, then call `vfscanf()`. The flush error is discarded and input parsing continues, so the caller may receive a successful scan result after output was not committed. **Affected configuration:** selected stdcio and POSIXC implementations and a handler/write-error condition. **Confidence:** high that the return is ignored and scanning proceeds; no stream or failure was induced. Check the flush result and return an input/output error before scanning when it fails. No I/O operation or build was run; source-only. See the [stdio formatted-input flush review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-vfscanf-flush-review-ek10654).


<a id="ek10655"></a>
### EK10655 — stdc and POSIXC `ungetc()` return the unconverted input value [low impact, high source confidence]

Both stdc and POSIXC `ungetc()` pass the original `int c` to DOS `UnGetC()` and return that same value on success (`compiler/crt/stdc/ungetc.c:59-82`; `compiler/crt/posixc/ungetc.c:65-80`). DOS stores the character in a byte-sized buffer (`rom/dos/ungetc.c:90-94`), so values outside the unsigned-byte range are truncated in the stream but not in the reported return value. The POSIX interface requires the successful result to be the character converted to `unsigned char`.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `ungetc(0x141, stream)` on a readable stream with pushback capacity. The pushed byte is `0x41`, but the function reports `0x141`; callers comparing the result to the character actually pushed can make an incorrect decision. **Affected configuration:** selected stdc and POSIXC `ungetc()` with DOS `UnGetC()`. **Confidence:** high for byte storage and unconverted return; no stream operation was run. Convert `c` to `unsigned char` before passing and returning the successful character, while retaining EOF handling. No I/O operation or build was run; source-only. See the [stdio ungetc conversion review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-ungetc-conversion-review-ek10655).


<a id="ek10656"></a>
### EK10656 — POSIXC `getpass()` reads with terminal echo enabled [medium impact, high source confidence]

The selected POSIXC `getpass()` prints its prompt and reads directly with `fgets()` from the normal stdin stream (`compiler/crt/posixc/getpass.c:54-61`). It does not switch the console to raw/no-echo mode or otherwise change terminal echo. The sibling `usergroup.library` implementation explicitly uses `SetMode(..., 1)` while reading and restores cooked mode afterward (`workbench/libs/usergroup/getpass.c:70-81`), demonstrating the available console control path. The documented getpass behavior disables character echo while reading ([getpass(3)](https://man.openbsd.org/getpass)).

**Trigger and consequence:** call POSIXC `getpass()` while stdin is a normal echoing console. Characters entered as the password are displayed as they are typed. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC implementation with an echoing stdin. **Confidence:** high that this implementation performs no echo control; terminal behavior was not run. Disable echo for the duration of input and restore the original console mode on every exit path, or report that no no-echo terminal is available. No input or terminal operation was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC getpass review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-identity-api-review-ek10656-ek10657).

<a id="ek10657"></a>
### EK10657 — POSIXC `getpass()` leaves excess password input queued [low impact, high source confidence]

`getpass()` reads at most `PASS_MAX` bytes by calling `fgets()` once (`compiler/crt/posixc/getpass.c:61`). The selected `fgets()` stops after filling that buffer and does not drain the rest of the line (`fgets.c:76-99`; DOS `FGets()` stops at `buflen - 1`, `rom/dos/fgets.c:55-75`). The sibling `usergroup.library` implementation continues reading through newline while storing only up to its maximum (`workbench/libs/usergroup/getpass.c:76-78`).

**Trigger and consequence:** enter more characters than fit in the POSIXC password buffer before newline. `getpass()` returns the prefix but leaves the suffix and newline on stdin, so the next input operation consumes stale password-line data. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC implementation when input exceeds the buffer. **Confidence:** high for the single bounded read and absence of a drain loop; no input was supplied. Consume and discard through newline after the buffer fills. No input operation or build was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC getpass review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-identity-api-review-ek10656-ek10657).


<a id="ek10658"></a>
### EK10658 — POSIXC `getpgid()` and `tcgetpgrp()` return zero without querying state [medium impact, high source confidence]

The selected implementations ignore their arguments and unconditionally return `(pid_t)0` (`compiler/crt/posixc/getpgid.c:43-45`; `tcgetpgrp.c:43-45`). POSIXC also marks `getpgrp()` as an explicit TODO, and the process-group setters are commented out of the export configuration (`posixc.conf:1045-1046,1058-1060`). These functions therefore return a success-shaped value without obtaining a process or terminal process-group ID.

**Trigger and consequence:** any caller invokes `getpgid(pid)` or `tcgetpgrp(fd)`. It receives zero regardless of PID, descriptor, or actual process-group state and cannot distinguish the stub from a successful query. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library. **Confidence:** high for the unconditional return and disabled setter exports; no process-group operation was run. Implement process-group tracking and validation, or return a documented unsupported-operation error rather than a fabricated ID. No process or terminal operation/build was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC terminal-control review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-terminal-control-review-ek10658).


<a id="ek10659"></a>
### EK10659 — POSIXC `sigismember()` tests the wrong bit [medium impact, high source confidence]

`sigaddset()` and `sigdelset()` address a signal with `1 << (signum & 0x1f)`, but `sigismember()` tests `set->__val[i] & (signum & 0x1f)` without shifting (`compiler/crt/posixc/sigaddset.c:38-41`; `sigdelset.c:38-41`; `sigismember.c:38-42`). Membership therefore disagrees with the corresponding add operation for ordinary signals; for example, adding signal 1 sets bit 1, while membership tests bit 0.

**Trigger and consequence:** add a signal to a set then query it with `sigismember()`, or test a signal mask in `sigsuspend()`. The query may report absent for a present signal or present due to a different set bit, so mask decisions are wrong. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC implementation. **Confidence:** high from the direct bit operations; no signal set was exercised. Use the same shifted unsigned bit mask in all three functions. No signal operation or build was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC signal-set review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-signal-set-and-build-review-ek10659-ek10661).

<a id="ek10660"></a>
### EK10660 — POSIXC signal-set mutators index out of bounds for invalid signal numbers [medium impact, high source confidence]

`sigaddset()`, `sigdelset()` and `sigismember()` compute `i = signum >> 5` and index the fixed four-element `sigset_t.__val` without validating the number (`compiler/crt/posixc/sigaddset.c:38-40`; `sigdelset.c:38-40`; `sigismember.c:38-40`; `include/aros/types/sigset_t.h:12-18`). The public signal header sets `_SIGMAX` to 64 and `NSIG` to 65 (`include/aros/posixc/signal.h:68-69`); a negative value or a number above that range can produce an invalid array index instead of `EINVAL`.

**Trigger and consequence:** pass a negative signal number or one above `_SIGMAX` to any of these set functions. The computed word index can address outside the `sigset_t` object, and the function does not return the specified invalid-signal error. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC signal-set functions. **Confidence:** high for missing range checks and the fixed array bound; no invalid value was passed. Validate `1 <= signum <= _SIGMAX` before indexing and return `EINVAL` on invalid values. No signal operation or build was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC signal-set review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-signal-set-and-build-review-ek10659-ek10661).

<a id="ek10661"></a>
### EK10661 — POSIXC includes unconditional `#error` signal-jump sources in its build list [high impact, high source confidence]

The `POSIXC` source list names `siglongjmp` and `sigsetjmp` (`compiler/crt/posixc/mmakefile.src:214,217`). Their only checked-in source files each contain an unconditional preprocessor error stating that the function must be implemented per CPU (`siglongjmp.c:62`; `sigsetjmp.c:1`). The same makefile's `POSIXC_ARCH` list contains only `vfork` and `vfork_longjmp` (`:304-307`), and a repository path search found no architecture-specific `sigsetjmp.c` or `siglongjmp.c` implementation.

**Trigger and consequence:** build the selected POSIXC module from this source manifest. Compiling either listed source stops at `#error`, preventing the module from building. **Affected configuration:** any `compiler-posixc` target that consumes the checked-in manifest without an external source override. **Confidence:** high for list membership, unconditional directives, and absence of checked-in replacements; no build was run. Supply architecture implementations or remove/conditionally exclude these entries until implemented. Source-only; build impact is inferred directly from the manifest and preprocessor directives. See the [POSIXC signal-set review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-signal-set-and-build-review-ek10659-ek10661).


<a id="ek10662"></a>
### EK10662 — Default signal reporting formats an unbounded task name into a 50-byte buffer [medium impact, high source confidence]

`__sig_default()` allocates `char s[50]` and formats the task's `tc_Node.ln_Name` with unbounded `sprintf()` in all three branches (`compiler/crt/stdc/__signal.c:74-90`). Task names supplied to `NewCreateTaskA()` are copied using their full `strlen()+1` allocation, without a length limit (`rom/exec/newcreatetaska.c:133-137,190-203`). For ordinary signal cases, even a task name only modestly longer than ten characters exceeds the local buffer.

**Trigger and consequence:** a task with a sufficiently long name receives a signal handled by the default action. Formatting the diagnostic writes past `s` before the requester/logging and exit path, so the default signal handler can corrupt its stack and fail during error reporting. **Affected configuration:** selected stdc default signal handler on all supported targets; task names need not be malformed. **Confidence:** high for unbounded formatting, fixed destination, and unrestricted copied name length; no signal was raised. Use bounded formatting with an explicit truncation policy. No task or signal was created; source-only. See the [POSIXC signal implementation review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-signal-implementation-review-ek10662-ek10663).

<a id="ek10663"></a>
### EK10663 — `raise()` ignores signal masks and `SA_NODEFER` [medium impact, high source confidence]

POSIXC `sigprocmask()` stores the caller mask in `PosixCIntBase->sigmask` (`compiler/crt/posixc/sigprocmask.c:53-94`), and `sigaction()` stores both `sa_mask` and `sa_flags` in shared signal state (`sigaction.c:90-106`). The stdc `raise()` implementation does not read either mask; it immediately runs the handler (`compiler/crt/stdc/raise.c:55-104`). It also always defers a same-signal raise while a handler is running via `__SIG_RUNNING`/`__SIG_PENDING` (`:60-66,72-102`), even when `SA_NODEFER` is set, although its own documentation says that flag is honored (`:38-42`).

**Trigger and consequence:** block a signal with `sigprocmask()` and call `raise()` for it, or raise a second signal from a handler whose `sa_mask` blocks it. The handler still runs synchronously. Conversely, a handler that raises itself with `SA_NODEFER` is queued until the outer handler returns instead of being invoked recursively. **Affected configuration:** POSIXC masks/actions with the stdc `raise()` implementation; asynchronous OS signal delivery is not required for these synchronous `raise()` cases. **Confidence:** high from the state writes and absence of mask/flag checks in dispatch; no signal handler was executed. Honor the current process mask and action mask when dispatching, and implement the documented `SA_NODEFER` behavior. No signal operation or build was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC signal implementation review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-signal-implementation-review-ek10662-ek10663).


<a id="ek601"></a>
### EK601 — POSIXC exec preparation dereferences unchecked pooled allocations [medium impact, high source confidence]

Three `AllocPooled()` results in `__exec.c` are used without checking for allocation failure: the copied PATH buffer is passed to `strcpy()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/__exec.c:156-158`); the initial argument buffer is written immediately (`:287-288`); and the script-interpreter filename buffer is passed to `strcpy()` (`:341-343`). The pool itself is checked when created, but later allocations from it can still fail.

**Trigger and consequence:** `execvp()`/`execlp()` can fail while copying PATH, ordinary `exec*()` preparation can fail while allocating the initial argument buffer, or script execution can fail while copying the interpreter name. The code then writes through NULL instead of returning `-1` with `ENOMEM`. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC exec implementation; requires the corresponding pooled allocation to fail. **Confidence:** high for all three unchecked results and immediate dereferences; no allocation failure or exec was induced. Check each allocation and use the existing cleanup path before writing. Source-only; see the [exec preparation review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-exec-wrapper-and-path-conversion-review-ek601-ek10664).

<a id="ek10664"></a>
### EK10664 — POSIXC exec paths pass failed Unix-to-Amiga conversions to DOS [medium impact, high source confidence]

`assign_filename()` passes the result of `__path_u2a()` directly to `Lock()` during PATH search (`compiler/crt/posixc/__exec.c:199-204`). Regular execution likewise passes the conversion result directly to `Open()` (`:281-292`), and script-interpreter setup converts then later passes the result to `LoadSeg()` (`:341-343,402-404`). `__path_u2a()` can return NULL with `ENOENT` for the blocked `/.attbin` path or `ENOMEM` when conversion allocation fails (`__upath.c:67-81,93-100`).

**Trigger and consequence:** call a selected `exec*()` path with Unix path handling enabled and a path rejected by the converter, or make conversion allocation fail. A NULL conversion result reaches DOS path consumers instead of the API returning `-1` with the conversion errno; the call can fault or fail through an unrelated DOS error path. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC exec implementation with `doupath` enabled; allocation failure also depends on conversion being required. **Confidence:** high for the NULL-producing converter branches and unchecked consumers; no path or allocation failure was induced. Check each conversion result before `Lock()`, `Open()` or `LoadSeg()` and preserve its errno through cleanup. No file operation or build was run; source-only. See the [exec preparation review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-exec-wrapper-and-path-conversion-review-ek601-ek10664).

<a id="ek10665"></a>
### EK10665 — POSIXC environment cache leaks a name when value-buffer growth fails [low impact, high source confidence]

When a cached environment value is shorter than the newly requested buffer, `__stdcio_env_getvar()` frees the old value and allocates a larger buffer (`compiler/crt/stdc/__env.c:122-125`). If that allocation fails, it unlinks the cache node and calls `free(*curr)` without freeing the separately allocated `(*curr)->name` (`:127-133`). The normal cache deletion path frees both `name` and `value` (`:144-159`), confirming the missing release.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `getenv()` for a variable, grow that variable, then have the cache's larger-value `malloc()` fail on a later `getenv()`. The lookup returns NULL and leaks the cached name allocation; the cache node is removed. **Affected configuration:** POSIXC `getenv()` using the stdcio environment cache; requires a cached value to grow and allocation failure. **Confidence:** high from the allocation and cleanup paths; no allocation failure was induced. Free the name before freeing the node, or preserve the node until reallocation succeeds. Source-only; see the [environment API and cache review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-environment-api-and-cache-review-ek10665).

<a id="ek10666"></a>
### EK10666 — POSIXC `uselocale()` neither queries nor changes the current locale [medium impact, high source confidence]

The selected implementation returns its input unchanged (`compiler/crt/posixc/uselocale.c:9-11`). It does not read or update current-locale state; stdc stores that state in `StdCIntBase->__locale_cur` and exposes it internally through `__get_current_locale()` (`compiler/crt/stdc/__locale.c:69-74`). POSIX `uselocale(0)` must query the calling thread's current locale, and a nonzero argument must install the locale and return the previous one.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `uselocale(0)` to query state or pass a valid locale handle to select it. The query returns NULL instead of the current handle, and selection has no effect (while the return value falsely reports the input as the previous locale). **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `uselocale()` vector. **Confidence:** high from the complete implementation and absence of state access; no locale call was executed. Implement per-thread current-locale storage and return the prior locale, including query-only behavior. Source-only; see the [locale-object API review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-locale-object-api-review-ek10666-ek10667).

<a id="ek10667"></a>
### EK10667 — POSIXC `newlocale()` discards unselected categories from `base` [medium impact, high source confidence]

`newlocale()` validates that the mask contains no bits outside `LC_ALL_MASK` and rejects `LC_GLOBAL_LOCALE`, but then returns the complete static C or C.UTF-8 object based only on `locale_name` (`compiler/crt/posixc/newlocale.c:97-119`). It does not combine the requested categories with `base`. The locale objects differ in `__lc_mb_max` (1 for C, 4 for C.UTF-8; `:27-51`), which controls multibyte conversion in stdc (`compiler/crt/stdc/mbstowcs.c:90`).

**Trigger and consequence:** on a build with `__WCHAR_MAX__ > 255`, use a C base and request only `LC_NUMERIC_MASK` from `C.UTF-8`. The returned object changes `LC_CTYPE` to UTF-8 even though that category was not selected; the inverse call can similarly discard an existing UTF-8 `LC_CTYPE`. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC locale API when C.UTF-8 is compiled; only partial category masks with a non-NULL base expose the mismatch. **Confidence:** high from the ignored mask/base and differing locale fields; no locale call or build was performed. Construct a locale preserving every category outside the mask, or reject combinations the implementation cannot represent. Source-only; see the [locale-object API review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-locale-object-api-review-ek10666-ek10667).

<a id="ek10668"></a>
### EK10668 — POSIXC `uname()` reverses the release major and minor components [low impact, high source confidence]

The `ArosInquire()` call stores `AI_ArosReleaseMajor` in `release_minor` and `AI_ArosReleaseMinor` in `release_major`, then formats `release_major.release_minor` (`compiler/crt/posixc/uname.c:60-69`). ArosInquire returns the requested major and minor values under those respective tags (`rom/aros/arosinquirea.c:183-191`), so `uname().release` is emitted as minor.major.

**Trigger and consequence:** call selected POSIXC `uname()` on a release whose major and minor components differ. Software reading `utsname.release` sees the reversed version components. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `uname()`; applies on any architecture with unequal release values. **Confidence:** high from the tag definitions and output formatting; no call was executed. Store each tag in its matching variable before formatting. Source-only; see the [uname and small API review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-uname-and-small-api-pass-ek10668).

<a id="ek10669"></a>
### EK10669 — POSIXC `mbsnrtowcs()` consumes input after filling the destination [medium impact, high source confidence]

`mbsnrtowcs()` continues its loop while input bytes remain, even after `count` reaches `len`; the `count < len` check guards only the destination write (`compiler/crt/posixc/mbsnrtowcs.c:69-92`). It therefore keeps converting and discarding characters, then advances `*src` past them.

**Trigger and consequence:** pass a non-NULL destination with room for one wide character and a source containing multiple characters. The function returns a count for characters it did not write and advances the source beyond those characters, so the caller cannot resume at the first unconverted character. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `mbsnrtowcs()`. **Confidence:** high from the loop and cursor update; no conversion was run. Stop when `len` output characters are produced and preserve `*src` at the first unconverted sequence. Source-only; see the [bounded conversion review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-multibyte-bounded-conversion-review-ek10669-ek10678).

<a id="ek10670"></a>
### EK10670 — POSIXC `mbsnrtowcs()` includes the terminating NUL in its result [low impact, high source confidence]

When `mbrtowc()` returns zero, the wrapper writes the wide NUL when it fits, increments `count`, and returns that incremented value (`compiler/crt/posixc/mbsnrtowcs.c:77-84`). The conversion result should count characters before the terminating NUL.

**Trigger and consequence:** convert a NUL-terminated source with enough output space. The return value is one larger than the number of converted string characters, which misstates the required/written length. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `mbsnrtowcs()` when the NUL is within `nms`. **Confidence:** high from the zero-result branch; no conversion was run. Return the count before the terminator. Source-only; see the [bounded conversion review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-multibyte-bounded-conversion-review-ek10669-ek10678).

<a id="ek10671"></a>
### EK10671 — POSIXC `wcsnrtombs()` does not store the converted string terminator [medium impact, high source confidence]

The loop stops when `*s` is NUL (`compiler/crt/posixc/wcsnrtombs.c:70`), and the subsequent cursor update sets `*src` to NULL without writing a NUL byte to `dst` (`:93`). The selected `wcrtomb()` helper writes a NUL when asked to convert `L'\0'` (`compiler/crt/stdc/wcrtomb.c:50-58`), but the wrapper never makes that call.

**Trigger and consequence:** convert a NUL-terminated wide string into a non-NULL destination with enough space. The returned byte sequence is not NUL-terminated even though the source cursor reports successful terminator conversion. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `wcsnrtombs()` when the source NUL is reached. **Confidence:** high from the complete loop and helper contract; no conversion was run. Write the multibyte NUL when it fits while keeping it excluded from the returned count. Source-only; see the [bounded conversion review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-multibyte-bounded-conversion-review-ek10669-ek10678).

<a id="ek10672"></a>
### EK10672 — POSIXC `wcsnrtombs()` clears the source pointer when its input limit is reached [medium impact, high source confidence]

After converting, the implementation sets `*src` to NULL whenever `nwc == 0`, even if `*s` still points to an unconverted non-NUL character (`compiler/crt/posixc/wcsnrtombs.c:70-71,88-94`).

**Trigger and consequence:** pass an input limit shorter than the wide string. After converting exactly that many characters, the function signals that the source is exhausted; the caller loses access to the remaining suffix through the updated pointer. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `wcsnrtombs()` when `nwc` is the stopping condition. **Confidence:** high from the loop and final pointer expression; no conversion was run. Leave `*src` pointing at `s` when the input limit is reached before the terminator. Source-only; see the [bounded conversion review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-multibyte-bounded-conversion-review-ek10669-ek10678).

<a id="ek10673"></a>
### EK10673 — POSIXC `wcsnrtombs()` does not measure output when `dst` is NULL [medium impact, high source confidence]

The loop compares `count + res` to `len` even when `dst` is NULL (`compiler/crt/posixc/wcsnrtombs.c:78-81`). The documented query form ignores destination capacity, but a conventional query call with `dst == NULL` and `len == 0` stops before counting the first character.

**Trigger and consequence:** query a nonempty string with `dst == NULL` and zero length. The function returns zero instead of the number of bytes required. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `wcsnrtombs()` sizing form. **Confidence:** high from the query documentation and unconditional capacity check; no conversion was run. Do not apply the output-capacity stop when no destination is supplied. Source-only; see the [bounded conversion review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-multibyte-bounded-conversion-review-ek10669-ek10678).

<a id="ek10674"></a>
### EK10674 — stdc `mbrtowc()` reports impossible UTF-8 lead bytes as incomplete [low impact, high source confidence]

The incomplete-sequence branch returns `(size_t)-2` for short input based on `n < 2`, `n < 3` or `n < 4` before validating that the first byte is a legal UTF-8 lead (`compiler/crt/stdc/mbrtowc.c:78-85`). A continuation byte such as `0x80`, or an invalid lead such as `0xF5`, with `n == 1` is therefore classified as incomplete instead of an encoding error.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `mbrtowc()` on one of those bytes with a one-byte limit, or pass it through `mbsnrtowcs()`. The decoder reports an incomplete sequence and leaves the source unconsumed instead of returning `(size_t)-1` with `EILSEQ`, so callers can mistake malformed input for a valid prefix. **Affected configuration:** selected stdc UTF-8 decoder and POSIXC wrappers using it. **Confidence:** high from branch ordering and UTF-8 prefix validity; no conversion was run. Validate lead-byte class before treating a short sequence as incomplete. Source-only; see the [bounded conversion review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-multibyte-bounded-conversion-review-ek10669-ek10678).

<a id="ek10675"></a>
### EK10675 — POSIXC `wcsnrtombs()` dereferences a failed output-buffer allocation [medium impact, high source confidence]

`wcsnrtombs()` allocates a temporary multibyte buffer sized from the current locale's maximum character length, but does not check the `AllocVec()` result before passing it to `wcrtomb()` and copying from it (`compiler/crt/posixc/wcsnrtombs.c:58-71,83-86`). For a non-NULL destination with enough capacity, a failed allocation leaves `buf` NULL and the copy reads from it.

**Trigger and consequence:** convert a nonempty string to a real destination while the temporary `AllocVec()` fails. The function can fault instead of returning `(size_t)-1` with an allocation error. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `wcsnrtombs()`; requires allocation failure and a non-NULL destination with sufficient capacity. **Confidence:** high from unchecked allocation and subsequent indexed read; no allocation failure or conversion was induced. Check the temporary allocation before entering the conversion loop and return an error cleanly. Source-only; see the [bounded conversion review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-multibyte-bounded-conversion-review-ek10669-ek10678).

<a id="ek10676"></a>
### EK10676 — POSIXC `fchown()` reports success without changing ownership [medium impact, high source confidence]

The selected `fchown()` implementation is explicitly marked “Not implemented” and contains only a TODO, but returns `0` (`compiler/crt/posixc/fchown.c:26-27,38-43`). It does not validate the descriptor or call any ownership operation.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `fchown()` on any descriptor, including one requesting a new owner or group. The caller receives success while the object ownership remains unchanged, so permission/ownership bookkeeping can proceed on a false assumption. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `fchown()` vector. **Confidence:** high from the complete body; no ownership call was executed. Return an unsupported-operation error until ownership-by-descriptor is implemented. Source-only; see the [directory, ownership and truncate-wrapper review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-directory-ownership-and-truncate-wrapper-pass-ek10676).

<a id="ek10677"></a>
### EK10677 — POSIXC `setsid()` always fails without setting `errno` [low impact, high source confidence]

The selected `setsid()` implementation unconditionally returns `(pid_t)-1` and does not assign `errno` or inspect session state (`compiler/crt/posixc/setsid.c:42-44`). A failed POSIX call must report its reason through `errno`; the result here depends on whatever value the caller previously left there.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `setsid()` in any process state. It always reports failure, and callers cannot determine whether a session operation was unsupported, prohibited, or failed for another reason. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `setsid()` vector. **Confidence:** high from the complete implementation; no session call was executed. Implement session creation or return a documented error with a corresponding `errno`. Source-only; see the [process-ID and session API review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-process-id-and-session-api-pass-ek10677).

<a id="ek10678"></a>
### EK10678 — stdc multibyte conversion ignores the selected C locale [medium impact, high source confidence]

The selected `mbrtowc()` and `wcrtomb()` implementations hard-code UTF-8 conversion and do not read the current locale (`compiler/crt/stdc/mbrtowc.c:58-61,82-105`; `wcrtomb.c:57-65,73-81`). In contrast, stdc initializes the current locale to C with `__lc_mb_max = 1`, and `setlocale(LC_CTYPE, ...)` changes the selected locale and `mb_cur_max` (`compiler/crt/stdc/__locale.c:30-42,69-90`).

**Trigger and consequence:** use the initial or explicitly selected C locale and convert a multibyte sequence such as a UTF-8 encoded non-ASCII character, or convert that wide character back. The decoder accepts UTF-8 where the C locale uses a single-byte encoding, and the encoder emits multiple UTF-8 bytes instead of reporting a character not representable in the selected locale. **Affected configuration:** selected stdc multibyte conversion APIs while the current locale is C; also affects POSIXC wrappers that delegate to these helpers. **Confidence:** high from the locale state and helper implementations; no conversion was run. Make the conversion helpers honor `LC_CTYPE`, or constrain locale selection and API claims consistently. Source-only; see the [bounded conversion review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-multibyte-bounded-conversion-review-ek10669-ek10678).

<a id="ek10679"></a>
### EK10679 — POSIXC `posix_memalign()` overwrites the output pointer on failure [low impact, high source confidence]

`posix_memalign()` assigns `aligned_alloc()` directly to `*memptr` before checking whether allocation succeeded (`compiler/crt/posixc/posix_memalign.c:57-63`). If the allocation fails, the function returns the error number but leaves `*memptr` changed to NULL instead of preserving the caller's prior value.

**Trigger and consequence:** initialize the output pointer to a live allocation, then call `posix_memalign()` with a valid alignment when the new allocation fails. The caller loses the original pointer value even though the call failed, potentially leaking the existing allocation or disrupting its cleanup path. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `posix_memalign()` vector; requires allocation failure. **Confidence:** high from the direct output assignment and failure branch; no allocation failure was induced. Allocate into a temporary pointer and update `*memptr` only on success. Source-only; see the [aligned allocation and PRNG review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-allocation-and-reentrant-prng-pass-ek10679).

<a id="ek10680"></a>
### EK10680 — POSIXC `random()` starts with mostly uninitialized default state [medium impact, high source confidence]

`get_random_state()` allocates TYPE_3 storage, then `init_random_state()` copies `DEG_3 + 1` bytes from the initialized table (`compiler/crt/posixc/random.c:167-195`). `DEG_3 + 1` is 32, but `rst_randtbl` contains 32-bit words, so only eight words are copied into the 32-word allocation. `init_random_state()` does not seed or clear the remaining words; `random()` immediately passes the state to `random_r()`, which adds and reads through the whole degree-31 table (`:514-533`).

**Trigger and consequence:** call `random()` before `srandom()` or `initstate()`. After the front pointer advances beyond the copied words, generation reads uninitialized state and produces values unrelated to the documented initialized sequence. **Affected configuration:** first-use POSIXC `random()` state allocation when no explicit seed/state initialization has occurred. **Confidence:** high from allocation size, copy length, and pointer traversal; no random call was run. Copy the complete word array or initialize the entire state through `srandom_r()`. Source-only; see the [random-state initialization review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-random-state-initialization-review-ek10680-ek10681).

<a id="ek10681"></a>
### EK10681 — POSIXC `initstate()` treats a negative buffer size as the largest state size [high impact, high source confidence]

The public `initstate()` API takes `n` as an `int` and forwards it to `initstate_r()`'s `size_t sz` without rejecting negative values (`compiler/crt/posixc/random.c:398-420`). A negative `n` converts to a very large unsigned size, selects TYPE_4 (`:349-371`), and seeds 63 state words starting at `arg_state + 1` (`:373-375,250-266`).

**Trigger and consequence:** pass a non-NULL small state buffer with a negative size. The size check accepts the converted value and initialization writes beyond the supplied buffer. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `initstate()` API; requires a negative `n` and a small caller buffer. **Confidence:** high from the signed-to-unsigned call and selected state degree; no buffer or random-state call was run. Reject nonpositive/smaller-than-minimum sizes before conversion and before modifying the current state. Source-only; see the [random-state initialization review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-random-state-initialization-review-ek10680-ek10681).

<a id="ek10682"></a>
### EK10682 — POSIXC `posix_fadvise()` accepts invalid arguments for foreign descriptors [low impact, high source confidence]

For a descriptor not found in the POSIXC table, `posix_fadvise()` returns success as soon as `__getfdhooks()` finds another subsystem's registered descriptor (`compiler/crt/posixc/posix_fadvise.c:61-68`). That branch precedes the negative offset/length checks and advice-enum switch used for ordinary POSIXC descriptors (`:71-89`); the function's own contract lists those invalid values as `EINVAL`.

**Trigger and consequence:** use a valid fd owned by another registered subsystem, such as a socket, and pass a negative offset/length or an unrecognized advice value. The call returns zero instead of the documented error number, hiding an invalid request. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `posix_fadvise()` with a foreign fd.library owner hook. **Confidence:** high from the branch ordering and local contract; no descriptor call was run. Validate the arguments before the foreign-owner no-op path. Source-only; see the [advisory-file API review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-advisory-file-api-review-ek10682).

<a id="ek10683"></a>
### EK10683 — POSIXC `localeconv_l()` interprets locale handles with the wrong structure layout [medium impact, high source confidence]

`localeconv_l.c` defines `struct __locale` as a single embedded `struct lconv` and returns `&loc->locale_lconv` (`compiler/crt/posixc/localeconv_l.c:14-22,47-51`). The `newlocale()` implementation returns pointers to static objects whose actual `struct __locale` begins with `__lc_name`, `__lc_mb_max`, and classification-table fields (`compiler/crt/posixc/newlocale.c:27-51`; shared definition `compiler/crt/stdc/include/aros/types/locale_s.h:16-25`). The two translation units therefore interpret the same pointer with incompatible layouts.

**Trigger and consequence:** pass a valid non-NULL locale handle from `newlocale()` to `localeconv_l()` and read the returned `struct lconv`. The pointer aliases the locale object's beginning; its first members are the locale name and multibyte limit, not decimal/grouping/currency fields, so callers receive invalid field values and may dereference small integer values as pointers. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `localeconv_l()` with any valid handle returned by the selected `newlocale()`. **Confidence:** high from the conflicting structure definitions and returned pointer; no locale call was run. Use the shared locale layout and store locale-specific `lconv` data at a defined field, or return a proper `lconv` object. Source-only; see the [locale-specific wrapper review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-locale-specific-wrapper-review-ek10683).

<a id="ek10684"></a>
### EK10684 — POSIXC `*at()` helper can dereference a directory descriptor after concurrent close [medium impact, medium source confidence]

`__at_enter()` obtains an `fdesc *` from `__getfdesc()` and then reads `desc->fcb->privflags` and `desc->fcb->handle` before calling `DupLock()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/__at.c:42-58`). `__getfdesc()` protects only the descriptor-array lookup with `FD_LOCK`; it releases that semaphore before returning the pointer (`compiler/crt/posixc/__fdesc.c:116-144`). It does not retain the descriptor or FCB. Meanwhile `close()` obtains the same borrowed pointer, decrements the FCB reference count, closes/unlocks and frees the FCB at zero, then frees the descriptor and clears the table slot (`compiler/crt/posixc/close.c:53-79,98-119`). The `io_lock` does not protect `__at_enter()`'s lookup or lifetime window.

The helper comment says its duplicated directory lock is intended to keep the current directory valid "even if the descriptor is closed by another thread meanwhile" (`__at.c:54-57`). POSIXC routes pthread worker descriptor lookups to the creator's shared descriptor table (`__fdesc.c:750-763`), so the threads can reach the same `fdesc`/FCB. If `close(dirfd)` frees either object after `__getfdesc()` returns but before `__at_enter()` finishes reading the fields or duplicates the DOS lock, a relative `openat()`, `fstatat()`, `unlinkat()`, or `fchmodat()` can access freed descriptor state instead of safely retaining the directory lock. These wrappers all call this helper for relative paths (`openat.c:83-91`; `fstatat.c:69-78`; `unlinkat.c:67-77`; `fchmodat.c:68-77`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a pthread worker begins a relative `*at()` operation while another thread closes the same directory descriptor, with the close/free interleaving between descriptor lookup and `DupLock()`. This can dereference freed descriptor/FCB memory or pass an invalid lock to DOS. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `*at()` wrappers and pthread workers sharing the creator's descriptor table; requires concurrent close of the same descriptor. The legacy `close()` function comment warns against threaded use, so the candidate is limited to the helper's explicit concurrent-close safety claim and is not asserted as general POSIX close-vs-I/O semantics. **Confidence:** medium: lifetime operations and missing retention are explicit, but the precise schedule and intended API guarantee were not exercised. Pin the descriptor/FCB under a lifetime guard through `DupLock()`, or remove the concurrent-close guarantee and enforce/document caller synchronization. Source-only; see the [shared `*at()` helper review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-at-directory-lock-lifetime-review-ek10684).

<a id="ek10685"></a>
### EK10685 — POSIXC `strptime()` accepts failed numeric conversions and stores an indeterminate value [medium impact, high source confidence]

The `MATCHUINT` macro treats any `sscanf()` result other than `EOF` as a successful conversion (`compiler/crt/posixc/strptime.c:11-16`). A nonnumeric input makes `sscanf("%u%n", ...)` return zero, which passes that test; `matched` was initialized to zero, while `val` has not been assigned, and the macro writes `value` into the `struct tm` field anyway. For `%m`, that expression is `val - 1`. The `%u` conversion also receives `int *val` rather than the required `unsigned int *`, which does not match the conversion specification.

**Trigger and consequence:** call the selected `strptime()` with a supported numeric directive such as `%Y` and input beginning with a non-digit. The function returns a non-NULL pointer without consuming input and writes an indeterminate value into the corresponding `tm` field; later directives may then parse from the same input position. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `strptime()` API; it is exposed in the public POSIXC header and vector, though no maintained in-tree production caller of this implementation was found. **Confidence:** high for the result-count check and uninitialized assignment; no parse call was run. Require exactly one successful numeric conversion and use a correctly typed `unsigned int` temporary before updating `tm`. Source-only; see the [strptime parser review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-strptime-parser-review-ek10685-ek10686).

<a id="ek10686"></a>
### EK10686 — POSIXC `strptime()` returns a pointer before the input on a mismatched `%%` [medium impact, high source confidence]

For the `%%` format directive, the parser sets `matched` to `EOF` (negative one) when the next input character is not `%`, then unconditionally applies `s += matched` (`compiler/crt/posixc/strptime.c:34-38,72`). It does not return failure on the mismatch.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `strptime()` with a non-percent input character and a format consisting of `%%`. The function decrements the input pointer and, if the format ends there, returns a pointer before the supplied input buffer. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `strptime()` API; requires a mismatched literal-percent directive. No maintained in-tree production caller was found. **Confidence:** high from the signed `EOF` value and unconditional pointer addition; no parse call was run. Return `NULL` on a mismatch and advance only after a successful match. Source-only; see the [strptime parser review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-strptime-parser-review-ek10685-ek10686).

<a id="ek10687"></a>
### EK10687 — Shared `gmtime()` conversion leaves negative timestamps in negative clock fields [medium impact, high source confidence]

The common `__CRT_GMTIME` macro reads `time_t` into a signed `long`, then decomposes it using C's truncation-toward-zero division and signed remainder (`compiler/crt/common/__crt_time.h:32-45`). It does not borrow seconds/minutes/hours into the preceding unit or adjust the day count for a negative remainder. AROS defines `time_t` as a signed 32-bit type (`compiler/crt/stdc/include/aros/types/time_t.h:13-16`). For example, an input of -1 second yields `tm_sec == -1` while the day count remains 1 January 1970, rather than 31 December 1969 at 23:59:59.

**Trigger and consequence:** convert a representable negative timestamp with `gmtime()`, `gmtime_r()`, `localtime()`, or `localtime_r()`. The broken-down result can contain negative seconds/minutes/hours and the wrong calendar date; `ctime()`/`ctime_r()` then format that invalid tuple. **Affected configuration:** selected stdc and POSIXC time-conversion APIs sharing `__crt_time.h`; also affects `localtime*` after applying the configured GMT offset. **Confidence:** high from the signed `time_t` definition and the shared arithmetic; no conversion was run. Normalize negative remainders into the preceding minute/hour/day before calendar decomposition. Source-only; see the [reentrant time conversion review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-reentrant-time-conversion-review-ek10687).

<a id="ek10688"></a>
### EK10688 — `jrand48()` and `mrand48()` do not safely produce the required signed 32-bit result [medium impact, high source confidence]

Both implementations combine the high and middle 16-bit state words using signed `long` arithmetic without first constructing a signed 32-bit value (`compiler/crt/posixc/jrand48.c:41-43`; `mrand48.c:44-46`). POSIX specifies that these functions return signed long values in `[-2^31, 2^31)` and derives them from the high-order 32 bits of the updated state ([Open Group POSIX draft, `jrand48`/`mrand48`](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/open/n4217.pdf)).

**Trigger and consequence:** generate a state whose high bit of `xseed[2]` is set. On 32-bit-`long` targets, shifting that positive signed value left 16 bits and adding the next word exceeds `LONG_MAX`, which is undefined signed arithmetic. On targets where `long` is wider than 32 bits, the arithmetic is representable but returns a nonnegative value from `0x80000000` through `0xffffffff` instead of sign-extending it to the required negative result. The same issue occurs with caller state in `jrand48()` and global state in `mrand48()`. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC `jrand48()`/`mrand48()` vectors; behavior depends on the target C `long` width. **Confidence:** high from the expression and required signed result range; no generator call was run. Assemble the 32-bit result in an unsigned type, then explicitly convert/sign-extend it to the API's `long`. Source-only; see the [rand48 family review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-rand48-family-review-ek10688).

<a id="ek10689"></a>
### EK10689 — POSIXC declares `strtol_l()` and `strtoul_l()` but exports no library vectors [medium impact, medium source confidence]

The public POSIXC stdlib header declares both locale-aware integer conversion APIs under POSIX.1-2008/XSI/GNU feature selections (`compiler/crt/posixc/include/aros/posixc/stdlib.h:88-97`). Their implementation files are included in `POSIXC_LOCALE` and define the functions, but both bodies are explicit `AROS_FUNCTION_NOT_IMPLEMENTED` stubs returning zero (`compiler/crt/posixc/mmakefile.src:261-274`; `strtol_l.c:14-18`; `strtoul_l.c:14-18`). In the POSIXC library's `functionlist`, six vector slots are skipped at `posixc.conf:1143-1144`, followed by vectors for `strtof_l`, `strtod_l`, `strtold_l`, `strtoll_l`, and `strtoull_l`; there are no `strtol_l` or `strtoul_l` entries. Genmodule's `.skip` handling advances the library vector number without adding a function (`tools/genmodule/config.c:1713-1734`), so clients cannot call these declared functions through the generated POSIXC interface.

**Trigger and consequence:** a client enables the header's feature test macro and calls either function through POSIXC. The declaration permits compilation, but the selected library has no corresponding vector, so normal library linkage cannot resolve the API. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC library and its public stdlib header; limited to `strtol_l()` and `strtoul_l()`. **Confidence:** medium: the declaration, selected source and vector omissions are explicit; the omission may be an intentional consequence of the unimplemented stubs, but the header still advertises both interfaces. Either provide them with defined behavior or remove/guard the declarations until the API is callable. Source-only; see the [wide-string and locale-long API review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-wide-string-and-locale-long-api-review-ek10689).

<a id="ek10690"></a>
### EK10690 — POSIXC `getopt_long()` suppresses every requested option diagnostic [low impact, high source confidence]

The AROS build defines `warnx()` as an empty variadic function and marks it `FIXME: implement me` (`compiler/crt/posixc/getopt_long.c:65-68`). The selected parser calls `warnx()` for ambiguous long options, forbidden or missing arguments, unknown long options, and invalid short options (`:271-280,283-304,318-338,340-352,515-536,538-556,561-574`). These calls are guarded by `PRINT_ERROR`, which is true when `opterr` is nonzero and the option string does not begin with `:` (`:91`).

**Trigger and consequence:** use the selected `getopt_long()`/`getopt_long_only()` API with its default `opterr == 1` and supply an unknown, ambiguous, or malformed option. The functions return their error value, but emit no diagnostic on stderr, so command-line tools lose the requested explanation. **Affected configuration:** POSIXC static link library's `getopt_long` implementation on AROS; host-tool builds use their host libc and are excluded. **Confidence:** high from the explicit no-op helper and all guarded call sites; no parser call was run. Provide an AROS warning implementation or route these diagnostics through the existing stdio error path. Source-only; see the [getopt implementation review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-getopt-implementation-review-ek10690).


<a id="ek677"></a>
### EK677 — OpenSBI GOP framebuffer remap can leave the Sv39 lower canonical window [medium impact, high source confidence; conditional firmware placement]

The OpenSBI startup maps a GOP framebuffer above the 256 GiB identity limit at `FB_WINDOW + (framebuffer_base - SV39_IDENTITY_LIMIT)`, where `FB_WINDOW` is 128 GiB (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:313-321`). Sv39 lower-half virtual addresses must remain below 256 GiB. Consequently, the remapped framebuffer interval must end no later than 384 GiB physically: a base at or above 384 GiB starts at or above 256 GiB virtually, and a lower base whose span crosses 384 GiB has a tail at or above that noncanonical boundary. Startup passes that alias to `krnMMUMapPages()` and publishes it as `KRN_FBAddr` without checking the upper canonical bound (`:424-432,695-703`). The selected `efifbgfx` path then clears and writes through the published pointer (`rom/hidds/efifbgfx/efifbgfx_support.c:19-86,146-150`).

**Trigger and consequence:** boot the OpenSBI target with a remapped GOP framebuffer whose physical span extends beyond 384 GiB. The corresponding virtual span extends beyond Sv39's lower canonical range; accesses to the noncanonical portion fault instead of reaching the display. **Affected configuration:** UEFI-booted RISC-V OpenSBI using the selected EFI framebuffer HIDD, conditional on firmware placement at this boundary. **Confidence:** high for the arithmetic and the access path; no such firmware layout was established or booted. Validate that the complete remapped range fits the supported virtual window before publishing it, and fail or disable framebuffer use otherwise. Source-only; see the [framebuffer virtual-window trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L277).

<a id="ek678"></a>
### EK678 — OpenSBI framebuffer or high-device remap can overwrite virtual RAM still offered to the allocator [medium impact, medium source confidence; conditional memory layout]

OpenSBI places high device mappings in a fixed virtual window beginning at 128 GiB. For a GOP framebuffer range that starts below the 256 GiB identity limit but extends above it, `krnFBAddr()` computes an alias below the fixed window by unsigned subtraction. `krnMMUMapPages()` writes the device mapping into that alias, splitting/replacing any existing identity leaves there (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:313-321,695-703`; `kernel_mmu.c:149-197,360-399`). The same fixed-window remapping is used for high PCI BARs (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/hidd/pcidt/pcidt_driverclass.c:137-145,459-470`). Later startup publishes FDT-reported RAM banks as MemHeaders without subtracting any virtual span replaced by those mappings (`kernel_startup.c:781-782,890-895,979-993`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a selected firmware layout must both place usable RAM at an alias address overwritten by a crossing GOP framebuffer or high PCI BAR and publish that RAM to Exec. The MMU then directs the range to device memory while the allocator may still allocate it as RAM, so ordinary RAM use can corrupt device state or fail. **Affected configuration:** RISC-V OpenSBI with a crossing GOP range or a high PCI BAR, plus a reported usable-RAM bank overlapping the resulting virtual alias; no checked-in firmware map establishes this combination. **Confidence:** high for the mapping and MemHeader publication behavior; medium for practical reachability because the required firmware/device layout was not found in-tree. Exclude device aliases from the allocatable RAM ranges or reserve/validate them before publishing MemHeaders. Source-only; see the [framebuffer/RAM alias trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L279).

<a id="ek10693"></a>
## EK10693 — `mktime()` miscounts leap days for pre-1970 dates [conditional]

The year-count expression in `mktime()` uses C signed division for negative operands (`compiler/crt/stdc/mktime.c:125-140`). For 1968-01-01 (`tm_year == 68`), it sets `year` to 67 and evaluates `(year - 68) / 4` as `(-1) / 4 == 0` under C truncation toward zero. That yields `days == -730`; the correct epoch offset is -731 days because 1968 was a leap year. The resulting timestamp and recomputed weekday are one day late. `mktime()` is selected in the stdc source list (`compiler/crt/stdc/mmakefile.src:528`) and the project defines `time_t` as signed 32-bit (`compiler/crt/stdc/include/aros/types/time_t.h:13-17`). The maintained WirelessManager caller rejects years before 1970, so this candidate is scoped to other valid public API callers or future callers.

**Trigger and consequence:** a caller passes a valid pre-1970 calendar date whose elapsed-year count crosses a leap day, such as 1968-01-01. The returned timestamp and `tm_wday` are wrong by one day. **Affected configuration:** AROS stdc clients using `mktime()` for pre-epoch dates. **Confidence:** high for the arithmetic and example; occurrence depends on a caller needing pre-1970 conversion. Count leap days with floor-correct arithmetic for negative years. No time conversion or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10694"></a>
## EK10694 — `mktime()` overflows signed arithmetic past the 32-bit `time_t` limit [conditional]

`mktime()` stores the elapsed day count in `int`, then forms seconds using an expression whose operands remain `int` until assigned to `time_t` (`compiler/crt/stdc/mktime.c:79-83,125-164`). AROS `time_t` is signed 32-bit (`compiler/crt/stdc/include/aros/types/time_t.h:13-17`), but the function has no representability check before that expression. For 2038-01-19 03:14:08 UTC, the intermediate seconds value is 2,147,483,648, one above `INT32_MAX`; the signed multiplication/addition overflows before the assignment. The selected WirelessManager X.509 date conversion accepts years from 1970 onward and passes the result into certificate-time checks (`workbench/network/WirelessManager/src/utils/os_amiga.c:45-78`; `workbench/network/WirelessManager/src/tls/x509v3.c:636-648`), so post-limit certificate dates can receive a corrupted timestamp instead of a conversion failure.

**Trigger and consequence:** `mktime()` receives a date outside signed-32-bit epoch range, such as the second after the 2038 limit. Signed integer overflow makes the returned value incorrect/undefined instead of the required unrepresentable-time indication; in the WirelessManager path this can misclassify certificate validity. **Affected configuration:** AROS stdc users converting dates beyond the signed 32-bit `time_t` range, including the selected WirelessManager X.509 path. **Confidence:** high for the integer types, expression, and caller range; exact overflow result is compiler-dependent. Use a wider checked intermediate and return the documented failure value when the result cannot fit `time_t`. No certificate, time conversion, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10695"></a>
## EK10695 — `difftime()` can overflow before converting the result to `double` [conditional]

The implementation subtracts the two signed 32-bit `time_t` arguments before casting the result to `double` (`compiler/crt/stdc/difftime.c:50-53`; `time_t` definition: `compiler/crt/stdc/include/aros/types/time_t.h:13-17`). When the mathematical difference lies outside the signed 32-bit range, that subtraction overflows; the cast cannot recover the intended difference. For example, `difftime(INT32_MAX, INT32_MIN)` should return 4,294,967,295 seconds but instead evaluates an overflowing signed subtraction. This implementation is selected by `compiler/crt/stdc/mmakefile.src:507`; it is absent from the checked-in m68k `AROS_NOFPU` implementation branch. Repository search found no AROS production caller, so scope this to stdc clients on FPU-enabled targets.

**Trigger and consequence:** an FPU-enabled AROS caller compares timestamps whose difference exceeds `INT32_MAX` seconds, such as widely separated representable `time_t` endpoints. The function returns an incorrect value or invokes undefined signed-overflow behavior instead of the elapsed-seconds difference. **Affected configuration:** AROS stdc builds where `AROS_NOFPU` is not defined. **Confidence:** high for the signed operand width and cast ordering; occurrence depends on caller timestamp range. Convert each operand to `double` before subtracting, or use checked wider integer arithmetic. No time calculation or build was run; source-only.
