The ordinary StdC-linked path queues an exit callback and releases usergroup before the program closes its libraries (__optionallibs.c:38-90,111-117), avoiding the cycle. The defect is the explicit StdCBase == NULL fallback, which opens usergroup without that release callback.

**Trigger and consequence:** a task with a POSIXC base but no active StdC base calls a POSIXC user/group API that opens usergroup.library, then exits/closes its POSIXC library. The relative-library cycle can keep both per-task library bases and their dependency references alive after the caller is gone. **Affected configuration:** clients using the selected POSIXC user/group wrappers without a StdC exit-list base; the POSIXC library source is selected by compiler/crt/posixc/mmakefile.src:16. No checked-in caller exercising the no-StdCBase branch was found, so in-tree trigger reachability is not established. **Confidence:** high for the open and close-hook dependency cycle if this branch is entered; current in-tree caller likelihood is uncertain. Ensure every successful optional usergroup open has a release path independent of StdC, or reject/undo the open when no exit-list base is available. No library open, task exit, or build was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC optional-library lifecycle pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-optionallibs-cycle-ek10812).

<a id="ek10814"></a>
### EK10814 — POSIXC failed assertions call exit instead of abort [conditional termination-contract mismatch]

The POSIXC module aliases the assert implementation symbol to __posixc_assert (compiler/crt/posixc/posixc.conf:85-86). The selected stdc and stdcio implementations both call abort after reporting the assertion (compiler/crt/stdc/__assert.c; compiler/crt/stdc/__stdcio_assert.c).

**Trigger and consequence:** an assertion evaluates false in a POSIXC-linked program with NDEBUG undefined. The process exits normally with status 10 rather than following abort's abnormal-termination path; normal exit handlers and stream cleanup can run, and callers or supervisors cannot distinguish the assertion through the required abort behavior. **Affected configuration:** programs using the selected POSIXC assert implementation. **Confidence:** high for the selected alias, call to exit, and C99 contract. No assertion or process termination was run. Call abort() after writing the diagnostic, matching the selected stdc/stdcio implementations. Source-only. See the [POSIXC assertion implementation pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#posixc-assert-perror-missing-definition-ek10813).

<a id="ek10854"></a>
### EK10854 — AArch64 binary128 `sqrtl()` can return a result one ULP below the correctly rounded value [confirmed]

The selected binary128 `__ieee754_sqrtl()` uses `feholdexcept()` to save/clear state, sets round-toward-zero before computing a quotient that it calls “chopped,” tests `FE_INEXACT` to decide whether that quotient is exact, and then selects a final correction from `fegetround()` (`compiler/crt/stdc/math/e_sqrtl.c:94,130-151`). On AArch64, the selected inline fenv header stores only zero in `feholdexcept()`, leaves `fesetround()` unsupported, makes `fetestexcept()` always return zero, and makes `fegetround()` return -1 (`arch/aarch64-all/include/aros/fenv.h:58-81`). Thus the quotient is computed in the caller's existing mode, every quotient is treated as exact, and the final correction handles neither nearest nor upward mode. A source-derived exact binary128 arithmetic trace for `sqrtl(11.0L)` under round-to-nearest gives `0x1.a887293fd6f34168ef24f1987215p+1`; correctly rounded binary128 is `0x1.a887293fd6f34168ef24f1987216p+1`, one ULP higher. In this path `11/4` is inexact, but `fetestexcept()` reports zero, so the algorithm decrements the quotient as though exact and skips the nearest-mode correction because `fegetround()` returns -1. `e_sqrtl` is in `STDC_LONGDB_MATH` (`compiler/crt/stdc/mmakefile.src:271`); AArch64 selects the binary128 layout and precision (`math/fpmath.h:45-46`; `compiler/crt/stdc/include/aros/stdc/float.h:44-52`). This is a caller-level consequence distinct from EK10852's fenv API mismatch and EK10853's exact `fma()` result case.

**Trigger and consequence:** on the default AArch64 StdC path, `sqrtl(11.0L)` under round-to-nearest returns the binary128 value one ULP below the correctly rounded result, per the source-derived exact arithmetic trace above. **Affected configuration:** AArch64 StdC builds selecting the 113-bit `long double` implementation and default inline fenv header, when FPCR selects round-to-nearest. **Confidence:** high for the source path and exact arithmetic witness; no compiler build or runtime call was used. Restore the required environment operations or provide a square-root implementation that does not rely on them. Source-only.

<a id="ek10853"></a>
### EK10853 — AArch64 `fma()` and `fmal()` can take the upward-rounding branch when the mode is unknown [conditional]

The selected `fma()` and distinct-long-double `fmal()` implementations save `fegetround()` in `oround` and, when the scaled product is more than their mantissa width below `z`, switch on that value to choose the correctly rounded adjacent result (`compiler/crt/stdc/math/s_fma.c:202-235`; `s_fmal.c:188-221`). The default AArch64 fenv header returns `-1` from `fegetround()` (`arch/aarch64-all/include/aros/fenv.h:63-66`); this matches none of the named cases, so each switch's `default` treats the mode as `FE_UPWARD`. For example, `fma(0x1p-28, 0x1p-28, 1.0)` has `spread == -55`, and its positive product is much smaller than half an ULP at 1. Under round-to-nearest the result is exactly `1.0`, but the fallback branch returns `nextafter(1.0, INFINITY)` (`s_fma.c:230-234`). The same calculation applies to binary128 `fmal(0x1p-58L, 0x1p-58L, 1.0L)`: `spread == -115 < -LDBL_MANT_DIG`, so round-to-nearest returns `1.0L` while the fallback returns `nextafterl(1.0L, INFINITY)` (`s_fmal.c:199-220`). The common math list selects `s_fma` (`mmakefile.src:197`); `s_fmal` is selected in `STDC_LONGDB_MATH` (`:301`). These are concrete result errors in selected callers, distinct from EK10852's fenv API mismatch.

**Trigger and consequence:** on AArch64, call `fma()` or `fmal()` with finite nonzero operands whose product is much smaller than `z`, while hardware rounding is round-to-nearest. Since `fegetround()` returns `-1`, the distant-product path treats the mode as upward and can return the adjacent representable value instead of `z`. **Affected configuration:** AArch64 builds using the default inline fenv header; the common double body and distinct binary128 long-double body are both selected. **Confidence:** high for the source-derived mode and branches; the examples assume round-to-nearest hardware state. Correct the AArch64 fenv implementation or make both routines handle an unsupported `fegetround()` result without selecting an arbitrary directed mode. Source-only; no FP call or build was run.

<a id="ek10852"></a>
### EK10852 — AArch64 floating-point environment stubs report success without doing the operation

The default AArch64 `aros/stdc/fenv.h` inline implementations return success for exception/status and environment operations but do not access the floating-point environment (`arch/aarch64-all/include/aros/fenv.h:37-92`). In particular, `fegetenv()` leaves its output untouched; `feholdexcept()` writes zero rather than saving the current state or clearing flags; `fesetenv()` and `feupdateenv()` do nothing; `feclearexcept()` and `feraiseexcept()` do nothing; and `fetestexcept()` always returns zero. The same header explicitly returns `-1` from `fegetround()` and `fesetround()`, but the other APIs falsely signal success. The selected `aros/stdc/fenv.h` includes this header on AArch64 (`compiler/crt/stdc/include/aros/stdc/fenv.h:15-17`); the default build does not define `STDC_NOINLINE`, which would select the generic error-returning library stubs instead. The C fenv contract requires these success returns to correspond to the requested state operation ([WG14 N1570, §7.6.2 and §7.6.4](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf)). AArch64 floating-point instructions can set status flags in FPSR according to FPCR ([Arm A64 floating-point instruction reference](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/100069/0610/A64-SIMD-Scalar-Instructions/FRSQRTE--scalar-)).

**Trigger and consequence:** on the default AArch64 StdC header path, call `feraiseexcept(FE_INVALID)` or `fegetenv(&env)`: each returns zero although no exception is raised and no environment is stored. Likewise, after arithmetic sets a hardware flag, `fetestexcept()` reports none and a successful `fesetenv()` does not restore saved state. Selected `nearbyint()` depends on `fegetenv()`/`fesetenv()` to suppress `FE_INEXACT` (`compiler/crt/stdc/math/s_nearbyint.c:40-56`), so that flag is not restored/cleared by these stubs. **Affected configuration:** AArch64 StdC clients using the default inline fenv header; builds explicitly selecting `STDC_NOINLINE` instead reach the generic stubs that report failure. **Confidence:** high for the success-return/no-operation mismatch; exact downstream effects depend on the operation and whether it sets architectural status. Implement the advertised FPCR/FPSR operations, or return failure consistently when unsupported. Source-only; no FP instruction or fenv call was run.



<a id="ek10855"></a>
### EK10855 — `system(NULL)` dereferences NULL in native path mode

The POSIXC `system()` documentation promises that a NULL command checks for command-processor availability and returns 1 (`compiler/crt/posixc/system.c:35-50`). However, the implementation tests `doupath` and enters `system_no_sh()` before checking `string` for NULL (`:86-92`). The `system_no_sh()` path immediately calls `strdup(string)` (`:147`), whose implementation calls `strlen(orig)` without a NULL check (`compiler/crt/stdc/strdup.c:40-48`). `posixc.library` uses a per-opener base (`compiler/crt/posixc/posixc.conf:4-6`); `MakeLibrary()` clears the root base allocation (`rom/exec/makelibrary.c:105-113`), the generated per-opener constructor copies it (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1360-1375`), and ordinary POSIXC startup does not set `doupath` (`posixc_startup.c:14-23`). Only `__posixc_nixmain()` sets the flag to one (`__posixc_nixmain.c:41-45`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a native-mode POSIXC caller invokes the documented `system(NULL)` query while `doupath == 0`. The early branch sends NULL to `strdup()`, which reads it through `strlen()` instead of returning the documented availability result. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC clients using the native path mode; `system()` is in the POSIXC source list (`compiler/crt/posixc/mmakefile.src:232`). NIX-wrapper callers set `doupath` before reaching the NULL check and take the later return-1 branch. **Confidence:** high for the branch ordering, cleared default state, and null dereference. Handle `string == NULL` before selecting the path-mode fallback, and perform the documented availability check. No call or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10856"></a>
### EK10856 — `system_no_sh()` dereferences failed path conversions

The direct-command fallback passes its parsed command token to `__path_u2a()` and immediately uses the result in `strlen()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/system.c:147-157`). In Unix-path mode, `__path_u2a()` can return NULL for the deliberately blocked `/.attbin` prefix with `ENOENT`, or for failure to grow its conversion buffer with `ENOMEM` (`compiler/crt/posixc/__upath.c:67-81,88-100`). If `bin:sh` cannot be locked, `system()` selects `system_no_sh()` (`system.c:95-107`); it does not check the conversion result before computing the command buffer size.

**Trigger and consequence:** with `doupath` enabled and no shell available, a non-NULL command whose first token is a rejected path such as `/.attbin`, or an ordinary command whose path conversion fails for lack of memory, reaches `strlen(NULL)`. The process faults instead of returning an error with the path-conversion errno. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC NIX-path mode when `bin:sh` is unavailable and the command conversion returns NULL. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked converter result and subsequent `strlen()`; the conversion failure or missing-shell condition is required. Check and propagate `__path_u2a()` failure before sizing `fullcmd`. No command, allocation failure or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10857"></a>
### EK10857 — `system_no_sh()` dereferences failed command-buffer allocations

`system_no_sh()` does not check the command-copy allocation before tokenizing it (`compiler/crt/posixc/system.c:147-154`): if `strdup(string)` returns NULL, `strsep()` returns a NULL token, the path converter returns NULL, and the following `strlen(apath)` dereferences it. The function also does not check `fullcmd = malloc(...)` before `strcpy(fullcmd, apath)` (`:156-159`), so failure of this second allocation passes NULL as the destination. Both allocation APIs can report failure with NULL (`compiler/crt/stdc/strdup.c:44-51`; `compiler/crt/posixc/system.c:156-157`).

**Trigger and consequence:** the no-shell fallback receives a non-NULL command and either its `strdup()` or assembled-command `malloc()` fails. The unchecked result leads to a NULL dereference rather than `system()` returning an allocation error. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC builds whenever `system_no_sh()` is used and either allocation fails, including native mode or NIX mode without `bin:sh`. **Confidence:** high for both unchecked allocation results and their immediate use; allocation failure is required. Check each allocation and return `-1` with `errno = ENOMEM` after freeing any owned storage. No allocation failure or build was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek10859"></a>
### EK10859 — Unix-path `system(NULL)` reports a shell without checking for one

In Unix-path mode, `system()` returns 1 for either a NULL or empty command before reaching the code that tries to lock `bin:sh` (`compiler/crt/posixc/system.c:89-99`). Its own API documentation says a NULL command checks whether a command processor is available and returns 1 to indicate that one is available (`:35-50`). The NIX startup wrapper sets `PosixCBase->doupath = 1` (`compiler/crt/posixc/__posixc_nixmain.c:41-45`), while normal POSIXC startup leaves the mode unchanged (`posixc_startup.c:14-23`), so this false-success path is selected for NIX-mode callers. For non-NULL commands the implementation performs the actual `Lock("bin:sh", ...)` check at `system.c:95-107` and deliberately falls back to direct execution when it fails.

**Trigger and consequence:** a Unix-path/NIX-mode caller invokes `system(NULL)` on a system where `bin:sh` cannot be locked. The function still returns 1, falsely reporting a command processor as available; callers relying on the query may select shell-dependent behavior that cannot run. **Affected configuration:** POSIXC NIX-mode callers (`doupath != 0`); native-mode NULL input follows the separate EK10855 failure path. **Confidence:** high for the early return and documented contract mismatch. Perform the shell availability check for the NULL query and return the result dictated by it. No command, shell lookup, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10860"></a>
### EK10860 — withdrawn: `rmdir()` double conversion does not free its input buffer

The reported use-after-free depended on the disproved EK10805 expansion. In source order, `__path_u2a("..")` returns `/` using its original three-byte request. The nested `remove()` conversion of `/` requests two bytes. `realloc_nocopy()` keeps the existing allocation for a shrink smaller than 4096 bytes (`compiler/crt/stdc/realloc_nocopy.c:65-80`), so this call does not free the buffer that supplies its input. The second conversion changes `/` to `:` through the leading-slash volume-root rule, but this review did not establish a distinct caller-visible consequence for the altered target. Withdraw the use-after-free candidate; no replacement finding is credited. No path or allocation was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10861"></a>
### EK10861 — OpenSBI FDT parser classifies any `memory*` root node as RAM [conditional]

`krnParseFDT()` accepts a depth-two node as a memory bank whenever its name has the prefix `memory` and it has a `reg` property (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_fdt.c:146-159`). The prefix check does not require the standard memory-node spelling `memory` or `memory@...`, and the parser does not check `device_type = "memory"`. A distinct root-level node such as `memory-controller@...` with a normal address/size `reg` therefore enters `info->regions` and can become `mem_base` if its advertised size is the largest parsed range (`:164-171`).

On a non-UEFI OpenSBI startup, the kernel treats every parsed region as RAM: `krnInitMMU()` maps non-primary regions read/write/execute (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_mmu.c:390-395`), and startup creates a public system `MemHeader` for any surviving region extent of at least 1 MiB (`kernel_startup.c:979-997`). Thus a memory-prefixed non-RAM root node can expose its device-register range as allocatable memory when its range meets that size and survives the existing exclusions. Smaller false matches are still mapped as RAM but do not reach this `MemHeader` path.

UEFI startup replaces `fdtinfo.regions` with EFI usable regions (`kernel_startup.c:575-590`), so a false secondary FDT bank is normally discarded from the later-bank map and allocator path. The parsed scalar `mem_base`/`mem_size` is retained, however, when the misclassified bank is larger than each individual EFI region; it can then supply the primary MemHeader span described separately in EK9042. This UEFI case requires that additional size relationship and is not asserted for every false-name node.

**Trigger and consequence:** OpenSBI receives a DTB with a root child other than the RAM node whose name begins `memory`, and that node has a `reg` tuple interpreted as a bank. On non-UEFI startup, if its range is at least 1 MiB above the kernel and is not excluded, Exec may allocate from device space; ordinary memory writes can then hit MMIO or an unmapped/reserved region. On UEFI startup, the same false node can instead affect the primary heap only when it becomes the largest parsed FDT bank and remains larger than every EFI usable region, as in EK9042. **Affected configuration:** RISC-V64 OpenSBI with an external firmware DTB containing the described node; the UEFI form additionally requires the EFI-region size condition. No matching in-tree DTB was found, so current deployment reachability is unestablished. **Confidence:** high that the prefix predicate admits non-RAM names and that native parsed regions feed mapping/allocator setup; high for the conditional scalar retention; conditional on external DTB and range relationships. Require exact `memory`/`memory@` naming or validate the node's `device_type` before accepting its `reg`. No DTB, boot, mapping, allocation, or build was run; source-only. See the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md).


<a id="ek10871"></a>
### EK10871 — `AddDosEntry()` returns failure without setting the documented `IoErr()`

The public contract says `AddDosEntry()` returns `DOSFALSE` on error and that `IoErr()` supplies the additional error (`rom/dos/adddosentry.c:37-40`). For non-volume entries, the routine detects an existing non-volume node with the same name and sets only its local `success` flag to `DOSFALSE` (`:93-104`). Neither this branch nor either subsequent `UnLockDosList()` call sets `IoErr()` (`rom/dos/unlockdoslist.c:48-63`). The caller therefore receives the previous task error value, which may be zero or unrelated to the duplicate-name failure. The codebase's `AssignPath()`, `AssignLate()` and `AssignLock()` duplicate checks explicitly use `SetIoErr(ERROR_OBJECT_EXISTS)` (`rom/dos/assignpath.c:96-102`; corresponding checks in `assignlate.c` and `assignlock.c`), confirming the established error convention.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `AddDosEntry()` with a non-volume node whose name duplicates an existing non-volume DOS-list entry, then inspect `IoErr()`. The function returns `DOSFALSE`, but the error value does not identify the rejection and can remain stale. Callers that report or branch on `IoErr()` produce a misleading or missing diagnostic. **Affected configuration:** all DOS callers reaching the duplicate-name branch. **Confidence:** high; the complete function and unlock helper contain no error assignment on this path. Set the appropriate DOS error before returning failure. No DOS list was modified and no API call or build was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10872"></a>
### EK10872 — `AssignAdd()` rejects a null lock without setting the documented `IoErr()`

`AssignAdd()` documents that a zero return has additional information in `IoErr()` (`rom/dos/assignadd.c:36-39`). Its first validation returns `DOSFALSE` immediately when `lock == BNULL` (`:57-58`), before setting an error. The later invalid-assignment and allocation-failure branches do set `ERROR_OBJECT_WRONG_TYPE` and `ERROR_NO_FREE_STORE` (`:64-70,75-81`), so this early path is inconsistent with both the API contract and the function's other failures. The selected `C:Assign` command reads `IoErr()` after an `AssignAdd()` failure (`workbench/c/Assign.c:590-605`), and Installer likewise treats false as an operation failure (`workbench/utilities/Installer/execute.c:1769-1771`).

**Trigger and consequence:** call `AssignAdd(name, BNULL)` and inspect `IoErr()`. The function fails but leaves the previous value intact, so callers that report the DOS error may show a stale or empty diagnostic. **Affected configuration:** all callers that pass a null lock; the selected C:Assign caller can print its stale error if such a value reaches the API. **Confidence:** high for the missing error assignment and contract mismatch; ordinary selected callers generally obtain a lock first, so their reachability to this argument is conditional. Set an appropriate DOS error before returning. No assign or lock was created and no API call or build was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10873"></a>
### EK10873 — DOS `CheckSignal()` can erase a signal delivered by another CPU [ExecSMP]

`CheckSignal()` disables local interrupts, reads `tc_SigRecvd & mask`, then clears the requested bits with an ordinary read/modify/write (`rom/dos/checksignal.c:67-75`). Exec documents that `Disable()` only affects the current processor on ExecSMP and that shared data also needs a spinlock (`rom/exec/disable.c:43-48`). The SMP `Signal()` path sets a task's received bits atomically while holding its task spinlock (`rom/exec/signal.c:44-70,293-306`), so another CPU can deliver a selected bit after `CheckSignal()` reads it but before the non-atomic clear; the clear can overwrite that newly delivered bit. The selected SMP `Wait()` path handles the analogous consume operation with the task spinlock and `__AROS_ATOMIC_AND_L()` (`rom/exec/wait.c:123-137`), which `CheckSignal()` omits.

**Trigger and consequence:** on ExecSMP, a task calls `CheckSignal(mask)` while another CPU signals that task with a bit in `mask` between the read and clear. The newly delivered signal can be lost, so polling loops may miss a break or other event until it is signaled again. Checked-in production uses include DOS pattern traversal (`rom/dos/matchnext.c:112-120`) and desktop/utility cancellation loops such as `AddDataTypes`, `Type`, and `Say`; this makes the API reachable from maintained code. **Affected configuration:** builds defining `__AROSEXEC_SMP__`, including the configured x86-64 PC SMP and Raspberry Pi SMP variants (`configure.in:1669,2197`); uniprocessor local interrupt masking prevents the cross-CPU interleaving. **Confidence:** high for the unsynchronized clear and concurrent atomic producer; conditional on signal delivery in the read/clear window. Protect the read-and-clear with the task spinlock and an atomic consume operation as in `Wait()`. No task or signal was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10874"></a>
### EK10874 — DOS packet wrappers can fail without setting the documented `IoErr()` on allocation failure

`dopacket()` allocates a standard packet, then for non-Process tasks may allocate a reply port. Either allocation failure returns `FALSE` without setting the optional Res2 result or the current Process's `pr_Result2` (`rom/dos/dopkt.c:96-115`). `allocdospacket()` returns NULL from `AllocVec()` without setting IoErr (`rom/dos/allocdosobject.c:161-175`). The packet-based DOS wrappers commonly pass `NULL` for the explicit Res2 output, so a resource-allocation failure leaves their documented `IoErr()` unchanged. `ChangeMode()` directly returns this result (`rom/dos/changemode.c:60-66`), and `DeleteFile()` and `ExNext()` likewise return the false packet result (`rom/dos/deletefile.c:53-64`; `rom/dos/exnext.c:73-81`). Selected POSIXC `F_SETFL` and `remove()` callers read IoErr after the first two failures (`compiler/crt/posixc/fcntl.c:199-210`; `compiler/crt/stdc/remove.c:41-45`); `readdir()` uses IoErr after `ExNext()` to distinguish `ERROR_NO_MORE_ENTRIES` from a real error (`compiler/crt/posixc/readdir.c:104-116`), so a stale end-of-directory code can truncate enumeration.

**Trigger and consequence:** a Process calls a packet-based DOS API while the standard packet allocation fails (or a non-Process caller cannot create its reply port). The API reports failure but leaves a stale/zero error value; selected `F_SETFL` and POSIXC `remove()` can report the wrong `errno`, while `readdir()` can mistake an allocation failure for end-of-directory or report an unrelated failure. **Affected configuration:** all configurations using affected packet-based DOS wrappers, conditional on packet or reply-port allocation failure; the cited POSIXC consequences require those callers. **Confidence:** high for the early returns, missing error update, and caller error reads; occurrence depends on allocation failure. Set a DOS allocation error on each helper allocation failure before returning. No allocation failure, file operation, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10875"></a>
### EK10875 — DOS packet helpers send a NULL BSTR after name allocation failure [non-fast-BSTR]

`getpacketinfo()` calls `C2BSTR(name)` in both the relative-path and device-qualified branches, but does not check whether the result is `BNULL` before returning success (`rom/dos/packethelper.c:17-38,39-48`). On non-`AROS_FAST_BSTR` builds, `C2BSTR()` calls `CreateBSTR()`, whose allocation failure returns `BNULL` (`rom/dos/dos_intern.h:295-302`; `compiler/arossupport/createbstr.c:12-20`). The selected `CreateDir()` wrapper then sends `phs.name` as the required name argument (`rom/dos/createdir.c:55-63`). In the selected RAM handler, `BStr()` dereferences the supplied BSTR to read its length without a NULL check (`rom/filesys/ram/handler.c:463-475`), so this path can fault in the handler rather than return a memory error. The same helper is used by DeleteFile, SetComment, SetOwner, SetProtection, SetFileDate and MakeLink.

**Trigger and consequence:** on a non-fast-BSTR target, a DOS call requiring packet-name conversion reaches `getpacketinfo()` while `CreateBSTR()` allocation fails. The helper reports success and the wrapper sends `BNULL` where a name BSTR is required; the selected RAM handler dereferences it, and other handlers receive an invalid argument. **Affected configuration:** DOS builds without `AROS_FAST_BSTR` (including the selected m68k path); conditional on BSTR allocation failure. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked NULL propagation and RAM-handler dereference. Check `C2BSTR()` and return failure with `ERROR_NO_FREE_STORE` before reporting packet information as ready. No allocation failure or DOS operation was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek10876"></a>
### EK10876 — `getpacketinfo()` leaks its converted name when device lookup fails [non-fast-BSTR]

In the device-qualified branch, `getpacketinfo()` allocates `bstrname` before calling `GetDeviceProc()` (`rom/dos/packethelper.c:39-42`). If device lookup fails, it exits through the shared `return FALSE` at `:50` without calling `FREEC2BSTR(bstrname)`. On non-`AROS_FAST_BSTR` builds, `C2BSTR()` allocates storage with `CreateBSTR()` (`rom/dos/dos_intern.h:295-302`; `compiler/arossupport/createbstr.c:12-29`). All selected `getpacketinfo()` callers only call `freepacketinfo()` on helper success, so this allocation is not reclaimed on the failure path.

**Trigger and consequence:** on a non-fast-BSTR target, repeatedly call a packet-based DOS operation with a device-qualified path for which `GetDeviceProc()` fails. Each call leaks the converted BSTR allocation. **Affected configuration:** DOS builds without `AROS_FAST_BSTR` (including the selected m68k path); requires failed device lookup. **Confidence:** high for allocation-before-lookup and the missing cleanup, and for the callers' success-only cleanup. Free `bstrname` before returning failure. No lookup or repeated operation was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10877"></a>
### EK10877 — Bootability rejection leaves the boot process current directory pointing at an unlocked lock

`__dos_IsBootable()` changes the calling Process's current directory to the candidate volume with `CurrentDir(lock)` and discards the old lock returned by `CurrentDir()` (`rom/dos/isbootable.c:30-33`; the alternate compile-time branch does the same at `:98-101`). `CurrentDir()` stores the new BPTR in `pr_CurrentDir` and returns the old BPTR; it does not duplicate or release either lock (`rom/dos/currentdir.c:53-63`). When the signature check returns false, the selected `CliInit` caller calls `UnLock(lock)` and clears its local variable, but does not restore the Process current directory (`rom/dos/cliinit.c:488-493`). The boot Process therefore retains a BPTR to the lock just freed, and the previously current directory lock is also no longer owned by a reachable field. The boot loop continues into failure cleanup and may inspect further boot nodes (`:495-529`).

**Trigger and consequence:** on a non-m68k build using the signature check, examine a candidate volume without a valid `AROS.boot` signature (or with an unreadable/missing file), causing `__dos_IsBootable()` to return false. `CliInit` frees the lock still stored in `pr_CurrentDir`; subsequent relative DOS operations in the boot Process can dereference the stale lock. The old current-directory lock reference is leaked on every call. **Affected configuration:** boot paths selecting `AROS_BOOT_CHECKSIG`, including non-m68k platforms; conditional on a rejected/unreadable candidate. **Confidence:** high for the current-directory replacement, missing restoration, and caller's unlock; reachability follows the selected boot-node rejection branch. Save and restore the old directory on every return, or make the ownership transition explicit so the caller does not free the active current directory. No boot check or lock operation was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10878"></a>
### EK10878 — `NextDosEntry()` indexes past its type table when a linked node has a corrupt type [conditional]

`NextDosEntry()` follows the next BPTR and indexes `flagarray` directly with `dlist->dol_Type + 1` (`rom/dos/nextdosentry.c:50-63`). The table has six entries for types -1 through `DLT_NONBINDING` (4), but this function does not validate the type range first. `FindDosEntry()` walks the same DOS list and explicitly checks that exact range before indexing its corresponding table, logging and stopping on an invalid type (`rom/dos/finddosentry.c:83-101`). A linked node whose type is outside -1..4 therefore causes an out-of-bounds table read in `NextDosEntry()` and can fault or select an unrelated flag value.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `NextDosEntry()` while walking a DOS list containing a node with a corrupted `dol_Type` outside the supported range. The table access is out of bounds, so enumeration can fault instead of terminating with a corruption report. This requires prior list corruption, such as a freed node remaining linked; no normal node construction path inspected here produces such a type. **Affected configuration:** all builds using DOS list enumeration; conditional on corrupt list contents. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked index and table bounds; low for ordinary reachability because the required list corruption is not established by this pass. <a id="ek10880"></a>
### EK10880 — `ExAll()` fallback indexes before its size table for negative data types

<a id="ek10881"></a>

<a id="ek10882"></a>
### EK10882 — Buffered DOS reads can spin forever when flushing a zero-progress write

Before `vbuf_fetch()` can read from a filehandle that is still in write mode, `handle_write_mode()` flushes pending bytes by repeatedly calling `Write()` until `pos == fh->fh_Pos` (`rom/dos/fread.c:86-102`). It returns on a negative result, but does not handle zero: `pos` remains unchanged and the loop repeats indefinitely. The public `Write()` contract explicitly permits a return of zero (“0 if the end of the file was reached”) (`rom/dos/write.c:41-44`). A zero result for a positive remaining byte count therefore leaves this flush with no progress and no error exit. `vbuf_fetch()` is reached by both `FRead()` and `FGetC()` (`rom/dos/fread.c:56-81`; `rom/dos/fgetc.c:62-67`), so switching a buffered stream from output to input can hang either call.

The flush loop repeatedly issues the same remaining write and the caller never returns. **Affected configuration:** all DOS builds; conditional on a handler returning zero without consuming pending bytes, which the `Write()` API permits. **Confidence:** high for the non-progress loop and documented zero result; the triggering handler response is conditional. Treat a zero result as a failed/incomplete flush and return an error rather than retrying without progress. No file operation, handler response or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10883"></a>
### EK10883 — stdc `fwrite()` loses completed elements after a later block write fails [unbuffered mode]

The DOS `FWrite()` contract returns either the number of blocks written or `EOF` on error (`rom/dos/fwrite.c:24-49`). It writes blocks sequentially and returns `EOF` as soon as `FWriteChars()` does not write a full block, even if earlier blocks completed (`:68-78`). In `BUF_NONE` mode, `FWriteChars()` forwards each block directly to `Write()` (`:133-147`; mode selected by `rom/dos/setvbuf.c:68-80`). The stdc `fwrite()` wrapper maps `FWrite()`'s `-1` to a return count of zero instead of preserving the completed block count (`compiler/crt/stdc/fwrite.c:60-69`).

This loss has a selected handler path. RAMFS `WriteData()` copies available bytes into the current data block, then requests another block when bytes remain (`rom/filesys/ram/filesystem.c:898-931`). If its muddy-pool allocation fails, `AddDataBlock()` sets `ERROR_DISK_FULL` and returns NULL (`:1282-1325`); `WriteData()` advances the file position and returns the positive prefix already copied (`:940-954`), and `CmdWrite()` returns that byte count with the error in IoErr (`rom/filesys/ram/commands.c:655-670`). The RAM handler is selected by Raspberry Pi ARM and AArch64 package manifests (`arch/arm-raspi/boot/mmakefile.src:128-135`; `arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/mmakefile.src:128-136`). Thus an unbuffered stdc stream can finish one full element, encounter a partial second element as RAMFS exhausts its pool, and receive `fwrite() == 0` instead of 1 completed element.

**Trigger and consequence:** use `fwrite()` with element size greater than one, at least two elements, and an unbuffered stream backed by RAMFS; a later element's write reaches the end of allocated RAMFS blocks and pool allocation fails after copying a prefix. The stream error flag and disk-full errno are set, but the return value loses all fully completed earlier elements. **Affected configuration:** stdc callers using unbuffered streams over RAMFS, including the checked Raspberry Pi ARM/AArch64 package routes; the trigger requires RAMFS pool exhaustion during a later element. **Confidence:** high for the count loss and the selected RAMFS short-write/error path; no file operation or allocation failure was induced. <a id="ek10899"></a>
### EK10899 — `StrToDate()` accepts invalid months and indexes outside the month table

The numeric date parser accepts any value returned by `StrToLong()` for `month` and `days`; it checks only whether parsing failed (`rom/dos/strtodate.c:221-250`). It later evaluates `Dos_DayTable[month - 1]` without validating that the month is 1 through 12 (`:287-313`). Thus month 0 indexes before the table and month 13 indexes after it. Day-of-month values are also not checked against the selected month's length, so impossible dates are converted into another day count rather than rejected.

**Trigger and consequence:** pass a syntactically numeric date with month 0 or 13 in a numeric format. `StrToDate()` reads outside `Dos_DayTable` and may return a bogus datestamp; invalid day values such as February 31 are likewise accepted. **Affected configuration:** all DOS builds; conditional on malformed/out-of-range input. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked month index and missing calendar-range validation. Validate month and day against the selected month and leap year before computing the stamp. No date string was parsed; source-only.

<a id="ek10900"></a>
### EK10900 — `SplitName()` treats a zero buffer size as an unbounded destination

`SplitName()` decrements the signed `size` before checking it, then copies while `size` is nonzero (`rom/dos/splitname.c:65-77`). With `size == 0`, the value becomes -1 and remains nonzero as bytes are copied, so the loop writes the entire current path component plus a terminator even though the caller supplied a zero-byte buffer capacity.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `SplitName()` with a nonempty component and `size == 0`. The function writes into `buf` without any capacity, potentially overwriting adjacent memory. **Affected configuration:** all DOS builds; conditional on a zero-size call. **Confidence:** high for the signed decrement and loop condition. Reject nonpositive sizes before decrementing or copying. No split operation was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10901"></a>
### EK10901 — `VFWritef()` reports successful byte counts after write errors

`VFWritef()` increments its output count after every `FPutC()` call but never checks whether that call returned EOF (`rom/dos/vfwritef.c:104-111,125-127,141-145,169-174`). Its numeric helper `putNumber()` has the same unchecked write loop (`:231-242`). `FPutC()` returns EOF when its one-byte write fails (`rom/dos/fputc.c:65-69`), while VFWritef's contract promises -1 on an error.

**Trigger and consequence:** write a formatted string to a filehandle whose handler fails during one of the character writes. VFWritef continues attempting later characters and returns a positive count as if output succeeded, so callers cannot detect the failed or partial output from the documented result. **Affected configuration:** all DOS builds; conditional on an output failure during formatting. **Confidence:** high for the ignored FPutC result and contract mismatch. Stop at the first failed FPutC and return -1. No write failure was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek10902"></a>
### EK10902 — i386 Exec startup dereferences a missing optional boot command line

The selected i386 Exec initializer reads `KRN_CmdLine` with a default value of zero, then immediately passes that value to `strstr()` without checking for NULL (`arch/i386-pc/exec/debug_init.c:19-28`). The file is selected in the i386 Exec target's `CFILES` list (`arch/i386-pc/exec/mmakefile.src`). The selected PC bootstrap adds `KRN_CmdLine` only when its Multiboot v1 command-line flag is set (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/multiboot1.c:65-89`; `arch/all-pc/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:469-481`); Multiboot v2 likewise emits it only when the command-line tag is present (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/multiboot2.c:108-146,219-224`). The kernel's boot-info getter returns the tag list as supplied and does not synthesize an empty command line (`rom/kernel/getbootinfo.c:43-50`).

**Trigger and consequence:** boot the selected i386 PC path with a valid Multiboot handoff that omits the optional command-line field. `LibGetTagData(KRN_CmdLine, 0, msg)` returns NULL, and `strstr(NULL, "debug=memory")` dereferences it during Exec initialization, preventing normal startup. **Affected configuration:** i386 PC builds using the selected PC bootstrap and a bootloader that omits the command line; x86-64 has a separate startup path and is not covered by this finding. **Confidence:** high for the NULL default, unguarded call, target selection, and conditional producer omission; no boot was run. Guard the search or substitute an empty string when the tag is absent. Source-only.


<a id="ek10903"></a>
<a id="ek10904"></a>
### EK10904 — NewCLI does not refresh `pr_WindowPtr` after an AUTO console opens its window [conditional]

`internal_CliInitAny()` calls `SetWindowPtrFromConsole()` when its standard input is interactive (`rom/dos/newcliproc.c:245-250`). That helper asks the input handler for `ACTION_DISK_INFO` and copies `id_VolumeNode` into `pr_WindowPtr` only when the returned value is nonzero (`:26-54`). The console handler accepts `AUTO` without creating a window at open (`rom/filesys/console_handler/con_handler.c:600-609`); its `ACTION_DISK_INFO` response then reports the current, NULL `fh->window` (`:1166-1181`). On the first read or write, `MakeSureWinIsOpen()` creates the window (`:390-400`), but the console handler has no later update of the Process's `pr_WindowPtr`.

**Trigger and consequence:** initialize a CLI with an interactive `CON:.../AUTO` standard-input handle before that console has a window. The initial query returns a null window and leaves the process's requester target unchanged; the console later opens a window on first read/write without updating it. A process whose target is the default null value (as for `NP_WindowPtr` default `0`, `rom/dos/createnewproc.c:140`) continues to direct requesters to the default public screen rather than its console window. **Affected configuration:** DOS NewCLI/Run initialization using an AUTO console that has not yet opened its window; conditional on a requester being opened after lazy creation. **Confidence:** high for the initial null report, later window creation, and lack of refresh; no in-tree shell invocation demonstrating this exact ordering was established. Update the process requester target when the AUTO console creates its window or arrange for the CLI to query again. No console, requester, or process was run; source-only.

**Coverage evidence:** [NewCLI AUTO-console requester-target trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#newcli-auto-console-requester-target-trace-2026-11-05).

<a id="ek10906"></a>
### EK10906 — DOS `DateToStr(FORMAT_DEF)` ignores the current locale's date format

The public `DateTime` definition says `FORMAT_DEF` means “Format of current locale” (`compiler/include/dos/datetime.h:48-55`), and the `DateToStr()` documentation repeats that contract (`rom/dos/datetostr.c:67-86`). Its format switch handles only `FORMAT_INT`, `FORMAT_USA`, and `FORMAT_CDN`; every other value, including `FORMAT_DEF`, selects the hard-coded `d-M-y` pattern (`rom/dos/datetostr.c:218-231`). Month names also come from the fixed English `Dos_MonthTable` (`:30-35,246-249`). By comparison, the selected Locale library's `LocDateToStr()` uses `loc->loc_ShortDateFormat` for `FORMAT_DEF` (`workbench/libs/locale/locdatetostr.c:120-140`). Selected in-tree clients including `List`, LogView, and Wanderer set `FORMAT_DEF` and call DOS `DateToStr()` directly (`workbench/c/List.c:293-300`; `workbench/system/LogView/logview.c:235-247`; `workbench/system/Wanderer/Classes/icon.c:1027-1039`).

**Trigger and consequence:** call DOS `DateToStr()` with `dat_Format == FORMAT_DEF` while the active locale uses a short date order other than day-month-year, or localized month names. The routine still emits the DOS hard-coded order and English month abbreviations, so displayed dates do not follow the documented current-locale format. **Affected configuration:** all DOS builds with a non-DOS locale format; the visible effect is limited to callers requesting `FORMAT_DEF`. **Confidence:** high for the contract/implementation mismatch and selected caller use; no locale-dependent output was run. Resolve `FORMAT_DEF` through the active locale's short-date format and localized month names, or document and consistently use a locale-aware API. No date conversion or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10907"></a>
### EK10907 — Buffered DOS reads omit `IoErr()` when allocating their first buffer fails [conditional]

When a filehandle has no buffer, `vbuf_fetch()` calls `vbuf_alloc()` and returns `FETCHERR` if allocation fails (`rom/dos/fread.c:156-164`). `vbuf_alloc()` returns NULL after failed `AllocMem()` without setting `IoErr()` (`rom/dos/setvbuf.c:120-143`). `FGetC()` converts the sentinel to EOF without setting an error (`rom/dos/fgetc.c:65-72`), despite documenting that `IoErr()` supplies the error detail. `FRead()` clears the Process error to zero on entry, then returns EOF for the same sentinel (`rom/dos/fread.c:65-86`), so its result is accompanied by `IoErr() == 0`. Ordinary `Open()` filehandles begin zeroed, and non-interactive handlers are not assigned a DOS buffer by `Open()`; their first buffered read therefore reaches this allocation path (`rom/dos/allocdosobject.c:58-70`; `rom/dos/open.c:70-76,231-240`).

**Trigger and consequence:** make the first buffered `FGetC()` or `FRead()` on a valid unbuffered filehandle while the internal buffer allocation fails. Both APIs report the EOF/error sentinel without `ERROR_NO_FREE_STORE`; `FGetC()` can expose an unrelated previous error, while `FRead()` reports a zero IoErr. Callers cannot distinguish resource exhaustion through the documented error channel. **Affected configuration:** all DOS builds; conditional on the first buffered read requiring allocation and allocation failure. **Confidence:** high for the allocation, sentinel and unset error state; no allocation failure was induced. Set `IoErr(ERROR_NO_FREE_STORE)` when the internal buffer allocation fails. No file operation or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10908"></a>
### EK10908 — NIX startup leaks the temporary default `PATH` buffer [low impact, conditional]

When Unix-style startup finds no existing `PATH`, `__posixc_nixmain()` calls `update_PATH()` to construct one from the CLI command-directory list (`compiler/crt/posixc/__posixc_nixmain.c:74-75,185-270`). `update_PATH()` allocates and grows a temporary buffer with `realloc()`, then calls `setenv("PATH", PATH, 1)` without freeing that buffer (`:202-270`). The selected `setenv()` implementation passes the value to DOS `SetVar()`, which copies the variable data, and does not retain the caller's pointer (`compiler/crt/posixc/setenv.c:62-73`; `rom/dos/setvar.c:119-140`). In the coroutine case, the environment is cloned/restored around each invocation, so the temporary allocation is not reclaimed with a process that exits (`__posixc_nixmain.c:58-65,101-112`). The in-tree Shell provides this route: `loadCommand()` loads a command segment and `executeLine()` invokes it with `RunCommand()` (`workbench/c/Shell/Shell.c:348-420,504-555`). The only checked-in `nix=yes` target found is the explicitly buildable DHCP client (`workbench/network/common/dhcp/client/mmakefile.src:27-31`); its AROSTCP service launcher instead uses `CreateNewProcTags()` for a separate process (`workbench/network/stacks/AROSTCP/bsdsocket/kern/amiga_dhcp.c:90-105). A source census found direct `RunCommand()` callers in Shell, Installer, POSIXC `__exec`, and DOS/hosted boot helpers (`workbench/c/Shell/Shell.c:555`; `workbench/utilities/Installer/execute.c:1285`; `compiler/crt/posixc/__exec.c:564-573`; `rom/dos/boot.c:215`; `arch/all-hosted/filesys/emul_handler/boot.c:95`). Shell supplies repeated same-task invocation; the boot helpers invoke the fixed `AROSMonDrvs` command, and the other callers do not establish automatic repeated invocation of this NIX target. The `Execute` shell command search match is only a comment about RunCommand input flushing, not a direct call.

**Trigger and consequence:** run a NIX-mode executable as a Shell command, repeatedly, in a process with no `PATH` variable and a nonempty CLI command-directory list. Each `RunCommand()` invocation clones the Shell's local variables; `update_PATH()` constructs a temporary `PATH` buffer, `setenv()` copies it into the clone, and startup restores the original variables on return. The temporary buffer is left allocated each time, so repeated Shell commands steadily consume process memory. AROSTCP's normal separate-process launch of `dhclient` does not take this repeated-coroutine route. **Affected configuration:** explicitly buildable POSIXC NIX programs, including the optional `network-dhcp-client` target, when invoked as Shell commands; requires absent `PATH` and at least one usable CLI path entry. **Confidence:** high for the leak and Shell-to-RunCommand route; invocation frequency and absent-PATH condition depend on user configuration. Free the temporary buffer after `setenv()` returns. No allocation, command, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10909"></a>
### EK10909 — NIX startup silently publishes an incomplete default `PATH` after allocation failure [conditional]

`update_PATH()` skips a CLI command-directory entry when `realloc(PATH, PATH_len + uname_len + 1)` fails, then continues constructing and publishes whatever partial string remains (`compiler/crt/posixc/__posixc_nixmain.c:226-248,263-268`). It also ignores the return from `setenv("PATH", PATH, 1)` (`:265-268`), although selected POSIXC `setenv()` returns failure when DOS `SetVar()` cannot store the value (`compiler/crt/posixc/setenv.c:62-73`). `__posixc_nixmain()` ignores `update_PATH()`'s result (the helper returns `void`) and proceeds to invoke the program's `main()` (`__posixc_nixmain.c:74-85`).

**Trigger and consequence:** start a NIX-mode program without an existing `PATH` while growth of the CLI-derived path buffer fails, or while storing the completed value through `setenv()` fails. Startup proceeds with some CLI directories omitted or with no default `PATH`; later `execvp()`/`execlp()` searches can therefore report a command missing even though it is in the omitted configured directory. **Affected configuration:** selected POSIXC NIX startup; conditional on path-buffer or environment-variable allocation/storage failure and later PATH-based command lookup. **Confidence:** high for the ignored failures and continued startup; no allocation failure or command lookup was induced. Propagate a failure from `update_PATH()` and avoid presenting a partial default as complete. No build or runtime operation was performed; source-only.

### EK10903 — timestamped `KrnBug()` reports the requested length after truncating output

In the x86-64 PC `DEBUG_TIMESTAMP` implementation, `krnBug()` formats into the fixed boot buffer and returns the result of `vsnprintf()` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/_bug.c:37-75`). When the formatted text is too long, `vsnprintf()` returns the length it would have produced, while the loop emits only the bytes present in the 1,024-byte buffer. The public `KrnBug()` vector documents its result as the number of successfully printed characters (`rom/kernel/bug.c:32-41`). The x86-64 startup path sets the buffer size to 1,024 bytes (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:33,347-348`).

**Trigger and consequence:** build x86-64 PC with `DEBUG_TIMESTAMP` and emit a formatted message longer than the remaining buffer capacity. The message is truncated, but `KrnBug()` returns the full would-have-written payload length, so callers such as `kprintf()` receive a count that overstates the emitted output (`compiler/arossupport/kprintf.c:68-77`). **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC builds with `DEBUG_TIMESTAMP` and the startup debug buffer enabled. **Confidence:** high for the truncation, return-value semantics, and selected buffer size; no build or output was run. Return the actual emitted count (and define whether timestamp-prefix characters count) or use a dynamically sized output path. Source-only.


<a id="ek10910"></a>
### EK10910 — `RXLIB` ignores initialization failure before using its Rexx message [conditional]

`init()` returns `FALSE` when it cannot find the `REXX` port, create a reply port, or allocate a `RexxMsg` (`workbench/rexxc/RXLIB.c:29-48`). `main()` ignores that return (`:63-70`), then the 2–5 argument branches write through the static `msg`, which remains NULL after each of those failures (`:92-108`). In the `CreateRexxMsg()` failure case, `replyport` has already been allocated and `init()` returns without deleting it; the ensuing null dereference occurs before `main()` reaches its normal cleanup calls. The adjacent `RX` program checks `init()` and cleans up before returning an error (`workbench/rexxc/RX.c:97-101`). The `RXLIB` executable has an explicit build rule, while the aggregate Workbench edge is commented out (`workbench/rexxc/mmakefile.src:5-12`; `workbench/mmakefile.src:28`).

**Trigger and consequence:** explicitly build/run `RXLIB` with two to five arguments while RexxMast has not published the `REXX` port, or when `CreatePort()`/`CreateRexxMsg()` fails. Initialization prints an error and returns, but `main()` proceeds and dereferences `msg`, terminating the utility instead of returning its error result; if message allocation failed, the previously created reply port is also left without the intended cleanup. **Affected configuration:** optional explicitly built Workbench `RXLIB` program; no default-image inclusion is claimed. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked return, null dereference, and missing cleanup path; no Rexx service or allocation failure was induced. Check `init()` in `main()` and call `cleanup()` before returning `RC_ERROR` on failure. No program or build was run; source-only. See the [RXLIB initialization-failure caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#rexxlib-initialization-failure-caller-trace-ek10910).


<a id="ek10911"></a>
### EK10911 withdrawn — duplicate AArch64 scope of EK10202

The AArch64 context leak is already covered by EK10202. The NULL-task continuation after bootstrap failure is separately covered by EK8904; this later entry added no independent defect and incorrectly described the SMP fatal path as a wait loop.


<a id="ek699"></a>
### EK699 — Console completion retains a writer task pointer after that task exits [conditional]

`answer_write_request()` saves the reply port's `mp_SigTask` in the shared console `filehandle` as `lastwritetask`, then replies to the write (`rom/filesys/console_handler/support.c:1095-1119`). Later Tab or Shift-Tab input calls `Completion()`. `InitCompletion()` dereferences `lastwritetask` to inspect its task type, and the directory/file requester and scan paths dereference it again as a `Process` to read `pr_CurrentDir` (`completion.c:64-100,212-220,400-414`). The stored pointer has no reference or lifetime protection. `CreateNewProc()` accepts caller-supplied `NP_Input` and `NP_Output`, and its close flags can be set false; a child sharing a console handle can therefore write to the same console state and then exit while the parent retains that handle (`rom/dos/createnewproc.c:126-130,334-352,434-462,913-925`). Exec later reclaims the terminated process's task storage (`rom/exec/remtask.c:115-181`; `service.c:63-90`). A subsequent completion before another write refreshes `lastwritetask` uses the stale pointer.

**Trigger and consequence:** create a child with the same interactive console handle as both `NP_Input` and `NP_Output`, set `NP_CloseInput` and `NP_CloseOutput` false, have the child write, then let it exit. If the surviving caller subsequently enters Tab or Shift-Tab before another write updates the saved pointer, completion reads reclaimed task storage and may use an invalid `pr_CurrentDir`, causing a fault or incorrect directory scan. **Affected configuration:** console.handler clients using shared DOS handles and the public `CreateNewProc()` API; no maintained in-tree client performing the full child-exit-then-completion sequence was established. **Confidence:** high for unowned pointer storage and the dereferences; the triggering client sequence is conditional and was not run. Retain a safe directory snapshot or clear/refresh the saved writer context when its task exits. No process, console input, completion or build was run; source-only. See the [console completion task-lifetime caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2738).


<a id="ek10912"></a>
### EK10912 — `StartNotify()` scans past a relative filename when the process has no current directory [conditional]

`GetDeviceProc()` treats a name with no volume separator as relative to `pr_CurrentDir`; when that lock is `BNULL`, it returns the boot handler with `dvp_Lock == BNULL` (`rom/dos/getdeviceproc.c:168-190`). `StartNotify()` interprets every null lock as a device or volume-root path and copies `notify->nr_Name` until it sees `:` without checking for the terminating NUL (`rom/dos/startnotify.c:74-89`). A valid relative filename contains no colon, so the scan reads beyond the caller's string and writes each byte into the fixed `name[MAXFILENAMELENGTH+1]` buffer; the read is unbounded and a sufficiently long adjacent-memory sequence can also overrun that buffer. The API accepts a file or directory name and does not document a device-prefix requirement (`startnotify.c:27-47`; `compiler/include/dos/notify.h:24-32`).

A selected in-tree caller can also supply a relative name. NetInfo reads the global DOS variables SYS/userdb and SYS/groupdb into its database filename fields without requiring a volume prefix (workbench/devs/netinfo/server.c:46-55). The passwd/group map carries those names to nim_Filename, and after opening and reading the database, entries.c assigns the same name to nr_Name and calls StartNotify() (passwdunit.c:48-59; groupunit.c:49-61; entries.c:391-440). The device starts this server process with CreateNewProcTags() but no NP_CurrentDir (netinfo.c:172-179). The selected CreateNewProc() default inherits the caller's current-directory lock only when its parent is a Process with non-NULL pr_CurrentDir; otherwise the new process has BNULL (rom/dos/createnewproc.c:131,364-379,434-435). Thus a relative global database path that opens successfully, combined with a device opener that has no current directory, reaches the reported StartNotify() path. No checked-in producer of those global path values or opener state was established, so this remains a conditional trigger.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `StartNotify()` with a relative name from a Process whose `pr_CurrentDir` is `BNULL`. The colon search reads beyond `nr_Name` and may continue writing beyond its local buffer before attempting to lock the fabricated root name; behavior depends on the following memory contents. **Affected configuration:** all DOS builds. A checked-in caller path is the Workbench-selected workbench-devs-netinfo target (workbench/devs/netinfo/mmakefile.src:13,20-22; workbench/devs/mmakefile.src:4-13,21-27; workbench/mmakefile.src:4-13), conditional on a relative SYS/userdb or SYS/groupdb value and an opener with no current directory. The optional developer/debug/test/dos/notify target also accepts arbitrary command-line names (notify.c:17-53; mmakefile.src:6-42) but does not establish the null-current-directory state. No checked-in caller was shown to satisfy both required conditions. **Confidence:** high for the missing terminator check, null-lock behavior, and NetInfo name propagation/current-directory inheritance. The relative database value and no-current-directory opener remain conditional; the extent/outcome depend on following memory contents. Handle relative paths without scanning for a colon, or bound the scan and return an error when the expected device prefix is absent. No notification or malformed path was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10913"></a>
### EK10913 withdrawn — duplicate EndNotify path of EK9883

The unlocked `Remove()` in `EndNotify()` is now included in EK9883 alongside `WaitIO()`'s removal from the same SMP-protected message-port list. Keeping a second active finding would count the shared port-lock defect twice. The 2026-11-08 Wanderer trace in EK9883 established a maintained shared-port caller; an append from a different active filesystem handler on another CPU remains a timing-dependent trigger.


<a id="ek10914"></a>
### EK10914 — RexxSupport `TYPEPKT` returns an uninitialized byte for an unsupported selector [conditional]

The optional RexxSupport command table registers `TYPEPKT` with one or two arguments, and `ArexxDispatch` validates only that count before calling the handler (`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/arexxdispatch.c:49,71-79`). With two arguments, `rxsupp_typepkt()` declares an uninitialized local `char c`; it assigns `c` only for selectors `A`, `C`, or `F`, has no `default` branch, then passes `&c` to `CreateArgstring()` (`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/typepkt.c:27-46`). `CreateArgstring()` copies the requested byte into the returned Rexx string (`workbench/libs/rexxsyslib/createargstring.c:49-68`). Thus an unsupported selector is still reported as success with an indeterminate result byte. No checked-in command documentation establishes a selector contract or defines the invalid-selector response; the defect is conditional on a two-argument call outside the three recognized selectors. The `toupper()` call also receives a plain `char`, so high-bit input can invoke undefined behavior on targets where `char` is signed.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `TYPEPKT` with two arguments and a second argument whose first byte is not `A`, `C`, or `F`. The command returns success and copies an uninitialized stack byte into its result string, producing nondeterministic output. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded `workbench-libs-rexxsupport`; aggregate package selection is not established. **Confidence:** high that this input reaches the uninitialized read through the selected dispatcher; medium that the unsupported selector should be rejected because no command manual or checked-in caller defines that case. Add an explicit invalid-selector response and convert the input to `unsigned char` before `toupper()`. No Rexx command or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10915"></a>
### EK10915 — RexxSupport `REPLY` parses its optional result code from the message-pointer argument [conditional]

`GETPKT` returns an argstring containing the raw bytes of the dequeued message pointer (`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/getpkt.c:29-32`). `REPLY` consumes argument 1 as that pointer (`reply.c:21-23`), and the selected dispatcher permits one or two arguments (`arexxdispatch.c:45,71-79`). When the optional second argument is present and the message is a Rexx message, the handler intends to parse a numeric `rm_Result1`, but calls `strtoul(ARG1(msg), ...)` instead of using `ARG2(msg)` (`reply.c:31-44`). For the pointer argstring returned by `GETPKT`, argument 1 contains binary pointer bytes rather than a decimal result code; the parse therefore normally fails the trailing-character check and returns `ERR10_018` before unlinking or replying the message. The request remains tracked on `PortNodeData.msgs` and its sender continues waiting. A one-argument `REPLY` bypasses the faulty parse, and a caller may be able to retry that form; no checked-in command caller establishes whether two-argument use is maintained.

**Trigger and consequence:** use `GETPKT` to obtain a `RexxMsg *`, then invoke the accepted two-argument `REPLY` form to set its result code. For a valid Rexx message, the handler parses the pointer token instead of the result-code argument, rejects it, and leaves the message unreplied until another cleanup/retry path handles it. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded `workbench-libs-rexxsupport`; aggregate package selection is not established. **Confidence:** high for the wrong argument and early return on the binary pointer token; medium for impact because no checked-in caller or command manual confirms two-argument `REPLY` use. Parse `ARG2(msg)` for the optional result code. No Rexx command or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10916"></a>
### EK10916 — RexxSupport `GETARG` parses its optional index from the message-pointer argument [conditional]

`GETARG` uses argument 1 as a pointer to the Rexx message, then, in its two-argument branch, passes that same `ARG1(msg)` to `strtoul()` as the requested argument index (`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/getarg.c:21-42`). The selected `GETPKT` command returns that message pointer as raw pointer bytes inside an argstring (`getpkt.c:29-32`); this is not a decimal index string, so the parse normally fails the trailing-character check and returns `ERR10_018` before retrieving any argument. The command table accepts one or two arguments (`arexxdispatch.c:36,71-79`), and the one-argument form defaults to index zero, so the optional indexed form is the affected path. The intended numeric index is the second command argument.

**Trigger and consequence:** invoke the accepted two-argument `GETARG` form with a valid message pointer returned by `GETPKT` and an argument index. The handler parses the binary pointer token instead of the supplied index and normally rejects the request, preventing retrieval of the selected Rexx argument. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded `workbench-libs-rexxsupport`; aggregate package selection is not established. **Confidence:** high for the wrong argument and pointer-byte format; medium for impact because no checked-in caller documents use of the two-argument form. Parse `ARG2(msg)` for the optional index. No Rexx command or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10917"></a>
### EK10917 — RexxSupport `NEXT` reads from the pointer token instead of the pointed-to object [conditional]

`NEXT` requires argument 1 to be an argstring exactly `sizeof(void *)` bytes long, which is the pointer-token format produced by the selected `GETPKT` command (`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/next.c:37-45`; `getpkt.c:29-32`). Its description says it obtains the pointer value stored at the pointed-to address, commonly the next list element. However, it sets `ptr` to `(char *)ARG1(msg) + offset`, using the argstring buffer address instead of decoding the pointer value first (`next.c:43`). The neighboring `OFFSET` helper decodes the same pointer-token format with `*(char **)ARG1(msg)` before adding its offset (`offset.c:31-37`). Therefore `NEXT` copies bytes from the Rexx argstring itself; at offset zero it returns the original pointer token, and at nonzero offsets it reads outside that pointer-sized token rather than reading the pointed-to object's field.

**Trigger and consequence:** call `NEXT` with a valid pointer token from `GETPKT` or another RexxSupport pointer-producing command, optionally supplying a field offset. It returns the token bytes instead of the pointer field at the pointed-to object; nonzero offsets can make `CreateArgstring()` copy bytes past the token allocation. The intended linked-list traversal result is therefore unavailable. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded `workbench-libs-rexxsupport`; aggregate package selection is not established. **Confidence:** high for the pointer-base mismatch against the function description and adjacent `OFFSET` contract; medium for caller impact because no checked-in `NEXT` caller was found. Decode the pointer token before applying the offset and copy from the target address. No Rexx command or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10918"></a>
### EK10918 — RexxSupport `ALLOCMEM` leaks an allocated block when result-string allocation fails [conditional]

`rxsupp_allocmem()` allocates the requested block, then stores its pointer in a newly allocated Rexx argstring (`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/allocmem.c:43-56`). `CreateArgstring()` returns NULL when its `AllocMem()` fails (`workbench/libs/rexxsyslib/createargstring.c:49-56`), but the caller does not check that result: it returns success with `*argstring == NULL` and never frees the already allocated block. `ArexxDispatch` forwards the success code and NULL result unchanged (`arexxdispatch.c:75-79`; `compiler/include/rexx/rexxcall.h:36-39`). The script receives no pointer value with which to call the paired `FREEMEM` command.

**Trigger and consequence:** explicitly call RexxSupport `ALLOCMEM` with a valid size and force the subsequent result-string allocation to fail. The command reports success without returning the block pointer, permanently losing the allocation to the script. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded `workbench-libs-rexxsupport`; aggregate package selection is not established. **Confidence:** high for the missing failure check and lost pointer; trigger depends on memory exhaustion at the second allocation. Free the block and return an allocation error if `CreateArgstring()` fails. No memory failure, Rexx command, or build was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek8787"></a>
### EK8787 — Task notification callbacks deadlock if they change the hook registry [conditional]

`taskres_NotifyTasks()` takes `trb_NotifySem` shared and keeps that hold while synchronously invoking every registered hook (`rom/task/task_support.c:130-145`). Both public registry mutators take the same semaphore exclusively before editing the list (`rom/task/AddTaskNotifyHook.c:49-58`; `RemTaskNotifyHook.c:41-52`). If a callback calls either mutator, `InternalObtainSemaphore()` cannot grant that exclusive acquisition while the callback's shared hold remains active; it queues the current task and waits (`rom/exec/semaphores.c:91-124`). The callback cannot return to release its shared hold, so the task blocks permanently inside registration change. The callback contract says hooks must not wait for other tasks, but does not prohibit calling AddTaskNotifyHook/RemTaskNotifyHook from a callback; this cycle waits on the callback's own lock hold.

**Trigger and consequence:** on a build selecting `task.resource`, a TNA_ADDED, TNA_FAILED, or TNA_REMOVED hook callback calls `AddTaskNotifyHook()` or `RemTaskNotifyHook()`. Notification never completes; the task creation or removal operation that is delivering the callback also remains blocked. **Affected configuration:** targets that include task.resource, conditional on an external or indirect callback mutating the registry. The selected in-tree Security callback does not do so, and no maintained in-tree mutating callback was found. **Confidence:** high for the shared-to-exclusive wait cycle and its non-returning behavior; occurrence is conditional on a client callback. Defer registry mutation until after the callback returns, or dispatch callbacks without holding the registry semaphore while preserving hook lifetime. No callback or task lifecycle event was run; source-only. See the [Task notification registry-mutation trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5041).

<a id="ek641"></a>
### EK641 — HPET enumeration omits the last comparator in every block

The ACPI HPET table's `Id` field carries the hardware timer-count field. The selected initializer extracts that field into `n`, initializes entries only for `i < n`, and adds only `n` units to the total (`arch/all-pc/hpet/hpet_init.c:32-44`). The Intel IA-PC HPET specification defines this field as the **last timer index**: three timers report 2, four report 3, and five report 4 ([specification §2.3.4](https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/public/us/en/documents/technical-specifications/software-developers-hpet-spec-1-0a.pdf)). The implementation therefore allocates and exposes one fewer comparator than the block reports, omitting index `n`.

**Trigger and consequence:** a PC system's ACPI HPET table describes a block with one or more timers. The resource's `CLOCKSOURCE_COUNT` and `AllocCSUnit()` range then omit the final comparator, making it unavailable to resource clients. The checked kernel registration only claims the first unit, so no kernel timing failure is established. **Affected configuration:** selected HPET resource on i386-PC and x86-64-PC. **Confidence:** high for the last-index specification and `n`-entry loop; impact is limited to the omitted resource unit. Count the field as an index (`n + 1`) and preserve the total across blocks. No firmware table or HPET hardware was queried; source-only. See the [HPET enumeration trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L899).

<a id="ek642"></a>
### EK642 — HPET reports a fixed 10 MHz rate instead of the hardware rate [external caller conditional]

The public `CLOCKSOURCE_FREQUENCY` tag means the frequency at which the time source operates (`compiler/include/resources/clocksource.h:17`). The HPET getter always returns `10000000` (`arch/all-pc/hpet/hpet_getcsattrsa.c:60-62`). HPET hardware reports its actual counter tick period in femtoseconds in the General Capabilities and ID register; the specification's 10 MHz value is a minimum recommended frequency, not a fixed rate ([specification §2.2 and §2.3.4](https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/public/us/en/documents/technical-specifications/software-developers-hpet-spec-1-0a.pdf)). The returned frequency can therefore disagree with the counter's actual rate.

**Trigger and consequence:** a client queries the frequency attribute and uses the returned value to convert counter ticks to elapsed time on hardware whose actual rate differs from 10 MHz. Such a client computes incorrect durations. **Affected configuration:** selected HPET resource on i386-PC and x86-64-PC; no checked-in `GetCSAttrsA()` caller was found, so no active in-tree timing consequence is claimed. **Confidence:** high for the fixed value and hardware-defined rate; the error magnitude depends on the platform and external caller. Derive the reported frequency from the hardware period. No HPET was queried; source-only. See the [HPET attribute caller census](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L900).

<a id="ek643"></a>
### EK643 — HPET advertises periodic mode for every comparator [external caller conditional]

The getter reports `CLOCKSOURCE_PERIODIC` as TRUE for every query (`arch/all-pc/hpet/hpet_getcsattrsa.c:63-65`), while HPET periodic-interrupt support is a per-timer capability: `Tn_PER_INT_CAP` may be clear, in which case that timer cannot be configured for periodic mode (Intel IA-PC HPET specification §2.3.8, [Timer N Configuration and Capabilities Register](https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/public/us/en/documents/technical-specifications/software-developers-hpet-spec-1-0a.pdf)). The public resource models these as per-unit attributes (`compiler/include/resources/clocksource.h:18`). Thus the getter can claim support for a comparator that lacks it. The adjacent one-shot TRUE value is consistent with the specification and is not part of this finding.

**Trigger and consequence:** a client queries periodic capability for a unit backed by a comparator with `Tn_PER_INT_CAP` clear, then selects periodic operation based on the returned TRUE value. That client attempts an unsupported mode. **Affected configuration:** selected HPET resource on i386-PC and x86-64-PC; no checked-in `GetCSAttrsA()` caller was found, so this is conditional on an external or future client. **Confidence:** high for the unconditional return and per-timer capability; actual client behavior is unverified. Report periodic support per comparator from its capability bit. No HPET attribute query or hardware operation was run; source-only. See the [HPET attribute caller census](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L900).

<a id="ek760"></a>
### EK760 — HPET name attributes write one byte of a string pointer [external caller conditional]

The HPET implementation handles `CLOCKSOURCE_ID` and `CLOCKSOURCE_FRIENDLY` by assigning `(IPTR)"HPET"` and `(IPTR)"High precision event timer"` through a `char *` lvalue (`arch/all-pc/hpet/hpet_getcsattrsa.c:54-59`). Each operation stores only one byte of the pointer value instead of returning the string pointer or copying the text. The public tag definitions describe these values as an ID and friendly name (`compiler/include/resources/clocksource.h:15-16`); the neighboring count, frequency, and capability tags use output storage sized as `IPTR` (`hpet_getcsattrsa.c:50-66`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a client queries either HPET name tag. Its output receives one byte derived from the string literal address, not a usable name; a pointer-valued output can therefore be left invalid, while a character-buffer output contains only one byte. **Affected configuration:** selected HPET resource in i386-PC and x86-64-PC builds. No checked-in `GetCSAttrsA()` caller was found, so impact is conditional on an external or future client. **Confidence:** high for the one-byte stores and mismatch with the declared string values; the consumer-visible result depends on the caller's output representation. Return a `CONST_STRPTR` through pointer-sized output storage, or copy into an explicitly sized buffer if that is the API contract. No HPET attribute query or build was run; source-only. See the [HPET inventory and caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L900).


<a id="ek10919"></a>
### EK10919 — RexxSupport `STATEF` leaks its file lock and skips failure checks [conditional]

`rxsupp_statef()` obtains a read lock and only releases it in no branch (`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/statef.c:46-82`). On every successful `Lock()`, it calls `Examine()` without checking its Boolean result, then allocates a 1,024-byte formatting buffer without checking for NULL before `my_sprintf()` writes through it (`:54-77`). If `Examine()` fails, the code formats fields from a `FileInfoBlock` whose contents are not established as valid. Even on the normal path, it frees the DOS object and formatting buffer but retains the DOS lock.

**Trigger and consequence:** call the explicitly selected RexxSupport `STATEF` command on a path that can be locked. Each call retains a lock on that object; repeated calls can pin directories/filesystem objects and prevent operations that require the corresponding lock to be released. A formatting-buffer allocation failure dereferences NULL, and an `Examine()` failure can produce a fabricated status from invalid metadata. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded `workbench-libs-rexxsupport`; aggregate package selection is not established. **Confidence:** high for the missing `UnLock()` and unchecked allocation; high for the unchecked `Examine()` result, with the returned metadata consequence dependent on DOS handler failure behavior. Release the lock on all post-lock paths, check `Examine()`, and handle buffer allocation failure. No Rexx command, allocation failure or filesystem operation was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10920"></a>
### EK10920 — RexxSupport `SHOWDIR` leaks locks and reports failed enumeration as success [conditional]

`rxsupp_showdir()` obtains a directory lock but does not call `UnLock()` on any path after acquisition, including the non-directory early return and normal enumeration completion (`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/showdir.c:71-138`). Its initial ExAll buffer, output string and `ExAllControl` allocations are not checked before dereference (`:95-100`); the output-buffer growth allocation is also unchecked before `strcpy()` (`:112-120`).
