DOS documents that `ExAll()` returns FALSE both when enumeration finishes and when an error occurs, distinguishing the cases with `IoErr()` (`rom/dos/exall.c:41-48`). The loop treats every FALSE as successful completion and returns the accumulated string with `RC_OK` without checking `IoErr()` (`showdir.c:101-138`).

**Trigger and consequence:** call the explicitly selected RexxSupport `SHOWDIR` command with a path that locks to a directory. Every call retains its directory lock; allocation failure can fault the command; and an `ExAll()` handler/filesystem error can produce a truncated listing reported as successful. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded `workbench-libs-rexxsupport`; aggregate package selection is not established. **Confidence:** high for lock retention, unchecked allocation results and ignored `ExAll()` error distinction. Release the lock on every path, check allocations and distinguish `IoErr() == ERROR_NO_MORE_ENTRIES` from enumeration failure. No Rexx command, allocation failure or filesystem operation was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10921"></a>
### EK10921 — RexxSupport `SHOWLIST` dereferences unchecked output-buffer allocations [conditional]

When no specific name is supplied, `rxsupp_showlist()` allocates a 1,024-byte output buffer and immediately writes `string[0]` without checking for NULL (`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/showlist.c:129-133`). Both the Exec-list and DOS-list branches grow that buffer with `AllocMem()` and immediately pass the result to `strcpy()` (`:147-166,183-204`), again without checking. The DOS list lock or Exec list read/disable section is active during these allocations. The function returns `RC_OK` only after it has built the entire string.

**Trigger and consequence:** call the explicitly selected RexxSupport `SHOWLIST` command without a name while memory allocation fails, either for the initial buffer or during growth for a large list. The command dereferences NULL and faults instead of returning an allocation error; the grow failure occurs while the relevant list protection remains held. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded `workbench-libs-rexxsupport`; aggregate package selection is not established. **Confidence:** high for each unchecked result and subsequent dereference; exact scheduling impact depends on allocator behavior while list protection is held. Check the allocation results and release list protection before error return. No Rexx command or allocation failure was induced; source-only.


<a id="ek10922"></a>
### EK10922 — RexxSupport `DELAY` converts unbounded decimal input with `atoi()` [conditional]

`rxsupp_delay()` accepts any nonempty sequence of decimal digits, then passes `atoi(arg)` directly to `Delay()` (`workbench/libs/rexxsupport/delay.c:28-44`). `atoi()` has no range reporting; the C library conversion has undefined behavior when the value is not representable as `int`. `Delay()` takes an `ULONG` timeout (`rom/dos/dos.conf:86`), so even a negative result on a target/compiler that wraps it would become a very large unsigned tick count.

**Trigger and consequence:** call the explicitly selected RexxSupport `DELAY` command with a decimal value greater than `INT_MAX`. Conversion is outside the representable `int` range, with compiler-dependent behavior; implementations that produce a negative `int` can turn it into a very long unsigned wait. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded `workbench-libs-rexxsupport`; aggregate package selection is not established. **Confidence:** high that accepted input exceeds the conversion range without a check; the resulting duration is compiler-dependent. Parse with a range-checked conversion and reject values that do not fit the `Delay()` argument. No Rexx command or wait was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10923"></a>
### EK10923 — m68kemu zero-extends negative trap sentinels before forwarding them [optional target]

The generated `AllocTrap()` and `FreeTrap()` thunks read D0 through `THUNK_D(0)` into an unsigned `ULONG` and pass that value directly to the native function (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2036-2048`). `THUNK_D` returns the 32-bit `ULONG` from `M68KEmu_GetD()` without sign extension (`m68kemu_thunks.h:27`; implementation `m68kemu_moira.cpp:306`). On the m68kemu target ABIs, `long` is 64 bits, while AROS `ULONG` is 32 bits (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:8,14-17`; `compiler/include/exec/types.h:38-39`). Therefore a guest D0 value of `0xffffffff` is widened as positive 4,294,967,295 when passed to the native `long` parameter declared by `exec.conf` and implemented by these vectors (`rom/exec/exec.conf:130-131`; `alloctrap.c:13-19`; `freetrap.c:13-19`).

`AllocTrap()` treats a negative `trapNum` as “any trap” and finds a free bit in the task's 16-bit mask (`rom/exec/alloctrap.c:50-73`). With the guest `-1` sentinel zero-extended, it instead enters the explicit-index branch and evaluates `1 << 4294967295`, which has undefined shift behavior. `FreeTrap()` explicitly treats `-1` as a no-op, but the same forwarded value fails that comparison and reaches another out-of-range shift (`rom/exec/freetrap.c:42-54`). The m68kemu makefile explicitly supports x86-64, AArch64 and RISC-V64 hosts, where this width mismatch applies; the library is a separately buildable optional target.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated m68k program calls `AllocTrap(-1)` to request any free trap, or calls `FreeTrap(-1)` as the documented-by-implementation no-op sentinel. The thunk passes a positive 64-bit value instead of the signed sentinel; `AllocTrap()` fails to take its automatic allocation path, and both vectors can execute an undefined shift instead of honoring their negative-argument behavior. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built and loaded `kernel-m68kemu-library` on x86-64, AArch64 or RISC-V64; the parent aggregate edges are commented out, so default-image inclusion is not claimed. **Confidence:** high for the unsigned D0 read, width conversion and mismatched branch/shift; no emulated caller was run. Sign-extend the guest 32-bit register according to each vector parameter's declared signed type before forwarding it. No emulated program, trap operation or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10924"></a>
### EK10924 — task.resource leaves hook lists uninitialized for existing READY/WAIT tasks [conditional]

`taskres_Init()` allocates a cleared `TaskListEntry` for each task already on the Exec task lists. In SMP builds, it calls `NEWLIST(&taskEntry->tle_HookTypes)` for entries copied from `TaskRunning` (`rom/task/task_init.c:86-108`), but omits it for `TaskSpinning` (`:111-132`), `TaskReady` (`:134-180`), and `TaskWait` (`:182-203`). In non-SMP builds, it also omits `NEWLIST()` for the current `ThisTask` entry (`:137-157`), as well as entries copied from `TaskReady` and `TaskWait` (`:159-203`). `MEMF_CLEAR` leaves the embedded list head and tail pointers zero; it does not create the sentinel links that `NEWLIST()` installs.

The selected C runtime startup opens `task.resource` and calls `InitTaskHooks()` for its current task whenever the resource is available (`compiler/startup/startup.c:90-97`). `InitTaskHooks()` and `AddTaskHook()` both pass that task entry's `tle_HookTypes` to `GetHookTypeEntry()` (`rom/task/InitTaskHooks.c:60-69`; `AddTaskHook.c:57-69`). `GetHookTypeEntry()` immediately traverses it with `ForeachNode` (`rom/task/task_support.c:65-75`); that macro reads `ln_Succ` through the list head, so a zero head dereferences NULL before a hook can be created.

**Trigger and consequence:** a task.resource snapshot entry that missed `NEWLIST()` faults when `InitTaskHooks()` or `AddTaskHook()` first traverses its hook list. The maintained C startup opens task.resource and calls `InitTaskHooks()` for the current task whenever the resource is available (`compiler/startup/startup.c:90-97`); therefore a pre-existing task without the list initialization can fail during program startup. The non-SMP `ThisTask` omission is especially direct if that task later reaches this startup path. **Affected configuration:** task.resource builds on both UP and SMP; the omitted snapshot categories differ by scheduler configuration as described above. **Confidence:** high for the missing sentinel initialization and NULL traversal; conditional on a task without an initialized hook list reaching the maintained hook API. Initialize `tle_HookTypes` for every allocated task entry before publishing it. No task startup, hook call, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10925"></a>
### EK10925 — task.resource failed-init rollback clears Exec vectors with NULL saved functions [conditional]

The resource's expunge hook `taskres_Exit()` unconditionally restores the `NewAddTask` and `RemTask` vectors from `trb_NewAddTask` and `trb_RemTask` (`rom/task/task_init.c:215-224`). Those fields are zero in the cleared base until the successful `SetFunction()` calls later in initialization (`:77-78`). Before reaching those calls, `taskres_Init()` can return FALSE when `kernel.resource` cannot be opened, the utility library cannot be opened, or the initial task-storage free-slot allocation fails (`:36-40,52-54,68-73`).

The selected generated resource initialization sets `initcalled` before invoking the `INITLIB` set; when an initlib function fails, `_set_libinit()` calls the registered `EXPUNGELIB` hooks in reverse order (`compiler/autoinit/functions.c:48-70`; the generated set contains `SETNAME(EXPUNGELIB)`, `tools/genmodule/writestart.c:987-1008`). Thus these early `taskres_Init()` failures invoke `taskres_Exit()` even though neither vector was replaced. Exec `SetFunction()` writes its `newFunction` argument into the vector without rejecting NULL (`rom/exec/setfunction.c:79-96`), so rollback replaces both core task vectors with NULL before generated `InitLib` frees the failed resource base.

**Trigger and consequence:** any of the pre-vector failure paths in task.resource initialization, including failure to allocate the first task-storage slot, enters failed-init rollback. `taskres_Exit()` then clears Exec's `NewAddTask` and `RemTask` vectors, leaving task creation/removal calls through those vectors to jump through NULL. **Affected configuration:** targets that build task.resource with `TASKRES_ENABLE`; this is the selected configuration in the inspected source. **Confidence:** high for each early return, rollback-hook execution, zero saved fields and unconditional vector write; the failure conditions were not induced. Guard restoration until each hook was installed, or track installation state before restoring. No resource initialization failure or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8786"></a>
### EK8786 — task.resource leaks each task's late-init hook-type record [conditional]

`InitTaskHooks()` obtains the current task's `TaskListEntry` and calls `GetHookTypeEntry(..., TRUE)` for the requested type (`rom/task/InitTaskHooks.c:60-70`). When the type is new, `GetHookTypeEntry()` allocates a separate `TaskListHookEntry` and links it into `tle_HookTypes` (`rom/task/task_support.c:81-110`). The selected C runtime opens `task.resource` and calls `InitTaskHooks()` for its late-init type whenever the resource is available (`compiler/startup/startup.c:94-96`), so the nested allocation occurs for ordinary C-started tasks even when no client adds a hook.

On task removal, the task.resource `RemTask` wrapper either removes and frees the `TaskListEntry` directly (`rom/task/task_execfuncs.c:121-130,141-151`) or marks it for later cleanup when task-list locks remain. `task_CleanList()` later also removes and frees only the parent `TaskListEntry` (`rom/task/task_support.c:13-38`). Neither path walks or frees `tle_HookTypes`; the declared `TaskHooksDispose()` and `TaskHookTypeDispose()` functions are empty stubs and have no callers (`task_support.c:116-124`). The nested hook-type record therefore becomes unreachable when the outer entry is freed.

**Trigger and consequence:** a task reaches C startup while `task.resource` is available, then exits through the task.resource `RemTask` wrapper. Each such task leaks its allocated late-init `TaskListHookEntry`, so repeated task launches consume unreclaimed memory. **Affected configuration:** builds with task.resource and `TASKRES_ENABLE`, which is defined in `rom/task/task_intern.h`; this is the selected configuration. **Confidence:** high for allocation, retained ownership through the task entry, and both cleanup paths omitting nested disposal; no task lifecycle was run. Dispose hook-type entries before freeing the parent task entry. Source-only; see the Exec/Kernel coverage ledger.

<a id="ek664"></a>
### EK664 — DynModule glue frees a public port name before removing its port [conditional]

`__dynglue_DisposeIFPort()` drains queued messages, frees `dmmport->mp_Node.ln_Name`, and only then calls `DeletePort()` (`compiler/dynmodule/dynmodule_glue.c:63-72`). The port was published with that name by `CreatePort()` (`:43-49`; `compiler/alib/createport.c:49-58`), which stores the caller's pointer in `ln_Name` and calls `AddPort()` without copying it. `DeletePort()` removes a named port only after checking the still-nonnull `ln_Name` pointer (`compiler/alib/deleteport.c:48-54`); `RemPort()` serializes the actual list removal with `PortListSpinLock` on ExecSMP (`rom/exec/remport.c:54-70`). In the interval after `FreeVec()` and before that removal, `FindPort()` can still encounter the listed node. Its SMP read lock does not help because the freeing path has not yet taken the corresponding write lock; `FindName()` checks `ln_Name` and calls `strcmp()` through the freed pointer (`rom/exec/findport.c:52-62`; `rom/exec/findname.c:72-78`). On a single-CPU build, a lookup can likewise run if the disposer is preempted between the free and `DeletePort()`.

The port is disposed on both the `DYNMODULE_Setup()` failure path and after the normal message loop (`dynmodule_glue.c:145-149,185-187`), so both teardown routes share this ordering. The issue is confined to the optional DynModule glue target; its aggregate dependency is commented out (`compiler/dynmodule/mmakefile.src:3-5,12-13`).

**Trigger and consequence:** while a DynModule glue process is disposing its named interface port, another task calls `FindPort()` before `DeletePort()` removes the node. The lookup may compare against freed name storage, causing an invalid read, fault, or incorrect lookup result. **Affected configuration:** explicit use of `linklibs-dynmodglue`; the race is possible with concurrent callers on ExecSMP and with a task preemption in the free-to-remove interval on a single-CPU build. **Confidence:** high for the free-before-unlink ordering and unlocked lifetime gap; occurrence requires a concurrent lookup in that interval. Remove the public port under the port-list synchronization before freeing its name. No port teardown, lookup, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek833"></a>
### EK833 — AROS `sched_yield()` does not request a task handoff [conditional]

The AROS build selects the non-Amiga/MorphOS branch in `sched_yield()` (`compiler/pthread/sched.c:46-68`): it gets the current task with `FindTask(NULL)`, calls `SetTaskPri(task, -10)`, and immediately restores the returned old priority. The AROS specs define `__AROS__` but not `__AMIGA__` (`config/specs.in:25-29`), and the pthread link-library compile rule adds `-D__AROS__` (`config/make.tmpl:2640-2643`). In `SetTaskPri()`, the current task's priority is assigned before the reschedule comparison (`rom/exec/settaskpri.c:98-129`); because the target is the current task, the new priority is then compared against the same task's already-updated priority, so the explicit `Reschedule()` condition is false. ExecSMP's corresponding `doResched` comparison has the same self-comparison (`:114-123,139-143`). `Enable()` only hands off if an independent pending switch or soft interrupt exists (`rom/exec/enable.c:90-125`), so neither priority update itself yields the processor.

The selected pthread implementation calls `sched_yield()` after each failed `pthread_spin_lock()` test-and-set on this AROS path (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:758-779`). A contending caller therefore continues polling its lock without the voluntary processor handoff promised by `sched_yield()`; a runnable lock owner or other worker can be delayed until ordinary scheduling preempts the spinner. The PC scheduler can select equal-or-lower-priority ready tasks once the current quantum expires (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:107-134`), so this is not an unconditional deadlock or permanent-starvation claim.

**Trigger and consequence:** an AROS pthread client calls `sched_yield()`, including from the in-tree spin-lock retry path, while another runnable task should receive processor time. The function returns success without requesting a context switch; under contention the caller may continue consuming CPU and delay the other task until normal scheduling occurs. **Affected configuration:** clients explicitly linking `linklibs-pthread` on AROS; MorphOS and Amiga builds use the separate explicit-Forbid/reschedule branch and are excluded. **Confidence:** high that neither AROS priority change requests a switch; caller impact is conditional on contention and scheduler timing. Use an Exec primitive that explicitly requests a scheduling handoff rather than self-priority changes. No task, lock, or scheduler event was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10926"></a>
### EK10926 — Multiboot2 extended memory-map entries are converted with the wrong stride [conditional]

`mmap_convert()` walks input entries by the loader-provided `tag->entry_size`, but advances its output cursor by the fixed `sizeof(struct mb_mmap)` (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/multiboot2.c:80-98`). It writes a legacy size field at each output cursor and returns a contiguous legacy map length, but does not move each source entry's address, length, and type fields into that compacted output layout. Both the current `struct mb2_mmap` and legacy `struct mb_mmap` are 24 bytes (`compiler/include/aros/multiboot2.h:180-196`; `compiler/include/aros/multiboot.h:132-145`). When `entry_size` exceeds 24, the first entry remains readable through the shifted view, but the second legacy entry begins 24 bytes after the first while the second Multiboot2 entry begins `entry_size` bytes after it. The kernel consumes the result as a legacy map and advances using each entry's `size + 4` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_mmap.c:129-185`), so later records are interpreted from extension bytes and mixed fields rather than their actual entries.

**Trigger and consequence:** the PC bootstrap receives a Multiboot2 memory-map tag with more than one entry and an `entry_size` larger than the local 24-byte base structure. The converted list then supplies incorrect address, length, or type values for later records to memory initialization, which can cause usable memory to be omitted or wrongly classified. **Affected configuration:** i386-PC and x86-64-PC boot paths selecting `arch/all-pc/bootstrap/multiboot2.c` for Multiboot2/GRUB2 input. No in-tree producer with an extended entry was found; the source comment explicitly anticipates extended Multiboot2 entries, so this is a conditional forward-compatibility defect. **Confidence:** high for the incompatible input/output strides and kernel consumer; occurrence depends on the loader supplying an entry size greater than 24. Compact each entry into the legacy output layout or preserve and correctly translate the source stride. No boot record, memory map, or build was used; source-only.

**Coverage evidence:** [Multiboot2 extended memory-map stride trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#multiboot2-extended-memory-map-stride-ek10926).


<a id="ek10927"></a>
### EK10927 — Multiboot2 module-alignment header type has framebuffer fields [conditional]

`struct mb2_header_tag_module_align` in `compiler/include/aros/multiboot2.h:104-110` repeats the three `width`, `height`, and `depth` fields from the framebuffer header tag. The Multiboot2 specification defines the module-alignment header tag (type 6) as only the common 8-byte tag header; its presence requests page-aligned modules and has no payload ([GNU Multiboot2 specification, §3.1.11](https://www.gnu.org/software/grub/manual/multiboot2/multiboot.pdf)). The declared AROS structure is therefore 20 bytes rather than 8. A client that uses this public type or its `sizeof` to construct the tag emits an invalid tag size and extra fields; a bootloader may reject or misinterpret the image header.

**Trigger and consequence:** an external boot-image producer uses this AROS structure to declare a module-alignment tag. The resulting image header does not match the specified tag layout and may not be accepted as intended. **Affected configuration:** external Multiboot2 image producers that include this public AROS header; no in-tree source references this type, and the selected PC bootstrap does not construct this tag. **Confidence:** high for the declaration/specification mismatch, low for in-tree impact because no maintained caller was found. Replace the fields with the common header only. No image was assembled, bootloader was run, or build was performed; source-only.

**Coverage evidence:** [Multiboot2 public-header and caller census](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#multiboot2-module-alignment-header-ek10927).


<a id="ek10928"></a>
### EK10928 — ARM unwind lookup treats linker boundary symbols as data [conditional]

`__gnu_Unwind_Find_exidx()` declares `__exidx_start` and `__exidx_end` as unsigned objects, subtracts their contents, divides by eight, and returns the contents of `__exidx_start` (`compiler/startup/arm-exidx-unwind.c:18-24`). These names are linker-defined `.ARM.exidx` boundary addresses. GCC's ARM unwinder contract uses the address of the start symbol as the table pointer and the difference between the boundary addresses as the number of entries; each entry is two words ([GCC ARM unwinder](https://github.com/gcc-mirror/gcc/blob/master/libgcc/unwind-arm-common.inc), [Arm EHABI32](https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/main/ehabi32/ehabi32.rst)). Thus this implementation returns table data as though it were an address and derives the count from data words, so an exception lookup can search an invalid table range.

The ARM startup makefile builds `arm-exidx-unwind.o` as a separate object for ARM targets (`compiler/startup/mmakefile.src:22-25,35-50`). Although generic `config/specs.in` does not show it, all nine checked-in GNU GCC AROS target patches inject the object into ARM links: GCC 6.5, 8.3, 11.2, and 12.2 use the start-file sequence, while 9.5, 10.5, 13.5, 15.2, and 16.2 use `ENDFILE_SPEC` (`tools/crosstools/gnu/gcc-*-aros.diff`, ARM target spec hunks). Configure also assigns it to `aros_target_nostartup_objects` for ARM (`configure.in:2939`). The lookup function itself is a strong definition in `arm-exidx-unwind.c` (it has no `weak` attribute); the weak attributes in that file apply only to separate `__cxa_*` fallback functions. Therefore their override behavior does not qualify the erroneous table lookup when this function is selected.

**Trigger and consequence:** a normal ARM link using the checked-in AROS GCC target configuration queries an exception index through this implementation. It may return an invalid table pointer/count, causing unwinding to fail or read the wrong index records. **Affected configuration:** GNU ARM toolchains patched by the checked-in AROS specs. The GCC 6.5, 8.3, 11.2, and 12.2 patches add `arm-exidx-unwind.o` to the start-file sequence; patches for GCC 9.5, 10.5, 13.5, 15.2, and 16.2 add it in `ENDFILE_SPEC` (`tools/crosstools/gnu/gcc-*-aros.diff`, ARM target spec hunks). The object is built for ARM targets by `compiler/startup/mmakefile.src:22-25,35-50`, and configure sets it as a no-startup object on ARM (`configure.in:2939`). **Confidence:** high for object selection and the symbol-contract mismatch in the checked-in GNU toolchain paths. Non-GNU/custom toolchains remain unverified. Use linker-symbol addresses for both the table pointer and count. No link, exception, boot, or build was run; source-only.

**Coverage evidence:** [ARM `.ARM.exidx` unwinder contract and link-selection trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#arm-exidx-unwind-linker-symbols-ek10928).


<a id="ek10929"></a>
### EK10929 — Static C++ `operator new` returns null on allocation failure [conditional]

The static C++ shim implements scalar and array `operator new` by directly returning `AllocVec(size, MEMF_PUBLIC | MEMF_CLEAR)` (`compiler/startup/static-cxx-ops.cpp:9-23`). Exec explicitly documents `AllocVec()` as returning NULL when allocation fails and guarantees NULL for a zero-byte request (`rom/exec/allocvec.c:24-27,48-58`). These are the ordinary throwing allocation functions, not `std::nothrow` overloads. The C++ allocation-function contract requires the ordinary replacement functions to return non-null storage or throw `std::bad_alloc` ([C++ draft, replacement `operator new`](https://eel.is/c++draft/new.delete.single)). Thus `new T[0]` reaches `AllocVec(0)` and produces a null result where a successful zero-length allocation must still yield a non-null pointer; memory exhaustion likewise propagates a null result instead of the documented allocation exception.

The shim is selected only when the GNU AROS target specs see the static C++ option: the checked-in GCC patches add `static-cxx-ops.o` with the other static C++ support objects (`tools/crosstools/gnu/gcc-*-aros.diff`, ARM and common target start-file hunks). In-tree targets use `-static-libstdc++`, including GLU, HEIC, JPEG XL, and the C++ test program (`workbench/libs/glu/mmakefile.src:149`; `workbench/classes/datatypes/heic/mmakefile.src:151`; `workbench/classes/datatypes/jpegxl/mmakefile.src:283`; `developer/debug/test/cplusplus/mmakefile.src:14`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a client linked with this static C++ shim performs a zero-length array allocation or its allocation request fails. The expression can yield NULL without `std::bad_alloc`, so a caller relying on standard throwing-new behavior may continue with an invalid pointer or miss its exception handling path. **Affected configuration:** GNU AROS C++ links that select the static C++ support objects; dynamic C++ runtime links are excluded. **Confidence:** high for the direct null-return path and option-controlled selection. Implement the ordinary forms so allocation failure follows the configured C++ exception policy and zero-size requests produce a valid allocation result. No allocation, C++ program, link, or build was run; source-only.

**Coverage evidence:** [static C++ allocation shim and option/caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#static-cxx-allocation-shim-ek10929).


<a id="ek10930"></a>
### EK10930 — CLI argument parsing leaks its copied buffer when argv allocation fails [conditional]

For a nonempty command line, `__initcommandline()` allocates and fills `__args`, counts arguments, then allocates `__argv` (`compiler/autoinit/commandline.c:39-57`). If the second allocation fails, it returns immediately without freeing `__args`; the only cleanup for that buffer is later in the normal continuation path (`:84-97`). The selected startup has already initialized `__startup_error` to `RETURN_FAIL` before entering the program-entry chain (`compiler/startup/startup.c:109-113`), and the failed entry does not advance to `main`, so the process returns startup failure. Exec's `AllocMem()` returns an ordinary allocation (`rom/exec/allocmem.c:45-53`); it is not automatically attached to the process for release at task exit, and `FreeMem()` must be called explicitly.

**Trigger and consequence:** a CLI-started program has a nonzero `__argsize`, the copied argument-buffer allocation succeeds, and the subsequent pointer-array allocation fails. Startup aborts before the program runs but leaves the copied argument buffer allocated. **Affected configuration:** C startup using the autoinit command-line entry (`compiler/autoinit/mmakefile.src:15-24`; startup imports it unless `__nocommandline` is supplied, `compiler/startup/startup.c:42-46`). Workbench launches and the zero-argument branch do not take this two-allocation path. **Confidence:** high for the allocation/early-return/cleanup ordering and selected startup path; occurrence requires the second allocation to fail after the first succeeds. Free `__args` before returning on `__argv` allocation failure. No allocation failure or process was run; source-only.

**Coverage evidence:** [startup entry ordering and command-line allocation-failure trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#startup-entry-order-and-command-line-allocation-failure-ek10930).


<a id="ek10931"></a>
### EK10931 — `NewCreateTaskA()` discards `TASKTAG_FLAGS` [conditional]

`NewCreateTaskA()` documents `TASKTAG_FLAGS` as the initial value for `tc_Flags` and saves the supplied value, then assigns it to the newly allocated task before calling `NewAddTask()` (`rom/exec/newcreatetaska.c:71,154-156,238-256`). `NewAddTask()` unconditionally resets `task->tc_Flags` to zero before initialization and publication (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:236-240`); it later adds only the flags needed for stack checking, switching, and launch (`:263-266,312-317`). Thus the caller-supplied initial flags never reach the created task. The implementation itself labels this tag as ignored in the `NewCreateTaskA()` BUGS documentation (`newcreatetaska.c:83-88`). A repository-wide search found no maintained `TASKTAG_FLAGS` call site, so impact through checked-in callers is not established.

**Trigger and consequence:** an external `NewCreateTaskA()` caller supplies a nonzero `TASKTAG_FLAGS` value and relies on the documented initial `tc_Flags`; the task starts without those bits. **Affected configuration:** all targets using the shared `NewCreateTaskA()`/`NewAddTask()` implementation; caller-visible impact requires a client that uses the tag. **Confidence:** high that the value is discarded; no maintained in-tree caller or concrete user-visible failure was established. Preserve the requested flags while adding the internal task-state bits. No task was created and no build was run; source-only.

**Coverage evidence:** [NewCreateTaskA flag-tag implementation review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#newcreatetaska-flags-ek10931).


<a id="ek10934"></a>
### EK10934 — Workbench skips launch cleanup when child creation fails [conditional]

Workbench duplicates the launch directory lock for `NP_HomeDir` and passes that lock in the `CreateNewProc()` tags (`workbench/libs/workbench/handler.c:312-332`). On success, `CreateNewProc()` stores the explicit tag value in `process->pr_HomeDir`, and DOS process-exit cleanup later unlocks it (`rom/dos/createnewproc.c:459,967-968`). On failure after the process structure has been allocated, DOS frees the per-process seg-array wrapper but does not unload an explicitly supplied `NP_Seglist` (`:496-514,594-598`). Its error cleanup only unlocks the local `homedir` variable used for the inherited-parent default; it does not release an explicitly supplied `defaults[21].ti_Data` (`:381-395,594-618`). The Workbench caller handles a NULL result by jumping to `done`, which restores the current directory but skips the `error` cleanup that unloads the segment, destroys the `WBStartup` message and its argument locks/names, and releases the `home` duplicate (`handler.c:334-356`). The enclosing handler then frees only the `WBCommandMessage` (`handler.c:95-116`); no startup reply is queued for this failed launch. `UnLoadSeg()` is the operation that releases the loaded segment (`rom/dos/unloadseg.c:90-112`).

**Trigger and consequence:** Workbench has successfully duplicated the launch directory lock, then `CreateNewProc()` fails during later process setup, such as stack/memlist allocation or task insertion. The failed launch can leave the loaded segment, startup message and argument locks/names, and duplicated home lock outstanding; repeated failures accumulate these resources and can keep the directory or volume in use. **Affected configuration:** Workbench-launched programs where process setup fails after `DupLock()` succeeds. The earlier `LoadSeg()` failure occurs before the duplicate is made and is excluded. **Confidence:** high for the ownership handoff on success and both missing release paths on failure; occurrence requires the conditional post-duplication process-creation failure. Route the NULL-result path through the existing launch cleanup, while preserving ownership rules for the explicit `NP_HomeDir` tag. No process creation failure or directory operation was induced; source-only.

**Coverage evidence:** [CreateNewProc explicit home-directory failure caller pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#workbench-np-homedir-failure-ek10934).

<a id="ek10935"></a>
### EK10935 — Timer device link library opens the device as a library [conditional]

`rom/timer/timer.conf` enables `options autoinit` for `timer.device` (`:1-8`). Genmodule turns this into a `timer_autoinit.c` object in the generated link library (`tools/genmodule/writeautoinit.c:15-21,36-49`; `writemakefile.c:79-85`), and `build_module` produces the ABI/link-library target (`config/make.tmpl:2809-2829`). The generated source uses `AROS_LIBSET("timer.device", ..., TimerBase)` (`writeautoinit.c:38-45`; `compiler/include/aros/symbolsets.h:118-128`), whose startup handler opens the named entry with `OpenLibrary()` (`compiler/autoinit/libraries.c:23-55`). Exec's `OpenLibrary()` searches only `SysBase->LibList` (`rom/exec/openlibrary.c:73-79`), while `InitResident()` publishes `NT_DEVICE` modules through `AddDevice()` to the separate DeviceList (`rom/exec/initresident.c:143-150`; `rom/exec/adddevice.c:52-70`). The matching `OpenDevice()` path searches that DeviceList (`rom/exec/opendevice.c:92-100`). Thus the generated timer link-library auto-open cannot obtain the device base through its configured opener.

**Trigger and consequence:** a client links the generated `linklibs-timer` archive and relies on its `TimerBase` auto-init. At startup, the required `OpenLibrary("timer.device", ...)` returns NULL because the resident is an `NT_DEVICE`, so the LIBS initialization set reports failure and prevents later startup/init callbacks from running. This does not affect normal clients that acquire TimerBase through `OpenDevice()` and do not link the timer auto-init object. **Affected configuration:** explicit use of the generated Timer link library; no checked-in target currently links `linklibs-timer`, and no default-image failure is claimed. **Confidence:** high for the generated `AROS_LIBSET`/`OpenLibrary` path and Exec's distinct library/device lists; the client-facing failure is conditional on using this link library. Remove the `autoinit` option for the device, or generate a device-open/close set with request ownership rather than an `AROS_LIBSET`. No link, startup or device operation was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10936"></a>
### EK10936 — MinGW accepts a zero VBlank frequency and divides by zero [conditional]

The MinGW platform init reads `KRN_CmdLine` and, when it finds `vblank=`, assigns `atoi(&s[7])` directly to `SysBase->VBlankFrequency` without checking conversion or range (`arch/all-mingw32/kernel/kernel_startup.c:198-208`; `compiler/include/aros/kernel.h:54`). It passes that value to the host module's `core_init()` (`:214`; `arch/all-mingw32/kernel/host_intr.c:252,353-356`). `core_init()` starts the clock through `StartClock()`, which computes `1000 / TimerHz` before calling `SetWaitableTimer()` (`host_intr.c:236-245`). A literal zero or a nonnumeric value immediately after `vblank=` makes `atoi()` return zero, so `StartClock()` performs integer division by zero during kernel platform initialization.

**Trigger and consequence:** a MinGW-hosted boot command line contains `vblank=0` or `vblank=` followed by a nonnumeric character. Platform initialization reaches `StartClock()` with zero and faults before the hosted kernel clock is initialized. A value above 1,000 also truncates `1000 / TimerHz` to a zero-millisecond period; Windows documents that `SetWaitableTimer()` then signals only once, so recurring VBlank delivery stops. **Affected configuration:** `arch/all-mingw32`; the default 50 Hz path is unaffected. **Confidence:** high for both outcomes: the integer conversion/division is direct, and the one-shot meaning of a zero period is specified by [Microsoft's SetWaitableTimer documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/synchapi/nf-synchapi-setwaitabletimer). Validate the parsed frequency and reject values that cannot produce a valid recurring host timer period before calling `core_init()`. No boot or timer was run; source-only.

**Coverage evidence:** [MinGW kernel startup full-file review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#mingw-kernel-startup-ek10936).


<a id="ek10938"></a>
### EK10938 — `CreatePool()` can construct a bogus plain memory header after size wrap [conditional]

`CreatePool()` adds `MEMHEADER_TOTAL`, allocator-context size, worst alignment, and optionally MungWall overhead to its `IPTR puddleSize`, then rounds the result without overflow checks (`rom/exec/createpool.c:100-107`). A caller can choose a value that makes these additions wrap to zero. If the compact handle allocation at `:129` comes from a managed header, the managed branch frees it and calls `AllocMemHeader(0)` (`:132-142`). `nommu_AllocMem()` skips only headers whose free-byte count is less than the requested size, so zero reaches matching headers with nonnegative free space (`rom/exec/memory_nommu.c:33-43`). A managed TLSF callback rejects zero (`rom/kernel/tlsf.c:489-498`), but the scan can continue to a matching plain header. There `stdAlloc()` rounds zero to zero, accepts an existing positive free chunk, and takes the non-consuming split path (`rom/exec/memory.c:566,581-586,638-669`). The returned chunk remains in the parent free list. `AllocMemHeader()` finds that plain parent and subtracts `MEMHEADER_TOTAL` from the zero size before writing `mh_Free` and the first chunk's `mc_Bytes` (`rom/exec/memory.c:905-907,958-976`), creating a wrapped extent over memory it did not reserve. The pool is then initialized using this fabricated header (`createpool.c:159-190`). On the normal consistency-checked path, the plain `Allocate()` call validates the impossible bounds, `stdAlloc()` returns NULL, and `CreatePool()` immediately uses `pool` in `NEWLIST()` without checking the allocation result (`rom/exec/memory.c:447-481,575-578`; `rom/exec/allocate.c:105-143`; `createpool.c:166-176`). Thus the same conditional setup can fail as a direct NULL dereference before returning a pool. If consistency checks are disabled, allocation instead proceeds against the corrupted header, with the parent free-list metadata already overwritten.

**Trigger and consequence:** `CreatePool()` receives a `puddleSize` whose unchecked overhead arithmetic wraps to zero; the compact handle must be allocated from a matching managed header, and a matching plain header with a nonempty free chunk must also be available to the subsequent zero-size `AllocMemHeader()` search. The parent free chunk is rewritten as an enormous free extent while remaining on the parent's free list, and the returned pool may allocate through a header whose bounds do not describe owned memory. This corrupts allocator state and can lead to out-of-region access. Maintained configurable routes exist in both MUI List and NList. Standard `List` stores the public `MUIA_List_PoolPuddleSize` `ULONG` tag in a signed `LONG`, then forwards it to `CreatePool()` (`workbench/libs/muimaster/classes/list.c:91,1197-1199,1289-1294`; public declaration: `workbench/classes/zune/nlist/include/libraries/mui.h:2163`). A tag value whose low 32 bits encode the negative overhead sum is converted back to `IPTR` as that negative value, so the unchecked addition can wrap to zero on both 32-bit and 64-bit targets. NList has a separate non-AmigaOS4 path that reads `MUIA_NList_PoolPuddleSize`/`MUIA_List_PoolPuddleSize` into `ULONG` and passes it directly to `CreatePool()` (`workbench/classes/zune/nlist/nlist_mcc/NList_mcc.c:621-633`; public NList attribute is documented as `[I..], ULONG` in `include/mui/NList_mcc.h:128` and `docs/MCC_NList.doc:1492-1498`); that route can wrap on 32-bit builds. Their defaults are 2,008 and 2,048 bytes respectively; no checked-in caller supplies a near-limit value. **Affected configuration:** MUI List with a caller-supplied boundary puddle tag on 32-bit or 64-bit builds, or NList on 32-bit non-AmigaOS4 builds, plus the required managed/plain header selection. **Confidence:** high for unchecked wrap, zero-size plain allocation, and fabricated header construction; conditional for callers choosing the boundary value and reaching the mixed-header order. Reject sizes whose overhead and alignment cannot be represented, and make `AllocMemHeader()` reject sizes smaller than the required header. No allocation, build or runtime behavior was exercised; source-only.

**Coverage evidence:** [CreatePool configured-size arithmetic reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#createpool-configured-size-arithmetic-reconciliation-ek10938).

<a id="ek10933"></a>
## EK10933 — `NewCliProc` releases the current-directory lock that the child still stores [conditional]

`SystemTagList()` reads an explicit `NP_CurrentDir` value from its cloned tag list, forwards that same BPTR in the `CreateNewProc()` tags, and later places the same lock in the CLI startup packet (`rom/dos/systemtaglist.c:393-405,448-461`). Network Preferences supplies its `Lock(ENV:SMB)` result this way while asynchronously starting `C:Mount` (`workbench/prefs/network/prefsdata.c:931-953`; `SYS_Asynch=TRUE` selects `CLI_ASYSTEM`, which sets `NP_Cli`). `CreateNewProc()` stores the explicit lock in `process->pr_CurrentDir` and sets `PRF_FREECURRDIR` (`rom/dos/createnewproc.c:434,459-468`). During CLI startup, `internal_CliInitAny()` passes the same lock as `newdir` to `CurrentDir()`. `CurrentDir()` simply replaces and returns the existing pointer; `NewCliProc` then unlocks the returned old lock under `PRF_FREECURRDIR` (`rom/dos/newcliproc.c:142-165`; `rom/dos/currentdir.c:47-59`). The child's `pr_CurrentDir` still contains that released BPTR, and ordinary child-exit cleanup later unlocks it again (`rom/dos/createnewproc.c:960-965`).

**Trigger and consequence:** launch an asynchronous CLI with an explicit non-null `NP_CurrentDir`, as the checked Network Preferences Mount caller does. CLI initialization releases the lock while leaving the child pointed at it, so relative-path DOS calls made by the child can use an invalid lock; process exit then attempts a second unlock of the same BPTR. **Affected configuration:** DOS CLI startup through `SystemTagList()` with explicit `NP_CurrentDir`; the in-tree Network Preferences caller is selected when configured server automounts are launched. **Confidence:** high for pointer identity, `CurrentDir()` behavior, the first unlock and retained child field; consequences require subsequent path use or cleanup. Preserve a separate lock reference for the child or transfer ownership without unlocking the installed directory. No process, lock or filesystem operation was run; source-only.

<a id="ek10939"></a>
## EK10939 — Network Preferences leaks the server-directory lock when no servers are configured [conditional]

`MountServers()` obtains a shared lock on `ENV:SMB`, but only calls `SystemTagList()` when `GetServerCount() > 0`; the function returns TRUE without `UnLock(dir)` in the zero-server case (`workbench/prefs/network/prefsdata.c:931-953`). `UseNetworkPrefs()` calls `MountServers()` after writing the active preferences (`:1017-1036`), and both the preferences editor Use method and the command's use/save flow reach `UseNetworkPrefs()` (`workbench/prefs/network/netpeditor.c:2134-2150`; `prefsdata.c:1014-1017,1658-1672`). Repeated apply/use operations with no configured server entries therefore retain one directory lock per call. The `GetServerCount() > 0` branch is separate: it passes the lock to the asynchronous CLI as `NP_CurrentDir` and is covered by EK10933.

**Trigger and consequence:** `Lock(ENV:SMB, SHARED_LOCK)` succeeds while there are no configured servers, and Network Preferences applies/uses the settings. The function drops its only local reference without unlocking it, leaving a filesystem lock retained; repeated uses accumulate locks. **Affected configuration:** Workbench Network Preferences when its server list is empty and the environment directory exists. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked zero-server return and missing unlock; requires successful lock acquisition and that branch. Unlock `dir` before returning when no child takes ownership. No preferences operation, directory lock or build was run; source-only.

### EK8840 — withdrawn duplicate of DOS finding D01

This identifier duplicated the `Close()` flush-result overwrite already documented as [D01](AROS-dos.md#d01). D01 is the canonical finding; handler-specific evidence from the Exec/Kernel revisit has been consolidated there. This anchor remains only for older coverage references.


<a id="ek10610"></a>
### EK10610 — withdrawn: unsupported cross-task RexxSupport query scenario

This candidate was withdrawn after reconciling the intended `ArexxDispatch` use: it is the Rexx library query function called inline by `rexxmast`, and the checked-in source does not establish distinct tasks for `OPENPORT` and `WAITPKT` during normal Rexx command execution. The signal-owner mismatch is source-real only for direct or concurrent external query-vector calls, which this review has not established as supported `WAITPKT` use. No active bug is claimed; the historical trace remains in the coverage ledger.

<a id="ek646"></a>
### EK646 — Efika vector 18 cache maintenance omits the copied handler's final instruction-cache line [conditional]

`init_interrupt()` copies 256 bytes of `__vector_dmissw` into the vector-18 slot, then calls `flush_cache(target, target + 0xff)` (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/intr.c:245-282`). `flush_cache()` treats `end` as exclusive and rounds it down to a 32-byte boundary before iterating in 32-byte steps (`:287-304`). For a 256-byte-aligned vector target, `target + 0xff` rounds down to `target + 0xe0`; the maintenance loops cover offsets 0 through 0xc0 and omit the line at offsets 0xe0–0xff. The copied vector's selected inline assembly is 60 four-byte instructions, with its final branch at offset 0xec (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/mmu.c:639-713`). Thus executable bytes occupy the omitted line. The function writes the vector bytes and then performs `dcbst`/`icbi` plus synchronization, but the last line receives neither cache operation.

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicit CHRP/Efika kernel path initializes vector 18 while the final instruction-cache line contains stale code. A subsequent data-store translation miss can execute the stale instruction(s) in that line instead of the copied handler tail, causing incorrect exception handling or failure to return through the intended path. If the line is not cached or already matches memory, this omission may have no visible effect. **Affected configuration:** Efika MPC5200B kernel builds using `arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/intr.c`'s vector-18 installation. **Confidence:** high for the 256-byte copy, exclusive-end rounding, omitted 32-byte line and executable instructions in that line; visible behavior depends on prior cache contents and processor cache state. Pass the true exclusive end (`target + 256`) or include the final line in the cache maintenance range. No boot, exception, cache operation, or build was run; source-only; see the [Efika interrupt/vector coverage](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1709).

<a id="m68kemu-childorphan-return-cross-reference-gd15091"></a>
## m68kemu `ChildOrphan()` return-value cross-reference (GD15091)

The generated Exec thunk calls `ChildOrphan()` but returns zero unconditionally (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2351-2355`). The public vector is `ULONG` (`rom/exec/exec.conf:200`), and its documented result is zero on success or a `CHILD_*` error (`rom/exec/childorphan.c:36-37,64-117`). The m68k emulator dispatches the thunk's `IPTR` result into guest D0 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:256-275`), so an emulated caller cannot observe an error. This is one instance of the shared generator misclassification documented as [GD15091](AROS-graphics-desktop.md#gd15091), which covers 20 non-void vectors across Graphics, Exec, Intuition, Layers, and Commodities; it is not a separate root cause. The m68kemu library's exact shipped-image inclusion and external guest callers remain unverified. Source-only; no task or emulator call was run.


<a id="ek10940"></a>
### EK10940 — Slow-stack varargs conversion mishandles `TAG_SKIP` [conditional]

On targets that define `AROS_SLOWSTACKTAGS`, `GetTagsFromStack()` first scans stack varargs to size a temporary `TagItem` array, then copies them (`compiler/alib/alib_util.c:192-203,235-246`). In both passes, its `TAG_SKIP` branch consumes the requested tag/value pairs without adding those entries to the output, while preserving the original `TAG_SKIP` and its count. Standard `NextTagItem()` implements `TAG_SKIP` by advancing over the next count of entries in the resulting array (`compiler/arossupport/libnexttagitem.c:28-30`). The converted array therefore skips the next live tag(s) a second time; when a positive `TAG_SKIP` consumes the final input pair, the output contains only `TAG_SKIP` followed by `TAG_DONE`, and iteration advances past the allocated terminator.

**Trigger and consequence:** a caller invokes a stack-tag varargs API with a positive `TAG_SKIP` followed by the number of tag/value pairs it should suppress. The A-form API's effective tag list then omits subsequent live tags and can make standard tag traversal pass the temporary array's terminator. **Affected configuration:** targets whose CPU ABI selects upward-growing stacks and `AROS_SLOWSTACKTAGS`, including maintained ARM, AArch64, PowerPC, RISC-V and x86-64 variants; the ordinary downward-stack conversion path does not use this helper. No checked-in varargs caller using `TAG_SKIP` was identified, so the finding is conditional on public clients exercising this supported tag-control form. **Confidence:** high for the converter's emitted layout and standard iterator behavior; external-call reachability is unverified. Preserve the skipped entries in the converted list, or normalize the control tag while removing its skipped entries. No varargs call, tag traversal or build was run; source-only; see the [full alib helper pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md).


<a id="ek10941"></a>
### EK10941 — EasyRequest varargs helpers dereference a failed format allocation [conditional]

The shared `CreateFormatStringFromEasyStruct()` computes a buffer size and calls `AllocVec()`, but does not check the returned pointer before copying either format or writing the terminating NUL (`compiler/alib/easystruct_util.h:13-26`). The final `format[...] = '\0'` dereferences NULL even when both source formats are empty; when either is nonempty, the earlier `CopyMem()` can already write through NULL. Both selected varargs wrappers call this helper before invoking the Intuition API and have no failure branch (`compiler/alib/easyrequest.c:43-50`; `buildeasyrequest.c:43-50`).

**Trigger and consequence:** `EasyRequest()` or `BuildEasyRequest()` is called with a valid EasyStruct while allocation of the temporary combined format fails. The wrapper faults while constructing the format instead of returning the underlying request failure value. **Affected configuration:** targets that link these selected `libamiga.a` helpers and call either varargs API; checked-in EasyRequest callers exist, while no direct BuildEasyRequest caller was found. Exact product-image inclusion and forced allocation-failure behavior were not established. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked allocation and unconditional write; reachability depends on the helper being linked/called and AllocVec failure. Return a failure result before copying when allocation fails. No requester, allocation failure or build was induced; source-only.


<a id="ek10942"></a>
### EK10942 — `InvertStringForwd()` mishandles an unterminated angle expression [conditional]

When the scan for `>` reaches the input's NUL terminator, `InvertStringForwd()` still sets that byte to NUL, calls `ParseIX()`, then unconditionally writes `>` and increments `str` (`compiler/alib/invertstringforward.c:124-140`). `ParseIX()` accepts an empty expression body and a single-key body as successful input (`workbench/libs/commodities/parseix.c:121-238,251-264`). For an input such as `"<a"`, the converter therefore advances beyond the terminator and the outer loop reads from that next byte. It also leaves the caller's input modified. The paired `FreeIEvents()` cleanup matches the `AllocMem(sizeof(struct InputEvent))` nodes; no separate ownership issue was found.

**Trigger and consequence:** pass a NUL-terminated string containing `<` without a later `>`, with a body that `ParseIX()` accepts. `InvertStringForwd()` can read beyond the string and returns an event list as if the malformed expression were valid. The selected FKey Insert Text caller reverses `ki->param`, invokes this helper, then reverses it back (`workbench/tools/commodities/FKey.c:824-848`); on malformed parameter `"<a"`, the helper replaces the terminator before that second reversal, so the stored text is changed. FKey's 257-byte fixed parameter buffer keeps this particular short example inside the field's allocation; no out-of-allocation read is claimed for that caller. **Affected configuration:** builds selecting the FKey commodity and `compiler/alib/invertstringforward.c`; external callers with exact-size NUL-terminated strings can also encounter the one-past-terminator read. **Confidence:** high for terminator overwrite/advance and FKey state mutation; the byte observed after NUL and any visible event behavior depend on the caller's surrounding storage. Reject a missing closing delimiter before calling `ParseIX()` and preserve the input terminator. No string conversion, event injection or build was run; source-only.


<a id="ek10943"></a>
### EK10943 — `RangeRand()` truncates the requested range to 16 bits [conditional]

The public prototype accepts and returns `ULONG` (`compiler/include/clib/alib_protos.h:56`), but `RangeRand()` stores `maxValue - 1` in a `UWORD` and casts both the generator state and `maxValue` to `UWORD` for its scaling result (`compiler/alib/rangerand.c:42-60`). Consequently, values above 65,536 cannot be returned. For example, `maxValue == 65,537` makes the loop counter zero and the scale factor one, so the function returns zero for every seed; larger values similarly produce a truncated range. The selected helper is listed in `compiler/alib/mmakefile.src:101`.

**Trigger and consequence:** a caller requests a range larger than 65,536. Results are restricted to 0–65,535 (and some such maxima collapse to much smaller ranges), contrary to a full-width `maxValue` range contract. **Affected configuration:** any target linking this selected alib function. No maintained in-tree caller was found, and no in-tree text states an explicit maximum-value precondition, so practical reachability and the full-width contract remain conditional. **Confidence:** high that the implementation truncates; medium that this violates the intended public contract. Widen the iteration and scaling arithmetic or document and enforce a 16-bit limit. No random sequence or build was run; source-only; see the [full alib helper pass](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md).

<a id="ek10944"></a>
### EK10944 — ARM32 Raspberry Pi can zero the live firmware DTB before copying it [conditional]

The selected ARM32 Raspberry Pi bootstrap parses the incoming DTB at `atags` and obtains the RAM upper bound from `/memory/reg` (`arch/arm-raspi/boot/boot.c:243,269-275,339-362,483-485`). It computes `kernel_phys` by subtracting the rounded kernel, package, and DTB storage sizes from that upper bound (`:487-557`), then zeroes the whole kernel interval before copying the original DTB from `atags` into its reserved kernel-image area (`:559,564-569`). There is no overlap check before the zeroing. The selected AArch64 sibling explicitly checks whether the firmware DTB overlaps the interval and moves the kernel lower before zeroing (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/boot.c:895-919`). The ARM32 path later reparses the copied DTB and publishes its address in `KRN_FlattenedDeviceTree` (`arch/arm-raspi/boot/boot.c:674-695,702-710`).

**Trigger and consequence:** firmware places the incoming ARM32 DTB so its `[atags, atags + dt_total_size())` extent intersects the kernel interval that `bzero()` clears. The later copy then contains zeroed or partially overwritten DTB bytes; the bootstrap's reparse and the kernel's published flattened-tree tag no longer contain the original tree, which can break firmware-tree consumers or prevent startup. The exact failure depends on which DTB bytes overlap. The AArch64 source documents that Pi firmware can place a live DTB near the top of ARM memory, but this review did not establish an ARM32 firmware layout that satisfies the overlap condition. **Affected configuration:** ARM32 Raspberry Pi bootstrap when its firmware-provided DTB overlaps the top-of-RAM kernel allocation. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked clear-before-copy ordering and resulting source corruption under overlap; conditional for ARM32 firmware reachability and boot consequence. Apply an overlap check before clearing and relocate the kernel below the live DTB, as the AArch64 path does. No firmware image, DTB, or boot was used; source-only; see the [ARM32 Raspberry Pi boot coverage](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2967).

<a id="ek10945"></a>
### EK10945 — TextEditor crashes when splitting its last line with `Insert(NULL, …)` [conditional]

TextEditor's `InsertLine(line, after)` macro deliberately calls Exec `Insert(NULL, line, after)` (`workbench/classes/zune/texteditor/mcc/private.h:665`). `SplitLine()` uses that macro to link the newly allocated line immediately after the line being split (`EditorStuff.c:779-789,995`). When `after` is the final line, its `ln_Succ` points at the list's tail sentinel, whose `ln_Succ` is NULL; Exec `Insert()` therefore takes its tail-node branch and writes through `list->lh_TailPred` (`rom/exec/insert.c:60-99`). The caller supplied a NULL `list`, so this branch dereferences NULL. The intended omitted-list shortcut works only when the predecessor has a non-NULL successor (an interior node), not when appending after the tail.

The selected input route reaches this case directly: `HandleInput()` dispatches the Return key to `Key_Return()` (`workbench/classes/zune/texteditor/mcc/HandleInput.c:372-374`), which passes `data->actualline` to `SplitLine()` (`:1357-1371`). The editor's navigation explicitly places `actualline` on `GetLastLine(&data->linelist)` (`Navigation.c:294-300`), so pressing Return while on the last line reaches the NULL-list tail branch. TextEditor is a separately declared module target in `workbench/classes/zune/texteditor/mcc/mmakefile.src:46-48`; this finding is limited to builds that include and load that class.

**Trigger and consequence:** use the TextEditor Return action while the cursor is on its last line. `SplitLine()` inserts the new line through `Insert(NULL, …, lastLine)`, and Exec dereferences the NULL list pointer in its tail insertion branch, faulting instead of appending the line. Other selected split and imported-text paths that pass the final line as predecessor share the same helper defect. **Affected configuration:** builds including the explicitly declared Zune TextEditor MCC; inclusion in a default image is not established here. **Confidence:** high for the list-sentinel branch and reachable last-line caller; no GUI input or fault was run. Pass the containing line list to `InsertLine`, or use a tail-safe insertion operation when the predecessor is last. Source-only; see the [Insert caller recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2051).
